title: Lawyer questions al-Qaida suspect's competence before USS Cole bombing trial
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A lawyer for the suspected organizer of a deadly al-Qaida attack on a U.S. warship in the year 2000 wants a military court to determine his competence before trial, arguing that he has a traumatic brain injury “arising from torture in CIA custody.”
A trial is scheduled to start this month for Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri in the killing of 17 U.S. sailors, who died when an explosives-laden skiff blew up alongside the USS Cole destroyer off the coast of Yemen. He faces a possible death penalty. The proceedings at a U.S. Navy base in Cuba, where he is detained, could last up to five weeks.
Captured in 2002, Nashiri underwent waterboarding, beatings, and confinement in a crate for years in CIA custody at clandestine detention facilities. Declassified documents released in 2018 graphically described how he was stripped naked, repeatedly slammed against walls and left “moaning, shaking and asking God to help him repeatedly.”
Nashiri’s attorney, Allison Ferber Miller, asked a federal court in Washington, D.C., on Thursday to delay the proceedings until the military commission has had enough time to determine his mental capacity.
A psychiatrist for the defense who examined Nashiri in August concluded that he is “not competent,” Miller wrote.
“He diagnosed a traumatic brain injury (TBI) arising from torture in CIA custody, a severe neurocognitive disorder, complex post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and major depression,” Miller wrote. “He concluded that Petitioner cannot understand the proceedings or assist his counsel.”
Miller wrote that Nashiri is not asking the federal judge to determine his competence but to delay the trial until the military commission has had “a meaningful opportunity” to do so.
The military judge had ordered a competency evaluation, “but left no time for a meaningful hearing” on whether al-Nashiri is fit for trial, Miller wrote, adding that the military judge has declined three times to stay the proceedings until the question of Nashiri’s competence was resolved.
Lawyers in the case were scheduled to travel to Guantanamo Bay on Saturday, Miller wrote. The military judge left open the possibility for a competency hearing on Monday morning, the same day the trial was scheduled to begin.
The trial has since been rescheduled to start a week later on Oct. 26, according to Ronald Flesvig, the spokesman for the Office of Military Commissions at Guantanamo Bay.
The Office of the Chief Prosecutor for military commissions at Guantanamo Bay did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.
Proceedings before the military commission were previously mired in delays and in legal challenges over admissibility of evidence from the torture-aided interrogations of Nashiri and over other circumstances of his trial and detention. Questions over the handling of Nashiri’s case, like those of other Guantanamo Bay detainees accused of planning and aiding al-Qaida’s 9/11 attacks on the United States, have led to constitutional debates and other problems.

title: Florida man killed ex-fiancee hours after their ‘People’s Court’ episode aired, police say
text:
ORLANDO, Fla. (AP) — A Florida man has been charged with killing the mother of his children nearly 15 years ago, after his ex-fiancee went missing just hours after their pretaped appearance on “The People’s Court” was broadcast, police said.
Orlando police announced the arrest Wednesday of Dale Smith Jr., 55, on a charge of second-degree murder. The body of 33-year-old Michelle Parker has not been recovered, but all evidence leads to Smith as the person responsible for her death, police said.
Smith’s attorney, Rajan Joshi, said during a hearing Thursday afternoon that he didn’t believe the state could meet its burden of proof to convict Smith based on the information presented in the criminal complaint. A judge ordered Smith to be held without bond pending a detention hearing, which wasn’t immediately scheduled.
Joshi said later Thursday during a phone interview that the prosecution’s case has many challenges that he plans to explore. The defense attorney said the investigation focused almost exclusively on Smith from the beginning and ignored other potential leads.
“Michelle Parker worked at a bar. She was a very attractive young lady,” Joshi said. “They (police) did not go out and investigate other possibilities that could have happened to her. This is one of those cases where they go and they immediately target the usual suspect, which is the ex.”
Orlando Police Chief Eric Smith, who is not related to Smith, said during the news conference on Wednesday that the case never stopped being a priority. Smith was the last known person to see or hear from Parker before she went missing on Nov. 17, 2011, when she dropped their children off at his home, the chief said.
“Over the past year, we expanded our investigative team looking into this case and took a fresh, focused look at all the evidence,” the police chief said. “We reexamined testimony and conflicting statements made by the suspect and used advances in digital forensics to uncover and analyze additional evidence.”
Police gave few details about what evidence they had against Smith, but Detective Phillip McMican confirmed that police had collected new evidence in the past year, as well as new insights into old evidence thanks to technological advancements.
“Vehicles, electronic devices, phones, computers — we’re able to better interpret that evidence today than what we were able to do back in 2011,” McMican said.
Police continue to search for Parker’s body. Her vehicle was found abandoned a day after her disappearance, and her cellphone was later recovered from an Orlando-area lake.
Investigators have not publicly stated a motive for Parker’s murder.
On the day of Parker’s disappearance, an episode of “The People’s Court” featuring her and Smith was broadcast. Smith had sued Parker, claiming that a $5,000 engagement ring that he bought for her was lost when she threw it at him during an argument. Judge Marilyn Milian ultimately ruled that both parties were responsible for the ring’s loss and ordered Parker to pay $2,500 to Smith for half of it.

title: Vatican says Pope Leo XIV resumes work from the hospital as doctors say he's 'recovered well'
text:
Vatican says Pope Leo XIV resumes work from the hospital as doctors say he's 'recovered well'
Pope Leo XIV’s lung has recovered well from surgery to remove a cancerous nodule, and he resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported.
Related video: Catholics in Chicago attend Mass and pray for Pope Leo after cancer diagnosis
Leo’s post-operative tests remained within normal levels and his physiotherapy session Thursday involved full mobility exercises, with the pope going about his daily activities independently, said the update from Leo’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
“The chest X-ray revealed good recovery of the operated lung,” they reported. “Overall, his postoperative recovery is proceeding as expected.”
Separately, the Vatican said Leo had resumed working from the hospital, looking at documents, and had for a second day celebrated Mass with other priests in a special chapel set up for him near his room on the 10th floor of the hospital.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower right lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Asked if any changes to Leo's planned trip to South America from Nov. 6-17 were expected, spokesman Matteo Bruni pointed to Leo's words on Sunday when he announced the discovery of the nodule and impending surgery.
“Thank you for your prayers for the pastoral visit I will make to Peru,” Leo said Sunday in Spanish, in a greeting delivered to a Peruvian group. The trip is also scheduled to include stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
Leo is expected to remain hospitalized until at least Oct. 20.
___
Colleen Barry reported from Milan.

title: Owens Becomes 11th Mainer to Qualify for Century Club
text:
Bernard Owens, 79, of Waldoboro, became the 11th Mainer to qualify for The Dressage Foundation’s Century Club.
To qualify, the combined ages of a rider and horse must equal 100 years or greater. Horse and rider perform a test at a judged event. Owens competed in a show at Hope Spring Stable in Winthrop with 26-year-old horse Pi, whose registered name is Kennebec Joyful Encounter.
“Horses in their mid-20s are usually retired, but Pi is still going strong,” said Carolyn Owens, Owens’ wife.

title: Why autoimmune disease is harder to catch in older adults — and what helps
text:
(Aging Untold) — Autoimmune conditions like type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus can be especially tricky to spot for older adults because the immune system naturally changes with age.
The good news is that early diagnosis can make a real difference in managing symptoms long-term.
What does “autoimmune” actually mean?
Autoimmune disease is a condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy body tissues, according to the National Institutes of Health.
“Think about it like your body has an army that’s there to protect you, and that’s your immune system,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “And it no longer knows who the enemy is. So it fights itself. And that’s what an autoimmune disease is.”
Rheumatoid arthritis affects the joints and bones, and lupus is systemic, Cradduck said. “It, unfortunately, can go after everything.”
Cradduck also shared her own experience being diagnosed.
“I was going to the doctor for well over a year and seeing a very good rheumatologist, and my lab work and my symptoms weren’t meeting the criteria all at the same time,” she said.
She said she would have symptoms, but her lab work would look OK.
Then she would have “terrible lab work,” but symptomatically she was OK.
“And sadly, oftentimes the treatment is worse than the disease in some ways, because the treatment only targets lowering your immune system and leaving you more susceptible,” Cradduck said.
Finding the source of inflammation
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, compared it to a “big ball of confusion.”
“It’s really the system is confused, so it doesn’t know what’s going on,” Rogers said. “So wherever that weakest link is, that’s where it’s going to attack. I think probably at the time when you were diagnosed several years ago, we didn’t have the recognition that we have now.”
Rogers said inflammation is usually the driver.
“Key is, you have to find out what drove it in the first place. Where is the inflammation coming from that’s allowed these other organs to get hit? It’s much more complex than people realize,” Rogers said.
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, offered a way to picture it.
“I had another doctor friend explain that these symptoms are like smoke, and you want to get to the fire, which is the inflammation,” Ambrose said.
Rogers pointed to the gut as a common source.
“And usually a lot of times it’s coming from the gut,” Rogers said. “So I tell people, if you figure out that you have some GI issues, and the breakdown there, go back to the foundation — go back to nutrition, go back to the sleep. You have to say, hey, my body is on fire. Am I going to use water or gas to put it out?”
Leaning on friends and community
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, talked about what she’s learned from a friend living with Crohn’s disease.
“She has a really great diet. I let her pick all the restaurants out because she knows what she can eat on any given day. And so I really encourage people that have friends that have autoimmune too, when they’re having a day that’s not a particularly great day and they’re tired and they’re worn out, be with them,” O’Rourke said.
And celebrate the good days.
“And then when they have a better day, celebrate that victory. Like, be there through thick and thin. Because it can be an inconsistent condition and some of the symptoms might preempt a plan that you might have had — and just be OK with that,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck added that the invisible nature of these conditions can be one of the hardest parts.
“What I found was so hard was everybody was saying, ‘But you look so good,’” Cradduck said. “When I felt so terrible... I couldn’t prepare a meal without having to take a break when I was first sick.”
It’s rarely just one cause
Rogers emphasized that autoimmune disease develops from a mix of factors, not a single trigger.
“It’s multifactorial. You also have to look at a combination of lifestyle factors and genetics. Genetics plays a huge role,” Rogers said. “And it’s an autoimmune disease — I tell people it’s not like catching a cold. You didn’t just catch it. It’s a combination of things that have led up to this point.”
So, you need to figure out what’s driving it.
“Keep looking for answers,” Ambrose said. “Because today many people are living longer, fuller lives, and there could be answers out there that make a difference.”
Key takeaways
When managing an autoimmune disease, keep these points in mind:
- It’s internal friendly fire. The immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissue, damaging joints, skin, nerves or organs.
- It’s often an invisible battle. These conditions rarely have visible signs, yet heavily impact daily life, careers and family.
- There are clues before crisis. Pay attention to early warning signs, make proactive choices and practice strong self-advocacy to help your body function at its best.

title: Dunlap and LePage debated, hotly, for the final time. Here are 3 takeaways
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage faced off Thursday— sometimes arguing — for the final time on the debate stage before Election Day.
The Democratic state auditor and Republican former governor are locked in one of the nation’s most competitive races for the U.S. House. The only major poll of the race, conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center in September, found Dunlap with a six-point edge.
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, the second-most rural in the country, has voted for President Donald Trump three times while also electing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden to a House seat since 2018. With Golden not running for reelection, the seat is wide open.
The race is of national importance. Democrats’ path to recapture the House — currently held by Republicans with a four-seat majority — would be significantly bolstered if Dunlap can hold off LePage, one of Maine’s most prominent Republicans.
Those were the stakes for the candidates coming into Thursday’s debate. It was hosted by WABI and WAGM.
Here are three takeaways.
1. There were quite a few spiky moments.
During discussion about declining healthcare access in Maine, Dunlap criticized PL 90, a law championed by LePage during his time as governor that set up a pool of high-risk patients and subsidized their insurance with a fee on all individual health insurance plans in Maine.
“It’s an all-you-can-eat buffet for the insurance companies,” Dunlap said, repeating criticisms about PL 90 from 2012.
“What are you reading?” LePage shot back. “PL 90 lowered the premiums by 76%.”
“That’s not true,” Dunlap said, leaving LePage seemingly exasperated.
“Matt, you’ve been lying a lot this campaign,” LePage said.
Dunlap later accused LePage of calling Social Security a “welfare program,” and quoted from a 2014 press release in which the LePage administration criticized transfer programs, where the federal government sends money to the state, which then disburses funds. The release lumped Social Security in with those programs.
“Quote: ‘It doesn’t matter what liberals call these payments, it is welfare, pure and simple,’ said Gov. LePage,” Dunlap said, pulling from the release. “Including those Social Security payments we just discussed.”
LePage and Dunlap sparred on this for a full minute and a half while moderators Jon Small and Kelly O’Mara attempted to go to a commercial break.
“I’ll just say this,” LePage said, getting the last word in before the halfway point. “If Jared doesn’t retire, you’re not here tonight.”
At the end of the debate, Dunlap challenged LePage about his time living in Florida. LePage has been back and forth between the two states since he left the Blaine House in 2019. He began renting an apartment in Augusta the same month he announced his candidacy for Congress last spring.
LePage said he was a “snowbird,” living in Florida during the winter and Maine during the summer. He said he never spent a full year in Florida and paid his taxes here.
That point emerged again in the candidates’ final remarks.
“He just got a Maine driver’s license right after he declared he was going to run for Congress here,” Dunlap said.
“I never said I didn’t have a Florida driver’s license,” LePage interrupted.
2. Global conflict was, again, a major focus.
The debate began with a question on increasing heating oil assistance. Heating oil, used by about half of Maine households, is hovering near its all-time record price — it rose to over $6 per gallon last month.
Dunlap said heating assistance through the Home Energy Assistance Program should be fully funded, and that the war in Iran was the primary driver of costs. The reduction of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began in February has caused oil prices to spike worldwide.
LePage agreed on the first point — that HEAP should have more backing from the federal government — but challenged the second. Instead of pulling out of Iran, he said, the U.S. Navy and Air Force should force regime change there, though he said the U.S. should not put “boots on the ground.”
“Too many Americans are getting killed in other countries by proxies and the regime in Iran,” LePage said. “So I do believe it’s time to take ’em out.”
“Paul LePage is talking about regime change, and yet not putting any boots on the ground,” Dunlap responded. “I’m not sure how that happens without having American troops committed in a combat situation.”
The moderators also asked about the U.S. trade war with Canada, which has put strain on Maine businesses.
LePage said he has urged the Trump administration to return to the negotiating table, not least because tariffs can be a useful negotiating tool.
Dunlap said he would hope to act instead as a check on Trump, challenging his power to unilaterally impose tariffs.
3. Healthcare kept coming back up.
The most spirited and substantive discussion during the first half of the debate took place in response to a question about healthcare access.
LePage said he wanted to return to the insurance subsidy program he championed as governor, and Dunlap said he hoped to move toward universal healthcare.
LePage had pivoted from a question on immigration to his intent to work across the aisle with Democrats in Congress, and said Dunlap would simply block efforts to take action. Dunlap further pivoted to universal healthcare, saying adopting such a system would, on average, save money. LePage said the cost would be “astronomical.”

title: Homicide victim found in barrel at Lake Mead identified more than 4 years after discovery
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) - Authorities in Las Vegas identified a homicide victim Thursday whose remains were found in a barrel at Lake Mead more than four years ago.
Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse identified the man as Edward Lelburian Jackson. Authorities said he was from Arkansas and in his mid-to-late 50s when he died.
Las Vegas police said Jackson’s remains were discovered in a barrel at Hemenway Harbor at Lake Mead on May 1, 2022. He died from a gunshot wound, and his death was ruled a homicide.
The case drew national attention as water levels at Lake Mead dropped to record lows.
Clark County released facial approximation images created by the FBI in hopes of generating leads.
“Our hope is to put the composite out there and see if we can get any good matches. As good as a DNA profile is, it’s only as good as what you have to compare it to,” Rouse previously said about the case. “Obviously, the next steps would be to get it out to the community in hopes that we have some good links to individuals that could be considered for testing.”
Investigators said Jackson’s family told them that he liked to travel, but it was unclear why he was in Las Vegas.
Authorities said they estimated Jackson was killed between the mid-1970s and early 1980s, based on the type of shoes found with him.
According to the county, this homicide was one of four cases involving remains found at Lake Mead in 2022. Three others were identified by DNA:
- Claude Russell Pensinger, 52, of Las Vegas — Skeletal remains found July 25, Aug. 6 and Aug. 16, 2022, near Boulder Beach were confirmed to be from the same person. Pensinger disappeared July 14, 1998. Cause and manner undetermined.
- Donald P. Smith, 39, of North Las Vegas — Remains found Oct. 17 and Oct. 19, 2022, in the Callville Bay area. Smith reportedly drowned in April 1974. Death ruled accidental drowning.
- Thomas Erndt, 42, of Las Vegas — Remains found May 7, 2022, in the Callville Bay area. Erndt reportedly drowned Aug. 2, 2002. Cause and manner undetermined.
In August of this year, more human remains were also discovered at Lake Mead amid the receding water level.

title: Groundbreaking ceremony celebrates new Cape Elizabeth middle school
text:
Cape Elizabeth’s new middle school is one step closer to completion.
The town will hold a ceremonial groundbreaking on Saturday at noon on the baseball field. The middle school band will perform, and there will be remarks from speakers, including the school board and town council chairs, teachers and current students.
The construction technically began this summer, and is scheduled to be completed by the 2028 school year. The new school should meet the town’s needs for at least 50 years, according to Superintendent Chris Record.
In June 2025, Cape Elizabeth voters passed a hotly contested $86.5 million school project after multiple attempts, funding a rebuild of the middle school and renovations and additions for the elementary school.
The bid for the primary contractor, which was awarded to Great Falls Construction of Gorham, came in at $64.9 million, about $8 million under budget. The school department is still fundraising, partially through selling naming rights to classrooms.
The new, V-shaped building will sit next to the baseball field, nestled into the hill, with a design that updates the school for modern education needs, including safety and flexibility.
The main office will be at the front of the building, and each wing of the school can be closed off in case of emergency.
The new school will also include more spaces for learning in groups of all sizes, according to Record. There will be what he calls a “collaborative staircase” or wide steps with benches on each wing of the building, which is a large enough space for each grade level to learn a concept together.
The performance space, a new cafetorium, will be able to fit the entire band. It’s also closer to the music wing, making it easier to set up for performances.
Great Falls started on some of the site work over the summer. “There’s been a lot of moving dirt and blasting granite,” Record said. They will pour the foundation soon.
“We’ll start seeing it come up out of the ground,” he said.

title: What kind of world are we building for our children?
text:
Ella D. Tabasky is a nonprofit worker, union steward and community organizer. She lives in Midcoast Maine.
Thanks to Ed Sheeran and Macklemore, the struggle for Palestinian liberation was recently thrust back into the mainstream.
The stars’ public dispute revived the familiar question of whether performing artists should “stay out of politics,” as if speaking about the suffering of millions is somehow more political than staying silent.
For me, there is no staying silent. I am Jewish, I am an activist, and I am the daughter of a Holocaust educator. And the fact that this conversation unfolded during the Days of Awe — the 10 days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur devoted to introspection and repentance — felt especially significant.
Judaism, at its core, is not neutral in the face of suffering. We are a people whose story is one of liberation from oppression. We are taught that pikuach nefesh, saving a life, is the most important obligation of every human being.
During the Days of Awe, we are asked to look honestly at ourselves. Teshuvah calls us to acknowledge our mistakes and resolve to do better. Tefillah asks us to engage in deep reflection. Tzedakah calls us to give to those in need.
So what does this require once the holiday is over? For me, it means continuing to look honestly at what is happening to Palestinians and to all oppressed people.
The genocide remains devastating. In June, the United Nations released a paper outlining the deliberate targeting and killing of Palestinian children across occupied Palestine. The Elimination Project, a recent report from B’Tselem, an Israeli human rights organization, documents more than 2,000 testimonies showing Israel dismantling the conditions necessary for Palestinian collective existence in the West Bank.
“Naza,” the new documentary from Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examines Israel’s bombing campaign in Gaza and the systems used to select targets. Its central question is difficult to ignore: What happens when technology and bureaucracy make it easier to reduce human beings to targets?
All people, but especially children, deserve safety and joy.
That conviction is inseparable, for me, from being Jewish. I grew up understanding the Holocaust as a warning about dehumanization and what happens when people decide someone else’s pain is none of their business.
My Judaism does not tell me that someone’s humanity matters more than anyone else’s. Quite the opposite. Jewish safety and Palestinian freedom are not opposing values. Our safety and liberation are intertwined.
And this is where Palestine connects, for me, to what is happening here in Maine. The histories and circumstances of these two places are profoundly different. But questions of power, safety and dignity follow us home.
In January, the federal government launched “Operation Catch of the Day.” The ACLU of Maine reports that roughly 200 people were detained. Maine subsequently enacted three “ICE Out” laws limiting cooperation between federal immigration enforcement and state and local institutions.
Then, in July, 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was murdered by an ICE agent with a well-documented history of violence. Left in the wake of this tragedy were Guerrero’s wife and 3-year-old child.
Again, the situations in Palestine and Maine are not the same. But I keep coming back to the same question: What kind of world are we building for future generations?
I am a member of Jewish Voice for Peace Maine, and we are organizing an event for children and families called From Maine to Palestine: Children Will Be Free on Oct. 18 in Portland. The fundraising event will include music, storytelling and community art-making, and 100% of the proceeds will support the Maine Solidarity Fund and Rawa, a Palestinian grassroots community fund.
The Days of Awe are over. But the work of asking what we owe one another continues. For me, that means continuing to build a world where all children and their families, regardless of their backgrounds, can be safe and experience joy. I invite you to commit to that work. Joining me on Oct. 18 is one way to start.

title: A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan's Upper West Side. New Yorkers are captivated
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Manhattan’s Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park.
This is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history, according to one expert, and the owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds.
“It was, like, totally shocking,” Andrew Farnsworth, a migration ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, said of the barn owls. “To the best of our knowledge, like the collective birding knowledge, there hasn’t been a nest in, you know, in Manhattan, at least in recorded history.”
Word of the barn owl family didn’t get around until last week, when Elisabeth Williams, an Upper West Side resident, notified a local news outlet on Oct. 6 that she and her husband saw multiple owls at the water tower atop a building on West 75th Street close to Central Park West.
The couple had previously seen a single owl on an apartment windowsill a few days earlier and were shocked even then, Williams recalled.
“In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature,” she said. “And here it was, just sort of right outside our window.”
Barn owl sightings are rare in New York City
It’s not the first time that birds have captivated New Yorkers. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan’s Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. And after Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year.
But barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl’s range and the barn owl population has declined “at an alarming rate” over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.
“There’s lots of excitement among New Yorkers, both birders and non-birders alike, about these owls because owls really capture the attention,” said Jessica Wilson, executive director of NYC Bird Alliance. “They’re magical, they’re nocturnal, they are secretive, they’re not commonly seen, especially on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. And to have this chance to see these birds is really thrilling.”
Photographers and casual onlookers have gathered on the street on a nightly basis to spot the owls.
“I’ve only seen one barn owl ever, and that was in California,” said Val Coleman, a retired New York City resident who was on the Upper West Side earlier this week trying to spot the owls. “At dusk, we hope they will come out to hunt. We hope they don’t eat poisoned rats with rodenticide in ’em.”
David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert, said he’s observed at least one adult barn owl and five fledglings at the water tower. He’s also seen an adult owl carrying rodents back to the water tower. There are believed to be two adult owls, and some photographers have claimed to have seen six fledglings, Barrett added.
“Having one barn owl is a rarity, but it’s not national news. Having a family, for the first time ever, breeding in Manhattan in recorded history, that’s special news,” Barrett said.
Screeching was heard by residents
Before the recent barn owl sightings, Williams and her husband heard periodic screeching noises outside going back to early September. They initially assumed it was a bird of some kind but were skeptical when a phone app indicated the noise was from a barn owl.
Thomas Obersteiner said that he first heard bizarre screeching and wailing noises from outside one evening in mid-September. It sounded like someone was “being murdered outside,” he said.
“That lasted for two or three weeks, every night, sometimes more, sometimes less, coming from different directions,” Obersteiner added. “But I had no idea what that was.”
On multiple occasions, Obersteiner or his wife ran into their children’s bedroom after mistaking the owls’ screech for a child in pain, he said. It wasn’t until he saw a news report that he realized that owls were making the sounds.
Farnsworth said the screech is typical of barn owls, who use it to communicate with one another. The screech is like a “horror movie kind of experience,” he said.
Obersteiner, who said his roof deck is the “probably the best location in town right now” to watch the owls, has been letting nature photographers access that perch to observe the owls “almost every night” since news of the barn owls spread. On one night last week, 20 people had gathered.
“We can’t say no because it’s so much fun and these people are so serious,” Obersteiner added. “It’s beautiful.”
Williams and her husband were not bird watchers before the barn owl family moved in to the water tower. But that may change soon after their “delightful” experience.
“I think we’re about to become birders,” Williams said.
__
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: Hunters help save seriously injured woman ‘left out there to die,’ sheriff says
text:
FARGO, N.D. (KVLY/Gray News) - Two friends checking hunting cameras likely saved the life of an injured and bloody 28-year-old woman in North Dakota.
According to Cass County Sheriff Jesse Jahner, the woman was spotted Tuesday on cameras that resident Jay Schueler had set up near County Road 81. The woman was walking alone along the Wild Rice River, appearing to be missing clothing, badly injured and bleeding.
Jahner said Schueler called his friend Jeff Jones, whose property the cameras were located on, and the two went to the area to check on the woman and call 911.
They reached the woman before first responders. Jahner said she had multiple cuts on her neck, describing the injuries as severe and life-threatening, and noted she was wet when they found her.
The woman, who was not immediately identified by police, was treated at the scene, then taken to Sanford in Fargo.
Jahner said the woman had been “left out there to die,” and credited Schueler and his friend with likely saving her life.
Despite her injuries, authorities said she was able to give investigators a suspect’s name and information about a vehicle.
The woman told medical personnel she had been attacked with a knife, Jahner said.
A witness also came forward, helping investigators pinpoint where they believed the assault happened.
Jahner said investigators identified the suspect as 60-year-old Tracy Vaughn Peters.
Cass County authorities and the U.S. Marshals Task Force located and arrested Peters on Wednesday.
Peters was booked into the Cass County Jail on a charge of attempted murder.
Jahner said the reported victim and Peters knew each other but did not elaborate on their connection.
Investigators noted the case remains an open investigation, with deputies continuing to search for the knife that was said to have been used and gathering additional evidence.

title: US coach who recorded young gymnasts undressing sentenced to 90 years in prison
text:
IOWA CITY, Iowa (AP) - A once prominent youth gymnastics coach was sentenced to 90 years in prison Wednesday for secretly recording his young female students undressing and using the bathroom at a Mississippi gym, in a case that rocked the sport.
U.S. District Judge Kristi Johnson gave the maximum sentence possible to Sean Gardner, ordering that he serve 30 years in prison for each of the three federal child pornography production charges to which he pleaded guilty. The sentence likely amounts to life in prison for Gardner, 39.
Gardner’s arrest last summer by the FBI, first reported by The Associated Press, renewed questions about whether U.S. gymnastics authorities had done enough to protect athletes from sexual abuse at the hands of an influential coach.
Gardner pleaded guilty to placing a hidden camera in a bathroom at a gymnastics studio in Purvis, Mississippi, between December 2017 and April 2018 to record his students. Investigators say he created videos showing close-up images of at least 10 minors naked or undressing, which they recovered from his computers years later while investigating claims that he sexually abused gymnasts in Iowa.
Several of his former students at Chow’s Gymnastics and Dance Institute in West Des Moines, Iowa, have alleged to police and in civil lawsuits that he used his position to prey on them. The institute was founded by prominent coach Liang “Chow” Qiao, who is known for producing Olympic champions. Gardner coached several youth prospects and served as director of an annual winter meet that drew hundreds of gymnasts to Iowa.
Gardner has not been charged in connection with any of the Iowa allegations, and police have said they would wait to determine how to proceed after the federal case concludes.
Lawyers for some of the women have also alleged the sport’s oversight bodies, USA Gymnastics and the U.S. Center for SafeSport, were told about inappropriate behavior by Gardner in 2017 but failed to take action to remove him from the sport for years. SafeSport temporarily suspended Gardner in 2022 after a Chow’s gymnast alleged sexual abuse, and Chow’s fired him then.
SafeSport has said it learned during its investigation that Chow and other coaches had been aware of allegations of sexual misconduct against Gardner but failed to report them to the center as required by its policy. A judge dismissed SafeSport in May as a party from two lawsuits alleging it did not properly investigate Gardner, finding it was entitled to immunity under federal law.
Several lawsuits remain pending against Gardner, USA Gymnastics and Chow’s Gymnastics.

title: Incidental killing of New England’s endangered species no longer illegal
text:
October 15, 2026 Listen to the story HERE. By Kathryn Carley North Atlantic right whales were hunted to near extinction prior to being listed as an endangered species in 1970. The North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium estimated the 2024 population at 384, up from 376 in 2023. (Adobe Stock) Environmental groups warn federal regulators have stripped the Endangered Species Act […]
October 15, 2026
Listen to the story HERE.
By Kathryn Carley
North Atlantic right whales were hunted to near extinction prior to being listed as an endangered species in 1970. The North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium estimated the 2024 population at 384, up from 376 in 2023. (Adobe Stock)
Environmental groups warn federal regulators have stripped the Endangered Species Act of decades-old protections, making it easier to kill imperiled wildlife or destroy their habitats.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has reinterpreted language within the law to ensure the incidental killing or injuring of a protected animal, known as a “take,” is illegal only if it was intentional.
Jim Murphy, associate vice president of legal advocacy for the National Wildlife Federation, said the Trump administration is attempting to write the Endangered Species Act out of existence.
“This is a unilateral move by the executive branch to basically undo one of Congress’s most successful acts without Congress or anyone else having a say, and that’s a very, very troubling development,” Murphy stressed.
Murphy pointed out oil and gas drilling or mining operations can now proceed without concern for endangered species. Federal regulators said the administrative changes return the interpretation of the Endangered Species Act to its original intent and will end years of federal overreach.
At least nine animals listed under the federal Endangered Species Act reside in Maine, including the Canadian lynx, the northern long-eared bat and leatherback sea turtle. The state is also home to more than 800 nesting pairs of bald eagles, which are considered a premier example of the law’s success.
Marine researchers warned changes to the law could drive the remaining North Atlantic right whale population to extinction. Murphy noted the Endangered Species Act would offer little protection unless it can be shown the intent of a ship, for example, was to hit and kill a whale.
“We are going to lose a lot of species if we don’t take the measures to protect their habitat and we don’t take the measures to protect them from activities that incidentally harm them,” Murphy contended.
Vessel strikes and fishing net entanglements are the greatest threat to North Atlantic right whales, which have been slowly increasing in number thanks to Endangered Species Act protections.
Murphy added the National Wildlife Federation and several other groups are challenging the revision made to habitat protections in court and are hopeful the rule will be overturned. A coalition of state attorneys general has filed two separate lawsuits.

title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
text:
Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia’s Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
Zelenskyy complains about U.S. stance toward Ukraine
The strike could further complicate Kyiv’s relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.
Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump’s demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. Both are vital for Ukrainian defenses and attack operations.
The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. “We’re done,” he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist’s YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
“Really, yes, between us,” Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. “Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump.”
He said that the U.S. behavior “was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us.”
Zelenskyy says U.S. position isn't ‘on the right side of history’
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that “we are losing a strong partner” in the United States.
He said that “it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he’s in the middle.”
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is “not the right side of history.”
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Ukraine looks to Europe for more help
Amid fears that the Trump administration may be withdrawing support for Ukraine, Zelenskyy was due in Brussels for talks with European Union leaders attending a summit.
He was traveling to Belgium after visiting London, where he won pledges of more help from U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Asked whether the EU still trusts Trump, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, replied: “We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender.”
“Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that is why Europe is standing beside Ukraine,” Kallas told reporters at the summit, which Zelenskyy is scheduled to attend on Friday.
Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians
Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine’s Emergency Services said Thursday.
Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came “precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted.”
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security.”
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.
___
Samya Kullab in Kyiv, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this story.

title: World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
text:
World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
Archaeologists working off the coast of Turkey have found a shipwreck dating back around 4,700 years, making it the oldest in the world.
A number of ancient storage vessels known as amphorae were recovered during excavations at the wreck, which was found at a depth of around 100 feet near Kekova Island off the coast of southern Turkey, according to a statement from the country’s culture ministry, published Wednesday.
The amphorae date from 4,400-4,700 years ago and provide new information on maritime history, the daily lives of mariners and trade connections at the time.
Related video above: Divers explore world's oldest shipwreck
The vessels are thought to mainly have been used for transporting olive oil or wine. However, one amphora features a distinctive set of marks and two holes in its body, which suggest it could have been used to make cheese or butter.
Researchers said the presence of this amphora may mean that sailors took goats with them on their voyages, using their milk to make dairy products.
The excavations were led by Hakan Öniz, a professor at Akdeniz University, Antalya, who told CNN that the shipwreck was first discovered four years ago.
The amphorae were initially thought to be much more recent, but then Öniz read a publication on amphorae that had been found near the Giza pyramids in Egypt — the oldest of which was believed to have been under construction at the same time as the ship sank.
“These resembled the amphorae in our shipwreck,” Öniz told CNN on Wednesday, adding that a team of researchers made a follow-up dive at the site.
They then invited a leading expert on amphorae, Australian archaeologist Karin Sowada, to visit the shipwreck and examine the evidence.
“We reached a consensus and proceeded with further analysis,” said Öniz, who added the team is “generally confident” that this is the oldest shipwreck in the world.
“It is not just the amphorae; the anchors and other artifacts found at the shipwreck site also point to the same centuries,” he said.
Turkey’s culture and tourism minister, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, said the amphorae appear to have moved around the Eastern Mediterranean.
“Clay analyses indicate that the amphorae were likely produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley,” Ersoy said in the statement.
“The fact that similar examples have been found in Egypt, Troy, and Crete is of great importance for understanding the trade networks that connected different geographies via sea routes,” he said.
Researchers believe the ship may have been traveling from the Levantine coast, which runs from Turkey in the north to Egypt in the south, to Troy or Crete when it was wrecked.

title: Speaker Johnson dismisses skeptics as he campaigns for House GOP in Maine battleground
text:
BANGOR — Speaker Mike Johnson made a campaign swing Wednesday through Maine’s picturesque second congressional district, convinced Republicans will defy history and maintain their House majority, as he worked to boost GOP candidate Paul LePage in what is one of the party’s best hopes to flip a Democratic-held seat.
The speaker told a small crowd at the Sea Dog Brewing Co. that he disagrees with the polling and the growing sense that Republicans are heading toward defeat on Nov. 3. Instead, he said he believes that the party in power will maintain its narrow grip on the House — thanks in part to candidates like LePage, the two-term former governor.
“I’m telling you, we’re going to surprise them,” Johnson told the few dozen gathered for lunches of burgers, fish and chips and pot pies at the Bangor eatery.
Johnson has been crisscrossing the country in a campaign blitz that will total more than 20 states and 40 districts in October, in a final sprint ahead of the elections that will determine control of Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term in the White House.
Republicans have increasingly been forced to play defense in the final weeks, trying to shore up their candidates in GOP strongholds nationwide as voters reel from high gas prices, Trump’s tariff policies and the war against Iran. Democrats are reaching deep into districts where Trump has had support, trying and preparing a first 100-day agenda if they win back control.
Johnson said what he’s seeing on the campaign trail tells a different story — of crowds turning out to support the party’s candidates, including earlier this week in southern Texas, a key battleground region.
“Now we have to defy history to do this,” Johnson said, noting that rarely does the president’s party win in midterm elections.
But he said, echoing Le Page’s own message to the room, “voter turnout is critical.”
With a narrow split, every House district matters
While much of the attention in Maine has been on the state’s volatile Senate race between incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, the House race for the open seat held by retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden is another key battleground.
LePage and Democratic state auditor Matt Dunlap are vying for the sprawling district that encompasses much of the rural northern part of the state. The two are set to debate this week.
LePage acknowledged that getting out the vote is what will make the difference.
The district is one Trump carried in the past, but that Golden has held as a leader of the conservative Blue Dog Coalition, a caucus of more centrist Democrats. The retiring congressman has at times bucked House Democratic leadership in voting with Republicans.
It’s also one of the few remaining Trump-won districts represented by a Democrat, which makes it a prime opportunity for Republicans as they work to backfill losses elsewhere and keep their majority.
This week, the main House Republican super PAC aligned with Johnson, the Congressional Leadership Fund, canceled spending in four House races, including Iowa and New Jersey, and increased its investment in others from Texas to Pennsylvania.
Democrats, however, are confident they will seize control, as they begin planning an ambitious agenda focused on affordability issues and anti-corruption investigations of Trump and his administration.

title: CAR T-cell therapy offers new hope for lupus patients
text:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. (Aging Untold) — A treatment first developed to fight cancer is now being used in a clinical trial at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine to treat lupus, an autoimmune disease that affects an estimated 1.5 million Americans.
What is lupus?
Lupus is a lifelong autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy cells and tissues, which can lead to inflammation and organ damage. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the disease is difficult to diagnose due to its many signs and symptoms. Nine of 10 lupus diagnoses are in women ages 15 to 44.
There is currently no cure.
A patient’s two-decade battle
Rachel Dib, a military wife and mother of three in North Carolina, was diagnosed with lupus in December 2007, when she was a college sophomore.
At first, she said it hurt to breathe or laugh. Over time, her joints began to fail.
“My thumb just like popped out of the socket. I didn’t even know what was happening. I went to like do this and my thumb popped out and that’s the start of like multiple hand surgeries,” Dib said.
The disease cost her the ability to play musical instruments. She had been a clarinetist, pianist, tenor saxophone player — and she could no longer run or hike.
“On a good day I used a cane. On a bad day I used a walker and on a really bad day, it was just, I just couldn’t get out of bed. I would hurt my hip just like rolling over in bed. It was bad,” Dib said.
How CAR T-cell therapy works
After nearly 20 years of suffering and hospital stays, Dib enrolled in a CAR T-cell therapy clinical trial at UNC.
CAR T, which stands for chimeric antigen receptor therapy, integrates immunotherapy, genetic engineering and personalized medicine. It has been used in the treatment of blood cancers.
Dr. Saira Sheikh, a rheumatologist and researcher at UNC and one of only a handful of doctors in the world offering the therapy, said the connection between cancer and lupus treatment comes down to B cells.
“In these particular cancers, B cells are at play and in autoimmune diseases such as lupus, B cells are also involved. And these are what are called autoreactive B cells in which the body’s immune system starts to attack itself,” Sheikh said.
The process begins by drawing the patient’s blood to extract T-cells, which the body uses to fight infection. Those T-cells are then genetically reprogrammed in a lab.
“It’s as though you give the T-cells a GPS to go back into the body and find the target cell. In this case, the B cells are the targets,” Sheikh said.
After three days of preconditioning with chemotherapy, the patient receives the CAR T-cell infusion.
“It’s often referred to as a living drug because it uses the patient’s own immune system to fight whatever disease you’re targeting,” Sheikh said.
Results and risks
Dib said she felt results the day after her infusion.
“After I got it, the day after, I had the most energy I’d ever had, ever. I was like, ‘I feel like I’m 20 again and I’m stuck in a hospital room,’” Dib said.
More than a year later, she said she is able to get up with her children in the morning, take them to school and manage household tasks.
“If I had had this treatment when I was 19, my life would be completely different now,” Dib said.
Sheikh said the therapy holds “incredible promise,” but is not without risks.
The CAR T-cell therapy clinical trial is conducted by a team of specialists that oversees preparation, administration and follow-up therapy. The clinical care team includes a rheumatologist, an oncologist or hematologist, an immunologist and a nephrologist to monitor the kidneys.
“I would say it’s just really groundbreaking in a way that we had never imagined,” Sheikh said.

title: Why now is the time for a pre-holiday debt audit

text:
(InvestigateTV) — Carrying credit card debt into the holiday season can quickly spiral into a painful “debt hangover” come January. Debt relief attorney Leslie Tayne said now, before the holiday pressure sets in, is the time to review budgets for the upcoming season.
Tayne said that includes planning for Thanksgiving, Hanukkah, Christmas and Kwanzaa.
“At this time you should be gathering your lists, thinking about who you’re giving gifts to and how you’re going to be paying for those,” Tayne said. “If there’s sales on items you’re going to be purchasing, now is the time to be taking advantage of those. Start looking for coupons and other opportunities, like Black Friday sales that might be coming up.”
Tayne said planning ahead is key to staying on budget, and smart online shopping can make a real difference. For big-ticket items like toys or electronics, she recommends checking prices across multiple retailers now.
“It’s an opportunity to think now: What does this item cost? Will this particular item go on sale? Where can I get the best possible deal?” Tayne said. “Be very proactive about finding that opportunity to save as much money as possible and budget your spending for the holidays.”
Tayne said the holiday season tends to arrive quickly, and rising prices due to inflation can mean even more debt for families who are not prepared. She said the current challenge for shoppers is making sure every dollar goes as far as possible.

title: NTSB preliminary report: Pilot error caused plane crash involving Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate﻿
text:
Pilot error caused plane crash involving Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate, NTSB preliminary report finds
Pilot error caused the plane crash involving Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany in September, according to the National Transportation Safety Board Preliminary Report. 
Pilot error caused plane crash involving Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate, NTSB preliminary report finds
Pilot error caused the plane crash involving Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany in September, according to the National Transportation Safety Board Preliminary Report. 
"The pilot said the loss of engine power was due to his delay in switching fuel tanks and not turning on the electric fuel boost pump" during flight, according to the report.
The sheriff's office identified the pilot as 73-year-old Leonard Boltz from Pearson after the crash.
The left main fuel tank was empty, while the right main tank and both auxiliary tanks were full, the report stated.
The fuel selector was set to the right main tank, and the boost pump switch was off. The airplane had taken off earlier that day with 70 gallons of fuel and was not refueled before the flight to Wausau, according to the NTSB.
"Tom will always be grateful to the pilot for his composure during the emergency. In a life-threatening situation, he remained calm and did what was necessary to ensure they both survived," the Tiffany campaign said Wednesday.
The crash
While landing, the pilot noticed a higher-than-normal engine exhaust temperature and switched the fuel selector to the right main tank. He advanced the mixture and throttle controls but said the engine did not respond. He did not turn on the electric fuel boost pump while trying to restore power.
The Beech K35 airplane struck water while the pilot was trying to reach the runway at Wausau Downtown Airport, damaging the plane.
The Marathon County Sheriff's Office said the initial 911 call came in at 8:49 p.m. Saturday.
"After the crash, we called 911," Tiffany said in a statement. "As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat."
Tiffany's campaign said he received stitches above his right eye at Aspirus Wausau Hospital overnight and was released. The pilot also received stitches and was released.
The 911 call
The 911 call was made in the moments after the crash, and the dispatcher can be heard asking Tiffany and his pilot, Boltz, if they can swim to safety.
Only the dispatcher can be heard in the 911 call. The sheriff's office released a statement, saying, "The missing audio was not captured by the recording equipment. The problem that caused the audio to not be recorded has been resolved for future calls, but the missing audio is not recoverable."
Listen to the full 911 call and see what the scene and removal of the plane looked like below.
The dispatcher tells them how to help the rescuers find them, including using lights to be seen faster.
"Just try to have a flashlight or your phone out," the dispatcher said. "Still waving it around like one of you guys has a phone. You can just wave in the air with a flashlight on or something. It'll help too, because they're looking from the shoreline right now."
The rescue
Tiffany said when the plane crashed, they called for help and then stood on the top of the plane as it began to sink. They ended up swimming to shallow waters, where they waited for rescuers.
Video shows a crew member calling in what they believed was going to be a fuel spill after the crash. It showed the plane in the water in the dark with flashlights surrounding the area.
"We just got the pilot and the passenger out," the man said.
Sister station WISN spoke with Wausau Fire Battalion Chief Kraig Kruzan on Sunday. He was asked about the upgrades to boats that fire stations have done over the past few years.
"The boat that we use for a river system is very important," Kruzan said. "You have to be able to manage very shallow water, as well as very deep water. Having a shallow-running boat is very important to our success. Even crossing from the boat landing, we had to cross water that was as little as a foot deep. Standard tiller boats might run aground and get you stuck. Having the proper equipment is key to the success of a situation like this."
When he realized the crew had rescued a sitting member of Congress who was running for governor, he said, "That reaction didn't come until I watched them both safely walk onto shore from the boat, and I was just pleased that, regardless of who they are. I'm glad they were safe. And for the most part had very minor injuries. So I think everybody on our crew was very relieved to find that the injuries were so minor, they were able to walk under their own power. Things could have been a lot worse."
Witnesses
Video obtained by WISN from a neighbor Monday night shows the moment the plane crashed into the lake.
A 911 call also came in from someone who was hanging out in the back of their truck at DC Everest Park and reported the crash.
"There was a water plane that came in, and they crashed," the man said.
He continued to tell the dispatcher that he saw some lights for a bit, but then it was dark.
"They were coming down pretty smooth," the man said to the dispatcher. "And then they just. They just went nose first."
Full statement
Tom Tiffany issued the following statement after the crash.
"While returning home from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner, the plane I was traveling in lost power as we approached the Wausau Downtown Airport. The pilot made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau.
"After landing, we called 911. As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat.
"I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly. They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care. Thankfully, both the pilot and I sustained only minor injuries.
"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side. An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is."
Emotional thanks
In a news conference Sunday afternoon, Tiffany thanked everyone who reached out with prayers and kind words, and said he was especially grateful to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, law enforcement, first responders and the team at Aspirus Wausau Hospital for their care and quick response.
"(I'm) just grateful for the Lord for sparing us another day," Tiffany said.
Watch the full news conference in the video player below.
Plane removal
Officials removed the plane from Lake Wausau Monday. It had been partially submerged since the crash happened, and people were asked to avoid the area.
Crowley responds to the incident
Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley spoke after hearing about the crash.
"I’m grateful to God that Congressman Tiffany and no one else was hurt in this horrifying incident, which could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot. I wish them and the Congressman a quick recovery and that they can find solace with their loved ones," he said.

title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, as Zelenskyy says he feels betrayed by Trump
text:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine attacked a Russian oil refinery Thursday, abandoning a brief truce involving energy-related targets that it said Moscow did not heed, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow in Russia’s Ryazan region, according to the Russian Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov. Russia’s Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv’s relations with Trump, which have soured again in recent days amid deepening tensions with Washington.
Zelenskyy said he was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks.
Despite going along with Trump’s demand for a truce, Zelenskyy complained, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes, and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. Both are vital for the Ukrainian military.
He said his patience had run out, telling the Financial Times in an interview published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume.
“We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying.
A senior Ukrainian official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to speak publicly, confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
Zelenskyy slams US deal to buy Russian diesel
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Ukraine never stopped its strikes on refineries that have hurt Russia. It wasn’t possible to independently verify each side’s claims.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov labeled Ukraine’s strikes on oil facilities as a “direct and crude challenge to President Trump.”
Another point of tension with Ukraine is a deal Trump made with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
In an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist’s YouTube show, Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink limits that restricted the use of Ukrainian drones.
“Really, yes, between us,” Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. “Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump.”
He said the behavior of the U.S., including restricting the Starlink system, “was really strange.”
Zelenskyy says U.S. position isn’t ‘on the right side of history’
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “losing a strong partner” in the United States.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he’s in the middle,” he said.
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is “not the right side of history.”
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
A Ukrainian official said the country has not received an explanation from either SpaceX, the company that maintains the Starlink satellites, or the Pentagon, on the slowdown. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive situation.
The Pentagon has not answered questions about the slowdown from The Associated Press either.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn’t stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Ukraine looks to Europe for more help
Amid fears that the Trump administration may be withdrawing support for Ukraine, Zelenskyy went to Brussels on Thursday for talks with European Union leaders attending a two-day summit.
Zelenskyy said he would meet with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, French President Emmanuel Macron, and the prime ministers of Poland, Denmark and Belgium.
The previous day, he visited London, where he won pledges of more help from U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Asked whether the EU still trusts Trump, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, replied: “We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender.”
“Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that is why Europe is standing beside Ukraine,” Kallas told reporters.
Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians
In other developments, three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine’s Emergency Services said Thursday.
Between midnight and Thursday morning, Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, Zelenskyy said on X, adding that the barrage came “precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted.”
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security.”
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian air force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
A Ukrainian missile destroyed six warplanes at an airfield in southwestern Russia, Zelenskyy said. The aircraft were used to launch powerful glide bombs, he said.
“Russia is dragging out the war, so our long-range operations will continue,” he said on social media.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight and that Russian forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.
___
Associated Press writers Samya Kullab in Kyiv, Ukraine; Lorne Cook in Brussels; and Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Who protects the farmers?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Regarding an Oct. 7 news report (“Maine’s top court rejects eviction appeal by Midcoast farmers”), the farmers’ appeal was reportedly lost because it was found they had “failed to pay rent and grow crops as they had once agreed.”
Crops, for most non-farmers, usually means fruits and vegetables. Not all soils in Maine are suitable for growing fruits and vegetables. Some soils are best used for pasture and hay (a valuable crop) or for growing livestock, which might also be called a valuable crop.
The Maine Farmland Trust ought to carefully review its policies regarding farmers on leased land; the situation that happened in Harpswell will happen again. It is one thing to protect farmland. Who protects the farmers? No farmers, no food.
Jeanne Johnson
Juniper Edge Farm
Brunswick

title: Troy Jackson raises millions more than Susan Collins, but trails her in money race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign raised $3.9 million in the third quarter of 2026 — a figure that paled in comparison to the $20.4 million raised by her opponent, Troy Jackson.
But Republicans are still badly outspending Democrats on the Senate race overall. So far, Republican-aligned groups have spent or reserved $151.5 million on ads, compared to $110.7 million by Democrat-aligned groups, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
Collins’ campaign spent almost $11 million from July through September, Thursday’s quarterly finance report showed.
Jackson released detailed campaign finance numbers at 6:15 p.m. Thursday, despite promising to do so by Wednesday morning. His upstart campaign raked in more than $19.4 million in donations and about $1 million from other groups.
Collins is running to win a sixth term in the U.S. Senate and, as the lone Republican in Congress from New England, is facing political headwinds in the final three weeks of the campaign. Polling has repeatedly shown Jackson ahead or within the margin of error.
It’s going to be a close race. Here’s how Collins’ and Jackson’s camps used their money — and raised it, in the campaign’s crucial months.
COLLINS’ SPENDING
Collins’ biggest area of spending, unsurprisingly, was advertising. About 85% of the campaign’s $10.8 million spent between July and the end of September was on advertising.
The campaign spent nearly $6.5 million on media buys, the report shows, almost entirely through Mentzer Media Services, which is based in Towson, Maryland. Collins’ team also spent more than $2.8 million on digital fundraising and advertising through the Arlington, Virginia-based consulting firm Targeted Victory.
Using out-of-state consultants to buy media and place advertisements is par for the course. Prior to these new three-month reports being filed Thursday, less than 4% of the money in Maine’s federal races was being spent in this state, and the overwhelming majority of it was going toward advertising.
According to media tracker AdImpact, Collins’ campaign has spent or reserved space for almost $12.4 million in advertising. The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Collins’ campaign have bought an additional $2.6 million in advertising and a Collins joint fundraising committee has about $1.6 million lined up.
But it’s the outside money — from political action committees, or PACs — that is dominating Maine’s airwaves. Collins is a bigger beneficiary than her opponent, Jackson, AdImpact’s figures show.
JACKSON’S SPENDING
Jackson’s campaign spent about $16.4 million during its first quarter, and still had almost $4 million in cash at the end of the period.
About three-quarters of the campaign’s spending was on advertising, mostly to Chevy Chase, Maryland-based TKO Buying LLC and the Washington D.C. firm Sage Media Planning & Placement, Inc.
Jackson’s campaign has bought or reserved $20.4 million in advertisements, according to AdImpact. Again, though, Democrats are being heavily out-spent on advertising in the race, to the tune of about $40 million.
The second-largest expense for Jackson’s campaign was “list acquisition” — or, in other words, buying donor information. The campaign spent $1.5 million for that purpose.
COLLINS’ FUNDRAISING
The Collins campaign had $11 million on hand at the start of this filing period, in July. Most of that was spent down, but Collins also brought in an additional $3.9 million.
Collins’ most notable donor in this report cycle was George W. Bush, the former Republican president who has long summered in Kennebunkport. Bush gave $3,500 on Aug. 26, the report shows.
Collins also received $3,500, the maximum for individual donors, from U.S. Secretary of Education and wrestling executive Linda McMahon. Thomas Klingenstein, the conservative megadonor who helped bankroll a political committee for failed gubernatorial candidate Garrett Mason, also gave the personal max to Collins’s campaign.
Almost all of Collins’ fundraising came from individuals — about $3.7 million. But almost all of those individual contributions came from out-of-state. Among Collins’ donations from individuals, two-thirds were less than $100.
Only 11% of the money from individual donors during this three-month period came from Maine. Florida, Texas, California and New York donors gave more than three times what Collins’ Maine donors gave — though some of those funds were subject to refund.
JACKSON’S FUNDRAISING
Jackson sprinted out of the gate and, despite his late start, raised well over $20 million in his first quarter.
Almost all of that was from individual donors. Jackson’s campaign said they raised money from nearly 200,000 individual donors, including from every Maine county. About 95% of the contributions were $100 or less, the campaign said.
Dan Kleban, Jackson’s opponent, briefly, for the nomination after Graham Platner dropped out, donated $3,500. Jordan Wood, another candidate in that short secondary race, donated the personal maximum.
Jackson, a union supporter, was also backed by several union PACs with tens of thousands in donations.

title: Water cooler stops falling tree just inches away from crushing man and his dog
text:
PRESCOTT, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - A water cooler miraculously saved a man and his dog from a falling tree in Arizona, authorities say.
Deputies with the Yavapai County Sheriff’s Office responded Sunday afternoon to reports that a massive tree fell onto a van parked in a camping spot just outside of Prescott.
“When deputies arrived, they braced for the worst. Instead, they found a man and his dog, miraculously unharmed, though the van itself was a total loss,” officials said in a statement.
Deputies looked inside the van to see what could’ve stopped the tree from crushing the man and dog and found an ordinary Igloo water cooler.
“As the tree smashed into the vehicle, the sturdy cooler took the brunt of the impact, stopping the trunk just inches from crushing the man in the driver’s seat,” officials said.
High winds and saturated soil can make falling trees an unpredictable and deadly hazard, officials said. Avoid parking under large, dead or leaning trees, especially during high winds.
