title: Did Maine Democrats decriminalize several crimes if the offender says they are homeless?
text:
No.
Maine law does not exempt people from any crimes simply because they say they are homeless.
A 2021 bill sponsored by state Rep. Victoria Morales, D-South Portland, initially proposed barring arrests and prosecutions for certain offenses committed because someone lacked housing. But lawmakers removed that provision before enactment.
Instead, the law requires officers to ask whether someone accused of certain crimes has a home. It covers five offenses: trespassing, disorderly conduct, public urination, drug possession for illegal use and drinking alcohol in prohibited public places.
For those without housing, police must follow their department’s homelessness crisis protocol. Protocols include referrals to crisis services, mental health and substance use professionals, emergency housing and case management. The Maine attorney general’s model favors referrals over citations or arrests, which it calls a last resort.
However, departments can adopt different protocols, and police still may issue citations or make arrests when warranted.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: Mainers who import prescription drugs face new customs rule
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A new Customs and Border Protection rule would make it nearly impossible for personal prescription shipments from pharmacies outside the U.S. to enter the country, affecting Mainers who rely on lower-cost prescriptions from Canada and elsewhere.
The change was supposed to start next week on Oct. 22, but CBP on Wednesday delayed the deadline 90 days to Jan. 20.
The group Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation says the reprieve came after its members sent more than 107,000 letters to Congress. The group says it is seeking a permanent solution.
Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, said some patients may not be able to afford their drugs under the new rule.
“Some patients are going to be in the situation of not being able to afford their drugs,” Hunter said. “We’re not talking about a, you know, 10 or 15 dollar price increase. This is hundreds of dollars per month. Then you multiply that across multiple prescriptions that, for instance, a senior might take, you can see that can be a couple of thousand dollars.”
“It’s going to be very important that we get personal pharmaceuticals carved out and set aside from this new rule, because it’s really a matter of life and death,” Hunter said.
Senators sign letter to CBP
Hunter said a number of senators, including Angus King, signed a letter to CBP demanding personal prescriptions be exempted, arguing the rule won’t help with tariffs or stopping fentanyl, its intended purpose. Hunter says Sen. Susan Collins was not among the senators signed on to the letter, but he’d welcome her support.
Hunter is urging people to keep pressuring Congress at personalimportation.org.

title: Maine’s unsung heroes, caregivers, deserve support. AARP Maine is in their corner.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Family caregivers are among Maine’s most important resources, yet their contributions often go unrecognized. Every day, they help aging parents, spouses, friends, neighbors, and other loved ones live safely and independently at home. They support their loved ones by helping with daily activities that many of us do but take for granted, such as making a meal or managing our medications. They do this not because they are paid to, but because someone they love needs help.
In Maine, nearly three in ten adults are family caregivers or have provided care within the past year. Together, they represent over 300,000 people whose dedication helps make it possible for countless older adults to remain in their homes and communities, where they want to be.
Caregiving is rewarding, but it can be demanding. Many caregivers work full- or part-time jobs, and some raise children while caregiving. Others find themselves navigating complicated health care systems, making difficult decisions, and handling responsibilities they never expected to take on. The physical, emotional, and financial challenges can be overwhelming.
Get the family caregiving help you need with resources in Maine.
The AARP Family Caregiver Resource Guide for Maine helps family caregivers access key programs, services and agencies in their community.
To order a copy of the guide, call the AARP Family Caregiving Resource Line at 1-877-333-5885 and request the AARP Family Caregiver Resource Guide for Maine. Or view it online at aarp.org/CaregiverResources.
Find us at aarp.org/me | [email protected] | @aarpmaine
That is why AARP Maine is committed to standing with family caregivers. We know they are the unsung heroes of Maine’s long-term care system, and we believe they deserve practical support, reliable information, and policies that make caregiving easier.
One of the most important ways AARP Maine has supported caregivers is through our advocacy for Paid Family and Medical Leave. We heard repeatedly from caregivers who were forced to choose between caring for a loved one and earning a paycheck. Many family caregivers are still working while providing care, often using vacation time, unpaid leave, or flexible schedules to meet their caregiving responsibilities.
AARP Maine fought for Paid Family and Medical Leave because no one should have to choose between family and financial security. The program gives eligible workers access to paid, job-protected leave when they need time to care for a loved one, recover from a serious health condition, welcome a new child, or address other qualifying family needs. It is a major step forward for Maine caregivers and working families.
Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) gives eligible Maine workers up to 12 weeks of paid, job-protected leave to care for themselves or a loved one. AARP Maine proudly advocated for PFML, helping ensure working caregivers no longer have to choose between family and a paycheck.
Learn more at maine.gov/paidleave
Advocacy is only part of the equation. Caregivers also need resources they can use today.
That is why AARP Maine offers a free Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide. Whether someone is just beginning a caregiving journey or has been providing care for years, the guide serves as a valuable roadmap to programs, services, and support available across the state. It includes information on caregiver support services, transportation assistance, financial resources, legal help, respite care, and other programs that can make caregiving more manageable.
The guide also encourages caregivers to prioritize their own well-being. Too often, caregivers focus entirely on the needs of others while neglecting their own health. Yet caregivers need support, rest, and resources if they are to continue providing care over the long term.
AARP Maine has also partnered with 211 Maine to help family caregivers connect with assistance in their communities. Through this collaboration, caregivers can contact 211 and be connected to trained specialists who help identify local resources tailored to their needs.
Caregiving will touch nearly every Maine family at some point. Most of us will either provide care, receive care, or love someone who does. As Maine’s population continues to age, supporting family caregivers becomes even more important.
At AARP Maine, we want caregivers to know they are not alone. We will continue fighting for policies that help them save time and money, providing resources that help them navigate challenges, and elevating their voices in Augusta and beyond.
If you are caring for a loved one, AARP Maine is in your corner. To learn more about Paid Family and Medical Leave, download the Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide, explore caregiver tools, and learn about the 211 Maine partnership, visit aarp.org/mecares.
Caregivers spend so much of their time caring for others. Let us help care for you.

title: Letter: Paul LePage is wrong choice for Maine’s 2nd District
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I’m deeply concerned about Paul LePage’s bid for the 2nd Congressional District. In my view, his positions and priorities simply don’t align with the values of our state.
He proudly claimed in 2016 that he was Trump before Trump and “we are one of the same cloth.” I don’t think we want another Trump representing Maine in Washington, D.C., with a 35% approval rating and LePage’s historically offensive, belligerent, racist behavior.
LePage has made it clear he opposes clean, renewable energy that is bringing jobs and economic growth to Maine while protecting our environment. Instead, he supported Trump’s call for offshore oil drilling, the only eastern state governor in either party to support Trump’s proposal, which threatened our fisheries and tourism industries.
LePage refused to fund 55% of school funding, thus raising everyone’s property taxes. Thank you to Gov. Janet Mills for fully funding education at 55%.
LePage opposed legislation to reduce toxic chemicals in our food, even saying that it was no big deal if women grew “little beards” due to the toxicity. Even more troubling, LePage doesn’t seem to live here. His wife has claimed a homestead exemption in Ormond Beach, Florida since 2018.
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District deserves a representative who believes in sustainable energy, safeguards our natural resources, and understands our way of life because they live here. Paul LePage is not that person.
Vote for Matt Dunlap who is highly qualified after being a legislator, secretary of state, and state auditor.
Steve Kahl
Waterville

title: Pumpkinfest Regatta Draws Thousands to Damariscotta
text:
Puffins, multiple Dolly Partons, time travelers from the 1980s, and more gathered in downtown Damariscotta to face off while captaining boats made of pumpkins during the Damariscotta Pumpkinfest Regatta on Sunday, Oct. 11.
Thousands crowded Riverside Park and the municipal parking lot to watch the competition live. Pumpkinfest and Regatta Executive Director Jed Weiss said the turnout was the biggest ever, viewers seen all the way past Oysterhead Pizza Co., in surrounding yards, and out on the water.
“Thankfully, it went off without a hitch,” Weiss said.
Before participants took to the water, Char Corbett blessed the fleet. She recognized the traditional homeland of the Wabanaki people and encouraged gratitude to the land. Corbett said racing a “giant, hollowed-out” squash is the ultimate test of “seaworthiness.”
“There is no truer American freedom that cramming oneself into a several 100-pound pumpkin for the amusement of family, friends, neighbors, and strangers,” Corbett said. “May we first and forever celebrate your freedom to be absolutely and delightfully ridiculous, together.”
Throughout the event, there were winners for each heat. Notable wins include the puffin team, which consisted of Mael Glon and Jen Libby. Glon won the third heat for the individual category for nonmotorized pumpkin boats and the duo won the first relay race together.
Glon started volunteering for Damariscotta Pumpkinfest last year and grew some pumpkins that were featured in the Oct. 4 weigh-off. The snail pumpkin located outside of Barn Door Cafe in Damariscotta was one from his garden.
The pumpkin Glon and Libby used for the race was inspired by Eastern Egg Rock, the location where puffin populations were restored in Muscongus Bay. Glon said some of their luck came from how well their pumpkin was balanced.
“I’m just really competitive,” Glon said. “So, I got out there and I know there’s a little trophy on the line and I was like, I want a trophy.”
Riding inside a pumpkin decorated to resemble a red apple, Andrew Cox won the first individual heat. Cox was invited as a special guest, known for his Wicked Mainer social media accounts. When he is not racing or flipping over his pumpkin boat, Cox spends is a lobsterman.
Going into the competition, Cox said he knew he was going to get wet.
“It’s all mind over matter,” Cox said. “I get wet everyday on the job, so this sounds like a fun blast. So, take a day off and come get wet down this way.”
If invited back next year, Cox said he will definitely attend.
Other notable wins this year include the Dolly Parton-themed team. Former regatta winner Jaja Martin was joined by her family, Valerie and Robert Watts. Dressed in blonde wigs and racing in a pink pumpkin, the team paid homage to the late country singer.
Josh Felter took home the win for the motorized pumpkin boat races. Riding in a boat shaped to look like a rubber duck, Felter sported a bathrobe and blew bubbles as he sped through the water.
“One of the Maine questions I’m getting is ‘When is the regatta next year?’” Weiss said. “I haven’t even looked at the tide scheduled. That is what creates when the regatta is.”
For more information, go to mainepumpkinfest.com.

title: Mt. Blue field hockey bests Messalonskee in double overtime
text:
OAKLAND — The Mt. Blue field hockey team is finding its stride with the playoff quickly approaching.
The Cougars earned the fifth straight win Thursday, beating Messalonskee 2-1 in double overtime. With the win, Mt. Blue (8-5) overtakes the Eagles for fourth place in the Class A North Heal point standings.
Reese Nye scored the first goal for the Cougars, and the game-winner was an own-goal after a scramble in front of the cage with 6:34 left in the second overtime.
“We knew we had to play strong,” said Nye, a senior. “The way we practice really translates to how we play on the field. The way we push ourselves and prepare (is key). And our pregame mentality has been really good.”
Senior Addie Hafford scored for Messalonskee (6-7), which is now fifth in A North.
How did they get there?
Pure grit. The Cougars put constant pressure on the Eagles, but goalie Baylee Dillon, who finished with 12 saves, and Messalonskee were able to knock away every attack.
Nye gave Mt. Blue a 1-0 lead with 6:05 left in the first quarter. Hafford tied it just two minutes later.
“We just pushed each other and kept each other going,” Nye said. “We just keep telling each other to keep our heads in the game.”
From there, it was a midfield battle for the remaining three quarters, and then some, before the Cougars prevailed.
What does it mean?
Mt. Blue continued its winning streak and continues to climb up the A North standings. The Cougars trail No. 1 Skowhegan (12-1), No. 2 Mt. Ararat (12-0), and No. 3 Camden Hills (10-2).
“It’s not where you start, it’s where you finish,” said Mt. Blue coach Julie Lajoie of her team’s current streak.
The Cougars wrap up the regular season at Oxford Hills (3-9-1) on Monday.
Messalonskee is 1-2 in its last three games and remains in the middle of the A North playoff mix. The Eagles finish at Skowhegan on Friday.
Unsung hero
Mt. Blue senior goalie Gwen Lesperance had four saves, including a key stop on a breakaway opportunity in the first overtime.
“That’s a very hard thing to do, to get a save in overtime, point blank (on a breakaway),” Lajoie said.
Statistical leaders
• Mt. Blue: Reese Nye (1 goal), Gwen Lesperance (4 saves)
• Messalonskee: Addie Hafford (1 goal), Baylee Dillon (12 saves)

title: Toyota recalls thousands of RAV4s because vehicles could shut down. Here’s why
text:
(CNN) - More than 30,000 Toyota vehicles have been recalled due to a software issue that could cause the car to shut down.
The recall affects the 2026 Toyota RAV4 plug-in hybrid.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said the software issue could cause the hybrid system to reduce power or even shut down when the vehicle is driven at higher speeds.
As a result, the issue could increase the risk of a crash.
Toyota dealers will update the software for free.
Owners will be notified by early December.

title: Doctors say Pope Leo’s lung has recovered well from surgery and say his post-operative tests normal
text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV met with a top aide on Thursday and resumed working from the hospital, as doctors reported his lung had recovered well from surgery to remove a cancerous nodule.
Leo’s post-operative tests remained within normal levels and his physiotherapy session Thursday involved full mobility exercises, with the pope going about his daily activities independently, said the update from Leo’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
“The chest X-ray revealed good recovery of the operated lung,” they reported. “Overall, his postoperative recovery is proceeding as expected.”
Separately, the Vatican said Leo had received the Vatican chief of staff, or “substitute,” Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, and had resumed working from the hospital. Rudelli handles much of the day-to-day administrative work of the Holy See.
For a second day Leo celebrated Mass with other priests in a special chapel set up near his room on the 10th floor of the hospital, spokesman Matteo Bruni said.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower right lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Asked if any changes to Leo’s planned trip to South America from Nov. 6-17 were expected, Bruni pointed to Leo’s words on Sunday when he announced the discovery of the nodule and impending surgery.
“Thank you for your prayers for the pastoral visit I will make to Peru,” Leo said Sunday in Spanish, in a greeting delivered to a Peruvian group. The trip is also scheduled to include stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
Leo is expected to remain hospitalized until at least Oct. 20.
___
Barry reported from Milan.

title: Norridgewock man gets 45 years for murder of then-girlfriend’s son
text:
SKOWHEGAN — A 61-year-old Norridgewock man was sentenced Thursday to 45 years in prison for the shooting death of his then-girlfriend’s son.
Daniel V. Markey, however, was not in court to learn his fate.
Markey, who was convicted by a jury in August of intentional or knowing murder for the March 1, 2025, death of 39-year-old Christopher Nickerson, chose not to attend his sentencing hearing at the Skowhegan District Court.
Markey’s attorneys had mentioned that possibility previously, Superior Court Justice Daniel Mitchell wrote in an order last week. He called another conference Wednesday to further inquire of Markey’s intentions in a recorded proceeding.
Mitchell said in court at the beginning of Thursday’s hearing that he explained to Markey he had the right to attend or skip the sentencing, but it would proceed regardless of his decision. Markey understood his rights, Mitchell said.
One of Markey’s court-appointed attorneys, Stephen Smith of Steve Smith Trial Lawyers in Augusta, declined to comment on Markey’s decision after the hearing.
Markey’s other defense attorney, Justine Barry, also of Smith’s firm, asked Mitchell not to consider Markey’s absence as a sentencing factor. The judge ultimately did not include it in his analysis.
But prosecutor Jennifer Ackerman, an assistant attorney general, said that Markey’s choice not to attend his sentencing was noteworthy.
“That, from the state’s point of view, certainly reveals his character,” Ackerman said.
Ackerman asked for a prison sentence of 48 years, plus restitution of $3,700 to the state victims’ compensation fund to cover the expenses for Nickerson’s funeral.
Barry asked for a sentence of 25 years, the statutory minimum. Murder in Maine carries a sentence of 25 years to life and the sentence cannot include a term of probation.
Mitchell, with the 45-year sentence he imposed, landed much closer to prosecutors’ recommendation. He also ordered Markey to pay the
In laying out how he arrived at the sentence, Mitchell noted Markey used a firearm to commit the crime; fired at Nickerson multiple times at close range; had sufficient time between a fight and the shooting to do something other than retrieve a gun; killed Nickerson in the presence of his mother; and was motivated by some desire for revenge against Nickerson.
The subjective impact on Nickerson’s family, including his two children, was a key aggravating factor, Mitchell said. It, along with Markey’s future risk to public safety, outweighed mitigating factors, including Markey’s lack of criminal history and his willingness to turn himself into authorities immediately after the shooting.
The fact that a sentence of this length at Markey’s age likely means he will die in prison was not something that could be taken into consideration, Mitchell said.
In a statement read by a victim witness advocate with the attorney general’s office, Kathleen Nickerson said the killing of her son was the worst thing that has ever happened in her life. She could not understand how someone who said he loved her — Markey — could do something so horrible, the statement read.
“My hopes, my dreams, and my sense of purpose have all been changed forever,” said Nickerson, who the advocate said was listening via videoconference, in the statement. “I only wanted to help Chris. I never imagined that trying to help my son would lead to something so devastating.”
The advocate also read letters from Christopher Nickerson’s cousin and her 13-year-old son. Another cousin spoke via videoconference. All told Mitchell about how the loss of Nickerson has affected their lives.
Markey’s brother-in-law, Keith Whitehouse, who was in the courtroom along with another friend of Markey, said he has known Markey for decades and spent a significant amount of time with him.
“I have never known Dan to be violent,” he said.
A jury, after a trial over four days, took about 40 minutes to return its guilty verdict on the murder charge.
Markey’s attorneys argued Markey acted in self-defense after an altercation between him and Christopher Nickerson. Prosecutors, meanwhile, argued Markey was seeking revenge.
Prosecutors’ case relied heavily on testimony from Kathleen Nickerson, Markey’s then-girlfriend and Christopher Nickerson’s mother, who was the only eyewitness to the shooting.
According to her testimony, Christopher Nickerson had been living with her and Markey for a couple of months at their home at 471 River Road in Norridgewock, over Markey’s initial objections. The morning of the shooting, Kathleen Nickerson testified, the three went to bring Christopher Nickerson to a job interview at Walmart. Upon returning home, Markey and Christopher Nickerson got into a verbal argument.
The two exchanged insults, Christopher Nickerson took a swing at Markey and he then went outside the home. He and Markey then got into a physical scuffle outside.
Christopher Nickerson began to pack up his items to be picked up by his cousin, while Markey went to another structure on the property that was being used as a marijuana growing facility. That’s where, prosecutors said, Markey got the gun.
Markey returned to the house and shot Christopher Nickerson four times, missing with a fifth shot. One hit him in the chest, a wound that an autopsy determined was rapidly fatal.
At the time, Kathleen Nickerson testified, Christopher Nickerson was near the door and about to leave and put his hands up when he saw the gun. Markey’s attorneys questioned that version of events during the trial.
After the shooting, Markey drove away and turned himself in to police in Skowhegan. He was evaluated at Redington-Fairview General Hospital and found to have minor injuries, including a cut on his head, a hematoma on his face and a scrape on his chest.
A shooting reconstruction by a state police detective was consistent with Kathleen Nickerson’s account. Among other things, Landry concluded Christopher Nickerson was not moving or charging forward when he was struck by the bullets.
Markey, who has been held at the Somerset County Jail in Madison since his arrest, chose not to testify at trial.
The jury, however, did hear part of his side of the story in video clips of him speaking to police and medical personnel in the hours after the shooting. He told them Christopher Nickerson had attacked him and was repeatedly beating him.
Markey plans to file an appeal, Smith said.

title: Kelly Clarkson and a Brooklyn store are clashing on social media over mechanical bird. Here’s why
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — It was something most people have likely done at one time or another: complain to others about feeling judged or dismissed during an interaction, maybe even take to social media to post about it.
But just because we might all have the same impulse, we all don’t have the same reach and impact. Exhibit A: a dispute between singer Kelly Clarkson and a small store in Brooklyn that’s brought out angry fans and heated commentary.
The conflict from over the weekend, involving a high-priced mechanical bird, is raising more issues than just the quality of customer service. It’s also a case study in power dynamics, and the differential that exists between someone with a high profile and those without.
It started Saturday when Clarkson went to Art of Play, a store in Brooklyn that offers items like books, games and playing cards and also hosts magic shows. But the interaction turned negative, she said in a social media post, when she “was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it” and went on to say the store had “just lost a huge sale.” She named the store and gave it a thumbs down.
A back-and-forth ensued, with the store making its own posts saying initially that the item wasn’t for sale and then adding that they had tried to find her an alternative. Clarkson said that wasn’t true.
Since Clarkson’s initial post, there’s been a barrage of commentary online — and, the store owners say, in the real world. There have been hateful messages and reviews, and even someone showing up at the store, said Adam Rubin, one of the partners.
“I don’t understand why these people are willing to debase themselves on behalf of a celebrity they never met,” he said. Representatives for Clarkson did not respond to repeated attempts to get comment.
The power of celebrity is potent
Celebrities have power in different ways. They can influence what people feel as well as impact what they think or believe, said Alfred Archer, assistant professor at Tilburg University in the Netherlands, who has done research around the ethics and politics of fame.
In a situation like Clarkson’s, the influence is heavily weighted in the celebrity’s favor as a result, he said. That doesn’t mean celebrities should be censored or barred from speaking, but they should be cognizant of that reality in determining what they say and how they say it.
“You can’t hold the celebrity responsible for everything that their followers do, of course,” Archer said, but those who have influence should remember that their words can resonate widely and “be careful about what they put on social media and what they communicate in public for that reason.”
That power can also have positive ripples — like when Ms. Rachel, the children’s educator and YouTube star, asked people on social media for Black-owned businesses to support. She gave recognition to small businesses like a coffee shop in New Jersey, leading to a huge jump in sales and popularity.
“I think really the responsibility here is to use this power in a responsible way,” Archer said. “And of course, what that looks like in any individual case is going to be a decision for a particular celebrity to make. But they do have to think about it a bit more carefully than an ordinary member of the public does.”
Social media changed the equation
While everyday people have always been fascinated by the famous, the explosion of social media and the glut of information — and the way we follow our family and friends right along with our favorite stars — means there’s more of a likelihood that people can develop parasocial, or one-sided, unreciprocated relationships with celebrities. That can lead to the kind of harsh messages and bad reviews that the Brooklyn store says it has experienced.
That aspect of modern life is baffling to Franchesca Ramsey, a writer, podcaster, and content creator.
“I think social media itself has heightened people’s ability to feel a connection to a celebrity or a public person that they don’t know,” she said.
“Back in my day, you liked a musician, you put up a poster on the wall. You read the magazine articles about them. You maybe went to their concert. You watched their music videos. But beyond that, it didn’t feel like a two-way relationship. It felt like I’m the fan and this is the person that I really enjoy,” she said.
“Social media has ... kind of created this false sense of reality where, I really think even the act of watching someone’s content on your phone and it looks like they’re talking directly to you,” she said.
Asked what advice he would give another small-business owner facing this kind of situation, Rubin didn’t have any. “This is not something that a small business owner has the capability to deal with,” he said. “This is something that happens on a level of fame and celebrity that I don’t have access to, (that) most normal people don’t have access to.”
Watching the crowd of reporters from his plumbing supply store next door to Art of Play, Daniel Graffeo couldn’t believe the uproar was still going on several days after the initial encounter, but wasn’t totally surprised. “Nowadays everybody’s looking for something, you know, publicity,” he said.
He hoped it would never find him. “I would not want to be in that situation.”

title: CLT’s ‘Cabaret’ opens this weekend
text:
AUBURN, ME – The L/A Community Little Theatre (CLT) opens its 87th season this weekend with a daring and powerful interpretation of the Tony Award winning musical “Cabaret.”
Set in a seedy Berlin cabaret called the Kit Kat Klub in 1929, the show tells the story of two doomed romances set against the emergence of antisemitism and fascism in Germany. Winner of eight Tony Awards during its original run, “Cabaret” has been revived on Broadway during every decade since the 1970s. Musical numbers include “Willkommen,” “Cabaret,” “Don’t Tell Mama” and “Two Ladies.”
This CLT production of “Cabaret” is based on the 1998 Broadway revival, widely considered the most revolutionary re-envisioning of this innovative musical. It emphasizes the creeping threat of fascism, underscoring the parallels between the rising threat of Nazism in 1929 Berlin and contemporary anxieties about authoritarian resurgence. The show instills a chilling sense of impending doom in between the lively numbers at the Kit Kat Klub. More than anything, “Cabaret” serves as a cautionary tale, denouncing hedonism and highlighting the importance of morality.
The show is directed by Brandon Chaloux assisted by musical director Paul G. Caron, choreographer Adelyn Bell, producer Sarah Chaloux, stage manager Sarah Greaton, and lead costumer Jackie Ahlquist.
Performances of “Cabaret” will be held on October 16, 17, 22, 23, and 24 at 7:30 p.m., and October 18 and 25 at 2:00 p.m. All shows will be held at CLT on 30 Academy Street in Auburn. Tickets are available online at www.laclt.com. Due to the mature themes in this production, parental discretion is advised.
Lead roles in the CLT production of “Cabaret” are played by Owen Lewis as the Emcee and Hillary Perry as Sally Bowles. The show opens Friday, October 16 and will run through October 25. www.laclt.com/. Photo by Aaron Skolfield.

title: Troy Jackson raises millions more than Susan Collins, but trails her in money race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign raised $3.9 million in the third quarter of 2026 — a figure that paled in comparison to the $20.4 million raised by her opponent, Troy Jackson.
But Republicans are still badly outspending Democrats on the Senate race overall. So far, Republican-aligned groups have spent or reserved $151.5 million on ads, compared to $110.7 million by Democrat-aligned groups, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
Collins’ campaign spent almost $11 million from July through September, Thursday’s quarterly finance report showed.
Jackson released detailed campaign finance numbers at 6:15 p.m. Thursday, despite promising to do so by Wednesday morning. His upstart campaign raked in more than $19.4 million in donations and about $1 million from other groups.
Collins is running to win a sixth term in the U.S. Senate and, as the lone Republican in Congress from New England, is facing political headwinds in the final three weeks of the campaign. Polling has repeatedly shown Jackson ahead or within the margin of error.
It’s going to be a close race. Here’s how Collins’ and Jackson’s camps used their money — and raised it, in the campaign’s crucial months.
COLLINS’ SPENDING
Collins’ biggest area of spending, unsurprisingly, was advertising. About 85% of the campaign’s $10.8 million spent between July and the end of September was on advertising.
The campaign spent nearly $6.5 million on media buys, the report shows, almost entirely through Mentzer Media Services, which is based in Towson, Maryland. Collins’ team also spent more than $2.8 million on digital fundraising and advertising through the Arlington, Virginia-based consulting firm Targeted Victory.
Using out-of-state consultants to buy media and place advertisements is par for the course. Prior to these new three-month reports being filed Thursday, less than 4% of the money in Maine’s federal races was being spent in this state, and the overwhelming majority of it was going toward advertising.
According to media tracker AdImpact, Collins’ campaign has spent or reserved space for almost $12.4 million in advertising. The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Collins’ campaign have bought an additional $2.6 million in advertising and a Collins joint fundraising committee has about $1.6 million lined up.
But it’s the outside money — from political action committees, or PACs — that is dominating Maine’s airwaves. Collins is a bigger beneficiary than her opponent, Jackson, AdImpact’s figures show.
JACKSON’S SPENDING
Jackson’s campaign spent about $16.4 million during its first quarter, and still had almost $4 million in cash at the end of the period.
About three-quarters of the campaign’s spending was on advertising, mostly to Chevy Chase, Maryland-based TKO Buying LLC and the Washington D.C. firm Sage Media Planning & Placement, Inc.
Jackson’s campaign has bought or reserved $20.4 million in advertisements, according to AdImpact. Again, though, Democrats are being heavily out-spent on advertising in the race, to the tune of about $40 million.
The second-largest expense for Jackson’s campaign was “list acquisition” — or, in other words, buying donor information. The campaign spent $1.5 million for that purpose.
COLLINS’ FUNDRAISING
The Collins campaign had $11 million on hand at the start of this filing period, in July. Most of that was spent down, but Collins also brought in an additional $3.9 million.
Collins’ most notable donor in this report cycle was George W. Bush, the former Republican president who has long summered in Kennebunkport. Bush gave $3,500 on Aug. 26, the report shows.
Collins also received $3,500, the maximum for individual donors, from U.S. Secretary of Education and wrestling executive Linda McMahon. Thomas Klingenstein, the conservative megadonor who helped bankroll a political committee for failed gubernatorial candidate Garrett Mason, also gave the personal max to Collins’s campaign.
Almost all of Collins’ fundraising came from individuals — about $3.7 million. But almost all of those individual contributions came from out-of-state. Among Collins’ donations from individuals, two-thirds were less than $100.
Only 11% of the money from individual donors during this three-month period came from Maine. Florida, Texas, California and New York donors gave more than three times what Collins’ Maine donors gave — though some of those funds were subject to refund.
JACKSON’S FUNDRAISING
Jackson sprinted out of the gate and, despite his late start, raised well over $20 million in his first quarter.
Almost all of that was from individual donors. Jackson’s campaign said they raised money from nearly 200,000 individual donors, including from every Maine county. About 95% of the contributions were $100 or less, the campaign said.
Dan Kleban, Jackson’s opponent, briefly, for the nomination after Graham Platner dropped out, donated $3,500. Jordan Wood, another candidate in that short secondary race, donated the personal maximum.
Jackson, a union supporter, was also backed by several union PACs with tens of thousands in donations.

title: Maine immigrants could lose work authorization under federal rule change, advocates say
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Trump administration is finalizing a rule change this week ending automatic work permit extensions for many immigrants.
The regulation makes permanent a change that was first implemented last year.
Panagioti Tsolkas, with the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition, said it undermines immigrants’ ability to support themselves.
“Stripping people’s certainty about whether or not they’re allowed to actually go to work and collect a paycheck for their work, you know, it has the effect of creating a second-class citizen,” he said, adding that it would also create a domino effect of uncertainty for workers and their employers.
“Many of Maine’s key industries that the state’s so well known for rely on immigrants with work permits, and so that’s thrown into uncertainty,” he said.
In a written public comment, the Maine State Chamber of Commerce warned the new rule could create unnecessary gaps in employment authorization for Maine workers.
The Department of Homeland Security said the change is about “proper screening and vetting.”
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Police: Pennsylvania man fatally strangles wife, who was a doctor, before setting her body on fire
text:
Pennsylvania man fatally strangles wife, who was a UPMC pediatrician, before setting body on fire, police say
Police noted that the couple's young daughter was sleeping in the home at the time
Pennsylvania man fatally strangles wife, who was a UPMC pediatrician, before setting body on fire, police say
Police noted that the couple's young daughter was sleeping in the home at the time
A Pennsylvania man is accused of strangling his wife, who was a UPMC doctor, to death before setting her body on fire inside their home, according to the Harrisburg Bureau of Police.
Authorities identified the suspect as 41-year-old Jonathan Gatto of Dauphin County, in south-central Pennsylvania.
Fire reported at Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, home
Emergency crews responded around 7:05 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 10, to the couple’s home in Harrisburg, which is the state's capital and is located outside of Hershey, Pennsylvania.
Firefighters saw light smoke coming from the home before finding Julia Pederson in a first-floor bedroom, the affidavit stated.
Police said first responders performed CPR before taking Pederson to Penn State Health Holy Spirit Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead.
Investigators say fire was intentionally set
Investigators described the fire as "very small."
A Pennsylvania State Police fire marshal examined the scene and determined that the fire had been intentionally set, according to court documents.
Gatto told police marriage was 'not good'
Police interviewed Gatto at the Harrisburg police station.
"During the interview, Gatto indicated that his marriage with Julia Pederson was not good," the affidavit stated. "He indicated that they were getting separated and they were trying to work together to come up with a time and how they were going to tell their 7-year-old daughter this news."
Police said Gatto told investigators that Pederson had not been feeling well after recently starting medication for migraines. He said he heard a loud noise around 11 p.m. or midnight that sounded like someone falling down the stairs, according to the affidavit.
Gatto said he set an alarm for 2 a.m. to bring Pederson ibuprofen, but she told him she did not need anything, according to the documents. He said he later awoke to smoke detectors, took his daughter outside and called 911, police said.
Gatto told investigators he went back inside and attempted to reach Pederson but burned his hand when he opened her bedroom door, the affidavit stated. He said he then returned outside and waited for emergency crews.
Autopsy shows Pederson died before fire
An autopsy conducted on Oct. 13 determined that Pederson died from multiple traumatic injuries before the fire was set, according to police. Her death was ruled a homicide.
Investigators said Gatto strangled Pederson before setting her body on fire inside the home. Police noted their daughter was asleep in an upstairs bedroom at the time.
Charges
Gatto was charged with the following:
- First-degree murder
- Abuse of a corpse
- Tampering with or fabricating physical evidence
- Endangering the welfare of a child
- Arson involving danger of death or bodily injury
- Aggravated arson involving a person inside the property
He was denied bail and remains in Dauphin County Prison.
UPMC says Pederson was a 'beloved pediatrician'
UPMC spokesperson said Pederson was a doctor and member of its UPMC Children's Community Pediatrics team. They shared the following message with Harrisburg sister station WGAL:
"We are deeply saddened by the tragic passing of Dr. Julia Pederson, a beloved pediatrician and valued member of our UPMC Children's Community Pediatrics team. Dr. Pederson devoted her career to caring for children and supporting families, and her loss is felt deeply by colleagues, patients and communities she served. We extend our heartfelt condolences to her family, friends and loved ones, and ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time."

title: Trump says Pentagon won’t livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it.
Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan.”
But, he continued, “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
The Pentagon has said Hasan’s execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, “if they so choose.”
The announcement earlier this month from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan’s execution would be public — and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be livestreamed — prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalization.
Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said Trump and Hegseth discussed the decision to drop the livestream plans before the president’s announcement on social media.
“The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned,” Parnell said.
Catholic bishop called the plan ‘barbaric’
When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said, adding, “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”
Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops had condemned the Trump administration’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution, with Archbishop Paul S. Coakley saying the move was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”
Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., voiced similar sentiments.
For his part, the president has defended his decision to approve the use of a firing squad, but had for days distanced himself from Hegseth’s announcement that it would be public.
“Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump said Friday when asked about the livestream. As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: “He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement and now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.
The U.S. military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

title: Innocent bystander, 81, killed in gunfire outside Walmart, police say

Gunfire broke out in the parking lot of the store on Shallowford Road just after 7 p.m. Wednesday, striking 81-year-old James Edward McDaniel, police said.

title: 2 women file lawsuit accusing former US Rep. Matt Gaetz of sex trafficking, reports say
text:
(Gray News) — Former Republican congressman Matt Gaetz has been accused of sex trafficking two young women in a new lawsuit filed Thursday in Florida.
Gaetz resigned from Congress in November 2024. The allegations are the latest of a long-running sexual abuse scandal involving Gaetz.
In a statement to The Guardian, Gaetz denied the claims.
“I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” he wrote. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee Report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.”
The lawsuit alleges that Gaetz and two others “coordinated the recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts” from two young women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2. The lawsuit said they were recent high school graduates at the time of the alleged sex trafficking.
The alleged events happened “from 2017 through January 2019,” according to the lawsuit.
According to the Miami Herald, after the lawsuit was filed, Gaetz posted a photo on X in an effort to dox the Jane Does in the lawsuit. He posted a photo of three young women in bikinis, writing, “Jane Doe Strikes Again! Two adult women sued me today alleging they were sex trafficked to the Bahamas. I’m shocked nobody responded to their repeated cries for help, posted to Instagram.”
The Miami Herald said Gaetz admitted to a reporter that he was not sure if the women in the photo were any of the Jane Does in the lawsuit.

Drought Monitor shows no relief to extreme drought conditions
Despite Tuesday and Wednesday's rain, no improvements were made.
Drought Monitor shows no relief to extreme drought conditions
Despite Tuesday and Wednesday's rain, no improvements were made.
The Maine Drought Monitor remains mostly unchanged this week, with drought conditions continuing across much of the state. We did see an expansion of severe drought conditions in Piscataquis County, indicating that some areas continue to experience the effects of prolonged dryness.
Along the coast and midcoast, extreme drought conditions saw only a slight improvement. The area classified as experiencing extreme drought decreased from 4.84% last week to 4.64% this week. While this is a small step in the right direction, the overall change remains minimal, and extreme drought conditions persist in parts of the region.
Overall, the latest update suggests that drought conditions across Maine are largely holding steady, with limited improvement in some coastal areas and worsening conditions in parts of the state. Scattered, widespread showers will be needed over the next few months in helping to ease these dry conditions. The concern is that as we get colder temperatures and the ground freezes, it doesn't allow water to replenish the soil and we could see prolonged drought into spring 2027.

title: Community college students send radiation experiment to International Space Station
text:
Community college students send radiation experiment to International Space Station
The three students will compare radiation measurements from space with readings taken on Earth.
Community college students send radiation experiment to International Space Station
The three students will compare radiation measurements from space with readings taken on Earth.
Three community college students are getting the opportunity to take their classroom research into space after their experiment was selected for the Student Spaceflight Experiments Program.
See the report in the video above
From Omaha, Nebraska, the Metropolitan Community College students developed an experiment to measure neutron radiation during the sun’s current period of high activity. Their experiment is traveling to the International Space Station, where they hope to learn more about radiation levels in orbit.
The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched on Tuesday, causing a spectacular "space jellyfish" to be seen in the pre-dawn sky.
MCC student Nikoli Vanosdall said seeing the project launch was rewarding after the work that went into developing it.
"To see that come to life and not just be like, on paper or whatever, but to actually physically be sent abroad, is amazing," Vanosdall said.
The students plan to compare radiation readings collected in space with measurements taken on Earth. Eric Tomjack said he is interested in whether the data will reveal a noticeable difference between the two readings.
The experience also included a trip to Kennedy Space Center, where the students watched the rocket launch and toured NASA facilities.
The rocket lifted off around 5:30 a.m. Central Time on Tuesday and is expected to arrive at the space station Thursday. The experiment will remain aboard for several weeks before returning to Earth for analysis.

title: Can Maine use natural methods to stop shoreline erosion?
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND — On a mild afternoon, sailboats glided across Casco Bay while Southern Maine Community College students sat at picnic tables studying, knitting and talking politics. Just steps away, however, this beloved stretch of coastline is crumbling.
Back-to-back winter storms battered the Willard Beach area three years ago, eating away at fragile bluffs beneath a campus science building and city pump house and closing a popular shoreline walking path.
Now city, regional and state officials are coming together to try to protect the shoreline and infrastructure, using natural methods when they can and hoping to forestall rising seas and worsening storms for as long as they can.
The proposal to protect this small stretch of shoreline, which would involve the combination of riprap, vegetation and a relocated walking path, is one of three that the Greater Portland Council of Governments is using federal grants to help draft.
The plans for South Portland, Mitchell Field in Harpswell and the Yarmouth wastewater treatment plant are far from complete. Variations abound. Nothing is permitted. Nobody knows who might foot the bill.
“It’s clear that something has to be done,” said Sara Mills-Knapp, the sustainability director at Greater Portland Council of Governments and the leader of a nature-based shoreline erosion workshop at Willard Beach on Wednesday.
The Willard Beach workshop serves as a crucial test case for how vulnerable communities can adapt, if not turn back, rising waters without smothering their shorelines under a rigid granite seawall. Instead of concrete, think plants, coir logs and buried trees to rebuild the dune system.
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection now favors such methods during permitting, said Nathan Robbins, the department’s climate change specialist. The state is publishing a new reference guide to help promote nature-based erosion control this week, Robbins said.
Maine sea levels have been rising at a rate of about a half-foot a century. The pace has sped up as the world burns more fossil fuels, producing heat-trapping emissions that warm both air and sea.
Maine sea levels are projected to rise between 1.1 and 3.2 feet by 2050 and 3 and 9.3 feet by 2100, depending on how successful and quick we are at curbing global emissions rates, according to the scientists who advise the Maine Climate Council.
The $800,000 to $1 million Willard Beach proposal would give engineers room to replace the steep, failing bank with a gentler sloped bluff. Unlike hard seawalls that reflect wave energy downward and scoop out beach sand, the sloped bluff dissipates waves.
Heavy vegetative riprap — stone embedded with deep-rooted native plants — would bind the slope, paired with a newly engineered sand dune at the base. As much as they wanted to avoid stone, the consultants agreed Willard Beach requires a mixed approach.
“Plants alone just won’t cut it,” said Lisa Vickers, senior coastal specialist at GEI Consultants.
The proposal, which is about 30% complete, would require moving the walking path a couple hundred feet inland, behind the science building. But that extra space means it will not encroach upon the sandy beach below, a favorite among sunbathers and dog walkers.
Nature-based methods have sparked some tension. Hard seawalls offer immediate structural defense, while living shorelines require two to three growing seasons for native roots to bind sands. Marine contractors are used to dumping heavy granite boulders, not installing soil lifts.
And they could fail with the next winter storm, warned Pete Slovinsky, a marine geologist with the Maine Geological Survey. But so could traditional seawalls and even jettys, even with a high price tag and the harder-to-win permits required to build them, he said.
At the workshop Wednesday, Slovinsky told a crowd of about 30 people that ranged from local residents to engineers working on other erosion control projects that the proposed bluff project would help protect the city pump house for now, but the city should plan to eventually move it.
“The one thing I can guarantee you is that the sea will keep rising,” Slovinsky said. He pointed at the pump house behind him, which sits a couple dozen feet back from the 22-foot bluff. “That’s going to fail. Maybe not today, or next year, but sooner than you think.”
For state leaders, however, these pilot designs mark an essential turning point.
“Rocks don’t have roots,” Robbins said. “Plants have roots, deep roots that can help stabilize from the top of the bluff to the dunes to the beach. And rocks are expensive and require maintenance. Over time, plants will take over and do a lot of our work for us.”

title: The Latest: AP-NORC poll: Strong majority of voters believes Trump is failing at home and abroad
text:
A strong majority of voters believe that President Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad, and they want major change in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a new AP-NORC poll that raises serious warning signs for the Republican Party at a critical moment.
House Democrats are preparing an ambitious 100-day agenda focused on delivering their campaign promises — making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the Trump administration — if voters return them to majority control in the Nov. 3 elections. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become House speaker, said Democrats will be united “right out of the gate.”
And Trump’s new press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role. Katie Zacharia has long described herself as a lawyer, but so far, she and the White House have offered no evidence that she passed a bar exam.
The Latest:
Albania protests: Anti-government movement targets Kushner-linked project
Student-led demonstrators clashed Thursday with Albanian police in the capital Tirana for a third day running, joining a broader anti-government movement launched in opposition to a major development project promoted by Trump’s daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Youths protesting Albania’s long-serving Socialist government hurled rocks at a police cordon outside the Education Ministry, and riot police responded with tear gas and water cannons. Wednesday’s riots featured protesters attacking government buildings, banks and businesses, leaving 89 people injured including 61 police officers, according to the Health Ministry.
Student groups seeking education reforms have joined the so-called flamingo movement — named for the birds in a nature reserve where the luxury tourism development is planned — which is calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama over allegations of widespread corruption and in opposition to the Kushner venture.
The number of Americans filing for jobless aid remain at historically low levels below 200,000
U.S. applications for unemployment benefits inched up last week as layoffs remain historically low and most American workers enjoy job security.
Initial jobless claims for the week ending October 10 ticked up by 1,000 to 199,000 from the week before, the Labor Department said Thursday. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, rose by 250 to 198,500.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have remained at a historically low level below 220,000.
The total number of Americans filing for unemployment benefits for the previous week ending October 3 fell by 4,000 to 1.71 million, also a historically healthy figure.
Wholesale inflation jumped last month by most in four years as gas prices soared
Wholesale inflation rose more quickly than expected last month on a big jump in fuel costs, a sign that stubbornly rising prices remain an economic challenge for consumers and a political problem for Republicans as Americans begin to vote.
The Labor Department’s producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers — soared 6.3% in September from a year ago, up from 5.6% in August and the biggest increase since December 2022, the government said Thursday.
Thursday’s data amplifies the better-known consumer price index, released Wednesday, which also accelerated in September as gas prices jumped. A broad range of goods and services also got more expensive. Both inflation reports raise pressure on the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate. Inflation has now topped the central bank’s 2% target for five and a half years.
Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal probe, AP source says
Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork. Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17 years old, five years after she arrived with her family after obtaining asylum in the United States.
The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the Democrat for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
AP-NORC Poll: Trump’s numbers on the economy and costs remain weak
Voters are deeply frustrated with Trump’s leadership on the issues they say matter most, the new poll found.
The economy and the cost of living are high priorities for voters on both sides of the aisle. The survey found that the vast majority of Republican and Democratic voters say both issues are among the most important for the upcoming election.
But about 8 in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living and about three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy.
Even among Republican voters, only 44% approve of Trump’s performance on the cost of living, while 54% approve of his leadership on the economy. That’s a sharp contrast with other issues, like crime, where Republican approval is much higher.
AP-NORC Poll: The vast majority of voters want change
One thing is crystal clear on the eve of the 2026 midterms: Voters want change.
About half of voters say they want “substantial change” in how the country is run, according to the new AP-NORC poll. Roughly 3 in 10 want “complete and total upheaval.”
Democrats and independents are much likelier than Republicans to want a full overhaul of the country’s direction. But even Republican voters are still looking for something different. Slightly fewer than half, 45%, want substantial change, while 13% want upheaval.
“I’m kind of tired of sending people there, and nothing gets done,” Krista Kohles, a 70-year-old Republican told the AP. “Nothing’s changing.”
AP-NORC Poll: Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans
Democratic voters are more enthused than Republican voters about casting a ballot, according to a new AP-NORC poll conducted weeks before the midterm elections.
The survey finds that registered voters who identify as Democrats are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about voting, and more voters want Democrats to win control of Congress. The Democratic advantage is small in some cases, but taken together, the findings paint a challenging picture for Republicans.
Overall, about two-thirds of registered voters say it’s “extremely” important to vote in the upcoming election, while about 2 in 10 say it’s “very” important. But about three-quarters of Democratic voters say this is “extremely” important, compared to roughly 6 in 10 Republicans.
Alaska U.S. House candidates highlight contrasting priorities, style in debate
Clear contrasts were on display during a statewide debate between Alaska’s top two U.S. House candidates, starting with their attire.
Republican Rep. Nick Begich donned a suit and tie. Independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman, wore jeans, a dress shirt and zip-up vest and a cap with a fishing company logo.
Begich said he’s been effective. He expressed support for Trump, the president’s use of tariffs and the war in Iran. He said he wants to continue seeing expanded oil development in Alaska.
Hill asked Alaskans to look at their grocery bills and health care costs and ask if they’re better off than they were two years ago. He said many Alaskans are upset about U.S. involvement in “never-ending” wars.
The debate came a day after Trump held a rally in Wasilla in support of Begich and U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Alaska House candidate says that as an independent, his vote would be ‘greatest piece of leverage’
Alaska independent U.S. House candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich for Alaska’s only House seat. Hill faced criticism early on for declining to say which party he would caucus with were he to win next month’s election. He has been endorsed by the state Democratic Party.
During a debate Wednesday, Hill said he’d like to caucus with people who are “tired of this party-line partisanship” and who would support addressing issues like health care costs and pushing back against an overreaching executive branch.
Begich, an ally of Trump, said Hill is “too progressive” for Alaska and that it’s clear who he’d caucus with. Hill, meanwhile, accused Begich of being a rubber stamp for Trump.
Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia faces scrutiny over claims she’s a lawyer
The new White House press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration.
Katie Zacharia has long described herself as a lawyer as she has worked to establish herself as a commentator for conservative outlets like Fox News and Newsmax. But so far, she and the White House have offered no evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.
The questions add to the confusion surrounding Trump’s decision to hire Zacharia, who had worked for his social media company for only a few months when he announced her appointment and whose debut at the podium on Tuesday has been widely panned.
Afterward, the president was asked by reporters where Zacharia had passed the bar exam, following a report by the independent outlet Popular Information that she did not appear to be licensed in any state.
House Democrats plan a first 100-days agenda if they sweep to power in midterm elections
House Democrats are preparing an ambitious 100-days agenda focused on delivering their campaign promises — making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the Trump administration — if the party seizes majority control in next month’s elections.
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker if the party wins power, said the Democrats will be united “right out of the gate” on reinstating Affordable Care Act tax breaks, reversing Republican Medicaid cuts, holding votes against the Iran war and undoing President Donald Trump’s tariff regime.
They expect to launch the agenda in the first 100 hours, once the new Congress is seated in January.
“Fighting for an affordable America — that’s what unites Democrats all across the country,” Jeffries said recently at the party campaign headquarters in Washington.
“That’s our commitment to the American people, because the cost of living is way too high and far too many people who are working hard, playing by the rules, can’t thrive and can barely survive — and are drowning — in the Trump economy.”

title: Accrediting body decision won’t affect existing UMPI YourPace programs
text:
Accreditors have temporarily limited the University of Maine at Presque Isle’s ability to offer new competency-based educational programs, but that won’t affect existing offerings, University of Maine System officials said.
The system previously had permission to bring new programs online without prior approval by the New England Commission of Higher Education.
Now, following an investigation sparked by a Washington Post article that suggested YourPace students were obtaining degrees in weeks rather than years, the commission temporarily suspended that permission.
“This is really only about potential future expansion, which we do not have plans to do,” Sam Warren, the University of Maine System’s chief external and governmental affairs officer, said Thursday. “It only changes the process between now and April, so it functionally does not change anything for us.”
According to the commission’s Oct. 7 decision letter to Chancellor Dannel Malloy, obtained by the Bangor Daily News on Thursday, the commission suspended the university’s general approval to offer competency-based education programs at University of Maine at Presque Isle.
“General approval,” a term that may be misleading to non-academics, allows institutions to add new programs and locations without getting additional approval from the commission, but it does not mean the program has been suspended, according to the commission.
“Should [the university] plan to offer new competency-based education programs at any of its campuses, it needs to submit a report to the commission, in keeping with the Policy on Substantive Change,” the letter stated.
As part of the routine April investigation, the commission asked the University of Maine System questions about the YourPace program, to which the system supplied a 20-page response for review, commission President Larry Schall previously told the BDN.
“We have the ability to take notice of things in the press and then the commission needs to decide if it is worthy of the commission looking into it further,” Schall said at the time. “In this case, they thought it was.”
As part of that process, the commission reviewed and accepted the university’s extensive response at its late September meeting, university officials said.
Many working adults enter YourPace with 15 or more years of professional experience and transfer an average of at least 90 college credits — equivalent to three years of full-time study — allowing them to complete the remaining requirements for a four-year degree typically in a year or less, according to some of the data the University of Maine System supplied to the commission.
Most YourPace undergraduate students, on average, earn 18 credit hours a semester, consistent with their traditional peers, according to a system release.
Despite the Post’s reporting calling the program’s quality into question, UMPI President Ray Rice and Warren said YourPace competency-based courses are fully accredited and follow the same learning outcomes and assessment standards as in-person courses.
The fact that traditional full-time faculty design, teach and test the students makes a public university’s competency-based program unique, Rice said in a September interview.
“There’s no world in which I can view this as a negative because it is actually doing what it was intended to do,” he said. “This incredible growth is a reflection of that success.”
The speed at which students complete their degrees in competency-based education varies because of their experience, Rice said. Someone with 20 years professional work experience will complete the work much faster than an 18-year-old just starting out.
“For nearly a decade, YourPace has reopened a door to higher education that many working adults thought was closed to them,” Malloy said in a statement. “We are incredibly proud of the success of YourPace and the thousands of adult learners it serves, many of whom are earning life-changing credentials while balancing the demands of work and family.”
Malloy said the system welcomes the commission’s review and is committed to “demonstrating that the innovation and accessibility that make YourPace so impactful are matched by the academic quality and rigor our students, employers and accreditors expect.”
As part of its review, the commission said it was concerned about the “dramatic growth” of YourPace in part due to the speed at which students completed degrees.
Before its planned spring 2027 visit, the commission has asked the university system to prepare a report detailing such items as actual student enrollment, the ratio of faculty to students in each competency-based education program, an analysis of transfer credits, and procedures to verify that the student who registers in a competency-based course is the same student who participates in and completes the program.
This commission decision doesn’t affect any programs currently being offered or those that have recently been approved, including the master’s in healthcare administration approved by the Board of Trustees in September, Warren said.
“The only thing that has actually changed is that they have asked us to come to their April commission meeting to discuss the findings of the site visit,” she said.

title: Watch: Fryeburg soccer is the Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Fryeburg Academy soccer
Coach Bob Hodgman-Burns saw signs during a preseason game against Laconia, New Hampshire, that this could be a successful season for the Fryeburg Academy boys soccer team.
“My local players are a year more experienced, and I don’t want to say they suffered through last year, but they had a tough year last year,” Hodgman-Burns said. “I think they learned a lot. So after that first week, it was all coming together.”
With an 8-2-1 record, Fryeburg ranked second in the Class B South Heal point standings heading into Wednesday’s game against Traip Academy. In 2025, the Raiders finished 3-8-3.
Fourth-year player and team captain Abram Grace said the Raiders took a little time to find their footing before settling into the grind of the Western Maine Conference schedule. They had a loss and a tie in their first five games but then won five of their next six.
“Our season started, obviously, not how we’re doing now,” Grace said. “We were struggling with communication, and our passes were a little bit sloppy at times, but throughout the season, we’ve been working hard and getting quite a few wins that we didn’t really expect.”
That includes a 1-0 win over defending Class B champion Yarmouth on Sept. 17 and a 2-1 victory over perennial power Cape Elizabeth on Sept. 22. It’s the first time since 2011 that Fryeburg, ranked 10th in the Varsity Maine poll, has beaten both of those schools in the same season.
Last week, the Raiders offense exploded in a 7-0 win over Lake Region and a 9-1 victory over Sacopee Valley.
The Raiders have scored 39 goals, and nine players have contributed to that total.
“I think that in the games that we come out strong and really try to push from the start and don’t give (opponents) any time, don’t let the team kind of play with the ball, we’re doing better,” Grace said. “So I think for the rest of the season, we’re being aggressive and going at every team we play, because we’re not going to overlook any team.”

title: Father, child found dead following Amber Alert for the 4-year-old boy
text:
GAINESVILLE, Texas (KXII/Gray News) — A father and 4-year-old child were found dead in Texas on Wednesday amid a search connected to an Amber Alert issued out of Oklahoma.
The Gainesville Police Department said that early Wednesday morning, they got in contact with a relative of Caleb Furley, 25, and missing 4-year-old Andres Furley, who were the subjects of an Amber Alert out of Norman, Oklahoma.
The relative told officers that the two went missing after last being seen at an area business early Monday evening.
A police investigator went to the business when it opened and found surveillance video from Monday that appeared to show the two walking away from the area.
Authorities said they searched the surrounding area for the father and son, which led to the discovery of their bodies.
Gainesville Police Chief Kevin Phillips said their investigation began on Monday after someone reported a suspicious interaction involving a father and son.
“The contact just appeared to be suspicious. So they notified the police department and we responded,” Phillips said.
Officers searched at the time but did not find anyone.
“The officers searched the area extensively, and we also used a drone to search the area, but we weren’t able to locate anyone,” Phillips said.
Police said they also looked for a vehicle possibly associated with the two but were unable to locate it during that initial search.
Norman police confirmed the bodies found were those of 4-year-old Andres and Furley.
Police in Oklahoma said they are working with Texas authorities regarding the case.
“We do extend our deepest condolences to the persons who are impacted,” Phillips added.
