title: Maine's CD2 candidates face off in last debate before election
text:
Maine's CD2 candidates Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage face off in last debate before election
Thursday's debate hosted by WMTW media partners WABI and WAGM
Maine's CD2 candidates Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage face off in last debate before election
Thursday's debate hosted by WMTW media partners WABI and WAGM
State Auditor Matt Dunlap (D) and former Gov. Paul LePage (R), the candidates for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, debated for the second and final time ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
Thursday's hourlong debate was hosted by WMTW media partners WABI and WAGM from WABI's studio in Bangor. You can watch the full debate in the YouTube video embedded below.
This debate was held two weeks after Dunlap and LePage squared off in a debate hosted by Maine's Total Coverage. Throughout our debate, LePage took swings at Dunlap as the candidates answered questions on topics including the trade war with Canada, immigration enforcement and Social Security. Both candidates found common ground on the importance of Maine's town clerks in ensuring the state's elections run smoothly. They also agreed that there does not need to be an age limit to serve in Congress.
You can watch the entire Maine's Total Coverage debate in the video player embedded below, or on the WMTW-TV YouTube channel.
More about the candidates
LePage was the only Republican candidate to qualify for the primary ballot. He served as the mayor of Waterville (2004-11) before serving two terms as Maine governor (2011-2019). LePage has often aligned himself with President Donald Trump, who has won Maine's 2nd Congressional District in each of the last three presidential elections. LePage, however, has different opinions on some of the president's policies, including tariffs and immigration. Other priorities for LePage include securing the border and lowering costs for Americans, and he is calling on Trump and Gov. Janet Mills to suspend all taxes on fuel.
Dunlap won a four-way race in the Democratic primary following a ranked-choice voting tabulation. He formerly served in the Maine House of Representatives (1996-2005) and had two stints as Maine's secretary of state (2005-11, 2013-21). Dunlap has said that universal healthcare is one of his top priorities and he blames Trump for the affordability challenges many people are facing, citing the war with Iran. Dunlap's other priorities include labor issues and a woman's right to choose when it comes to abortion.
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat, announced in November 2025 that he will not seek reelection in the 2nd Congressional District.

title: Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy chief endorses Susan Collins in U.S. Senate race
text:
MAINE (WABI) - The Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy Tribe announced their endorsement of Sen. Susan Collins for her re-election.
In their letter, the tribe cited Collins’ recent work on a new wastewater treatment plant, securing $5 million of federal funding for the project.
“I am honored to have the endorsement of the Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy Tribe,” Collins said. “I look forward to our continued work together to ensure Maine’s tribes have the resources they need to strengthen their communities, protect their residents, and build a stronger future.”
Collins will face Democratic nominee Troy Jackson in the general election on Nov. 3.

title: Maine's final Senate debate with Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The fourth and final debate in the Maine U.S. Senate race was a spirited affair that plowed some new ground, with Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican Susan Collins weighing in on gun control and the possible reform of the U.S. Supreme Court.
Thursday’s debate at the Gracie Theater at Husson University in Bangor was the only one to have a live audience, invited by the campaigns. It allowed for crowd reactions — and at one point an interruption by a protester — leading to a memorable exchange.
Jackson, a 58-year-old former logger, continued to tie Collins to President Donald Trump, whose actions and policies Jackson argued are driving up the prices of consumer goods, energy and fuel.
Collins, meanwhile, continued to focus on her seniority, which she says has brought $1.5 billion in federal earmarks to Maine in recent years. The 73-year-old has also sought to distance herself from Trump and shift blame onto Jackson for high energy prices, citing his votes in support of solar energy as Maine Senate president.
Here are the major takeaways from the final debate before the Nov. 3 election. It was conducted in partnership with Maine Public, the Portland Press Herald and NEWSCENTER Maine.
1. Protester interrupts, Jackson snaps
About 15 minutes into the debate, someone in the crowd stood up and began shouting about data centers. The moderator took a brief pause as security removed the young man, who appeared to be wearing a press badge.
“That’s obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Collins quipped.
Jackson shot back.
“Oh shut up,” Jackson said. “I don’t even know that kid.”
Event organizers said the individual was not on the pre-registered media list, but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in.
In an email Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send a reporter to the debate, and that the credential must have been fabricated.
2. Jackson stumbles on campaign finance
Collins and Jackson each had the opportunity to ask each other a question. And Collins appeared to get the best of both exchanges.
Collins called out Jackson for vowing not to take money from billionaires and corporate PACs. But Collins noted that Jackson’s campaign has been running joint ads with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which she said received money from 28 billionaires and 190 corporate PACs.
Jackson appeared to have been caught off guard, at first confusing the joint ads, which contain his endorsement, with independent super PACs, which he cannot legally coordinate with.
Jackson, who earlier in the day announced he’d give away $15,000 in donations from oil and pharmaceutical lobbyists, also acknowledged that billionaires are supporting his campaign — a statement that drew a reaction from the audience.
“As far as billionaires that I might have on my campaign, that is accurate, but I haven’t made any deals like Sen. Collins has with those billionaires,” he said. “I don’t owe (them) my votes. I’m going to tax those billionaires when I get the U.S. Senate.”
During his turn, Jackson brought up his working class roots and asked Collins if she looks down at him or all working people. Collins talked about how she started working in potato fields in Aroostook County at the age of 10.
“I do not look down on you or on anyone,” Collins said. “I have enormous respect for all the people of Maine.”
3. Supreme Court reform
The two candidates sparred over whether the U.S. Supreme Court needs reforming.
The Democrat said he supports term limits and enforceable ethics standards and would be open to adding members to the court, which he said is currently working for Trump and “the billionaire class.”
“It’s just gross the way that this has ended up,” Jackson said. “And we have to do something meaningful to actually give people’s confidence back.”
Collins disagreed. She said increasing the number of justices would go “completely against the vision of those who wrote the Constitution.” She stuck to her position when a moderator noted that the current number of nine justices was not in the Constitution.
“It’s inconsistent with the whole idea of the Supreme Court being insulated from politics,” Collins said. “That would make it a totally political body.”
Jackson, however, would get the last word.
“We have the best court that money can buy right now,” he said.
4. Through the looking glass on guns
A question about assault weapons produced some surprising answers.
Collins noted that she was a supporter of the original ban on assault weapons passed by Congress in the 90s. She accused Democrats of allowing that ban to expire because they wanted to expand it. And she said she voted to ban bump stocks, which increase the rate of fire in a weapon.
She said she supports “reasonable limits” on magazine capacity and would be open to increasing the age to legally obtain an assault weapon.
Jackson seemed more pro-gun by comparison.
“I’m not in favor of increasing the age,” he said. “It actually comes down to the person. I mean, we do have a culture here in Maine of people being able to buy guns.”
Jackson said he would not oppose an assault weapons ban, but he would oppose taking weapons away from people who already have them.
“I don’t see a good reason for assault weapons,” he said. “You can’t use them for hunting or anything like that. And so I would not be opposed to banning them.”

title: Wiscasset Developers Bring Proposal to Residents at Informational Meeting
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Developers are proposing a 170-unit apartment complex at 257 Bath Road in Wiscasset across from the intersection of Birch Point Road.
Patrick Boothe, a partner and principal architect at Portland-based architecture design and construction firm Woodhull, described the structure as holding a possible 170 units with multiple road-facing buildings and a four-story structure in the back. Designs display a total of five structures and 172 units.
The developers met residents at an informational meeting on Oct. 7. Wiscasset Economic Development Director Aaron Chrostowsky said the team requested the meeting because the project is unique in Wiscasset.
According to Chrostowsky, the proposed development aligns with the town’s comprehensive plan and is in a place with access to sewer and water infrastructure.
“This is an opportunity to bring new residents and families to the community, hopefully for our schools,” Chrostowsky said. “This is an opportunity to help support major employers like Bath Iron Works in the region and our local businesses attract and retain employees. This is an opportunity to increase the tax base.”
Boothe said at this point nothing is “set in stone” or submitted for approval from the town. Recent legislation altering land use ordinances including L.D. 1829, “An Act to Build Housing for Maine Families and Attract Workers to Maine Businesses by Amending the Laws Governing Municipal Land Use Decisions” signed by Gov. Janet Mills on June 20, 2025, impacts their ability to build the complex, he said.
Code Enforcement Officer George Chase said in an interview that L.D. 2003, “An Act to Implement the Recommendations of the Commission to Increase Housing Opportunities in Maine by Studying Zoning and Land Use Restrictions,” signed by Mills in 2022, is also causing a need for a revision of ordinances.
All towns are required to adjust ordinances to align with the state law. In Wiscasset, revised ordinances are reviewed by the Wiscasset Planning Board. Chase said in an interview the legislation has to be adopted by July.
Changes caused by the legislation will create the ability for denser housing, Chase said. One change happening in Wiscasset will be the expansion of the Village I district to include more of U.S. Route 1, meaning more businesses can open on the road.
The ordinance review committee examined ways to “mitigate the dramatic impact and maintain the integrity of the districts” by adding road frontage requirements and slight increases in setback requirements to drafted ordinance changes, Chase said.
Boothe said new housing is necessary.
“We in the United States haven’t built enough housing since the recession in 2008,” Boothe said. “We’ve been under built for two decades and we’re really hitting the ramification of that through our crisis of affordable housing.”
Construction is expensive and scaling the project up will lower the cost per unit, Boothe said.
“It’s beneficial to have the opportunity to build a four-story building in the back just to help offset the infrastructure cost of the rows, the parking, the sewer connections, and all these other things so that it can be spread out over the course of more units,” Boothe said.
Seth Kimball, a principal and partner at Portland landscape architecture firm Aceto. During a site walk, Kimball said the team found the area has wetlands that are connected to tributaries. To avoid building on top of them, he said the team is building the structures closer to the road.
Kimball said the site will have a public trail system and commercial space.
Wiscasset resident David Flynn asked the designers if they had examined any traffic studies of the corridor.
“Adding 170 units on this proposed spot is going to bottleneck traffic during the summer months even more, which then dumps the traffic onto the Old Bath Road, which is currently where my wife and I live, and it’s going to turn it into a super highway,” David Flynn said. “Does Wiscasset really need 170 more units for living space when there’s no work in this area?”
As the project continues, Boothe said the team will look at traffic studies.
Woodhull Business Development Manager Andrew Sturgeon represented the landowners. Offsite improvements such as an additional traffic lane are possible to avoid “making a problem a bigger problem,” Sturgeon said.
Wiscasset resident Mary Finn said she appreciates the design.
“I think it’s aesthetically really pleasing,” Finn said. “I love the design and how you worked with the land to kind of preserve most of the wetlands that are there.”
Jean Flynn, of Wiscasset, said she does not think 172 parking spots will be enough for the total amount of units.
The amount of parking is not fully determined, Boothe said. The trailhead will include its own parking lot. However, parking spots come at a cost, he said.
“We can’t just provide over parking,” Boothe said. “It would mean that there’s less area to build housing and there’s more disruption to natural resources, it’s more costly per unit.”
Wiscasset Select Board member Cassaundra Rose said she appreciates the attention to detail the firm provided in walkability to downtown, and the preservation of the wetlands.
“This does meet a real need or more affordable and smaller housing, and meeting that need, where a lot of folks looking for entry-level housing, other folks just cannot find it, which I hear consistently,” Rose said.
In response to a question from Rose, Boothe said the trail would be accessible to all interested persons and said amenities are a priority of the firm.
Wiscasset resident Tara Servilio asked if the firm could provide examples of previous housing projects. She added she does not think the apartment design matches the town’s aesthetic.
“It’s not just superficial, but I am saying if you could show us examples of towns with the population size, the infrastructure, same as here, where this was built, and not just like it provided housing for these many people,” Servilio said. “How did it make the community better? How did it fit into the holistic picture of the community?”
Kimball discussed a project the firm completed replacing the Scarborough Downs racetrack with a mixed-use town center and neighborhood.
“We think that’s the sort of thing that allows for a piece of land that doesn’t do anything for the community, doesn’t produce tax revenue, but it can actually do something really special for the community,” Kimball said.
Wiscasset Superintendent of Schools Kimberly Andersson said she welcomes the development.
“I hear from employees and families all the time that housing is a real challenge,” Andersson said.
Brie DiPerri, of Wiscasset, said she recognizes the need for housing but thinks the development “creates an impression that’s not really in keeping with this historic village.”
“It seems very close to the road, and I wouldn’t agree that I like the design,” DiPerri said. “I don’t think it really fits in with our vernacular. And the fact that there’s a four story apartment building is concerning to me since that seems to be not in keeping anything in the region.”
DiPerri said she would prefer the building not be placed within a driver’s view entering Wiscasset.
Boothe said new development can be jarring but is done for “a good reason.” Kimball added the location was so people could walk into town.
“There’s a certain vernacular that you’re speaking of, and it’s a nostalgia we all have,” Kimball said. “I appreciate it. But towns grow, we evolve, and we’re thinking about the next generation in proximity, on the U.S. Route 1 corridor.”
The developers are currently in a “holding pattern” as they discuss next steps and wait for the ordinance changes to allow for the development, Sturgeon said in an interview.
Chrotowsky said Bath Road is the “ideal” location for this development, as it is close to Wiscasset’s infrastructure and transport systems. People may not necessarily work in Wiscasset but could commute to Brunswick, Bath, or other towns, he said.
“This is really good potential for a positive effect,” Chrotowsky said. “It also achieves some of our goals here, a lot of people want affordable houses.”
For more information, go to wiscasset.gov, call 882-8200, or email [email protected].

title: Aging Untold: Decoding Medicare Advantage
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down Medicare Advantage to help you navigate coverage options, costs and hidden limits.
We also explore the complex world of autoimmune conditions, what happens when the immune system turns on itself and tips for managing daily life.
Finally, we highlight a daily check-in call program giving older adults living alone a vital safety net and peace of mind.
It can feel overwhelming to make the choice between Medicare Advantage, which is also known as Medicare Part C, and traditional Medicare.
As you weigh your decision, the Aging Untold experts say to start with your budget and your health history.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said family health history matters just as much as the monthly premium.
Patients should also confirm whether their own doctors accept the plan — and that those doctors have stayed in the plan’s network, O’Rourke said.
Diagnosing an older adult with an autoimmune condition like type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus can be especially tricky because the immune system naturally changes with age.
But an early diagnosis can make a real difference in managing symptoms long-term.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said inflammation is usually the driver.
“Key is, you have to find out what drove it in the first place. Where is the inflammation coming from that’s allowed these other organs to get hit? It’s much more complex than people realize,” Rogers said.
There is currently no cure for lupus, but a treatment that was developed to fight cancer is now being used in a clinical trial to treat the autoimmune disease that affects an estimated 1.5 million Americans.
Rachel Dib, a military wife and mother of three in North Carolina, was diagnosed with lupus when she was a college sophomore.
After nearly 20 years of suffering, she enrolled in a CAR T-cell therapy clinical trial at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine.
Older adults who live alone in Phoenix are receiving daily phone calls to check on them and provide help in case of an emergency.
The program, called R.U. OK ,stands for Are You OK?
Seniors receive computerized calls instructing them to push one number to let the system know they are OK or another to alert it that they need help.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal probe, AP source says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Washington D.C. U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also probing issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the Democrat for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

title: Bear wanders into hospital, stops to eat Halloween candy
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - A bear walked into a hospital early Monday and treated itself to Halloween candy.
A black bear roamed the hallway at a hospital on Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson around 2 a.m., stopping only when it found a bucket of donated Halloween candy.
“This is like being in a tunnel with a bear,” said Sherri Warnke, who had been at the hospital helping her mother settle in after being transferred.
Warnke, who does not work at the hospital, said she was walking toward the exit through the emergency department when the bear stepped out of a side hallway ahead of her. She said the bear was about 30 feet away.
“And if I was like 15 seconds faster, we would have ran into each other,” she said.
The doors along the hallway she was in open only with a badge.
“I don’t have a badge,” Warnke said. “I can’t get through any doors. They’re all locked.”
The closest way for her to get out was a door about 60 yards behind her. So she began backing away, slowly and quietly, betting the bear had not spotted her in the dim hallway.
The bear suddenly stopped and started digging in something.
“I got a whiff of what I thought initially was trash,” Warnke said.
It was not trash. Doctors later told her the bear had found a Halloween candy donation bucket.
Soon after, an announcement over the intercom warned that a bear was in the building. Shortly after the announcement, several doctors working in the building came down the hallway to take a picture of the bear.
“They wanted pictures,” Warnke said. “But approaching a bear that’s having this dessert is not my first option.”
Warnke started taking video and pictures. In one of her videos, she said, she can be heard calling out, “Exit plan, guys, because the bear thinks you’re going to steal his food.”
Warnke said she was worried that there would be a lag between one of the doctors swiping their badge and a door unlocking.
“And that delay can be a death sentence to you if a bear is really mad at you,” she said.
The candy, however, bought everyone time.
“I was like, candy, donation, he’s going to be there for a while, he’s not going to give up that candy, that’s for sure,” Warnke said.
Staff let her out through a back way, and she did not see how the bear left the building.
When Warnke returned the next day, she said a door leading into the main part of the hospital was closed, and the staffer at the emergency department front desk told her it had been shut because of the bear. Staff said the bear left the same way it came in.
The staffer also showed her a photo of the bear standing at the same front counter where she stood. Staff joked that the bear had been checking in.
“I said, ‘Well, actually, I think he’s checking out now,’” Warnke said.
Warnke said she is not easily rattled by wildlife.
“I was born and raised in Alaska,” she said. “So I’m in the mountains all the time, and I’m a mountain runner.”
Warnke said it was not her first encounter with a bear, but she was surprised to see one in the hospital.
“And this is not a small bear,” she said. “He was a pretty big black bear.”
With hibernation approaching, the bear looked well fed already.
“And he was fat and ready for hibernation,” Warnke said. “I was like, ‘Well, did you eat something before you came for dessert?’”
Warnke told a friend the bear had simply been out trick-or-treating, “and good thing he chose the treat and not for me to do a trick.”

title: Troy Jackson got $15k from big oil, pharma lobbyists. He’s giving it to charity.
text:
Troy Jackson is donating about $15,000 in political contributions from oil and pharmaceutical lobbyists, his campaign said on Thursday.
Jackson, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, said in a news release that he will donate $5,000 each to Keep ME Warm/Project Heat and the Good Shepherd Food Bank, and $2,500 each to Maine Needs and the Augusta Food Bank.
The lobbyists’ donations are a small fraction of the $20.4 million his campaign says it raised since Jackson secured the nomination on July 25. In giving the donations to charity, Jackson said he’s keeping the”Dirigo Pledge” he made during the abbreviated Democratic primary to replace Graham Platner in July.
“I said I wouldn’t take money from Big Oil or Big Pharma lobbyists, and I meant it,” Jackson said in a written statement. “That money is better spent helping Mainers heat their homes, put food on the table, afford the things they need, and get through a tough winter.”
Jackson also pledged, among other things, to refuse donations from corporate PACs and the pro-Israel AIPAC; to fully disclose his campaign finances; to advocate for a Constitutional amendment to get big money out of politics; and to advocate for a ban on congressional stock trading.
The announcement came hours before his fourth and final debate with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, 73, who has called out the 58-year-old former logger for accepting corporate contributions as state Senate president.
And it comes as polls show that inflation and high gas prices are among the top issues on voters’ minds.
The deadline for campaign finance reports to be filed is midnight Thursday. Jackson has yet to release his full campaign finance report, despite saying in a televised debate that he would release it on Wednesday morning.
Collins, meanwhile, released hers Thursday afternoon, reporting a total of $3.9 million from July 1 through Sept. 30. Her total for the campaign is now nearly $17.7 million. She reported $5.4 million in cash for the final stretch of the campaign.
Despite Jackson’s fundraising, Republicans have a clear money advantage in the Maine’s closely watched race.
So far, Republican-aligned groups have spent or reserved $151.5 million on ads, compared to $110.7 million by Democrat-aligned groups, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

title: Breaching whale attempts to jump on fishermen’s boat deck
text:
(CNN) - A pair of fishermen witnessed a breaching whale try to jump onto their boat.
The massive mammal was caught on camera breaching and then bursting through the rear door of a boat.
It happened after the pair, who was fishing off the coast of Long Island, spotted the whale and started recording.
In the surreal moment, the whale burst onto the boat’s deck, bringing with it a frenzy of flipping and flopping fish.
The fishermen said that in more than a decade of fishing together, they’ve never seen anything that big or close.

title: Pennsylvania man who killed family had controlled their movements and finances: police
text:
A Pennsylvania man who fatally shot eight others, including seven family members, before killing himself had exercised strict control over his relatives, including their finances and interactions with others, police said Thursday.
Investigators still don’t know why family patriarch Matthew Stone Sr. gunned down his wife, their three children, two grandchildren and two women who had rushed to the home and were shot outside, Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said at a news conference.
Lorah painted a picture of a family living in a home in isolated, filthy conditions. He said the authoritarian behavior of Stone, 45, started after his wife became pregnant with their first child more than two decades ago.
The adult victims of the Oct. 9 shooting previously were identified as Stone’s wife, Michelle Stone, 44; their daughter, Angelina Stone, 24, who was due to give birth Monday, three days after the shooting; sons Jonathan Stone, 19, and Matthew Stone Jr., 21; and two women who lived at other addresses: Lora Roberts, 37, and Twila Tanner, 51. Roberts was Michelle Stone’s sister.
A 5-year-old boy and a 22-month-old girl who were identified by relatives as Angelina Stone’s children also were killed. State law prevented authorities from releasing their names.
Family members told detectives that the elder Stone “restricted when family members could leave the residence or spend time with relatives,” Lorah said. In addition, Michelle Stone “stopped maintaining contact with friends.”
The elder Stone also kept a tight grip over the family’s money, including supplemental government income received for one of the grandchildren, Lorah said.
In 2019, Stone was arrested and charged with threatening his wife with the same .40-caliber handgun that he used in the Oct. 9 shootings. However, at a preliminary hearing, Michelle Stone “changed her original statement and those charges were withdrawn,” Lorah said.
A year ago, daughter Angelina filed a petition to change her last name, citing concerns about the elder Stone’s “declining mental health,” according to Lorah. She had planned to pursue a career in medicine and didn’t want her last name associated with her father. But that application was closed in April 2026.
Angelina Stone posted ultrasound photos of her unborn child on social media on Sept. 25. Lorah said she had been sending messages to others indicating she was going to leave the home after giving birth. She also said her father had been physically abusive toward her brothers. After the shootings, detectives found bags and boxes that were packed in Angelina Stone’s bedroom.
Detectives described conditions in the home as “extremely filthy.” A shower, toilet and kitchen sink didn’t appear to be working, and there were numerous soda bottles filled with urine throughout the house. Water service remained active but had an outstanding balance of $1,900, the chief said.
During their search, detectives also found drug paraphernalia, “but we cannot establish what role, if any, mental health or substance use played in the shooting,” Lorah said.
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before Roberts and Tanner arrived and began pounding on the door. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside. Tanner was the only nonrelative killed, Lorah said.
As circumstances of the family’s living conditions and history came to light, Mayor Daria Devlin said some difficult questions, too, have surfaced.
“Were there opportunities to recognize that this family was struggling?” Devlin said. “Were there places where our systems could have responded differently? And how do we make sure that families in this community who are suffering and struggling like this don’t fall through the cracks?
“We cannot assume that any one intervention could have prevented what happened on Friday. But that can’t stop us from examining where each one of us can do better.”

title: High schools Thursday: Leavitt football turns back Nokomis
text:
Landon Marquis rushed for two touchdowns and passed for two more, and Leavitt remained unbeaten Thursday night by defeating Nokomis 36-12 in a Class C football game in Turner.
The Hornets (7-0) capitalized on a Nokomis fumble to open the scoring in the first quarter, as Landon Reny tip-toed his way down the sideline for a 57-yard touchdown run.
Marquis scored on a 2-yard run in the second quarter, and Darren Flagg turned a screen pass into a 68-yard touchdown that made it 22-0 at halftime.
Nokomis (2-5) threw a scare into the Hornets with two quick touchdowns in the third quarter. First, Maxx Demchak ripped the ball away from a Leavitt defender to catch a 16-yard touchdown pass from Colt Robinson. The Warriors then recovered an onside kick, and Stephone Ross cut the deficit to 22-12 with a 40-yard run.
Leavitt quickly regained control, however, as Marquis capped a drive with a 16-yard run early in the fourth. Cooper Morin caught a 4-yard pass for the final touchdown.
WINTHROP 29, MOUNTAIN VALLEY 7: The Ramblers (6-1) finally pulled away in the second half to earn a Class D South victory over the Falcons (1-6) at Chet Bulger Field in Rumford.
Through the first two-and-a-half quarters, Mountain Valley’s defense rarely allowed the Ramblers extra yards after contact. Winthrop started to break away midway through the third quarter, however, scoring on a 13-yard pass from Porter Lavigne to Clyde Moody for a 15-7 lead.
In the final minute of the third, Tristyan Ortiz added a 28-yard touchdown run. Winthrop’s last touchdown as a 2-yard run by Carter Rand in the fourth, set up a by a 26-yard Moody reception.
Mountain Valley opened the game with an 89-yard kickoff return for a score by Cole Curtis, who made many of the game’s biggest plays. He intercepted two passes, and had a couple of long runs and nice returns.
The Falcons forced a turnover on downs and two punts on Winthrop’s first three drives. On the fourth possession, Rand scored on a 21-yard run, but a missed kick kept Mountain Valley in the lead, 7-6.
Interceptions by Curtis ended the next two Winthrop drives, but in between those, a safety put the Ramblers ahead 8-7. Falcons quarterback Jimmy Arsenault was called for intentional grounding in the end zone.
Winthrop’s defense was stout throughout. Mason Fish had an interception and Canyon Peaslee recovered fumble. For Mountain Valley, Josh Pollis deflected a punt.
GIRLS SOCCER
LEAVITT 1, WINSLOW 1: Reese Bilodeau scored off a corner kick with one second left in regulation, and Leavitt (5-6-2) escaped with a tie against Winslow (8-4-1) in Turner.
Winslow took the lead midway through the second half on a goal by Mirra Meak.
SPRUCE MOUNTAIN 4, TELSTAR 1: Lexi Hebert notched two goals in the first half to lead the Phoenix (7-3-2) past the Rebels (3-8) in Jay.
Natasha McDonald and Shaylin Hoyt also scored, Ashley Nelson set up two goals and Aubrey Mitchell had one assist. Phoenix keeper Jayda McDonald made four saves.
Mya Buck stopped 10 shots for Telstar.
HALL-DALE 8, WINTHROP 0: Clare Sturtevant’s two goals paced the Bulldogs (9-2-2) to their fifth consecutive victory, a shutout win over the Ramblers (4-9) in Farmingdale.
Maya Hammonds contributed a goal and two assists for Hall-Dale, and Robin Asch had one goal and one assist. Lexi Tinkham, Audra Schaab, Megan Inch and Sandra Corpion also scored, while Ella Lawrence, Isabel Tinkham, Vera Krajewski and Fiona Breslin each recorded an assist.
Goalie Genevieve Ciccarelli made three saves for the Bulldogs, who are vying four the second seed in Class C South.
Winthrop’s Kylee Savage stopped 21 shots. The Ramblers are trying to maintain their hold on C South’s eighth and final postseason berth.
GRAY-NEW GLOUCESTER 3, WAYNFLETE 2: The Patriots (4-10) scored twice in the second half to beat the Flyers (4-7-1) in Gray.
Ida Waterman tallied two goals and an assist, Bri Burbank added a goal, and Ainsley Harris had an assist for Gray-New Gloucester. Patriots keeper Mallory Hardiman made five saves.
Quinn Culley and Amara Redon scored for Waynflete. Rachel Yordon made three stops.
CAPE ELIZABETH 3, GREELY 2: Addie Miller scored two goals, Alexa Mallory added a goal and an assist, and the Capers (11-1-1) held off the Rangers (6-4-2) in Cape Elizabeth.
Miller scored in each half before Mallory broke a 2-2 tie a little over 14 minutes into the second half.
Greely rallied to tie twice, on goals by Victoria Zandan in the first half and Lydia Berthiaume in the second.
Kelsie Law made five saves for the win. Greely’s Rylee Begin stopped nine shots.
BOYS SOCCER
PINE TREE ACADEMY 1, TELSTAR 0: Lucky Kabeya tapped in a rebound midway through the second half, lifting the Breakers (10-0) to an eight-player win over the Rebels (10-1) in Freeport.
Abner Poland stopped a breakaway en route to the shutout.
LEAVITT 6, WINSLOW 0: Angelo Toscano scored three times in the first half as the Hornets (8-3-2) jumped out to a 5-0 lead and beat the Raiders (8-6) in Winslow.
Tyler Mates added two goals in the first half and Ryder Sawyer Brown scored on a penalty kick in the second half. Avery Schlobohm, Jacob Gibbs and Sawyer Brown each had an assist.
Leavitt keepers Luke Horn and Andrew Sutton combined for nine saves, while Maddox Lambert made 10 saves for Winslow.
FIELD HOCKEY
SPRUCE MOUNTAIN 10, TELSTAR 0: Zoe Groomes scored three times and the Phoenix (11-2) cruised past the Rebels (1-12) in Bethel.
Reese Gat and Ryley Wright each added two goals. Elyssa Yannelli, Kylie Blair and Lily Niedner also scored.
Madelyn Cooley made 22 saves for Telstar.

title: FBI agents and analysts fired for roles in Trump classified files probe sue to get their jobs back
text:
FBI agents and analysts fired for roles in Trump classified files probe sue to get their jobs back
FBI employees fired for their roles in the investigation of President Donald Trump's retention of classified documents at his Florida estate sued on Thursday to get their jobs back, calling their terminations unlawful acts of “political retribution.”
The complaint adds to the growing list of legal challenges to the mass terminations under FBI Director Kash Patel of agents who participated in investigations of the Republican president or are seen as opposed to Trump administration interests.
The suit was filed in federal court in Washington on behalf of nine agents, intelligence analysts and staff operations specialists who were fired in February following earlier dismissals of agents who had worked on the investigation into Trump's efforts to overturn his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.
Patel has said in congressional testimony that employees he has fired had “weaponized” the FBI. But the agents deny that claim in the lawsuit, noting that between them they had more than a century of distinguished and apolitical FBI service that involved responding to the Boston Marathon bombing, hostage recoveries and the investigation into the 2024 assassination attempt of Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.
Their firings, the lawsuit says, create an “immeasurable loss” to “America's national security."
“In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did to follow the facts and law without bias or favor. To this administration, this is an offense. To the rest of us, it is heroic,” said a statement from their attorneys, Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio.
“This lawsuit will prove their unlawful dismissal and hold the administration accountable for this blatant attack on the rule of law,” the statement added.
The Mar-a-Lago investigation produced criminal charges against Trump
The suit lays out a detailed recitation of the allegations against Trump, describing how he improperly stored dozens of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, that he took with him after leaving the White House, showed them off to people not authorized to see them and obstructed FBI efforts to get them back.
The investigation resulted in a dramatic 2022 FBI search of Mar-a-Lago that recovered classified records and later produced an indictment in federal court in Florida charging Trump with dozens of felony counts.
Trump denied wrongdoing, and the case was dismissed in 2024 by a Trump-appointed judge, Aileen Cannon, who ruled that the special counsel who filed the charges, Jack Smith, had been illegally appointed by the Biden administration Justice Department.
The nine fired FBI employees did not volunteer for the investigation but were rather assigned to it as part of their work on specialized counterintelligence and counterespionage squads, according to the lawsuit, which says they were nonetheless terminated because of baseless perceptions that the performance of their law enforcement duties had run “afoul of the political and personal loyalty to Trump that Defendants demanded.”
“By casting Plaintiffs’ work on the Plasmic Echo investigation as ‘politically weaponized,’ Defendants incorrectly presumed to know the personal political convictions of Plaintiffs and took unlawful action based on that presumption,” the lawsuit says, using the FBI code name for the classified documents investigation. “Worse still, Defendants incorrectly concluded that those personal political convictions affected or drove their work.”
The lawsuit seeks, among other remedies, reinstatement to the FBI, an awarding of back pay and a court order declaring that the firings were unlawful.
The suit says the firings were the culmination of a retribution campaign
Lawyers for the fired employees suggest their clients' “fate was sealed” well before the February terminations, casting the ousters as the culmination of a long-running retribution campaign that kicked into gear once Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
The lawsuit notes how Patel, in his capacity as a conservative podcaster before becoming Trump's FBI director, had derided the FBI's Mar-a-Lago search as “unlawful” and had accused the agents who had participated in it as being “corrupt government gangsters.”
Days after Trump was inaugurated, a top Justice Department official demanded that the FBI turn over a list of bureau employees who had participated in Trump-related investigations, an order that the then-director, Brian Driscoll, resisted and that was seen within the workforce as a potential prelude to mass firings.
Over the following year, the FBI and the Justice Department fired waves of employees involved in investigations of Trump, without hearings or proper notice that the plaintiffs' lawyers say are required by law.
The lawsuit says that the Mar-a-Lago agents and analysts were fired last February after Patel disclosed to Reuters that the FBI, as part of the investigation, had subpoenaed his toll records, which show the date, time and length of a phone call but not the content of the communications.
“The Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President’s personal vendetta,” the lawsuit states. “The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal.”

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate for a final time
text:
The fourth and final debate between Troy Jackson and Susan Collins is here.
After a whirlwind two weeks in which the candidates repeatedly faced questions from Maine journalists, they will meet for a final time onstage Thursday in Bangor.
Tonight’s debate is hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine.
As always, we’ll be following along live. The event starts at 7 p.m., and you can watch a livestream below.
And that’s a wrap!
Thanks so much for following along with us, not just for this debate, but for all the debates!
We’ll see you next time.
A Maine Mount Rushmore?
The candidates ended by answering a question about who should be on a Maine-themed Mount Rushmore, if such a thing were to exist.
Collins took a beat before answering Joshua Chamberlain, who fought for the Union in the Civil War. Jackson said Frances Perkins, the former Labor Secretary, and the first woman to hold a Cabinet position.
Collins said she is a strong supporter of Ukraine and that she “adamantly opposed” the Russian invasion of the country. She noted that she signed a letter criticizing Trump’s recent move to buy some oil from Russia.
Jackson said he’s not in favor of increasing the age limit to buy the weapons, but said he’s not opposed to banning them. He noted he would not advocate for taking away the weapons from people who already have them.
“We are resilient and strong. I’ve seen the executive branch over the years, regardless of whether it was Democratic president or a Republican president, try to get more and more power,” Collins said.
Jackson seems to be settling in
If he was stilted in previous debates, Jackson seems to be finding more a comedic stride tonight. He’s slipped in a number of these one-liner jabs such as his jab about the Supreme Court, and they’re playing well in the room.
“What we want is a Supreme Court that is insulated from politics,” Collins said.
Jackson shot back with a joke.
“We have the best court that money can buy,” Jackson said.
Jackson criticized Collins for not doing enough for everyday Mainers.
Jackson countered that as senator, Collins has presided in a huge spike in gas prices.
Jackson was asked why he prefers Customs and Border Protection to take over ICE’s responsibilities given that CBP officers fatally shot a Minnesota man earlier this year.
Jackson said she wouldn’t give immigration officers a “blank check” like Collins did.
This is an emerging theme of the night: Jackson expresses a number of things he wouldn’t do, but doesn’t express clearly what he would do.
A note on the audience
The audience is getting rowdy. People were laughing and “oohing” and “ahhing” at several of the pithier lines in Jackson’s answer to Collins’ question about his campaign finance filing
She also reiterated Iran should not be allowed to make a nuclear weapon.
When pressed on the beginning of the war, Collins said Congress should have been consulted on the war.
“Under the War Powers Act, the president, as commander-in-chief, for the first 60 days, has very broad authority to do whatever he wants, essentially, when it comes to a military conflict,” Collins said. “After 60 days, that’s when I voted every single time with the Democrats to bring the conflict to a halt.”
She pivoted to talking about how heating assistance has been funded at record levels, and noted that she supports social safety net programs.
Jackson said he may have gotten some support by billionaires, drawing a reaction from the room. But he said he still plans to tax them.
“They know that I don’t owe them a thing like Sen. Collins,” Jackson said.
However, he noted he would vote to impeach Hegseth, Trump’s Defense Secretary.
Does Collins regret RFK vote?
Collins noted the areas where she disagrees with the controversial U.S. Health and Human Services department secretary. For example, she doesn’t believe vaccines cause autism — a link Kennedy has made in the past.
But she said she agrees with him on his focus on chronic diseases. Overall, she’t said she didn’t regret the vote.
A look at the instigator from the room
A young man just stood up from the fourth row and interrupted Collins before she could answer a question. He was quickly escorted out of the room to applause.
Jackson’s response was muffled, but it sounded like he said, “oh, shut up,” noting he didn’t know the person.
“I don’t know what world Sen. Collins is in where she started out, we had $4 trillion in debt, now we have $40 trillion in debt under her watch, and somehow it’s my fault,” Jackson responded. “In Maine, we have a balanced budget. Has it grown? Yes. But it’s still balanced.”
He noted that tax cuts for wealthy Americans contribute to the debt.
Collins noted Maine is running a potential budget deficit of about $1 billion — you can read about that here — and Jackson noted that he hasn’t been in the Legislature since 2024.
Pressed on that point, Collins pivoted to attacking Jackson, arguing she’d vote the Democratic party line if elected.
Jackson contended that Collins would be a rubber stamp for Trump in her sixth term, and the two squabbled over how often Collins supports Trump.
When asked the same question about her party, Collins said her party has worked to secure the border.
But Collins also said she would vote independently during her sixth term.
“We need more people in the center. We don’t need more people who are going to vote a straight party line,” Collins said.
Jackson’s opening statement hits on chaos in our politics
Following a familiar line of attack, Jackson hit Collins for voting to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Collins did not ultimately support the measure, but Jackson has repeatedly attacked her for a vote to advance the bill. (She’s argued it would have made the floor anyway, and that because of her vote, she was able to get a $50 billion fund for rural hospitals amended onto it.)
“I ask for your support so I can continue my work for you,” Collins said.
Jackson’s campaign finance report is in
He promised to deliver the numbers Wednesday morning. They came about 36 hours later — though still before the statutory deadline.
Take a look at our rundown of the third quarter fundraising by Collins and Jackson. The Democrat had a heck of a quarter — but he’s still being badly outraised by Collins and her allies.
The candidates take the stage
The candidates have arrived! The room is full mostly of Collins and Jackson supporters, who broke out into applause as the candidates took the stage. The two met in a cordial handshake and are now at their podiums taking last minute notes.
Pictures tell the story
Here’s a look a the scenes outside the debate. Might be a bit more raucous inside than the past three.
Coming into tonight, Jackson’s campaign said the former logger will try to focus on healthcare — something that he’s done in each debate so far. He will undoubtedly continue to tie Collins to President Donald Trump, who’s deeply unpopular here.
Expect Collins to continue to highlight her seniority in the Senate as a strength and try to shift blame for the high cost of — whether its property taxes or electricity rates — onto Jackson, who served as state Senate president for six years.
Let’s hope the candidates break some new ground. But after three televised debates in two weeks, that may be difficult to do.
Update from on the ground from Bangor
Just under an hour before the candidates are set to take the stage, supporters of each have gathered in the parking lot outside the venue. Jackson’s supporters are blasting music and holding a large banner that reads “Let them eat road salt” — a zinger from the first debate.
Across the lot, Collins supporters are doing a call-and-response with the senator’s first and last name in front of a large tour bus.
One hour to go!
We are about an hour from go time.
Get caught up on our past debate coverage before we get started. You can read our takeaways from the first debate here, from the second debate here and from the third debate here.

title: Crash during ICE detainment in Sanford prompts local police response
text:
Sanford police responded to the scene of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention Thursday morning after federal agents reported a car crash and unattended children.
ICE detained a man during a traffic stop near Brook and High streets around 9 a.m., Sanford police say. As agents attempted to stop the man, he reversed into one of their vehicles, according to a police account and a video shared with the Portland Press Herald.
Footage captured by a nearby resident’s bird feeder camera shows the two SUVs block the driver in, at which point he reverses into the vehicle behind him. The short clip doesn’t show the rest of the detention.
Sanford police Chief Eric Small said federal agents called dispatch after the crash, prompting a response by Sanford police. Police officers also assisted with a 1-year-old who was found in the man’s car.
Officials say no one was injured, though the 1-year-old was taken to a hospital as a precaution.
Immigration officials did not immediately respond to questions about the man’s detention.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree criticized the incident as “yet another instance of ICE’s aggressive operations putting public safety at risk,” pointing to the fatal July shooting of a Biddeford man during an attempted traffic stop.
‘PRETTY SCARY’
Federal agents told police they used two of their vehicles to block the front and back of the car that the man was driving, according to the Sanford Police Department. A neighbor who witnessed the detention, Wendy Deflaminis, said the man had just pulled out of his driveway when the two ICE vehicles drove up from either side and cornered his vehicle.
The man then reversed, crashing into one of the federal vehicles. Deflaminis said it looked as though the man was trying to navigate around the vehicles until he backed into the one behind him. Small said there was no major damage and that the driver was moving at a “very low speed.”
After the crash, the agents told the driver to stop and put his hands up, and he appeared to comply, Deflaminis said. Federal agents then escorted him into a car.
Once the man had been detained, agents appeared to notice that a 1-year-old was sitting in a car seat in the rear of the vehicle, Deflaminis said. She recalled asking whether someone should call an ambulance to ensure the baby was safe, to which the agents responded that they had already called for one.
“It was pretty scary,” Deflaminis said.
Sanford police say the baby was not properly restrained in a car seat and was taken to MaineHealth Maine Medical Center Sanford out of “an abundance of caution.” Small and Assistant Fire Chief Brian Watkins both said no one was injured.
Small said the police department did not assist with the federal detention and that he did not know the man’s name. Deflaminis did not know the man’s name either but said he lived nearby.
Emergency personnel also evaluated the driver, who is the baby’s father, while he was handcuffed in the back of a federal vehicle, Small said. The man “was under a lot of stress,” Small said, and reportedly told federal agents that he had two more children unattended at his nearby home.
Child Protective Services and the Maine Department of Health and Human Services were contacted to ensure the welfare of the other two children, who are 9 and 2 years old, according to a news release from the Sanford Police Department. Small said those children are now with a family friend who was able to take them in via an arrangement with CPS.
“(The ICE agents) were very forthcoming,” Small said. “They wanted what was best for the children as well.”
Small said the man’s vehicle was towed from the scene.
PINGREE CALLS FOR VIDEO RELEASE
Officials with ICE, U.S. Border Patrol and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond Thursday to requests for more information about the incident.
In a written statement, Pingree, D-1st District, called on the federal agencies to promptly release any footage of the incident, including from body-worn and dashboard cameras.
Referencing the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the congresswoman said that “it is entirely understandable that a father confronted by ICE — with his one-year-old in the car and two more children at home — would be terrified when federal agents box in his car.”
Durán Guerrero, 25, was shot and killed by an ICE agent on the morning of July 13 while driving in a Biddeford neighborhood; officials have said he was not the intended target of ICE’s operation.
A spokesperson for U.S. Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said the senator has been “very clear” about his opposition to how ICE is operating under the Trump administration.
Spokespeople for Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd District, did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this report.

title: ‘He’s not violent’: 911 call made before man allegedly kills aunt, grandmother with chainsaw
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — Transcripts reveal a call for help was made before police in Alabama said a 47-year-old man killed two of his family members.
Crime scene tape surrounded a home on Carolina Court in Mobile on Oct. 12 as investigators canvassed the area.
911 call details
According to transcripts, a woman called 911 after 11 a.m. on Monday.
In the call, she said her nephew, later identified as Thomas Steele, was “off his medication for Lithium” and she wasn’t “sure who to call or contact.”
“He gave away his phone and giving his car away. He’s doing some bizarre things, and I don’t know if that’s good. He says he’s just going to live for God and not going to have any kind of electronics,” the woman said to 911 dispatchers.
The operator asked if she needed medical help.
The woman said Steele is bipolar and “it’s in his mind. He’s following God.”
As the call continued, the caller said her nephew was acting out.
The operator asked what she meant and if he was being harmful.
“I just needed to figure out what to do. I called 988 and tried to talk to him. He’s calm! He’s not violent or anything. So, I guess I’ll just let it play itself out,” the caller responded.
The operator gave the woman the number for the police department and the call ended.
Police respond to home
According to a source, about two and a half hours later, police were called to the home and were told Steele was waiting outside.
Officers said they found Steele’s grandmother and aunt inside the home decapitated with a chainsaw.
Mobile police identified the victims in the double homicide on Carolina Court as Christy Deloach, 65, and Dora Boone, 85.
The source also told FOX10 News that a woman with special needs was inside the home at the time of the killings. She was unharmed.
Steele remains behind bars without bond.
It is unclear how long after the 911 call the aunt and grandmother were killed. It is also unclear if the caller was able to reach Mobile police after the operator gave her that number.

title: Suspicious letters with white powder mailed to election and congressional offices
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities are investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and are urging recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.”
The investigation by the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Thursday by The Associated Press. The notice, sent to Senate offices, said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but “it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations.”
In Congress, the threat appeared limited to the Senate, though the House was monitoring the situation, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly.
The office of Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, a Delaware Democrat, said in a statement that it was sent a letter with a “suspicious substance” that was intercepted by Capitol Police. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said the Postal Service intercepted a suspicious package before it reached his office. And Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said postal inspectors intercepted a suspicious piece of mail addressed to her New York City office.
An FBI statement said the bureau and the Postal Inspection Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the statement read. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said their election offices either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said in a statement that it received a letter and the white powder enclosed in it was not hazardous, according to tests. “Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us,” Wisconsin elections administrator Meagan Wolfe said.
News of the letters comes just three weeks before Election Day and is reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when election offices in six states received mailings that contained a white powder. In some cases, the incidents disrupted work around local elections.
Some of those letters contained threats and traces of the powerful opioid fentanyl, leading some election offices to stock up on the overdose reversal medication naloxone.
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement condemning what they said were threats against election staff.
“Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” they said in their statement.
Deputy Postal Inspector Brendan Donahue told reporters Thursday that “any threat or attack on election officials is unacceptable” and that “we are also working with our partners on identifying the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
___
Associated Press writers Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin; Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia; and Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this report.

title: US coach who recorded young gymnasts undressing sentenced to 90 years in prison
text:
IOWA CITY, Iowa (AP) - A once prominent youth gymnastics coach was sentenced to 90 years in prison Wednesday for secretly recording his young female students undressing and using the bathroom at a Mississippi gym, in a case that rocked the sport.
U.S. District Judge Kristi Johnson gave the maximum sentence possible to Sean Gardner, ordering that he serve 30 years in prison for each of the three federal child pornography production charges to which he pleaded guilty. The sentence likely amounts to life in prison for Gardner, 39.
Gardner’s arrest last summer by the FBI, first reported by The Associated Press, renewed questions about whether U.S. gymnastics authorities had done enough to protect athletes from sexual abuse at the hands of an influential coach.
Gardner pleaded guilty to placing a hidden camera in a bathroom at a gymnastics studio in Purvis, Mississippi, between December 2017 and April 2018 to record his students. Investigators say he created videos showing close-up images of at least 10 minors naked or undressing, which they recovered from his computers years later while investigating claims that he sexually abused gymnasts in Iowa.
Several of his former students at Chow’s Gymnastics and Dance Institute in West Des Moines, Iowa, have alleged to police and in civil lawsuits that he used his position to prey on them. The institute was founded by prominent coach Liang “Chow” Qiao, who is known for producing Olympic champions. Gardner coached several youth prospects and served as director of an annual winter meet that drew hundreds of gymnasts to Iowa.
Gardner has not been charged in connection with any of the Iowa allegations, and police have said they would wait to determine how to proceed after the federal case concludes.
Lawyers for some of the women have also alleged the sport’s oversight bodies, USA Gymnastics and the U.S. Center for SafeSport, were told about inappropriate behavior by Gardner in 2017 but failed to take action to remove him from the sport for years. SafeSport temporarily suspended Gardner in 2022 after a Chow’s gymnast alleged sexual abuse, and Chow’s fired him then.
SafeSport has said it learned during its investigation that Chow and other coaches had been aware of allegations of sexual misconduct against Gardner but failed to report them to the center as required by its policy. A judge dismissed SafeSport in May as a party from two lawsuits alleging it did not properly investigate Gardner, finding it was entitled to immunity under federal law.
Several lawsuits remain pending against Gardner, USA Gymnastics and Chow’s Gymnastics.

title: Three Maine football storylines to follow against Bryant
text:
It’s been two weeks since the University of Maine football team dropped its fifth straight game with a 24-16 loss to Sacred Heart on Oct. 3 in Orono. Maine had a bye last week, during which it fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters.
The Black Bears (1-5, 1-2 Coastal Athletic Association) return to action when they host Bryant (4-2, 2-0 CAA) at 1 p.m. Saturday (FloSports; ABC in Bangor market). Here are three storylines to watch as Maine looks to end the skid.
Green-er pastures?
With Waters gone, running backs coach Sean Green takes over as interim offensive coordinator. Green is well-known in Maine, having won state titles as head coach of Cape Elizabeth High School in 2021 (Class C) and Portland in 2024 (Class A).
Green takes over a Maine offense ranked 121st of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in points per game (14.5). In Monday’s CAA press conference, coach Jordan Stevens said the goal is to “continue to find ways to be more balanced” offensively and praised his team’s response to the change.
“I thought the guys have handled that type of change really well in how they’ve approached practice, and Coach Green has done an excellent job,” Stevens said. “This is not something that’s foreign to him in calling plays; it’s something he’s done in the past, so I have full confidence in his ability.”
The quarterback question
Through the first four games, Eddie Buehler was Maine’s unquestioned starter at quarterback. Yet in the second half at Elon on Sept. 26, Caden Drezek took over under center. Buehler again got the start against Sacred Heart before Stevens turned to Drezek in the second quarter.
So, with a new offensive coordinator, what will the plan be this weekend? Will Buehler make his seventh straight start? Will the Black Bears turn to Drezek instead? Or will we see some combination of the two, as has been the case the past two games?
“In a perfect world, you’d always probably have one guy,” Stevens said. “I don’t have any answer for you on that right now, but we are working through the quarterback position and how we’re going to manage that this week.”
Up-and-down Bulldogs
On one hand, Bryant boasts an impressive 21-14 win over Princeton, which is 3-1. Yet the Bulldogs also needed a miracle — 10 points in the final 40 seconds — to pull out a win over North Carolina A&T, which might be the worst team in the CAA. Bryant also lost 28-13 at Brown.
This is an opportunity, then, for the Black Bears, who have had two weeks to prepare. The numbers don’t suggest a lopsided game — in fact, ESPN’s SP+ has the Bulldogs as just 1.3-point favorites. A win will be difficult, but it’s not impossible — and if Maine can pull it off, the trajectory of the season could change.
