title: Bird flu caused the death of Jackie, a California bald eagle who captured hearts
text:
BIG BEAR LAKE, Calif. (AP) — Bird flu caused the death of a bald eagle named Jackie who had become an internet sensation and a symbol of the species’ recovery in California, officials said.
A necropsy and additional testing found that the primary underlying cause of Jackie’s death in August was highly pathogenic avian influenza, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said Wednesday in a news release.
In the weeks before she died, Jackie was being treated at the Ojai Raptor Center for various ailments, including anemia. Chris Eksteen, the center’s director, said in the news release that the necropsy results “have helped connect many of the findings” they saw during her hospitalization.
“In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis,” Steve Kubiski, the disease investigations director at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, where the necropsy was conducted, said in the news release.
For more than a decade, nature lovers watched via an online video feed as Jackie and her partner, Shadow, tended to their nest each year atop trees near Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains east of Los Angeles. There’s no evidence Shadow is ill, according to the news release.
The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015 and documented the successes and failures of each breeding season.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been circulating in bird populations throughout the U.S. While waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts for bird flu viruses, eagles and other raptors can be exposed through contact with infected birds or by eating them, according to the news release.
Jackie’s remains were cremated to prevent transmission of the virus, it said.
American bald eagles teetered on the brink of extinction until the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were established, leading the species to rebound and be removed from the federal endangered list.

title: Eliot Cutler begins jail sentence for probation violations
text:
Eliot Cutler, convicted sex offender and former Maine gubernatorial candidate, begins jail sentence for probation violations
Hancock County Jail confirms Cutler reported Thursday morning, as scheduled
Eliot Cutler, convicted sex offender and former Maine gubernatorial candidate, begins jail sentence for probation violations
Hancock County Jail confirms Cutler reported Thursday morning, as scheduled
Convicted sex offender Eliot Cutler, who twice ran to become governor of Maine, returned to jail Thursday morning to begin serving the sentence he received for violating his probation.
Cutler, 80, was found guilty of three probation violations after being accused of violating his probation six times since September 2025. According to WMTW media partner WABI, a Hancock County Superior Court judge considered three of Cutler's alleged probation violations during a hearing last month. One violation involved Cutler having a phone with internet access, another involved an internet search that led Cutler to access pornographic material, and the third was an incident in South Portland, where police said Cutler was found in possession of pornographic DVDs.
The judge sentenced Cutler to 6 months in jail with 107 days of credit for previous time served in connection with the probation violation allegations.
The Hancock County Jail confirmed to Maine's Total Coverage that Cutler reported to the facility as scheduled Thursday morning to serve the 73 days remaining on his sentence.
According to WABI, the judge said during last month's hearing that Cutler will not have to attend the Maine Department of Corrections recovery program as long as he continues treatment with his therapist.
What Cutler was convicted of and details of probation violation allegations
In May 2023, Cutler pleaded guilty to four counts of possession of sexually explicit materials of children as part of a plea deal. Prosecutors said investigators had found tens of thousands of images and videos of child sexual abuse material on Cutler's electronic devices.
As part of his plea deal, Cutler was sentenced to four years in prison with all but nine months suspended and received six years of probation. He reported to the Hancock County Jail in June 2023. In January 2024, Cutler was released from jail about six weeks early for good behavior.
The first probation violation case surfaced in November 2025. Cutler was accused of using an external USB drive on Sept. 8, 2025, to access content related to massage parlors in the San Francisco area. An affidavit also indicates Cutler was accused of answering questions about his desired preferences in an escort through a menu on the website. The alleged activity coincided with a request Cutler made for a travel permit to go to California to see friends, the affidavit states. Cutler appeared in court on Dec. 16, 2025, and denied claims that he accessed prohibited websites, used unmonitored electronic devices and failed to report that activity to his probation officer.
On Jan. 13, 2026, Cutler turned himself in to authorities after prosecutors alleged he violated the terms of his release at his home in Brooklin on Dec. 28, 2025, and again on Jan. 2, 2026. Court documents state that on both dates, Cutler was accused of accessing a website that displayed sexually explicit materials and obscene or sexually explicit conduct.
On Feb. 9, 2026, Cutler was arrested by Maine State Police detectives at a South Portland hotel for violating his probation. State police said those detectives were conducting a separate, unrelated investigation in Cumberland County when they encountered Cutler at the hotel. Court documents state that Cutler was holding a brown paper bag and a stack of DVD cases. After an officer identified himself, Cutler allegedly hid the items behind his back. The court documents state, "Mr. Cutler began to loudly cry and say he can't help himself and that he has had this problem for 65 years." Officers searched Cutler's room at the hotel and found 10 tapes, along with a receipt and packaging for a DVD player that was plugged into the hotel TV. Cutler denied the claims when he appeared in Cumberland County Court two days later.
A fourth motion to revoke Cutler's probation was filed on Feb. 20, 2026, because he was unsatisfactorily discharged from court-ordered specialized problematic sexual behavior treatment on Feb. 18 for failing to attend and participate in that treatment, according to court documents. Court records indicate that at this time, Cutler was still being held on $50,000 bail at the Cumberland County Jail. Cutler made a request to amend that bail to personal recognizance so that he could be transferred from Cumberland County to Hancock County, where he would be held without bail. A judge granted that request on Feb. 24.
On April 8, a judge denied Cutler's request to be let out on bail while a case regarding a previous alleged probation violation moves forward.
The fifth motion for revocation states that Cutler violated his probation conditions on April 21 in the city of Ellsworth by maintaining encrypted files upon or within a computer or account under his control without written permission from a parole officer. The motion also states that Cutler violated his probation by failing to disclose passwords or passkeys used to access electronic devices that were in his possession.
An affidavit from a probation officer, which was filed with the motion to revoke Cutler's probation, states that on April 17, the officer received an email from a member of the Maine State Police Major Crimes Special Victims Unit (SVU), who was tasked with examining several of Cutler's electronic devices. The SVU member said she was provided with three different passcodes that would provide her access to one of Cutler's electronic devices, and that the passcodes were provided to her by Washington County District Attorney Robert Granger, who had received them from Cutler's lawyer. The probation officer said all three passcodes provided to the SVU member did not work, and she could not get into the device.
While in court on May 22, Cutler testified that he was allowed to have encrypted files if they relate to his finances or medical records. The court determined Cutler did not object to random searches of his devices, but noted that he did have devices that could not be accessed.
Cutler was released from the Hancock County Jail on May 22 amid the proceedings to revoke his probation. A judge ordered Cutler to be released on $10,000 bail, which he posted in January, while continuing the probation revocation hearing to June 1.
At the June 1 hearing, the judge said Cutler could use the internet while he was on probation, but only while supervised by either his wife or his brother between the hours of 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Cutler was also ordered to notify his probation officer when he used the internet, and his computer and phone must continue to be monitored by an independent agency, with compliance reports sent to the probation officer.
Cutler was arrested on June 11 for violating his probation and booked at the Penobscot County Jail. Court documents state that Cutler was arrested because he refused to sign a contract to receive specialized treatment for problematic sexual behavior, which is a condition of his release.
During a June 16 hearing at the Washington County Courthouse, Cutler’s attorney argued that the contract his client refused to sign contained restrictions on Cutler's internet use that did not align with what had previously been ordered by a judge. District Attorney Bob Granger said Cutler's probation officer did inform Cutler that the contract's restrictions that differed from the judge's orders would not be enforced.
Cutler was then released from jail after the judge ruled that there was no probable cause to keep him in jail and that instead of being arrested, Cutler should have been allowed more time to speak with his attorney and instead been issued a summons to appear in court. In addition, the judge said he would not require Cutler to appear in problematic sexual behavior treatment until the matter was resolved.
On July 22, a judge amended two of Cutler's bail conditions. The judge modified the condition that Cutler was prohibited from using the internet after 5 p.m., allowing Cutler to use the internet from 6 to 8 p.m. on Wednesdays to solely attend Sex Addicts Anonymous meetings. The judge also amended another condition to specify that Cutler's internet supervision should be random and unannounced.
More on Cutler's campaigns for governor
Cutler ran twice for governor of Maine as an independent candidate. In 2010, Cutler lost to Republican candidate Paul LePage by fewer than 10,000 votes and finished nearly 99,000 votes ahead of Democratic candidate Libby Mitchell. But in 2014, Cutler finished well behind the incumbent LePage and Democratic nominee Mike Michaud.
In July 2024, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court officially ordered that Cutler be disbarred after he agreed to stop practicing law in the state in February. Cutler was also disbarred in the state of New York.

title: MDI Marathon is this Sunday
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — In October, runners from around the world flock to Mount Desert Island for what may be one of the country’s most scenic marathons.
Alongside the 23rd running of the MDI Marathon, Half, and Relay on Sunday, Oct. 18, the Acadia Chamber of Commerce will host its annual Finish Line Festival in Southwest Harbor, greeting runners as they finish.
Starting in Bar Harbor and winding through MDI’s beautiful landscape, racers will pass through six villages while enjoying scenic views of the island’s rolling hills adorned with vibrant fall colors.
The marathon starts in Bar Harbor at 8 a.m. sharp. The route travels south, passing by the Tarn, then towards Otter Creek and briefly through Acadia National Park. Half marathon runners will start at 5 Manchester Rd. in Northeast Harbor at 8:30 a.m.
As runners drop into Seal Harbor, they will take Cooksey Drive, overlooking Cranberry Islands and Bunker Ledge, eventually passing the fountain in Seal Harbor and running past the beach entrance to Acadia National Park.
From there, runners will pass Seal Harbor Beach, then continue toward Asticou on Peabody Drive.
The landscape changes as runners make their way through Northeast Harbor toward Sargeant Drive. The road follows Somes Sound, with ocean views on the left and pink cliff formations and forests on the right leading to Somesville.
After passing Somesville, runners will be in the home stretch of their 26-mile journey, which includes an elevation gain of 1,386 feet, before dropping into Southwest Harbor.
Race founder Gary Allen encourages anyone watching to set up along the race route.
“As ever, we encourage folks to set up anywhere on the course with music, costumes, signs and even host a roadside viewing BBQ,” said Allen. “The creativity of Mainers and islanders always shines on marathon day, and we encourage more.”
The race presents an opportunity to bring the entire island together, said Allen. “We of course called it the Mount Desert Island Marathon vs. Acadia or Bar Harbor because this is our entire island’s marathon, and we just push down on the gas pedal and help steer it,” he explained. “Of course, the course design links our island communities, much like that historic Boston Marathon route does. It’s a ton of work, but oh so satisfying when all the pieces come together.”
This year’s Finish Line Festival will be front and center for the Acadia Chamber’s new location, located right on the finish line in Southwest. Live music, food, and drink will be plentiful from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Roads on the race route will be closed to thru traffic.
Parking in Southwest Harbor during the event will be available at: Golf of Maine Miniature Golf, 55 Main St.; Seal Cove Road Shops, Seal Cove Road; the former Northern Lights Clinic on Herrick Road; former Morris Yacht parking lot on Clark Point Road and Ships Way; Upper town dock, Clark Point Road; Lower town dock, Clark Point Road; Lot behind Southwest Harbor Town Office/Police Department; Community Health Centers, Community Way; Dry Dock Inn paid parking lot, Main Street; Post office parking lot, Clark Point Road and behind Pemetic Elementary School on Maple Lane. Town Dock areas are paid parking and metered.
For those interested in a pre-race pasta dinner hosted by the Mount Desert Island High School Music Boosters, visit runmdi.org/race-weekend-info. The dinner will take place at MDI High School, 1081 Eagle Lake Rd. (Route 233) in Bar Harbor, on Saturday, Oct. 17, from 5:30 to 7 p.m.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Snow Mixes to Rain Friday, Colder and Breezy Saturday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Thursday. Quiet but cold conditions are expected tonight before our next storm system arrives Friday. Precipitation will initially fall as snow across portions of northern Maine Friday morning before warmer air changes most locations over to rain during the afternoon. The system moves away Friday night into Saturday, but colder and breezy weather will follow for the start of the weekend.
Cloud cover will gradually increase overnight as our next storm system approaches from the west. Before those clouds arrive, temperatures will fall quickly under mostly clear skies and light winds.
Most of Aroostook County will drop into the mid to upper 20s tonight. Presque Isle is forecast to reach around 26 degrees, Caribou around 27 and Houlton near 24. Some of the normally colder spots across northern and western Aroostook County could fall into the lower to mid 20s.
A strong low pressure system will approach Maine Friday, spreading widespread precipitation across the region during the morning. Snow will likely be the initial precipitation type across much of northern Maine, particularly across northern Aroostook County and the higher terrain. As warmer air moves north during the day, snow will gradually mix with and change to rain. Accumulation should remain relatively limited. A dusting to around one-half inch is possible across much of northern Aroostook County, with amounts approaching an inch over the higher terrain and portions of northwestern Aroostook County. There’s also the possibility of some freezing rain during the transition Friday afternoon. However, temperatures are expected to rise fairly quickly, meaning icing. Farther south toward Houlton, little or no snow accumulation is expected before precipitation changes to rain.
Once the transition occurs, Friday becomes predominantly a rain event across the region. The latest rainfall forecast generally shows around a quarter to half inch across much of Aroostook County through the weekend system, with somewhat higher amounts possible farther west. Rain continues into Friday evening before becoming more scattered overnight as the system begins pulling away.
Temperatures will behave a little differently than a typical night. They may continue climbing for part of Friday evening as warmer air moves north before colder air rushes back into the region behind the system overnight. By Saturday morning, temperatures should fall into the lower 30s across much of northern and northeastern Aroostook County, including around 32 degrees in Presque Isle and Caribou. Some colder locations farther north and west could fall into the upper 20s. As that colder air returns, some rain could briefly mix back with snow before precipitation ends.
Northwest winds increase behind the system Friday night and remain breezy through Saturday. The latest forecast shows gusts generally reaching around 30 to 35 mph across northern Maine, with the strongest gusts expected across northeastern Aroostook County. That is noticeably lower than some earlier forecasts that suggested gusts could approach or exceed 40 mph. Saturday afternoon itself looks mainly dry, although a few snow showers could linger during the morning. High temperatures will struggle to climb out of the upper 30s across far northern Maine, with lower to mid 40s farther south. Combined with the wind, it will feel considerably colder.
Conditions improve considerably as we move deeper into the weekend. Saturday night turns clear and cold, with widespread temperatures falling into the lower 20s. Sunshine returns Sunday as high pressure builds into the region. Highs rebound into the mid to upper 40s, and an extended stretch of mainly dry weather is then expected to continue through much of next week. Temperatures moderate quickly as well, with highs returning to the 50s Monday and Tuesday.
For the latest details on Friday’s snow and rain, the breezy conditions Saturday and the quieter weather returning Sunday, check out the First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Study says global warming did more than El Niño to turbocharge Hurricane Polo
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A new study finds that climate change and El Niño combined to rev up last month’s explosively intensifying Hurricane Polo, which was the longest-lasting Category 5 storm ever to churn in the Pacific.
Global warming caused by the burning of coal, oil and gas was the bigger of the two culprits, adding about 6 mph (nearly 10 kph) to its already monstrous strength, according to a joint study published Thursday by the science teams World Weather Attribution and Climate Central. El Niño contributed a bit less, about 5 mph (8 kph), a study co-author said.
Climate change made the conditions that fueled the hurricane 23 times more likely, while El Niño — the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific — made it 14 times more likely, the study found. It all has to do with the 88-degree Fahrenheit (31.2 degrees Celsius) waters that were as much as 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (2 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal, the study said.
This year, with a super strong El Niño, has set records for strength and longevity of Pacific storms. Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 in the Pacific at two-and-a-half days.
“El Niño and climate change both made this hurricane stronger than it would have otherwise been, but the effect of climate change is even bigger than the one of El Niño,” said climate scientist and study co-author Friederike Otto, who coordinates the international science team behind World Weather Attribution.
“El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse. That means that now every hurricane that will occur in the East Pacific has at least this climate change signal making it stronger. And as long as we keep burning fossil fuels, that will only get bigger,” Otto added.
Researchers found that without climate change and El Niño, Polo would have been a monster storm anyway. But every bit of additional wind speed can dramatically increase the damage.
Decoding Polo’s rapid strengthening
While Hurricane Polo ultimately weakened considerably before it hit a sparsely populated part of Mexico, scientists remain fascinated by how it turbocharged from a tropical storm to a top-of-the-chart Category 5 hurricane in about 24 hours.
The study puts the different atmospheric dangers in perspective, said Kristina Dahl, a climate scientist and vice president of science at Climate Central, a science and journalism nonprofit out of New Jersey.
“It’s a powerful reminder that even though El Niño right now is shifting hazards around the globe and changing where it’s flooding and getting dry, the really dominant signal behind all of this remains climate change,” she said.
The study looked at the warm water that fuels storms, using a measure of how strong they can get. But the study didn’t focus on the upper level wind shear where El Niño has a huge footprint. El Niño usually increases those storm-decapitating high altitude winds in the Atlantic. However, in the Pacific because of changes in wind patterns, El Niño decreases the winds that weaken storms.
The two sets of researchers measured conditions slightly differently and used different techniques but came to the same general conclusion, making them more confident in the result. However, the rapid study has not had time to be peer-reviewed, which is the gold standard of science.
To calculate the impact of climate change on Polo, both teams used the scientifically accepted method of comparing what happened in our warmer real world to a hypothetical world that hasn’t warmed by 2.5 degrees (1.4 degrees Celsius) since pre-industrial times.
How El Niño and climate change interact
Study co-author Daniel Gilford, a Climate Central scientist, said the process they looked at was similar to cars on a road. Wind shear from El Niño can be a red light, as it is in the Atlantic, or a green light, as it is in the Pacific. In the Pacific that green light says go, and then the water warmed by both climate change and El Niño acts like a driver flooring the accelerator.
University at Albany atmospheric scientist Brian Tang, who wasn’t part of the study, said he was initially surprised that the research found climate change to be the bigger influence on Polo, “given how extreme this El Niño is, but from a long-term standpoint, perhaps the result isn’t as surprising as it might seem.”
But three other outside scientists — Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections, University of Pennsylvania’s Michael Mann and North Carolina State University’s Carl Schreck — said they believe the study underestimates how much climate change has added to Polo’s strength. Masters pointed to Gilford’s own 2024 study that found climate change added 16 mph (30 kph) to hurricanes in the Atlantic from 2019 to 2023.
Gilford acknowledged that Thursday’s report could be underestimating climate change’s impact a bit, but said he was factoring in other conditions and being conservative.

title: Eliot Cutler reports to jail for previous probation violations
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - Former gubernatorial candidate Eliot Cutler has reported back to jail for past probation violations.
A judge ordered Cutler, 80, to return to custody on Thursday, Oct. 15, at a hearing last month to address three charges of violating his probation.
One violation involved Cutler having a phone with internet access. Another was an internet search that led Cutler to access pornographic material. The third was an incident in South Portland in October of last year in which Cutler was found in possession of pornographic DVDs.
Cutler’s bail conditions barred him from possessing or viewing explicit images.
The judge sentenced Cutler to six months in jail with credit for time served. He will spend roughly two-and-a-half months behind bars. He is being held at Hancock County Jail.
Cutler has about three years of probation left from his original sentence for possession of sexually explicit materials.

title: Pringles is offering a can-shaped urn for one die-hard fan to be buried in. Here’s how to get it
text:
(Gray News) — Pringles is offering one fan the chance to be buried in an urn shaped like a Pringles can.
The spooky season campaign will award one fan a one-of-a-kind Pringles can-shaped urn to be buried in, as well as an “afterlifetime” supply of Pringles. According to the campaign, this amounts to 200 years’ worth of snacks.
From now through Oct. 22, fans can visit OnceYouDrop.com to sign the “will and taste-ament” for a chance to be randomly selected to win.
A winner will be notified on or around Oct. 31.
“Leaning into Halloween’s dark humor and Gen Z’s taste for absurdist storytelling, we’re putting Pringles on the salty side of Halloween and rewarding the ultimate fan in the most lasting way possible — by making the Pringles can part of their legacy,” said Mauricio Jenkins, Salty Snacks Brand & Content lead, Mars Snacking North America.
Pringles said the campaign is inspired by the real-life story of the Pringles inventor, whose ashes were buried in a Pringles can in 2008.

title: Listen to the emergency calls made after Christa Pike’s failed execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Authorities have released emergency calls made from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution the night of Christa Pike’s attempted execution.
Metro Nashville Emergency Communications Center released the audio on Monday.
The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications first received notification of the incident at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in a 911 call at 9:40 p.m. ET on Sept. 30.
What happened the night of Christa Pike’s attempted execution?
The failed attempt happened after a day of back-and-forth among the courts about whether the procedure would proceed.
Pike was scheduled to be executed at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution the morning of Sept. 30, but shortly before, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ordered that her execution be paused.
The pause was issued because the court believed that she should be allowed to challenge the legality of her sentence. Pike’s attorneys then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to maintain that pause while a federal appeals court reviewed a new legal challenge.
That evening, the Supreme Court said in a 6-3 decision that the execution would be allowed to proceed. She would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be executed in Tennessee. She is the only woman on death row in the state.
Things went wrong when an attempt was made to administer the two doses of pentobarbital.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” witnesses heard Pike say as she was undergoing lethal injection.
The state administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to be lethal. But witnesses and her attorneys say that they did not have the intended effect. Instead, one witness said, “heavy snoring is the best description we can get you for the noises she was making.”
Shortly after, WSMV observed ambulances arriving at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution and leaving soon after, followed by police.
Pike was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
Attorneys later confirmed that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. It was revealed that on Oct. 5, her attorneys and medical team believed she was brain dead and would be taken off life support within days, but she regained consciousness the following morning.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery,” one of her attorneys, Randy Spivey, said.
Pike’s attorneys announced on Saturday that she had been released from the hospital and was returned to the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years.
Why is Christa Pike on death row?
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
The case revealed that Pike, who was 18 at the time, worked with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson to plan and carry out the killing, which became known as the “Job Corps Murder.” Pike and Slemmer had both been Job Corps members at the time of the murder, which took place at the University of Tennessee campus.
Phil Keith, who was the Knoxville police chief during the 1995 murder, described it as “an incredibly grotesque crime scene, one of the most brutal I’ve ever seen.”
According to Keith, Pike had tortured Slemmer for nearly an hour with a box cutter, “carving a pentagram on her chest before she crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.”
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her upbringing was not given enough consideration in her case. According to her defense, Pike was a victim of child abuse and multiple rapes, details they say were kept from the jury during her trial.
Tennessee previously claimed Pike was lying about her childhood, but has since acknowledged the abuse in open court.
For Keith, the upbringing is not an excuse.
“If everyone that had an abusive lifestyle killed someone, there’d be a lot more murders in this country,” he said. “This is not about how she’s become reformed, or that those days are past. Her values or morals have been set for a long time, and somewhere along the way, they got twisted.”
While Keith said that Pike never showed any remorse for the crime, Pike’s friend, Misty Armstrong, said otherwise.
According to Armstrong, Pike spent much of her time in prison trying to help other inmates.
“It took years of therapy for her to get there, but she did,” she said. “She changed and became a completely different person.”

title: Jackson backs sovereignty, Collins delivers cash. Which matters to Wabanaki communities?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Weeks after he was sworn in as president of the state Senate, Democrats Troy Jackson and House Speaker Sara Gideon called a meeting of the Wabanaki chiefs at the capitol. All five attended.
There, the lawmakers posed a question: “How do you want to fix this?”
By early 2019, there was a growing appetite to address the fraught relationship between the state and the Wabanaki Nations, which stems from a 1980 settlement that placed unique limits on the tribes’ jurisdiction. But Gov. Janet Mills was known to oppose sweeping changes to that agreement, and so the can of worms Jackson and Gideon were opening was a politically inconvenient one.
Tribal officials in the room were struck by the earnestness of the new leaders’ approach.
“That was refreshing to hear,” recalled Maulian Bryant, who attended as the ambassador for the Penobscot Nation. “I think for a long time the tribes were being told by the state what was good for us.”
Now locked in a furiously tight U.S. Senate race against Republican incumbent Susan Collins, Jackson’s past is serving him well in tribal communities.
“Troy is one of the leaders that we can credit with changing tribal-state relations in the state of Maine, and I am so honored to be his friend and supporter,” Bryant, who now serves on the Penobscot tribal council, told a crowd Saturday as she introduced Jackson at a campaign rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders.
Collins has not championed tribal sovereignty — the notion that Wabanaki Nations’ authority over tribal lands should not be curtailed by state oversight — in Congress the way Jackson did in the State House, and she’s generally perceived to be at odds with tribal leaders on the issue. Congress adopted the settlement with the tribes and could consequently crack it open again.
For some Wabanaki voters, Collins has won support with the depth of her personal connections paired with millions in federal spending she’s directed to Indigenous communities.
In different ways, Collins and Jackson have both proven themselves to be worthy advocates of tribal issues.
Will it win over tribal members and their allies?
‘SHE DOESN’T FORGET’
The cornucopia of the Collins campaign is her power as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
She’s taken credit for nearly $6 million for housing improvements on the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Motahkomikuk (Indian Township); $5 million to improve the wastewater system on the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Sipayik (Pleasant Point); $530,000 to improve sidewalks in a Mi’kmaq affordable housing development; and several million more for programs run by Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness.
“She’s been instrumental in so much relating to our community,” said William Nicholas Sr., the long-serving chief of Motahkomikuk and a one-time Republican who is now an independent.
When the Trump administration went on a slashing spree last year and halted payouts on federal grants, Sipayik found itself stuck, rather literally, in the water, when a $4 million grant to protect the wastewater treatment system from climate-related flooding was frozen.
Tribal officials met with Collins on the hill, and she swiftly persuaded the administration to release the funds.
On Thursday, the Collins campaign picked up an endorsement from Sipayik Chief Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett. In a letter announcing the decision, Bassett cited Collins’ successful efforts to direct and secure funding for the tribe.
Like her ability to wield congressional funding at home, Collins can effectively leverage strong interpersonal relationships in some tribal communities.
She attended the inauguration of former Sipayik Chief Fred Moore in 2015.
When Collins visits Motahkomikuk — the Wabanaki community she has directed the most money to — “it’s always about how she can help people and help the tribe,” said Chief Nicholas, who describes the senator as “a friend.”
“What I hear when I’m around my elders is the fact that she doesn’t forget them,” he said.
Shane Hill, the director of transportation, realty and asset management for the Mi’kmaq Nation, is an anti-Trump Republican. He lives in Caribou, near Collins’ family farm, and his wife works for the family’s lumber supply company.
Hill ran into the senator at Tim Hortons several years ago, when he was the superintendent of the Northern Maine Veterans Memorial Cemetery, and mentioned an upcoming inspection by the Department of Veterans Affairs. He received a near-perfect score that year, and months later Collins called him up from the crowd at a ceremony to thank him, and later sent him a signed photograph of the two of them together.
“Maybe we wouldn’t agree politically on everything,” Hill said. “However, I think she’s done a great job with her high rank and being from the community that I’m from, you know, you’d be foolish to think that doesn’t have any pull.”
‘HE DIDN’T STAND DOWN’
In response to Jackson and Gideon’s question, “How do you want to fix this?” lawmakers established a task force.
The group published 300 pages of research, testimony and recommendations that have underpinned numerous bills and laws in the years since.
Although the most ambitious of those bills haven’t cleared Mills’ desk, Bryant — who now leads the Wabanaki Alliance, a coalition of tribes fighting for tribal sovereignty — said the work reframed tribal-state relations and forced Mills to wrestle with the issue.
“I think that was brave of (Jackson) and (Gideon) to take that on,” she said.
Jackson butted heads with the governor numerous times on the issue during his time leading the Senate, calling her veto of one sovereignty bill in 2023 “disappointing but unsurprising.”
The Mi’kmaq Nation endorsed Jackson in the gubernatorial primary, but has stayed silent since he entered the Senate race.
Teresita Hamel, the Mi’kmaq vice chief who spoke only for herself, said Jackson’s leadership and willingness to fight for tribal sovereignty have won her over.
“He didn’t stand down and turn his back on the Wabanaki Nations,” she said.
Even tribal leaders like Nicholas will praise Jackson’s affability and commitment to sovereignty, an issue that Collins has been mostly quiet about, or at times antagonistic.
There was a 2012 incident, when Collins confirmed with the Office of the Maine Attorney General that an amendment to federal disaster relief laws would usurp state authority and therefore not benefit the Wabanaki Nations. She elicited as much from the bill’s sponsor on the Senate floor: “This provision would not and should not apply within or to the State of Maine.”
Collins has maintained she was unaware of the chiefs’ objections at the time.
And in 2022, there was a bill sponsored by Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd-District, that would’ve made all beneficial federal laws applicable to the Wabanaki Nations going forward. It wouldn’t have restored full tribal sovereignty, but it was a step toward righting what Wabanaki leaders say is one of the 1980 settlement’s most pernicious wrongs.
In the Democratically controlled Senate, it was a member of the majority caucus, Maine’s independent Sen. Angus King, who blocked the bill.
Collins earned no favors when she stayed silent.
“We were never in a position to flesh out her position, because there were other people in the Senate who caucused with Democrats who were standing in the way of it,” Golden said in an interview.
STATE VS. FEDERAL
Tribal sovereignty is one of those rare divisive issues that transcends party politics. Among non-tribal politicians, the dividing line appears generational, observed Golden.
“There’s a lot of people that are very dug in against tribal sovereignty in Maine politics, and they’re all, let’s just say, above a certain age,” he said.
After King killed Golden’s bill, lawmakers and tribal leaders alike are aligned in feeling that sovereignty has to start with support at the state level.
That’s why four chiefs, including Nicholas, endorsed Democrat Hannah Pingree for governor last week. Pingree has promised to pass and sign tribal sovereignty legislation in her first 100 days.
Bassett, the sole chief to make an endorsement in the Senate race so far, was also the only chief who did not endorse Pingree.
A working group in the Maine Legislature is currently developing a proposal for state-level changes that would allow the Wabanaki Nations to benefit from all or most federal laws that apply to other Indian tribes.
State and tribal officials are confident that they can make the change at the state level.
A Collins spokesperson in a statement Tuesday reiterated the senator’s support for the applicability of individual federal laws, but declined to take a position on the matter at the federal level. A spokesperson for Jackson said “Troy believes the Wabanaki Nations deserve the same respect, rights and opportunities as other federally recognized tribes,” but did not take a stance on this specific issue.
People like Nicholas and Hill will overlook Collins’ past silence on sovereignty and take the wins — all $6 million of them — that are attainable until the issue is settled at the state level.
“When we get there, I think we’re going to have that discussion, but it’s not right now,” Nicholas said.
Hamel, the Mi’kmaq vice chief, looks at it differently.
“Having a champion for sovereignty at this time in our growth, I think that’s extremely important,” she said. “I think that that’s the fight we need to take on.”
Jackson and Collins both have their shortcomings: Jackson his lack of power and experience, and Collins her unwillingness to lead the charge.
Their supporters are not willing to let these imperfections be the enemy of their good.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 15 to add information about Chief Pos Bassett’s endorsement.

title: Letter: Russian diesel deal must be stopped
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I am deeply troubled by President Donald Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to waive sanctions and allow Russia to sell diesel to the United States and the world. Experts say that the diesel we would get from Russia would do little to offset the price of diesel in the United States. Rather, this deal would aid an adversary in its illegal war against Ukraine, reverse current U.S. policy on Russia oil trade, and subvert past U.S. efforts to help Ukraine.
Are we willing to waste the billions of tax dollars we’ve spent defending Ukraine by aiding Russia at this critical time? Russia is currently testing the resolve of NATO to defend against military threats in Europe, is aiding Iran in its conflict with the U.S., and continues to attack Ukraine’s civilians and infrastructure as another winter approaches.
Congress just passed a bill directing the president to increase sanctions against Russia, but President Trump is moving in the opposite direction. What would the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who the bill was named for, say?
I urge others to write to your representatives and ask them to speak out against the Russian diesel deal and to stop it.
Wally Jakubas
Hampden

title: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson split sharply on democracy’s future in final debate
text:
At a Thursday debate, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins said American democracy “will be just fine” while Democratic opponent Troy Jackson questioned whether President Donald Trump will leave office when his term ends.
The exchange came in response to a submitted question toward the end of the fourth and final debate of Maine’s toss-up U.S. Senate race, hosted by Maine Public, News Center Maine and the Portland Press Herald at the Gracie Theatre at Husson University in Bangor.
It was the clearest of the many philosophical divides in a race that could decide control of the Senate, and it gets at the central challenge for Collins. The five-term Republican is running in a Democratic-leaning state where Trump is unpopular, needing a significant share of voters who dislike the president to stick with her as they have in the past.
The question came from Bridget O’Brien of Harpswell, who asked in a video whether democracy is under attack and what it will look like in five to 10 years. Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash, said Republicans in Congress have handed Trump their power over wars and tariffs, pointing to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.
“I do think that our democracy is at risk,” Jackson said. “Donald Trump is trying every trick in the book to keep power.”
Collins, who was one of seven Republicans who voted to convict Trump on an impeachment charge related to the Capitol riot, took a longer view. She said she has worked with five presidents and supported the campaign of only one, George W. Bush, and that presidents of both parties have tried to take more power from Congress.
“I think that Congress does need to keep reasserting itself,” Collins said. “But I think our democracy will be just fine.”
Jackson went further on the night’s final policy question, about Trump’s warmer posture toward rivals like Russia and China. He said Trump “wants to be a dictator” and that the “single biggest problem with democracy” is whether he will “go away when his term is up.”
“We have to make damn sure” that happens, Jackson said. Trump has repeatedly floated a third term, which the 22nd Amendment bars.
The debate was held before an invited audience, with each campaign given 100 seats. It was interrupted early when a person wearing what appeared to be a press badge shouted as Collins began answering a taped question from a University of Maine student.
“This is obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Collins said.
“Oh, shut up,” Jackson replied. “I don’t even know that kid.”
The candidates also clashed over money. Collins asked how Jackson could say he does not benefit from corporate PAC or billionaire money while running “hybrid ads” with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which has taken money from billionaires and corporate PACs.
Jackson said he had “no knowledge of those ads” and that it “would be illegal” for him to make decisions on them. That is true of outside groups but not of hybrid ads, which a party and a campaign pay for jointly. Collins and the National Republican Senatorial Committee have spent about $2.4 million on such ads to about $835,000 for Jackson and the DSCC, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. After the debate, a Jackson spokesperson said he misspoke.
The candidates made their cases for Senate control at the top of the debate. Asked how the country would benefit from their party controlling the Senate, Jackson said a Democratic majority would block anti-abortion court picks, tax cuts for the wealthy and the war with Iran, which has driven up fuel prices.
“People are going to start losing their businesses, losing their homes because of the Republicans’ insistence on doing what Donald Trump wants,” Jackson said.
Collins pointed to “totally open borders” under President Joe Biden and to her own record. She said studies show she is the most bipartisan member of the Senate.
“We need more people in the center,” she said. “We don’t need more people who are going to vote a straight party line.”
BDN writer Benjamin Kail contributed to this report.

title: Norridgewock man sentenced to 45 years in prison for murder of girlfriend’s son
text:
SKOWHEGAN, Maine (WABI) - A Norridgewock man will spend 45 years in prison for the murder of his girlfriend’s son.
Daniel Markey, 60, was convicted of killing Christopher Nickerson back in August.
Nickerson, 38, was shot to death at the home Markey shared with Nickerson’s mother in Norridgewock in March 2025. Nickerson’s mother, Kathleen, said tensions had grown between the pair leading up to the shooting.
Defense attorneys claimed that Markey killed Nickerson in self-defense during a physical altercation that left him injured and disoriented. Prosecutors argued that Nickerson was shot while attempting to surrender. It took a jury only 40 minutes to convict him.
Kathleen Nickerson, the victim’s mother, wrote a letter to the judge asking him to consider the pain her family has felt since her son’s murder in his sentencing decision Thursday.
“It feels as though a part of my identity was taken from me,” victim advocate Jamie Miller read on Nickerson’s behalf. “My hopes, my dreams, and my sense of purpose have all been changed forever. What makes this even harder is that this was done by someone who claimed to love me. I cannot understand how someone who said he loved me could do something so horrible.“
A judge ruled Markey will serve 45 years behind bars and ordered him to pay $3,700 to cover Nickerson’s funeral costs.
Markey was not present in court for the sentencing.

title: ‘Doomsday’ glacier is melting more aggressively than previously projected, study says
text:
(CNN) - A new study suggests the Thwaites Glacier, nicknamed the “Doomsday Glacier,” is melting “more aggressively” than previously projected.
Thwaites Glacier is located in West Antarctica. It got its nickname due to the impact its collapse would have on the rise of sea levels.
The glacier’s melting is driven by processes at the point where the ice rises up from the seabed and starts to float on the ocean as an ice shelf. That point is known as the “grounding line.”
Researchers say satellite data shows that line is actually a “grounding zone” that is sometimes miles wide. They say it is allowing warm ocean water to reach deep underneath the ice sheets and cause vigorous melting.
Using a new ice sheet model, the researchers predict the glacier could contribute up to 1.2 inches of sea level rise by the year 2100. That is twice the amount of previous estimates.

title: East Windham Conservation Area and Lowell Preserve united as Windham Community Forest
text:
Naming ceremony and Universal Access Trail ribbon-cutting planned for Saturday
WESTBROOK – The crowd-favorite natural spaces of East Windham Conservation Area and Lowell Preserve have been officially united under one identity. On Sept. 8, the Windham Town Council voted to formally rename the combined property as Windham Community Forest.
“As we learned more about how people use the spaces and began thinking about long-term management plans, it became clear that unifying the two preserves under one identity would make a lot of sense,” Linda Brooks, director of Windham Parks and Recreation, said.
The Council established the East Windham Steering Committee in January to recommend a new name that unifies the two preserves and to develop a process for establishing a master plan for further development and management of the property. This committee is composed of 11 representatives from town committees, recreational groups, nearby residential associations, and the general public and is staffed by Brooks and Presumpscot Regional Land Trust’s Executive Director Will Sedlack.
The committee brainstormed names over the course of several sessions and sent the top four choices for public input via FlashVote in mid-August, then shared survey results with the Council to make the final name selection. The Council also approved new names for the two entrances to the preserve: the trailhead and parking area formerly for East Windham Conservation Area will be called Atherton Hill Trailhead (189 Falmouth Road) and the one formerly for Lowell Preserve will be called Lowell Farm Trailhead (45 Falmouth Road), honoring the history of both locations.
The land now known as Windham Community Forest consists of 1,104 acres of hilly and forested terrain with a mix of hardwood trees and scenic views of the White Mountains and Little Duck Pond. It is part of an over 2,000-acre conservation corridor–larger than any state park in Southern Maine.
“The scale of this project is considerable and is an incredible asset to our community,” Mark Morrison, chair of the Windham Town Council, said. “We believe that the name change will help promote this area as a recreation hub, bringing more visitors to Windham to experience this outdoor destination.”
The Town of Windham and PRLT have jointly managed Lowell Preserve since 2021 and East Windham Conservation Area since it was opened in 2023.
“With the Town as the property owner and PRLT holding a conservation easement, we have collaborated to make sure these spaces provide both a great place for the community to recreate year-round and for wildlife to thrive in perpetuity,” Sedlack said. The purchase of East Windham Conservation Area was made possible by the Land for Maine’s Future program, the Federal Land and Water Conservation Fund, the Town of Windham’s conservation bond, lead business partner Maine Community Bank and over 400 local individuals, businesses and foundations.
The preserve offers over 16 miles of trails for hiking, mountain biking, trail running and cross-country skiing. The newest trail is a Universal Access Trail, designed with a low grade and smooth path so wheelchairs, strollers, and other users with mobility concerns have access to the outdoors. The one-mile trail stretches from Atherton Hill Trailhead to the White Mountains Overlook and was partially funded by the Land and Water Conservation Fund.
To celebrate the new name and the completion of the Universal Access Trail, PRLT and the Town are hosting a naming ceremony and ribbon-cutting on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 9 a.m. at the Atherton Hill Trailhead. All are welcome to come recognize and celebrate these community milestones. Weather permitting, following the ceremony, attendees will be invited to enjoy a guided walk along the UA Trail and experience the improved access it provides for all visitors to the preserve.
These changes are all part of continued strategic improvements at the preserve to elevate the user experience and to make the spaces easier for PRLT and the Town to manage. The steering committee will continue meeting to develop a management plan for the property. For future updates on the committee’s work, visit https://www.windhammaine.us/880/East-Windham-Steering-Committee.
For more information about the celebration, visit https://www.windhammaine.us/m/calendar/event/detail/7881.
For more information about Windham Community Forest, visit https://www.prlt.org/windham-community-forest.

title: Showers on Friday, cold wind Saturday
text:
Rain Friday, cold wind Saturday
Rain Friday, cold wind Saturday
Widespread rain arrives from west to east Friday morning as winds pick up, gusting to 20 to 30 mph from the south. A soggy morning is expected, with a lull likely in the afternoon before a cold front crosses with more rain during the evening.
Expected rainfall amounts range from around 0.25 i to 1 inch by Saturday morning. As cold air flows in Friday night, mountain showers change from rain to snow.
Sprinkles may linger along the coast Saturday morning but will give way to a mostly sunny afternoon. Mountain snow showers continue and flurries may spill farther south. Winds from the north-northwest gust to around 35 mph, creating wind chills in the 20s, 30s, and low 40s.
Temperatures fall below freezing across the state Saturday night, setting the stage for our coldest morning yet. Sunshine then dominates the forecast into next week, with temperatures climbing closer to average.

title: Soggy Friday in Maine with a taste of November this weekend
text:
Soggy Friday in Maine with a taste of November this weekend
Soaking rains arrive Friday, with windy and cold weather arriving for the weekend.
Soggy Friday in Maine with a taste of November this weekend
Soaking rains arrive Friday, with windy and cold weather arriving for the weekend.
High pressure quickly sweeps across New England today, giving Maine one last dry, mild day before damp and cold weather takes over for the weekend. Rain moves from west to east Friday morning as a low-pressure system tracks along or just northwest of the Canadian border.
The storm will bring a half-inch to an inch of beneficial rain to most of the state Friday afternoon and evening, with heavy downpours possible at times. Temperatures will remain high enough for rain across most areas, though flurries could mix in across the higher western mountains early Friday morning before changing to rain. As cold air moves in Friday night, rain will taper to snow showers in the mountains and northern valleys.
Late fall conditions arrive Saturday as strong winds push cold air across the region. High temperatures will top out in the 40s to near 50 along the coast, while mountains stay in the 30s. Combined with northwest wind gusts up to 30 mph regionwide and 40 mph in the foothills, wind chills will drop into the 20s and 30s. Mountain areas will see upslope snow showers, and conditions could become hazardous for hikers above treeline.
After a very cold Saturday night with lows in the 20s and lower 30s, conditions improve through the day on Sunday. High pressure will build over the state, bringing dry conditions and a gradual warming trend through early to midweek next week, with temperatures climbing back into the 50s and 60s.

title: 4 takeaways from the final debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The fourth and final debate in the Maine U.S. Senate race was a spirited affair that plowed some new ground, with Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican Susan Collins weighing in on gun control and the possible reform of the U.S. Supreme Court.
Thursday’s debate at the Gracie Theater at Husson University in Bangor was the only one to have a live audience, invited by the campaigns. It allowed for crowd reactions — and at one point an interruption by a protester — leading to a memorable exchange.
Jackson, a 58-year-old former logger, continued to tie Collins to President Donald Trump, whose actions and policies Jackson argued are driving up the prices of consumer goods, energy and fuel.
Collins, meanwhile, continued to focus on her seniority, which she says has brought $1.5 billion in federal earmarks to Maine in recent years. The 73-year-old has also sought to distance herself from Trump and shift blame onto Jackson for high energy prices, citing his votes in support of solar energy as Maine Senate president.
Here are the major takeaways from the final debate before the Nov. 3 election. It was conducted in partnership with Maine Public, the Portland Press Herald and NEWSCENTER Maine.
1. Protester interrupts, Jackson snaps
About 15 minutes into the debate, someone in the crowd stood up and began shouting about data centers. The moderator took a brief pause as security removed the young man, who appeared to be wearing a press badge.
“That’s obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Collins quipped.
Jackson shot back.
“Oh shut up,” Jackson said. “I don’t even know that kid.”
Event organizers said the individual was not on the pre-registered media list, but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in.
In an email Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send a reporter to the debate, and that the credential must have been fabricated.
2. Jackson stumbles on campaign finance
Collins and Jackson each had the opportunity to ask each other a question. And Collins appeared to get the best of both exchanges.
Collins called out Jackson for vowing not to take money from billionaires and corporate PACs. But Collins noted that Jackson’s campaign has been running joint ads with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which she said received money from 28 billionaires and 190 corporate PACs.
Jackson appeared to have been caught off guard, at first confusing the joint ads, which contain his endorsement, with independent super PACs, which he cannot legally coordinate with.
Jackson, who earlier in the day announced he’d give away $15,000 in donations from oil and pharmaceutical lobbyists, also acknowledged that billionaires are supporting his campaign — a statement that drew a reaction from the audience.
“As far as billionaires that I might have on my campaign, that is accurate, but I haven’t made any deals like Sen. Collins has with those billionaires,” he said. “I don’t owe (them) my votes. I’m going to tax those billionaires when I get the U.S. Senate.”
During his turn, Jackson brought up his working class roots and asked Collins if she looks down at him or all working people. Collins talked about how she started working in potato fields in Aroostook County at the age of 10.
“I do not look down on you or on anyone,” Collins said. “I have enormous respect for all the people of Maine.”
3. Supreme Court reform
The two candidates sparred over whether the U.S. Supreme Court needs reforming.
The Democrat said he supports term limits and enforceable ethics standards and would be open to adding members to the court, which he said is currently working for Trump and “the billionaire class.”
“It’s just gross the way that this has ended up,” Jackson said. “And we have to do something meaningful to actually give people’s confidence back.”
Collins disagreed. She said increasing the number of justices would go “completely against the vision of those who wrote the Constitution.” She stuck to her position when a moderator noted that the current number of nine justices was not in the Constitution.
“It’s inconsistent with the whole idea of the Supreme Court being insulated from politics,” Collins said. “That would make it a totally political body.”
Jackson, however, would get the last word.
“We have the best court that money can buy right now,” he said.
4. Through the looking glass on guns
A question about assault weapons produced some surprising answers.
Collins noted that she was a supporter of the original ban on assault weapons passed by Congress in the 90s. She accused Democrats of allowing that ban to expire because they wanted to expand it. And she said she voted to ban bump stocks, which increase the rate of fire in a weapon.
She said she supports “reasonable limits” on magazine capacity and would be open to increasing the age to legally obtain an assault weapon.
Jackson seemed more pro-gun by comparison.
“I’m not in favor of increasing the age,” he said. “It actually comes down to the person. I mean, we do have a culture here in Maine of people being able to buy guns.”
Jackson said he would not oppose an assault weapons ban, but he would oppose taking weapons away from people who already have them.
“I don’t see a good reason for assault weapons,” he said. “You can’t use them for hunting or anything like that. And so I would not be opposed to banning them.”

title: Jackson backs sovereignty, Collins delivers cash. Which matters to Wabanaki communities?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Weeks after he was sworn in as president of the state Senate, Democrats Troy Jackson and House Speaker Sara Gideon called a meeting of the Wabanaki chiefs at the capitol. All five attended.
There, the lawmakers posed a question: “How do you want to fix this?”
By early 2019, there was a growing appetite to address the fraught relationship between the state and the Wabanaki Nations, which stems from a 1980 settlement that placed unique limits on the tribes’ jurisdiction. But Gov. Janet Mills was known to oppose sweeping changes to that agreement, and so the can of worms Jackson and Gideon were opening was a politically inconvenient one.
Tribal officials in the room were struck by the earnestness of the new leaders’ approach.
“That was refreshing to hear,” recalled Maulian Bryant, who attended as the ambassador for the Penobscot Nation. “I think for a long time the tribes were being told by the state what was good for us.”
Now locked in a furiously tight U.S. Senate race against Republican incumbent Susan Collins, Jackson’s past is serving him well in tribal communities.
“Troy is one of the leaders that we can credit with changing tribal-state relations in the state of Maine, and I am so honored to be his friend and supporter,” Bryant, who now serves on the Penobscot tribal council, told a crowd Saturday as she introduced Jackson at a campaign rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders.
Collins has not championed tribal sovereignty — the notion that Wabanaki Nations’ authority over tribal lands should not be curtailed by state oversight — in Congress the way Jackson did in the State House, and she’s generally perceived to be at odds with tribal leaders on the issue. Congress adopted the settlement with the tribes and could consequently crack it open again.
For some Wabanaki voters, Collins has won support with the depth of her personal connections paired with millions in federal spending she’s directed to Indigenous communities.
In different ways, Collins and Jackson have both proven themselves to be worthy advocates of tribal issues.
Will it win over tribal members and their allies?
‘SHE DOESN’T FORGET’
The cornucopia of the Collins campaign is her power as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
She’s taken credit for nearly $6 million for housing improvements on the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Motahkomikuk (Indian Township); $5 million to improve the wastewater system on the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Sipayik (Pleasant Point); $530,000 to improve sidewalks in a Mi’kmaq affordable housing development; and several million more for programs run by Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness.
“She’s been instrumental in so much relating to our community,” said William Nicholas Sr., the long-serving chief of Motahkomikuk and a one-time Republican who is now an independent.
When the Trump administration went on a slashing spree last year and halted payouts on federal grants, Sipayik found itself stuck, rather literally, in the water, when a $4 million grant to protect the wastewater treatment system from climate-related flooding was frozen.
Tribal officials met with Collins on the hill, and she swiftly persuaded the administration to release the funds.
On Thursday, the Collins campaign picked up an endorsement from Sipayik Chief Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett. In a letter announcing the decision, Bassett cited Collins’ successful efforts to direct and secure funding for the tribe.
Like her ability to wield congressional funding at home, Collins can effectively leverage strong interpersonal relationships in some tribal communities.
She attended the inauguration of former Sipayik Chief Fred Moore in 2015.
When Collins visits Motahkomikuk — the Wabanaki community she has directed the most money to — “it’s always about how she can help people and help the tribe,” said Chief Nicholas, who describes the senator as “a friend.”
“What I hear when I’m around my elders is the fact that she doesn’t forget them,” he said.
Shane Hill, the director of transportation, realty and asset management for the Mi’kmaq Nation, is an anti-Trump Republican. He lives in Caribou, near Collins’ family farm, and his wife works for the family’s lumber supply company.
Hill ran into the senator at Tim Hortons several years ago, when he was the superintendent of the Northern Maine Veterans Memorial Cemetery, and mentioned an upcoming inspection by the Department of Veterans Affairs. He received a near-perfect score that year, and months later Collins called him up from the crowd at a ceremony to thank him, and later sent him a signed photograph of the two of them together.
“Maybe we wouldn’t agree politically on everything,” Hill said. “However, I think she’s done a great job with her high rank and being from the community that I’m from, you know, you’d be foolish to think that doesn’t have any pull.”
‘HE DIDN’T STAND DOWN’
In response to Jackson and Gideon’s question, “How do you want to fix this?” lawmakers established a task force.
The group published 300 pages of research, testimony and recommendations that have underpinned numerous bills and laws in the years since.
Although the most ambitious of those bills haven’t cleared Mills’ desk, Bryant — who now leads the Wabanaki Alliance, a coalition of tribes fighting for tribal sovereignty — said the work reframed tribal-state relations and forced Mills to wrestle with the issue.
“I think that was brave of (Jackson) and (Gideon) to take that on,” she said.
Jackson butted heads with the governor numerous times on the issue during his time leading the Senate, calling her veto of one sovereignty bill in 2023 “disappointing but unsurprising.”
The Mi’kmaq Nation endorsed Jackson in the gubernatorial primary, but has stayed silent since he entered the Senate race.
Teresita Hamel, the Mi’kmaq vice chief who spoke only for herself, said Jackson’s leadership and willingness to fight for tribal sovereignty have won her over.
“He didn’t stand down and turn his back on the Wabanaki Nations,” she said.
Even tribal leaders like Nicholas will praise Jackson’s affability and commitment to sovereignty, an issue that Collins has been mostly quiet about, or at times antagonistic.
There was a 2012 incident, when Collins confirmed with the Office of the Maine Attorney General that an amendment to federal disaster relief laws would usurp state authority and therefore not benefit the Wabanaki Nations. She elicited as much from the bill’s sponsor on the Senate floor: “This provision would not and should not apply within or to the State of Maine.”
Collins has maintained she was unaware of the chiefs’ objections at the time.
And in 2022, there was a bill sponsored by Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd-District, that would’ve made all beneficial federal laws applicable to the Wabanaki Nations going forward. It wouldn’t have restored full tribal sovereignty, but it was a step toward righting what Wabanaki leaders say is one of the 1980 settlement’s most pernicious wrongs.
In the Democratically controlled Senate, it was a member of the majority caucus, Maine’s independent Sen. Angus King, who blocked the bill.
Collins earned no favors when she stayed silent.
“We were never in a position to flesh out her position, because there were other people in the Senate who caucused with Democrats who were standing in the way of it,” Golden said in an interview.
STATE VS. FEDERAL
Tribal sovereignty is one of those rare divisive issues that transcends party politics. Among non-tribal politicians, the dividing line appears generational, observed Golden.
“There’s a lot of people that are very dug in against tribal sovereignty in Maine politics, and they’re all, let’s just say, above a certain age,” he said.
After King killed Golden’s bill, lawmakers and tribal leaders alike are aligned in feeling that sovereignty has to start with support at the state level.
That’s why four chiefs, including Nicholas, endorsed Democrat Hannah Pingree for governor last week. Pingree has promised to pass and sign tribal sovereignty legislation in her first 100 days.
Bassett, the sole chief to make an endorsement in the Senate race so far, was also the only chief who did not endorse Pingree.
A working group in the Maine Legislature is currently developing a proposal for state-level changes that would allow the Wabanaki Nations to benefit from all or most federal laws that apply to other Indian tribes.
State and tribal officials are confident that they can make the change at the state level.
A Collins spokesperson in a statement Tuesday reiterated the senator’s support for the applicability of individual federal laws, but declined to take a position on the matter at the federal level. A spokesperson for Jackson said “Troy believes the Wabanaki Nations deserve the same respect, rights and opportunities as other federally recognized tribes,” but did not take a stance on this specific issue.
People like Nicholas and Hill will overlook Collins’ past silence on sovereignty and take the wins — all $6 million of them — that are attainable until the issue is settled at the state level.
“When we get there, I think we’re going to have that discussion, but it’s not right now,” Nicholas said.
Hamel, the Mi’kmaq vice chief, looks at it differently.
“Having a champion for sovereignty at this time in our growth, I think that’s extremely important,” she said. “I think that that’s the fight we need to take on.”
Jackson and Collins both have their shortcomings: Jackson his lack of power and experience, and Collins her unwillingness to lead the charge.
Their supporters are not willing to let these imperfections be the enemy of their good.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 15 to add information about Chief Pos Bassett’s endorsement.

title: Is the Michigan Senate race make-or-break for the progressive movement?
text:
Is the Michigan Senate race make-or-break for the progressive movement?
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed says he's not thinking much about the progressive movement, but his Senate race is seen as a high-stakes test case for a growing faction of the Democratic Party.
Is the Michigan Senate race make-or-break for the progressive movement?
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed says he's not thinking much about the progressive movement, but his Senate race is seen as a high-stakes test case for a growing faction of the Democratic Party.
Progressive candidates beat out moderates in some key primaries this year, but now, the movement is gearing up for an even bigger test as it looks to prove its viability in high-stakes battlegrounds that will determine control of Congress.
A Brookings Institution study of this year's most competitive races found mainstream candidates were more successful in 2026's most competitive primaries, with progressive Democrats winning 18% of the time.
The Michigan Senate race is seen as the biggest test case of the progressive brand in a swing state that President Donald Trump carried twice. The contest between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is on a short list of races considered "toss ups" in this fall's midterm elections.
"I'm not really thinking that much about the progressive movement," said El-Sayed when asked whether he views his candidacy as a make-or-break moment for the movement. "I'm more thinking about the lives of the 10 million people I'm hoping to serve. This is a make-or-break moment for their lives."
Ron Stockton, a political science professor at the University of Michigan-Dearborn, views the contest as the most important Senate race in the country for the direction of the Democratic Party.
"Even if every single progressive loses, the issues have won, because those issues are not going away," Stockton said.
The risk, according to Stockton, is that Democrats could lose voters who feel alienated by progressive positions, as Republicans frame the growing faction as radical.
The Democratic Socialists of America's metro-Detroit chapter has more than doubled its membership since the last presidential election, from roughly 700 to over 1,600 people, according to the organization's internal tally.
"We need real change. Things have gotten to a really bad place, and so these policies that maybe that you're, you know, calling 'progressive' just aren't really considered all that radical anymore," said Lila Brickner, who co-chairs the DSA chapter.
The national DSA platform includes establishing public ownership of the largest corporations. It calls for universal healthcare, rent control and free college. The organization also supports abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and even prisons long-term, going well beyond the positions of establishment Democrats.
"There are a lot of establishment Democrats that I've idolized over the years, and I kind of look back and realize that their messaging was really vague and opaque," Brickner said. "Your average voter sees through that, and they're looking for people who actually stand for something."
The DSA has not officially endorsed El-Sayed, but Brickner is planning to support him because he has embraced policies like Medicare for All and eliminating ICE.
El-Sayed does not identify as a Democratic Socialist and has said that he believes in capitalism. He declined to offer specifics when asked whether he would distance himself from other parts of the DSA platform.
"I don't think about myself with reference to any other group," he said during a brief interview last month.
But El-Sayed's overlap with the DSA is a major concern for Michigan voter Chelsea Rebeck. She describes herself as a lifelong Democrat, but she is planning to back Rogers in the Senate race.
"This could be the end of the Democratic Party as we know it, and they need to wake up," Rebeck said. "We have been completely hijacked by people that don't share the same values that the traditional Democratic Party shares."
It's a sentiment that Trump has tried to seize on in an effort to link the progressive movement to communism.
“They use the word 'social Democrat' because it sounds so nice, but it’s really communism you’re talking about,” Trump told reporters in June.
"I don't think we need to respond to those points at all," said Mara Matta, co-chair of the Detroit DSA's Black-Brown Alliance. "I'm more interested in having those deep, meaningful conversations on what actually matters to people in their everyday lives than trying to rebut these boogeyman claims."
The Rogers campaign did not respond to multiple interview requests.
