title: How do I know my loved ones’ ashes are real? Behind the scenes of the cremation process
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Death can be an uncomfortable conversation, but leaving your loved ones without a plan puts you at risk of ending up in the wrong hands.
Cremation has surpassed traditional burial in popularity in the country. The North American Cremation Association said in 2025 the cremation rate was 62.8%.
Dr. Joe Paciarelli, a grief counselor in Greenville, has seen the importance of ashes to loved ones through his work.
“There’s one case of somebody who, they had such a powerful emotional connection and attachment with their spouse that they actually kept the urn on their body, in a bag,” Paciarelli said. “When they were sleeping, when they were at work, when they went on vacation.”
When you choose cremation, you’re trusting a stranger with something irreplaceable. So how do you know it’s really your loved one coming home? Horror stories of mishandled cremations have sparked doubt in some minds.
Paciarelli said the concern comes up a lot.
“People mention maybe offhandedly, I don’t really know if it’s actually them or not,“ Paciarelli said. ”There’s no way for me to tell."
Our investigation went inside South Carolina funeral homes to find out what you need to know. We came away with three questions you should ask any funeral home.
Does it include a private viewing?
For Jay McAfee, the CEO of Thomas McAfee Funeral Homes, the death care industry isn’t just business; it’s a century-old promise to his community. McAfee’s great-great-grandfather started the company in 1913, making him and his cousin the fifth generation of McAfees to run the business.
“We’re going to operate with absolute transparency,” McAfee said. “If anybody wants to come in and you know, get a behind the scenes look to our facilities, we are absolutely willing to be open about that.”
McAfee said one of the ways they ensure the integrity of the cremation process is through a private family viewing.
“It’s going to serve two purposes,” McAfee said. “They’re going to confirm the identity of their loved one who’s in the cremation container at the time... The second purpose it serves is as a meaningful way to say goodbye.”
McAfee said the viewing takes place in a serene setting and they work hard to make sure it’s not a clinical or transactional experience that many people fear.
Thomas McAfee offers public tours as part of their “Unmasking the Mysteries of Cremation” program. The next session will be held on May 28 at the Northwest location on White Horse Road.
How do they track the process?
Funeral Director Trevor Buchanan at Robinson Funeral Home said if a funeral home isn’t transparent, it’s a sign to walk away.
“You deserve transparency,” Buchanan said. “If a funeral home cannot answer your questions without hesitation, that is a major red flag.”
Buchanan took FOX Carolina Investigates through each step of their cremation process and how Robinson Funeral Home logs it all.
After a private family viewing, the family signs an identification form stating they saw their loved one. Then a barcode is placed on the loved one’s ankle, which is tracked through a software system.
Barcodes are also on the retort equipment and scanned at the start of cremation, for any changes during the cremation and at the end of cremation. Nothing can be scanned out of order.
“We take multiple steps that are above what the law requires,” Buchanan said. “Including having the cameras that record everything that occurs in our cremation center.”
A numbered medallion corresponding with the number of the cremation certificate also stays with the body the entire time and is attached to the bag of cremains.
“That medallion is the physical link to a family’s loved one’s identity after the cremation process,” Buchanan said.
Do they operate a crematory on-site?
Both Thomas McAfee and Robinson Funeral Homes operate their own crematories, and have rooms with a viewing window into the area where the retort is located.
“Any family that wishes to be present at the start of their loved ones’ cremation, this is the room that they come to,” Buchanan said.
Families can even push the button to start the loading process, which is important in some religious practices.
Both Buchanan and McAfee said they want the community to know that just because you choose cremation doesn’t mean you can’t have a service or a meaningful experience.
“We can do a memorial service, a celebration of life, a full service where your loved one is present in a casket for an open casket visitation and service,” Buchanan said.
“I wish families understood that cremation doesn’t have to be transactional,” McAfee said. “There’s so many options that they have when they choose cremation. We just see so often families coming to us with anxiety, you know, because they don’t know what to expect. And so, our job is to educate them and help them understand what the experience is going to be like for them and hopefully ease that anxiety.”
Pre-plan end of life
Experts say that pre-planning is crucial to protecting the people you leave behind from confusion and last-minute decision making.
They say guesswork can become a burden fast, especially when families are left to decide what their love one wanted. That includes how to pay for it and who has the authority to say yes.
“If you’re not legally divorced, that spouse has to sign,” Buchanan told us. “If you have five kids across the United States, all five of those kids would need to sign for cremation to occur.”
Pre-planning can give you your own voice in the legal process. In certain states, you can sign your own cremation authorization and pre-planning can lock in prices.
But the plan doesn’t have to start with a funeral contract. Experts suggest you write down your wish and put them somewhere your family can find them.
The more open of a conversation you have with loved ones about end of life care will mean less guesswork later on.

title: Troy Jackson got $15k from big oil, pharma lobbyists. He’s giving it to charity.
text:
Troy Jackson is donating about $15,000 in political contributions from oil and pharmaceutical lobbyists, his campaign said on Thursday.
Jackson, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, said in a news release that he will donate $5,000 each to Keep ME Warm/Project Heat and the Good Shepherd Food Bank, and $2,500 each to Maine Needs and the Augusta Food Bank.
The lobbyists’ donations are a small fraction of the $20.4 million his campaign says it raised since Jackson secured the nomination on July 25. In giving the donations to charity, Jackson said he’s keeping the”Dirigo Pledge” he made during the abbreviated Democratic primary to replace Graham Platner in July.
“I said I wouldn’t take money from Big Oil or Big Pharma lobbyists, and I meant it,” Jackson said in a written statement. “That money is better spent helping Mainers heat their homes, put food on the table, afford the things they need, and get through a tough winter.”
Jackson also pledged, among other things, to refuse donations from corporate PACs and the pro-Israel AIPAC; to fully disclose his campaign finances; to advocate for a Constitutional amendment to get big money out of politics; and to advocate for a ban on congressional stock trading.
The announcement came hours before his fourth and final debate with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, 73, who has called out the 58-year-old former logger for accepting corporate contributions as state Senate president.
And it comes as polls show that inflation and high gas prices are among the top issues on voters’ minds.
The deadline for campaign finance reports to be filed is midnight Thursday. Jackson has yet to release his full campaign finance report, despite saying in a televised debate that he would release it on Wednesday morning.
Collins, meanwhile, released hers Thursday afternoon, reporting a total of $3.9 million from July 1 through Sept. 30. Her total for the campaign is now nearly $17.7 million. She reported $5.4 million in cash for the final stretch of the campaign.
Despite Jackson’s fundraising, Republicans have a clear money advantage in the Maine’s closely watched race.
So far, Republican-aligned groups have spent or reserved $151.5 million on ads, compared to $110.7 million by Democrat-aligned groups, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal probe, AP source says
text:
Rep. Ilhan Omar's phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal probe, AP source says
Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker's phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar's immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Washington D.C. U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on" related to Omar and that her office is also probing issues concerning the lawmaker's financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar's home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the Democrat for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

title: Maine Wildness is the name of the state’s new women’s soccer team
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — The name was announced and was immediately greeted by an extended and hearty ovation.
The Maine Wildness, the newly named amateur women’s soccer club that will be a sister team to the Portland Hearts of Pine, is already a hit. And so is the club’s logo, a blend of new imagery with a clear connection to the Hearts.
“It’s perfect. All of it,” said Nicole Vinal, a native Mainer who lives in Brunswick. Vinal said the name and the story behind it represents her. “I’m scrappy. I’m a hard worker. I love the outdoors, the wilderness.”
Vinal, a season ticket-holder for both the Maine Wildness and the Hearts of Pine, was among a crowd of 500 supporters at Madrid’s in Portland for Thursday’s name and brand reveal.
The Maine Wildness will begin play in the spring and early summer of 2027, competing in the USL W League, which in 2026 had 96 teams across 16 regionalized divisions.
The name and logo were the result of months of planning and community outreach by the organization, which has achieved worldwide recognition for its Hearts of Pine branding and merchandise. Club representatives held town hall-style meetings and an online forum with U.S. Women’s National Team legends, including Michelle Akers, who has become a founding adviser for the Maine Wildness.
Hannah Sirois, the club’s vice president for fan experience and the point person for the women’s team, said the Wildness name was first isolated when staff members were huddled around a campfire, riffing on themes of wilderness and natural beauty.
“It’s about being your unapologetic self,” Sirois said.
Catherine Culley, one of the club’s founding co-owners, had tears in her eyes when the name was revealed and the crowd voiced their wholehearted endorsement.
“I think women need this right now as a positive environment that welcomes women for everything they are,” Culley said. “It’s something I feel the community needed right now. And I think it is important for young girls to see a path forward and it’s equal to the men. Not the same as the men.”
Prior to the name reveal, the audience heard from club personnel about how they had spent hours and hours going over 300-plus names and then shaping the asymmetrical crest logo that pays homage to Maine’s wilderness with stylized imagery of Katahdin, flowing waters and wildflowers.
In the presentation, the qualities of “Wildness” as it relates to Maine women were detailed as five main themes: resilience, communers, work ethic, leadership, and being grounded. Wildness, according to a club press release, connects the physical characteristics of Maine and “the trailblazing spirit” of Maine women.
“The name, it encapsulates everything a Maine women is,” said Justine Satterthwaite of Scarborough. Like Vinal, Satterthwaite is now a season-ticket holder for both the Maine Wildness and the Hearts of Pine.
By incorporating the Hearts of Pine’s distinctive Dirigo Heart image and blue-and-green colors into the Maine Wildness logo, designed by Portland-based artist Pame Chévez, the club was purposeful in connecting its two teams while providing the women’s team with its own identity. The crest emphasizes the natural beauty of wild spaces with images of Katahdin, flowing waters, and resilient flora like wild lupines, thistle, sea rose and fern.
“We asked people across Maine what they wanted for this team and we kept hearing the same response: a love for what we’ve created with Hearts and a deep desire for something distinct to the women of Maine,” said Gabe Hoffman-Johnson, the club’s founder and chief community officer, in a press release. “‘Wildness came from listening to that feedback, finding a name that captures the spirit intrinsic to both this place and the people who make it so special.”
Shortly after the name and brand were revealed, the crowded main room noticeably thinned out. That’s because half of the attendees went to the music venue’s lobby to line up and buy Maine Wildness T-shirts, sweatshirts and other swag. The women’s team items are now available on the club’s online store and its Club Shop at 127 Marginal Way in Portland.
The women’s team will consist of mostly college-age players. Because it is a pre-professional league (think wooden bat baseball leagues for a simple comparison), the players retain their college eligibility. Games are played mostly in May and June. The Maine Wildness will compete in the USLW’s Northeast Division.
The Wildness will immediately be one of top drawing clubs in the USLW. In June, the club sold 5,000 season-ticket deposits in an hour and have converted 4,400 of those deposits into season-ticket sales.
The men’s team, which has averaged 6,239 fans at city-owned Fitzpatrick Stadium this season, has 4,000 season-ticket holders.
The USLW does not report average attendance, but most teams draw less than 1,000 fans. Minnesota Aurora FC is a rare exception, reportedly bringing in over 5,000 fans per match. The Vermont Green, which will be a rival for the Wildness in the Northeast Division, consistently sold out 2,500-seat Virtue Field in Burlington in their first season in 2026.
“This team is intended to set the standard for what a pre-professional women’s team can accomplish,” Sirois said in the press release. “We want to grow the women’s game in this country. Consistently selling out a 6,000-person stadium has never been done at this level, and raising that standard is what we’re rallying this state around.”
The Hearts of Pine ownership announced in August its plans to build its own 9,000-11,000 seat stadium on Cassidy Point in Portland. The hope is to break ground sometime in 2027, with 2029 as the target year for both the men’s and women’s teams to move to their new home.

title: Waterville Filmmaker Ryan Cook Brings Donn Fendler's Survival Story To Audience At Gracie Theatre In Bangor Next Month
text:
Waterville Native Ryan Cook To Host Talk At Gracie Theater About How He Got To Make The Movie ‘Lost On A Mountain In Maine’
It's been a little over two years since one of Maine's most famous rescue stories, one many middle school students in the state have read in book form, debuted on the big screen.
The effort to bring the story of Donn Fendler's plight when he got "Lost On A Mountain In Maine" to a film form was spearheaded by Waterville native, Ryan Cook, who like many had read the book in school, and was captivated by the story.
Read More: 'Lost On A Mountain' Producer To Come Full Circle With Movie
Cook befriended Fendler and his family, and through his time with them, got even more of the story which he felt needed to be told, so in 2011, he put together a documentary called documentary about Fendler called “Finding Donn Fendler: Lost on a Mountain in Maine 72 Years Later" which he screened at the Waterville Opera House at the Maine International Film Festival. 
Fendler passed away a few years later, in 2016.
Almost a decade later, Cook's efforts to make a full-fledged movie based on the book came to fruition. With the backing of Sylvester Stallone's production company, Balboa Productions, and with the addition of producers Braden Aftergood and Dick Boyce the motion picture version of Lost On A Mountain In Maine debuted in 2024. It landed at #5 on the Netflix Global charts.
Read More: Check It Out: Trailer For New 'Lost On A Mountain In Maine' Movie
Next month, Cook will come to Bangor, bringing the documentary he made, which inspired the film, and behind-the-scenes footage of Fendler himself when he hosts a talk about his experience with the story at the Gracie Theatre on the campus of Husson University.
According to the Lost On A Mountain In Maine Facebook page, the special event will take place next month, with opportunities for the audience to ask questions of the man who made the movie. The talk is entitled "The Legacy of Donn Fendler; Perseverance Against All Odds.
"Friday, November 20th, at the Gracie Theater in Bangor. Join producer and Maine native Ryan Cook for a special evening celebrating the legacy of Donn Fendler. Hear and see documentary footage of Donn Fendler telling the story in his own words, followed by a discussion with Ryan about the years he spent working with Donn to make the feature film 'Lost on a Mountain in Maine'."
Doors will open at 5PM, with general admission opening at 5:30. The talk is scheduled to go from 6 PM to 7:30, with a question and answer portion available till 8 PM.
The event is free and appropriate for all ages. The first 150 participants who register will get a complimentary copy of the book that started it all, Lost On A Mountain In Maine.

The Galen Cole Family Foundation is sponsoring this special event.

title: R.U. OK? Older adults living alone in Arizona get daily check-in calls
text:
PHOENIX (Aging Untold) — A program in Phoenix is ensuring that older adults who live alone have a lifeline in case of an emergency.
Each year, there are about 3 million emergency room visits due to falls among older adults, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Multiple studies published between 2020 and 2025 found living alone may increase the risk of falls and the severity of injury among older adults.
Debbie Lane, 84, has lived in Arizona since 1977 after moving from New Jersey. She raised three children and has been involved with the Arizona Opera. Now she lives alone and has peace of mind knowing that the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office checks on her every day through its R.U. OK program, which stands for Are You OK?
How the program works
“It rings. I know the number. The voice says the number. I push it and they said, ‘This is R.U. OK and push one if you are OK, push three if you need assistance,’ which I like,” Lane said.
Sun City Posse Chaplain Don Erlitz said the residents receive up to three computerized calls every day. If they do not answer, deputies are dispatched to their homes.
Erlitz said the goal is to make sure residents are OK.
Lane participates in the R.U. OK program for her children. When she told them about it, they were thrilled, she said. It gives them peace of mind.

title: Did Maine Democrats decriminalize several crimes if the offender says they are homeless?
text:
No.
Maine law does not exempt people from any crimes simply because they say they are homeless.
A 2021 bill sponsored by state Rep. Victoria Morales, D-South Portland, initially proposed barring arrests and prosecutions for certain offenses committed because someone lacked housing. But lawmakers removed that provision before enactment.
Instead, the law requires officers to ask whether someone accused of certain crimes has a home. It covers five offenses: trespassing, disorderly conduct, public urination, drug possession for illegal use and drinking alcohol in prohibited public places.
For those without housing, police must follow their department’s homelessness crisis protocol. Protocols include referrals to crisis services, mental health and substance use professionals, emergency housing and case management. The Maine attorney general’s model favors referrals over citations or arrests, which it calls a last resort.
However, departments can adopt different protocols, and police still may issue citations or make arrests when warranted.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: Crews work on partial demolition of Old Town bridge following collapse
text:
OLD TOWN, Maine (WABI) - Construction crews are working on demolishing a portion of the Llewelyn Estes replacement bridge in Old Town.
Work began on Tuesday and is expected to continue into next week.
The bridge collapsed in August when concrete was being poured. Three workers were hurt.
Crews are separating the damaged span of the bridge from the pier and abutment, making the pieces smaller before removing them from the river.
Maine DOT says the temporary bridge will be closed for periods while crews work, although exact times are fluid.

title: More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — A growing number of amusement parks have shut down roller coasters as police and state regulators investigate what caused a man to fall out of his seat and plummet to his death at a Georgia park.
Sea World Orlando in Florida and La Ronde theme park in Montreal, Canada confirmed on Thursday they had temporarily closed rides, bringing the total number of roller coasters halted to 12.
Police and a state regulatory agency are investigating what caused Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, to fall from the Goliath coaster on Monday. Witnesses described seeing him ejected from the coaster; some people who rode the Goliath before him raised concerns about its restraints.
Ten of the roller coasters taken out of service have the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system as the Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia.
Mom says her son’s restraint didn’t work properly
Erica Billups said her son and daughter rode Goliath about an hour before Kariem’s death and encountered a problem with the restraint on one seat. Her son initially sat in that seat and tried to lock it, but then moved when it repeatedly became unlocked. The roller coaster embarked with the seat empty and the harness up, she said in a post on X.
She confirmed the post in a text message to The Associated Press on Thursday.
She said staff did not tell her kids there was a problem.
Summer Bates, who was at the Georgia park with her husband and three children and saw Kariem fall, told the AP previously that her older two children kept trying to push their restraints down tighter while on the ride. She understood why they were doing that later when she was on the coaster, she said, because the restraints didn’t feel secure.
Six Flags did not immediately respond to an email for comment on any issues with restraints.
At least one of the other closures is for safety
La Ronde in Montreal, Canada, said one of its coasters — also named Goliath — is offline “while we conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride’s manufacturer.”
Neither La Ronde nor Sea World Orlando said why those specific rides were closed. Both were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, which also built the Goliath ride in Georgia and eight of the additional coasters that Six Flags closed. Bolliger & Mabillard declined Thursday to answer questions about the shutdowns.
Online photos and videos of 10 of the closed coasters show each equipped with so-called “clamshell” restraints, mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider’s knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
It’s unclear from the images whether any of the 10 coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints.
Roller coaster manufacturers decide what type of restraints to use after considering speed, force and the track’s transitions, said Brian D. Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert.
He advocates the use of a backup restraint for riders, but there is a long-running debate in the industry over whether that would increase wait times, Avery said.
Bolliger & Mabillard says it is investigating
The company said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a “better understanding of what transpired” on Monday.
Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia’s headline attractions, towers above the park’s entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers).
Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead, said it looked like Kariem was hovering because the car was moving underneath him. He fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, and then was ejected from the ride on its final turn.
The park is scheduled to reopen Friday
The Goliath, however, is not expected to be running.
The park, which has about a dozen roller coasters, is in Austell, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. Associated Press writer Dylan Lovan in Louisville, Kentucky, contributed to this report.

title: Reny Wants to Address Affordability in Bid for Senate District 13
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Cameron Reny, D-Bristol, wants to continue the work she has started in her two terms representing Senate District 13.
Reny is up against Edwin W. Mitchell, I-Boothbay, to represent Senate District 13, which consists of all of Lincoln County excluding Dresden and including Washington and Windsor. Reny is the current holder of the seat and if reelected, she will enter her third term.
“Public service, it’s important to me,” Reny said. “My communities are important to me and I want our kids to stand a shot at a life here.”
Born and raised in Bristol, Reny continues to live in her hometown. She went to Guilford College in Greensboro, N.C., where she got a community and justice studies degree. She obtained her master’s degree in school counseling from the University of Southern Maine in Portland.
Most of Reny’s professional career before becoming a state senator was spent as a school counselor, a position she said she is “really passionate about.”
“I think when everyone pitches in, we are all better off and I am of a mindset that I want to leave the world better than I found it and school counseling was what I ended up gravitating towards because it’s helping kids and families,” Reny said.
Her career started out at Biddeford Middle School and when she decided she wanted to move closer to home, she worked at South Bristol School for a few years. She would go on to become the counselor at Woolwich Central School. The roles gave her experience dealing with people from different backgrounds and viewpoints, which she said has helped her with her problem solving skills and bringing together different stakeholders.
When she became a senator, Reny said she had a “hunch” that her school counselor skills would be useful in the new line of work.
“What matters when it comes to getting bills passed into law is your ability to relationship build, your ability to bring in all the appropriate stakeholders, your ability to work with people who don’t necessarily see eye to eye with you, which are all skills I’ve been using for years and years, and that have made me a very effective legislator and have made me very effective working across the aisle,” Reny said.
During her time in the school system, Reny said she has served on school-wide and district-wide committees, and served as the president of the Maine School Counseling Association for a few years.
If reelected, Reny said she wants to continue her public service. Her desire to run again also is fueled by her being raised in a “very strong community” that has a heart for helping each other out. This means to not just donate money, but to devote time and effort, she said.
“I feel like we’ve done a good job trying to insulate the state of Maine from sort of the federal uncertainty that has been prevalent over the last few years, and I want to see that work continue,” Reny said.
In this election, Reny said she believes her experience sets her apart. With this, she said she has been a capable legislator and has been effective in getting different policy “across the finish line.” This includes a bill that was passed last session that made it where medical debt will not affect someone’s credit score. Reny said a bill like this makes it where people are now able to access mortgages, business loans, and other financials that previously weren’t able to because they were sick or hurt.
Not only does Reny want to do better for the state now, she said she wants to set up a “bright future” where people can afford to live and raise their families.
“I want my kids and grandkids and everybody’s kids and grandkids to be able to live here and thrive here long after we’re gone,” she said.
Another achievement Reny is proud of from her time in office comes from her first term. She reflected on how when she was a school counselor, she faced the challenge of a student or their family having a mental health crisis and finding that when they needed to go to the emergency room, their insurance would not pay for the counseling they needed. Reny said this was usually because the referral came from an emergency room doctor instead of their primary care physician.
This encouraged her to push forward a bill that allowed emergency room referrals to be used to access counseling services.
“For people who are struggling with those sort of issues, and honestly, just getting an appointment, taking the time off work, getting yourself there, it’s something that’s seemingly simple that is a hurdle for a lot of people, understandably so,” Reny said.
Another effort Reny is proud of is her climate resiliency work. She said her district faces bigger and stronger storms and need to be ready for them.
“I know culverts aren’t sexy, but they’re very important,” she said.
Other work includes healthcare, where she pushed for a bill to strengthen the prescription drug affordability board which she said gave it direction and resources to use for policy. She said her “extremely bipartisan” Federally Qualified Health Center pharmacy bill presents grants to serve rural and underserved populations to expand pharmaceutical services and decrease the cost of prescriptions.
Reny currently serves on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and the Marine Resources Committee.
She said her time as a senator has allowed her to learn a lot about a wide range of topics. She used the example of how when she first started, she was placed on the Marine Resources Committee and Health Coverage Insurance and Financial Committee. The experience allowed her to fully understand different aspects of government and the people it serves, she said.
“Standing up for, you know, our farmers, our fisherman, our loggers, and really trying to insulate the state once again,” Reny said. “I hate to come back to it, but it’s sort of the weird world we’re in right now. It feels like there’s a lot of chaos coming from the federal level and trying to not let that chaos steer us off course, or harm our friends and neighbors.”
While on the campaign trail, Reny said the biggest concerns she has heard from people in the district is the cost of living.
Affordability issues are directly tied into cost increases controlled at the federal level, such as fuel, energy, and inflation, she said. At the state level, Reny said the legislature can tackle this issue in different ways.
Reny used the example of high energy costs and said she would like to see the state diversify its energy creation production, making sure it finds anything available to it. She said she would like to see more hydropower and the exploration of any alternative energy source.
She said she also wants public advocates to be able to “check” Central Maine Power when necessary by also having ways to pivot.
Affordability makes the economy do better and small businesses do better when people have buying power, Reny said. By creating more accessible and affordable necessities such as energy, childcare, prescription drug costs, and more, Reny said people can not only afford the bare minimum, but also extra to improve their lives.
“I can’t personally control inflation on my own,” Reny said. “You can do things to make life more affordable where you can.”
Affordable housing fits into this through Reny’s efforts to incentive the creation of new housing, as well as protects more affordable options such as mobile home parks. She mentioned previous bills she has worked on to protect mobile home parks from private equity investors that would buy them and raise the rents.
“When you can make other places in people’s lives more affordable, they can at least take a breath,” she said.
Reny has also been thinking of the impending closure of the labor and delivery unit at MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta. She said the closure of the addiction resource center in Damariscotta is also unacceptable.
To address these closures and prevent more from happening, Reny said she has a few ideas for the legislature. She wants more transparency in the decision making and financials, especially because of the healthcare system’s “virtual monopoly” in the state.
Reny said because of the district’s high need for substance use resources, it is irresponsible to take them away.
“We’re going to have to look into creative solutions and probably some alternative community service possibilities, but we can’t go without,” Reny said. “I don’t accept us going without.”
When it comes to the state’s working waterfront, Reny said there are ways to find balance between those making a living on the water and making sure others also have access for recreation. While she said she does not know a legislative fix for the balance, she said she is willing to listen and learn to see what people need.
Local infrastructure fits into two separate areas for Reny. She said the first is the community resiliency partnership, which is a state level program that provides grants to municipalities to upgrade infrastructure and prepare for weather events.
The other area is the potential for community and economic development partnerships throughout the state. Reny said there are possibilities that can grow out of it, especially since the state has an entire department for it.
In the past year, the state legislature has evaluated ways to change the funding formula for how education subsidy is sent out to different towns. Reny said a part of the reason people are frustrated with rising education costs is not only within the school system, but because of how everything else has raised in cost.
“Everything is so much more expensive that it was before and just the additional burden feels more daunting that I think it would otherwise,” Reny said.
To solve some of these increasing costs, Reny said she would like to see a higher tax rate on non-resident homes and see the homestead exemption raised. She would also like to see the federal government pay 40% of special education costs, but that is out of her control, she said.
Within the cost for education, Reny said if the state can get a handle on health insurance prices, it might ease the burden on residents. She said that if health insurance can be more “reasonable,” less money is needed for every school employee, town administrator, and staff of businesses across the district.
Reny has endorsements from Maine American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations, the Sierra Club, Maine Service Employees Associations, SEIU Local 1989; Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund PAC, Maine Conservation Voters Action Fund, Committee to Protect Health Care, EqualityMaine PAC, and the Wabanaki Alliance.
The election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: How Lewiston’s mayoral candidates want to move the city forward
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON — Voters on Nov. 3 will choose between five candidates for mayor: Mayor Carl Sheline, former City Councilor Rick LaChapelle, Jay Rodrigue, Brian Beaulieu and Charles Soule.
The Sun Journal asked each candidate how they would use the mayor’s office to address the major challenges facing Lewiston. Sheline was the only candidate to respond.
“From the beginning, I have viewed a large portion of my job as being a cheerleader for our city,” Sheline said when asked about the powers of the mayor’s office.
“Part of instilling pride in the hearts of residents is making progress on city beautification efforts and removing blight,” Sheline continued. “Through the efforts of code enforcement, the new murals, our new homeless shelter that is continually working to get people housed and many other initiatives, we are making progress.”
While LaChapelle did not respond to the question, in responses to the Maine Trust for Local News voter guide, he did note the city needs stronger leadership.
“With strong leadership, we can make Lewiston safer, attract new businesses and investment, and restore pride in our community,” LaChapelle said. “I want people inside and outside Lewiston to see a city that is safe, vibrant, growing and worth investing in.”
The Sun Journal also asked all five candidates how they would handle crime, taxes and the local economy. Again, Sheline was the only one to respond. For the other candidates the Sun Journal looked to their public statements and Facebook posts, as well as LaChappelle’s responses to the Maine Trust for Local News voter guide.
It appears Soule is the only candidate who has not issued public statements or social media posts offering his thoughts outlining his positions.
CRIME
Residents deserve to feel safe in their homes, neighborhoods and businesses, Rodrigue said in a Facebook post. Curbing crime and improving public safety is one of his top priorities.
“I will work to support effective policing, address the root causes of crime and hold people accountable,” Rodrigue said. “This campaign is about bringing common sense, accountability and responsible leadership back to City Hall.”
At the Aug. 4 City Council meeting, LaChapelle, once the council president, blamed Lewiston’s youth gun violence on a lack of city leadership.
“Last time we met was over at Lewiston High School and frankly that meeting was a joke,” LaChapelle said. “All we heard was just about every speaker get up saying we need more money, we need more money, we need more money. At the end of the meeting, our illustrious mayor closed saying we all love Lewiston — meeting adjourned with no plan, no guidance, no leadership. We need some leadership. I’m begging for leadership now.”
LaChapelle also said city leaders need to engage Lewiston’s delegation in Augusta to find solutions.
“I know you’re going to say you’re not responsible for what happens up in Augusta,” LaChapelle said. “Well, I say no, you have to know what happens up in Augusta, where it affects Lewiston. You should know everything. We should be getting on our state representatives. … We need some leadership.”
Sheline, who has been mayor since 2022, said the city’s efforts to curb crime are working, but that there are long-term solutions the city needs to address, and it will take the police and the community working together to combat crime and solve cases.
“Long-term solutions include increasing the access to (recreation) and after-school programs,” Sheline said. “Our youth are in crisis and I will make sure that they are prioritized during the upcoming budget process.”
Police recruitment is also a long-term issue the city has struggled with for some time, Sheline said.
During the last budget season, city councilors froze three officer positions. Now, police are short by more than a dozen positions.
“A new police station, take-home police cars, and competitive pay assist with those recruitment efforts and as a result, we are making great hires,” Sheline said. “This takes time and will not be fixed overnight, but progress is being made.”
For Beaulieu, the worst part has been watching other communities make strides toward a better future while Lewiston residents have become increasingly concerned with issues like crime and taxes.
“For too long, residents have watched crime and violence become an increasing concern,” Beaulieu said in a Facebook post. “We’ve watched taxes and property valuations climb while families wonder what they’re getting in return. We’ve watched other communities attract new businesses, new investment and new opportunities while Lewiston continues to fall short of its potential.”
ECONOMY AND TAXES
Rodrigue says city leaders must lower the property tax burden and control spending. Lewiston’s residents and homeowners are carrying too much of the cost, he said.
“We need to find responsible ways to reduce unnecessary expenses and make city government work more efficiently,” Rodrigue said. “Every taxpayer dollar matters. I will push for greater transparency, accountability, and careful review of city spending. Before asking residents for more money, we should make sure we’re using what we already have wisely.”
Among his top three priorities, according to the voter guide questionnaire, LaChapelle said the city needs to be more aggressive in recruiting new businesses. This can be achieved by revamping codes to make it easier to do business, an effort he led as city councilor that he said resulted in over 1,000 code changes.
The city also needs to freeze property taxes for 2027 at the same level as 2026, LaChappelle said.
“Then review the recent citywide evaluation (which the city delayed implementing by a year) to ensure everyone that uses our services is paying their fair share,” he said. “I want us to think outside the box, use technology, listen to the great minds within our city and challenge every department to do better.”
Lewiston needs more housing, Sheline said, adding that he has supported housing of all types, including senior housing at the former Martel School at 860 Lisbon St.
Sheline said Lewiston also needs to continue attracting new businesses and supporting the growth of current businesses.
“Through assisting new businesses, such as Mancini’s Deli, and supporting the expansion of our current businesses, Bourgeois Guitars for example, we can help grow our business community and tax base,” Sheline said.
Beaulieu said in his Facebook post that Lewiston needs leadership that will “focus on what matters” — attracting businesses; jobs that pay well; fighting “unnecessary increases in the burden on taxpayers”; addressing neglected neighborhoods and blight; addressing discarded needles; giving youths more opportunities; holding City Hall more accountable and responsive to residents; and restoring the city’s pride.
“I’m not a career politician,” Beaulieu said. “I’m a resident who believes Lewiston deserves better and that complaining about the problems isn’t enough. Someone has to be willing to stand up and work to fix them. I want Lewiston to become a city where businesses want to invest, families want to live, and residents are proud to say ‘This is my home.’”

title: Wrong to remove George Mitchell’s name without evidence or proof
text:
Douglas Rooks is the author of “Statesman: George Mitchell and the Art of the Possible” (Down East Books, 2016.) He welcomes comment at [email protected].
The University of Maine System Board of Trustees voted 9-5 on Sept. 28 to remove former Sen. George Mitchell’s name from university programs and scholarships — the latest in a series of such moves following release of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
The removal of Mitchell’s name from scholarships and institutes began back in February in Ireland, which had recognized Mitchell’s central role in the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, a deal that has brought lasting peace to Northern Ireland.
They never knew Mitchell as well as we do here in Maine.
One of the dissenting UMS trustees, Donna Loring, explained her position in a Bangor Daily News op-ed, writing, “My vote was not a declaration that every allegation concerning Mitchell is false. I do not know that. But neither has there been a finding that he committed wrongdoing. The university’s own task force acknowledged that fact.”
Loring’s point is inarguable. Before we remove names, portraits and statues from the public square, there must be an effort to establish the facts, and discern the truth as far as it can be known. Judging from its report, the task force did not attempt this, instead citing “serious allegations” and potential “reputational harm” to the university as deciding factors.
“I worry about a standard in which reputational harm can outweigh the absence of a finding of wrongdoing,” Loring wrote. We should all be worried.
Although the chaotic release of the Epstein files in 2025 by order of Congress was widely assumed to be in the public interest, there are serious doubts. Unedited investigative files and reports — such as those just inadvertently released by the Maine Attorney General’s Office — can be profoundly and unfairly damaging to lives and reputations. If such releases became routine, there would be few reputations left worth having.
Suspicions and allegations that would not normally be public are spread worldwide, with instantaneous reactions and conclusions that then drive policymakers to treat accusations, however serious, as facts, and suspicions as warranted.
News accounts focused on 300 “mentions” of Mitchell’s name among 2.5 million pages of documents; Donald Trump’s name appears more than 30,000 times. By itself, these numbers mean nothing. To this day, no one has been charged with any criminal offenses (except Epstein and his enabler, Ghislaine Maxwell).
If we use suspicion and allegation as the standard, we’re on a slippery slope. It’s a short distance from here to the 1950s McCarthyite “Red Scare,” where guilt by association among “fellow travelers” ruined lives, careers and reputations.
At least the UMS trustees made some attempt to balance the accusations against Mitchell’s lifetime of service. In his hometown, Waterville’s school board swiftly voted 5-2 to remove his name from an elementary school after a handful of complaints. The Legislature’s presiding officers, with no process at all, removed Mitchell’s portrait from the State House, where it had been installed to bipartisan acclaim in 2014.
There are public places in Maine and recognitions in Washington to which Mitchell’s name is still attached. This is far from unanimous.
We should also balance the accusations with an accounting of Mitchell’s achievements. Along with his unique contributions to world peace — among dozens of wars and rebellions in our times, there is hardly another example like it — Mitchell represented Maine with distinction in the U.S. Senate for 15 years. As majority leader, he shepherded dozens of important bills to passage — landmarks in protecting the environment, creating affordable housing and providing better lives for persons with disabilities. Surely this should count.
I am of course not privy to the UMS trustees’ deliberations. As Mitchell’s biographer, however, I can offer testimony from years of research, interviews and discussions involving his family, his staff, political supporters and opponents, those who knew him best in his personal and public life.
In all that time, I never heard of any lapses in personal integrity lending credence to the anonymous, unsourced Epstein allegations. Rather the reverse — in campaigning, in fundraising, in the sometime regrettable business of politics, Mitchell was a stickler for following the rules.
It may be impossible ever to lay to rest the suspicions created by the Epstein files. As so often in the digital age, we are drowning in data of variable quality, with understanding nowhere to be seen.
In the absence of proof, I suggest no further “de-namings” of Mitchell, with its implied public censure, until some reliable standards can be established. Ultimately, history will assess his virtues and flaws, like those of any other human being. The trustees’ majority judgment should not be the last word.

title: Local warehouse owner among the 6 people killed in Wisconsin plane crash
text:
A prominent local warehouse owner died along with five other people when the plane he owned crashed in Wisconsin after ice built up on the wings during a thunderstorm.
Menomonie Airport Commission Chairman Daniel Johnson said at a public meeting Wednesday night that longtime pilot Ron Riek died in the crash. Authorities have not yet released the names of the five others who died.
“He was simply a good man. A highly experienced pilot, and this was simply a tragedy,” Johnson said about the friend he had known for decades.
The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation. Its experts will certainly examine the history of icing-related crashes involving Piper PA-46 Malibu planes like the one that Riek owned. The agency did a safety study on seven Piper crashes between 1989 and 1991.
Johnson said “the aircraft has a reputation of not doing well in thunderstorms.”
This latest crash is hitting the aviation community around Menomonie hard because just last year four people died in a different plane crash. Riek helped organize a fundraiser afterward to raise money for the three young children of one couple that died.
“This is two fatal crashes in 18 months. We’ve lost a lot of friends,” Johnson said. “This creates a hole in the aviation community.”
The pilot in this week’s crash told an air traffic controller about icing on the wings of the Piper PA-46 Malibu as it flew at 24,000 feet (7,315 meters) and requested permission to descend, according to the NTSB. That is a major aviation hazard because even a thin layer of ice can make it difficult for a plane to remain airborne.
Air traffic control approved the descent, and the plane began a right descending turn that increased sharply in rate until communications and data tracking were lost shortly before 10 p.m. Tuesday. The six-seat, single-engine plane was traveling from Kenosha to Menomonie when it crashed in a wooded area near Mirror Lake State Park, not far from the popular tourist destination of Wisconsin Dells. No one on the ground was hurt.
The Wisconsin Dells sells itself as the “Waterpark Capital of the World” because of its high concentration of waterparks. The area drew more than 5 million visitors in 2025, according to state tourism officials.

title: Trump says Pentagon won’t livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it.
Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan.”
But, he continued, “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said Trump and Hegseth discussed the decision to drop the livestream plans before the president’s announcement on social media.
“The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned,” Parnell said.
Catholic bishop called the plan ‘barbaric’
When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said, adding, “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”
Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. The head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops had condemned the Trump administration’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution, with Archbishop Paul S. Coakley saying the move was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”
Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., voiced similar sentiments.
For his part, the president has defended his decision to approve the use of a firing squad, but had for days distanced himself from Hegseth’s announcement that it would be public.
“Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump said Friday when asked about the livestream. As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: “He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement and now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.
The U.S. military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
——-
Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin contributed to this report.

title: With anger spreading over Iran war, Democrats hope to flip Republican seats with veterans' help
text:
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo. (AP) — The doorbell chimed “The Star Spangled Banner” as retired Col. Lou Christensen stepped inside the large house on the northeastern edge of Colorado Springs. The registered Republican and 28-year Air Force veteran was doing something he never expected to do — attending a party for a Democratic congressional candidate.
“The legislative branch needs to put up guardrails from President Trump,” said Christensen, 70. “We need another branch of government that stands up and says, ‘Uh, boss, that’s not constitutional.’”
Christensen is backing Jessica Killin, a fellow veteran, over first-term Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, a conservative stronghold that includes five military facilities. The district is a longshot for Democrats but they’re investing money here for the first time in years, counting on an unpopular war with Iran and upheaval in the armed forces to put more seats in play as the party pushes for control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Democratic candidates who previously served in the military are also running in Florida, South Carolina and Virginia districts with significant veteran populations.
Although veterans hold all sorts of political beliefs, the population overall leans right — nearly 6 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago, according to AP VoteCast. Trump won Colorado’s 5th by 9 percentage points that year, and nearly one out of every nine people there is a veteran, according to federal statistics, making it one of the most veteran-heavy seats in the country. The district is home to NORAD, Fort Carson and the Air Force Academy.
“I know there’s a bunch of veterans in the room, so I don’t have to tell you where we are with foreign policy,” Killin told more than two dozen voters who gathered on a recent Friday evening. “For the first time in history, now the global community thinks more of China than of the United States.”
Iran war, Hegseth unsettle some veterans
One of the only comparable seats in terms of veteran population is in Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, centered in Virginia Beach and similarly dotted with military bases, with the massive Naval Station Norfolk just outside its boundaries.
Unlike Colorado’s 5th, elections in Virginia’s 2nd have zig-zagged back and forth over the last decade. Democrat Elaine Luria, a retired Naval Commander who deployed to the Middle East and Western Pacific and led a unit of 400 sailors over the course of her military career, ousted a Republican incumbent in 2018. She held the seat for two terms before Republican Jen Kiggans, a former Navy helicopter pilot, defeated her in 2022.
Now Luria is back for a rematch, hammering Kiggans and Trump for the Iran war that she called “an expanding economic crisis” as well as a geopolitical blunder. In an interview, she criticized Kiggans for voting against resolutions intended to halt military action without congressional approval.
Kiggans, whose 10 years of service included two deployments to the Persian Gulf, said she hopes the war can soon be brought to a close. But she argued that Luria, through her criticism, has “chosen the side of Iran.”
“It’s like the Democrats are now siding with the Iranians and not standing with our military,” she said in an interview.
Paul Krekorian, a Navy veteran and retired grade school teacher in Virginia Beach, said he worries the war may become a “quagmire” for Trump. But he still decided to support Kiggans because Democrats “have gone socialist.”
Still, plenty of veterans were casting early ballots for Luria, citing their frustration at Trump and his administration.
“I think we are less safe, not just because of the war in Iran, but because of the leadership or the lack of leadership we have,” said Phyllis Mihalas, a self-described independent and retired Army lieutenant colonel. She described Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth as “an enormously incompetent man whose ego consistently gets in the way.”
Democrats bet on veteran candidates
Democratic veterans are trying to make that argument in other races for Republican-held seats. In South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, Democrat Nancy Lacore, a former Navy vice admiral, is running against Republican lawyer Jennifer Honeycutt. Lacore was fired by Hegseth last year.
In Florida’s 13th Congressional District, retired Army Brigadier Gen. Leela Gray is challenging Republican Rep. Anna Paulina Luna. And in Florida’s 7th Congressional District, Bale Dalton, a former Navy Aviator and NASA chief of staff, is running against Ryan Elijah, a Republican and local news anchor.
In Colorado Springs, the Republican incumbent, Crank, is in his first term in Congress. Though his father and father-in-law are veterans and his son-in-law is currently in the Army, Crank has never been in the military.
A onetime aide to a longtime congressman representing the area, Crank ran the Colorado chapter of the conservative group Americans For Prosperity and then served as Colorado chairman of former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley’s bid for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024. He ran for the open congressional seat against a Trump-backed candidate and won the Republican primary, sparking some suspicion among Trump supporters about whether he’d be a team player for the president.
Now Killin’s campaign is airing an ad slamming Crank for voting with Trump “100% of the time.”
In an interview, Crank scoffed at the charge but said it wasn’t his style to pick public fights with Trump. “I’m going to try to check the president where I think he’s wrong,” Crank said, such as Trump moving U.S. Space Command from Colorado to Alabama.
‘Don’t let it be for nothing’
Crank said that one of the first casualties from the Iran war was stationed at Ft. Carson in Colorado Springs, and it fell to him to call the fallen soldier’s father. “He basically said to me, ‘Don’t let it be for nothing,’” Crank said. He added: “We’re reluctant to go, but once we’re there, let’s get the job done and go home. And I think that’s how people in my district feel.”
Mike Gould, a retired lieutenant general who once ran the Air Force Academy, agreed. “What our president did, taking on Iran the way he did, was exactly the right thing to do,” said Gould, who supports Crank.
Killin grew up in Colorado Springs and quips that she was the lone Democrat in her elementary school class. She joined the Army in the late 1990s and rose to captain, serving in the Balkan war before joining USAA, the company that provides insurance and banking services to members of the military and veterans.
At the house party, Killin said she was worried about what Trump had done to the country — and that Crank wasn’t trying to stop it. “I grew up in an era where the Department of Defense was apolitical and the Department of Justice was apolitical,” Killin said.
It was a theme that many other veterans sounded during the gathering, which was held in the home of an Air Force veteran and former Reagan administration official just a few miles from the Air Force Academy. One former Army Ranger worried about Hegseth’s attempts to infuse the military with conservative Christian cultural ideas. A newly discharged veteran worried about how he’ll find work. And Michael Stewart, a 75-year-old former Marine, made a confession about the level of his disgust over the Iran war.
“This is the first time,” Stewart said, “I’ve wanted to see my country lose.”
___
Rankin reported from Virginia Beach, Virginia.

title: Small dog that escaped into Yellowstone wilderness for over a month found safe
text:
Small dog that escaped into Yellowstone wilderness for over a month found safe
For over a month, Luna, a Jack Russell terrier that bolted from her family's cabin during a vacation at Yellowstone National Park, eluded capture as fears for her survival mounted and winter weather approached. On Wednesday, her ordeal came to a happy ending when she was caught and reunited with her owners.
The 10-year-old white dog with pointy ears and a gray collar had been spotted crossing intersections, strolling through employee housing and entering lodges through automatic doors at the sprawling park, home to grizzly bears, wolves and other predators.
Related video above | New webcam at Yellowstone National Park records 'small' eruption from Black Diamond Pool
Katie Boucher, the volunteer leading the rescue effort and a spokesperson for Luna's California owners, said she and one of the owners found the dog in the trap baited with scraps from a T-shirt and pillowcase belonging to the family. They took her to a veterinarian, where the owner held the dog as it was examined Wednesday afternoon.
“She's underweight, but that's to be expected. She's alert and in good spirits,” Boucher said. “I was crying all the way up here from the park."
Luna escaped Sept. 10. Boucher said the dog spent its first year on the streets before being adopted and showed strong survival instincts while on the loose. Based on sightings, Boucher said, Luna retraced her family’s steps from the day before she was lost -- sneaking into eateries or lodges they had visited and seeking shelter in employee residences and businesses.
An escape into the wilderness
The day of the escape, the family left her in their cabin with a “Do Not Disturb” sign while they ventured out to explore the park. They believe a housekeeping staffer accidentally opened a door, freeing the dog.
“The staff then proceeded to chase her around that area of the park for over two hours before the owners came back and discovered all the chaos and their dog missing,” Boucher said.
Yellowstone was the first U.S. national park and covers about 3,500 square miles (some 9,000 square kilometers), including portions of Wyoming, Montana and Idaho.
Luna's family searched for the dog, which is part chihuahua, but were told it likely died, possibly killed by a coyote, Boucher recounted. Days after leaving Yellowstone, the owners learned Luna had been spotted, and contacted Boucher, president of the Norris Ark Training and Recovery Center in Norris, Montana, north of the park.
“I cannot fathom how I would feel if I had been taking the vacation of a lifetime, and looking for all these memorable experiences in one of the most beautiful places on earth, and lost one of my family members there,” Boucher said.
Locals and tourists called out Luna’s name or chased her, triggering her fight-or-flight response and driving her further into the park, Boucher said. The volunteers set a live trap using the family's scent to lure Luna in, avoiding food that could attract bears or other wildlife.
Time was running out as winter closes in
Boucher said this was the last week she would have been able to search for Luna. She was sleeping at an RV park for seasonal employees that closes next Monday.
The search had rallied locals and tourists alike. Marie Jaskula, an area resident who runs one of the park's general stores, posted signs at every park entrance urging visitors to be on the lookout for the dog.
“It’s really hard to stress the importance of do not chase,” said Jaskula. “Everybody sees this little dog buzz across the intersection or maybe around their employee housing, and the first instinct is to call her name and chase her.”

title: Florida man killed ex-fiancee hours after their ‘People’s Court’ episode aired, police say
text:
ORLANDO, Fla. (AP) — A Florida man has been charged with killing the mother of his children nearly 15 years ago, after his ex-fiancee went missing just hours after their pretaped appearance on “The People’s Court” was broadcast, police said.
Orlando police announced the arrest Wednesday of Dale Smith Jr., 55, on a charge of second-degree murder. The body of 33-year-old Michelle Parker has not been recovered, but all evidence leads to Smith as the person responsible for her death, police said.
Smith’s attorney, Rajan Joshi, said during a hearing Thursday afternoon that he didn’t believe the state could meet its burden of proof to convict Smith based on the information presented in the criminal complaint. A judge ordered Smith to be held without bond pending a detention hearing, which wasn’t immediately scheduled.
Joshi said later Thursday during a phone interview that the prosecution’s case has many challenges that he plans to explore. The defense attorney said the investigation focused almost exclusively on Smith from the beginning and ignored other potential leads.
“Michelle Parker worked at a bar. She was a very attractive young lady,” Joshi said. “They (police) did not go out and investigate other possibilities that could have happened to her. This is one of those cases where they go and they immediately target the usual suspect, which is the ex.”
Orlando Police Chief Eric Smith, who is not related to Smith, said during the news conference on Wednesday that the case never stopped being a priority. Smith was the last known person to see or hear from Parker before she went missing on Nov. 17, 2011, when she dropped their children off at his home, the chief said.
“Over the past year, we expanded our investigative team looking into this case and took a fresh, focused look at all the evidence,” the police chief said. “We reexamined testimony and conflicting statements made by the suspect and used advances in digital forensics to uncover and analyze additional evidence.”
Police gave few details about what evidence they had against Smith, but Detective Phillip McMican confirmed that police had collected new evidence in the past year, as well as new insights into old evidence thanks to technological advancements.
“Vehicles, electronic devices, phones, computers — we’re able to better interpret that evidence today than what we were able to do back in 2011,” McMican said.
Police continue to search for Parker’s body. Her vehicle was found abandoned a day after her disappearance, and her cellphone was later recovered from an Orlando-area lake.
Investigators have not publicly stated a motive for Parker’s murder.
On the day of Parker’s disappearance, an episode of “The People’s Court” featuring her and Smith was broadcast. Smith had sued Parker, claiming that a $5,000 engagement ring that he bought for her was lost when she threw it at him during an argument. Judge Marilyn Milian ultimately ruled that both parties were responsible for the ring’s loss and ordered Parker to pay $2,500 to Smith for half of it.

title: Crumbl Cookies locations closing across the country, reports say
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - Dozens of Crumbl Cookies locations are reportedly closing their doors.
According to a report by Restaurant Business, at least 57 locations have closed this year, with more at risk. The outlet also reported at least 55 franchises were listed for sale.
The closures come even after Crumbl, known for its rotating line of cookies, launched dirty sodas to bring in sales. Rather than improving sales, unit volumes declined by about 16%.
Sales overall didn’t look any better. USA Today reported that sales in August were 70% lower than two months before.
Co-founders Sawyer Hemsley and Jason McGowan stepped down from the company earlier in the year.
Still, the company has more than 1,000 locations and 29,000 employees, according to its website.
Crumbl was formed in 2017 in Utah and was generating $1 billion in revenue each year within its first seven years, Restaurant Business reported. The company went viral during and after the pandemic and became widely known for its pink boxes across social media.

title: Maine’s unsung heroes, caregivers, deserve support. AARP Maine is in their corner.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Family caregivers are among Maine’s most important resources, yet their contributions often go unrecognized. Every day, they help aging parents, spouses, friends, neighbors, and other loved ones live safely and independently at home. They support their loved ones by helping with daily activities that many of us do but take for granted, such as making a meal or managing our medications. They do this not because they are paid to, but because someone they love needs help.
In Maine, nearly three in ten adults are family caregivers or have provided care within the past year. Together, they represent over 300,000 people whose dedication helps make it possible for countless older adults to remain in their homes and communities, where they want to be.
Caregiving is rewarding, but it can be demanding. Many caregivers work full- or part-time jobs, and some raise children while caregiving. Others find themselves navigating complicated health care systems, making difficult decisions, and handling responsibilities they never expected to take on. The physical, emotional, and financial challenges can be overwhelming.
Get the family caregiving help you need with resources in Maine.
The AARP Family Caregiver Resource Guide for Maine helps family caregivers access key programs, services and agencies in their community.
To order a copy of the guide, call the AARP Family Caregiving Resource Line at 1-877-333-5885 and request the AARP Family Caregiver Resource Guide for Maine. Or view it online at aarp.org/CaregiverResources.
Find us at aarp.org/me | [email protected] | @aarpmaine
That is why AARP Maine is committed to standing with family caregivers. We know they are the unsung heroes of Maine’s long-term care system, and we believe they deserve practical support, reliable information, and policies that make caregiving easier.
One of the most important ways AARP Maine has supported caregivers is through our advocacy for Paid Family and Medical Leave. We heard repeatedly from caregivers who were forced to choose between caring for a loved one and earning a paycheck. Many family caregivers are still working while providing care, often using vacation time, unpaid leave, or flexible schedules to meet their caregiving responsibilities.
AARP Maine fought for Paid Family and Medical Leave because no one should have to choose between family and financial security. The program gives eligible workers access to paid, job-protected leave when they need time to care for a loved one, recover from a serious health condition, welcome a new child, or address other qualifying family needs. It is a major step forward for Maine caregivers and working families.
Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) gives eligible Maine workers up to 12 weeks of paid, job-protected leave to care for themselves or a loved one. AARP Maine proudly advocated for PFML, helping ensure working caregivers no longer have to choose between family and a paycheck.
Learn more at maine.gov/paidleave
Advocacy is only part of the equation. Caregivers also need resources they can use today.
That is why AARP Maine offers a free Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide. Whether someone is just beginning a caregiving journey or has been providing care for years, the guide serves as a valuable roadmap to programs, services, and support available across the state. It includes information on caregiver support services, transportation assistance, financial resources, legal help, respite care, and other programs that can make caregiving more manageable.
The guide also encourages caregivers to prioritize their own well-being. Too often, caregivers focus entirely on the needs of others while neglecting their own health. Yet caregivers need support, rest, and resources if they are to continue providing care over the long term.
AARP Maine has also partnered with 211 Maine to help family caregivers connect with assistance in their communities. Through this collaboration, caregivers can contact 211 and be connected to trained specialists who help identify local resources tailored to their needs.
Caregiving will touch nearly every Maine family at some point. Most of us will either provide care, receive care, or love someone who does. As Maine’s population continues to age, supporting family caregivers becomes even more important.
At AARP Maine, we want caregivers to know they are not alone. We will continue fighting for policies that help them save time and money, providing resources that help them navigate challenges, and elevating their voices in Augusta and beyond.
If you are caring for a loved one, AARP Maine is in your corner. To learn more about Paid Family and Medical Leave, download the Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide, explore caregiver tools, and learn about the 211 Maine partnership, visit aarp.org/mecares.
Caregivers spend so much of their time caring for others. Let us help care for you.

title: High schools Thursday: Bonny Eagle football stays unbeaten

title: Trudy strengthens to a hurricane as system nears Mexico’s coast with major storm expected
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Trudy intensified into a Category 1 hurricane as it approached the Pacific coast of Mexico, authorities said Thursday.
Trudy was located about 300 miles (480 kilometers) southwest of Acapulco, Mexico, with maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami.
The hurricane was moving northwest at 9 mph (15 kph) and was expected to approach the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico this weekend, the center said.
Trudy was on track to become a major hurricane on Friday, bringing rainfall of 4 to 8 inches (101 to 203 millimeters) through the weekend across Colima and Jalisco states, the center said.

More than 60 of King’s published works have been adapted into feature films or miniseries, with even more projects in development. Pennywise the Dancing Clown is practically made for Halloween! With creepy small-town secrets, childhood fears, and plenty of nightmare fuel, this terrifying adaptation is a perfect pick for a spooky movie night.

An isolated hotel, an increasingly unhinged caretaker, and an atmosphere of pure dread make The Shining an all-time horror classic. If you're looking for a movie that will leave you feeling uneasy long after the credits roll, this one belongs on your Halloween watchlist. Oh, and the genius of Jack!
