title: Farmington approves $1.42M Main Street construction change
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — The Select Board approved a $1.42 million change order for the second phase of Main Street reconstruction Oct. 13, nearly 20% above the original construction estimate, allowing the town to continue with its existing contractor rather than begin another competitive bidding process.
The $1,419,539 proposal from Scully Construction of Smithfield is $229,264 higher than the $1,190,275 preliminary estimate included in a February application to the Maine Department of Transportation’s Municipal Partnership Initiative program.
The project covers Main Street from South Street to Anson Street, and Broadway from Main Street to High Street. Improvements include roadway milling and paving, concrete sidewalks, granite curbing, drainage adjustments, accessible crosswalk features and new pavement markings.
A comparison of the February estimate and Scully’s proposal shows the same quantities for all 12 construction items, although individual costs vary considerably.
The largest difference involves mobilization and demobilization, which increased from an estimated $45,000 to $298,204. Concrete sidewalk costs rose from $219,000 to $268,955, while pavement milling decreased from $308,000 to $136,430.
Public Works Director Philip Hutchins said continuing with Scully would avoid approximately $30,000 in additional engineering and administrative expenses associated with another bidding process, while reducing delays and allowing materials to be purchased ahead of potential price increases.
Hutchins said MDOT encouraged the town to proceed through a change order because both phases are part of a larger Main Street reconstruction project.
The February funding application proposed a 50% municipal contribution toward construction costs. The application did not establish the final funding split for the higher approved amount.
The application anticipated construction during spring and summer 2027, with completion by September. Scully’s proposal identifies a broader 2026-27 construction period.
Dirigo Engineering of Fairfield is overseeing engineering services for the project.
The board also reviewed progress on the first phase, which extends from Center Bridge to South Street and includes granite curbing, paving and improvements near the Hippach Field wall.
Paving was scheduled for Oct. 14, with cleanup and smaller construction tasks expected before winter.
Construction of the Hippach Field wall has been delayed by outstanding property easements and is now expected to begin in spring 2027. Materials for the wall have already been delivered.
Hutchins said the project’s engineer is preparing documentation allowing Farmington to seek reimbursement for completed portions of the first phase.
The Select Board also voted to accept a MDOT Municipal Partnership Initiative award associated with the second phase.

title: Ex-fiancé charged nearly 15 years after mother who was on ‘People’s Court’ vanished
text:
ORLANDO, Fla. (Gray News) - Nearly 15 years ago, a Florida mother vanished after she and her former fiancé appeared on “The People’s Court.” Now, he’s accused of her murder.
Orlando Police say 55-year-old Dale Smith Jr. was arrested Wednesday on a charge of second-degree murder in relation to the presumed death of his former fiancée, Michelle Parker.
Parker, 33, disappeared on Nov. 17, 2011, after dropping her then-3-year-old twins off at Smith Jr.’s Orlando home. Hours earlier, Parker and Smith Jr. appeared on an episode of “The People’s Court” in a dispute over a lost engagement ring, WESH reports.
Police say Smith Jr., who has been the prime suspect in the case for years, was the last known person to see or hear from Parker. While Parker’s remains have never been found, all the evidence points to her former fiancé as being responsible for her murder, according to police.
Orlando Police Chief Eric Smith credited the suspect’s arrest to a renewed, focused look at the case over the past year as well as advances in digital forensics.
“This case never stopped being a priority. Our detectives kept working. They kept asking questions. They kept examining the evidence,” said Smith at a press conference.
Nearly 15 years after her daughter’s disappearance, Parker’s mother, Yvonne Stewart, said Smith Jr.’s arrest brings some measure of closure.
“This is the happiest day,” Stewart told The Orlando Sentinel. “I was hopeful this day would come but never really knowing if it will and the fact that he could get away with it and not ever be arrested – that’s just a hard pill to swallow.”
Stewart also said she hopes Smith Jr. will reveal where her daughter’s remains are.
“There’s not one day that’s gone by that I don’t think of her or look at her pictures or talk to her,” she said. “I’m just going to take it minute by minute.”
Smith Jr. has denied having anything to do with Parker’s disappearance.

title: Hoda Kotb to appear on ‘Aging Untold’ in Gray Media partnership
text:
(Gray News) - Gray Media is teaming up with journalist Hoda Kotb and her wellness company Joy 101 to bring new health segments to local newscasts and “Aging Untold” starting in January 2027.
The partnership centers on a weekly feature called “The Doctor’s In with Joy 101.”
The segments will air nationwide inside “Aging Untold” episodes and in Gray Media newscasts to highlight insights about wellness, resilience and intentional living.
Kotb is expected to make several special appearances on the nationally syndicated program.
“The Doctor’s In with Joy 101” is produced by Joy 101 and pairs co-founder Karen Swensen with Dr. Stephanie Moore.
Swensen is an award-winning journalist whose work has appeared on NBC’s TODAY with Hoda and Jenna. Moore is a triple-board-certified cardiologist with a background in heart transplantation who spent more than 20 years on the faculty of Harvard Medical School.
Each week, the two will break down healthy aging and everyday vitality into clear steps families and caregivers can use.
“Partnering with Gray Media allows us to bring trusted, uplifting conversations about health and longevity directly to viewers across the country,” Kotb said. “We want to give ‘Aging Untold’ audiences and local news viewers practical tools that inspire genuine vitality and joy.”
“Aging Untold” is now in its second season. The 30-minute conversation series focuses on answers for older adults and their caregivers, with returning experts “Sam” Cradduck, Amy Cameron O’Rourke, Katherine Ambrose and Dr. Rhea Rogers.
The first season, which debuted in March 2026, reached more than 7 million viewers age 18 and older. The show has since added stations outside Gray markets and is now cleared in nearly 40% of U.S. TV households.
“Our viewers look to ‘Aging Untold’ and our local news teams for honest guidance on issues that touch every household,” said Sandy Breland, Gray’s chief operating officer. “This partnership unites Joy 101’s dynamic wellness insight with Gray’s trusted reporting.”
Viewers can check local listings or visit aginguntold.com for broadcast times and streaming options.
Gray said it will also offer the Joy 101 app and its expert-led resources to participating team members as part of a new workplace wellness effort.

title: Maine artist’s pinecone sculpture debuts at governor’s residence
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -A new sculpture unveiled Thursday at the Blaine House, the governor’s official residence, is giving Maine’s state flower a distinctly industrial look.
Maine artist Patrick Plourde created “Pinecone Pair with Tassel” using repurposed steel shovels, materials that reflect the state’s working history.
The sculpture was selected through a statewide artist selection process.
Plourde said seeing his work displayed at the Blaine House is a humbling experience.
“You know, I’m really humbled by this whole process,” Plourde said. “Because there were 34 other artists involved in this and I know their work. For me to be chosen, you know, from that group and to see them displayed this way, it’s just, I mean, look at this.”
The Maine Arts Commission said it selected the sculpture in part because of its compatibility with the Blaine House grounds and because it reflects Maine’s forests and fields.
The white pinecone was designated as Maine’s state flower in 1895.

title: Farmington approves $1.42M Main Street construction change
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — The Select Board approved a $1.42 million change order for the second phase of Main Street reconstruction Oct. 13, nearly 20% above the original construction estimate, allowing the town to continue with its existing contractor rather than begin another competitive bidding process.
The $1,419,539 proposal from Scully Construction of Smithfield is $229,264 higher than the $1,190,275 preliminary estimate included in a February application to the Maine Department of Transportation’s Municipal Partnership Initiative program.
The project covers Main Street from South Street to Anson Street, and Broadway from Main Street to High Street. Improvements include roadway milling and paving, concrete sidewalks, granite curbing, drainage adjustments, accessible crosswalk features and new pavement markings.
A comparison of the February estimate and Scully’s proposal shows the same quantities for all 12 construction items, although individual costs vary considerably.
The largest difference involves mobilization and demobilization, which increased from an estimated $45,000 to $298,204. Concrete sidewalk costs rose from $219,000 to $268,955, while pavement milling decreased from $308,000 to $136,430.
Public Works Director Philip Hutchins said continuing with Scully would avoid approximately $30,000 in additional engineering and administrative expenses associated with another bidding process, while reducing delays and allowing materials to be purchased ahead of potential price increases.
Hutchins said MDOT encouraged the town to proceed through a change order because both phases are part of a larger Main Street reconstruction project.
The February funding application proposed a 50% municipal contribution toward construction costs. The application did not establish the final funding split for the higher approved amount.
The application anticipated construction during spring and summer 2027, with completion by September. Scully’s proposal identifies a broader 2026-27 construction period.
Dirigo Engineering of Fairfield is overseeing engineering services for the project.
The board also reviewed progress on the first phase, which extends from Center Bridge to South Street and includes granite curbing, paving and improvements near the Hippach Field wall.
Paving was scheduled for Oct. 14, with cleanup and smaller construction tasks expected before winter.
Construction of the Hippach Field wall has been delayed by outstanding property easements and is now expected to begin in spring 2027. Materials for the wall have already been delivered.
Hutchins said the project’s engineer is preparing documentation allowing Farmington to seek reimbursement for completed portions of the first phase.
The Select Board also voted to accept a MDOT Municipal Partnership Initiative award associated with the second phase.

title: Dementia cases to double worldwide by 2050, study says
text:
(CNN) — A new study suggests the number of people worldwide who develop dementia each year is expected to more than double by 2050.
Researchers studied data from 22 studies involving more than 38,000 people from 18 countries.
After following the participants over a period of time, the researchers estimate there will be nearly 25 million new annual cases of dementia by 2050.
For comparison, more than 11 million people developed dementia in 2023.
The researchers said they found women and those living in low- and middle-income countries were at higher risk of developing dementia.
The study’s authors said the research did not show why those disparities existed, but they highlighted the challenge for countries with lesser health care resources to deal with the condition.
The study was published Monday in JAMA Neurology.

title: When hearing loss affects the whole household
text:
“Did my spouse ignore a request because they forgot it, or because they never heard it?”
“Did Mom respond strangely because she is experiencing cognitive changes, or because she misunderstood what was said?”
“Did I confuse the date and time again?”
At Dirigo Hearing Center in Biddeford, co-owners Dr. Tarja Oliver and Dr. Abigail Sedenka regularly see older patients and their families trying to answer questions like these, sometimes acting as relationship coaches as much as audiologists.
In fact, they say that the first call to the office often comes from a caregiver, a loved one, or a family member who notices the person struggling in whatever way and convinces them to get the appointment.
Sometimes the signs are obvious: The television keeps getting louder or conversations need to be repeated. Others are easier to miss. Someone who once dominated the conversation around the game table now plays quietly. Restaurant invitations are turned down. Family gatherings feel exhausting.
Age-related hearing loss often develops gradually, making it easy for someone to adapt without realizing how much they are missing.
“And then people gradually make changes that often make their world smaller and smaller,” Dr. Sedenka said. That shrinking world is one reason hearing loss can affect far more than the person’s ability to hear.
When someone’s world gets smaller
Age-related changes in hearing can sometimes look like changes in memory, comprehension or behavior, and the two can occur together.
A 12 year long study of 639 adults at John Hopkins University researchers found that even mild hearing loss, when untreated, doubled the risk of developing dementia. Moderate loss tripled the risk, and people with severe hearing impairment “were five times more likely to develop dementia.”
Scientists are still studying exactly why hearing loss in older adults is connected to greater cognitive decline. Johns Hopkins researchers point out that hearing helps us balance, so possible explanations include the additional cognitive effort required to move through the world or process degraded sound. Other reasons include physical changes to the brain and increased social isolation.
However, hearing aids and communication changes can help. An NIH-funded clinical trial followed nearly 1,000 adults ages 70 to 84 with untreated hearing loss for three years. While hearing intervention did not reduce cognitive decline across the study population as a whole, among a group of participants at higher risk for cognitive decline, it reduced the rate by nearly 50%.
Understanding a person’s hearing ability can help families and health care providers get a clearer picture of what may be happening. For individuals or caregivers who are noticing changes, Dr. Oliver recommends starting in two places: Talk with a primary care provider and request a hearing test.
“That way you can know, did they not do what I asked them to do, or did they respond in a weird way because they didn’t hear me?” Dr. Oliver said. “Is there something else going on? Or both?”
Dirigo Hearing Center does not perform cognitive assessments, but Dr. Sedenka and Dr. Oliver regularly work with patients experiencing cognitive decline.
Better communication can support hearing loss
A hearing test and hearing aids, when appropriate, are only part of the solution.
When caregivers or family members accompany patients to appointments at Dirigo Hearing Center, Dr. Sedenka and Dr. Oliver can also teach them how to make communication easier at home.
The strategies are simple (and perhaps good advice for all of our relationships).
• No more yelling across the house or talking over the television.
• Get the person’s attention before speaking.
• Pause or turn off the TV, headphones or other distracting sounds.
• Be in the same room and face each other directly.
“Our ultimate goal is that you put the hearing aid in your ear and you don’t have to touch it,” Dr. Sedenka said, but even with ever-advancing technology (see below) hearing aids cannot restore perfect hearing.
Instead, they make communication “less effortful,” as the doctors describe it, so people feel confident participating again. Patients return to Dirigo Hearing Center and say they could hear their grandchildren during a visit or are rediscovering sounds they hadn’t realized they were missing.
For an older adult, better hearing makes it easier to stay part of the conversation. For family, caregivers and friends, it can mean fewer misunderstandings and less frustration. And for the whole household, it keeps an important person connected to the experiences and relationships that make up their world.
Hearing aid technology is the best it’s ever been
According to the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, fewer than one in three adults age 70 and older with hearing loss who could benefit from hearing aids has ever used them. Among adults ages 20 to 69 who could benefit, the figure is just 16%.
For people whose image of a hearing aid comes from a grandparent constantly adjusting a bulky device, Dr. Oliver and Dr. Sedenka said sleek-to-near-invisible designs and modern technology can be a surprise.
Artificial intelligence is everywhere, so it’s not surprising that hearing aid manufacturers have put this type of computing to use in designing today’s devices.
Some use AI to distinguish speech from background noise and change settings accordingly, while directional microphones can help prioritize sound coming from the person a wearer is facing.
Meanwhile, Bluetooth technology is becoming more standard. Many hearing aids can connect to smartphones or Bluetooth-equipped televisions, allowing phone calls or TV audio to stream directly through the hearing aids.

title: Mitchell Pushes for Larger Homestead Exemption in Bid for Senate District 13
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Edwin W. Mitchell, I-Boothbay, wants to represent both sides of the political aisle in his run for Senate District 13.
Mitchell, who goes by Win, faces Cameron Reny, D-Bristol, to represent Senate District 13, which consists of Lincoln County, excluding Dresden and including Washington and Windsor.
“I don’t have the answers to everything, but I sure have talked to a lot of people that have some great ideas,” Mitchell said. “Their voices need to be shared and heard.”
Originally from Southport, Mitchell volunteered with the Southport Fire Department and later attended Southern Maine Vocational Technical Institute for Marine Science Deck to get his mate’s or captain’s license. Instead of taking the usual route of shipping off on a tanker or tug boat, Mitchell went into the private boat trade, he said.
After a few years of running a boat up and down the East Coast, Mitchell was hired as a boat captain to run boats for the Maine Marine Patrol, first stationed in Southwest Harbor and then Boothbay.
Mitchell retired from the patrol after 12 years and spent his time after lobstering and running different businesses, such as woodcutting and lot cleaning. In 2006, Mitchell and his wife bought the property that his brewery and RV park now sit on. Boothbay Craft Brewery, Tavern, and RV is celebrating 20 years in business this year.
“We did everything ourselves,” Mitchell said.
With the creation of the brewery, Mitchell became a figure in reviving the Maine Brewer’s Guild. He partnered with the owner of Maine Beer Company, Daniel Kleban, and former state representative and senator Heather Sanborn, to reshape the organization. The effort took the guild from 25 breweries to just over 150.
Mitchell has “never been in politics” before because of his employment at the state level. He said he is familiar with numerous laws and how bills are passed.
“But I’m more interested in representing all my fellow Lincoln County people,” Mitchell said.
Mitchell is running as an independent because he believes he can converse with both political parties by being in the middle. During his campaign, he said he has found that more people are willing to talk to him because he is not affiliated with a party.
“I can state unequivocally that I am doing it because I think that’s the only proper way to represent a diverse political area like Lincoln County,” he said.
Mitchell decided to run because his sons are now old enough to start taking over the business. As they do so, he said his plan is to give back to the community.
He said he believes that his experience working in marine patrol and connections across the state from his business make him a good candidate. He referenced his campaign videos that highlight why he loves his community and local industries throughout the district.
“They’re intended to tell why I love living here, why my boys love living here, and we want to be able to stay here and succeed,” Mitchell said.
Another motivator for Mitchell to run was a perceived disconnect between elected officials and the communities they represent. In the 20 years he has run his business, he said that Reny has not stopped by.
Mitchell said once someone is elected to office, it should not be the end of their door knocking.

title: R.U. OK? Older adults living alone in Arizona get daily check-in calls
text:
PHOENIX (Aging Untold) — A program in Phoenix is ensuring that older adults who live alone have a lifeline in case of an emergency.
Each year, there are about 3 million emergency room visits due to falls among older adults, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Multiple studies published between 2020 and 2025 found living alone may increase the risk of falls and the severity of injury among older adults.
Debbie Lane, 84, has lived in Arizona since 1977 after moving from New Jersey. She raised three children and has been involved with the Arizona Opera. Now she lives alone and has peace of mind knowing that the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office checks on her every day through its R.U. OK program, which stands for Are You OK?
How the program works
“It rings. I know the number. The voice says the number. I push it and they said, ‘This is R.U. OK and push one if you are OK, push three if you need assistance,’ which I like,” Lane said.
Sun City Posse Chaplain Don Erlitz said the residents receive up to three computerized calls every day. If they do not answer, deputies are dispatched to their homes.
Erlitz said the goal is to make sure residents are OK.
Lane participates in the R.U. OK program for her children. When she told them about it, they were thrilled, she said. It gives them peace of mind.

title: Chicago Catholics rally for prayer in Pope Leo's hometown after his lung cancer diagnosis
text:
Pope Leo XIV’s hometown of Chicago sends cards, prayers and support after diagnosis
Gail Spreen goes most days to Mass just a few blocks from her home in Chicago, but the service at Holy Name Cathedral on Wednesday — dedicated to Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV — felt different.
“Knowing that everybody is behind him, it was very special to be there today," Spreen said. "The church was full and everybody was praying. You could just see all those prayers going up and being received.”
Catholics in Chicago and around the world met the news of Leo's lung cancer diagnosis with shock, concern and support for the 71-year-old, whose candor around his health broke with the Vatican's tendency to be tight-lipped around papal health. Leo himself announced that he had a nodule and was undergoing surgery, which confirmed that he has lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Surgeons on Tuesday removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
Spreen, whose husband died from cancer, said the pope going public with his diagnosis can “wake up the whole world” to the importance of early detection.
“If the pope can have cancer, anybody can," she said.
The first American-born pope, Leo undertook his ministry in Peru, but he was born in 1955 in the south side Chicago neighborhood of Bronzeville and grew up in suburban Dolton, near St. Mary of the Assumption, where he attended Mass and elementary school.
He later studied theology at the Catholic Theological Union of Chicago in Hyde Park and taught in local Catholic schools, including at St. Rita High School. Leo is also a White Sox fan, a fact embraced by the team.
Cardinal Blase J. Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago, encouraged fellow Chicagoans and people worldwide to “join me in asking the Lord to return this son of Chicago to wellness.”
"He has much more good work to do, many more wise words to preach and many more ways to inspire others," Cupich said in a statement.
Earlier Wednesday, students at Our Lady of Mount Carmel Academy made get-well cards and a care package, complete with a White Sox blanket, to send to the Vatican. The Rev. Charles Rubey, a retired priest, planned to offer a Sunday Mass in the apartment where he lives in the suburbs of Chicago.
“I’m praying very hard, asking God to spare him illness, so he’ll be successful in the treatment,” he said.
“I think he’s a hero,” Rubey said of Pope Leo. “He’s highly revered here, highly loved.”
The Vatican said late Wednesday that the pope had celebrated Mass with his secretaries in the afternoon in a special chapel set up for him on the 10th floor of the hospital. He had also resumed his regular diet and begun walking.
For Katrina Coker, Leo has been an authentic embodiment of true Catholicism, which she said should be open and welcoming and loving. Coker of Johns Creek, Georgia, said it was meaningful to her that she happened to be in Chicago this week and she wanted to attend Mass in his hometown to pray for Leo's recovery.
“I feel somewhat of a kindred spirit, and hopefully he can get a little bit of healing from home,” she said. “I think there’s just so much more that he can do, and I pray that he gets well soon."

title: ‘Street Fighter’ Review: This Video Game Movie Will Beat You Into Submission
text:
Review: ‘Street Fighter’ Will Beat You Into Submission With ’90s Nostalgia
If Mountain Dew directed a movie (with editing by Surge and music by Crystal Pepsi) it might look like Street Fighter. Relentless, loud, and bursting with color, it’s as much an adaptation of the Capcom fighting game as it is of the vibe of a ’90s mall arcade: Flashing lights, blaring chiptunes, and overcaffeinated people screaming at one another to be heard over the din. And like a trip to a ’90s mall arcade, Street Fighter’s pretty fun — for about 30 minutes, until the sensory overload starts to pummel your overstimulated brain into submission.
Credit where credit’s due: This movie goes for it. Unlike the ’90s Street Fighter movie, which clearly disdained its source material, the 2026 edition was made for fans by fans. It’s got most of the game’s classic cast of fighters, all in their signature costumes and hair – no matter how outlandish they might look in live-action. (Kudos to WWE wrestler Cody Rhodes for possessing the confidence and the sense of humor to rock the biggest and flattest flattop in cinema history as macho military man Guile).
At the center of them all are Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken (Noah Centineo). Former training partners and best friends, the duo have not spoken since a tragedy at the World Warrior Tournament. After an animated prologue establishes the reason for their estrangement, the story picks up six years later, when a power-mad dictator named M. Bison (David Dastmalchian) relaunches the same street fighting contest for brazenly nefarious purposes. His competition attracts top pugilists from around the globe, including stretchy-limbed Indian Dhalsim (Bollywood actor Vidyut Jammwal), claw-handed Spaniard Vega (country music star Orville Peck), and burly Russian grappler Zangief (Dutch bodybuilder Olivier Richters).
READ MORE: The Best Movies of the Year So Far
But wait! There are many, many more! There’s also 50 Cent as the boxer Balrog, Mel Jarnson as Bison’s henchwoman Cammy, MMA star Alexander Volkanovski as Joe, and no less than three pro wrestlers — Cody Rhodes, Joe “Roman Reigns” Anoa’i, and New Japan’s Hrooki Goto —all playing different Street Fighter mainstays (Guile, Akuma, and E. Honda, respectively.) Oh and Jason Momoa voices the beastly, quirky Blanca, who looks like the Hulk’s stoner cousin and possesses electricity powers because he was raised by electric eels. (That’s a thing that happens, right?) Blanka also likes to sniff his armpits and say stuff like “Mm, smell like hot dogs.”
Momoa is not the only character to smell himself or others in Street Fighter. The script by Sakurai and T.J. Fixman (with a story credit for Dalan Musson and Gary Dauberman) is big on B.O. humor, perhaps intended as another nod to those old arcades, which could get pretty funky if they weren’t properly ventilated. Or maybe it’s just part of this movie‘s broader strategy to fill the space between the fight scenes with as much weirdness as possible.
Said weirdness includes: Eric André screaming basically every one of his lines into a star-spangled microphone, Dastmalchian rolling his eyes into the back of his head as he monologues about his desire for “psycho power,” and Centineo’s Ken lugging around the ashes of his dead master and occasionally singing 4 Non Blonde’s “What’s Up?” You’ll lose track of why most of the characters care about this tournament or what’s at stake, but hey — Kyle Mooney gets a couple of chuckles as some kind of government agent with a desk job with a pathetic crush on the ferocious and beautiful Chun-Li (Callina Liang).
“What’s Up?” is hardly the only sing-along needle drop; the ironic soundtrack faves fly at the viewer nearly as fast as E. Honda’s hundred-hand slap. Street Fighter is all manic attitude. It’s self-aware enough to acknowledge the silliness baked into the Street Fighter mythology, even as it dedicates two full hours to getting as much of it onscreen as possible.
It doesn’t help that the movie is almost all set up; introducing and bringing together the enormous cast of the characters. By the time the tournament begins — and the film begins skipping multiple rounds of matches — Street Fighter begins to feel like the movie version of when you’d take a multiple-choice test in school, spend too much time solving the first five questions, and then have to rush to randomly fill in the bubbles for the last 20 answers. The film’s one-note go-for-broke freneticism gets tiresome long before Street Fighter stops and the credits roll. (Note I didn’t say it ends. It doesn’t. It simply stops.)
Everything rushes by in such a blur, it’s tough to single out highlights. There are so many characters that a lot of them fade to the background, although Roman Reigns brings an impressive amount of aggression and presence to the role of the supernaturally powered Akuma. Centineo brings a lot of rough charisma to Ken, despite spending a lot of the movie playing off Andrew Schulz as the bumbling Dan.
Street Fighter did make me smile a fair number of times. The sheer absurdity and fevered intensity of the pacing, not to mention some very athletic fight choreography, is good enough to carry things along through the jittery first act. (The best scene in the entire film is a confrontation between Ken and Ryu where the latter is trying everything he can think of not to beat up his friend and instead resorts of dodging his attacks and yanking off his socks.) But you can only mainline caffeine for so long before it starts to give you a headache.
Additional Thoughts:
-I generally sit through the closing credits of Hollywood movies out of professional obligation. (For the record, Street Fighter contains one brief mid-credits scene, and zilch after the credits.) With Street Fighter, that obligation was also a pleasure, because the end credits are backed by Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson’s fist-pumping electronic score. The pair previously wrote the music for Cobra Kai, which very much tracks. If you need composers for a nostalgic action movie or show about aggro dudes with gushy hearts, they’re the men for the job.
-Maybe it’s the ’90s kid in me, but I cannot help but observe that Street Fighter’s perennial rival in arcades, Mortal Kombat, got its own movie in 2026 — and that the heroes of both films share the same backstory, the same motivation, and the same arc. Street Fighter’s Ken and Mortal Kombat II’s Johnny Cage (Karl Urban) are both famous fighters who have fallen on hard times and now resort to taking embarrassing, emasculating gigs for cash. They both enter tournaments filled with garish, mega-powerful warriors, where they must regain their own confidence and sense of self-worth as they battle their way to victory. Is there no other storyline that can ground this kind of video-game adaptation? I’ll say this right now: If they make a Primal Rage movie about an insecure raptor god who needs to rediscover his belief in himself, I quit.
RATING: 5/10

title: Luna, a small dog missing for over a month in Yellowstone, is reunited with her owners
text:
(AP) - For over a month, Luna, a Jack Russell terrier that bolted from her family’s cabin during a vacation at Yellowstone National Park, eluded capture as fears for her survival mounted and winter weather approached. On Wednesday, her ordeal came to a happy ending when she was caught and reunited with her owners.
The 10-year-old white dog with pointy ears and a gray collar had been spotted crossing intersections, strolling through employee housing and entering lodges through automatic doors at the sprawling park, home to grizzly bears, wolves and other predators.
Katie Boucher, the volunteer leading the rescue effort and a spokesperson for Luna’s California owners, said she and one of the owners found the dog in the trap baited with scraps from a T-shirt and pillowcase belonging to the family. They took her to a veterinarian, where the owner held the dog as it was examined Wednesday afternoon.
“She’s underweight, but that’s to be expected. She’s alert and in good spirits,” Boucher said. “I was crying all the way up here from the park.”
Luna escaped Sept. 10. Boucher said the dog spent its first year on the streets before being adopted and showed strong survival instincts while on the loose. Based on sightings, Boucher said, Luna retraced her family’s steps from the day before she was lost -- sneaking into eateries or lodges they had visited and seeking shelter in employee residences and businesses.
An escape into the wilderness
The day of the escape, the family left her in their cabin with a “Do Not Disturb” sign while they ventured out to explore the park. They believe a housekeeping staffer accidentally opened a door, freeing the dog.
“The staff then proceeded to chase her around that area of the park for over two hours before the owners came back and discovered all the chaos and their dog missing,” Boucher said.
Yellowstone was the first U.S. national park and covers about 3,500 square miles (some 9,000 square kilometers), including portions of Wyoming, Montana and Idaho.
Luna’s family searched for the dog, which is part chihuahua, but were told it likely died, possibly killed by a coyote, Boucher recounted. Days after leaving Yellowstone, the owners learned Luna had been spotted, and contacted Boucher, president of the Norris Ark Training and Recovery Center in Norris, Montana, north of the park.
“I cannot fathom how I would feel if I had been taking the vacation of a lifetime, and looking for all these memorable experiences in one of the most beautiful places on earth, and lost one of my family members there,” Boucher said.
Locals and tourists called out Luna’s name or chased her, triggering her fight-or-flight response and driving her further into the park, Boucher said. The volunteers set a live trap using the family’s scent to lure Luna in, avoiding food that could attract bears or other wildlife.
Time was running out as winter closes in
Boucher said this was the last week she would have been able to search for Luna. She was sleeping at an RV park for seasonal employees that closes next Monday.
The search had rallied locals and tourists alike. Marie Jaskula, an area resident who runs one of the park’s general stores, posted signs at every park entrance urging visitors to be on the lookout for the dog.
“It’s really hard to stress the importance of do not chase,” said Jaskula. “Everybody sees this little dog buzz across the intersection or maybe around their employee housing, and the first instinct is to call her name and chase her.”

title: Why now is the time for a pre-holiday debt audit
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Carrying credit card debt into the holiday season can quickly spiral into a painful “debt hangover” come January. Debt relief attorney Leslie Tayne said now, before the holiday pressure sets in, is the time to review budgets for the upcoming season.
Tayne said that includes planning for Thanksgiving, Hanukkah, Christmas and Kwanzaa.
“At this time you should be gathering your lists, thinking about who you’re giving gifts to and how you’re going to be paying for those,” Tayne said. “If there’s sales on items you’re going to be purchasing, now is the time to be taking advantage of those. Start looking for coupons and other opportunities, like Black Friday sales that might be coming up.”
Tayne said planning ahead is key to staying on budget, and smart online shopping can make a real difference. For big-ticket items like toys or electronics, she recommends checking prices across multiple retailers now.
“It’s an opportunity to think now: What does this item cost? Will this particular item go on sale? Where can I get the best possible deal?” Tayne said. “Be very proactive about finding that opportunity to save as much money as possible and budget your spending for the holidays.”
Tayne said the holiday season tends to arrive quickly, and rising prices due to inflation can mean even more debt for families who are not prepared. She said the current challenge for shoppers is making sure every dollar goes as far as possible.

title: Portland Hearts of Pine unveil new women's team name, crest
Portland upholds opinion that Maine Irish Heritage Center is not tax-exempt
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Eric Brown dropped a check for $22,000 at Portland City Hall this week. Written on the check’s memo line were the words: “filed under protest.”
After reapplying for tax exempt status this spring, Brown, the executive director of the Maine Irish Heritage Center, received a 23-page response from the city assessor outlining their opinion that MIHC does not meet the definition of a charitable organization.
It was sent just days before local property tax bills are due. The building is assessed at $3.5 million.
Now, the nonprofit will lobby for state legislation, after losing an exemption that it held for two decades. Brown has been among the most vocal critics of the city’s recent decisions on exemptions, arguing that assessing staff continues to apply a “narrow interpretation of case law” in its decision.
In a statement posted to social media this week, Brown said that while several nonprofits have faced the same denials, the group’s position is “especially precarious because of the disproportion in the assessed value of our building and our actual operating budget.”
Brown said the assessor reviewed the organization’s finances and recognized that MIHC would operate at a loss without government grants and membership dues, but said the decision “registers clearly that the city is prepared to shutter the Irish Center permanently, despite there being no material change in our operations or service to the community.”
The assessor’s decision hinges on several points, including an opinion that the center on Gray Street does not meet the definition of a public building and is used for non-exempt private functions through rentals and events.
“The applicant’s activities may be ‘charitable’ in a broad sense of the word, but not within the legal meaning of the charitable exemption statute,” the city’s decision states.
Brown said he challenges the opinion that MIHC’s preservation of the former St. Dominic’s church — a historic landmark in Portland — does not fall under the mission of maintaining public buildings.
While some nonprofit leaders and officials have questioned whether assessing staff has been working under a new interpretation of state law, city staff have repeatedly said the revocations are not the result of any policy changes, and that the city now has the ability, with increased staff, to conduct reviews more thoroughly.
Municipal tax assessors in Maine are considered agents of the state and must follow state statutes for assessments, but they are also granted the authority to make decisions on exemptions locally.
Brown said the assessor’s decision is based on a definition of “charitable” that comes from case law stemming from a 1867 Massachusetts case. He’d like to see legislation to amend the state statute to explicitly extend protection to arts and culture organizations as providing a public and charitable good.
He said organizations with arts, culture and heritage missions have traditionally been viewed in other municipalities as charitable work and have qualified for exemptions by other assessing offices.
Despite some momentum among lawmakers this past spring, a bill that would have remedied the situation did not move forward. However, Brown is hopeful that with more “runway” to iron out the details on the language and what organizations would qualify, a bill could advance in the next legislative session.
“Despite this setback, I continue to be encouraged by the affirmations we have received at almost every turn in pursuing remedies to the assessor’s damaging decision,” he said in a statement on social media.
In August, Maine Public was informed it had also been denied tax-exempt status as it prepared to move into its new headquarters in the former Portland Public Market building on Cumberland Avenue. It was the media organization’s fourth attempt at gaining an exemption in Portland. Maine Public holds an exemption in Bangor and previously held an exemption at its former property in Lewiston.
The Press Herald requested an updated list of organizations that have had exemptions denied or revoked in the past year, but had not received it Thursday.

title: ‘It feels like punishment’: School district cancels ‘Little Shop of Horrors’ after female cast as male lead
text:
GRAND PRAIRIE, Texas (WFAA) - Grand Prairie ISD has scrapped its production of “Little Shop of Horrors” after district officials learned of the show’s casting and themes, according to the district.
Ana Mota, a senior at South Grand Prairie High School, was cast as the male lead, Seymour, before school leaders told her on Oct. 6 that she would no longer play the role.
Casting changed before cancellation
Ana said callbacks are for specific roles and students do not choose which roles they audition for. She said she initially got the role of Seymour.
“Initially, I got it,” Ana said. “And now we’re here.”
Ana said school leaders offered her the chance to split the female lead with another student instead.
“I was frustrated because I had earned a role and I worked hard for it and I wasn’t allowed to play it,” Ana said.
District cites state law
Grand Prairie ISD canceled the entire production after learning about the casting and the musical’s themes, which include the male lead character developing a romantic relationship with the female lead and an abusive relationship. The district said it plans to find something it called more appropriate.
“It’s not a compromise at all. It feels more like a punishment to everyone in the cast,” Ana said.
In a statement, the district said the decision was made as part of its effort to ensure programs comply with Texas Senate Bill 12 and other applicable laws. The law restricts certain sexually oriented performances on public property in the presence of minors.
Student has played male roles before
Ana said playing male characters is not new for her.
“I played Jack in ‘Into the Woods’ and Pinocchio,” she said.
Ana and her family plans to push back on the district’s decision.
“If we keep our heads down then nothing’s going to get better,” she said.

title: Portland restaurant to offer Thai, Vietnamese cuisine under one roof
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Portland family-owned restaurant group known for its Vietnamese and Thai cuisine plans to offer both at a single location in the city’s Old Port neighborhood starting this fall.
Veranda Kitchen & Bar has signed a seven-year lease for 1,381 square feet at 425 Fore St., according to East Brown Cow, which is involved in the Old Port Square development.
Pete Harrington of Malone Commercial Brokers brokered the lease.
Veranda Kitchen & Bar plans to use the existing fast-casual restaurant buildout and outdoor patio along Fore Street. The space they’re moving into on Fore Street had been leased by 66S Fusion in 2016 and underwent a full buildout, but the business never launched.
An exact opening date has not been announced.
About the restaurant
The new location will expand the business founded in 2009 by husband-and-wife team Hai Pham and Sonka Nguyen in Portland’s East Deering neighborhood. They own Veranda Thai at 9 Veranda St. and Veranda Noodle Bar across the street, which focuses on Vietnamese cuisine.
The couple later opened Veranda Asian Market at 695 Forest Ave in Portland, Veranda Kitchen & Bar at 672 Main St. in Westbrook and most recently, another Veranda Kitchen & Bar in Coral Springs, Florida.
The Old Port restaurant will serve both Vietnamese and Thai dishes, including pho, the Vietnamese noodle soup dish.
“Portland has been home to our family and our restaurants for many years, and we’re excited to bring Veranda Kitchen & Bar to Old Port Square,” said Nguyen. “We look forward to welcoming longtime guests and meeting new diners and visitors from around the world.”
The restaurant will join Barkada, a Filipino restaurant, and Gelato Fiasco, on Fore Street.

title: Why stop there, Sec. Hegseth?

title: Suspicious letters with white powder mailed to election and congressional offices
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities are investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and are urging recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.”
The investigation by the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Thursday by The Associated Press. The notice, sent to Senate offices, said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but “it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations.”
In Congress, the threat appeared limited to the Senate, though the House was monitoring the situation, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly.
The office of Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, a Delaware Democrat, said in a statement that it was sent a letter with a “suspicious substance” that was intercepted by Capitol Police. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said the Postal Service intercepted a suspicious package before it reached his office. And Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said postal inspectors intercepted a suspicious piece of mail addressed to her New York City office.
An FBI statement said the bureau and the Postal Inspection Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”
“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the statement read. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said their election offices either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said in a statement that it received a letter and the white powder enclosed in it was not hazardous, according to tests. “Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us,” Wisconsin elections administrator Meagan Wolfe said.
News of the letters comes just three weeks before Election Day and is reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when election offices in six states received mailings that contained a white powder. In some cases, the incidents disrupted work around local elections.
Some of those letters contained threats and traces of the powerful opioid fentanyl, leading some election offices to stock up on the overdose reversal medication naloxone.
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement condemning what they said were threats against election staff.
“Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” they said in their statement.
Deputy Postal Inspector Brendan Donahue told reporters Thursday that “any threat or attack on election officials is unacceptable” and that “we are also working with our partners on identifying the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”
___
Associated Press writers Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin; Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia; and Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this report.

title: Medomak Volleyball Wins Three
text:
The Medomak Valley volleyball team swept Wiscasset 3-0 in a Class C tilt on Tuesday, Oct. 13 in Waldoboro.
The match got off to a very competitive start, with the Panthers outlasting the Wolverines 25-23 in the opening set. Medomak carried the momentum over to the second set, which they won 25-19. The Panthers completed the sweep with a 25-11 win in the third set.
Medomak improved to 10-3 on the season and are now in third place in the Class C Heal Point Standings. Wiscasset dropped to 4-8, and hold sixth place in division with eight teams advancing to the playoffs.
Medomak 3 – Camden Hills 2
The Medomak Valley volleyball team beat Camden Hills 3-2 on Thursday, Oct. 8 in Waldoboro. The Panthers won the fifth and deciding set 15-13 to earn the 3 2 victory. It was their second win over Windjammers this season, after the Panthers swept Camden 3-0 on Sept. 8.
Medomak won the first set in overtime, 27-25, before the Windjammers responded with a stunning 25-7 win in the second set. The momentum swung back in favor of the Panthers in the third set, with Medomak prevailing 25-18 to take a 2-1 lead in the best-of five sets match.
The Windjammers responded yet again, taking the fourth set 25-20 to knot the match 2-2. Medomak jumped out to a 5-0 lead in the deciding fifth set, which unlike the first four sets, is a tiebreaker set played to 15 points instead of 25.
The Windjammers rallied to knot the score 6-6. The Panthers reestablished their lead and held an advantage until Camden stormed back again to tie the set 11-11. The set would level out again at 13-13 before Medomak won two straight points to seal the win 15-13.
The Panthers improved to 9-3 on the season, while Camden Hills dropped to 6-6.
Medomak Valley 3 – Nokomis 1
Medomak Valley beat Nokomis 3-1 on Tuesday, Oct. 6 in Newport.
The Panthers took the first set 25 16, before the Warriors evened the match by winning the second set 25-19. The Panthers won the next two sets 25-15, and 25-15, to win the match 3-1.
Andi Winchenbach had a strong match serving for Medomak, with 10 aces, and Maggie Bruno was next with five. Brooke McNelly had the most kills with six, and Bruno had five. Katie Bickel led the Panthers in digs with three. Sienna Lee recorded the only block for the Panthers during the match.

title: ‘Doomsday’ glacier is melting more aggressively than previously projected, study says
text:
(CNN) - A new study suggests the Thwaites Glacier, nicknamed the “Doomsday Glacier,” is melting “more aggressively” than previously projected.
Thwaites Glacier is located in West Antarctica. It got its nickname due to the impact its collapse would have on the rise of sea levels.
The glacier’s melting is driven by processes at the point where the ice rises up from the seabed and starts to float on the ocean as an ice shelf. That point is known as the “grounding line.”
Researchers say satellite data shows that line is actually a “grounding zone” that is sometimes miles wide. They say it is allowing warm ocean water to reach deep underneath the ice sheets and cause vigorous melting.
Using a new ice sheet model, the researchers predict the glacier could contribute up to 1.2 inches of sea level rise by the year 2100. That is twice the amount of previous estimates.

title: Gorgeous Fall Day Today... Then Rain Moves In Friday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - High pressure building into the area will bring us a beautiful fall day today with plenty of sunshine. Strong low pressure over the Maritimes combined with high pressure moving in from our west... will make for a breezy day with a northwest wind gusting to 25-35 MPH at times. Temperatures will be more seasonable with highs in the upper 40s to low 50s north and low to mid-50s elsewhere. Clouds will move back in tonight as our next weathermaker approaches. Temperatures will drop to the 30s for nighttime lows.
Low pressure is forecast to move from the Eastern Great Lakes Region Friday morning to the east/northeast... passing over Northern Maine Friday evening then exiting to our east Friday night. There’s a chance we may see some wet snow or mixed rain and snow across Northern Aroostook County at the onset of precipitation Friday morning... otherwise this northerly route will allow enough warm air to move in so that precipitation falls mainly as rain. Plan on rain spreading west to east across the state during the early to mid-morning with periods of rain continuing through the afternoon and evening before tapering off Friday night as the storm exits to our east. Temperatures on Friday will reach the mid to upper 40s north and mainly 50s elsewhere. Overall rainfall totals look a bit lighter than previously forecast... with most spots averaging .25″ to .75″ by later Friday evening. A few scattered snow showers will be possible Saturday morning.... mainly across the north and in the mountains otherwise expect morning clouds to give way to clearing skies as the day progresses. The pressure gradient will tighten up again on the backside of our departing storm leading to a strong northwest wind Saturday with gusts to 30-40 MPH possible. This will usher colder air into the region too with highs on Saturday only reaching the upper 30s to low 40s north and low to mid-40s elsewhere but will feel colder of course with the wind factored in. The wind will begin to diminish Saturday night as high pressure builds towards the area... allowing the pressure gradient to relax. The diminishing wind combined with clear skies and a colder air mass in place will lead to a cold night with lows dropping to the 20s to near 30° for most spots. High pressure will continue to build into the area for the second half of the weekend giving us lots of sunshine Sunday. It looks like the northwest wind will still be a bit breezy Sunday....especially over eastern areas but overall wind speeds will be much lighter as the pressure gradient continues to relax. After a cold start to the day... temperatures will be a bit better with highs in the mid-40s to near 50° north and low to mid-50s elsewhere. High pressure will provide us with a nice start to the work week with sunshine and seasonable temps Monday. Monday’s high temperatures will reach the 50s to near 60°.
Rest of Today: Mostly sunny and breezy. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s. Northwest wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-35 MPH possible.
Tonight: Increasing clouds. Diminishing wind. Lows in the 30s. Light and variable wind.
Friday: Rain likely. Some rain/snow mix possible across the north during the morning. Highs in the mid-40s to around 50° north and low to mid-50s elsewhere. Southeast wind 10-20 MPH.
Saturday: Morning clouds giving way to increasing sunshine. Breezy and colder. Highs in the upper 30s to low 40s north and low to mid-40s elsewhere. Northwest winds could gust to 30-40 MPH at times.
Sunday: Mostly sunny and breezy. Highs in the mid-40s to near 50° north and low to mid-50s elsewhere.
Monday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to near 60°.

title: Car registered to man accused of planning mass shooting was at temple he targeted, police say
text:
Car registered to man accused of planning mass shooting was at temple he targeted, police say
Illinois authorities believe a 19-year-old man charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago entered the building’s parking lot on Sunday, hours before police arrested him near his home after receiving a tip about the alleged attack plan.
Authorities announced Wednesday that they had arrested Alexandros Paporakis and provided the additional detail about his suspected movement during a news conference Thursday. The leaders of Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in a statement said a security threat had “targeted our Temple” and announced an increased security presence.
Palatine Police Chief William Nord said a red Acura RDX registered to Paporakis entered a temple parking lot on Sunday around 12:25 p.m. and left less than 15 minutes later. He was seen alone inside the car around 2 p.m., driving near his home in another suburb about 40 miles away.
Paporakis faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle. Prosecutors have said his co-workers at a Taco Bell location called 911 after Paporakis told them he “couldn't wait to kill Indian people” and said Sunday would be the “special day.”
Temple adds security after threat
Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, around 40 miles west of downtown Chicago, said leaders were in contact with police.
“Please know that the safety of our devotees, employees and volunteers is our highest priority, and we have implemented additional security measures effective immediately, including increased armed security presence at the Temple,” a statement said.
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois' 8th congressional district, said he was at the Hindu temple on Sunday.
“I visited not knowing that there was an attacker lying in wait with a sinister motive to commit a mass shooting, and only because his AR-15 weapon jammed was he not able to commit a massacre that day," Rep. Krishnamoorthi told The Associated Press on Thursday.
Rep. Krishnamoorthi said he had increased his security in response to the alleged planned attack. He called on the FBI to “investigate and prosecute this particular matter as a hate crime,” and the Trump administration to release federal nonprofit security grants to bolster security at religious institutions.
“People are really shaken up,” he added.
Court records detail the accused attacker's words
Paporakis told a coworker on Sunday afternoon that his gun jammed and he left quickly, but promised to “retry,” according to prosecutors. He sent the coworker a video showing an AR-style rifle and a photo of himself wearing a tactical vest, they added.
Paporakis also sent the coworker an eight-page manifesto called “Why I fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto)" in which he described non-white people as “subhumans” and expressed a plan to “sacrifice myself to take revenge on the world," according to prosecutors. In the document, he described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi," they say.
Police arrested Paporakis later that day. Detectives who searched his home found an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines and “hundreds of rounds” of ammunition, a gas canister labeled with a slur referring to South Asians, a tactical vest and a patch depicting Nazi symbolism, authorities say.
Paporakis' mother was questioned, but she is not cooperating with the investigation, police said on Thursday.
At a Wednesday court appearance, a judge ordered Paporakis to remain in detention. His next court hearing is scheduled for Oct. 30.
“This case is in the earliest stage of what will likely be a lengthy process,” the office of the Cook County Public Defender, which is representing Paporakis, said in a statement emailed to The AP. "We would remind the public that statements made by police and prosecutors are only allegations and that cases can change significantly as they continue to be investigated.”
The targeting of the Hindu temple is another example of heightened threats in the last few years against South Asians in the U.S., according to Stop AAPI Hate, the national reporting center for anti-Asian hate incidents. Online slurs and threats have risen significantly, co-founder Manjusha Kulkarni said in a statement.
“We are grateful this violent plot was thwarted and that no one was hurt – but it doesn’t erase the fear Hindu, Indian, and South Asian people feel after years of escalating hate,” Kulkarni said. “Violence against South Asian people is not inevitable. It is fueled when leaders stoke fear of immigrants and people of color for political gain.”
She attributed some of the anti-South Asian sentiment to the Trump administration’s rhetoric around Indian immigrants who hold work visas. She also pointed to a Texas Republican last month posting a social media video of South Asian students cheering at a University of Texas football game and referring to them as “foreigners.”
The temple, like other Hindu temples and households around the country, has been celebrating Navratri, a Hindu festival that lasts nine days. It “should be a time for celebration and unity, not terror and hate,” Kulkarni said.

title: Listen to the emergency calls made after Christa Pike’s failed execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Authorities have released emergency calls made from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution the night of Christa Pike’s attempted execution.
Metro Nashville Emergency Communications Center released the audio on Monday.
The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications first received notification of the incident at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in a 911 call at 9:40 p.m. ET on Sept. 30.
What happened the night of Christa Pike’s attempted execution?
The failed attempt happened after a day of back-and-forth among the courts about whether the procedure would proceed.
Pike was scheduled to be executed at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution the morning of Sept. 30, but shortly before, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ordered that her execution be paused.
The pause was issued because the court believed that she should be allowed to challenge the legality of her sentence. Pike’s attorneys then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to maintain that pause while a federal appeals court reviewed a new legal challenge.
That evening, the Supreme Court said in a 6-3 decision that the execution would be allowed to proceed. She would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be executed in Tennessee. She is the only woman on death row in the state.
Things went wrong when an attempt was made to administer the two doses of pentobarbital.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” witnesses heard Pike say as she was undergoing lethal injection.
The state administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to be lethal. But witnesses and her attorneys say that they did not have the intended effect. Instead, one witness said, “heavy snoring is the best description we can get you for the noises she was making.”
Shortly after, WSMV observed ambulances arriving at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution and leaving soon after, followed by police.
Pike was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
Attorneys later confirmed that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. It was revealed that on Oct. 5, her attorneys and medical team believed she was brain dead and would be taken off life support within days, but she regained consciousness the following morning.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery,” one of her attorneys, Randy Spivey, said.
Pike’s attorneys announced on Saturday that she had been released from the hospital and was returned to the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years.
Why is Christa Pike on death row?
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
The case revealed that Pike, who was 18 at the time, worked with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson to plan and carry out the killing, which became known as the “Job Corps Murder.” Pike and Slemmer had both been Job Corps members at the time of the murder, which took place at the University of Tennessee campus.
Phil Keith, who was the Knoxville police chief during the 1995 murder, described it as “an incredibly grotesque crime scene, one of the most brutal I’ve ever seen.”
According to Keith, Pike had tortured Slemmer for nearly an hour with a box cutter, “carving a pentagram on her chest before she crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.”
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her upbringing was not given enough consideration in her case. According to her defense, Pike was a victim of child abuse and multiple rapes, details they say were kept from the jury during her trial.
Tennessee previously claimed Pike was lying about her childhood, but has since acknowledged the abuse in open court.
For Keith, the upbringing is not an excuse.
“If everyone that had an abusive lifestyle killed someone, there’d be a lot more murders in this country,” he said. “This is not about how she’s become reformed, or that those days are past. Her values or morals have been set for a long time, and somewhere along the way, they got twisted.”
While Keith said that Pike never showed any remorse for the crime, Pike’s friend, Misty Armstrong, said otherwise.
According to Armstrong, Pike spent much of her time in prison trying to help other inmates.
“It took years of therapy for her to get there, but she did,” she said. “She changed and became a completely different person.”

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate for a final time
text:
The fourth and final debate between Troy Jackson and Susan Collins is here.
After a whirlwind two weeks in which the candidates repeatedly faced questions from Maine journalists, they will meet for a final time onstage Thursday in Bangor.
Tonight’s debate is hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine.
As always, we’ll be following along live. The event starts at 7 p.m., and you can watch a livestream below.
And that’s a wrap!
Thanks so much for following along with us, not just for this debate, but for all the debates!
We’ll see you next time.
A Maine Mount Rushmore?
The candidates ended by answering a question about who should be on a Maine-themed Mount Rushmore, if such a thing were to exist.
Collins took a beat before answering Joshua Chamberlain, who fought for the Union in the Civil War. Jackson said Frances Perkins, the former Labor Secretary, and the first woman to hold a Cabinet position.
Collins said she is a strong supporter of Ukraine and that she “adamantly opposed” the Russian invasion of the country. She noted that she signed a letter criticizing Trump’s recent move to buy some oil from Russia.
Jackson said he’s not in favor of increasing the age limit to buy the weapons, but said he’s not opposed to banning them. He noted he would not advocate for taking away the weapons from people who already have them.
“We are resilient and strong. I’ve seen the executive branch over the years, regardless of whether it was Democratic president or a Republican president, try to get more and more power,” Collins said.
Jackson seems to be settling in
If he was stilted in previous debates, Jackson seems to be finding more a comedic stride tonight. He’s slipped in a number of these one-liner jabs such as his jab about the Supreme Court, and they’re playing well in the room.
“What we want is a Supreme Court that is insulated from politics,” Collins said.
Jackson shot back with a joke.
“We have the best court that money can buy,” Jackson said.
Jackson criticized Collins for not doing enough for everyday Mainers.
Jackson countered that as senator, Collins has presided in a huge spike in gas prices.
Jackson was asked why he prefers Customs and Border Protection to take over ICE’s responsibilities given that CBP officers fatally shot a Minnesota man earlier this year.
Jackson said she wouldn’t give immigration officers a “blank check” like Collins did.
This is an emerging theme of the night: Jackson expresses a number of things he wouldn’t do, but doesn’t express clearly what he would do.
A note on the audience
The audience is getting rowdy. People were laughing and “oohing” and “ahhing” at several of the pithier lines in Jackson’s answer to Collins’ question about his campaign finance filing
She also reiterated Iran should not be allowed to make a nuclear weapon.
When pressed on the beginning of the war, Collins said Congress should have been consulted on the war.
“Under the War Powers Act, the president, as commander-in-chief, for the first 60 days, has very broad authority to do whatever he wants, essentially, when it comes to a military conflict,” Collins said. “After 60 days, that’s when I voted every single time with the Democrats to bring the conflict to a halt.”
She pivoted to talking about how heating assistance has been funded at record levels, and noted that she supports social safety net programs.
Jackson said he may have gotten some support by billionaires, drawing a reaction from the room. But he said he still plans to tax them.
“They know that I don’t owe them a thing like Sen. Collins,” Jackson said.
However, he noted he would vote to impeach Hegseth, Trump’s Defense Secretary.
Does Collins regret RFK vote?
Collins noted the areas where she disagrees with the controversial U.S. Health and Human Services department secretary. For example, she doesn’t believe vaccines cause autism — a link Kennedy has made in the past.
But she said she agrees with him on his focus on chronic diseases. Overall, she’t said she didn’t regret the vote.
A look at the instigator from the room
A young man just stood up from the fourth row and interrupted Collins before she could answer a question. He was quickly escorted out of the room to applause.
Jackson’s response was muffled, but it sounded like he said, “oh, shut up,” noting he didn’t know the person.
“I don’t know what world Sen. Collins is in where she started out, we had $4 trillion in debt, now we have $40 trillion in debt under her watch, and somehow it’s my fault,” Jackson responded. “In Maine, we have a balanced budget. Has it grown? Yes. But it’s still balanced.”
He noted that tax cuts for wealthy Americans contribute to the debt.
Collins noted Maine is running a potential budget deficit of about $1 billion — you can read about that here — and Jackson noted that he hasn’t been in the Legislature since 2024.
Pressed on that point, Collins pivoted to attacking Jackson, arguing she’d vote the Democratic party line if elected.
Jackson contended that Collins would be a rubber stamp for Trump in her sixth term, and the two squabbled over how often Collins supports Trump.
When asked the same question about her party, Collins said her party has worked to secure the border.
But Collins also said she would vote independently during her sixth term.
“We need more people in the center. We don’t need more people who are going to vote a straight party line,” Collins said.
Jackson’s opening statement hits on chaos in our politics
Following a familiar line of attack, Jackson hit Collins for voting to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Collins did not ultimately support the measure, but Jackson has repeatedly attacked her for a vote to advance the bill. (She’s argued it would have made the floor anyway, and that because of her vote, she was able to get a $50 billion fund for rural hospitals amended onto it.)
“I ask for your support so I can continue my work for you,” Collins said.
Jackson’s campaign finance report is in
He promised to deliver the numbers Wednesday morning. They came about 36 hours later — though still before the statutory deadline.
Take a look at our rundown of the third quarter fundraising by Collins and Jackson. The Democrat had a heck of a quarter — but he’s still being badly outraised by Collins and her allies.
The candidates take the stage
The candidates have arrived! The room is full mostly of Collins and Jackson supporters, who broke out into applause as the candidates took the stage. The two met in a cordial handshake and are now at their podiums taking last minute notes.
Pictures tell the story
Here’s a look a the scenes outside the debate. Might be a bit more raucous inside than the past three.
Coming into tonight, Jackson’s campaign said the former logger will try to focus on healthcare — something that he’s done in each debate so far. He will undoubtedly continue to tie Collins to President Donald Trump, who’s deeply unpopular here.
Expect Collins to continue to highlight her seniority in the Senate as a strength and try to shift blame for the high cost of — whether its property taxes or electricity rates — onto Jackson, who served as state Senate president for six years.
Let’s hope the candidates break some new ground. But after three televised debates in two weeks, that may be difficult to do.
Update from on the ground from Bangor
Just under an hour before the candidates are set to take the stage, supporters of each have gathered in the parking lot outside the venue. Jackson’s supporters are blasting music and holding a large banner that reads “Let them eat road salt” — a zinger from the first debate.
Across the lot, Collins supporters are doing a call-and-response with the senator’s first and last name in front of a large tour bus.
One hour to go!
We are about an hour from go time.
Get caught up on our past debate coverage before we get started. You can read our takeaways from the first debate here, from the second debate here and from the third debate here.

Watch: Fryeburg soccer is the Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Fryeburg Academy soccer
Coach Bob Hodgman-Burns saw signs during a preseason game against Laconia, New Hampshire, that this could be a successful season for the Fryeburg Academy boys soccer team.
“My local players are a year more experienced, and I don’t want to say they suffered through last year, but they had a tough year last year,” Hodgman-Burns said. “I think they learned a lot. So after that first week, it was all coming together.”
With an 8-2-1 record, Fryeburg ranked second in the Class B South Heal point standings heading into Wednesday’s game against Traip Academy. In 2025, the Raiders finished 3-8-3.
Fourth-year player and team captain Abram Grace said the Raiders took a little time to find their footing before settling into the grind of the Western Maine Conference schedule. They had a loss and a tie in their first five games but then won five of their next six.
“Our season started, obviously, not how we’re doing now,” Grace said. “We were struggling with communication, and our passes were a little bit sloppy at times, but throughout the season, we’ve been working hard and getting quite a few wins that we didn’t really expect.”
That includes a 1-0 win over defending Class B champion Yarmouth on Sept. 17 and a 2-1 victory over perennial power Cape Elizabeth on Sept. 22. It’s the first time since 2011 that Fryeburg, ranked 10th in the Varsity Maine poll, has beaten both of those schools in the same season.
Last week, the Raiders offense exploded in a 7-0 win over Lake Region and a 9-1 victory over Sacopee Valley.
The Raiders have scored 39 goals, and nine players have contributed to that total.
“I think that in the games that we come out strong and really try to push from the start and don’t give (opponents) any time, don’t let the team kind of play with the ball, we’re doing better,” Grace said. “So I think for the rest of the season, we’re being aggressive and going at every team we play, because we’re not going to overlook any team.”
