title: States sue AI giant OpenAI, saying its popular chatbot is hurting children and deceiving adults
text:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults.
The company’s chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to hurt others or commit suicide, Iowa’s lawsuit said. At the same time, the chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable, according to the lawsuit.
“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.
In a statement, OpenAI said it has already built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model.
The wave of lawsuits are the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.
In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends.
ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, according to the lawsuits.
In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an $18 billion landmark legal settlement that ended a trial over teen social media addiction and settled claims filed by nearly every state.
Coordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit. Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said in a statement that the company is committed to working with states on “advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.”
ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens has safeguards that are designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said.
Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said.
ChatGPT provides break reminders for periods of extended use and OpenAI said it works with external experts who review policies and the model’s behavior.
___
Follow Marc Levy at http://x.com/timelywriter

title: Maine has a shortage of home health workers. Is there any way to fix it?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Maine is struggling with workforce shortages in the home healthcare industry, which means the state isn’t able to meet the growing demand, industry experts say.
The problem is far from unique to Maine.
“Like many home health providers across the country, we are experiencing a challenging workforce environment,” said Patty Buiocchi, chief operating officer for post-acute care at MaineHealth who also oversees their home health and hospice programs.
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
Nancy Polito, 78, of Portland, said she struggled to find the caregiving help her mom needed, especially after a stroke.
“It was hard to get anyone to come in and do anything,” said Polito, who was her mother’s primary caregiver until she died in 2010. “I couldn’t leave her alone, and couldn’t find anyone to come in.”
Polito said she’s heard the problem has only gotten worse.
Shawna Ferris, a direct care worker from Mattawamkeag, said access to care and working conditions have worsened over the past two years.
“The cost of living has increased significantly, and the pay has not moved,” Ferris said. “You can go work in a different field and make the same or more money with less responsibilities.”
Home health includes a number of services, such as skilled nursing care for patients rehabilitating at home after a surgery, or patients who need help with daily tasks.
According to the Maine Center for Economic Policy, a progressive think tank, 23,500 hours per week of home health assistance go unfilled in the state because there aren’t enough workers.
“In the next 10-15 years, there’s going to be a lot more people 75 and older who are going to need these services. The demand for workers is growing while the number of people able to fill those roles is plateauing,” said James Myall, an economic policy analyst for the center.
Myall said the 23,500 hours is an undercount because it only looks at people who signed up for Medicaid home health services. It doesn’t consider people who need the services but didn’t bother putting their name down because they know there aren’t enough workers.
SOLUTIONS HARD TO COME BY
Myall said the state has an extreme shortage of direct care workers. Maine needs over 2,000 additional direct care employees, according to a Maine Center for Economic Policy analysis. Those are the staffers who help with daily tasks like cooking, picking up groceries, laundry, and helping people remember to take medications.
“The agencies have not been able to pay their workers enough,” Myall said. “They are getting outbid by retailers like Walmart.”
He said increasing the pay of direct care employees to 140% of the state minimum wage and then giving automatic cost-of-living raises would help alleviate the shortage.
Myall said the Maine Legislature in recent years has approved state reimbursement increases for the nonprofits that hire direct care workers, resulting in modest wage increases. But despite those efforts, wages in other industries, like retail, have increased by more, dampening the effectiveness.
Nonprofit agencies that provide home health services can currently pay their workers 125% of minimum wage, based on what the state’s Medicaid program will reimburse.
The state so far has not substantially increased wages for direct care workers, but lawmakers, including Democratic House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, have advocated for the boost to 140% of minimum wage. The state minimum wage will be $15.70 starting in January, so if that proposal passes, care workers could earn $21.98 per hour.
The Maine Essential Care and Workforce Partnership, a group advocating for better working conditions for direct care workers, is also proposing to improve training, benefits and technology for workers.
DEMAND FOR HELP IS GROWING
Myall said the shortages result in a system where it’s primarily “relatives taking care of their family members, juggling work and caregiving,” Myall said.
“It forces some people out of the workforce,” he said.
Noël Bonam, Maine’s AARP state director, said having a strong home health system will help keep older Mainers from having to move to nursing homes and hospitals. It’s also healthier for them.
“You are keeping that person in the community, and having strong social connections, and that helps them thrive,” Bonam said. “It costs a whole lot less to keep them in the home than taking up a bed in a nursing home.”
Buiocchi said they are able to run the MaineHealth program without workforce shortages, but they have advantages over other employers in that they can offer competitive wages and benefits and a flexible schedule. Also, because they’re a large employer, they have robust training programs and have many pathways for promotions.
Myall said much of the home health industry in Maine consists of nonprofits who don’t have the flexibility to pay higher wages.
Buiocchi said demand for home health services is expected to keep growing.
“The need has increased exponentially over the past five years,” she said.

title: UMaine Presque Isle loses blanket approval for new YourPace programs after reports of ‘speed runners’
text:
The accreditor for the University of Maine at Presque Isle has revoked the school’s blanket approval to offer new competency-based degree programs following an investigation into concerns about the rapid speed at which students were getting degrees through its online program, YourPace.
If the University of Maine System wants to introduce new competency programs going forward, it will need to submit them directly to the accreditor for approval.
“Given its concern about the dramatic growth of the YourPace program attributed in part to the speed at which students have been able to complete the credits required to earn a degree, both undergraduate and graduate, the Commission suspends University of Maine System’s general approval to offer competency-based education programs at University of Maine at Presque Isle,” the New England Commission of Higher Education wrote.
In addition, the commission will monitor the university’s progress through reports and requests, including site visits to UMPI and the other system schools that offer the degree programs in spring of 2027.
YourPace is a fully asynchronous competency-based program designed for adults, meaning students can earn credit whenever they demonstrate that they’ve mastered the course content, without set lecture or exam times.
The program — which has seen explosive 700% growth over the last four years and is now behind most of the enrollment growth across whole University of Maine System — came under scrutiny following reporting from The Washington Post that many YourPace students were completing bachelor’s degrees in as little as eight weeks.
The New England Commission of Higher Education, which accredits not just UMPI but the whole University of Maine System collectively, released its decision last Wednesday.
System spokesperson Samantha Warren said forthcoming YourPace programs already approved by the board of trustees, including a Master of Healthcare Administration approved at its latest meeting in September, will not be affected.
In a press release about the decision, UMPI President Ray Rice said YourPace has worked exactly as intended, by recognizing the knowledge and experience working adults already have and “providing an affordable, flexible pathway to a degree that will improve their career opportunities and economic mobility.”
System Chancellor Dannel Malloy, also quoted in the statement, said he was proud of the impact YourPace has had on thousands of adult learners who were able to get a degree while balancing work and their families.
“We welcome NECHE’s continued review and are committed to demonstrating that the innovation and accessibility that make YourPace so impactful are matched by the academic quality and rigor our students, employers and accreditor expect,” Malloy said.
The Post story profiled college “speed runners” who race to get their degrees in as little time as possible by transferring in the maximum number of non-collegiate online tutorial credits, then completing as many YourPace courses as they can in a session.
UMPI offers a flat rate of $1,800 per undergraduate session, so students pay the same cost regardless of how many courses they complete, and students are allowed to transfer in up to two-thirds of the credits needed for a bachelor’s degree.
About 90% of YourPace students get their degree in under a year, and 48% finish in one 16-week semester, according to data from the latest school year. Students transferred in an average of 91 credits, and that number is higher for undergrads.
As is standard practice, the accreditor, known as NECHE, requested a response from the university about the concerns raised in the article. UMPI submitted that update in August, in which it said the Post’s focus on rapid completers, “describes only the end of an academic journey, not the history of that journey itself” and that they make up a minority of students.
The university reported that about a fifth of YourPace students students finished 10 or more courses, or 30 credits, in a semester, and 11% completed 12 courses or more.
About half of the average YourPace student’s credits don’t come from an accredited college source. Nearly half of those noncollege credits are from Sophia Learning, a low-cost online tutorial site.
The school acknowledged a need for more monitoring of students who accelerate through their degrees rapidly, and a hard look at its transfer credit policy. But school and system leaders said they were confident the accreditation review process would not find any issues, since NECHE has accredited the YourPace program at every step of the way.
The commission discussed the university’s response at its latest regular meeting in late September.
NECHE will begin conducting visits to UMPI, the University of Maine at Farmington and University of Maine at Fort Kent — where the system has rolled out a much smaller number of YourPace programs — in order to assess the system’s “oversight and implementation” of its competency-based programs.
The system must also submit a report with detailed data, including faculty-to-student ratios, an analysis of transferred credits, the length of time it took graduates to complete degrees and details about procedures to verify that the students who register for courses are the ones actually completing the work.
System and UMPI representatives must appear before the commission in April 2027 for a review of the evaluation’s results.

title: A blueprint for disaster for Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Luisa S. Deprez, Ph.D., of Cape Elizabeth is professor emerita of sociology and social policy at the University of Southern Maine.
Once again, the notorious, dangerous and ultra-conservative Maine heritage foundation, the Maine Policy Institute, has gone out of its way to attempt to undermine the safety and security and well-being of Maine families.
Its newest approach to doing so is described in the recently released 2026 Maine Policy Blueprint, a dictum that leaves no stone unturned when it comes to proposals that will threaten the lives of children and families while undermining communities and, ultimately, the state.
Perhaps the children and families of the institute’s staff and collaborators will not suffer but be assured that hundreds of thousands throughout the state will.
Its impact would be similar to its national predecessor, Project 2025, which Donald Trump and his Republican loyalists used to decimate the federal government and unleash a flurry of executive orders, rule changes and (il)legal maneuvers designed to inflict harm on millions of Americans.
They include cuts to Medicaid and food programs; reduction and elimination of education programs for special needs children and low-achieving communities; decreased regulations of toxic chemicals both in the air and in your food and water; purging of research programs studying cancer, heart disease, diabetes and other chronic diseases; erasure of vaccination protocols; disregard for national park protections; and on the horizon, plans to upend Head Start by “stripping away standards on health and literacy … and brushing teeth.” Who knows what’s in store Social Security and Medicare?
The Blueprint purports to promote a Maine where “people are freer, more prosperous, or better able to afford happy lives.” To do so it suggests overall reforms in every sector.
Among them:
Environmental: End “state-level hostility toward fossil fuel and nuclear power” while removing regulatory and permitting barriers; end vehicle inspection mandates (ever been behind a vehicle with no brake lights on a dark road at night?); repeal all emissions reductions goals as well as nuclear referendum requirements; reduce funding for water quality by 15%; ban subsidies on EV sales.
Education: Allow public schools to transition to a charter school if they wish, reducing state expenditures for public schools and turning over educational standards and curriculum to a private enterprise; eliminate funding for adult education and turn over adult and community education, adult basic education, adult high school diploma programs, high school equivalency diploma testing, family literacy, job skills training, and college transition programs to the private sector; eliminate funding for the Department of Education’s office of student supports; reduce the state reimbursement rate for school administration encouraging central office staffing, and management functions; give authority for public school curriculum and learning wholly to parents.
Housing: Eliminate rent control; eliminate the Housing Opportunity Program targeting low- and moderate-income households and community workforce housing needs; abolish minimum lot sizes and parking mandates.
Health: Repeal the paid family medical leave program; repeal Medicaid expansion (30% of Mainers had MaineCare coverage in 2025, most children and elders); increase state employees’ share of health insurance premiums; contract-out prison medical services.
Food: Eliminate funding for Maine’s universal school meals program; eliminate statewide hunger relief program — breakfast, lunch, after-school, weekends, summer; expand work requirements for those receiving SNAP (about 40,000 of 170,000 current recipients); move food programs to DHHS.
Economy: Repeal the 2% income tax hike on incomes above $1 million for single filers; freeze the minimum wage and deregulate occupational licensing; targeted 10% reduction in central administrative units (567 jobs); lease or concession-manage Maine’s most visited, highest cost parks to eliminate payroll, seasonal staffing, overtime pay and day-to-day maintenance; eliminate funding for international commerce that promotes exports, international student recruitment and overseas trade opportunities for Maine businesses.
Veterans services: A 10% cut focused on outreach, technology and central-office staffing.
Law enforcement: Require all state and local police to cooperate with ICE.
This is not Maine as it should be nor as it is. The intent of the Blueprint is not to ensure that Maine “people are freer, more prosperous or better able to afford happy lives” but to slash expenditures that actually enable Mainers to be freer, more prosperous, safer, and able to live lives of value. Like Project 2025, it guarantees that only the private sector flourishes.
This Blueprint will be the agenda for every Republican up for election in any race in the state. We have seen this played out before. Project 2025 devastated the federal government and the state and continues to do so.
As you go to the polls, ask yourself this question: Do you want this Blueprint to be our future? If you say “No,” know who you are voting for. Be sure they share your sentiments.

title: Deputies: 9 kids endured day-long wall squats in house of ‘horror’
text:
ETNA TOWNSHIP, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) - Nine children have been removed from what investigators describe as “appalling and unsafe living conditions” in Ohio.
“The living conditions were horrific, disgusting,” said Captain Jay Cook with the Licking County Sheriff’s Office.
Detectives arrested Jonathan Parr and Jacqueline Coleman on child endangerment charges Tuesday after carrying out a search warrant at a home in Etna Township, according to the Licking County Sheriff.
Twelve people lived at the home, including nine children, detectives said.
“Part of the disclosure from the children was the abuse. Sometimes it was punishment. Sometimes it was for no good reason at all, where they would have to stand with their back against the wall. As like a wall squat type situation. It was reported that they would have to sometimes stand there all day,” Cook said. “There was a disclosure of nails in the floor, and it was mentioned that it was there for like a marker to put their feet.”
All nine children are now in the custody of child protective services.
The sheriff’s office said additional charges against the suspects are possible.

title: County Business Summit Sees Increased Interest

CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - From marketing to HR, business leaders across Aroostook County spent the day sharpening their skills at the Central Aroostook Business summit.

title: Landing School confirms it is closing for good
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine's Landing School of Boatbuilding and Design confirms it is closing for good
The Landing School of Boatbuilding and Design in Arundel confirms that it is closing for good.
In August, the school suspended its academic programs for the 2026-27 school year due to declining enrollment and ongoing funding challenges.
School leaders said in August that the closure was not permanent, but the Board of Trustees ultimately could not find a viable way to keep the school open, despite exploring possible partnerships and other options.
"For generations of students, TLS was a place where they learned to build with their hands, solve problems, work as a team, and take pride in what they created. For faculty and staff, it was a place where we had the privilege of watching students learn and grow. And for our alumni, donors, employers, volunteers, and friends, it was a school worth believing in," the Board of Trustees said in a statement. "The legacy of The Landing School will carry on in the boats our graduates built, the businesses they started, the skills they brought to their careers, the people they mentored, and the countless lives they touched."
The Landing School will be holding two auctions through Keenan Auction Company: one for the contents of the building and another for the school's real estate property.
"We hope that many of these tools and pieces of equipment will find new homes where they can continue to be used to build, teach, create, and inspire," the board said.
The auction of the building's contents features a collection of equipment accumulated over the years, including woodworking, welding and fabrication equipment, computer numerical control (CNC) machinery, marine manufacturing equipment, vessels, rolling stock, tools, classroom furnishings and office equipment. Among the highlights are a Crown forklift, MultiCam CNC router, SCM and Laguna woodworking equipment, SawStop table saw, Miller and Lincoln welders, Powermatic and Grizzly equipment, Festool tools and dust extractors, air compressors and dust-collection systems, a finishing booth, gantry and hoist equipment, and an Instron 5582 universal testing machine.

title: Prince Harry and Meghan to visit charities in Nottingham
text:
Prince Harry and Meghan cheered as they make first joint appearance since returning to UK
Prince Harry and his wife Meghan appeared together Thursday in front of cheering children in what is their joint public appearance since moving back to England, as the couple seek to rebuild their brand in Britain after walking away from royal duties six years ago
The couple arrived at the Community Recording Studio, in the city of Nottingham in central England, which uses music, performance and athletic programs to help young people build confidence and develop practical skills.
The crowd cheered as the couple got out of their car, before one woman shouted, “We love you Duchess Meghan, we love you.”
Video above: Harry and Meghan moving back to the UK
Harry and Meghan, who wore a long burgundy coat, stopped to take selfies, give hugs and shake hands with fans, many of them young children. They spent a few minutes talking to members of the public and the children.
The visit was the first of three they will make in Nottingham, where they made their first joint appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.
The day’s events are being presented with touches of royal style, including an announcement that features Harry and Meghan’s titles as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and a prearranged media pool chronicling their movements. Archewell, the philanthropic venture that often took center stage when they were living in the U.S., is hardly mentioned.
But King Charles III, Harry’s father, has made clear that the couple remain non-working members of the royal family, a status they accepted when they abandoned royal duties and moved to California.
In a letter sent on behalf of the king to senior government officials shortly after Harry and Meghan returned to the U.K. in September, the palace stressed that the couple would continue to refrain from using their royal forms of address — His Royal Highness or Her Royal Highness — and any charity work they undertake would be carried out as private citizens.
The decision to send the letter and, more importantly, to release it to the media demonstrated the concern among some palace officials that Harry and Meghan’s celebrity could allow them to become a sort of parallel royal court, competing with the Prince and Princess of Wales and other working royals for press coverage and public support.
The couple are back to working with familiar partners
After the Community Recording Studio, the couple will make go Himmah, central England’s biggest food bank and Epic Partners, which offers sports, education and mentoring programs for disadvantaged young people.
Harry has been involved with the Community Recording Studio and Epic Partners for more than a decade, and Meghan worked with Himmah on “Together: Our Community Cookbook,” published in 2018.
While the couple continued to support charities in the U.K. after they left Britain, their focus was elsewhere.
Harry and Meghan gave up their royal duties and moved to California more than six years ago, saying they wanted to earn their own living. They later signed lucrative contracts with Netflix and Spotify.
Video below: Harry and Meghan sit-down with Oprah
While the couple continued to support charities in the U.K. after they left Britain, their focus was elsewhere.
Relations with the rest of the royal family quickly deteriorated as the couple said palace staff had been insensitive to Meghan’s mental health and leveled charges of racism and media manipulation at other members of the family.
Harry wants his children to get to know their grandfather
But tensions began to ease in recent months as Harry expressed a desire for reconciliation with the king, saying he wanted his children to have a chance to get to know their 77-year-old grandfather. Charles is undergoing treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer that was discovered in 2024.
The couple and their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, are reportedly living at a private, nonroyal residence in the Cotswolds, a rural area of rolling hills, villages and farms to the west of Oxford.
While the couple have expressed their happiness about returning to the U.K., the move hasn’t been without controversy.
Harry continues to lobby for publicly funded police protection, which was canceled when he and Meghan gave up royal duties.
The prince says he and his family remain under threat simply because of his royal status. Just days into the new school year, the children have changed schools because of security issues.
___
Kirka reported from London. Pan Pylas in London contributed to this report.

title: NFL Week 6 schedule, predictions and more
text:
NFL Week 6 schedule, predictions and more
NFL Week 6 schedule, predictions and more
The first tie of the 2026 NFL season came in Week 5. Since the league introduced overtime rules in 1974, 31 ties have been recorded in NFL games.
Nobody could have predicted that — not even Matthew Peaslee of the Hearst National Team, who has been making selections all season long.
Video above: Saints’ home woes have left New Orleans desperate to avoid a 6th straight lost season
Before last week's 27-27 tie between the Washington Commanders and New York Giants, the most recent tie was the Sept. 28, 2025, contest between the Green Bay Packers and the Dallas Cowboys, which ended 40-40.
Could another tie come this week? There are some tight, intriguing matchups.
Here's a look at what's ahead this week, as Peaslee continues his predictions. Peaslee went 8-6-1 in his Week 5 predictions and sits at 45-33-1 on the year.
All game times are in Eastern Standard Time.
Thursday, Oct. 15
Seattle Seahawks (3-2) vs. Denver Broncos (3-2), 8:15 p.m.
Last season, the Seahawks and Broncos combined to go 32-7 — among the best in the sport. While the two teams are both above .500 in the young season now, there have been struggles on both sides. Seattle's defense is better than its offense and Denver's offense is going through a multitude of changes as well. This will be a close one.
Prediction: Seahawks 28, Broncos 24
Sunday, Oct. 18
Houston Texans (1-4) vs. Jacksonville Jaguars (4-1), 9:30 a.m.
The Jaguars may not be America's team, but they could be considered Europe's team. This is the 16th time Jacksonville will play an overseas contest, and it enters this contest with the Eagles at 8-7 in international games, after beating the Eagles in dramatic fashion a week ago — also in London. Houston just doesn't have enough going for it this year to keep up.
Prediction: Jaguars 38, Texans 24
Chicago Bears (3-2) vs. Atlanta Falcons (2-3), 1 p.m.
Chicago looked ugly last week and is a good enough team to be primed for a bounceback. Quarterback Caleb Williams looks to return to give the Bears' offense a boost. The Falcons can go toe-to-toe with them, though, with the NFL's leading rusher in Bijan Robinson, who has 580 yards this season. The Bears lead the league's rushing attack, though, with 173.2 yards per game.
Prediction: Bears 33, Falcons 28
Baltimore Ravens (4-1) vs. Cleveland Browns (3-2), 1 p.m.
Lamar Jackson missed the Ravens' last game and is questionable this week. Tyler Huntley was formidable filling in for the injured quarterback, leading Baltimore to a great win against the Falcons. The Cleveland offense has been surprisingly solid as quarterback Deshaun Watson has developed a good sense of things, with wide receiver Denzel Boston and tight end Harold Fannin Jr. emerging as reliable targets. This could be the most important game in the AFC North so far.
Prediction: Ravens 21, Browns 17
Tennessee Titans (0-5) vs. Indianapolis Colts (2-3), 1 p.m.
The Colts might be better than their record indicates, but that is not the case for the Titans. Tennessee comes in with the worst offense in the league, only scoring 11.6 points per game. The Colts defense isn't the best, but it doesn't have much to work against in this one.
Prediction: Colts 17, Titans 10
New York Jets (2-3) vs. New England Patriots (3-2), 1 p.m.
The Patriots are riding a two-game winning streak after struggling through the first couple weeks. Quarterback Drake Maye has been extremely efficient, throwing a combined eight touchdowns in the past two games. New England has won 40 of its last 50 regular-season games against the Jets since December 2001.
Prediction: Patriots 38, Jets 23
New Orleans Saints (1-4) vs. New York Giants (3-1-1), 1 p.m.
Coming off the first tie of the 2026 NFL season, can the Giants get the bittersweet taste out of their mouths and rally for a win? The defense better be on their toes because the Saints have one of the better passing attacks, with sure-handed receiver Chris Olave racking up 537 receiving yards, good for second in the league. New Orleans has beaten the Giants in three straight years and could make it a fourth.
Prediction: Saints 23, Giants 21
Carolina Panthers (2-2) vs. Philadelphia Eagles (2-3), 1 p.m.
The Eagles will face the Panthers coming off a bye week, just the fifth time in NFL history a team coming off an international game has faced a team coming off a bye. The team returning from overseas is 0-4 in the previous four matchups. With Jalen Hurts out, it's likely the Eagles will make that 0-5.
Prediction: Panthers 38, Eagles 27
Pittsburgh Steelers (3-2) vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4), 1 p.m.
The Steelers have Jaylen Warren, the reigning AFC Offensive Player of the Week. He handled the running game well, and Aaron Rodgers has been controlling the offense as a whole, as he should be in his 18th professional season. The Buccaneers and Steelers have only met 12 times, with Pittsburgh holding a 10-2 advantage.
Prediction: Steelers 24, Buccaneers 20
Arizona Cardinals (1-4) vs. Los Angeles Rams (2-3), 4:05 p.m.
The Rams come in with the best offense in the league with 424.4 yards per game, with 307.6 coming through the passing game led by Matthew Stafford. The veteran quarterback leads the NFL with 1,572 passing yards this season, so it's about time Los Angeles faces a team like the Cardinals. The Rams have faced a tough schedule, so playing the 1-4 Cardinals at home couldn't have come at a better time for the once-Super Bowl favorites.
Prediction: Rams 42, Cardinals 24
Los Angeles Chargers (0-5) vs. Kansas City Chiefs (4-0), 4:25 p.m.
The Chiefs will remain unbeaten, and the Chargers will sink deeper in despair. Through four games, Mahomes has thrown for 1,037 yards and nine touchdowns with just two interceptions, giving the Chiefs a productive passing attack. Justin Herbert has been uncharacteristically bad in every game this season.
Prediction: Chiefs 38, Chargers 12
Buffalo Bills (4-1) vs. Las Vegas Raiders (3-2), 4:25 p.m.
Maybe it was just a mirage. The Raiders came out of the gates as the most surprising team in the league. It's been a rough couple of weeks for Las Vegas and it gets even tougher when Josh Allen and the Bills come to town. Aside from Allen, running back James Cook III has shown he is among the game's best with 532 yards on the ground this season.
Prediction: Bills 31, Raiders 24
Dallas Cowboys (2-3) vs. Green Bay Packers (3-2), 8:20 p.m.
The Cowboys and Packers are the two worst running offenses in the game, ranking near the bottom with just 80 and 60 yards per game, respectively. Luckily, their quarterbacks are among the game's best. Dak Prescott is fifth in the league in passing and Jordan Love dominated the game last week against the rival Bears. Green Bay's Xavier McKinney has three interceptions this year, but the overall Dallas defense gives them the upper hand.
Prediction: Cowboys 28, Packers 24
Monday, Oct. 19
Washington Commanders (1-3-1) vs. San Francisco 49ers (5-0), 8:15 p.m.
Brock Purdy should have a huge game as the 49ers look to improve to 6-0. The Commanders are reeling after their tie last week, as they should have won the game against the Giants. It's not the right time to "get right" this week, as the 49ers are simply too good, especially on offense.
Prediction: 49ers 37, Commanders 17

title: Trailblazing doctor, 47, dies of the cancer she was working to cure
text:
Trailblazing doctor, 47, dies of the cancer she was working to cure
A trailblazing doctor has died from the very same cancer she spent years trying to cure.
Dr. Rachna Shroff, one of the leading pioneers and experts in stomach cancer research, has died. She was 47.
Shroff, an associate director of clinical investigations at the University of Arizona Cancer Center, spent much of her career researching gastrointestinal cancers.
Related video above | Cancer cases soar for young people and experts aren't sure why
She died following a brief “battle with an aggressive cancer,” the university states. Multiple reports state that cancer was the same one at which she spent decades seeking a cure.
Shroff was diagnosed with terminal adenocarcinoma earlier this year – an advanced and incurable cancer originating in glandular tissues.
She developed a swollen lymph node in May. Weeks later, it had spread elsewhere in her body. Doctors said it likely originated in her stomach or intestines.
One of the foremost experts on pancreatic and biliary tract cancer, Shroff authored more than 80 publications and spoke at more than 130 professional engagements.
“She was internationally recognized for her work in bile duct cancer, or cholangiocarcinoma, turning her focus to the rare and historically difficult-to-treat disease when few treatment options existed and no Food and Drug Administration-approved therapies were available. Today, the field has changed dramatically, due in part to the landmark clinical trials Dr. Shroff led as a principal investigator,” a statement from the University of Arizona reads in part.
Shroff's research trajectory was ignited early on by a Conquer Cancer Young Investigator Award (YIA), sparking decades of dedication to finding lifesaving advancements.
To celebrate her life and work, friends, colleagues, and supporters raised $1.35 million to create an endowed YIA in her name.
Shroff is survived by her husband, Dr. Puneet Shroff, and children, Simran and Sachin.

title: Mitchell Leads Lincoln Academy Golf Team To First State Title
text:
The Lincoln Academy golf team won the Class B state championship on Saturday, Oct. 10 at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro.
Junior captain Colin Mitchell led the way, carding a two-over-par 74 that earned him the individual state championship title. The team championship, and the individual title for Mitchell, are both firsts for the Lincoln Academy program, which also won the KVAC championship on Oct. 1.

title: Man accused of shooting at teens toilet papering neighbor’s house in prank gone wrong
text:
ARNAUDVILLE, La. (KATC/Gray News) - A Louisiana man is facing multiple charges after authorities say he shot at a group of high school students during a toilet-papering prank gone wrong.
Travis Frederick, 71, was arrested and booked on charges of attempted manslaughter, aggravated assault with a firearm and aggravated criminal damage to property. His bond has not yet been set.
St. Martin Parish Sheriff Becket Breaux said deputies responded to a shooting on a street right outside Arnaudville just before midnight Monday. Several high school students had been in the area throwing toilet paper on neighborhood homes as part of a homecoming prank, according to deputies.
Frederick, who lives next door to one of the targeted homes, went outside with a gun and fired a shot toward at least five of the students, Breaux said.
Breaux added that as the students tried to leave in a vehicle, Frederick fired a second shot, striking the car.
No injuries were reported, but Breaux said the shooting was an overreaction that could have turned deadly.
“You use deadly force on someone toilet papering someone’s house. That’s a little bit overboard, and basically, you’re sending someone to a death sentence for toilet papering,” Breaux said.
Breaux noted the case highlights how quickly a neighborhood prank escalated into a criminal investigation. He urges the public not to take the law into their own hands.
”You elected me to be your sheriff to enforce the law, enforce public safety, and we have 240 deputies here who do the same thing. Let them earn their money, call them and let us go do our job."

title: Susan Collins has delivered for Maine veterans
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Brad Farrin of Norridgewock served nearly three decades in the Maine Air National Guard, retiring in 2013 as the state’s highest-ranking enlisted airman. A veteran of Operations Iraqi Freedom and Enduring Freedom, he earned more than 18 military awards and decorations, including the Legion of Merit and the Air Force Meritorious Service Medal. He also has more than a decade of legislative experience, having served in the Maine House of Representatives and is currently a member of the Maine Senate.
I spent nearly 30 years in the Maine Air National Guard, including deployments in support of Operations Iraqi Freedom and Enduring Freedom. I know what it means to serve, and I know the sacrifices military families make. When our men and women come home, we have an obligation to make sure they get the care and benefits they earned.
That’s why I took issue with the recent Bangor Daily News opinion column criticizing Sen. Susan Collins over veterans’ health care.
Let’s be clear. The VA has problems. Veterans still face long wait times, staffing shortages and challenges getting appointments. That’s unacceptable, and we need to keep working to fix it. Every veteran deserves access to quality care.
But it’s one thing to point out problems. It’s another to suggest Collins hasn’t been fighting for veterans. Her record tells a different story.
As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins helped advance the fiscal year 2026 VA funding bill, which provides $164.9 billion for VA medical care. That includes $18.9 billion for mental health services and $6.4 billion for telehealth programs, serving veterans in rural areas, $1.4 billion for women veterans, and $3.5 billion combat veteran homelessness and support caregivers.
Those dollars matter. They help veterans get care, support families and make services available to those who need them.
And we’ve seen results here in Maine. In April, a new residential rehabilitation treatment facility opened at the Togus VA Medical Center. Maine veterans who needed this level of treatment for PTSD, depression and substance use disorders often had to travel out of state. Now, they can receive that care closer to home.
That’s a big deal. If you’ve ever had a family member struggle with mental health or substance use, you understand how important it is to get help close to home. This is the kind of investment that makes a real difference in veterans’ lives.
Collins has also supported the PACT Act, which expanded care and benefits for veterans exposed to toxic substances, and efforts to strengthen mental health services and improve access to care.
Is there more to do? Absolutely. I would never tell a veteran who is struggling to get an appointment that everything is fine. But I also won’t ignore the work being done to improve the system.
The column also raises allegations involving campaign contributions and a defense contractor. Those allegations should be examined based on the evidence. But they should not be confused with proof of wrongdoing, or used to dismiss Collins’ record on veterans’ issues.
I believe in accountability. I spent my military career holding myself and others to a standard, and I expect the same from our elected officials. But accountability also means being fair and giving credit where it is due.
That’s one reason I’m proud to serve as a co-chair of Veterans for Collins alongside Kelly Hoffses, who recently retired after 41 years of military service. Veterans from across Maine and every branch of the armed forces have joined this coalition because we believe Susan Collins has worked to deliver for those who served.
We know there are challenges facing our veterans. We also know the difference between pointing out a problem and working to solve it.
Maine veterans deserve honest answers and real results. They deserve leaders who will fight for the funding, services and care they need.
Our veterans did their duty. We owe it to them to do ours.

title: Lockheed Martin showered Susan Collins with cash as F-35 program hit turbulence
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In May 2023, the Pentagon’s shiny new fighter jet was not looking so shiny or new.
Already a decade late and nearly $200 billion over its original cost estimate, the F-35 program faced a new crisis. An internal government watchdog report detailed a cascade of new problems with the program, which was in a period of flux amid plans to upgrade the jet’s engine and cooling system.
The report from the Government Accountability Office criticized the Pentagon for lumping those upgrades in with the overall purchase of the planes. Conflating the two, the authors said, would limit congressional insight into cost increases. And they criticized the contractors behind the aircraft for failing to deliver the F-35 in a timely manner.
For Lockheed Martin, the main defense giant overseeing the development of the F-35, the timing was far from ideal. In a few weeks, Congress was set to debate the Pentagon’s mammoth budget — and with it, new funding for the military’s purchase of F-35 jets.
So Lockheed and its lobbyists went on a charm offensive in Washington. The weapons maker shelled out hundreds of thousands over a two-month period, in what the money-in-politics watchdog Open Secrets described as “one of the largest coordinated lobbying efforts” around that year’s military budget.
No member of Congress benefited more than Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who at the time served as the ranking member on the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee.
From May 1 to June 30, 2023, employees and top executives from Lockheed Martin donated $59,500 to Collins’s campaign committee. The donations were outliers during that period: Collins was among the largest recipients of Lockheed cash; the company was her largest single donor over those two months; and it was the largest spending blitz on Collins by Lockheed compared to the same period in other years.
The effort appeared to pay off for Lockheed. In July 2023, less than two months after the release of the Government Accountability Office report, Collins voted in favor of appropriating funds to purchase 83 new F-35 jets. Later that year, when the final version of the military budget was signed into law, Collins celebrated the economic boon she said it would bring to the state of Maine.
In response to questions from The Intercept, Phoebe Keller, a spokesperson for the Republican-controlled Senate Appropriations Committee, said Collins’s support for the jet had nothing to do with donations from Lockheed or any other firm.
“Sen. Collins did not support the F-35 because of donations that she received,” Keller said.
“The F-35 jet program is a longstanding bipartisan defense priority,” Keller said. “Sen. Collins has always publicly supported the F-35 jet program, as dozens of both Republican and Democratic Senators.”
Collins’s position on the Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee likely played a role in the outsized donations, according to analyst Dan Grazier. And Collins, for her part, would have good reason to approve the spending: The F-35 program, Lockheed claims, has had a nine-figure economic impact in Maine.
FIGHT OF HER POLITICAL LIFE
In the final weeks of the biggest fight of her political career against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, fresh scrutiny on Collins’s donations from defense contractors has become a sore spot for her campaign.
In some cases, the senator’s interactions with defense firms are the routine for Washington: glad-handing, lobbying, contributions, and directing pork-barrel spending back home. Not all of it, though, is standard.
Last month, a bombshell report in ProPublica detailed an FBI investigation into an alleged pay-to-play scheme. A former defense contractor claimed to federal agents that he worked with figures tied to Collins to disguise campaign donations — and got federal contracts totaling $32 million in return. (The FBI probe fizzled after Trump returned to office and purged the bureau; Collins denied wrongdoing, pushing back on elements of the report.)
On Wednesday, more than 250 Mainers signed a letter to the state’s attorney general asking the official to investigate the allegations of corruption, according to Maine Morning Star, a local news outlet.
And earlier this month, The Intercept reported on donations from another defense contractor, AM General, and its parent company, whose employees gave $58,000 to fundraising committees associated with Collins after a damning assessment from the Army put its federal contracts in jeopardy.
As with the AM General donations, the contributions by employees and lobbyists of Lockheed Martin do not indicate wrongdoing by Collins or her donors.
“This is an example of what’s wrong with our approach to buying weapons,” said William Hartung, an analyst who has written critically of defense spending and influence peddling in Washington. “If we buy things because they’re in the state of a powerful member, we’re not going to have a coherent arsenal.”
LOCKHEED GIVING
Collins was not the only member of Congress to push for funding the F-35, which enjoyed broad bipartisan support — especially from lawmakers with eligible firms and facilities in their states. And she was not the only one to benefit from the largesse of Lockheed Martin.
From May 1 to June 30, 2023, Lockheed’s corporate PAC doled out $421,000 in a bipartisan blitz to various campaign political action committees, campaign funds, state parties, and charitable foundations. (Aside from 2024, the year of the presidential election, contributions in that two-month period in 2023 eclipsed subsequent years. In the same period this year, Lockheed’s corporate PAC made 128 donations totaling $236,000; last year, it gave $286,000 across 158 donations during the same period.)
Collins was by far the biggest single beneficiary of the influx of cash — which came at a time when she was not actively campaigning. And, unlike the donations spread out to other campaign committees, the cash going from Lockheed into Collins’s coffers during those months came exclusively in the form of individual donations by employees and executives, including the firm’s CEO and chief operating officer, data from the Federal Election Commission shows.
Lobbyists working for Lockheed contributed another $5,000 to Collins during that period, and corporate PACs for Lockheed’s lobbying firms shelled out another $5,500 total, according to FEC disclosures.
Among individual contributions by Lockheed employees, donations to Collins made up more than 10 percent of all donations during the two-month period surrounding the watchdog report.
Only the firm’s in-house employee PAC, which received 75 percent of all employee donations, took in more from figures tied to Lockheed. Collins got more than twice as much as the next highest recipient, ActBlue, the Democratic Party-aligned fundraising vehicle, which received 4 percent of all Lockheed employee contributions in that period, according to FEC data.
The vast majority donations from Lockheed employees and officials were under $1,000. Of the 60 donations of $1,000 or more during May and June 2023, 56 went to Collins.
Virtually all employee contributions from Lockheed workers and executives to Collins during her current term came during that two-month window, according to the FEC.
Lockheed donations made up a quarter of all contributions during May and June 2023 to Collins’s main fundraising arm, Collins for Senator. The next runner-up was telecom giant Charter Communications, whose employee contributions made up just 8 percent of gifts to the Collins campaign in the second quarter of the 2023 fiscal year.
A spokesperson for Lockheed did not answer specific questions regarding the reason for the sudden influx of individual contributions to Collins in 2023.
“Our employee PAC program continues to observe long-standing principles of bi-partisan political engagement in support of our business interests,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
ANOTHER VEHICLE ARMY DIDN’T WANT
Two years later, a similar pattern played out in miniature when a lesser-known defense firm with a troubled product enjoyed Collins’s support on Capitol Hill.
Collins went out of her way last year to slam the Pentagon for canceling its plans to purchase robotic combat vehicles from Textron and its subsidiary Howe & Howe, the Maine-based developer of the Ripsaw.
Collins has repeatedly hyped the unmanned robotic combat vehicle in Senate hearings and official statements. On June 18, 2025, she took issue with the fact that the vehicle had appeared in a recent military parade, but did not make the cut for further spending.
“It’s the height of irony that you would feature this combat vehicle in your parade as the future of the Army at the same time that you’ve canceled the contract — the cancellation of a contract that was won over a lot of other competitors,” Collins said, describing the decision as “terribly unfair and a real mistake.”
A month later, after the military budget cleared the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins singled out Howe & Howe, and its plant in Waterboro, Maine, as a potential beneficiary of a portion of $44 million allotted to outfit the U.S. Marine Corps with amphibious and autonomous vehicles.
She gave another shoutout to Howe & Howe in January, after the 2026 military budget was signed into law. This May, during the congressional testimony by then-Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, Collins again took the military to task for cutting its planned purchase of the Ripsaw.
Textron’s corporate PAC made contributions totaling $4,000 to various PACs associated with Collins just ahead of her vote on the 2026 military budget. $3,000 of the gifts came days after Collins criticized the military for cutting its plans for the Ripsaw program that would have brought millions of dollars to Howe & Howe.
Later in the year, the Textron corporate PAC donated another $7,000 to Collins for Senator and the Collins-linked Dirigo PAC, according to FEC filings. (A spokesperson for Textron and Howe & Howe did not respond to a request for comment.)
Keller, the Senate Appropriations Committee spokesperson, said that Collins was not a member of the Armed Services Committee that voted on funding the Ripsaw.
“She doesn’t have the agency to fund or not fund the vehicle because it wasn’t through the Appropriations Committee,” Keller said, adding that Collins’s longtime support for the Ripsaw was not motivated by the Textron and Howe & Howe donations.
Employees of Textron and its subsidiary, meanwhile, made contributions to various Collins-linked PACS totaling nearly $15,000 between September 2025 and October 15, 2026, FEC data shows.
The donations, relatively small in the post-Citizens United era of campaign finance, still illustrate a troubling pattern of how influence plays out in Washington, according to Hartung, the analyst critical of military spending.
“A lot of members lobby to get more units of something built in their state, or craft legislation for a system that only their local firm can produce,” Hartung said. “It’s kind of business as usual, but sometimes business as usual causes great harm.”
This story was updated to include further statements from Phoebe Keller, a spokesperson for the Senate Appropriations Committee, that were made after publication.

title: Maine has a shortage of home health workers. Is there any way to fix it?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Maine is struggling with workforce shortages in the home healthcare industry, which means the state isn’t able to meet the growing demand, industry experts say.
The problem is far from unique to Maine.
“Like many home health providers across the country, we are experiencing a challenging workforce environment,” said Patty Buiocchi, chief operating officer for post-acute care at MaineHealth who also oversees their home health and hospice programs.
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
Nancy Polito, 78, of Portland, said she struggled to find the caregiving help her mom needed, especially after a stroke.
“It was hard to get anyone to come in and do anything,” said Polito, who was her mother’s primary caregiver until she died in 2010. “I couldn’t leave her alone, and couldn’t find anyone to come in.”
Polito said she’s heard the problem has only gotten worse.
Shawna Ferris, a direct care worker from Mattawamkeag, said access to care and working conditions have worsened over the past two years.
“The cost of living has increased significantly, and the pay has not moved,” Ferris said. “You can go work in a different field and make the same or more money with less responsibilities.”
Home health includes a number of services, such as skilled nursing care for patients rehabilitating at home after a surgery, or patients who need help with daily tasks.
According to the Maine Center for Economic Policy, a progressive think tank, 23,500 hours per week of home health assistance go unfilled in the state because there aren’t enough workers.
“In the next 10-15 years, there’s going to be a lot more people 75 and older who are going to need these services. The demand for workers is growing while the number of people able to fill those roles is plateauing,” said James Myall, an economic policy analyst for the center.
Myall said the 23,500 hours is an undercount because it only looks at people who signed up for Medicaid home health services. It doesn’t consider people who need the services but didn’t bother putting their name down because they know there aren’t enough workers.
SOLUTIONS HARD TO COME BY
Myall said the state has an extreme shortage of direct care workers. Maine needs over 2,000 additional direct care employees, according to a Maine Center for Economic Policy analysis. Those are the staffers who help with daily tasks like cooking, picking up groceries, laundry, and helping people remember to take medications.
“The agencies have not been able to pay their workers enough,” Myall said. “They are getting outbid by retailers like Walmart.”
He said increasing the pay of direct care employees to 140% of the state minimum wage and then giving automatic cost-of-living raises would help alleviate the shortage.
Myall said the Maine Legislature in recent years has approved state reimbursement increases for the nonprofits that hire direct care workers, resulting in modest wage increases. But despite those efforts, wages in other industries, like retail, have increased by more, dampening the effectiveness.
Nonprofit agencies that provide home health services can currently pay their workers 125% of minimum wage, based on what the state’s Medicaid program will reimburse.
The state so far has not substantially increased wages for direct care workers, but lawmakers, including Democratic House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, have advocated for the boost to 140% of minimum wage. The state minimum wage will be $15.70 starting in January, so if that proposal passes, care workers could earn $21.98 per hour.
The Maine Essential Care and Workforce Partnership, a group advocating for better working conditions for direct care workers, is also proposing to improve training, benefits and technology for workers.
DEMAND FOR HELP IS GROWING
Myall said the shortages result in a system where it’s primarily “relatives taking care of their family members, juggling work and caregiving,” Myall said.
“It forces some people out of the workforce,” he said.
Noël Bonam, Maine’s AARP state director, said having a strong home health system will help keep older Mainers from having to move to nursing homes and hospitals. It’s also healthier for them.
“You are keeping that person in the community, and having strong social connections, and that helps them thrive,” Bonam said. “It costs a whole lot less to keep them in the home than taking up a bed in a nursing home.”
Buiocchi said they are able to run the MaineHealth program without workforce shortages, but they have advantages over other employers in that they can offer competitive wages and benefits and a flexible schedule. Also, because they’re a large employer, they have robust training programs and have many pathways for promotions.
Myall said much of the home health industry in Maine consists of nonprofits who don’t have the flexibility to pay higher wages.
Buiocchi said demand for home health services is expected to keep growing.
“The need has increased exponentially over the past five years,” she said.

title: Meet the 81-year-old artist behind thousands of painted rocks
text:
TUALATIN, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - Every morning, rain or shine, painted rocks appear around Tualatin’s Jurgens Park like Easter eggs waiting to be found.
The artist behind the rocks has been a mystery until now.
Phillip Roberts, 81, has spent the last eight years hiding thousands of rocks during his daily walks with his wife.
“I take at least four dozen over a week, so it adds up,” Roberts said.
Roberts is a professional artist whose career has taken him around the world.
“For the past 20 years the pieces that I’ve been working on,” Roberts said, gesturing to his home studio. “I had galleries in Kansas City, I’ve had galleries in San Francisco, I’ve shown in England.”
His inspiration has constantly changed throughout his career.
“I started going to Mexico to find the subject matter of impressionist painters,” Roberts said. “We’d drive around France and Spain, painting.”
All of it has led him back to his home studio in Tualatin, where he spends hours each day.
“I’m usually in here at 1 o’clock, until after 10 in the evening,” Roberts said.
The size of his canvas has changed, and so has the complexity of his subject matter.
“Rather than throwing away the paint on my palette, I started painting rocks,” Roberts said.
Roberts said the rocks are simpler than his oil paintings, and they’re free. His oil paintings are not free.
He gathers his supplies from his backyard, washing and drying the rocks before deciding what to paint.
“I get the rocks from my backyard, I wash them, dry them and look at them,” Roberts said. “Some of them do dictate what they might be.”
Roberts said he is creating animal rocks now, using a hot glue gun and rope.
While the expressive river rocks bring joy to Roberts as he creates them, his real motivation comes from the joy they bring others.
“This lady came up and asked me if we were the ones that put out the rocks and said yes and she said her daughter had a very serious illness, and she said one of the things that got her daughter by was coming over and looking for the rocks,” Roberts said.
Roberts said he plans to continue hiding rocks as long as he can walk.
At 81 years old, Roberts credits his daily three-mile walks for his good health and wellbeing.

title: Ex-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro is returning to federal court to face torture allegations
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife return Thursday to a New York courtroom to face a rewritten indictment accusing them of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were expected to plead not guilty in Manhattan federal court to charges added to a drug trafficking indictment brought months earlier against the two. They were seized from their Caracas home by the U.S. military in a nighttime raid in January.
Attorney Barry Pollack said when the charges were announced last week that Maduro, 63, denies them and “looks forward to his day in court.”
According to the rewritten indictment, Maduro oversaw a violent torture system that beat, asphyxiated, and delivered electric shocks to its victims. He is accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims’ treatment, and threatening to kill one prisoner’s child as a form of psychological torture.
Flores, 69, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.
Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied wrongdoing.
Earlier this year, Maduro and his wife pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case, which said they conspired to flood the U.S. with cocaine. Their attorneys say the case should be dismissed on immunity grounds because they were the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.

title: Deer have built-in detection systems that make hunting a challenge
text:
This story was originally published in November 2023.
As most hunters are aware, Nature has blessed the whitetail deer with a danger detection system that is remarkably keen and effective.
Experts differ on which of the big three, smell, hearing or vision, play the most prominent role in helping our November quarry steer clear of predators, humans among them.
If you had to pick one from among the deer’s trifecta of danger-avoidance mechanisms, which would you choose?
Sense of smell? This one usually gets the nod during deer camp debates.
Modern whitetail hunters go the distance to keep their human scent in check, using everything from special body soap to scent-blocking clothing and earth-scent sprays.
A man with a lot of credentials has stepped forward to challenge this conventional wisdom. Dr. Leonard Lee Rue II, who is an American icon when it comes to deer photography and deer behavior, argues, quite convincingly, that a deer’s hearing, not smell, should be at the top of the list.
In his new book “Whitetail Savvy,” which is destined to become a classic comprehensive publication on deer behavior, Rue asserts that a deer’s sense of smell, which is acute, only works some of the time.
Wind, temperature and other weather conditions can really compromise a deer’s ability to smell danger.
Rue, whose credentials in this area are rock solid, believes that a deer’s keen hearing is its key defense.
Here is an excerpt from Rue’s book on the deer’s auditory system:
“A deer can be in a deep sleep, but its ears never stop moving, winnowing its surroundings for the slightest sound of danger. What is more remarkable is that even while a deer sleeps, its brain is analyzing and filtering out sounds that don’t represent danger.”
Rue says that a noisy squirrel or a falling limb won’t cause a deer to awaken, but a distant human footfall will bring a deer to full alert.
A deer, he points out, also can use its large ears like a revolving radar dish. Unlike humans, who turn their heads to hear a distant sound better, a deer can move its ears toward a sound without turning its head.
Additionally, a deer has a hearing frequency range that can go as high as 30,000 cycles, which is twice that of humans.
Scientists and wildlife professionals are learning more about a deer’s third important sense, its vision.
Although a deer’s eyesight is not as good as ours, 20/60, it more than compensates with other vision attributes. Because, unlike humans, deer have more rods than cones, they see a lot better than you do in low-light conditions, in fact, 18 times better than we do.
They don’t do so well discerning color. They see hunter orange as gray. And, for some unexplained reason, they see the color blue 20 times better than humans. (No blue jeans in the woods, folks).
Most interesting of all, deer can spot and process any movement much faster than humans. And, because their eyes are set differently, they have an uncanny field of vision that extends 300 degrees.
All of this may explain a couple of common beliefs that are engraved in the longstanding protocols of Maine deer hunting.
Deer hunting is a challenge and, under fair-chase practices, only one in four hunters fill their tags.
The most successful deer hunters keep their scents down, sit still as long as patience will allow, and always, always play the wind.

title: Wells taps police captain as next town manager
text:
The town of Wells has announced that police Capt. Adam Shaw will become its next town manager early next year.
Shaw will succeed Michael Pardue upon his retirement on Jan. 18.
The Select Board unanimously voted last week to appoint Shaw. In a news release Wednesday, the town said Shaw’s public safety, leadership and community service experience demonstrated his commitment to the community.
“Knowing that the members of the Board, elected by the people of Wells, unanimously believe I am the right person to help guide the Town forward and build upon the strong foundation established by current Town Manager Michael Pardue is truly humbling,” Shaw said in a written statement.
“I also recognize that this appointment represents a significant level of trust, not only from the Board, but from the entire community,” Shaw added. “I have always believed that trust is something to be earned, and never taken for granted.”
Select Board Chair Timothy Roche said in the release that the board is confident that Shaw will serve the town “exceptionally well.”
The town said Shaw will work with Pardue and other town officials over the coming months to prepare for the transition.
Wells also recently announced that Brian Pellerin, chief deputy for the Cumberland County Sherriff’s Office, has been appointed as the town’s next chief of police.

title: Old South Church Concerts presents UK’s Sarah McQuaid
Did Maine Democrats decriminalize several crimes if the offender says they are homeless?
text:
No.
Maine law does not exempt people from any crimes simply because they say they are homeless.
A 2021 bill sponsored by state Rep. Victoria Morales, D-South Portland, initially proposed barring arrests and prosecutions for certain offenses committed because someone lacked housing. But lawmakers removed that provision before enactment.
Instead, the law requires officers to ask whether someone accused of certain crimes has a home. It covers five offenses: trespassing, disorderly conduct, public urination, drug possession for illegal use and drinking alcohol in prohibited public places.
For those without housing, police must follow their department’s homelessness crisis protocol. Protocols include referrals to crisis services, mental health and substance use professionals, emergency housing and case management. The Maine attorney general’s model favors referrals over citations or arrests, which it calls a last resort.
However, departments can adopt different protocols, and police still may issue citations or make arrests when warranted.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Higher interest rates fuel 'affordability squeeze,' as Maine home sales decline
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The number of Maine homes sold in September fell 4.15% from a year earlier, marking the second straight monthly decline.
But the median sales price, which indicates that half of the homes were sold for more and half sold for less, increased by 2.6%, to $415,000, according to Maine Listings numbers released by the Maine Association of Realtors.
National data show a similar pattern, with the number of homes sold down 1.9% even as the median home price rose by 1.2%, to $422,700.
“The affordability squeeze continues as mortgage interest rates hover at the highest levels in three years,” says Judy Oberg, 2026 president of the Maine Association of Realtors and an associate broker at Oberg Insurance & Real Estate Agency in Bridgton.
“We’re seeing more homes on the market and a modest sales volume decline as we move into the fourth quarter,” she added. “Aside from the traditional slowdown from the summer months, increasing inflationary pressure and higher mortgage rates without a comparable downward adjustment in pricing have sidelined some buyers, especially first-time buyers with no equity from previous home purchases.”
Cumberland County numbers
Maine’s priciest county remains Cumberland, which includes Portland.
The number of homes sold in September declined by 2.24%, while the median sales price increased by 3.44%, to $599,950.
Portland, South Portland, Scarborough and Westbrook all saw double-digit gains in home sales.
Median home prices ranged from $492,500 in Westbrook to $730,000 in Scarborough.
Declines were reported in Windham, Gorham and Falmouth.
“September’s results show a mixed market across Cumberland County,” said Yvonne Myer, president of the Greater Portland Board of Realtors. “The countywide median sale price increased, while closed sales edged lower. Several larger communities experienced increased sales, while others recorded declines in activity. Higher borrowing costs and household expenses can create affordability challenges.”
“We are monitoring pending sales, inventory, and marketing times to better understand how those pressures are affecting buyers and sellers,” she added.
