title: Hot weather and winds raise California wildfire threat as power shutoffs start
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Large swaths of California are expected to see fire weather starting Thursday and thousands of people could lose power as utilities try not to spark wildfires during hot and windy conditions expected to last through Saturday.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who has faced criticism for her city’s response to deadly fires in 2025, said she’s directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds. The fire department has also requested assistance from the state’s office of emergency services, she said.
“It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Dry, warm and gusty northeast winds known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior of Southern California toward the coast and offshore, are expected, with the strongest winds forecast for Thursday afternoon through Friday afternoon.
The winds are expected to reach 20 to 40 mph (32 to 64 kph), with gusts from 50 to 70 mph (80 to 113 kph), in the San Gabriel mountains in Los Angeles County and the Santa Susana mountains, which are mostly in Ventura County, Schoenfeld said. Elevated, though brief, critical fire weather conditions are also forecast for portions of the Santa Lucia mountains in San Luis Obispo County.
Dangerous conditions began earlier in Northern California, with some communities in the Sierra Nevada and its foothills experiencing strong winds, high temperatures and low humidity starting Wednesday night, the National Weather Service said.
The service issued a Red Flag Warning for parts of central and Northern California starting Thursday and lasting through Friday morning, saying that any fires would spread rapidly. Such warnings are issued when weather conditions create an increased risk of wildfires.
Pacific Gas and Electric Company had notified 88,000 customers in 29 counties that it may need to proactively turn power off to reduce the risk of winds toppling over energized power lines that could start a fire. The planned shutoffs had started for some customers by Wednesday night.
The potential interruption in service to customers from the Central Coast to the upper corners of the Sierra Nevada could last through Saturday afternoon, the company said.
In Southern California, the Red Flag Warning for the mountainous areas in Ventura and Los Angeles counties will be in effect from Thursday morning through Friday night.
“We are augmenting our staffing, positioning our people and pre-deploying equipment ahead of this weather so we are ready before the first call comes in,” Los Angeles Fire Chief Jaime Moore said. “We are asking residents to do their part, too. Clear the streets, have a plan and stay informed.”
In January 2025, the Palisades Fire — fanned by Santa Ana winds — ripped through a hillside Los Angeles neighborhood, killing 12 people and destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views. Another fire that burned at the same time in the city of Altadena, in Los Angeles County, killed 19 people and destroyed more than 9,400 homes and businesses.
Schoenfeld said the Santa Ana winds are not going to be as strong as during those fires, when they were gusting 60 to 100 mph (96 to 160 kph).
Authorities determined the Palisades Fire was a carryover fire from the Lachman Fire. The Eaton Fire was caused by sparks from an idle transmission tower owned by Southern California Edison, officials said.
Southern California Edison’s online dashboard on Wednesday showed it was considering public safety shutoffs that could affect 245,000 customers in Kern, Los Angeles, Santa Barbara, Tulare and Ventura counties. Most of those customers — 124,000 — are in Ventura County, just north of Los Angeles.

title: Speaker Johnson dismisses skeptics as he campaigns for House Republicans in Maine battleground
text:
BANGOR — Speaker Mike Johnson made a campaign swing Wednesday through Maine’s picturesque second congressional district, convinced Republicans will defy history and maintain their House majority, as he worked to boost GOP candidate Paul LePage in what is one of the party’s best hopes to flip a Democratic-held seat.
The speaker told a small crowd at the Sea Dog Brewing Co. that he disagrees with the polling and the growing sense that Republicans are heading toward defeat on Nov. 3. Instead, he said he believes that the party in power will maintain its narrow grip on the House — thanks in part to candidates like LePage, the two-term former governor.
“I’m telling you, we’re going to surprise them,” Johnson told the few dozen gathered for lunches of burgers, fish and chips and pot pies at the Bangor eatery.
Johnson has been crisscrossing the country in a campaign blitz that will total more than 20 states and 40 districts in October, in a final sprint ahead of the elections that will determine control of Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term in the White House.
Republicans have increasingly been forced to play defense in the final weeks, trying to shore up their candidates in GOP strongholds nationwide as voters reel from high gas prices, Trump’s tariff policies and the war against Iran. Democrats are reaching deep into districts where Trump has had support, trying and preparing a first 100-day agenda if they win back control.
Johnson said what he’s seeing on the campaign trail tells a different story — of crowds turning out to support the party’s candidates, including earlier this week in southern Texas, a key battleground region.
“Now we have to defy history to do this,” Johnson said, noting that rarely does the president’s party win in midterm elections.
But he said, echoing Le Page’s own message to the room, “voter turnout is critical.”
With a narrow split, every House district matters
While much of the attention in Maine has been on the state’s volatile Senate race between incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, the House race for the open seat held by retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden is another key battleground.
LePage and Democratic state auditor Matt Dunlap are vying for the sprawling district that encompasses much of the rural northern part of the state. The two are set to debate this week.
LePage acknowledged that getting out the vote is what will make the difference.
The district is one Trump carried in the past, but that Golden has held as a leader of the conservative Blue Dog Coalition, a caucus of more centrist Democrats. The retiring congressman has at times bucked House Democratic leadership in voting with Republicans.
It’s also one of the few remaining Trump-won districts represented by a Democrat, which makes it a prime opportunity for Republicans as they work to backfill losses elsewhere and keep their majority.
This week, the main House Republican super PAC aligned with Johnson, the Congressional Leadership Fund, canceled spending in four House races, including Iowa and New Jersey, and increased its investment in others from Texas to Pennsylvania.
Democrats, however, are confident they will seize control, as they begin planning an ambitious agenda focused on affordability issues and anti-corruption investigations of Trump and his administration.

title: Lockheed Martin showered Susan Collins with cash as F-35 program hit turbulence
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In May 2023, the Pentagon’s shiny new fighter jet was not looking so shiny or new.
Already a decade late and nearly $200 billion over its original cost estimate, the F-35 program faced a new crisis. An internal government watchdog report detailed a cascade of new problems with the program, which was in a period of flux amid plans to upgrade the jet’s engine and cooling system.
The report from the Government Accountability Office criticized the Pentagon for lumping those upgrades in with the overall purchase of the planes. Conflating the two, the authors said, would limit congressional insight into cost increases. And they criticized the contractors behind the aircraft for failing to deliver the F-35 in a timely manner.
For Lockheed Martin, the main defense giant overseeing the development of the F-35, the timing was far from ideal. In a few weeks, Congress was set to debate the Pentagon’s mammoth budget — and with it, new funding for the military’s purchase of F-35 jets.
So Lockheed and its lobbyists went on a charm offensive in Washington. The weapons maker shelled out hundreds of thousands over a two-month period, in what the money-in-politics watchdog Open Secrets described as “one of the largest coordinated lobbying efforts” around that year’s military budget.
No member of Congress benefited more than Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who at the time served as the ranking member on the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee.
From May 1 to June 30, 2023, employees and top executives from Lockheed Martin donated $59,500 to Collins’s campaign committee. The donations were outliers during that period: Collins was among the largest recipients of Lockheed cash; the company was her largest single donor over those two months; and it was the largest spending blitz on Collins by Lockheed compared to the same period in other years.
The effort appeared to pay off for Lockheed. In July 2023, less than two months after the release of the Government Accountability Office report, Collins voted in favor of appropriating funds to purchase 83 new F-35 jets. Later that year, when the final version of the military budget was signed into law, Collins celebrated the economic boon she said it would bring to the state of Maine.
In response to questions from The Intercept, Phoebe Keller, a spokesperson for the Republican-controlled Senate Appropriations Committee, said Collins’s support for the jet had nothing to do with donations from Lockheed or any other firm.
“Sen. Collins did not support the F-35 because of donations that she received,” Keller said.
“The F-35 jet program is a longstanding bipartisan defense priority,” Keller said. “Sen. Collins has always publicly supported the F-35 jet program, as dozens of both Republican and Democratic Senators.”
Collins’s position on the Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee likely played a role in the outsized donations, according to analyst Dan Grazier. And Collins, for her part, would have good reason to approve the spending: The F-35 program, Lockheed claims, has had a nine-figure economic impact in Maine.
FIGHT OF HER POLITICAL LIFE
In the final weeks of the biggest fight of her political career against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, fresh scrutiny on Collins’s donations from defense contractors has become a sore spot for her campaign.
In some cases, the senator’s interactions with defense firms are the routine for Washington: glad-handing, lobbying, contributions, and directing pork-barrel spending back home. Not all of it, though, is standard.
Last month, a bombshell report in ProPublica detailed an FBI investigation into an alleged pay-to-play scheme. A former defense contractor claimed to federal agents that he worked with figures tied to Collins to disguise campaign donations — and got federal contracts totaling $32 million in return. (The FBI probe fizzled after Trump returned to office and purged the bureau; Collins denied wrongdoing, pushing back on elements of the report.)
On Wednesday, more than 250 Mainers signed a letter to the state’s attorney general asking the official to investigate the allegations of corruption, according to Maine Morning Star, a local news outlet.
And earlier this month, The Intercept reported on donations from another defense contractor, AM General, and its parent company, whose employees gave $58,000 to fundraising committees associated with Collins after a damning assessment from the Army put its federal contracts in jeopardy.
As with the AM General donations, the contributions by employees and lobbyists of Lockheed Martin do not indicate wrongdoing by Collins or her donors.
“This is an example of what’s wrong with our approach to buying weapons,” said William Hartung, an analyst who has written critically of defense spending and influence peddling in Washington. “If we buy things because they’re in the state of a powerful member, we’re not going to have a coherent arsenal.”
LOCKHEED GIVING
Collins was not the only member of Congress to push for funding the F-35, which enjoyed broad bipartisan support — especially from lawmakers with eligible firms and facilities in their states. And she was not the only one to benefit from the largesse of Lockheed Martin.
From May 1 to June 30, 2023, Lockheed’s corporate PAC doled out $421,000 in a bipartisan blitz to various campaign political action committees, campaign funds, state parties, and charitable foundations. (Aside from 2024, the year of the presidential election, contributions in that two-month period in 2023 eclipsed subsequent years. In the same period this year, Lockheed’s corporate PAC made 128 donations totaling $236,000; last year, it gave $286,000 across 158 donations during the same period.)
Collins was by far the biggest single beneficiary of the influx of cash — which came at a time when she was not actively campaigning. And, unlike the donations spread out to other campaign committees, the cash going from Lockheed into Collins’s coffers during those months came exclusively in the form of individual donations by employees and executives, including the firm’s CEO and chief operating officer, data from the Federal Election Commission shows.
Lobbyists working for Lockheed contributed another $5,000 to Collins during that period, and corporate PACs for Lockheed’s lobbying firms shelled out another $5,500 total, according to FEC disclosures.
Among individual contributions by Lockheed employees, donations to Collins made up more than 10 percent of all donations during the two-month period surrounding the watchdog report.
Only the firm’s in-house employee PAC, which received 75 percent of all employee donations, took in more from figures tied to Lockheed. Collins got more than twice as much as the next highest recipient, ActBlue, the Democratic Party-aligned fundraising vehicle, which received 4 percent of all Lockheed employee contributions in that period, according to FEC data.
The vast majority donations from Lockheed employees and officials were under $1,000. Of the 60 donations of $1,000 or more during May and June 2023, 56 went to Collins.
Virtually all employee contributions from Lockheed workers and executives to Collins during her current term came during that two-month window, according to the FEC.
Lockheed donations made up a quarter of all contributions during May and June 2023 to Collins’s main fundraising arm, Collins for Senator. The next runner-up was telecom giant Charter Communications, whose employee contributions made up just 8 percent of gifts to the Collins campaign in the second quarter of the 2023 fiscal year.
A spokesperson for Lockheed did not answer specific questions regarding the reason for the sudden influx of individual contributions to Collins in 2023.
“Our employee PAC program continues to observe long-standing principles of bi-partisan political engagement in support of our business interests,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
ANOTHER VEHICLE ARMY DIDN’T WANT
Two years later, a similar pattern played out in miniature when a lesser-known defense firm with a troubled product enjoyed Collins’s support on Capitol Hill.
Collins went out of her way last year to slam the Pentagon for canceling its plans to purchase robotic combat vehicles from Textron and its subsidiary Howe & Howe, the Maine-based developer of the Ripsaw.
Collins has repeatedly hyped the unmanned robotic combat vehicle in Senate hearings and official statements. On June 18, 2025, she took issue with the fact that the vehicle had appeared in a recent military parade, but did not make the cut for further spending.
“It’s the height of irony that you would feature this combat vehicle in your parade as the future of the Army at the same time that you’ve canceled the contract — the cancellation of a contract that was won over a lot of other competitors,” Collins said, describing the decision as “terribly unfair and a real mistake.”
A month later, after the military budget cleared the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins singled out Howe & Howe, and its plant in Waterboro, Maine, as a potential beneficiary of a portion of $44 million allotted to outfit the U.S. Marine Corps with amphibious and autonomous vehicles.
She gave another shoutout to Howe & Howe in January, after the 2026 military budget was signed into law. This May, during the congressional testimony by then-Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, Collins again took the military to task for cutting its planned purchase of the Ripsaw.
Textron’s corporate PAC made contributions totaling $4,000 to various PACs associated with Collins just ahead of her vote on the 2026 military budget. $3,000 of the gifts came days after Collins criticized the military for cutting its plans for the Ripsaw program that would have brought millions of dollars to Howe & Howe.
Later in the year, the Textron corporate PAC donated another $7,000 to Collins for Senator and the Collins-linked Dirigo PAC, according to FEC filings. (A spokesperson for Textron and Howe & Howe did not respond to a request for comment.)
Keller, the Senate Appropriations Committee spokesperson, said that Collins was not a member of the Armed Services Committee that voted on funding the Ripsaw.
“She doesn’t have the agency to fund or not fund the vehicle because it wasn’t through the Appropriations Committee,” Keller said, adding that Collins’s longtime support for the Ripsaw was not motivated by the Textron and Howe & Howe donations.
Employees of Textron and its subsidiary, meanwhile, made contributions to various Collins-linked PACS totaling nearly $15,000 between September 2025 and October 15, 2026, FEC data shows.
The donations, relatively small in the post-Citizens United era of campaign finance, still illustrate a troubling pattern of how influence plays out in Washington, according to Hartung, the analyst critical of military spending.
“A lot of members lobby to get more units of something built in their state, or craft legislation for a system that only their local firm can produce,” Hartung said. “It’s kind of business as usual, but sometimes business as usual causes great harm.”
This story was updated to include further statements from Phoebe Keller, a spokesperson for the Senate Appropriations Committee, that were made after publication.

title: Commercial goods are no longer entering Gaza, raising fears of worsening shortages in the territory
text:
Commercial goods are no longer entering Gaza, raising fears of worsening shortages in the territory
No commercial goods have entered the Gaza Strip for two days, Israeli authorities said Thursday, blaming the suspension on merchants angered by taxes imposed by Hamas — a claim that Palestinian importers say isn't true.
The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of food and other critical supplies as fears grow about procuring supplies needed to get through winter in the territory.
The move stands to immediately reduce Gaza's supplies, because the closed-off territory is completely reliant on whatever goods Israel allows in through border crossings.
Aid groups generally bring in staples such as flour, while merchants import more perishable foods like fruits and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza.
The suspension is raising fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control.
“The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council, an aid group. “The markets need to be functioning.”
COGAT announced the suspension of commercial shipments Wednesday. Its deputy spokesperson, Lt. Daniel Kantorovich, said the agency was acting on a decision made by Palestinian merchants a day earlier and could reverse it at their behest.
“We were prepared to coordinate the entry of their trucks as usual, but the vendors informed us that they were cancelling the coordination due to Hamas’s taxation mechanism and threats against them,” Kantorovich said. “The merchants don’t want to bring goods into Gaza.”
The world’s leading authority on food insecurity reported earlier this year that conditions in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but were still at crisis levels. Most families in the war-battered enclave weren’t getting nearly enough to eat, said the report, adding that “even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains.”
Merchants in Gaza coordinate directly with vendors outside the territory, whose shipments are examined by Israel's military before entering Gaza.
In announcing the measure, COGAT claimed to be communicating a decision made by local merchants in Gaza who had grown tired of Hamas taxing their trucks and threatening them. Israel has long accused the militant group of levying fees on imports to fund its operations.
COGAT said no private-sector vendors had attempted to import goods to Gaza since the merchants alerted Israel on Tuesday.
But the head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, disputed Israel's account, saying they were the ones who had made the decision.
“The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments,” he said. “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.”
Following COGAT's announcement, Sheheiber's union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods.
The ministry had been asking merchants to pay 10,000 shekels (about $3,226) per truck entering Gaza, Sheheiber said. At the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab told the union that the amount was not a tax, but rather a donation sought by the ministry to help pay civil servants in the strip.
It was not clear from the COGAT announcement if aid agencies would be allowed to increase shipments into Gaza to compensate for the loss in commercial goods.
The agency claimed that Gaza's population — of roughly 2 million people — required approximately 250 truckloads of goods each day. That's far below the minimum of 600 trucks a day stipulated by a ceasefire brokered by the U.S. a year ago.
The war started when Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people on Oct. 7, 2023, and took 251 hostages. Israel responded with a massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
That includes over 1,400 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire took effect, the ministry says. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
Mroue reported from Beirut.

title: US reportedly considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ as part of new strike plans against Iran
text:
WASHINGTON — The United States is considering using a so-called “mother of all bombs” as part of new strike plans in the war in Iran.
Military sources told CNN that the plans are in place in case President Trump decides to resume combat operations, either before or after the midterm elections.
What is the MOAB
The GBU-43-B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, is the most powerful non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal.
Using it for the first time in the war with Iran would be a notable escalation.
It has the capability of destroying an area equal to nine city blocks.
Concerns over effectiveness and casualties
However, there are concerns it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough to destroy suspected nuclear facilities.
The big blast radius also raises concerns about civilian casualties.
White House response
When asked about possible military plans in Iran, a White House official told CNN that the president is keeping all options on the table.
Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war, as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the midterm elections.
There is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of U.S. bombing.

title: UMaine Extension offers six-part online series for youth on machine learning
text:
University of Maine Cooperative Extension will offer two sessions of a six-part online 4-H series on six Mondays from Nov. 9 through Dec. 14. The sessions are identical. One will be held from 4 to 5:15 p.m. and the other from 6 to 7:15 p.m. Sessions will be held via Zoom.
“Machine Learning: Intro to AI” is designed primarily for youth ages 9 to 12, though teens are welcome. Through hands-on activities, participants will explore how machine learning models make predictions, practice training AI models and build beginner computer science skills. More information and registration is available at the event webpage.
If reasonable accommodation is needed, please contact Sarah Sparks at 207-581-8206 or sarah.sparks@maine.edu by Oct. 26.

title: Maine Mariners restocked, eager for more after lengthy playoff run
text:
PORTLAND — Rick Kowalsky sat on a bench at Troubh Ice Arena and flashed a smile as he untied and kicked off his skates following a Maine Mariners practice Monday afternoon.
“My feet are frozen,” he said.
There were more reasons besides the relief of warm shoes for the Mariners’ second-year coach to smile. The start of the new ECHL season is fast approaching, and with training camp in the books, the Mariners are starting the season on much better footing than they did last season, which ended up being among the franchise’s most memorable.
“We feel pretty good about what we’ve got and where we’re at,” Kowalsky said. “We started (last year) with probably 15 skaters, and not even half of those guys ended up sticking with us. … We started camp (last week) with 25, 26.
“It has a completely different feel than last year did.”
The NHL extended its regular season and shortened its preseason this year, speeding up when players landed with affiliated minor league teams. So the Mariners, rather than being largely TBD in early October, arrived for training more fully assembled.
“This is the first time, probably ever, other than when I was in the NHL, where we implemented systems for an exhibition game,” said Kowalsky, a former assistant with the New Jersey Devils. “You feel like you can hit the ground running.”
The season may have a different feel, but Kowalsky and the Mariners hope to build on last year’s success. Maine went deeper in the playoffs than ever before, reaching Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals before falling to Wheeling.
For the 14 players who made that run and are on this year’s roster, there are higher expectations.
“We know our goal, and our standard is to fight for a Kelly Cup,” said forward Wyllum Deveaux, who has served as the team’s captain since January 2025. “From the start of camp, it’s been known. We’ve picked up where we left off.”
A familiar face will be able to help with that. Maine brought back defenseman Connor Doherty, who captained the Mariners from 2021-24 and then played two seasons with the Florida Everblades, where he won the Kelly Cup last year.
As an ECHL veteran, Doherty had the choice of where to continue his career. The Mariners were interested in the reunion, and so was the 33-year-old Doherty, who played all 20 of Florida’s playoff games last season and led the team in plus-minus.
“I loved my time playing here,” Doherty said. “My wife and I wanted to try something for a couple of years, move down south and check that out. Obviously, we had some success in hockey, but now we’re just excited to be back here. I want to keep dragging this organization further and further, and hopefully accomplish something sweet up here.”
He didn’t have to make much of an adjustment.
“I feel like the first couple of days walking into the rink, it’s kind of like ‘Did I ever leave?'” he said.
Both Kowalsky and Deveaux said Doherty’s presence as a veteran leader and championship player will be important for a group of teammates looking to take a step closer to a title of their own.
“Bringing that championship pedigree is huge,” Deveaux said. “He plays the right way, he stands up for teammates and he plays on the edge. And he brings it every night.”
He’ll help anchor a defense that should be strong. Owen Gallatin, Michael Underwood, Nick Anderson and Jaxon Bellamy are back from last year’s playoff roster.
Brad Arvanitis is gone after a strong season in net, but Luke Cavallin (2.02 goals-against average in 10 playoff games) is back after leading the Mariners through the postseason, and Max Lundgren, last year’s Hockey East Tournament MVP at Merrimack College, will battle him for playing time.
“We definitely feel very good about goaltending again,” Kowalsky said. “(And) we’re way ahead of the game with our defense. Last year, we didn’t even have a right-shot defenseman, and I think three of the seven defensemen we started with didn’t even make it until Christmas.”
The big question marks come on offense, where three of the top six scorers from a season ago are gone. Max Andreev, Robert Cronin and Linus Hemstrom bring back some scoring punch, Ryan Francis and Mason Primeau should factor in, and the team also gets Deveaux back for a full season after an injury in last year’s opener limited him to seven regular-season games.
“That’s first and foremost (my focus), is being healthy, playing every single game this year,” he said. “As a leader as well, that’s my biggest thing. Taking care of myself, making sure I’m ready to go and showing the other guys that that’s the standard here.”
Or at least, one of them. The Mariners hope they set a new one last year.
“We feel pretty good about the group,” Kowalsky said. “We want winners, we want leaders, we want character people, that was a big part of my recruiting process, and I think we’ve done a good job of that.”

title: We tested Amazon's 'About You' feature. Here's what it got right — and wrong
text:
We tested Amazon's 'About You' feature. Here's what it got right — and wrong
The National Consumer Unit tried Amazon's personalization feature with several co-workers and asked the company how it builds customer profiles.
We tested Amazon's 'About You' feature. Here's what it got right — and wrong
The National Consumer Unit tried Amazon's personalization feature with several co-workers and asked the company how it builds customer profiles.
Amazon shoppers may have noticed a feature called "About You" making the rounds on social media.
The feature, which Amazon introduced in May, gives customers a look at some of the information the company uses to personalize their shopping experience. It can include details such as a customer's interests, household makeup and shopping habits.
You can find the feature by going into your account and looking for the section that says "About You." Alternatively, you can ask Alexa for Shopping, Amazon's AI tool, "What do you know about me?"
What Amazon knew about me
Naturally, I wanted to know what my "About You" profile looked like.
Amazon correctly identified that I likely live in New York. It knew my household has two adults. It also said I have a cat — technically true, although I actually have two.
Another detail caught my attention. Amazon said I consistently repurchase skincare staples and even listed some of the brands I've purchased.
Overall, there wasn't anything in my profile that surprised me or felt inconsistent with my shopping habits.
What Amazon knew about my teammates
I asked several co-workers to open their "About You" pages for the first time to see what they found.
One co-worker found that Amazon correctly identified crocheting as a hobby.
Another was surprised to see Amazon believed he had a 2-year-old child. He doesn't have children, but he has spent the past couple of years buying gifts for friends with young kids. It's possible those purchases led Amazon to make that assumption.
Then there was the result that prompted me to call Amazon: One co-worker discovered that Amazon not only listed that she owns a cat, but it also listed her cat's name.
How these profiles are built
Amazon told me the "About You" feature is built using customers' activity across Amazon.
That can include purchase history, searches, shopping lists, product reviews and conversations with Alexa for Shopping.
Amazon says the goal is to personalize features such as product recommendations and other content customers see while shopping.
Can you turn it off?
Amazon says customers cannot opt out of the "About You" feature entirely.
If you find something that's inaccurate, you can edit or remove individual details from your profile.
If you'd rather not receive interest-based ads, Amazon also lets you adjust your advertising preferences in your account settings.
You can also learn more about the information Amazon collects in its Privacy Notice.
Stay Connected With the National Consumer Unit
Get clear, actionable consumer reporting delivered across platforms.
Follow National Consumer Correspondent Allie Jasinski for real-time updates on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube.
Have a question you'd like us to investigate? Email us at askallie@hearst.com

title: Homicide victim found in barrel at Lake Mead identified more than 4 years after discovery
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) - Authorities in Las Vegas identified a homicide victim Thursday whose remains were found in a barrel at Lake Mead more than four years ago.
Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse identified the man as Edward Lelburian Jackson. Authorities said he was from Arkansas and in his mid-to-late 50s when he died.
Las Vegas police said Jackson’s remains were discovered in a barrel at Hemenway Harbor at Lake Mead on May 1, 2022. He died from a gunshot wound, and his death was ruled a homicide.
The case drew national attention as water levels at Lake Mead dropped to record lows.
Clark County released facial approximation images created by the FBI in hopes of generating leads.
“Our hope is to put the composite out there and see if we can get any good matches. As good as a DNA profile is, it’s only as good as what you have to compare it to,” Rouse previously said about the case. “Obviously, the next steps would be to get it out to the community in hopes that we have some good links to individuals that could be considered for testing.”
Investigators said Jackson’s family told them that he liked to travel, but it was unclear why he was in Las Vegas.
Authorities said they estimated Jackson was killed between the mid-1970s and early 1980s, based on the type of shoes found with him.
According to the county, this homicide was one of four cases involving remains found at Lake Mead in 2022. Three others were identified by DNA:
- Claude Russell Pensinger, 52, of Las Vegas — Skeletal remains found July 25, Aug. 6 and Aug. 16, 2022, near Boulder Beach were confirmed to be from the same person. Pensinger disappeared July 14, 1998. Cause and manner undetermined.
- Donald P. Smith, 39, of North Las Vegas — Remains found Oct. 17 and Oct. 19, 2022, in the Callville Bay area. Smith reportedly drowned in April 1974. Death ruled accidental drowning.
- Thomas Erndt, 42, of Las Vegas — Remains found May 7, 2022, in the Callville Bay area. Erndt reportedly drowned Aug. 2, 2002. Cause and manner undetermined.
In August of this year, more human remains were also discovered at Lake Mead amid the receding water level.

title: CAR T-cell therapy offers new hope for lupus patients
text:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. (Aging Untold) — A treatment first developed to fight cancer is now being used in a clinical trial at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine to treat lupus, an autoimmune disease that affects an estimated 1.5 million Americans.
What is lupus?
Lupus is a lifelong autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy cells and tissues, which can lead to inflammation and organ damage. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the disease is difficult to diagnose due to its many signs and symptoms. Nine of 10 lupus diagnoses are in women ages 15 to 44.
There is currently no cure.
A patient’s two-decade battle
Rachel Dib, a military wife and mother of three in North Carolina, was diagnosed with lupus in December 2007, when she was a college sophomore.
At first, she said it hurt to breathe or laugh. Over time, her joints began to fail.
“My thumb just like popped out of the socket. I didn’t even know what was happening. I went to like do this and my thumb popped out and that’s the start of like multiple hand surgeries,” Dib said.
The disease cost her the ability to play musical instruments. She had been a clarinetist, pianist, tenor saxophone player — and she could no longer run or hike.
“On a good day I used a cane. On a bad day I used a walker and on a really bad day, it was just, I just couldn’t get out of bed. I would hurt my hip just like rolling over in bed. It was bad,” Dib said.
How CAR T-cell therapy works
After nearly 20 years of suffering and hospital stays, Dib enrolled in a CAR T-cell therapy clinical trial at UNC.
CAR T, which stands for chimeric antigen receptor therapy, integrates immunotherapy, genetic engineering and personalized medicine. It has been used in the treatment of blood cancers.
Dr. Saira Sheikh, a rheumatologist and researcher at UNC and one of only a handful of doctors in the world offering the therapy, said the connection between cancer and lupus treatment comes down to B cells.
“In these particular cancers, B cells are at play and in autoimmune diseases such as lupus, B cells are also involved. And these are what are called autoreactive B cells in which the body’s immune system starts to attack itself,” Sheikh said.
The process begins by drawing the patient’s blood to extract T-cells, which the body uses to fight infection. Those T-cells are then genetically reprogrammed in a lab.
“It’s as though you give the T-cells a GPS to go back into the body and find the target cell. In this case, the B cells are the targets,” Sheikh said.
After three days of preconditioning with chemotherapy, the patient receives the CAR T-cell infusion.
“It’s often referred to as a living drug because it uses the patient’s own immune system to fight whatever disease you’re targeting,” Sheikh said.
Results and risks
Dib said she felt results the day after her infusion.
“After I got it, the day after, I had the most energy I’d ever had, ever. I was like, ‘I feel like I’m 20 again and I’m stuck in a hospital room,’” Dib said.
More than a year later, she said she is able to get up with her children in the morning, take them to school and manage household tasks.
“If I had had this treatment when I was 19, my life would be completely different now,” Dib said.
Sheikh said the therapy holds “incredible promise,” but is not without risks.
The CAR T-cell therapy clinical trial is conducted by a team of specialists that oversees preparation, administration and follow-up therapy. The clinical care team includes a rheumatologist, an oncologist or hematologist, an immunologist and a nephrologist to monitor the kidneys.
“I would say it’s just really groundbreaking in a way that we had never imagined,” Sheikh said.

title: Hilary Swank, 52, is pregnant with third child
text:
(Gray News) - Hilary Swank is pregnant with her third child at the age of 52.
The “Million Dollar Baby” star and her family shared the news on social media with a video showing them dancing with glowsticks taped to their bodies, which then revealed the mom’s baby bump.
The caption reads, “A lot of people have been asking what project I’m doing next, this one releases in December.”
In 2023, the Oscar winner gave birth at the age of 49 to twins, daughter Aya and son Ohm.
Swank told People in May that she felt fortunate to be able to prioritize time with her children.
Swank said her career had been a priority earlier in life, describing it as “such a baby of mine.” She won the best actress Oscar in 2000 for “Boys Don’t Cry” and in 2005 for “Million Dollar Baby.”
“I knew I wanted kids someday, but I wasn’t planning what that would look like,” Swank said. “I know it’s so different for everyone, but for me, if I had had a kid in my 20s or my 30s, I think I’d be a much different parent than I am now.”

title: ICE vehicle struck during Sanford traffic stop; toddler taken to hospital, police say
text:
SANFORD, Maine (WMTW) - A person who was stopped by ICE agents in Sanford is accused of backing into an ICE vehicle with a one-year-old inside their car.
That’s according to authorities.
Sanford police said officers were called to Brook Street around 9:30 a.m. Thursday at the request of ICE agents, who had a person in custody.
ICE agents told Sanford police they had made a traffic stop and positioned one of their vehicles in front of the detainee’s vehicle and another ICE vehicle behind.
The ICE agents reported the detainee had put their vehicle in reverse and struck the ICE vehicle positioned behind them.
ICE agents told police the toddler was not properly secured in a child safety seat.
Sanford police said as precaution, the child was medically evaluated.
During the incident, officers say they also learned two of the detainee’s other children, ages 2 and 9, had been left inside a nearby home without adult supervision.
Police called Maine DHHS to the home to check on the kids.

title: Snapchat messages show how Nolan Wells' friends reacted to his death
text:
Nolan Wells' family releases messages revealing friends' reactions to his death
The family of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teen who died over the Fourth of July weekend during a trip to Horn Island, released a digital forensic report of the late teen's phone. It includes hundreds of pages of messages across multiple platforms, revealing what friends said while Wells was missing and after his death.
The release of this report comes after a grand jury did not indict anyone in connection with Wells' death, and two autopsy reports list his cause of death as undetermined.
The names and identities of people who sent the messages are concealed in the report, prepared by the company Garrett Discovery.
Frantic messages
The report, which is almost 300 pages long, begins with an unidentified group of friends discussing Wells' disappearance.
The messages begin the night of July 4, when the group of friends asked if anyone had heard from or seen Nolan.
One message discussed Nolan being last seen with a girl and not getting on a boat with his friends to return to the island.
"He came and was hanging out with us and around us. He never disappeared with (redacted) when it was time to leave around like 6; he got off our boat with this other guy and they started walking back to their boat," the message read.
The group chat continued late into the night, with one friend calling his disappearance suspicious.
"There is a def some sus s---- going on," the message read.
The group chat also questioned why Nolan stayed behind, with one person writing it wasn't like him, a sentiment his parents have shared in the media on a number of occasions.
"That's not like Nolan bro just to get left," a message read.
Messages also showed the friends discussing why Nolan would leave his phone on the boat. The group discusses the issue with the boat that resulted in his friends leaving without him to get help.
Day after Nolan's disappearance
The day after Nolan's disappearance, the group chat continues, this time with his friends discussing the police investigation.
In one message, a friend encourages others to look at their camera rolls to see if they caught anyone speaking with Nolan.
"Yeah no luck on the island. Officials got that island covered miles out," one message received after 12:30 p.m. July 5 reads. "Hes gotta be shlumped somewhere rn hopefully," it continues.
"It's already noon though," one person replies.
"He might've got drugged or something," one reply reads.
A message received just before 12:40 p.m. the same day reads "I've woken up for work at 7 am before and he was still up from the night before on the couch and went to bed and woke up at like later that night so that's what I'm hoping."
Before 2:40 p.m. July 5, messages were sent regarding some members of the group chat getting calls from the sheriff's office. One person writes "[Whatever] gets him home the fastest."
Another message instructed the group not to speak to anybody or read articles posted online because they were "being blasted on Facebook."
A message received before 7:15 p.m. on July 5 reads "So much bs these people online don't know anything about the story and are just saying we are pieces of s---."
Reacting to Nolan's death
Once the news broke that Nolan had died, the group chat was flooded with messages reacting to his death.
One message from a friend expressed disbelief, calling Nolan "the best person."
"Nolan was the most nice and caring guy we knew," one message received before 10:20 a.m. July 6 reads. "He's in a better place now and we'll get through this together."
Members of the chat expressed support for several of his friends.
The group also discussed why anyone would think they had anything to do with Nolan's death once the story began making national headlines.
"All i keep seeing is white folk made it home and the one black kid didn't," one message reads.
One person replied, "It ain't ever been like that with us bro."
"If they knew how much we love him they wouldn't say that," another reply reads.
The chat continues to discuss the online discourse surrounding Nolan's death.
"Idc what anyone has to say I wanna know where the f--- my friend is bro," one friend writes.
One message from a friend urges the group not to speculate or post anything online and to turn off location services, with another offering advice to ask for an attorney if approached.
"If we get called in for questioning, the smart move is to ask for an attorney. That doesn't mean we're guilty, it just is smart so we don't get played by some potential bias cop," the message read.
Messages sent directly to Nolan following his death are also included in the report. One message reads, "Tell me this isn't true bro please open this text and let me know you're safe."
"You will never be forgotten," one person wrote after 11:30 a.m. July 6.
Funeral discussions
The group chat members also discussed whether they should attend the funeral.
One message from a friend suggests they go together and sit with Black friends to "make a statement."
"We need to go to Nolan's funeral and get with all our other black friends to prove a statement for the media," the message read.
Another person suggested they ask Nolan's mother, Christine Wonsley, if they should attend.
The chat became critical of how Nolan's funeral was being handled, calling the announcement of a reward in his case "a disservice and ignorant."
The group also discussed putting up a memorial for Nolan, which included a cross and burying his flip-flops.
The full report can be read online here.
Sister station WDSU has reached out to Ben Crump, the Wells family's attorney, for a statement regarding the messages. At the time of this publication, a response had not been received.
President Trump considering investigation
President Donald Trump said last week that he is considering an investigation into Wells' death.
This comes after weeks of Wells' family pushing for the FBI to take up the case.
Ben Crump, the attorney for Wells' family, issued the following statement, stating that he is ready to work with the federal government to ensure an investigation is conducted.
"Sunday will mark 100 days since we have been looking into the death of Nolan Wells, so when President Trump responds to news reporters that 'we’re looking into it,' we believe that carries more weight than the response given by the FBI. Our team stands ready to work with the federal government to ensure Nolan's death is investigated to the fullest extent," Crump said.
Snapchat conversations, a state autopsy report and context from a forensic analyst regarding the examination of a Mississippi teen's phone were shared in a news conference last month as the family continues to seek answers surrounding their son's death.
Crump was joined by Andrew Garrett, CEO of Garrett Discovery, to release the findings from the extraction of Nolan Wells' phone.
Crump and his team called for further investigation into his death, arguing that messages from his friends, forensic phone data and injuries documented during his autopsy raise questions about the conclusion made by a grand jury that he accidentally drowned.
The news conference comes after a grand jury in Jackson County, Mississippi, declined to charge anyone criminally in Wells' death.
Crump read excerpts from Snapchat messages exchanged among Wells’ friends but did not identify the people who wrote them. According to Crump, the messages described two "sketchy-looking guys" in nearby boats as "felons."
In another message, a friend said their father had escorted a woman to her boat and warned, "You don’t want to be left alone with those guys, especially if you were drunk."
Other messages shared the day after Wells' death expressed concern about encountering "racist people" on Horn Island.
Crump said the conversations indicate that some of Wells’ friends also questioned whether he drowned.
Analyst video details phone activity
Garrett, from the digital forensics company hired by Wells' family, said Wells rarely communicated through text messages.
Garrett said about 90% of Wells' communications were through Snapchat and Instagram, including group conversations involving numerous people.
Garrett said his team used two forensic tools to examine the device, but the version of Snapchat installed on Wells’ phone was too new to be processed by the software. His team then spent about a week manually decoding and extracting the Snapchat information, according to Garrett.
Garrett said his investigation of the phone showed Wells used Face ID, communicated with others and opened several apps on his phone on the day he died. Investigators later relied on GPS and other device data to trace the phone’s movements after Wells stopped using it.
Garrett said his analysis identified activity involving the phone both before and after Wells’ death. He also confirmed that some material had been deleted but declined to speculate about who deleted it or why.
Messages continued syncing to the phone after Wells’ death because other participants remained active in group conversations, according to Garrett.
Garrett presented a video tracing the phone’s movements. Houses, names and street information were not shown in an effort to protect privacy.
The timeline showed Wells visiting a McDonald’s at 8:24 a.m. the day of his death, and arriving at another person’s home at 8:37 a.m. Snapchat was used on Wells' phone during portions of that trip, according to Garrett.
According to Garrett, Wells boarded a boat at approximately 9:31 a.m. and arrived at Horn Island around 11:18 a.m. Snapchat messages were sent between the time he boarded the boat and the group’s arrival at the island.
Garrett identified 2:18 p.m. as the last time Wells personally locked the phone. Sea Tow was called at approximately 4:35 p.m. because of a problem with one of his friend's boat's bilges. The boat later traveled to a dock at about 6:30 p.m. and then to a boat ramp around 7 p.m., clearing the ramp at 7:25 p.m.
At 8:51 p.m., the phone traveled to a home, according to Garrett. Wells’ parents retrieved it at approximately 3 a.m.
Garrett said his reports and the underlying phone data were given to the district attorney.
He said the state’s forensic examiners use the same principal tools as his company. Garrett also penned a letter to Crump's legal team, disputing District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath's version of the events regarding the extraction of Wells' phone.
McIlrath responds to new findings
McIlrath issued a new statement Thursday night, standing by the grand jury investigation and its decision to not pursue criminal charges linked to Wells' death.
She also accused Crump’s legal team of withholding information and attempting to control the public narrative surrounding Wells' death and the investigation.
In her statement, McIlrath disputed claims surrounding data recovered from Nolan’s cellphone. She said a 30-hour digital download referenced by Garrett was never provided to her office. Instead, prosecutors received two emails containing approximately 300 pages of what she described as "selected findings" from the phone, according to McIlrath.
McIlrath said her office and the public had previously been told that no one possessed or accessed Nolan’s phone between his last known use and the time it was returned to his parents. She also maintained that the user activity discussed by Crump during his news conference came from other Snapchat users, not Nolan’s phone.
She said if Crump’s team has evidence showing otherwise, it should have provided that to investigators and the grand jury.
McIlrath maintained that the state was willing to participate in a mutual examination of the phone. She alleged that the Wonsley family decided "at the 11th hour" to arrange a private extraction of the device and then provided the grand jury with only portions of the results.
She also said Snapchat messages recovered during the investigation demonstrated Nolan’s close relationship with his friends. McIlrath criticized the Crump team for allowing those friends to be publicly accused and subjected to threats.
As far as the autopsy report, McIlrath said both the state’s autopsy and an independent examination found no evidence of a fatal injury or disease. She added that neither examination ruled out drowning.
McIlrath further claimed that Crump’s team previously told her office it had no evidence that a crime had been committed against Nolan. She accused Crump's team of publicly raising questions that only they may be able to answer.
"Mr. Crump, why are you asking the public to ask us, what was deleted?" McIlrath said. "What witness or piece of evidence on the phone or otherwise supports what you keep claiming, Mr. Crump? Tell us."
McIlrath said Crump’s team and the Wonsley family have her personal cellphone number and knew they had an open invitation to present information to the grand jury.
"The truth is the Crump team was offered a standing invitation to provide any evidence or witnesses that they wished to present to the grand jury, including any expert they retained," McIlrath said. "They have chosen to grandstand."
She added that Crump’s conduct during the case had "demonstrated that he is not worthy of our trust."
McIlrath also released a text message she sent to Nolan’s mother, saying it demonstrated her compassion for the Wonsley family and her intentions throughout the investigation.
She ended her statement by calling on Crump’s team to immediately turn over any new information it believes shows Nolan was murdered.
WDSU has reached out to Crump's team for a response to McIlrath's allegations. At the time of this publication, a response had not been received. 
Grand jury decision
Wells was found dead on Horn Island over the Fourth of July weekend.
According to the grand jury report, the grand jury engaged in a thorough and complete investigation into Wells' death, including reviewing witness testimony, physical and digital evidence, GPS data, cellphone records, videos and investigative reports.
The report states that the grand jury recognizes the public assertion that Wells was the only Black individual on Horn Island on July 4, but it found that he was not the only Black person there that day and says that these false assertions have led to misidentification, speculation and rumors concerning Wells' death.
In a video statement, the Jackson County district attorney also addressed those concerns, stating, "The narrative that three white boys and a Black boy went to an island and only the white friends returned spread like wildfire; this was false."
The grand jury found that Wells traveled to Horn Island on July 4 with a group of friends on three different boats and chose to remain at Horn Island after the three boats departed the island.
No credible evidence was found to support allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on the three boats on July 4 engaged in any criminal conduct related to Wells' death, according to the grand jury.
The report also states that the grand jury acknowledges that there is no statute of limitations on homicide cases in the state of Mississippi and that if credible evidence comes to light in the future that suggests Wells' death was not accidental, the matter should be presented to the grand jury for further consideration.
Nolan Wells' family reacts to grand jury decision
Crump, along with other attorneys working the case, was critical of the grand jury's decision, specifically citing injuries to the back of Wells' head.
Crump said the team believed the grand jury did not consider the circumstances involving how the injuries were caused when making the decision.
He also stressed that the injuries were noted in the independent autopsy and that the Mississippi medical examiner's report identified the injuries to Wells' head.
"It just does not add up. If it was your child, would they accept what that grand jury said?" Crump said. "If they wouldn't accept it, Nolan's parents don't have to accept it."
According to Crump, his team will not stop seeking information on what caused Wells' death.
Wells' mother, Christine Wonsley, also spoke, stating that she felt the grand jury could not determine her son's death was an accidental drowning when his death certificate says his cause of death is undetermined.
Wonsley said she felt like her son did not receive a fair or transparent investigation due to narratives that were circulating online regarding her son's death.

title: 5 Ellsworth residents are competing for 2 school board seats
text:
Five Ellsworth residents seek to fill two open seats on the local school board at a time when some of Maine’s elected supervisory school bodies have become hyperpoliticized.
Incumbents Kelly McKenney and Christopher Walters and hopefuls John Linnehan, Karen Shea Arkin and Brittany Rumery are vying for two open seats on the Ellsworth School Board.
It’s the first contested race for the city’s school board in five years, according to the Ellsworth American.
School board races in Maine for a long time were considered predominantly civil contests, but that has changed for some in recent years. Roughly since the COVID pandemic, first with mask and vaccination mandates, hot-button social topics such as transgender and other diversity issues have become more openly debated at school board meetings — and at times have drawn funding from outside groups that seek to have their preferred candidates elected.
In Ellsworth, the candidates differ how the school system — which governs Ellsworth High School, Ellsworth Elementary Middle School, Hancock County Technical Center and the city’s adult ed programs — can cultivate student success.
As Ellsworth’s school budget accounts for more than 40 percent of city spending, each of the candidates have stressed the importance of balancing student needs and fiscal responsibility.
But they don’t all agree on how to meet that balance.
Two candidates, Linnehan, a longtime area businessman and repeat political candidate who has never held public office, and Arkin, a self-described conservative social worker who is in the middle of her first bid for public office, want to slash unnecessary costs by reviewing the school system’s $34.6 million budget line-by-line.
“I would reduce spending in the Ellsworth Schools,” Linnehan wrote in an email to the Bangor Daily News. “Like my own and any family’s household spending, Ellsworth schools need to review each individual line spending item. Once an item is identified as being either ‘a need or a greed,’ only then can any item be chosen to be cut, reduced or approved. Like any household, I believe there are many items of spending that can be cut and eliminated from our school budget.”
Linnehan and Arkin share campaign signs posted around the city.
Rumery, a finance director at a Maine nonprofit who formerly served in the finance department at a community college and private university, said education was among the most vital ways to invest in a city. She supports exploring grants and partnerships to supplement local dollars, she said.
McKenney, who is running for her fourth school board term, said she’s seen her taxes nearly double in the past decade, but pointed out that fixed costs account for roughly 90 percent of the school budget.
“Our district is not frivolous with money, but educating and providing services to our students come with a hefty price tag,” McKenney said. “Fortunately, our very talented administrative team applies for and is awarded hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funds.”
Walters was appointed to the school board in June after former member Elizabeth Alteri resigned from her post to move out of the city. He said he would prioritize reviewing administrative costs, contracts, purchasing, technology expenses and underutilized resources before cutting budget items that are directly related to student academics like staff, special education resources and building maintenance.
McKenney and Walters said deferred building maintenance is a pressing challenge the schools will face soon. Rumery said Ellsworth’s growing population would bring significant change to the city’s school system.
Linnehan said the board should focus on repairing what he described as a “low level of quality education.” Linnehan cited declining student scores in core subjects as a matter that needed immediate attention.
Arkin wants to zero in on retaining high quality teachers and ensuring they have “time for teaching.”
The candidates had varying assessments of how shifting enrollment trends could impact Ellsworth students. Arkin does not think enrollment is “much of an issue at the moment,” while Linnehan, Walters, Rumery and McKenney agreed it should inform where and how the district invests in its programs and facilities.
“Enrollment and facility needs go hand in hand,” Rumery said. “We should be watching enrollment trends and listening to staff about how our buildings are actually working for students day to day. If we can identify needs early, we have more time to plan, explore funding options, and make thoughtful financial decisions instead of waiting until a need becomes urgent.”
The candidates also weighed in on how the district can best improve students’ quality of life.
McKenney believes the district should continue to invest in social services, including by providing mental, physical and emotional health services to students. The district is already offering many of these services, like access to food, clothing and hygiene products for homeless students and families.
Rumery wants to hear from students on what would enhance their school experience, but she said her own child has asked for longer lunches, more recesses and later start times. Rumery acknowledged that such changes would come with downsides — like interrupting family work schedules and absorbing educational time — that would also need consideration.
Linnehan would like to expand career and vocational training opportunities, noting the school district should be focused on preparing students for a successful career.
“I want to move away from technology teaching and bring back paper, pencils [and] textbooks,” Arkin said.
Walters, a firefighter, echoed some of McKenney and Linnehan’s points, tying a student’s quality of life to the opportunities at their disposal — both in terms of real-world skills and mental health resources.
“We need to look at the whole student,” Walters said. “Students should have trusted adults they can go to when they need help. We should also continue looking for ways to give students meaningful opportunities outside the traditional classroom. Not every student learns the same way or has the same goals.”

title: A dog with a legacy in Brunswick, Chowder gets his turn to speak
text:
Well, it’s about time. All the other dogs at Thornton Oaks have told their stories in the Oak Leaves newsletter but what about me? Just because I’ve moved on doesn’t mean I don’t have something to say. Here goes.
When I was 3 months old my stepbros gave me to Mom and Dad for a wedding present. I remember Dad saying, “Is it a boy or a girl?” What a dumb question. Believe me, I was all boy until they had me “fixed.” Ah well, I just had to satisfy my other appetites. Like, well, food. All food. That’s why they were smart to name me Chowder.
Here are some of the many delicacies I savored over the years: Being health conscious, I was partial to seafood, like dead seals washed up on the shore. Or the sand shark I found at Cape Hatteras. I also enjoyed good red meat, like dead squirrels and, yes, a frozen rat. Once I found a deer leg in the woods and carried it back to Mom and Dad. They weren’t impressed.
I also liked regular human food. Leftovers. Egg McMuffins (Dad was generous). Meat left on the counter when Mom was on a phone call. Or cheese on a coffee table when the guests weren’t paying attention. A neighbor once said to Mom and Dad, “Do you know your dog likes brie?” I got in trouble when I chomped a cake that was supposed to be for a baptism ceremony. I loved anything but onions. After all, I had to keep my breath sweet because I might find a girl dog who was also fixed and we could have a platonic relationship. I was always a lover, not a fighter.
One time I went into someone else’s house when the door was open, walked upstairs and jumped onto a bed with a couple in it, people who Mom and Dad didn’t even know. They seemed surprised, but they were good about it.
I did like other things beside eating. Like taking long walks in the woods or around this huge field that Mom and Dad called “the tundra.” I loved swimming. I liked hanging out with my four stepbros. They sometimes called me “Chow,” which was fair given my eating habits. I peaked at 110 pounds, prompting the lawnmower guy to call me “Porkchop,” but my fighting weight was about 90.
I loved coming to Maine on weekends from Massachusetts during the summer. I got to run loose at Mere Point, which was always great, except for the times I got quilled by a porcupine and sprayed by a skunk. I got pretty famous there. Everybody loved telling Chowder stories.
One of my favorite things was lying on the floor in the den while Mom and Dad watched television. Dad would use my stomach for a pillow. It was a good time to bond. I still remember the night before I died. I didn’t know I was going to die, but something seemed wrong. I remember staring right at Dad for a long time. He later told people that that was unusual. The next day Dad went away on a business trip and I felt awful.
Mom took me to this veterinary hospital. The vet told Mom and Dad they’d have to operate and it would cost $4,000 and I might not even survive. They decided to have the operation done — I always knew they loved me despite my mischievous ways — and I died anyway.
Don’t worry. This story has a happy ending. They took my ashes out to Seal Rock on Casco Bay along with the ashes of Dad’s mother (Moo) and had a double ash-sprinkling ceremony. My stepbro Andy read a neat poem about me called “Ode To Chowder.” Dad said some nice things about Moo. And then they tossed our ashes into the water. Pure heaven!
Mom and Dad sometimes talk about getting another dog, but they wouldn’t dare, not as long as I’m around. They do like walking Kami, the neighbor’s dog, at night. Kami seems nice, but no one can fill my shoes. Believe me.
So now you know something about me. When you walk by Apartment 219 you’ll see the black Lab rug. You can pat me if you want. It gets lonely being a guard dog 24 hours a day. Oh, and here’s some advice: Spread some love around like I tried to do. And never miss a meal. Or a snack. You’ll be just fine. Trust me.
David Treadwell, a Brunswick writer, welcomes commentary and suggestions for future “Just a Little Old” columns at [email protected].

title: Suspicious letters containing unknown substances sent to election offices and lawmakers
text:
Suspicious letters containing unknown substances sent to election offices and lawmakers
Federal authorities are investigating suspicious letters, some containing unknown substances, sent to election offices and lawmakers across the U.S., prompting evacuations and security warnings ahead of Election Day.Article:
Suspicious letters containing unknown substances sent to election offices and lawmakers
Federal authorities are investigating suspicious letters, some containing unknown substances, sent to election offices and lawmakers across the U.S., prompting evacuations and security warnings ahead of Election Day.Article:
Federal investigators are working to intercept suspicious letters, some containing unknown substances, sent to election offices and lawmakers across the country, sparking evacuations and a federal investigation less than three weeks before Election Day.
"I can confirm that we have intercepted some of these letters and they are in law enforcement possession," Brendan Donahue, U.S. Postal Inspection Service deputy chief inspector, said.
The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the mailings that have been sent nationwide to some lawmakers and election officials.
Letters containing powdery substances led to evacuations at election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. In Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New Mexico, the Postal Service intercepted similar letters before they reached the secretary of state’s office.
"Nothing's gonna take our eye off the ball. We're not deterred or in any way distracted by this," Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said.
On Capitol Hill, Senate offices were warned to treat suspicious mailings as potentially hazardous. Lawmakers were informed that, despite efforts to intercept the letters, some could still arrive.
"We're also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters," Donahue said.
Election officials say security and contingency plans are in place to ensure operations continue uninterrupted.
Separately, the U.S. Postal Service has urged voters to mail completed ballots at least one week before their state’s deadline. Starting Oct. 24, USPS will implement "extraordinary measures" to expedite ballot delivery, including extra collections, special pickups, expanded processing hours, and bypassing normal procedures to deliver ballots directly to election officials.
USPS reported that in 2024, 99.9% of ballots sent by voters to election officials arrived within seven days, with delivery averaging about one day.
In another development, the Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit against California over more than 20,000 registered voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens. The lawsuit does not establish that those individuals have voted illegally, but the federal government says they were identified as likely noncitizens and were sent mail ballots by California.
The DOJ is seeking a federal judge’s order to segregate any ballots returned by individuals on the list and to withhold counting them until their citizenship is verified. California has pushed back, arguing that the federal government has not demonstrated the reliability of its data and that the state already requires voters to be U.S. citizens.
The matter is now a court battle over whether those ballots can be set aside before the Nov. 3 election.

title: Chicago students pray for Pope Leo XIV and send care package to Rome
text:
Chicago students pray for Pope Leo XIV and send care package to Rome
A group of young students in Chicago gathered Wednesday to pray for Pope Leo XIV and send love and hometown support his way.
Students at Our Lady of Mount Carmel Academy prayed and sent messages of love and support to the pope after learning of his surgery and lung cancer diagnosis, WLS reports.
The students, some of whom met the pontiff at the Vatican last year, belong to “Team 14,” a student organization named for Pope Leo XIV.
They made the care package together, including a White Sox tie blanket and get-well cards.
“It feels really nice to wish him well because he's like a close friend, and I was really sad when I heard he was sick,” Ines Martins, a sixth-grade student, told WLS' Lissette Nuñez.
“I was a little bit nervous for Pope Leo because I've met him, and he has a big role, and I want him to stay healthy,” eighth-grader Lucas Knudsen said.
Students also shared personalized notes, including messages that asked the pope to feel better and said the school is praying for him and his doctors.
School officials said they will send the gifts to the hospital in Rome where the pope is receiving care.
“It’s important to us to model for our students how we can live our faith in small ways, and sometimes just accompanying someone through prayer and a small action can be really impactful in hard times,” Allison Foerster said.
