title: Your voice in elections shapes Maine’s future
text:
The first election that really captured my attention came before I was old enough to vote. I knew I wouldn’t turn 18 in time, but I wanted to participate. So I organized a voter registration drive at my high school and helped people get to the polls. I couldn’t cast my own ballot yet, but I could help others make their voices heard. That experience taught me that we all have a role in shaping our communities and helping a neighbor participate matters too. It also inspired me to run for office, because I saw how much it matters to have someone who listens to you in the room where decisions are being made, and voting is how we choose who takes that seat.
Earlier this year, I traveled to Normandy to study D-Day and the sacrifices made by those who fought there. Learning more about their courage really brought home how fortunate we are to have a say in our government, and how much others have sacrificed to defend that freedom.
The right to vote for the vast majority of Americans was hard won over centuries. Generations of people before us organized, marched, and challenged exclusion so more people could participate in our democracy. Whenever we cast a ballot and use our voice to shape the world we want to live in, we honor that work and take responsibility for the future we share. Each of us brings our own experiences, concerns, and hopes to the ballot box. When Mainers show up to the polls, we are thinking about our children’s schools, whether we can afford to stay in our hometown, or how to care for an aging parent. Voting is an essential right that gives us a voice in the intimate decisions that affect our day-to-day lives.
Here in Maine, civic engagement is the root of who we are. We believe deeply in local control, we show up at town meetings, volunteer for local organizations, ask the hard questions of our elected officials, and always look out for our neighbors. Maine is consistently a national leader in voter turnout, and our incredible election laws help people participate through options like no-excuse absentee voting.
With Election Day coming up on Tuesday, Nov. 3, now is a good time to make your voting plan.
If you plan to vote in person on Election Day, make sure you know where to go. The Secretary of State’s voting place report for the general election lists polling locations and opening times by municipality. Check your location ahead of time, especially if you have moved since the last election, and contact your town or city clerk if you have questions.
You can also vote absentee without giving a reason. Whether you have a busy work schedule, caregiving responsibilities, travel plans, or simply prefer to vote ahead of time, this option is available to you. You can request a ballot through Maine’s online absentee ballot service or contact your municipal clerk. You can also vote absentee in person at your clerk’s office.
The deadline to request an absentee ballot or vote absentee in person without an excuse is close of business on Thursday, Oct. 29. Your completed ballot must be received by your municipal clerk by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3. A postmark by that date is not enough, so be sure to allow plenty of time if you plan to return your ballot by mail.
If you are eligible but have not registered, you can still register in person through Election Day. First-time registrants should bring proof of identity and residency. Your municipal clerk can explain what you need and walk you through the process.
A voting plan is as simple as deciding when you will vote, knowing where you will go, and how you will get there. Set aside time to learn about the candidates and questions on your ballot. Check in with friends or neighbors who might need help finding information or getting to the polls.
I also would be remiss if I didn’t thank our incredible municipal clerks, election workers, and volunteers. Their careful work on the frontlines of democracy makes it possible for neighbors across Maine to cast their ballots and have their voices heard.
We all have hopes for the future that get us out of bed in the morning, worries that keep us up at night, and people we want a better future for. For all of those reasons, make a plan, cast your ballot, and help shape what comes next for our communities.
You don’t have to leave your hopes and worries at the door, bring them to the polls! They’re exactly why your voice belongs. Your voice matters, so let it be heard!
Mattie Daughtry represents State Senate District 23, Brunswick, Chebeague Island, Freeport, Harpswell, Pownal, and part of Yarmouth in the Maine Senate. She also serves as Maine’s Senate President. She can be reached at [email protected] or 207-287-1515.

title: Your employees may be caregivers. Here’s how your business can support them.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When someone is preparing to welcome a child, there’s often time to plan, at home and at work. Managers can adjust schedules, colleagues can prepare for an absence and there’s often a party. Everyone generally understands that their co-worker’s life is about to change.
But what happens when an employee’s mother falls and can no longer live independently? Or when a spouse develops dementia and needs help with everyday activities?
For many working Mainers, caring for an older loved one begins unexpectedly, and there’s certainly no party at work to mark the change.
“In general, people don’t plan for this part of life,” said Megan Walton, CEO of AgeMaine, formerly Southern Maine Agency on Aging. “With elder care, or caring for an adult loved one, it often happens suddenly, and after a moment of crisis.”
AgeMaine has long advocated for stronger support systems for family caregivers, including Maine’s Paid Family and Medical Leave program (PFML), which provides qualifying workers with paid time away from their jobs to care for themselves or loved ones. AgeMaine is also piloting a dementia respite care program for rural communities and administers the state’s Veteran-Directed Care program.
But Walton and AgeMaine believe employers can do more to support working caregivers before they reach a crisis point.
Maine has the oldest average population in the country, and as people remain in the workforce longer, more employers are navigating the intersection of work and family caregiving. Yet many people shouldering those responsibilities may not identify themselves as caregivers, much less discuss their situations with an employer.
Walton said many caregivers hesitate to disclose their role — according to national research, only 49% say their supervisor knows they are a caregiver. That means businesses may have employees managing significant responsibilities outside work without knowing what support they need.
Start by knowing your employees
Supporting caregivers doesn’t necessarily require a new benefits package or major financial investment. According to Walton, one of the most effective things managers can do is simply get to know their teams.
“Don’t just ask the question of, ‘Do you have kids? Do you have a partner?’” Walton suggested. “There are all types of working people who are caring for older adults or loved ones, or helping with transportation, medications or household tasks.”
Creating an environment where employees feel comfortable discussing those responsibilities can help employers anticipate challenges rather than respond only when a crisis occurs.
Make flexibility part of workplace culture
An employee may need to leave early for a parent’s medical appointment, work remotely because a paid caregiver called out sick or adjust their schedule while visiting potential assisted living facilities.
Walton encourages employers to approach those requests with the same understanding they might offer an employee managing a personal health condition or caring for a child. Family caregivers are often very effective at handling multiple responsibilities, she said, “so give them the benefit of the doubt.”
That flexibility can also be an employee retention strategy. Rather than losing an experienced worker who cannot maintain a traditional schedule, employers may be able to adjust hours, duties or other expectations to help that person succeed.
Beyond accommodating individual requests, employers can train managers to recognize signs of stress, understand PFML or other leave benefits and respond compassionately when employees need support or time away.
Peer connections matter, too. AgeMaine offers caregiver support groups, and Walton said she recently learned of a local employer establishing an employee resource group specifically for family caregivers.
Connect employees with trusted resources
Smaller employers don’t need to become experts in Medicare, dementia care or long-term care planning. They do, however, benefit from knowing where to send employees who need guidance.
That’s part of the thinking behind the new name AgeMaine.
After years of serving older adults, people with disabilities and caregivers under the name Southern Maine Agency on Aging, the organization has introduced a new identity intended to make its services easier to understand and access.
“For us, AgeMaine simplifies the message,” Walton said, explaining that the organization wants to be a “first stop” for people navigating aging, caregiving, Medicare enrollment and the services available to help.
Make room for caregivers, literally
AgeMaine is putting its philosophy of flexibility into practice at the upcoming Maine Family Caregiver Summit by offering on-site respite care for attendees’ loved ones.
“We believe that this is soon going to be the norm,” Walton said, comparing the programming to child care at conferences and community events.
By providing trained staff and engaging activities such as music, puzzles and crafts, AgeMaine is removing a major barrier for caregivers, who can become socially and professionally isolated as they lose free time.
For Walton and the event organizers, the service also makes a larger point: If employers and community organizations want caregivers to participate, they need to recognize the responsibilities those caregivers cannot simply leave at home.
“We’re actually living so much longer than we ever did before, and this is a gift,” Walton said. “It means we need to kind of rearrange our own systems or places of employment or the ways we’ve been doing things for years.”
For Maine businesses, that work can start with a conversation, a little flexibility and a willingness to think differently about what employees need to succeed.
AgeMaine helps older adults, people with disabilities and family caregivers navigate services and resources throughout York and Cumberland counties. Visit agemaine.org, call 207.396.6500 or email [email protected]. They’ll listen, talk through your options, and help you find a place to start.
Aging in Maine: Caregiving
Sunday, Oct. 18: Read “Aging in Maine: Caregiving,” a special publication from the newsrooms of the Maine Trust for Local News, focused on the needs of current and soon-to-be caregivers.
Friday, Oct. 23: Attend the Maine Family Caregiver Summit. A morning session focuses on employers supporting caregivers on their team, and the afternoon session offers caregivers practical tips and direct connections to resources and experts.

title: Police say at least 2 were hospitalized after shooting at elementary school, and the shooter is dead
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — At least two people were injured Thursday in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, and the attacker was shot and killed, authorities said.
Bend police spokesperson Sheila Miller said two people were transported to a hospital. The conditions of those injured were not immediately known, as well as whether there were additional casualties.
“We don’t have a number at this point. We know children are among the victims,” Miller said during a media briefing.
Authorities received a call about a shot fired into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary at 12:59 p.m. and arrived on scene within minutes. Further 911 calls came from inside the school, she said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school soon after police arrived, she said.
It was not immediately clear if it was by police, a bystander or self-inflicted.
Spokespeople for the city and police department did not immediately return emails seeking comment from The Associated Press.
Silver Rail Elementary was under lockdown, the Bend-La Pine school district wrote on Facebook.
“We’re in the process at this time of going room by room and evacuating each of the people who are in that school. … This is the kind of thing we never want to see happen in Bend. It’s devastating,” Miller said, pausing to control her emotions.
The school in Bend, Oregon, which is more than 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Portland, had 459 enrolled students as of last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. The school serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade.

title: ICE vehicle struck during Maine traffic stop; toddler taken to hospital
text:
ICE vehicle struck during Sanford traffic stop; toddler taken to hospital, police say
Person who was being detained reportedly backed their vehicle into ICE vehicle | 1-year-old who was in detainee's vehicle taken to hospital for medical evaluation
ICE vehicle struck during Sanford traffic stop; toddler taken to hospital, police say
Person who was being detained reportedly backed their vehicle into ICE vehicle | 1-year-old who was in detainee's vehicle taken to hospital for medical evaluation
A man who was stopped by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Sanford stands accused of backing into an ICE vehicle with a 1-year-old passenger inside his SUV, according to authorities.
The Sanford Police Department said officers responded to Brook Street, near the High Street intersection, shortly before 9:20 a.m. Thursday at the request of ICE agents, who had a person in custody.
In a statement shared with Maine's Total Coverage on Friday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said that ICE arrested Manucho Nseka on Thursday during a targeted enforcement operation.
DHS said that Nseka, who is originally from Angola, illegally entered the United States in March 2024 through the southern border and was arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Nseka was released from custody at that time but last month, on Sept. 9, an immigration judge issued Nseka a final order of removal because he failed to show up to his mandatory immigration proceedings.
Sanford police said that ICE agents told officers that they had made a traffic stop and positioned one of their vehicles in front of Nseka's vehicle and another ICE vehicle behind. The ICE agents reported that Nseka had put his vehicle in reverse and struck the ICE vehicle that was positioned behind him.
A bird feeder camera at a Brook Street home captured footage of the crash. The video, which was shared with Maine's Total Coverage, shows a black SUV driving on Brook Street toward High Street when a silver vehicle with flashing lights approaches the SUV from the front and cuts it off. The footage then shows the SUV begin to back up as another vehicle approaches from behind and then crash into that approaching vehicle while in reverse. Watch the footage in the video player embedded below.
"I noticed a Black male being arrested, yelling, being preceded to put in the car, continuing to — what seemed like — put up a little bit of a fight, continuing to yell," said witness Sarah Vachon.
Sanford police officers, along with emergency medical personnel from the Sanford Fire Department, responded to the scene after learning that a 1-year-old child was inside Nseka's vehicle. ICE agents told police that the toddler was not properly secured in a child safety seat. Sanford police said that out of an abundance of caution, the 1-year-old was taken to Southern Maine Health Care to be medically evaluated.
Witnesses told Maine's Total Coverage reporter Jim Keithley that Nseka could be heard yelling: "My baby. My baby." The witnesses said Nseka was so distraught that he passed out.
"It all seemed really calm, cool and collected from all the professionals, and the only person I saw yelling was the man being arrested," Vachon said.
During the incident, Sanford police officers also learned that two of Nseka's other children, ages 2 and 9, had been left inside a nearby home without adult supervision. The Sanford Police Department then contacted the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), which responded to the home to ensure the children's safety and welfare.
"The Sanford Police Department's involvement in this incident was limited to responding to a request for assistance, addressing immediate public safety concerns, and ensuring the safety and welfare of the children involved," Sanford police said in a news release shared on Facebook. "The federal enforcement action was conducted by ICE."
In July, a new law that restricts local law enforcement's collaboration with federal immigration authorities went into effect in Maine. LD 1971 was passed by both chambers of the Maine Legislature in June 2025, but Gov. Janet Mills decided to hold the bill, which became law without her signature in January.
DHS said Nseka will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the country. It is unclear where Nseka is being held as of Friday morning, as a search in ICE's Online Detainee Locator System did not yield any results.
As of Friday morning, it is unclear if the toddler is still in the hospital or if Nseka's other children are in DHHS custody.

title: Susan Collins is criticizing a Troy Jackson mortgage. She did something similar.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For about eight months in 2004, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins was bound by two mortgages that each named a different house as her principal residence, one in Washington and one in Bangor.
Collins, a Republican seeking a sixth term, has used a similar arrangement as a line of attack against her Democratic opponent, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson. At their Oct. 6 debate, she hit Jackson over the federally backed mortgage on an Augusta house that listed it as his primary home while he represented Allagash in the Maine Senate.
“How can he have a primary residence in Allagash for which he was reimbursed $160,000 for travel back and forth, and have a primary residence in Augusta?” Collins said, citing a figure for legislative travel reimbursements from 2019 to 2023 reported by The Maine Wire, the conservative media arm of the Maine Policy Institute.
Collins has made the same kind of claims about her homes in Maine and Washington, according to records reviewed by the Bangor Daily News. She twice signed mortgage documents pledging to use a Washington rowhouse as her principal residence while she owned a home in Bangor, where she has claimed Maine’s homestead exemption.
In 2004, she went a step further. Four months after refinancing the Washington house, she told a Bangor bank that a new house there would be her principal residence, while her D.C. pledge was still in effect.
The records do not show that Collins broke the law. But they show she made the same kind of pledge she and her allies are criticizing Jackson for as they joust in the final weeks of a toss-up race that could help decide control of the U.S. Senate. The incumbent is leaning on her seniority to stave off national Democrats in a state tilting their way.
The BDN asked Collins’ campaign whether her loans were priced as primary-residence mortgages and whether she claimed the federal tax break on home-sale profits when she sold the rowhouse in 2010. The campaign did not directly answer either question.
Collins spokesperson Blake Kernen said Jackson’s loan was different because it was backed by the Federal Housing Administration, which requires the home to be the borrower’s primary residence. Kernen described the program as meant for first-time and low-income buyers, but FHA loans have no income limits and are not restricted to first-time buyers.
“By contrast, Senator Collins used conventional loans which aren’t just meant for primary homes,” Kernen said. “She does not claim a D.C. homestead exemption, and she has accurately claimed her house in Maine as her primary residence.”
Tax records confirm Collins does not claim Washington’s homestead property tax break on her townhouse there. But neither Collins nor her campaign provided tax records or a letter from her accountant after BDN requests. Jackson’s campaign provided a letter from his accountant saying he did not claim a home-sale tax break when he sold the Augusta house in 2021.
Unlike Collins in 2004, Jackson was not bound by two principal-residence pledges at once. The one-year requirement on his Allagash mortgage had expired in 2016, before he bought the Augusta house.
The standard forms Collins signed require buyers to live in the house as their principal residence for at least a year, unless the lender agrees otherwise in writing. Kernen said Collins relied on professionals who were aware of her Senate role when she signed the documents.
Conventional loans can be used for second homes, but the borrower’s pledge stays in place unless the lender attaches a page called a “second home rider.” Mortgages on a home the buyer lives in can often cost less because lenders see them as less risky.
Collins first agreed to the terms when she bought the Capitol Hill rowhouse in 2000. Her Bank of America mortgage listed her address as Bangor, but it required her to live primarily in the Washington house.
The senator has used the second-home option on other properties, including an Enfield camp she bought in 2000 and Capitol Hill townhouse she bought with Tom Daffron, now her husband, in December 2010.
A single homeowner can avoid federal taxes on up to $250,000 in profit from selling a primary residence, but only if they lived there for at least two of the five years before the sale. Federal rules allow only one primary residence at a time.
Collins sold the rowhouse for $511,000 in November 2010 after buying it for $240,000 about 10 years earlier. Her interest rates and tax returns are not public, so it is not clear whether either benefit applied to her.
Jackson’s Augusta home was central to a 2023 complaint to the Maine Ethics Commission. He told the commission he used the house as “a temporary place to stay” and that he still voted and claimed the homestead exemption in Allagash. Yet his Augusta mortgage listed the house as his primary one. Commissioners voted 5-0 against an investigation after Jackson’s lawyer noted federal mortgage residency requirements differed from state ones.
The issue has still found its way into attack ads, including one from the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results PAC. It spent nearly $2.4 million to run it for more than two months, ending earlier this week, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
“Troy Jackson: falsifying documents, ripping off taxpayers, and a bully we can’t trust,” it closes.

title: 2 accused of selling crack and fentanyl in Bangor
text:
The Maine Drug Enforcement Agency and Bangor police have arrested two people in Bangor for allegedly trafficking crack cocaine and fentanyl.
State and local agents executed a search warrant Thursday morning at 73 First St. based on a month-long investigation into drug trafficking there, which included undercover purchases, according to the MDEA.
Agents found and seized 65 grams of cocaine base (crack), 9.8 grams of fentanyl and $4,630 in suspected drug proceeds, according to the agency, who valued the drugs at $7,000.
Morgan McNealy, 23, of Bangor, and Anthony Diaz, 21, of Malden, Massachusetts, were arrested without incident at the residence and taken to Penobscot County Jail, the agency said.
McNeally was charged with two counts of Class A aggravated trafficking Schedule W drugs. Diaz was charged with three counts of Class A aggravated trafficking Schedule W drugs.
The MDEA said it expects more arrests and charges based on the investigation.

title: Frustrated with Trump, voters overwhelmingly want change in Washington, an AP-NORC poll finds
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A strong majority of voters believe that President Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad, and they want major change in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a new AP-NORC poll that raises serious warning signs for the Republican Party at a critical moment.
The survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, conducted less than four weeks before Election Day, finds that registered voters who identify as Democrats are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about casting a ballot. More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans.
The Democratic advantage is small in some cases, but, taken together, the findings paint a challenging picture for Republicans, who are clinging to control of Congress under the weight of an unpopular war with Iran and surging prices at home.
About 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump — like immigration or crime — are lower priorities.
“The world is going backwards. We can barely afford anything,” said Diana Walker, a 65-year-old Democrat from Decatur, Georgia. “Everybody’s down. I don’t care if you’re a Democrat or Republican, we’re all catching hell.”
Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans
Less than a month before the final midterm votes are cast, the poll finds that Democratic voters are more motivated to vote.
Overall, about two-thirds of registered voters say it’s “extremely” important to vote in the upcoming election, while about 2 in 10 say it’s “very” important.
But about three-quarters of Democratic voters say that voting in this November’s midterm elections is “extremely” important, compared with roughly 6 in 10 Republicans.
Ryan Longbrake, a 52-year-old Democrat from Columbus, Ohio who works in technology marketing, said he’s especially excited about casting his ballot, and he’s already taken steps to ensure that his wife and two college-age daughters will vote as well.
“I believe that there is change on the horizon and there is an excitement within our party,” he said, pointing to Democrats’ momentum in Ohio’s elections for governor and U.S. Senate. The party is also investing resources in Republican-leaning states, like Iowa and Kansas, where the political environment has put Democratic candidates on friendlier footing.
Republicans have controlled Congress for the past two years, but about half of registered voters now say they’d prefer to see the Democratic Party control the House or the Senate. A smaller percentage, roughly 4 in 10, say they want the Republican Party to control each chamber, while 15% are undecided.
The vast majority of voters want change
One thing is crystal clear on the eve of the 2026 midterms: Voters want change.
About half of voters say they want “substantial change,” and roughly 3 in 10 want “complete and total upheaval” in the way the country is run.
Democrats and independents are much likelier than Republicans to want a full overhaul of the country’s direction. But even Republican voters are still looking for something different. Slightly fewer than half, 45%, want substantial change, while 13% want upheaval.
“I’m kind of tired of sending people there and nothing gets done,” said Krista Kohles, a 70-year-old Republican from near Davey, Nebraska. “Nothing’s changing.”
Trump’s numbers on key issues are weak
Voters are deeply frustrated with Trump and his leadership on the issues they say matter most.
Only about one-third of registered voters overall have a “very” or “somewhat” favorable view of the Republican president, and a similar share approve of his performance as president.
Voters continue to be frustrated by the high cost of living, an issue that Trump vowed to address before winning a second term in the White House.
Nearly two years after his successful election, about 8 in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, in line with a September AP-NORC poll. About three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy.
Even among Republican voters, only 44% approve of Trump’s performance on the cost of living, while 54% approve of his leadership on the economy. That’s a sharp contrast with other issues, like crime, on which Republican approval is much higher.
There are cracks in Trump’s Republican base on other issues, too. Just 69% of Republican voters support Trump on foreign policy as the war in Iran stretches into its eighth month, despite his promises that it would only last four or five weeks.
DonnaJean Weber, a 72-year-old Republican from Manistee, Michigan, says she will continue to support Republican candidates this fall, but she’s not happy with the state of the economy under Trump’s leadership.
“Everything’s going up,” she said, pointing to the impact of the war with Iran, among other Trump decisions. “I don’t agree with him fully on all of these tariffs, either. It’s making this country look bad.”
The economy and the cost of living are high priorities for voters on both sides of the aisle. The survey found that the vast majority of Republican and Democratic voters say both issues are among the most important for the upcoming election.
Voters aren’t any higher on one of Trump’s potential successors in the next presidential election, Vice President JD Vance: About half have a “somewhat” or “very” negative view of Vance, compared with about one-third who have a positive opinion.
Enthusiasm for the Democrats isn’t overwhelming
Trump’s struggles do not mean that voters are particularly excited about the direction of the Democratic Party.
Overall, about 4 in 10 voters have a “very” or “somewhat” favorable view of the Democrats, while about half view the party unfavorably. That’s roughly similar to views of the GOP, although about 6 in 10 voters view the Republicans unfavorably.
Democratic and Republican voters are equally enthusiastic about their own side, with about 8 in 10 saying they have a favorable view of their own party.
But the critical bloc of voters who identify as independents is much more likely to have a negative view of the Republicans than of the Democrats. About two-thirds of independent voters view the GOP negatively, compared with about 4 in 10 who view Democrats negatively.
Michael Russo, a 51-year-old Texas voter who is not registered with either party, described the state of the country under Republican control as “a nightmare.”
Does he want Republicans to maintain control of Congress? “No, I want them in prison — several of them,” he said. But he’s not thrilled with the Democratic Party, either.
“I’m not confident they’re going to do anything if they get into power,” Russo said.
___
Peoples reported from New York.
___
The AP-NORC poll of 1,119 adults, including 925 registered voters, was conducted Oct. 8-12 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 3.9 percentage points, and the margin of error for registered voters is plus or minus 4.2 percentage points.

title: Norridgewock man sentenced to 45 years for murder of girlfriend's son
Mid-Coast Energy Donates Thousands to Improve Firefighter Training and Equipment
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Tuesday, Oct. 7, Mid-Coast Energy Systems presented a $42,000 check to the Massasoit Engine Co., of Damariscotta to assist in the purchase of new fire equipment, training resources, and a countywide personnel accountability system.
The donation comes after Mid-Coast Energy Systems Vice President Eric Morgner said that he and his father, Bill Morgner, had been talking about the company’s 50th anniversary for a couple of years and a part of their mission is to donate money to community partners.
“Fifty years in business all in Damariscotta, we owe everything to the community that has supported us,” Eric Morgner said.
Bill Morgner went on to contact Damariscotta Fire Chief John Roberts for a wish list for the Massasoit Engine Co., which functions as the Damariscotta Fire Department. Eric Morgner said the two were not in the position to pick which items were more necessary for the department, so they decided to fund them all.
Damariscotta Fire Chief John Roberts said funding will help with the department’s efficiency and that the donation is “incredibly generous.”
“I was very surprised when Bill and Eric from Mid-Coast wanted to fund the entire list,
Roberts said. “We tried to provide a list of items that would allow for them to choose which projects best lined up with their goals with the donation.”
With the funding, Roberts said the department will be able to purchase equipment that will enhance its ability to respond to emergencies not only in Damariscotta, but the surrounding areas. One definite purchase is a forcible entry training prop, which is used to allowed firefighters to train on several methods on gaining entry to a structure as quickly as possible.
The funds will also be used to purchase a Blitzfire portable monitor, which extends the range of water flow while fighting fires.
On July 31, Chasse Marine Co. in Damariscotta experienced an explosion and fire that brought in five other departments to help put it out. During the event, Roberts said responders found that Damariscotta department’s ability to put large quantities of water on fires was limited. Portable monitors from other departments were used to put the fire out.
Roberts said the department also hoped to buy a chart plotter or GPS for navigating rescue boat searches. A plotter with sonar will provide better information about what is under the surface and assist in navigating different waterways, Roberts said.
In regard to personnel accountability, Roberts said it is a “critical component” for ensuring the safety of all first responders at any emergency. Roberts called the current system in place “cumbersome” and presents challenges with noting who is on scene doing what.
Regional accountability will create a system where the department knows what people and resources are at each and every emergency scene. The transition will include going to a passport system that puts two tag holders in each truck. The system will also be vital in mutual aid efforts to track who is on scene and when.
“Personnel accountability is a critical task in emergencies, to make sure all people and units responding are known, and to have the ability to perform a check that everyone is safe in cases where the situation degrades,” Roberts said. “The current system in the county has several issues that reduce the effectiveness of the system and does not offer the same situational awareness that the proposed passport system will.”
As Mid-Coast Energy continues to donate to the surrounding community, Eric Morgner said the business is built on the idea of helping people.
“It’s a team effort in a small town and we are just trying to help out,” Eric Morgner said.

title: Troy Jackson raises millions more than Susan Collins, but trails her in money race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign raised $3.9 million in the third quarter of 2026 — a figure that paled in comparison to the $20.4 million raised by her opponent, Troy Jackson.
But Republicans are still badly outspending Democrats on the Senate race overall. So far, Republican-aligned groups have spent or reserved $151.5 million on ads, compared to $110.7 million by Democrat-aligned groups, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
Collins’ campaign spent almost $11 million from July through September, Thursday’s quarterly finance report showed.
Jackson released detailed campaign finance numbers at 6:15 p.m. Thursday, despite promising to do so by Wednesday morning. His upstart campaign raked in more than $19.4 million in donations and about $1 million from other groups.
Collins is running to win a sixth term in the U.S. Senate and, as the lone Republican in Congress from New England, is facing political headwinds in the final three weeks of the campaign. Polling has repeatedly shown Jackson ahead or within the margin of error.
It’s going to be a close race. Here’s how Collins’ and Jackson’s camps used their money — and raised it, in the campaign’s crucial months.
COLLINS’ SPENDING
Collins’ biggest area of spending, unsurprisingly, was advertising. About 85% of the campaign’s $10.8 million spent between July and the end of September was on advertising.
The campaign spent nearly $6.5 million on media buys, the report shows, almost entirely through Mentzer Media Services, which is based in Towson, Maryland. Collins’ team also spent more than $2.8 million on digital fundraising and advertising through the Arlington, Virginia-based consulting firm Targeted Victory.
Using out-of-state consultants to buy media and place advertisements is par for the course. Prior to these new three-month reports being filed Thursday, less than 4% of the money in Maine’s federal races was being spent in this state, and the overwhelming majority of it was going toward advertising.
According to media tracker AdImpact, Collins’ campaign has spent or reserved space for almost $12.4 million in advertising. The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Collins’ campaign have bought an additional $2.6 million in advertising and a Collins joint fundraising committee has about $1.6 million lined up.
But it’s the outside money — from political action committees, or PACs — that is dominating Maine’s airwaves. Collins is a bigger beneficiary than her opponent, Jackson, AdImpact’s figures show.
JACKSON’S SPENDING
Jackson’s campaign spent about $16.4 million during its first quarter, and still had almost $4 million in cash at the end of the period.
About three-quarters of the campaign’s spending was on advertising, mostly to Chevy Chase, Maryland-based TKO Buying LLC and the Washington D.C. firm Sage Media Planning & Placement, Inc.
Jackson’s campaign has bought or reserved $20.4 million in advertisements, according to AdImpact. Again, though, Democrats are being heavily out-spent on advertising in the race, to the tune of about $40 million.
The second-largest expense for Jackson’s campaign was “list acquisition” — or, in other words, buying donor information. The campaign spent $1.5 million for that purpose.
COLLINS’ FUNDRAISING
The Collins campaign had $11 million on hand at the start of this filing period, in July. Most of that was spent down, but Collins also brought in an additional $3.9 million.
Collins’ most notable donor in this report cycle was George W. Bush, the former Republican president who has long summered in Kennebunkport. Bush gave $3,500 on Aug. 26, the report shows.
Collins also received $3,500, the maximum for individual donors, from U.S. Secretary of Education and wrestling executive Linda McMahon. Thomas Klingenstein, the conservative megadonor who helped bankroll a political committee for failed gubernatorial candidate Garrett Mason, also gave the personal max to Collins’s campaign.
Almost all of Collins’ fundraising came from individuals — about $3.7 million. But almost all of those individual contributions came from out-of-state. Among Collins’ donations from individuals, two-thirds were less than $100.
Only 11% of the money from individual donors during this three-month period came from Maine. Florida, Texas, California and New York donors gave more than three times what Collins’ Maine donors gave — though some of those funds were subject to refund.
JACKSON’S FUNDRAISING
Jackson sprinted out of the gate and, despite his late start, raised well over $20 million in his first quarter.
Almost all of that was from individual donors. Jackson’s campaign said they raised money from nearly 200,000 individual donors, including from every Maine county. About 95% of the contributions were $100 or less, the campaign said.
Dan Kleban, Jackson’s opponent, briefly, for the nomination after Graham Platner dropped out, donated $3,500. Jordan Wood, another candidate in that short secondary race, donated the personal maximum.
Jackson, a union supporter, was also backed by several union PACs with tens of thousands in donations.

title: CMMC warned by federal government about patient safety violations
text:
Central Maine Medical Center warned by federal government about patient safety violations
The federal government is warning Central Maine Medical Center (CMMC) about patient safety violations, telling the Lewiston hospital to correct a slew of issues or risk losing its ability to participate in Medicare.
A letter sent by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to the hospital's CEO, Allen Stefanek, states that the State of Maine Survey and Certification Unit completed a complaint investigation survey at CMMC on Aug. 26.
Inspectors found conditions at the hospital that, at one point, posed an immediate threat to patient health and safety. CMS said it found that the conditions no longer posed an immediate jeopardy to the health and safety of patients, but substantial noncompliance remains with infection prevention, the hospital's physical environment and leadership oversight.
"This deficiency has been determined to be of such character as to substantially limit the hospital's capacity to furnish adequate care and/or as to adversely affect the health and safety of patients," a CMS nurse consultant said in the letter. "We have determined that Central Maine Medical Center is no longer deemed to meet the Medicare Conditions of Participation and will be subject to the federal requirements applied to unaccredited hospitals. Consequently, Central Maine Medical Center is now under the jurisdiction of the State Survey Agency."
CMS said the finding that the hospital is not in compliance with the conditions of participation does not affect the facility's accreditation, its Medicare payments or its current status as a participating supplier of hospital services in the Medicare program. CMMC, however, is now required to submit an acceptable correction plan regarding the deficiencies. The federal government said that it will continue the state agency's survey jurisdiction after the approved correction plan has been implemented, and CMS has found that all conditions for participation have been met.
In the letter, CMS warned the hospital that if it fails to achieve compliance by Jan. 6, 2027, the federal government may begin administrative steps to terminate CMMC's Medicare agreement.

title: Spruce Mountain schools update meals, staffing and recipes
text:
JAY — Regional School Unit 73 is updating its school nutrition operations, including standardizing recipes, introducing employee evaluations and working to fill a kitchen management vacancy, while two schools have not qualified for a federal fresh fruit and vegetable program.
Sharon Searles, the district’s food service director, told the board of directors Oct. 8 that only Spruce Mountain Primary School in Livermore qualified for the Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program. Spruce Mountain Elementary School and Spruce Mountain Middle School, both in Jay, did not qualify.
Searles said the state would notify the district if additional funding became available.
The department also is developing standardized recipes to ensure consistency across school kitchens following the departure of employees who previously prepared meals.
“The state requires that we have standardized recipes,” Searles said. “So we need to have recipes so that everybody’s doing it the same way.”
Searles reported that written job procedures have been completed and posted in all district kitchens, allowing employees filling in for absent coworkers to follow established routines.
She has also developed staff evaluation forms and plans to begin individual evaluations.
The department is working to replace a kitchen manager who left for another job. Searles said she had interviewed a candidate and hoped to have a replacement hired within a few weeks.
Meanwhile, the district has begun preparing muffins for students at Spruce Mountain Primary School.
Searles reported that 243 students received pumpkin chocolate chip muffins during the first offering, followed by double chocolate chip muffins the following week.
She said the department plans to continue providing the muffins every other week as part of its school food service operations.
RSU 73 also includes Livermore Falls.

title: Hallowell voting location in question beyond 2026
text:
HALLOWELL — Residents may no longer be able to vote at Hall-Dale Elementary School following the upcoming November election.
Regional School Unit 2 Superintendent Rick Amero and the board of directors told city officials in June last year that Hall-Dale Elementary School can no longer be used as a voting location. The decision was made out of concerns related to safety, parking and traffic and issues connected with remote learning on voting days.
City Manager Ross McLellan, City Clerk Lisa Gilliam, Amero and Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows met after the board’s decision, and decided the city could continue to use the school’s gymnasium as a voting place, Gilliam said.
In the months after that discussion, the school board independently decided the city could not use the school for voting following the November 2026 election, Gilliam said.
Councilors and members of the public debated a potential location change Tuesday during the City Council meeting, questioning how and where a new voting location would work.
Despite the school board’s decision, the final decision to request a polling location change from the Department of Secretary of State must be voted on by the City Council.
Hallowell residents have voted at Hall-Dale Elementary School since it opened in 2006. About 11% of polling locations in Maine are in schools, Chief Deputy Secretary of State Kate McBrien said at the meeting. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, Hall-Dale students have had remote learning days and are not present at the school on voting day.
State Rep. Daniel Shagoury spoke about his time asschool board chair when the school was built. He referenced the process it took to raise money to fund a larger cafeteria so it could be used for community purposes such as voting.
Prior Hall-Dale’s construction, residents voted in five different polling locations representing each ward, causing confusion as many people were unaware what ward they lived in.
Charlotte Warren, former Hallowell mayor and state representative, also emphasized that Hallowell and Farmingdale residents worked hard to make sure Hall-Dale was large enough to be used as a polling location, a decision she called a “great solution” to the confusion of ward-based voting.
“I hope we consider, what it means, the honor of elections. … We want to keep kids close to that process,” Warren said. “I think the fact that voting happens in a school does matter, and I think we’re a community that gets that, and I hope that we can remember our history and make sure we preserve that as a place for more than just voting, for other things that happen there as well.”
Alice Gifford, a parent of two Hall-Dale students, urged the council to schedule a public hearing before taking any action. Gifford added that moving the polling location would allow Hall-Dale students to return to in-person learning on voting day like the rest of the district, sparing parents the strain of trying to find childcare on remote learning days and maintaining in-school safety for students and staff.
She said the threat of a violent tragedy in the city feels more pressing than it would have 20 years ago, citing the 2023 Lewiston mass shooting and increasing political polarization.
“A new location could serve the needs of all of our community members, remain accessible to our most vulnerable citizens, keep our youngest citizens safe and restore equity for the 300 students and their working families … who are not in school or able to work due to lack of childcare options two to three days every year on election days,” Gifford said.
If a city or town requests a polling location change, the Secretary of State’s office would have to review the proposed alternate location to ensure it met requirements regarding space, parking and accessibility, McBrien said. If there is not an adequate alternate location, the office would have to reject the request. They can also approve locations on a temporary basis, allowing use for one year to see how it goes before reevaluating.
The school board and superintendent proposed the RSU 2 central office on Reed Street as a potential new location.
In a letter to the council, McLellan said he, Gilliam and Deputy Clerk Dan Kelley toured the location with Amero and Kelleen Longfellow, director of finance for RSU 2. McLellan said the building might meet the minimum standards for a voting location, but limited space and access would make it an inadequate option.
Councilors voted unanimously to have McLellan meet with Superintendent Amero to discuss the matter further before any action like a public forum is decided.

title: Maine man who killed his girlfriend's son to be sentenced for murder
text:
Maine man who killed his girlfriend's son sentenced to 45 years in prison for murder
A Norridgewock man who was convicted of murdering his girlfriend's son in March 2025 was sentenced to 45 years in prison on Thursday.
In August, it took a jury just 40 minutes to find Daniel Markey, 60, guilty of murder and decide that he did not act in self-defense.
Christopher Nickerson, 38, was shot four times.
Markey claimed that he shot Nickerson because Nickerson attacked him and was beating him.
On March 1, 2025, police were called to a home on River Road in Norridgewock just before 9 a.m. State Police were called about half an hour later to help investigate a shooting.
Investigators say Nickerson had been staying at the home and that the home was owned by Markey and Nickerson's mother, Kathleen Nickerson, who was Markey's girlfriend.
Court documents state that Christopher Nickerson had confronted Markey over how he spoke to his mother when Markey shot him.
A letter written by Kathleen Nickerson was read in court on Thursday by a victim advocate. In the letter, Nickerson asked the judge to consider the pain her family has felt since her son's murder.
"It feels as though a part of my identity was taken from me. My hopes, my dreams, and my sense of purpose have all been changed forever," Kathleen Nickerson said in her letter. "What makes this even harder is that this was done by someone who claimed to love me. I cannot understand how someone who said he loved me could do something so horrible."
Markey, who did not appear in court for the sentencing, was also ordered to pay $3,700 to cover the funeral costs.

title: New report: Cause of death of famed bald eagle, Jackie, revealed
text:
Cause of death of beloved bald eagle, Jackie, revealed
Officials have revealed the cause of death of Jackie, the beloved California bald eagle whose life was watched by millions around the world via video livestreams.
The California Department of Fish and Wildlife released the results of the necropsy and additional diagnostic testing, revealing the bald eagle from the Big Bear Valley died from avian influenza complications.
Related video: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie rescued by Los Angeles wildlife officials after fight with other eagles
"Jackie's necropsy confirmed Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) as the primary underlying cause of her decline," Director of Disease Investigations, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Steve Kubiski, said in the report. "In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis."
Jackie was also said to have shown signs of "chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird’s stomach, commonly called the gizzard," the release said. A toxicology screening also detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide, in the liver, as well as persistent environmental contaminants.
Jackie had been nesting in the Big Bear area for years, where she and her partner, Shadow, raised eaglets together. Their nest sat high in a Jeffrey pine tree near Big Bear Lake, more than 7,000 feet above sea level.
Jackie, who died on Aug. 10, 2026, became especially popular for her dedicated parenting, dramatic interactions with Shadow and the challenges she faced protecting eggs and chicks from harsh mountain weather.
Shadow, the release said, remains in Big Bear, California. Wildlife officials said that there is nothing to indicate he or their eaglets, Sandy and Luna, are sick.
"Jackie's story brought unprecedented public attention to bald eagles and the importance of protecting the habitats they depend on," the CDFW said. "Her life and the public's connection to her highlights the powerful role that wildlife can play in connecting people to conservation."

title: 2 women file lawsuit accusing former US Rep. Matt Gaetz of sex trafficking, reports say
text:
(Gray News) — Former Republican congressman Matt Gaetz has been accused of sex trafficking two young women in a new lawsuit filed Thursday in Florida.
Gaetz resigned from Congress in November 2024. The allegations are the latest of a long-running sexual abuse scandal involving Gaetz.
In a statement to The Guardian, Gaetz denied the claims.
“I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” he wrote. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee Report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.”
The lawsuit alleges that Gaetz and two others “coordinated the recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts” from two young women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2. The lawsuit said they were recent high school graduates at the time of the alleged sex trafficking.
The alleged events happened “from 2017 through January 2019,” according to the lawsuit.
According to the Miami Herald, after the lawsuit was filed, Gaetz posted a photo on X in an effort to dox the Jane Does in the lawsuit. He posted a photo of three young women in bikinis, writing, “Jane Doe Strikes Again! Two adult women sued me today alleging they were sex trafficked to the Bahamas. I’m shocked nobody responded to their repeated cries for help, posted to Instagram.”
The Miami Herald said Gaetz admitted to a reporter that he was not sure if the women in the photo were any of the Jane Does in the lawsuit.

title: Former UMaine hockey player Bradly Nadeau called up by NHL’s Hurricanes
text:
Former University of Maine All-Hockey East winger Bradly Nadeau, whose 59 goals over the past two seasons with the Chicago Wolves is the third-most in the American Hockey League, has been called up by the National Hockey League’s Carolina Hurricanes.
The 21-year-old Nadeau had a strong training camp for the reigning Stanley Cup champions, notching two goals and an assist and 11 shots on goal in his three exhibition games. He was sent down due to the Hurricanes’ depth at the forward position.
But three of their top veteran forwards are injured, he was called up earlier this week.
Seth Jarvis is still recovering from off-season shoulder surgery. Captain Jordan Staal is facing a one- or two-month stint on the injured list with a partial calf tear and Taylor Hall suffered an upper-body injury in a game against the Washington Capitals on Tuesday.
Nadeau had one goal in four games with the Wolves.
He had 27 goals and 29 assists in 52 regular season games with the Wolves last season and added seven goals and 10 assists in 21 playoff games. In addition, he spent 12 games with the Hurricanes and scored three goals.
Two seasons ago, he led all AHL rookies in goals with 32 and was second in points with 58. He became just the sixth teenager since 1940 and third in the last 50 years to score at least 30 goals in an AHL season.
“The No. 1 thing is every time you watch him, you know you’ve got the NHL offensive upside and, every game, he’s continuing to add other NHL aspects to his game,” Hurricanes assistant general manager Darren Yorke told NHL.com. “It’s only a matter of time before he’s in the NHL full-time.”
The 5-foot-11, 181-pound Nadeau was a first round draft pick of the Hurricanes in 2023. He was the 30th overall selection.
During his one season at UMaine (2023-24), he registered 19 goals and 27 assists for 46 points in 37 games. He led the team in goals and points, and tied with older brother and linemate Josh Nadeau for the assists lead.
In addition to being chosen to the All-Hockey East second team, the Saint-Francois-de-Madawaska, New Brunswick, native was also picked to the league’s All-Rookie team and selected to the New England Hockey Writers Association’s all-star squad.
The Hurricanes play in Winnipeg on Saturday at 3:30 p.m. and in Calgary on Sunday at 8 p.m.

title: Meet Tow Mater, our Adoptable Pet of the Week
text:
Meet Tow Mater, our Adoptable Pet of the Week in Greater Portland
This week's featured adoptable pet from the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland is Tow Mater, a 9-month-old pup who is the textbook definition of a social butterfly.
Tow Mater loves to meet new people, play with toys and run around the yard, and he is generally up for any adventure.
Matt Blanchard of the Animal Refuge League said Tow Mater is very smart but does have a lot of energy and displays typical puppy tendencies, so Tow Mater will need training and structure to work on things like walking on a leash.
"He's going to be a really good fit for a family that can kind of keep up with that training, that is willing to put the work into him," Blanchard said. "I think, you know, you're going to put a lot of work into this dog, and you're going to get a lot of reward in return."
More information about Tow Mater is available on the Animal Refuge League's website, as long as he is still looking for his forever home.
Anyone who is interested in meeting Tow Mater or other adoptable pets can visit the Animal Refuge League's shelter at 217 Landing Road in Westbrook between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., except on Wednesdays, when the shelter is closed for adoptions.
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland does adoptions on a first-come, first-served basis. On the days the shelter is open, sign-in sheets will be placed on the front door at 9 a.m. to track the order of arrival of adopters who show up early. People who arrive early are asked to remain on the campus once they sign in.
Dog owners who are interested in adopting dogs that are older than 6 months are required to have their dogs meet the adoptable pet before a new pet can be brought home.

title: Medicare open enrollment begins: What to expect for 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Open enrollment for Medicare plans begins Thursday and enrollees will face a slew of changes that go into effect in 2027.
During the enrollment period, which ends Dec. 7, people will have the opportunity to choose between traditional Medicare and privately run Medicare Advantage plans in their area, as well as prescription drug plans. Those changes go into effect on Jan. 1.
Open enrollment also comes as inflation adds pressure on seniors whose healthcare costs have risen and as midterm elections are weeks away. Voters have consistently said that the cost of living is a major concern heading into the elections.
The Medicare enrollment period also comes as the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, which translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
New changes to Medicare coming in 2027 include higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies, and new drug price negotiations.
Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, said the open enrollment period offers enrollees “an opportunity to evaluate the coverage they have and see if there might be better options for them in terms of accessing the care that they need at possibly a lower cost.”
Here are a few of the biggest changes:
Medicare Part D
The cap on annual out-of-pocket expenses for Medicare Part D drugs will increase to $2,400, up from $2,100 in 2026, and the standard deductible will increase from $615 to $700.
The temporary Part D premium subsidy will also end early.
The Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums.
It was initially implemented by former President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024 to lower patients’ Medicare Part D prescription drug costs in response to the effects of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected only modest price increases for most people. CMS did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
David Lipschutz, co-director of the Center for Medicare Advocacy, points out that there could be greater disruptions in coverage for some Medicare enrollees since some Medicare Advantage plans are pulling out of specific geographic areas and scaling back benefits, such as dental coverage, while potentially increasing cost-sharing.
Plans, insurance companies make business decisions about what they’re going to offer the following year, if they’re going to offer anything at all. And by that very nature, it causes disruption to the system. And it looks like this time there’s more disruption than usual.
Drug price negotiations
New Medicare-negotiated prices, part of a Biden-era law that allows the haggling for Medicare, will go into effect for 15 drugs, including weight-loss and diabetes medications Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.
Additionally, Trelegy Ellipta, Xtandi, Pomalyst, Ibrance, Ofev, Linzess, Calquence, Austedo/Austedo XR, Breo Ellipta, Tradjenta, Xifaxan, Vraylar, Janumet/Janumet XR, and Otezla will be covered by Medicare as of Jan. 1.
CMS expects the change to lower prescription drug coverage for people enrolled in Medicare by $685 million in 2027.
AARP’s Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Nancy LeaMond said in a statement that “higher healthcare costs are making it harder for older Americans to afford the care they need.”
“It’s more important than ever to shop around, compare your options, and choose the coverage that’s best for you,” she said.
Other Trump administration promises
Along with the changes, President Donald Trump in recent weeks made a series of promises to Medicare enrollees and retirees.
Last week, Trump said his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person in October to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees — or less than one third of enrollees — pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion.
Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients.
According to the CMS website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October.
Trump also announced recently that roughly 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums.

title: Hoda Kotb to appear on ‘Aging Untold’ in Gray Media partnership
text:
(Gray News) - Gray Media is teaming up with journalist Hoda Kotb and her wellness company Joy 101 to bring new health segments to local newscasts and “Aging Untold” starting in January 2027.
The partnership centers on a weekly feature called “The Doctor’s In with Joy 101.”
The segments will air nationwide inside “Aging Untold” episodes and in Gray Media newscasts to highlight insights about wellness, resilience and intentional living.
Kotb is expected to make several special appearances on the nationally syndicated program.
“The Doctor’s In with Joy 101” is produced by Joy 101 and pairs co-founder Karen Swensen with Dr. Stephanie Moore.
Swensen is an award-winning journalist whose work has appeared on NBC’s TODAY with Hoda and Jenna. Moore is a triple-board-certified cardiologist with a background in heart transplantation who spent more than 20 years on the faculty of Harvard Medical School.
Each week, the two will break down healthy aging and everyday vitality into clear steps families and caregivers can use.
“Partnering with Gray Media allows us to bring trusted, uplifting conversations about health and longevity directly to viewers across the country,” Kotb said. “We want to give ‘Aging Untold’ audiences and local news viewers practical tools that inspire genuine vitality and joy.”
“Aging Untold” is now in its second season. The 30-minute conversation series focuses on answers for older adults and their caregivers, with returning experts “Sam” Cradduck, Amy Cameron O’Rourke, Katherine Ambrose and Dr. Rhea Rogers.
The first season, which debuted in March 2026, reached more than 7 million viewers age 18 and older. The show has since added stations outside Gray markets and is now cleared in nearly 40% of U.S. TV households.
“Our viewers look to ‘Aging Untold’ and our local news teams for honest guidance on issues that touch every household,” said Sandy Breland, Gray’s chief operating officer. “This partnership unites Joy 101’s dynamic wellness insight with Gray’s trusted reporting.”
Viewers can check local listings or visit aginguntold.com for broadcast times and streaming options.
Gray said it will also offer the Joy 101 app and its expert-led resources to participating team members as part of a new workplace wellness effort.

title: Accreditor suspends any new offerings within UMPI’s YourPace program
text:
The University of Maine at Presque Isle can’t offer any new YourPace competency-based programs without accreditor approval, according to the New England Commission of Higher Education.
“We didn’t suspend it,” said commission President Larry Schall. “We suspended any expansion of it — new programs, new locations — until they appear before us in the Spring.”
The news comes after an investigation, launched in April after a Washington Post article criticized the competency-based programs and suggested students were obtaining degrees in weeks rather than years.
The commission asked the University of Maine System to answer questions about YourPace, and was to review the system’s 20-page response, its president, Larry Schall, said earlier this month.
About 8,000 students have come through YourPace since January, and the program accounts for the majority of this fall’s enrollment, UMPI President Ray Rice previously told the Bangor Daily News.
BDN writer Kathleen Phalen Tomaselli contributed to this report.

title: Trump administration sues California over alleged noncitizens on the state's voter rolls
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month’s midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their status can be confirmed.
The lawsuit comes after a top Justice Department official warned California in a letter of possible legal action if the state did not review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan said in a statement that his office received the letter and thumb drive this week, along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.”
The Justice Department’s lawsuit says the federal government sought to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and “California made no serious effort to do so.”
“The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined,” the lawsuit says.
In a statement issued late Wednesday, the secretary of state’s office suggested the federal government’s outreach had not been collaborative.
Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat who also is named in the lawsuit, said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them.
Her office and the office of Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment on Thursday. In a social media post Wednesday, Newsom called the Trump administration’s request “more dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality.”
“California’s elections are NOT Donald Trump’s to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election,” Newsom wrote.
The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
___
Austin reported from Sacramento, California.

title: Hannaford app, website still offline over 2 days after company identified security issue
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford’s website and mobile app remained offline Friday, more than three days after the supermarket’s parent company says it disabled some systems as a precautionary measure while addressing a network cybersecurity issue.
Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch food giant that owns Maine’s largest grocer, announced in a brief news release late Monday that it was experiencing an internal network issue and had taken some systems offline to protect them, including the Hannaford website and app.
Online ordering has been disabled since then, though stores have remained open as usual.
On Thursday morning, the notification of the outage on Hannaford’s website was updated to include a note that customers can still shop online via third-party delivery services such as DoorDash, Instacart and Uber Eats.
Caitlin Cortelyou, a spokesperson for the Scarborough-based grocery store chain, said in an email Thursday that Hannaford is continuing to work with Ahold Delhaize to resolve the issue. While the investigation into the outage is ongoing, Cortelyou said, the companies “have no evidence at this moment that customer or associate data was taken in this cybersecurity incident.”
Ahold Delhaize says it has contacted external cybersecurity experts to help with its response and is “engaging with the appropriate authorities” as necessary.
“We know how important it is for our customers to be able to shop with us when and how they choose, and we apologize for the disruption,” Cortelyou said. “We appreciate our customers’ continued patience and understanding as we work to resolve the issue.”
If the cybersecurity issue is deemed to have been a data breach, then Maine law requires it be reported to the Office of the Maine Attorney General. The AG’s office said neither Hannaford nor Ahold Delhaize had reported the issue as of Wednesday.
A 2024 breach of Ahold Delhaize’s systems affected more than 95,000 Mainers and over 2 million people worldwide. Hannaford said most of the Mainers whose information was exposed were current or former employees.
Ahold Delhaize, one of the world’s largest food retailers, operates more than 2,000 U.S. stores under several brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant Food. Hannaford is the state’s largest grocer, with almost 70 stores across Maine.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 16 to indicate that the outage has continued into Friday.

title: Everyone has the same question in the midterms — where's the beef? (And how much does it cost?)
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In the midterm elections, meat is on the menu.
As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war, they’re also having a food fight over who’s the most red-blooded carnivore.
The latest example came this week in Mississippi, where Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom released a video with a snippet of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith saying that if consumers are upset over high beef prices, “you know you have so many proteins to choose from.”
The video cuts to a man grilling burgers who says, “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
The Mississippi race is somewhat unusual because it’s the Democrat hammering the Republican over beef. Elsewhere, Republicans have branded Democrats as vegans or otherwise opposed to meat, trying to show that they’re culturally out of step with voters, hostile to local cattle industries or just not manly enough.
In Texas, Republicans seized on an old interview in which Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico boasted that his campaign, then for the Texas statehouse, was going vegan. Talarico has since been publicly scarfing down barbecue to rebut allegations that his dietary choices mean he’s not a real Texan.
In Colorado, Republicans have gone after Democratic congressional candidate Manny Rutinel for his activism against meat production and factory farming. In college, he was photographed shirtless with a banner for the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals around his chest. In 2021, Rutinel founded Climate Refarm, which advocated for cutting down on the use of meat and has signed onto letters advocating for raising taxes on meat and dairy. He also supported a 2024 ballot measure to ban a lamb slaughterhouse in Denver, which failed.
Rutinel, 31, is now running against Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado’s 8th district, which includes a vast swath of the northeastern part of the state dotted with ranches, dairy farms and meat processing facilities, including the headquarters of beef production titan JBS Swift. Republicans have hammered Rutinel over advocating veganism, to the point that the conservative media group Daily Wire this week released an undercover video of a campaign official saying Rutinel eats meat “as little as possible.”
Rutinel, who’s made a point of publicly eating steak tacos on the campaign trail, scoffed at such arguments. “I don’t think Coloradans care about what’s on my plate, I think they care more about what’s on theirs,” Rutinel said in an interview after a recent campaign stop.
Evans said the issue goes beyond Rutinel’s meal preferences. “I don’t care what he eats personally,” Evans said in an interview. “I care that he wants to use the power of the government to make everyone eat that way.”
Republicans have gone after two other Democratic House candidates on meat — hammering Lindsay James in Iowa’s 2nd district, an area filled with hog farms, for supporting “meatless May” in a 2020 Facebook post, and Amish Shah in Arizona’s 1st district for his longstanding vegetarianism and animal rights activism.
Also in Iowa, Republican Senate candidate and current Rep. Ashley Hinson slammed her opponent, state lawmaker Josh Turek, for opposing a bill banning lab-grown meat from being sold in the state. “He’d rather have meat that comes from a lab than from our family farms,” she said at a campaign appearance.
Democrats have hammered on meat as well, but mainly just as one of the staples that cost more under Trump, squeezing voters’ pocketbooks. Trump has tried to lower prices by opening U.S. markets to beef imports, especially from Argentina, which is governed by a close Trump ally.
However, those moves have angered U.S. producers as prices have remained stubbornly high, creating a potential weakness in Republican-leaning states where Democrats hope to gain ground this year. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average pound of ground beef cost $6.79 last month, up from $5.55 in January of 2025, when Trump returned to office.
That was the dynamic that Hyde-Smith, a cattle rancher and former state agriculture commissioner, was addressing in her interview that was clipped in Colom’s video. The prosecutor — who also delivers the “pick another senator” line in the spot — is running a longshot challenge in Mississippi.
A spokesman for Hyde-Smith’s campaign argued that the Democrats deserve blame for high prices. “It is Scott Colom who supports Biden-era policies that drove up inflation,” said Nathan Calvert.
___
Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.
