title: At least 2 hospitalized after active shooter reported at elementary school in Oregon
text:
Teen shooter kills 4 at Oregon elementary school before being shot by a witness
A 16-year-old shot his way through locked doors to get into an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher. He was then shot by a person at the scene who followed him inside, authorities said.
The suspect was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to the hospital in critical condition, he said.
The first 911 call came just before 1 p.m. from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz said.
Further 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived on scene within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker, who police identified as a Bend resident, was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
Police said they did not know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or whether he had attended.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
The school in Bend, which is more than 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Portland, had 459 enrolled students as of last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. The school serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade.
Classes, sports and extracurriculars were canceled Friday for all 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine district.
At a news conference Thursday evening, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said her heart was “absolutely broken” and thanked the civilian who pursued the shooter.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she said.
Reunification of children with their parents was ongoing early Thursday evening.

title: Maine’s unsung heroes, caregivers, deserve support. AARP Maine is in their corner.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Family caregivers are among Maine’s most important resources, yet their contributions often go unrecognized. Every day, they help aging parents, spouses, friends, neighbors, and other loved ones live safely and independently at home. They support their loved ones by helping with daily activities that many of us do but take for granted, such as making a meal or managing our medications. They do this not because they are paid to, but because someone they love needs help.
In Maine, nearly three in ten adults are family caregivers or have provided care within the past year. Together, they represent over 300,000 people whose dedication helps make it possible for countless older adults to remain in their homes and communities, where they want to be.
Caregiving is rewarding, but it can be demanding. Many caregivers work full- or part-time jobs, and some raise children while caregiving. Others find themselves navigating complicated health care systems, making difficult decisions, and handling responsibilities they never expected to take on. The physical, emotional, and financial challenges can be overwhelming.
Get the family caregiving help you need with resources in Maine.
The AARP Family Caregiver Resource Guide for Maine helps family caregivers access key programs, services and agencies in their community.
To order a copy of the guide, call the AARP Family Caregiving Resource Line at 1-877-333-5885 and request the AARP Family Caregiver Resource Guide for Maine. Or view it online at aarp.org/CaregiverResources.
Find us at aarp.org/me | [email protected] | @aarpmaine
That is why AARP Maine is committed to standing with family caregivers. We know they are the unsung heroes of Maine’s long-term care system, and we believe they deserve practical support, reliable information, and policies that make caregiving easier.
One of the most important ways AARP Maine has supported caregivers is through our advocacy for Paid Family and Medical Leave. We heard repeatedly from caregivers who were forced to choose between caring for a loved one and earning a paycheck. Many family caregivers are still working while providing care, often using vacation time, unpaid leave, or flexible schedules to meet their caregiving responsibilities.
AARP Maine fought for Paid Family and Medical Leave because no one should have to choose between family and financial security. The program gives eligible workers access to paid, job-protected leave when they need time to care for a loved one, recover from a serious health condition, welcome a new child, or address other qualifying family needs. It is a major step forward for Maine caregivers and working families.
Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) gives eligible Maine workers up to 12 weeks of paid, job-protected leave to care for themselves or a loved one. AARP Maine proudly advocated for PFML, helping ensure working caregivers no longer have to choose between family and a paycheck.
Learn more at maine.gov/paidleave
Advocacy is only part of the equation. Caregivers also need resources they can use today.
That is why AARP Maine offers a free Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide. Whether someone is just beginning a caregiving journey or has been providing care for years, the guide serves as a valuable roadmap to programs, services, and support available across the state. It includes information on caregiver support services, transportation assistance, financial resources, legal help, respite care, and other programs that can make caregiving more manageable.
The guide also encourages caregivers to prioritize their own well-being. Too often, caregivers focus entirely on the needs of others while neglecting their own health. Yet caregivers need support, rest, and resources if they are to continue providing care over the long term.
AARP Maine has also partnered with 211 Maine to help family caregivers connect with assistance in their communities. Through this collaboration, caregivers can contact 211 and be connected to trained specialists who help identify local resources tailored to their needs.
Caregiving will touch nearly every Maine family at some point. Most of us will either provide care, receive care, or love someone who does. As Maine’s population continues to age, supporting family caregivers becomes even more important.
At AARP Maine, we want caregivers to know they are not alone. We will continue fighting for policies that help them save time and money, providing resources that help them navigate challenges, and elevating their voices in Augusta and beyond.
If you are caring for a loved one, AARP Maine is in your corner. To learn more about Paid Family and Medical Leave, download the Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide, explore caregiver tools, and learn about the 211 Maine partnership, visit aarp.org/mecares.
Caregivers spend so much of their time caring for others. Let us help care for you.

title: Search warrant offers new details after a woman killed her son and husband at a Pennsylvania resort
text:
Great Wolf Lodge killings: Search warrant offers new details after a woman allegedly killed her son and husband
Police have released a search warrant that provides new details about the woman accused of killing her husband and 3-year-old son inside a room at Great Wolf Lodge in Monroe County, Pennsylvania.
Metallica Harrison, 27, of Towanda, faces two counts of criminal homicide in the stabbing deaths of her husband, Charles Harrison, and their son on Monday, Oct. 12. The child's name has not been released.
Police search family's home
The Pocono Township Police Department requested a search warrant for the family's home in Towanda.
Located in northeastern Pennsylvania — not far from the New York State border — Towanda is about 100 miles from Pocono Township, which lies between Scranton and Allentown.
Pocono Township police said they contacted Towanda Borough police and asked them to check the property. Officers reported finding an electric utility shutoff notice posted on the front door, according to the warrant.
Police also contacted an employee of a local lawn-care company who asked if the residents were okay because he had not seen them in approximately a month, the documents stated.
The family had checked into Great Wolf Lodge on Sept. 21 and had been staying there for about three weeks before the deaths, according to police.
Knives, financial records and journals seized
Investigators seized 10 teal knives from the home, including two inside a knife block, according to an inventory filed with the search warrant.
Pocono Township police previously reported finding two teal-handled knives inside the Great Wolf Lodge room. Resort employees told investigators those knives were not the type maintained by Great Wolf Lodge.
Other property seized from the home included:
- Teal scissors
- Nine sealed envelopes addressed to Metallica Harrison
- Four sealed envelopes addressed to Charles Harrison
- A white, green and pink journal
- A red journal
- A book
- Financial records and a financial notebook
- Other miscellaneous records
- A black HP laptop and charger
- A Sentry 1100 safe
- A Penelec envelope
Pocono police said records inside the home could uncover valuable evidence in the investigation.
The documents do not disclose what was written in the journals or sealed envelopes or what information was stored on the laptop.
What we know about what happened at the resort
Pocono Township police responded around 3:13 p.m. Oct. 12 after Harrison called 911 and said she needed "help dying," according to the affidavit.
Officers found Metallica with injuries to her wrist and neck and discovered her husband and son dead on separate mattresses, police said. Investigators recovered two teal-handled knives, medication bottles and containers holding suspected blood.
During the 911 call and ambulance ride, Metallica made statements indicating her family was dead and expressing frustration that her apparent suicide attempt had failed, according to police.
If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters, please call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 (or 1-800-273-8255) to connect with a trained counselor. You can also text TALK to 741741
Surveillance video showed no activity at the room's door after Metallica and her husband returned from the resort's arcade the night before the deaths, according to police.
Investigators obtained search warrants and collected DNA evidence. Pocono Township police described the deaths as an "isolated domestic tragedy" that posed no continuing threat to the public.
Family members of her husband say Metallica Harrison was 'dominant, controlling,' police say
According to the search warrant, Pocono Township police spoke with Charles Harrison’s mother and his sister, while notifying them of his death on Oct. 12.
The women told investigators that Metallica Harrison was "dominant" and "controlling" and had isolated Charles and the 3-year-old from Charles' family during the last three years, according to the warrant.
The women also told investigators that Metallica appeared resentful toward her son and had said she never wanted to become pregnant, the documents stated.
The family members said that Metallica complained that their child took away one-on-one time between her and Charles, according to the warrant.

title: Police investigate report of sexual assault at a fraternity party near the University of Chicago
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Police are investigating a woman’s report that she was sexually assaulted during a fraternity party near the University of Chicago campus, an allegation that comes at a time of heightened awareness of sexual violence on college campuses.
Chicago police said no one had been charged Wednesday, a day after university officials posted an alert saying that a person of interest had been identified.
The Chicago case comes amid an uproar over Cornell University’s handling of a woman’s allegations that she was drugged and gang raped by fraternity members in 2024. A campus investigation led to internal disciplinary action by the university, but no criminal charges were ever filed.
The University of Chicago, a top-ranked U.S. research school with an enrollment of 18,000 students, said in a statement that a woman reported being sexually assaulted early Sunday during a party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house.
The university said the perpetrator fled the house after being confronted by another person.
The 21-year-old woman reported the assault to police and went to a hospital for treatment, according to Chicago police. The university said she is not a student.
Chicago police did not immediately provide a copy of the incident report on the alleged attack when The Associated Press requested it Wednesday.
The Chicago Sun-Times, citing the police report, said the woman told police she had been drinking and dancing at the party before she began feeling unwell. The Sun-Times said the report stated two of the woman’s friends then found her “not fully conscious” in a bathroom with a man and that both were partially undressed.
The friends told police that to get into the bathroom, they had to force their way through several men who were “cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside,” the Sun-Times reported.
Alpha Epsilon Pi said no fraternity members took part in the alleged attack or encouraged it. The fraternity’s University of Chicago chapter said in a statement that its members rushed to help the woman after being alerted by one of her friends and ended the party immediately.
“There is no evidence at all that any AEPi members participated in this assault or were aware of it while it was transpiring,” Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity’s national organization, said in a statement Wednesday.
The fraternity said the perpetrator was chased out of the house and was recorded by cameras while fleeing.
University officials said the person of interest who has been identified is not a student or otherwise affiliated with the school.
The Cornell case came to light last month after a woman filed a lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members, saying she was repeatedly assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024. She went to campus police three weeks later and gave a detailed interview, but local prosecutors never pursued charges. The men she accused have denied wrongdoing.
Cornell announced Tuesday it’s banning parties at fraternity houses until next year. The university said it will include New York State Police in investigations of campus sexual assaults.
Fraternities have also been under scrutiny at the University of Arizona, which suspended fraternity activities earlier this month following multiple reports of assault, hazing and other misconduct.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.

title: Man accused of shooting at teens toilet papering neighbor’s house in prank gone wrong
text:
ARNAUDVILLE, La. (KATC/Gray News) - A Louisiana man is facing multiple charges after authorities say he shot at a group of high school students during a toilet-papering prank gone wrong.
Travis Frederick, 71, was arrested and booked on charges of attempted manslaughter, aggravated assault with a firearm and aggravated criminal damage to property. His bond has not yet been set.
St. Martin Parish Sheriff Becket Breaux said deputies responded to a shooting on a street right outside Arnaudville just before midnight Monday. Several high school students had been in the area throwing toilet paper on neighborhood homes as part of a homecoming prank, according to deputies.
Frederick, who lives next door to one of the targeted homes, went outside with a gun and fired a shot toward at least five of the students, Breaux said.
Breaux added that as the students tried to leave in a vehicle, Frederick fired a second shot, striking the car.
No injuries were reported, but Breaux said the shooting was an overreaction that could have turned deadly.
“You use deadly force on someone toilet papering someone’s house. That’s a little bit overboard, and basically, you’re sending someone to a death sentence for toilet papering,” Breaux said.
Breaux noted the case highlights how quickly a neighborhood prank escalated into a criminal investigation. He urges the public not to take the law into their own hands.
”You elected me to be your sheriff to enforce the law, enforce public safety, and we have 240 deputies here who do the same thing. Let them earn their money, call them and let us go do our job."

title: 1 dead in Bangor apartment building fire

The Bangor Fire Department responded to 72 Cedar St. for a structure fire at about 6:35 a.m., Maine Department of Public Safety spokesperson Shannon Moss said in a news release Thursday.

Maine Bistro Named the No. 1 Family-Run Restaurant in America
Maine has plenty of incredible places to grab a delicious meal, but one Portland bistro just earned a pretty impressive distinction: It was ranked the No. 1 family-run restaurant in America!
Lovefood, a food website known for its restaurant rankings, food lists, and recommendations, named Isa Bistro the best family-run restaurant in the entire country. Not too shabby for a neighborhood spot in Maine!
For Maine food lovers, sometimes the best meals are worth the drive, and Isa Bistro is making a pretty strong case for a trip south.
Located in Portland’s Bayside neighborhood, Isa Bistro has a story that’s almost as charming as its food. Husband-and-wife team Isaul Perez and Suzie St. Pierre opened the restaurant on March 19, 2015, after meeting while working in New York City restaurants. Eventually, they made their way to Maine to open the neighborhood bistro they had always dreamed about.
Chef Isaul brings together his French and Italian culinary training with the Mexican cooking traditions he grew up with, creating a menu that puts a creative spin on comfort food. Suzie oversees the front of house and wine program, helping give the restaurant its warm, welcoming atmosphere.
Even the name has a personal touch. Isa Bistro is named after a shortened version of Isaul’s name, making the restaurant a true family labor of love.

With layers of flavor, seasonal ingredients, and plenty of attention to detail, the dish is a great example of how Isa Bistro takes classic favorites and makes them its own.
It's not just lasagna though, the restaurant offers a seasonal menu featuring handmade pastas, creative small plates, and dishes that reflect their impressive culinary background.
With a cozy atmosphere and personal touch, it’s the kind of place that makes a meal feel like more than just dinner, but a memorable night out.
Isa Bistro is located at 79 Portland St. in Portland.
Dinner is served Monday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Sunday from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. The restaurant is closed Tuesdays. On Fridays and Saturdays, brunch runs from 11:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., followed by dinner service.

title: Trump scraps livestream of Fort Hood shooter’s execution
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled plans to livestream the execution of the gunman responsible for the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting, following bipartisan criticism from lawmakers, religious leaders and some survivors of the attack.
The decision comes just one week after the Pentagon announced that Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others, would be executed by firing squad in a broadcast available to the public.
In a lengthy post on Truth Social, Trump defended the original proposal as a potential deterrent to terrorism but acknowledged concerns about broadcasting the execution.
“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan,” Trump wrote. “But, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
Trump had previously expressed support for the livestream, telling reporters Oct. 9 that he approved of the plan. But the proposed broadcast quickly drew opposition from across the political spectrum.
Vice President JD Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson stopped short of condemning the proposal but said they would not watch the execution. Other lawmakers, including some Republicans, publicly opposed the livestream.
Some survivors of the Fort Hood shooting also raised concerns about broadcasting Hasan’s death, while the Vatican’s Secretary of State criticized the proposed spectacle.
Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. During his military trial, Hasan acknowledged carrying out the shooting and presented his actions as religiously motivated.
Despite canceling the livestream, Trump said the firing squad execution would proceed as planned. However, he clarified that only the victims’ immediate family members would be allowed to watch the event if they chose to.
The controversy has prompted a legislative response. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) introduced legislation Thursday that would prohibit the public broadcasting of military executions, seeking to prevent similar proposals in the future.

title: Waterville Filmmaker Ryan Cook Brings Donn Fendler's Survival Story To Audience At Gracie Theatre In Bangor Next Month
text:
Waterville Native Ryan Cook To Host Talk At Gracie Theater About How He Got To Make The Movie ‘Lost On A Mountain In Maine’
It's been a little over two years since one of Maine's most famous rescue stories, one many middle school students in the state have read in book form, debuted on the big screen.
The effort to bring the story of Donn Fendler's plight when he got "Lost On A Mountain In Maine" to a film form was spearheaded by Waterville native, Ryan Cook, who like many had read the book in school, and was captivated by the story.
Read More: 'Lost On A Mountain' Producer To Come Full Circle With Movie
Cook befriended Fendler and his family, and through his time with them, got even more of the story which he felt needed to be told, so in 2011, he put together a documentary called documentary about Fendler called “Finding Donn Fendler: Lost on a Mountain in Maine 72 Years Later" which he screened at the Waterville Opera House at the Maine International Film Festival. 
Fendler passed away a few years later, in 2016.
Almost a decade later, Cook's efforts to make a full-fledged movie based on the book came to fruition. With the backing of Sylvester Stallone's production company, Balboa Productions, and with the addition of producers Braden Aftergood and Dick Boyce the motion picture version of Lost On A Mountain In Maine debuted in 2024. It landed at #5 on the Netflix Global charts.
Read More: Check It Out: Trailer For New 'Lost On A Mountain In Maine' Movie
Next month, Cook will come to Bangor, bringing the documentary he made, which inspired the film, and behind-the-scenes footage of Fendler himself when he hosts a talk about his experience with the story at the Gracie Theatre on the campus of Husson University.
According to the Lost On A Mountain In Maine Facebook page, the special event will take place next month, with opportunities for the audience to ask questions of the man who made the movie. The talk is entitled "The Legacy of Donn Fendler; Perseverance Against All Odds.
"Friday, November 20th, at the Gracie Theater in Bangor. Join producer and Maine native Ryan Cook for a special evening celebrating the legacy of Donn Fendler. Hear and see documentary footage of Donn Fendler telling the story in his own words, followed by a discussion with Ryan about the years he spent working with Donn to make the feature film 'Lost on a Mountain in Maine'."
Doors will open at 5PM, with general admission opening at 5:30. The talk is scheduled to go from 6 PM to 7:30, with a question and answer portion available till 8 PM.
The event is free and appropriate for all ages. The first 150 participants who register will get a complimentary copy of the book that started it all, Lost On A Mountain In Maine.

The Galen Cole Family Foundation is sponsoring this special event.

title: States sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT is hurting children and deceiving adults
text:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit.
The company’s chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to commit suicide or hurt or kill others, the lawsuits said.
At the same time, the lawsuits contend that chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and on teenagers, the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence.
“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.
The states also accused OpenAI of giving life to rogue AI models — or “cyberhacking agents” as one lawsuit called them — that hacked into other companies, lied to human users and wrote themselves new mission instructions.
In a statement, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model. It also said it is reviewing what it calls “misaligned models” and that it had found nothing close to the rogue incident discovered in July when an AI agent hacked into another AI company.
States join together in lawsuits
The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.
Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”
In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends.
The states say that the risks and harms — to teenagers and to the broader public from rogue agents — were foreseeable, but that OpenAI has misled people into thinking that ChatGPT undergoes adequate safety testing while the company undermines safety in the pursuit of profit.
“Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI’s) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content,” Idaho wrote in its lawsuit.
ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits.
The AI landscape is evolving
It’s possible all of the allegations in the states’ lengthy lawsuits date to incidents and findings before August, when OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT designed for teenagers, with stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats.
Still, the states said it is far from clear that the current version is any less dangerous.
A watchdog group, Common Sense Media, said last week that some of OpenAI’s protections in its ChatGPT for Teens product don’t work as intended and it urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until it can offer a safe product for teens.
Coordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit.
In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an $18 billion landmark legal settlement that ended a trial over teen social media addiction and settled claims filed by nearly every state.
Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures.
OpenAI is making a similar appeal.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company is committed to working with states on “advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.”
OpenAI also said it works with external experts who review its policies and ChatGPT’s behavior.
ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens is designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said.
Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said.
But Laura Zimmerman, Common Sense Media’s director of youth AI research, questioned the value of OpenAI’s statistics.
For one thing, ChatGPT can do a student’s homework in seconds, so even 15 minutes can have a big impact on a teenager’s development, Zimmerman said. She also questioned whether OpenAI knows which users are teenagers or children, given that her organization’s testing found that ChatGPT couldn’t or didn’t detect which user is a child.
___
Follow Marc Levy at http://x.com/timelywriter

title: Aging Untold: Decoding Medicare Advantage
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down Medicare Advantage to help you navigate coverage options, costs and hidden limits.
We also explore the complex world of autoimmune conditions, what happens when the immune system turns on itself and tips for managing daily life.
Finally, we highlight a daily check-in call program giving older adults living alone a vital safety net and peace of mind.
It can feel overwhelming to make the choice between Medicare Advantage, which is also known as Medicare Part C, and traditional Medicare.
As you weigh your decision, the Aging Untold experts say to start with your budget and your health history.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said family health history matters just as much as the monthly premium.
Patients should also confirm whether their own doctors accept the plan — and that those doctors have stayed in the plan’s network, O’Rourke said.
Diagnosing an older adult with an autoimmune condition like type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus can be especially tricky because the immune system naturally changes with age.
But an early diagnosis can make a real difference in managing symptoms long-term.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said inflammation is usually the driver.
There is currently no cure for lupus, but a treatment that was developed to fight cancer is now being used in a clinical trial to treat the autoimmune disease that affects an estimated 1.5 million Americans.
Rachel Dib, a military wife and mother of three in North Carolina, was diagnosed with lupus when she was a college sophomore.
After nearly 20 years of suffering, she enrolled in a CAR T-cell therapy clinical trial at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine.
Older adults who live alone in Phoenix are receiving daily phone calls to check on them and provide help in case of an emergency.
The program, called R.U. OK ,stands for Are You OK?
Seniors receive computerized calls instructing them to push one number to let the system know they are OK or another to alert it that they need help.

title: 🥇 WOW, MAINE! This Bistro Was Just Named the No. 1 Family-Run Restaurant in America!
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Bistro Named the No. 1 Family-Run Restaurant in America
Maine has plenty of incredible places to grab a delicious meal, but one Portland bistro just earned a pretty impressive distinction: It was ranked the No. 1 family-run restaurant in America!
Lovefood, a food website known for its restaurant rankings, food lists, and recommendations, named Isa Bistro the best family-run restaurant in the entire country. Not too shabby for a neighborhood spot in Maine!
For Maine food lovers, sometimes the best meals are worth the drive, and Isa Bistro is making a pretty strong case for a trip south.
Located in Portland’s Bayside neighborhood, Isa Bistro has a story that’s almost as charming as its food. Husband-and-wife team Isaul Perez and Suzie St. Pierre opened the restaurant on March 19, 2015, after meeting while working in New York City restaurants. Eventually, they made their way to Maine to open the neighborhood bistro they had always dreamed about.
Chef Isaul brings together his French and Italian culinary training with the Mexican cooking traditions he grew up with, creating a menu that puts a creative spin on comfort food. Suzie oversees the front of house and wine program, helping give the restaurant its warm, welcoming atmosphere.
Even the name has a personal touch. Isa Bistro is named after a shortened version of Isaul’s name, making the restaurant a true family labor of love.
Read More: 13 Bangor Mall Stores You'll Remember From The Good Old Days
Isa Bistro has earned attention for its incredible lasagna, including its eggplant lasagna, which puts a creative spin on a familiar comfort-food favorite.
With layers of flavor, seasonal ingredients, and plenty of attention to detail, the dish is a great example of how Isa Bistro takes classic favorites and makes them its own.
It's not just lasagna though, the restaurant offers a seasonal menu featuring handmade pastas, creative small plates, and dishes that reflect their impressive culinary background.
With a cozy atmosphere and personal touch, it’s the kind of place that makes a meal feel like more than just dinner, but a memorable night out.
Isa Bistro is located at 79 Portland St. in Portland.
Dinner is served Monday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Sunday from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. The restaurant is closed Tuesdays. On Fridays and Saturdays, brunch runs from 11:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., followed by dinner service.
Whether you’re going for the lasagna, the creative menu, or the chance to support a restaurant built around a husband-and-wife team’s dream, Isa Bistro is putting Maine on the national food map in a very tasty way.

title: Three Maine football storylines to follow against Bryant
text:
It’s been two weeks since the University of Maine football team dropped its fifth straight game with a 24-16 loss to Sacred Heart on Oct. 3 in Orono. Maine had a bye last week, during which it fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters.
The Black Bears (1-5, 1-2 Coastal Athletic Association) return to action when they host Bryant (4-2, 2-0 CAA) at 1 p.m. Saturday (FloSports; ABC in Bangor market). Here are three storylines to watch as Maine looks to end the skid.
Green-er pastures?
With Waters gone, running backs coach Sean Green takes over as interim offensive coordinator. Green is well-known in Maine, having won state titles as head coach of Cape Elizabeth High School in 2021 (Class C) and Portland in 2024 (Class A).
Green takes over a Maine offense ranked 121st of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in points per game (14.5). In Monday’s CAA press conference, coach Jordan Stevens said the goal is to “continue to find ways to be more balanced” offensively and praised his team’s response to the change.
“I thought the guys have handled that type of change really well in how they’ve approached practice, and Coach Green has done an excellent job,” Stevens said. “This is not something that’s foreign to him in calling plays; it’s something he’s done in the past, so I have full confidence in his ability.”
The quarterback question
Through the first four games, Eddie Buehler was Maine’s unquestioned starter at quarterback. Yet in the second half at Elon on Sept. 26, Caden Drezek took over under center. Buehler again got the start against Sacred Heart before Stevens turned to Drezek in the second quarter.
So, with a new offensive coordinator, what will the plan be this weekend? Will Buehler make his seventh straight start? Will the Black Bears turn to Drezek instead? Or will we see some combination of the two, as has been the case the past two games?
“In a perfect world, you’d always probably have one guy,” Stevens said. “I don’t have any answer for you on that right now, but we are working through the quarterback position and how we’re going to manage that this week.”
Up-and-down Bulldogs
On one hand, Bryant boasts an impressive 21-14 win over Princeton, which is 3-1. Yet the Bulldogs also needed a miracle — 10 points in the final 40 seconds — to pull out a win over North Carolina A&T, which might be the worst team in the CAA. Bryant also lost 28-13 at Brown.
This is an opportunity, then, for the Black Bears, who have had two weeks to prepare. The numbers don’t suggest a lopsided game — in fact, ESPN’s SP+ has the Bulldogs as just 1.3-point favorites. A win will be difficult, but it’s not impossible — and if Maine can pull it off, the trajectory of the season could change.

title: Kittery Point man charged after hit-and-run crash, seriously injures motorcyclist in Newry
text:
Kittery Point man charged after hit-and-run crash, seriously injures motorcyclist in Newry
Deputies say the driver struck a 67-year-old motorcyclist before fleeing the scene
Kittery Point man charged after hit-and-run crash, seriously injures motorcyclist in Newry
Deputies say the driver struck a 67-year-old motorcyclist before fleeing the scene
A Kittery Point man is facing charges after authorities say he struck a motorcyclist in Newry and fled the scene Saturday afternoon.
According to the Oxford County Sheriff's Office, deputies responded to a crash involving a vehicle and a motorcycle at the intersection of Mayville Road and Bear River Road around 3:46 p.m. on October 10.
Investigators say 23-year-old Henry Clark was driving a black 2020 Mazda CX-9 west on Mayville Road when he passed a stopped pickup truck and struck a motorcycle turning onto the road.
The motorcyclist, identified as 67-year-old Donald Dyer Jr. of Standish, was thrown from his motorcycle and suffered significant injuries. He was transported to Rumford Hospital.
Authorities say Clark fled the scene towards Bethel following the crash.
Later, deputies were able to locate Clark at an Irving gas station in Bethel. Investigators reported significant damage to Clark's car.
Clark was arrested and taken to the Oxford County Jail.
He faces charges of aggravated leaving the scene of an accident, aggravated reckless conduct, operating under the influence causing serious bodily injury and aggravated assault with a dangerous weapon.
The crash remains under investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Oxford County Sheriff's Office.

title: A new Medicare season begins, but some shifts will arrive in 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new Medicare season begins, but some shifts will arrive in 2027
WASHINGTON —
Open enrollment for Medicare plans begins Thursday and enrollees will face a slew of changes that go into effect in 2027.
Video above: Here's how to find out if you're eligible for Trump's $90 Medicare payments
During the enrollment period, which ends Dec. 7, people will have the opportunity to choose between traditional Medicare and privately run Medicare Advantage plans in their area, as well as prescription drug plans. Those changes go into effect on Jan. 1.
Open enrollment also comes as inflation adds pressure on seniors whose healthcare costs have risen and as midterm elections are weeks away. Voters have consistently said cost-of-living is a major concern headed into the elections.
The Medicare enrollment period also comes as the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, which translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
New changes to Medicare coming in 2027 include higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies, and new drug price negotiations.
Here are a few of the biggest changes:
Medicare Part D
The cap on annual out-of-pocket expenses for Medicare Part D drugs will increase to $2,400, up from $2,100 in 2026, and the standard deductible will increase from $615 to $700.
The temporary Part D premium subsidy will also end early.
The Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums.
It was initially implemented by former President Joe Biden's administration in 2024 to lower patients’ Medicare Part D prescription drug costs in response to effects of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected only modest price increases for most people. CMS did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
Drug price negotiations
New Medicare-negotiated prices, part of a Biden-era law that allows the haggling for Medicare, will go into effect for 15 drugs, including weight-loss and diabetes medications Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.
Additionally, Trelegy Ellipta, Xtandi, Pomalyst, Ibrance, Ofev, Linzess, Calquence, Austedo/Austedo XR, Breo Ellipta, Tradjenta, Xifaxan, Vraylar, Janumet/Janumet XR, and Otezla will be covered by Medicare as of Jan. 1.
CMS expects the change to lower prescription drug coverage for people enrolled in Medicare by $685 million in 2027.
AARP’s Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Nancy LeaMond said in a statement that “higher healthcare costs are making it harder for older Americans to afford the care they need."
“It’s more important than ever to shop around, compare your options, and choose the coverage that’s best for you," she said.
Other Trump administration promises
Along with the changes, President Donald Trump in recent weeks made a series of promises to Medicare enrollees and retirees.
Last week, Trump said his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person in October to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees — or less than one third of enrollees — pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion.
Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients.
According to the CMS website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October.
Trump also announced recently that roughly 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums.

title: More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall
text:
More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park
A growing number of amusement parks have shut down roller coasters as police and state regulators investigate what caused a man to fall out of his seat and plummet to his death at a Georgia park.
SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde theme park in Montreal, Canada, confirmed on Thursday they had temporarily closed rides, bringing the total number of roller coasters halted to 12.
Police and a state regulatory agency are investigating what caused Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, to fall from the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Witnesses described seeing him ejected from the coaster; some people who rode the Goliath before him raised concerns about its restraints.
Related video above: Riders evacuated from roller coaster at Six Flags in Atlanta, Ga., after man dies
Ten of the roller coasters taken out of service have the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system to the Goliath at Six Flags.
Mom says her son's restraint didn't work properly
Erica Billups said her son and daughter rode Goliath about an hour before Kariem’s death and encountered a problem with the restraint on one seat. Her son initially sat in that seat and tried to lock it, but then moved when it repeatedly became unlocked. The roller coaster departed with the seat empty and the harness up, she said in a post on X.
She confirmed the post in a text message to The Associated Press on Thursday.
She said staff did not tell her kids there was a problem.
Summer Bates, who was at the Georgia park with her husband and three children and saw Kariem fall, told the AP previously that her older two children kept trying to push their restraints down tighter while on the ride. She understood why they were doing that later when she was on the coaster, she said, because the restraints didn’t feel secure.
Six Flags did not immediately respond to an email for comment on any issues with restraints.
At least one of the other closures is for safety
La Ronde in Montreal said one of its coasters — also named Goliath — is offline “while we conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride’s manufacturer.”
Neither La Ronde nor Sea World Orlando said why those specific rides were closed. Both were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, which also built the Goliath ride in Georgia and eight of the other coasters that Six Flags closed. Bolliger & Mabillard declined Thursday to answer questions about the shutdowns.
Online photos and videos of 10 of the closed coasters show each equipped with so-called “clamshell” restraints, mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider’s knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.
It’s unclear from the images whether any of those coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints.
Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the similar restraint systems are almost certainly why most of the coasters were closed.
Speigel said they’re likely to remain shut down until investigators have determined what went wrong on the Georgia coaster, but he said that “obviously it was something with the restraint.”
Roller coaster manufacturers decide what type of restraints to use after considering speed, force and the track’s transitions, said Brian D. Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert.
He advocates the use of a backup restraint for riders, but there is a long-running debate in the industry over whether that would increase wait times, Avery said.
Bolliger & Mabillard says it is investigating
The company said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a “better understanding of what transpired” on Monday.
Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia's headline attractions, towers above the park's entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers per hour).
Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead, said it looked like Kariem was hovering because the car was moving underneath him. He fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, and then was ejected from the ride on its final turn.
Six Flags has faced legal trouble before
A class-action lawsuit filed by investors in 2025 alleges that Six Flags concealed the poor state of its amusement parks — including long-neglected maintenance — ahead of its merger with major amusement park operator Cedar Fair.
“Prior to the Merger, Legacy Six Flags had for years deferred or foregone basic park maintenance, operational improvements, infrastructure repairs, and ride design and development updates,” the complaint said. The company also cut staffing to reduce costs, it alleges.
Timothy Loranger, a California attorney who sued Six Flags in a fatal case, said it’s a positive step that the theme park chain closed down rides at other parks as a precaution. Loranger represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 roller coaster in 2022 at Six Flags Magic Mountain.
“In all instances, X2 had many reports of injury in the past, and instead of doing a deep dive investigation into the ride, they did things like blame the passengers, the injured person for not sitting properly or holding their head against the headrest or they blamed an imaginary pre-existing condition,” Loranger said.
Six Flags permanently closed the X2 ride last month.
The park is scheduled to reopen Friday
Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen on Friday. The Goliath, however, is not expected to be running.
The park, which has about a dozen roller coasters, is in Austell, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta.

title: FBI agents and analysts fired for roles in Trump classified files probe sue to get their jobs back
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — FBI employees fired for their roles in the investigation of President Donald Trump’s retention of classified documents at his Florida estate sued on Thursday to get their jobs back, calling their terminations unlawful acts of “political retribution.”
The complaint adds to the growing list of legal challenges to the mass terminations under FBI Director Kash Patel of agents who participated in investigations of the Republican president or are seen as opposed to Trump administration interests.
The suit was filed in federal court in Washington on behalf of nine agents, intelligence analysts and staff operations specialists who were fired in February following earlier dismissals of agents who had worked on the investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.
Patel has said in congressional testimony that employees he has fired had “weaponized” the FBI. But the agents deny that claim in the lawsuit, noting that between them they had more than a century of distinguished and apolitical FBI service that involved responding to the Boston Marathon bombing, hostage recoveries and the investigation into the 2024 assassination attempt of Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.
Their firings, the lawsuit says, create an “immeasurable loss” to “America’s national security.”
“In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did to follow the facts and law without bias or favor. To this administration, this is an offense. To the rest of us, it is heroic,” said a statement from their attorneys, Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio.
“This lawsuit will prove their unlawful dismissal and hold the administration accountable for this blatant attack on the rule of law,” the statement added.
The Mar-a-Lago investigation produced criminal charges against Trump
The suit lays out a detailed recitation of the allegations against Trump, describing how he improperly stored dozens of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, that he took with him after leaving the White House, showed them off to people not authorized to see them and obstructed FBI efforts to get them back.
The investigation resulted in a dramatic 2022 FBI search of Mar-a-Lago that recovered classified records and later produced an indictment in federal court in Florida charging Trump with dozens of felony counts.
Trump denied wrongdoing, and the case was dismissed in 2024 by a Trump-appointed judge, Aileen Cannon, who ruled that the special counsel who filed the charges, Jack Smith, had been illegally appointed by the Biden administration Justice Department.
The nine fired FBI employees did not volunteer for the investigation but were rather assigned to it as part of their work on specialized counterintelligence and counterespionage squads, according to the lawsuit, which says they were nonetheless terminated because of baseless perceptions that the performance of their law enforcement duties had run “afoul of the political and personal loyalty to Trump that Defendants demanded.”
“By casting Plaintiffs’ work on the Plasmic Echo investigation as ‘politically weaponized,’ Defendants incorrectly presumed to know the personal political convictions of Plaintiffs and took unlawful action based on that presumption,” the lawsuit says, using the FBI code name for the classified documents investigation. “Worse still, Defendants incorrectly concluded that those personal political convictions affected or drove their work.”
The lawsuit seeks, among other remedies, reinstatement to the FBI, an awarding of back pay and a court order declaring that the firings were unlawful.
The suit says the firings were the culmination of a retribution campaign
Lawyers for the fired employees suggest their clients’ “fate was sealed” well before the February terminations, casting the ousters as the culmination of a long-running retribution campaign that kicked into gear once Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
The lawsuit notes how Patel, in his capacity as a conservative podcaster before becoming Trump’s FBI director, had derided the FBI’s Mar-a-Lago search as “unlawful” and had accused the agents who had participated in it as being “corrupt government gangsters.”
Days after Trump was inaugurated, a top Justice Department official demanded that the FBI turn over a list of bureau employees who had participated in Trump-related investigations, an order that the then-director, Brian Driscoll, resisted and that was seen within the workforce as a potential prelude to mass firings.
Over the following year, the FBI and the Justice Department fired waves of employees involved in investigations of Trump, without hearings or proper notice that the plaintiffs’ lawyers say are required by law.
The lawsuit says that the Mar-a-Lago agents and analysts were fired last February after Patel disclosed to Reuters that the FBI, as part of the investigation, had subpoenaed his toll records, which show the date, time and length of a phone call but not the content of the communications.
“The Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President’s personal vendetta,” the lawsuit states. “The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal.”

title: Portland gets money for housing crisis but may not be able to accept it
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A philanthropic organization announced Thursday that Portland will receive hundreds of thousands of dollars to tackle its pervasive housing crisis.
But city officials say they never applied for the funding. They can’t even use it.
Bloomberg Philanthropies selected Portland as one of 15 cities to test whether housing reforms that have worked in other parts of the country can have the same impact locally, the group announced Thursday.
Using successful models from California, Texas and Georgia, the selected cities will receive between $450,000 and $750,000 as well as expert support to tackle permitting times, accessory dwelling unit approvals and a backlog of stalled affordable housing projects.
Bloomberg did not say which initiative Portland will take on or how much money it will receive.
Mayor Mark Dion was perplexed by Portland’s inclusion in the list. Bloomberg contacted him about the opportunity a few weeks ago, he said, and he ran the possibility by staff, but they ultimately determined it wasn’t a good fit.
The money, which is largely for staff, comes with strict criteria, Dion said, and Portland has already undertaken many of the initiatives the organization is trying to pilot.
For example, Austin, Texas, legalized up to three homes on most single-family lots and shrank minimum lot sizes to encourage more accessory dwelling units. Permits nearly quadrupled, according to Bloomberg.
But Maine already implemented similar zoning mandates statewide in 2022, and next year, another law will go into effect that further loosens zoning laws.
In San Diego, officials moved permit reviews online and set a 30-day limit on approvals. The number of homes cleared for construction jumped 82% in one year, the most in 20 years.
Portland’s permitting process is already digitized, Dion said.
In Atlanta, the mayor pulled every agency involved in housing into a Housing Strike Force, which got more than 2,000 stalled affordable homes moving again, according to Bloomberg.
Portland is already working on that issue, too.
Last year, the city launched a Social Housing Task Force to explore how to establish middle-income housing that would be owned, operated and managed by the city. And the City Council is currently reviewing potential changes to its inclusionary zoning policy, which developers have criticized as the main barrier to completing housing projects in Portland.
Dion said he’d love to be able to accept the money, but Portland doesn’t have a way to use it.
“Staff fully considered whether there was a match …. It’s not a match right now,” he said.
Dion said as much to Bloomberg officials last week and said that Luke McGowan, who works on the organization’s Government Innovation team told him Portland was included because it’s still considered “eligible.”
If the city develops an initiative in line with Bloomberg’s criteria, it can still move forward.
“But at this time we’re not there,” Dion said. “We feel we’re in a good position” with permitting and ADUs.
Bloomberg Philanthropies did not immediately respond to an email seeking clarification.
Portland, which has a population of about 70,000, was by far the smallest city on the list and is one of only two in New England.
Other selected cities include Miami, Florida; Albuquerque, New Mexico; San Jose, California; Omaha, Nebraska; Providence, Rhode Island; and Nashville, Tennessee.

title: ‘An incredible amount of panic’: As Maine faces record-high heating oil prices, Aroostook County will be hit the hardest
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Northern Maine saw its first snowfall of the season Tuesday night. Nighttime temperatures have barely dipped below freezing and most Mainers have yet to turn on their heat, but the threat of winter looms.
As the Iran war and other global conflicts have skyrocketed the price of oil, Maine will uniquely feel the burden once the weather turns cold. It is the most dependent state in the U.S. on home heating oil, which more than 57% of households use as a fuel source.
The average price of heating oil is roughly 80% higher than this time last year, lingering around a record high of $6 per gallon for the last month. That means a standard 275-gallon tank will cost upwards of $740 more to fill, multiplied by several fillups over the course of a winter.
In Aroostook County, Maine’s coldest and among its poorest counties, that economic pain will be its most pronounced. Nearly 70% of households in The County use heating oil, further squeezing a population already dealing with the rising cost of groceries, electricity and other expenses fueling the affordability crisis.
And the federal programs meant to help alleviate the burden are overwhelmed.
“Last year was really challenging, but this year, with the price of oil hovering at about $6 a gallon, it’s just been an incredible amount of panic on the part of a lot of folks who just don’t know how they’re going to be able to heat their home this winter,” said Jason Parent, the CEO of Avec Community Action.
Avec, which recently rebranded from the Aroostook County Action Program, administers heating assistance programs in Aroostook, Washington and Hancock counties. The organization has seen a surge in applications for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) in the years following the pandemic.
In Aroostook County alone, Avec expects to receive more than 7,600 applications for this heating season, 16% higher than last year and accounting for more than a quarter of all households in The County.
“I’ve been in community action for 18 years and I have never seen the need as horrible as it is so early on in the season,” Avec Chief Program Officer Heidi Rackliffe said. “We’re not even in freezing temperatures yet. And to have this, I don’t even want to know what the next month is going to bring.”
The organization has 1,200 unanswered voicemails from people looking to apply for LIHEAP funds, and has already received around 1,000 online applications, Rackliffe said. It has a staff of 11 conducting intake interviews, and around five others certifying applications, but the sheer demand has created a bottleneck that Avec is struggling to keep up with. It is currently scheduling interviews into February.
Each interview takes about 45 minutes, so each of the staff members can only do around eight per day. The organization is working to hire more employees to take on the job, but its contract to administer the assistance program requires background checks for new hires, which can delay the process by more than a month, Parent said.
“Oftentimes, we might have a candidate that we fully vetted, that we’ve gone through the interview process, checked references, make a job offer, sent their name off for a background check, and a month later we’re still not able to have them on staff,” Parent said. “And then you end up losing them because they were seeking other employment.”
Online applications allow households to avoid the months-long wait for interviews, but strict documentation requirements mean a family could wait weeks to be approved for assistance, only to have their application denied on a technicality, such as having a corner of a Social Security card missing in a photo submission.
Then they apply again, adding to the bottleneck.
“The list keeps growing and growing and growing because we’re denying, unfortunately, more applications than we’re approving because the proof we’re getting through customers is not meeting the guidelines of the program,” Rackliffe said.
Avec has the most success with applications submitted through in-person interviews or phone appointments, she said, a step she recommended for older adults or those who don’t feel comfortable with technology.
Aroostook is one of seven Maine counties where more than a quarter of residents are 65 or older, many living on fixed incomes, who are disproportionately affected by rising costs.
“[They’re] truly worried. ‘How will I make it through this winter?’” said Vi Belanger, manager of Community & Memory Services for Aroostook Agency on Aging, which provides programming and services for older adults in The County. “This is real. This is raw.”
Many clients the agency works with are changing their diets in ways that stretch their money further, such as switching from fresh to canned meats, Belanger said. Some are considering foregoing heating oil to instead use space heaters or wood.
“There are quite a few of our clients that are also now going to food pantries and they’ve never had to before,” Belanger said. “This is a big deal.”
Maine is working with roughly $42 million in heating assistance funding this winter, including $4 million leftover from last winter and $38 million newly appropriated by the Department of Health and Human Services. The total is around what the state typically receives in LIHEAP funds, but with the high price of heating oil and the soaring need for assistance, those resources will be stretched thin.
MaineHousing — the quasi-state housing finance agency — is pushing LIHEAP administrators to process online applications “pretty immediately,” Parent said. They also face a contractual requirement to resolve applications from households with seniors and children under 6 — those most vulnerable to the cold — within 120 days.
Avec has tasked staff who already work with some young families in other programs, such as Head Start or WIC, with the administration of their LIHEAP applications to speed up the process. But it simply does not have the staff to meet all of the program’s requirements, Rackliffe said.
“I had a conversation with MaineHousing and I said, ‘I’m going to be out of compliance in one area, pick which is the lesser evil for you,’” Rackliffe said. “If I have to stay true to importing all these onlines, I’m no longer going to be able to make sure that all of the individuals with a vulnerability to hypothermic temperatures are going to be [processed] in the 120 days.
“It’s like [I’m] playing a game where I’m losing anywhere I look at it.”

President Donald Trump has canceled plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting.
The president said he still believes publicly showing the execution could have served as a deterrent but acknowledged that "many people would rather not watch someone die."
The decision comes after bipartisan backlash, with House Speaker Mike Johnson opposing the livestream and Vice President JD Vance saying he "wouldn't watch it."
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood. He is still scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, which would mark the first U.S. military execution in more than 65 years.
Victims' immediate family members will still be allowed to witness the execution in person.

title: More Beneficial Rainfall Friday!
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - High pressure will continue to slide in the evening, bringing lighter winds and mostly clear skies for the first half of the night. After midnight, the high slides east and clouds will increase. How fast those clouds arrive will set overnight lows, ranging from 30° to 40°.
Friday: More Rain & Breezy
Our next round of rainfall will arrive on Friday and does look to move in slightly faster than anticipated. Areas west of Bangor see light rain before sunrise Friday, filling in across the rest of the region through late Friday morning. Enough cold air stays trapped across the County for light snow to start. Accumulations stay light and wash away as snow changes to rain by Friday afternoon.
Showers continue through Friday afternoon, ending near sunset, with a few quick passing showers possible early Friday evening.
Rainfall totals for most will average from 0.25″ to 0.75″ with some pocket locally up to an inch.
Saturday: Cold and Windy
As the low departs Friday night into early Saturday, winds increase and colder air moves in behind it.
Expect morning clouds giving way to afternoon sunshine Saturday. Highs in the upper 30s to mid 40s, but feeling at or below freezing with a strong northwest wind gusting to 40 mph. Wrap-around light snow will be possible in the Mountains and north with little to no accumulation.
Saturday night into Sunday morning turns very cold, lows in the 20s in what could be one of the coldest nights so far this season. The breeze makes it feel even colder Sunday morning.
Sunday: Less Wind & Warmer
Mostly sunny skies Sunday with highs in the 40s to low 50s. West winds much weaker, gusts to 20 mph.
Warmer and less breezy conditions arrive early next week.

title: Police investigate report of sexual assault at a fraternity party near the University of Chicago
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Police are investigating a woman’s report that she was sexually assaulted during a fraternity party near the University of Chicago campus, an allegation that comes at a time of heightened awareness of sexual violence on college campuses.
Chicago police said no one had been charged Wednesday, a day after university officials posted an alert saying that a person of interest had been identified.
The Chicago case comes amid an uproar over Cornell University’s handling of a woman’s allegations that she was drugged and gang raped by fraternity members in 2024. A campus investigation led to internal disciplinary action by the university, but no criminal charges were ever filed.
The University of Chicago, a top-ranked U.S. research school with an enrollment of 18,000 students, said in a statement that a woman reported being sexually assaulted early Sunday during a party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house.
The university said the perpetrator fled the house after being confronted by another person.
The 21-year-old woman reported the assault to police and went to a hospital for treatment, according to Chicago police. The university said she is not a student.
Chicago police did not immediately provide a copy of the incident report on the alleged attack when The Associated Press requested it Wednesday.
The Chicago Sun-Times, citing the police report, said the woman told police she had been drinking and dancing at the party before she began feeling unwell. The Sun-Times said the report stated two of the woman’s friends then found her “not fully conscious” in a bathroom with a man and that both were partially undressed.
The friends told police that to get into the bathroom, they had to force their way through several men who were “cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside,” the Sun-Times reported.
Alpha Epsilon Pi said no fraternity members took part in the alleged attack or encouraged it. The fraternity’s University of Chicago chapter said in a statement that its members rushed to help the woman after being alerted by one of her friends and ended the party immediately.
“There is no evidence at all that any AEPi members participated in this assault or were aware of it while it was transpiring,” Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity’s national organization, said in a statement Wednesday.
The fraternity said the perpetrator was chased out of the house and was recorded by cameras while fleeing.
University officials said the person of interest who has been identified is not a student or otherwise affiliated with the school.
The Cornell case came to light last month after a woman filed a lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members, saying she was repeatedly assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024. She went to campus police three weeks later and gave a detailed interview, but local prosecutors never pursued charges. The men she accused have denied wrongdoing.
Cornell announced Tuesday it’s banning parties at fraternity houses until next year. The university said it will include New York State Police in investigations of campus sexual assaults.
Fraternities have also been under scrutiny at the University of Arizona, which suspended fraternity activities earlier this month following multiple reports of assault, hazing and other misconduct.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.

LEWISTON, ME – The City Clerk’s Office would like to inform voters about election details for the November 3 election. There are two ballots for this election – a state ballot and a city ballot.
