title: Can Maine use natural methods to stop shoreline erosion?
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND — On a mild afternoon, sailboats glided across Casco Bay while Southern Maine Community College students sat at picnic tables studying, knitting and talking politics. Just steps away, however, this beloved stretch of coastline is crumbling.
Back-to-back winter storms battered the Willard Beach area three years ago, eating away at fragile bluffs beneath a campus science building and city pump house and closing a popular shoreline walking path.
Now city, regional and state officials are coming together to try to protect the shoreline and infrastructure, using natural methods when they can and hoping to forestall rising seas and worsening storms for as long as they can.
The proposal to protect this small stretch of shoreline, which would involve the combination of riprap, vegetation and a relocated walking path, is one of three that the Greater Portland Council of Governments is using federal grants to help draft.
The plans for South Portland, Mitchell Field in Harpswell and the Yarmouth wastewater treatment plant are far from complete. Variations abound. Nothing is permitted. Nobody knows who might foot the bill.
“It’s clear that something has to be done,” said Sara Mills-Knapp, the sustainability director at Greater Portland Council of Governments and the leader of a nature-based shoreline erosion workshop at Willard Beach on Wednesday.
The Willard Beach workshop serves as a crucial test case for how vulnerable communities can adapt, if not turn back, rising waters without smothering their shorelines under a rigid granite seawall. Instead of concrete, think plants, coir logs and buried trees to rebuild the dune system.
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection now favors such methods during permitting, said Nathan Robbins, the department’s climate change specialist. The state is publishing a new reference guide to help promote nature-based erosion control this week, Robbins said.
Maine sea levels have been rising at a rate of about a half-foot a century. The pace has sped up as the world burns more fossil fuels, producing heat-trapping emissions that warm both air and sea.
Maine sea levels are projected to rise between 1.1 and 3.2 feet by 2050 and 3 and 9.3 feet by 2100, depending on how successful and quick we are at curbing global emissions rates, according to the scientists who advise the Maine Climate Council.
The $800,000 to $1 million Willard Beach proposal would give engineers room to replace the steep, failing bank with a gentler sloped bluff. Unlike hard seawalls that reflect wave energy downward and scoop out beach sand, the sloped bluff dissipates waves.
Heavy vegetative riprap — stone embedded with deep-rooted native plants — would bind the slope, paired with a newly engineered sand dune at the base. As much as they wanted to avoid stone, the consultants agreed Willard Beach requires a mixed approach.
“Plants alone just won’t cut it,” said Lisa Vickers, senior coastal specialist at GEI Consultants.
The proposal, which is about 30% complete, would require moving the walking path a couple hundred feet inland, behind the science building. But that extra space means it will not encroach upon the sandy beach below, a favorite among sunbathers and dog walkers.
Nature-based methods have sparked some tension. Hard seawalls offer immediate structural defense, while living shorelines require two to three growing seasons for native roots to bind sands. Marine contractors are used to dumping heavy granite boulders, not installing soil lifts.
And they could fail with the next winter storm, warned Pete Slovinsky, a marine geologist with the Maine Geological Survey. But so could traditional seawalls and even jettys, even with a high price tag and the harder-to-win permits required to build them, he said.
At the workshop Wednesday, Slovinsky told a crowd of about 30 people that ranged from local residents to engineers working on other erosion control projects that the proposed bluff project would help protect the city pump house for now, but the city should plan to eventually move it.
“The one thing I can guarantee you is that the sea will keep rising,” Slovinsky said. He pointed at the pump house behind him, which sits a couple dozen feet back from the 22-foot bluff. “That’s going to fail. Maybe not today, or next year, but sooner than you think.”
For state leaders, however, these pilot designs mark an essential turning point.
“Rocks don’t have roots,” Robbins said. “Plants have roots, deep roots that can help stabilize from the top of the bluff to the dunes to the beach. And rocks are expensive and require maintenance. Over time, plants will take over and do a lot of our work for us.”

title: Wrong to remove George Mitchell’s name without evidence or proof
text:
Douglas Rooks is the author of “Statesman: George Mitchell and the Art of the Possible” (Down East Books, 2016.) He welcomes comment at [email protected].
The University of Maine System Board of Trustees voted 9-5 on Sept. 28 to remove former Sen. George Mitchell’s name from university programs and scholarships — the latest in a series of such moves following release of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
The removal of Mitchell’s name from scholarships and institutes began back in February in Ireland, which had recognized Mitchell’s central role in the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, a deal that has brought lasting peace to Northern Ireland.
They never knew Mitchell as well as we do here in Maine.
One of the dissenting UMS trustees, Donna Loring, explained her position in a Bangor Daily News op-ed, writing, “My vote was not a declaration that every allegation concerning Mitchell is false. I do not know that. But neither has there been a finding that he committed wrongdoing. The university’s own task force acknowledged that fact.”
Loring’s point is inarguable. Before we remove names, portraits and statues from the public square, there must be an effort to establish the facts, and discern the truth as far as it can be known. Judging from its report, the task force did not attempt this, instead citing “serious allegations” and potential “reputational harm” to the university as deciding factors.
“I worry about a standard in which reputational harm can outweigh the absence of a finding of wrongdoing,” Loring wrote. We should all be worried.
Although the chaotic release of the Epstein files in 2025 by order of Congress was widely assumed to be in the public interest, there are serious doubts. Unedited investigative files and reports — such as those just inadvertently released by the Maine Attorney General’s Office — can be profoundly and unfairly damaging to lives and reputations. If such releases became routine, there would be few reputations left worth having.
Suspicions and allegations that would not normally be public are spread worldwide, with instantaneous reactions and conclusions that then drive policymakers to treat accusations, however serious, as facts, and suspicions as warranted.
News accounts focused on 300 “mentions” of Mitchell’s name among 2.5 million pages of documents; Donald Trump’s name appears more than 30,000 times. By itself, these numbers mean nothing. To this day, no one has been charged with any criminal offenses (except Epstein and his enabler, Ghislaine Maxwell).
If we use suspicion and allegation as the standard, we’re on a slippery slope. It’s a short distance from here to the 1950s McCarthyite “Red Scare,” where guilt by association among “fellow travelers” ruined lives, careers and reputations.
At least the UMS trustees made some attempt to balance the accusations against Mitchell’s lifetime of service. In his hometown, Waterville’s school board swiftly voted 5-2 to remove his name from an elementary school after a handful of complaints. The Legislature’s presiding officers, with no process at all, removed Mitchell’s portrait from the State House, where it had been installed to bipartisan acclaim in 2014.
There are public places in Maine and recognitions in Washington to which Mitchell’s name is still attached. This is far from unanimous.
We should also balance the accusations with an accounting of Mitchell’s achievements. Along with his unique contributions to world peace — among dozens of wars and rebellions in our times, there is hardly another example like it — Mitchell represented Maine with distinction in the U.S. Senate for 15 years. As majority leader, he shepherded dozens of important bills to passage — landmarks in protecting the environment, creating affordable housing and providing better lives for persons with disabilities. Surely this should count.
I am of course not privy to the UMS trustees’ deliberations. As Mitchell’s biographer, however, I can offer testimony from years of research, interviews and discussions involving his family, his staff, political supporters and opponents, those who knew him best in his personal and public life.
In all that time, I never heard of any lapses in personal integrity lending credence to the anonymous, unsourced Epstein allegations. Rather the reverse — in campaigning, in fundraising, in the sometime regrettable business of politics, Mitchell was a stickler for following the rules.
It may be impossible ever to lay to rest the suspicions created by the Epstein files. As so often in the digital age, we are drowning in data of variable quality, with understanding nowhere to be seen.
In the absence of proof, I suggest no further “de-namings” of Mitchell, with its implied public censure, until some reliable standards can be established. Ultimately, history will assess his virtues and flaws, like those of any other human being. The trustees’ majority judgment should not be the last word.

title: Buckle Up: Belfast boat building group aims for 100 mph lobster boat record
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BELFAST, Maine (WABI) - A Belfast-based boat building company is working on a lobster boat designed to exceed 100 miles per hour.
Holland Custom Boats is building the vessel with the goal of breaking lobster boat racing speed records.
“The first thing I’d like to do is scare the competition a little bit,” said Gavin Holland, boat builder.
Gavin Holland has been working around boats since birth.
“I mean, one of the biggest parts is the speed, trying to make things go fast and figure out how to do that,” Gavin Holland said.
A family history of speed
The Holland family has a history of exceeding lobster boat speed expectations.
“I can remember back, they said if we ever made 40 miles an hour, we’re doing good. And the guy that was a naval architect that told me that by that time, by the time he told us we were already pushing 50, he said we’d never get by 40. I said, ‘we’ve passed that a while back,’” said Glenn Holland, boat builder.
The Hollands are seeking to double that 40 mile per hour mark with the new boat.
“There have been rumors, people hitting 80. Never seen it in a race, though. 70s have been achieved. This one did about 60 (Red Baron). But she was a work boat. I mean, it would, like I said, lobster during the week and racing on the weekends. I mean, it wasn’t built for that specific purpose,” Gavin Holland said.
Continuing a family legacy
Gavin Holland said setting the record would continue the family’s legacy of fast boats.
“Continuing that on, I mean, it’s an important thing to me. I don’t want to see it die. I mean, from my great-grandfather, starting out lobstering and my grandfather, designing these and building the reputation that we have, the whole family’s been involved in it forever. I mean, everyone has had a hand in it at some point in my family. So to keep that going, pretty important to me,” Gavin Holland said.
“It’s something I’ve been wanting to do for a long time. And I’m finally getting around to doing it, but he’s going to do it instead of me, which is all right with me,” Glenn Holland said.
Gavin Holland said the new boat might create a new class for lobster boat racing if the project goes to plan.
The team is working on prepping the molds for the new boat. The process will be documented on their website.

title: Watch: Spruce Mountain soccer is the Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week
text:
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Spruce Mountain soccer
Winning hasn’t come easy for the Spruce Mountain girls soccer team over the past handful of years.
The Phoenix won only eight games from 2023-25. It looked like the 2026 season would be more of the same when they started with three straight losses, but then the victories started to pile up.
Since Sept. 11, Spruce Mountain is 6-0-2, including 6-0 and 3-2 wins last week against Wiscasset/Boothbay and Wells, respectively. The Phoenix were ranked sixth in Class C South Heal points going into Wednesday’s games.
“So I think our team is clicking more … in a sense of just distributing the ball and finding that open player and looking for crosses,” Spruce Mountain coach Jacob Turner said. “I think that’s really helped, and I saw that the most in Wells.”
Both Turner and senior captain Ashley Nelson said three freshmen — midfielder Lexus Hebert, forward Evangeline “Gigi” DiPasquale and defender Harlee Foss — have played a big part in the turnaround.
“I think we have the most talent that we have had in a very long time,” Nelson said. “We’ve had three amazing freshmen (who) have stepped up and (taken) on some very important roles on our team.”
Turner said the Phoenix are well balanced throughout the lineup.
“We have a great back system,” Turner said. “Our midfield is strong, and we’re aggressive in the midfield. We have Lexus Hebert and Natasha (McDonald) that can score on some of these really good teams.”
Nelson said she’s been waiting for a postseason push since entering high school.
“We’ve gone hard at practices; everyone wants to be here,” Nelson said. “We’ve wanted this since I was a freshman. We’ve really wanted to pull through and make playoffs.”

title: Luna, a small dog missing for over a month in Yellowstone, is reunited with her owners
text:
(AP) - For over a month, Luna, a Jack Russell terrier that bolted from her family’s cabin during a vacation at Yellowstone National Park, eluded capture as fears for her survival mounted and winter weather approached. On Wednesday, her ordeal came to a happy ending when she was caught and reunited with her owners.
The 10-year-old white dog with pointy ears and a gray collar had been spotted crossing intersections, strolling through employee housing and entering lodges through automatic doors at the sprawling park, home to grizzly bears, wolves and other predators.
Katie Boucher, the volunteer leading the rescue effort and a spokesperson for Luna’s California owners, said she and one of the owners found the dog in the trap baited with scraps from a T-shirt and pillowcase belonging to the family. They took her to a veterinarian, where the owner held the dog as it was examined Wednesday afternoon.
“She’s underweight, but that’s to be expected. She’s alert and in good spirits,” Boucher said. “I was crying all the way up here from the park.”
Luna escaped Sept. 10. Boucher said the dog spent its first year on the streets before being adopted and showed strong survival instincts while on the loose. Based on sightings, Boucher said, Luna retraced her family’s steps from the day before she was lost -- sneaking into eateries or lodges they had visited and seeking shelter in employee residences and businesses.
An escape into the wilderness
The day of the escape, the family left her in their cabin with a “Do Not Disturb” sign while they ventured out to explore the park. They believe a housekeeping staffer accidentally opened a door, freeing the dog.
“The staff then proceeded to chase her around that area of the park for over two hours before the owners came back and discovered all the chaos and their dog missing,” Boucher said.
Yellowstone was the first U.S. national park and covers about 3,500 square miles (some 9,000 square kilometers), including portions of Wyoming, Montana and Idaho.
Luna’s family searched for the dog, which is part chihuahua, but were told it likely died, possibly killed by a coyote, Boucher recounted. Days after leaving Yellowstone, the owners learned Luna had been spotted, and contacted Boucher, president of the Norris Ark Training and Recovery Center in Norris, Montana, north of the park.
“I cannot fathom how I would feel if I had been taking the vacation of a lifetime, and looking for all these memorable experiences in one of the most beautiful places on earth, and lost one of my family members there,” Boucher said.
Locals and tourists called out Luna’s name or chased her, triggering her fight-or-flight response and driving her further into the park, Boucher said. The volunteers set a live trap using the family’s scent to lure Luna in, avoiding food that could attract bears or other wildlife.
Time was running out as winter closes in
Boucher said this was the last week she would have been able to search for Luna. She was sleeping at an RV park for seasonal employees that closes next Monday.
The search had rallied locals and tourists alike. Marie Jaskula, an area resident who runs one of the park’s general stores, posted signs at every park entrance urging visitors to be on the lookout for the dog.
“It’s really hard to stress the importance of do not chase,” said Jaskula. “Everybody sees this little dog buzz across the intersection or maybe around their employee housing, and the first instinct is to call her name and chase her.”
__

title: CMP sues to block Maine law forcing grid participation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s biggest electric utility is suing in federal court to block a new state law that requires participation in the regional electric grid, and strips away a longstanding financial bonus for joining ISO-New England.
Maine’s Office of Public Advocate has stated that removing that incentive, or “adder,” would save electric customers $2 million a year.
In a complaint filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Maine, Central Maine Power said the law, LD 2038, was preempted by the authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which is responsible for setting prices of electric transmission and oversight of regional transmission organizations, or RTOs, such as ISO-New England.
The incentive was granted in recognition that it gave up significant control over its transmission assets, such as construction planning, power dispatch, outage scheduling and approval of new interconnections by power generators, according to CMP.
Requiring CMP to participate in the grid operator “undermines the federal policy regime of voluntary membership in RTOs and forces utilities like plaintiffs to concede property interests and contracted-for rights without compensation,” the utility said in its complaint.
A utility spokesperson declined to comment on the complaint. CMP is joined in the lawsuit by the Maine Electric Power Co., a transmission utility owned jointly by CMP and Versant Power that owns the wires connecting the New England grid to New Brunswick.
An Act to Require Maine Transmission and Distribution Utility Participation in a Regional Transmission Organization was enacted this spring. In September, the Office of Public Advocate petitioned FERC to remove the bonus that gives CMP an added profit margin for their transmission infrastructure.
But the office noted that federal appeals courts and the energy commission have found that utilities no longer qualify for the bonus once state law compels them to join a regional transmission organization.
“Maine electricity customers are paying for something they no longer need to pay for,” Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said in a statement at the time. “Eliminating this outdated adder would mean real savings on their electric bills,” Sanborn added. Sanborn declined to comment on the lawsuit.
The complaint also names Maine Public Utilities Commission Chair Phil Bartlett and acting Commissioner Celina Cunningham of the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
The lawsuit comes as CMP is requesting an increase in the amount its customers pay for service at the same time many Mainers are concerned with the rising cost of energy and other household necessities. The utility serves more than 646,000 customers.
The utilities commission recently rejected the utility’s request for short-term temporary rates until long-term prices are set next year. The company has said its financial situation is precarious and has cut back on infrastructure spending and hiring.

title: Maine has a shortage of home health workers. Is there any way to fix it?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Maine is struggling with workforce shortages in the home healthcare industry, which means the state isn’t able to meet the growing demand, industry experts say.
The problem is far from unique to Maine.
“Like many home health providers across the country, we are experiencing a challenging workforce environment,” said Patty Buiocchi, chief operating officer for post-acute care at MaineHealth who also oversees their home health and hospice programs.
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
Nancy Polito, 78, of Portland, said she struggled to find the caregiving help her mom needed, especially after a stroke.
“It was hard to get anyone to come in and do anything,” said Polito, who was her mother’s primary caregiver until she died in 2010. “I couldn’t leave her alone, and couldn’t find anyone to come in.”
Polito said she’s heard the problem has only gotten worse.
Shawna Ferris, a direct care worker from Mattawamkeag, said access to care and working conditions have worsened over the past two years.
“The cost of living has increased significantly, and the pay has not moved,” Ferris said. “You can go work in a different field and make the same or more money with less responsibilities.”
Home health includes a number of services, such as skilled nursing care for patients rehabilitating at home after a surgery, or patients who need help with daily tasks.
According to the Maine Center for Economic Policy, a progressive think tank, 23,500 hours per week of home health assistance go unfilled in the state because there aren’t enough workers.
“In the next 10-15 years, there’s going to be a lot more people 75 and older who are going to need these services. The demand for workers is growing while the number of people able to fill those roles is plateauing,” said James Myall, an economic policy analyst for the center.
Myall said the 23,500 hours is an undercount because it only looks at people who signed up for Medicaid home health services. It doesn’t consider people who need the services but didn’t bother putting their name down because they know there aren’t enough workers.
SOLUTIONS HARD TO COME BY
Myall said the state has an extreme shortage of direct care workers. Maine needs over 2,000 additional direct care employees, according to a Maine Center for Economic Policy analysis. Those are the staffers who help with daily tasks like cooking, picking up groceries, laundry, and helping people remember to take medications.
“The agencies have not been able to pay their workers enough,” Myall said. “They are getting outbid by retailers like Walmart.”
He said increasing the pay of direct care employees to 140% of the state minimum wage and then giving automatic cost-of-living raises would help alleviate the shortage.
Myall said the Maine Legislature in recent years has approved state reimbursement increases for the nonprofits that hire direct care workers, resulting in modest wage increases. But despite those efforts, wages in other industries, like retail, have increased by more, dampening the effectiveness.
Nonprofit agencies that provide home health services can currently pay their workers 125% of minimum wage, based on what the state’s Medicaid program will reimburse.
The state so far has not substantially increased wages for direct care workers, but lawmakers, including Democratic House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, have advocated for the boost to 140% of minimum wage. The state minimum wage will be $15.70 starting in January, so if that proposal passes, care workers could earn $21.98 per hour.
The Maine Essential Care and Workforce Partnership, a group advocating for better working conditions for direct care workers, is also proposing to improve training, benefits and technology for workers.
DEMAND FOR HELP IS GROWING
Myall said the shortages result in a system where it’s primarily “relatives taking care of their family members, juggling work and caregiving,” Myall said.
“It forces some people out of the workforce,” he said.
Noël Bonam, Maine’s AARP state director, said having a strong home health system will help keep older Mainers from having to move to nursing homes and hospitals. It’s also healthier for them.
“You are keeping that person in the community, and having strong social connections, and that helps them thrive,” Bonam said. “It costs a whole lot less to keep them in the home than taking up a bed in a nursing home.”
Buiocchi said they are able to run the MaineHealth program without workforce shortages, but they have advantages over other employers in that they can offer competitive wages and benefits and a flexible schedule. Also, because they’re a large employer, they have robust training programs and have many pathways for promotions.
Myall said much of the home health industry in Maine consists of nonprofits who don’t have the flexibility to pay higher wages.
Buiocchi said demand for home health services is expected to keep growing.
“The need has increased exponentially over the past five years,” she said.

title: Wells taps police captain as next town manager
text:
The town of Wells has announced that police Capt. Adam Shaw will become its next town manager early next year.
Shaw will succeed Michael Pardue upon his retirement on Jan. 18.
The Select Board unanimously voted last week to appoint Shaw. In a news release Wednesday, the town said Shaw’s public safety, leadership and community service experience demonstrated his commitment to the community.
“Knowing that the members of the Board, elected by the people of Wells, unanimously believe I am the right person to help guide the Town forward and build upon the strong foundation established by current Town Manager Michael Pardue is truly humbling,” Shaw said in a written statement.
“I also recognize that this appointment represents a significant level of trust, not only from the Board, but from the entire community,” Shaw added. “I have always believed that trust is something to be earned, and never taken for granted.”
Select Board Chair Timothy Roche said in the release that the board is confident that Shaw will serve the town “exceptionally well.”
The town said Shaw will work with Pardue and other town officials over the coming months to prepare for the transition.
Wells also recently announced that Brian Pellerin, chief deputy for the Cumberland County Sherriff’s Office, has been appointed as the town’s next chief of police.

title: Husson wins NAC men’s golf championship
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Husson Eagles are NAC men’s golf champions.
Husson won its fifth conference title over the course of six seasons in a nine-shot victory over second-place SUNY Delhi on Saturday at Bangor Municipal Golf Course.
Husson’s Juan Carlos Hernandez won the individual medal with four Eagles finishing in the top six.
“Being able to get it done at home is probably the best feeling we could have asked for going into the weekend. I hit the last putt of the tournament. Once that putt goes in, it’s over, and you guys are winners,” said Ty Dickson, senior.
“Definitely our final four holes of the first day really helped. We were down probably by like 15 strokes, but we went 13-under in the last four holes as a team. That really helped us on the first day. Then the second day, the same four holes helped us accomplish the victory,” said Chase Farnsworth, sophomore.
Next up is the New England Intercollegiate Golf Association Championship this weekend in Brewster, Mass. to close out the fall season.
With their conference title, the Eagles have qualified for the NCAA Championship in May 2027 at Kingsmill Resort in Williamsburg, Va.
Their next goal is to make the cut there.

title: Foreign exporters are pricing Maine lumber mills out of the market
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Foreign exporters are pricing Maine lumber mills out of the market
"He would have never imagined that you could take a truckload of logs from Boston in a container ship to China or Vietnam for $400"
Foreign exporters are pricing Maine lumber mills out of the market
"He would have never imagined that you could take a truckload of logs from Boston in a container ship to China or Vietnam for $400"
Foreign exporters are putting Maine lumber mills in jeopardy.
Kennebec Lumber Company has already closed one sawmill. Its remaining mills are operating at 75% capacity. President Dennis Carrier thinks the industry needs more regulation to level the playing field for American lumber manufacturers.
"You can't get raw material, you can't run a facility," Carrier said.
It costs less to produce manufactured lumber overseas, where labor is cheaper and where mills don't face the same costly safety and environmental regulations.
When asked whether he wanted to lower those standards for mills in the United States, Carrier said, "No, I’d rather raise it. People need to make a living. We believe in that. The American dream. Right? Raise a family, have a nice home."
Lower manufacturing costs allow foreign mills to pay a premium for American logs. Carrier says it's chipping away at the local supply and pricing Maine mills out of the market.
"We can’t afford to pay the same prices for raw material," he said.
Exporters keep calling Carrier, asking to buy the limited supply of logs he has on hand. In between fielding calls, Carrier searches for ways to keep the business his grandfather started afloat.
"He would have never imagined that you could take a truckload of logs from Boston in a container ship to China or Vietnam for $400," Carrier said. "I can't go from Solon to Skowhegan for $400 on truck."
Industry experts say the issue is especially prevalent in China and Vietnam. According to the Hardwood Federation, U.S. mills used to export $1.5 billion worth of hardwood lumber to China each year. That figure has dropped to roughly $701 million annually.
Amid ongoing tariff negotiations, a group of senators and House members, including Sen. Angus King (I) and Rep. Jared Golden (D), wrote to U.S. trade representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer, urging U.S. negotiators to focus on American lumber during trade talks. The lawmakers urged Greer to seek a commitment from China to buy more hardwood lumber, rather than logs.
"In my industry, it seems like they started on the wrong end of the pole, where you have tariffs for furniture coming in and such," Carrier said. "That worked, but all they did is circumvent that by buying our logs and manufacturing on the other side cheaper."
Carrier met with members of Sen. Susan Collins’ office but said he has not seen any changes.
8 Investigates reached out to each member of Maine's congressional delegation to ask whether they had plans to take action on this issue. None provided concrete examples of proposed legislation
Responses from Maine's Congressional Delegation
Sen. Susan Collins (R)
A Collins spokesperson pointed to meetings with Kennebec Lumber Company.
"When Kennebec Lumber Company reached out to Sen. Collins’ office, staff helped to facilitate two separate conversations with the relevant officials at the Department of Commerce," wrote a spokesperson for Collins. "These meetings ensured that the mill was able to make its case to the Administration officials overseeing the rules governing export caps.”
Rep. Chellie Pingree (D)
Rep. Chellie Pingree’s office touted the fact that she's a co-sponsor of the Fair Trade for Working Families Resolution, which aims to boost domestic manufacturing.
A spokesperson for Pingree wrote, "I’m also working to grow demand for homegrown wood. As Ranking Member of the Interior Appropriations Subcommittee, I was proud to secure $30 million for Wood Innovation grants and $15 million for the Community Wood Energy program for Fiscal Year 2026. I also support the Wildfire Reduction Market Expansion Act, which modernizes the Renewable Fuel Standard to recognize more woody materials as renewable biomass."
Rep. Jared Golden (D)
A spokesperson for Golden said his office is in contact with forest products industry leaders.
"Congressman Golden and his staff are in regular contact with leaders and workers from the forest products industry and he’s committed to doing what he can to ensure fair competition across the border," a spokesperson wrote.
King’s team declined 8 Investigates' request for comment.
8 Investigates also reached out to candidates in Maine’s midterm elections.
Responses from Maine Midterm Candidates
Troy Jackson (D)
"President Trump and Susan Collins’ illegal tariffs and war in Iran are pushing Maine’s economy toward the brink," wrote a spokesperson for U.S. Senate candidate and former state Senate President Troy Jackson. "Troy understands firsthand that many of Maine’s bedrock industries are paying the price. We’re headed for a disaster if Congress doesn’t take back its authority, end the war, and bring common sense to trade policy. When Troy is elected, that’s what he will do."
Ron Russell (R)
"If elected I will do everything in my power to help legacy industries continue to survive in this great state," wrote congressional district one candidate Ron Russell, who's challenging Pingree. "It would seem like putting a cap on log exports might help this particular mill owner so it is something that I would certainly take a look at."
Candidates for Maine's Second Congressional District, former Gov. Paul LePage and state auditor Matt Dunlap, have not responded to 8 Investigates' request for comment.
While some call for tighter trade regulations, not everyone is in agreement.
Forest economist Eric Kingsley doesn't think export caps are the solution.
"Anything but increased market demand is a Band-Aid on a gaping wound," said Kingsley during a call with 8 Investigates.
Kingsley believes lawmakers should start by improving the economy and paving the way for more home construction. Increased demand would help both loggers and lumber manufacturers.

title: A blueprint for disaster for Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Luisa S. Deprez, Ph.D., of Cape Elizabeth is professor emerita of sociology and social policy at the University of Southern Maine.
Once again, the notorious, dangerous and ultra-conservative Maine heritage foundation, the Maine Policy Institute, has gone out of its way to attempt to undermine the safety and security and well-being of Maine families.
Its newest approach to doing so is described in the recently released 2026 Maine Policy Blueprint, a dictum that leaves no stone unturned when it comes to proposals that will threaten the lives of children and families while undermining communities and, ultimately, the state.
Perhaps the children and families of the institute’s staff and collaborators will not suffer but be assured that hundreds of thousands throughout the state will.
Its impact would be similar to its national predecessor, Project 2025, which Donald Trump and his Republican loyalists used to decimate the federal government and unleash a flurry of executive orders, rule changes and (il)legal maneuvers designed to inflict harm on millions of Americans.
They include cuts to Medicaid and food programs; reduction and elimination of education programs for special needs children and low-achieving communities; decreased regulations of toxic chemicals both in the air and in your food and water; purging of research programs studying cancer, heart disease, diabetes and other chronic diseases; erasure of vaccination protocols; disregard for national park protections; and on the horizon, plans to upend Head Start by “stripping away standards on health and literacy … and brushing teeth.” Who knows what’s in store Social Security and Medicare?
The Blueprint purports to promote a Maine where “people are freer, more prosperous, or better able to afford happy lives.” To do so it suggests overall reforms in every sector.
Among them:
Environmental: End “state-level hostility toward fossil fuel and nuclear power” while removing regulatory and permitting barriers; end vehicle inspection mandates (ever been behind a vehicle with no brake lights on a dark road at night?); repeal all emissions reductions goals as well as nuclear referendum requirements; reduce funding for water quality by 15%; ban subsidies on EV sales.
Education: Allow public schools to transition to a charter school if they wish, reducing state expenditures for public schools and turning over educational standards and curriculum to a private enterprise; eliminate funding for adult education and turn over adult and community education, adult basic education, adult high school diploma programs, high school equivalency diploma testing, family literacy, job skills training, and college transition programs to the private sector; eliminate funding for the Department of Education’s office of student supports; reduce the state reimbursement rate for school administration encouraging central office staffing, and management functions; give authority for public school curriculum and learning wholly to parents.
Housing: Eliminate rent control; eliminate the Housing Opportunity Program targeting low- and moderate-income households and community workforce housing needs; abolish minimum lot sizes and parking mandates.
Health: Repeal the paid family medical leave program; repeal Medicaid expansion (30% of Mainers had MaineCare coverage in 2025, most children and elders); increase state employees’ share of health insurance premiums; contract-out prison medical services.
Food: Eliminate funding for Maine’s universal school meals program; eliminate statewide hunger relief program — breakfast, lunch, after-school, weekends, summer; expand work requirements for those receiving SNAP (about 40,000 of 170,000 current recipients); move food programs to DHHS.
Economy: Repeal the 2% income tax hike on incomes above $1 million for single filers; freeze the minimum wage and deregulate occupational licensing; targeted 10% reduction in central administrative units (567 jobs); lease or concession-manage Maine’s most visited, highest cost parks to eliminate payroll, seasonal staffing, overtime pay and day-to-day maintenance; eliminate funding for international commerce that promotes exports, international student recruitment and overseas trade opportunities for Maine businesses.
Veterans services: A 10% cut focused on outreach, technology and central-office staffing.
Law enforcement: Require all state and local police to cooperate with ICE.
This is not Maine as it should be nor as it is. The intent of the Blueprint is not to ensure that Maine “people are freer, more prosperous or better able to afford happy lives” but to slash expenditures that actually enable Mainers to be freer, more prosperous, safer, and able to live lives of value. Like Project 2025, it guarantees that only the private sector flourishes.
This Blueprint will be the agenda for every Republican up for election in any race in the state. We have seen this played out before. Project 2025 devastated the federal government and the state and continues to do so.
As you go to the polls, ask yourself this question: Do you want this Blueprint to be our future? If you say “No,” know who you are voting for. Be sure they share your sentiments.

title: A 14-year-old was shot in the face, losing his eye. His friend is now facing charges
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - A 14-year-old South Carolina boy is traumatized after he was shot in the face and lost an eye. His 17-year-old friend is now facing charges, police say.
Derrick Simmons, 14, is facing a long road to recovery after he was shot in the face Friday, losing his left eye. His mother, Davida Simmons, says the incident has changed her son’s life.
“He was like, ‘Mom, I can’t play football no more.’ And I tell him, ‘You can still do anything that’s possible. Don’t let this hinder you,’” Simmons said.
Charleston Police say officers responded to a downtown apartment complex around 1 p.m. Friday and found Derrick with a gunshot wound to the face. Police say the 14-year-old and a 17-year-old friend were handling a gun when the older teen pointed the gun at Derrick and fired.
A call from the hospital changed everything for Derrick’s mother.
“I got the first call around 1:35. I had, like, 20-something missed calls... So, I was panicking,” Simmons said. " So, I came down to the hospital and talked to one of the nurses. She was telling me that my son was shot twice. He was shot once in the eye. Then, he was shot once in the shoulder. So, I asked the doctor, ‘Can you save his eye?’ His eye is not savable at all. His eye is completely gone."
Simmons says her son is recovering from surgery, but the trauma is still with him.
“He was telling me that he was scared, and I told him, ‘The best birthday gift was you still here,’” Simmons said.
She says her son has had nightmares since the shooting.
“He was trying to figure out why he can’t open his eyes. He was trying to open his eyes. So, he finally grasped the idea last night when I told him, ‘You can’t open your eyes because your eye is not there anymore.’ So, he started crying because he was trying to figure out why. Why did this happen to me?” Simmons said.
As her son begins a long recovery that will include getting a prosthetic eye, Simmons is urging gun owners to make sure children can’t access their firearms.
“If you own a firearm, the best thing for you to do, if you have kids that’s active or any situation, it’s best to keep it locked up because things like this can happen. I don’t want another mother to go through what I’m going through,” she said.
Police say the 17-year-old suspect admitted to shooting Derrick. He was arrested and charged with assault and battery of a high and aggravated nature, possession of a firearm during the commission of a violent crime and possession of a firearm under 18.
He was booked into the South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice.
Keeping guns out of teens’ hands
Jerome Smalls, developer of youth outreach for the Charleston Police Department, said preventing gun violence takes a community effort.
“There’s a culture around firearms, right? Around it being exciting or cool or part of a facade or an identity. We need to do a better job, both in schools and our communities and as a whole, in changing that culture and that narrative of what it means to be cool and to be associated with firearms,” Smalls said.
Smalls said many young people access firearms through unlocked vehicles.
“The kids call it poking, where they go pull loose door handles, and if it’s unlocked, that’s the number one way firearms are getting in the hands of not just young people but other folks in our community,” he said.
Smalls said the department is working with local organizations, including Representation Matters, on youth programs focused on keeping guns out of young people’s hands.
“If we can get a better hold in marketing and understanding that hey, you have a very dangerous piece of machinery that you own, and you need to be accountable and responsible with that machinery, I think that right there – it doesn’t end it all – but it can curve a lot of young people getting their hands on firearms,” he said.
Carlos DeVeaux, co-executive director of the Representation Matters Foundation, said he works directly with the teen suspect and his family.
“It’s a very unfortunate situation, and it’s kind of personal because I work hand-in-hand with the children in the community. The teenager that it happened to, I work hand-in-hand with him and his parents,” DeVeaux said. “I just think that parents need to pay more attention to the children and don’t give them too much options... But most of all, men, more Black men need to step up and get into these children’s lives, pay attention to their movement, pay attention to what bothers them because too much guns are getting into these children’s hands.”
DeVeaux said his organization works to show young people role models who look like them.
“If you show a child that somebody that looks like them have done it before, they feel that they can do it,” he said.

title: New documentary 'The Eyes of Ghana' produced by the Obamas and streamer IShowSpeed
text:
New documentary 'The Eyes of Ghana' shows the rise and fall of an African leader
Produced by Barack and Michelle Obama's production company
New documentary 'The Eyes of Ghana' shows the rise and fall of an African leader
Produced by Barack and Michelle Obama's production company
A new documentary produced by Barack and Michelle Obama and the popular streamer IShowSpeed is coming to theaters.
Related video above: Sylvester Stallone digs into painful memories and the making of 'Rocky'
"The Eyes of Ghana" is a documentary about Chris Hesse, the personal cameraman of the revolutionary African leader Kwame Nkrumah. In 1957, Nkrumah became the first democratically elected president of Ghana, after it won independence from the United Kingdom. In 1966, Nkrumah's government was deposed in a military coup while he was on a state visit to China.
Hesse, now 93 years old, was there to document it all. He even, as the film claims, hid and protected rolls of archival film from Nkrumah's enemies, who sought to destroy it. The documentary follows Hesse as he uncovers the film after years and screens it publicly in Ghana's capital of Accra for the first time.
The film is directed by Ben Proudfoot, an Academy Award-winning short film director. It is produced by the Obamas' production company, Higher Ground Productions, as well as Darren Watkins Jr., a popular internet streamer known as IShowSpeed, or simply Speed.
The film originally premiered at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival and will be released in U.S. theaters on Oct. 28.

title: ’Some sus s--- going on’: What Nolan Wells’ friends said in texts after he mysteriously disappeared
text:
(Gray News) - Phone records reveal how Nolan Wells’ friends privately talked about his death and what they planned to tell police.
Wells went to Horn Island in Mississippi with friends to celebrate the July 4 holiday but never came home. His body was found two days later on the shore of the island.
The Wells family’s outside analysis of his phone, compiled by Garrett Discovery, has since been publicly released, People reported.
The 292-page report includes private messages from 29 group chats in which Wells’ phone was included.
The messages show Wells’ friends reacting in real time to news that he was found dead as well as to accusations that they were involved in his death.
In a message sent on July 5, a user indicated that Wells seemed fine in the early evening on July 4: “he came and was hanging out with us and around us, he never disappeared with [redacted] when it was time to leave around like 6 he got off our boat with this other guy and thy started walking back to their boat.”
In the early morning hours of July 5, several messages were sent to Wells asking where he was and whether he was OK, CBS News reported.
At 11:59 a.m. on July 5, a user wrote in one of the chats: “There is def some sus s--- going on.”
Soon after, a user said that thousands of people had been “on that damn island and nobody knows who he was with.”
Another user said at 11:12 a.m., “They did sum wit bra.”
And at 12:24 p.m. that day, members of one of the group chats appeared to question the account that Wells had chosen to remain on Horn Island: “if he was gone ride with somebody else why would he leave his phone on the boat,” one user wrote.
In one of the group chats, a user told everyone on July 5 sent at 12:56 p.m., to check their camera rolls for photos or videos in which Wells might appear in the background.
“See if he was talking to anyone we don’t know,” read a message.
One person wrote that Wells appeared in a video recorded at 12:39 p.m., and at 4:28 p.m. on July 5, someone wrote that their friend group was getting blasted on “fb” and warned “dont read that bs or or be running yalls mouth bc ppl will make an inch turn into a mile.”
“No one say anything to anyone out of our friendgroup,” read another message.
On July 5 at 6:52 p.m., a user wrote that police had just contacted them. “They’ve called everyone,” another message reads.
On July 6 at 9:22 a.m., a user issued what they described as “a little advice,” writing that “if we get called in for questioning” then “the smart move is to ask for an attorney and that doesn’t mean we’re guilty it just smart so we don’t get played by some potential bias cop.”
Less than 30 minutes later, a user reported that Wells’ body had been found, writing, “They got him.”
“There’s no [expletive] way,” one user responded, adding that Wells was “the best [expletive] person.”
“I love Nolan he would want us to stay together through this and be there to live on his lecacy [sic],” another message read.
“It’s nationwide,” a message sent at 11:35 a.m. on July 6 read.
On July 6 at 12:44 p.m. one user said “Don’t speculate about s--- yall.”
Another message warned, “Bc they can try to get your ass.” And another advised: “just stick to what you know happened.”
On July 6 at 12:45 p.m., a user wrote, in part, “We have nothing to hide.”
By July 7, the conversation had turned to accusations of a cover-up.
On July 7 at 1:40 p.m., a user wrote, “They posted this update and every single comment is just abt how we’re covering it up.”
On July 13 at 4:08 p.m., a user, identified as Tracestin Shepherd, who was quoted in a July 12 Rolling Stone article, wrote that they were sorry if an interview they had done caused any backlash: “that wasn’t my intention at all was just tryna clear our group of what I know was the truth.”
On July 14 at 9:43 a.m., someone wrote, “We need to go to Nolan’s funeral and get with all our other black friends to prove a statement for the media. It would shut everything down.”
Less than an hour later, someone said, “It’s almost like their brainwashing Nolan’s parents and taking advantage of them while their overwhelmed and grief.”
On July 20, the day of Wells’ funeral, a user reacted to the news that a reward was being offered in Wells’ death investigation.
“They are doing such a disservice at a funeral and so ignorant,” the message read, in part.
The same day, there was a discussion about putting up a cross for Wells. “Bring his flip flops,” a user wrote on the night of July 20. “We can bury those as well.”
Last month, Jackson County’s district attorney announced a Mississippi grand jury found no criminal wrongdoing in Wells’ death.
The grand jury said the position, condition and location of his body, along with the time it was discovered, were “consistent with drowning.”
Liza Park, an attorney on Wells’ family attorney Ben Crump’s team, said the state autopsy found two 2-inch contusions — or bruises — on the back of Nolan’s head. This is consistent with what Dr. Roger Mitchell found when he conducted the independent autopsy.
Park emphasized that Dr. Mitchell found no white blood cells, meaning the injury to Nolan’s head happened within a short period of time before he died.
Park noted that the state autopsy report says the larynx and hyoid bone are without hemorrhages and fractures, and the interior spine was “unremarkable.”
The toxicology results included in the report say chest decomposition fluid contained 270 mg/dL of ethanol. Cannabinoids, nicotine, cotinine and caffeine were all “presumptive positive,” but it said confirmatory testing did not reveal cannabinoids in the decomposition fluid.
Experts said there was no fluid or debris in his airways, his GI tract was “unremarkable” and his stomach was empty.
His lungs and throat did not contain any water.

title: Dunlap and LePage debated, hotly, for the final time. Here are 3 takeaways
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage faced off Thursday— sometimes arguing — for the final time on the debate stage before Election Day.
The Democratic state auditor and Republican former governor are locked in one of the nation’s most competitive races for the U.S. House. The only major poll of the race, conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center in September, found Dunlap with a six-point edge.
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, the second-most rural in the country, has voted for President Donald Trump three times while also electing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden to a House seat since 2018. With Golden not running for reelection, the seat is wide open.
The race is of national importance. Democrats’ path to recapture the House — currently held by Republicans with a four-seat majority — would be significantly bolstered if Dunlap can hold off LePage, one of Maine’s most prominent Republicans.
Those were the stakes for the candidates coming into Thursday’s debate. It was hosted by WABI and WAGM.
Here are three takeaways.
1. There were quite a few spiky moments.
During discussion about declining healthcare access in Maine, Dunlap criticized PL 90, a law championed by LePage during his time as governor that set up a pool of high-risk patients and subsidized their insurance with a fee on all individual health insurance plans in Maine.
“It’s an all-you-can-eat buffet for the insurance companies,” Dunlap said, repeating criticisms about PL 90 from 2012.
“What are you reading?” LePage shot back. “PL 90 lowered the premiums by 76%.”
“That’s not true,” Dunlap said, leaving LePage seemingly exasperated.
“Matt, you’ve been lying a lot this campaign,” LePage said.
Dunlap later accused LePage of calling Social Security a “welfare program,” and quoted from a 2014 press release in which the LePage administration criticized transfer programs, where the federal government sends money to the state, which then disburses funds. The release lumped Social Security in with those programs.
“Quote: ‘It doesn’t matter what liberals call these payments, it is welfare, pure and simple,’ said Gov. LePage,” Dunlap said, pulling from the release. “Including those Social Security payments we just discussed.”
LePage and Dunlap sparred on this for a full minute and a half while moderators Jon Small and Kelly O’Mara attempted to go to a commercial break.
“I’ll just say this,” LePage said, getting the last word in before the halfway point. “If Jared doesn’t retire, you’re not here tonight.”
At the end of the debate, Dunlap challenged LePage about his time living in Florida. LePage has been back and forth between the two states since he left the Blaine House in 2019. He began renting an apartment in Augusta the same month he announced his candidacy for Congress last spring.
LePage said he was a “snowbird,” living in Florida during the winter and Maine during the summer. He said he never spent a full year in Florida and paid his taxes here.
That point emerged again in the candidates’ final remarks.
“He just got a Maine driver’s license right after he declared he was going to run for Congress here,” Dunlap said.
“I never said I didn’t have a Florida driver’s license,” LePage interrupted.
2. Global conflict was, again, a major focus.
The debate began with a question on increasing heating oil assistance. Heating oil, used by about half of Maine households, is hovering near its all-time record price — it rose to over $6 per gallon last month.
Dunlap said heating assistance through the Home Energy Assistance Program should be fully funded, and that the war in Iran was the primary driver of costs. The reduction of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began in February has caused oil prices to spike worldwide.
LePage agreed on the first point — that HEAP should have more backing from the federal government — but challenged the second. Instead of pulling out of Iran, he said, the U.S. Navy and Air Force should force regime change there, though he said the U.S. should not put “boots on the ground.”
“Too many Americans are getting killed in other countries by proxies and the regime in Iran,” LePage said. “So I do believe it’s time to take ’em out.”
“Paul LePage is talking about regime change, and yet not putting any boots on the ground,” Dunlap responded. “I’m not sure how that happens without having American troops committed in a combat situation.”
The moderators also asked about the U.S. trade war with Canada, which has put strain on Maine businesses.
LePage said he has urged the Trump administration to return to the negotiating table, not least because tariffs can be a useful negotiating tool.
Dunlap said he would hope to act instead as a check on Trump, challenging his power to unilaterally impose tariffs.
3. Healthcare kept coming back up.
The most spirited and substantive discussion during the first half of the debate took place in response to a question about healthcare access.
LePage said he wanted to return to the insurance subsidy program he championed as governor, and Dunlap said he hoped to move toward universal healthcare.
LePage had pivoted from a question on immigration to his intent to work across the aisle with Democrats in Congress, and said Dunlap would simply block efforts to take action. Dunlap further pivoted to universal healthcare, saying adopting such a system would, on average, save money. LePage said the cost would be “astronomical.”

title: 104-year-old Brewers fan hopes for World Series win as 105th birthday gift
text:
104-year-old Brewers fan hopes for World Series win as 105th birthday gift
Ruth Werning, a 104-year-old Milwaukee Brewers fan turning 105 next month, predicts a 6-2 win and hopes for a World Series birthday gift.
104-year-old Brewers fan hopes for World Series win as 105th birthday gift
Ruth Werning, a 104-year-old Milwaukee Brewers fan turning 105 next month, predicts a 6-2 win and hopes for a World Series birthday gift.
Ruth Werning is 104 years old and will celebrate her 105th birthday next month. She said there would be no better present than seeing the Brewers win the World Series.
“Oh my, would it ever,” Werning said when asked whether a championship would be a big gift. “I’m able to get around. Put me on a bus, put me on an airplane. Oh, I think I’d have something to look forward to.”
The Brewers are one win away from a World Series.
Werning, a lifelong fan, remembers the Brewers’ 1982 World Series appearance, when Milwaukee faced the St. Louis Cardinals.
More than four decades later, she is hoping to see the team return to baseball’s biggest stage.
She may also be a familiar face to Brewers fans.
Shortly before the 2024 postseason, Werning threw out the ceremonial first pitch at a game against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Milwaukee won that game 6-4.
For NLCS Game 3, Werning predicted another Brewers victory — this time by a score of 6-2.
She also had a plan for celebrating with the people watching alongside her.
“There will be several people here probably watching games together,” Werning said. “Maybe I could say I would treat them all to a drink. We can get that here.”
When asked about her secret to longevity, Werning said she drinks a glass of wine a day and a gin and tonic on Sunday.

title: Jackson backs sovereignty, Collins delivers cash. Which matters to Wabanaki communities?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Weeks after he was sworn in as president of the state Senate, Democrats Troy Jackson and House Speaker Sara Gideon called a meeting of the Wabanaki chiefs at the capitol. All five attended.
There, the lawmakers posed a question: “How do you want to fix this?”
By early 2019, there was a growing appetite to address the fraught relationship between the state and the Wabanaki Nations, which stems from a 1980 settlement that placed unique limits on the tribes’ jurisdiction. But Gov. Janet Mills was known to oppose sweeping changes to that agreement, and so the can of worms Jackson and Gideon were opening was a politically inconvenient one.
Tribal officials in the room were struck by the earnestness of the new leaders’ approach.
“That was refreshing to hear,” recalled Maulian Bryant, who attended as the ambassador for the Penobscot Nation. “I think for a long time the tribes were being told by the state what was good for us.”
Now locked in a furiously tight U.S. Senate race against Republican incumbent Susan Collins, Jackson’s past is serving him well in tribal communities.
“Troy is one of the leaders that we can credit with changing tribal-state relations in the state of Maine, and I am so honored to be his friend and supporter,” Bryant, who now serves on the Penobscot tribal council, told a crowd Saturday as she introduced Jackson at a campaign rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders.
Collins has not championed tribal sovereignty — the notion that Wabanaki Nations’ authority over tribal lands should not be curtailed by state oversight — in Congress the way Jackson did in the State House, and she’s generally perceived to be at odds with tribal leaders on the issue. Congress adopted the settlement with the tribes and could consequently crack it open again.
For some Wabanaki voters, Collins has won support with the depth of her personal connections paired with millions in federal spending she’s directed to Indigenous communities.
In different ways, Collins and Jackson have both proven themselves to be worthy advocates of tribal issues.
Will it win over tribal members and their allies?
‘SHE DOESN’T FORGET’
The cornucopia of the Collins campaign is her power as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
She’s taken credit for nearly $6 million for housing improvements on the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Motahkomikuk (Indian Township); $5 million to improve the wastewater system on the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Sipayik (Pleasant Point); $530,000 to improve sidewalks in a Mi’kmaq affordable housing development; and several million more for programs run by Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness.
“She’s been instrumental in so much relating to our community,” said William Nicholas Sr., the long-serving chief of Motahkomikuk and a one-time Republican who is now an independent.
When the Trump administration went on a slashing spree last year and halted payouts on federal grants, Sipayik found itself stuck, rather literally, in the water, when a $4 million grant to protect the wastewater treatment system from climate-related flooding was frozen.
Tribal officials met with Collins on the hill, and she swiftly persuaded the administration to release the funds.
On Thursday, the Collins campaign picked up an endorsement from Sipayik Chief Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett. In a letter announcing the decision, Bassett cited Collins’ successful efforts to direct and secure funding for the tribe.
Like her ability to wield congressional funding at home, Collins can effectively leverage strong interpersonal relationships in some tribal communities.
She attended the inauguration of former Sipayik Chief Fred Moore in 2015.
When Collins visits Motahkomikuk — the Wabanaki community she has directed the most money to — “it’s always about how she can help people and help the tribe,” said Chief Nicholas, who describes the senator as “a friend.”
“What I hear when I’m around my elders is the fact that she doesn’t forget them,” he said.
Shane Hill, the director of transportation, realty and asset management for the Mi’kmaq Nation, is an anti-Trump Republican. He lives in Caribou, near Collins’ family farm, and his wife works for the family’s lumber supply company.
Hill ran into the senator at Tim Hortons several years ago, when he was the superintendent of the Northern Maine Veterans Memorial Cemetery, and mentioned an upcoming inspection by the Department of Veterans Affairs. He received a near-perfect score that year, and months later Collins called him up from the crowd at a ceremony to thank him, and later sent him a signed photograph of the two of them together.
“Maybe we wouldn’t agree politically on everything,” Hill said. “However, I think she’s done a great job with her high rank and being from the community that I’m from, you know, you’d be foolish to think that doesn’t have any pull.”
‘HE DIDN’T STAND DOWN’
In response to Jackson and Gideon’s question, “How do you want to fix this?” lawmakers established a task force.
The group published 300 pages of research, testimony and recommendations that have underpinned numerous bills and laws in the years since.
Although the most ambitious of those bills haven’t cleared Mills’ desk, Bryant — who now leads the Wabanaki Alliance, a coalition of tribes fighting for tribal sovereignty — said the work reframed tribal-state relations and forced Mills to wrestle with the issue.
“I think that was brave of (Jackson) and (Gideon) to take that on,” she said.
Jackson butted heads with the governor numerous times on the issue during his time leading the Senate, calling her veto of one sovereignty bill in 2023 “disappointing but unsurprising.”
The Mi’kmaq Nation endorsed Jackson in the gubernatorial primary, but has stayed silent since he entered the Senate race.
Teresita Hamel, the Mi’kmaq vice chief who spoke only for herself, said Jackson’s leadership and willingness to fight for tribal sovereignty have won her over.
“He didn’t stand down and turn his back on the Wabanaki Nations,” she said.
Even tribal leaders like Nicholas will praise Jackson’s affability and commitment to sovereignty, an issue that Collins has been mostly quiet about, or at times antagonistic.
There was a 2012 incident, when Collins confirmed with the Office of the Maine Attorney General that an amendment to federal disaster relief laws would usurp state authority and therefore not benefit the Wabanaki Nations. She elicited as much from the bill’s sponsor on the Senate floor: “This provision would not and should not apply within or to the State of Maine.”
Collins has maintained she was unaware of the chiefs’ objections at the time.
And in 2022, there was a bill sponsored by Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd-District, that would’ve made all beneficial federal laws applicable to the Wabanaki Nations going forward. It wouldn’t have restored full tribal sovereignty, but it was a step toward righting what Wabanaki leaders say is one of the 1980 settlement’s most pernicious wrongs.
In the Democratically controlled Senate, it was a member of the majority caucus, Maine’s independent Sen. Angus King, who blocked the bill.
Collins earned no favors when she stayed silent.
“We were never in a position to flesh out her position, because there were other people in the Senate who caucused with Democrats who were standing in the way of it,” Golden said in an interview.
STATE VS. FEDERAL
Tribal sovereignty is one of those rare divisive issues that transcends party politics. Among non-tribal politicians, the dividing line appears generational, observed Golden.
“There’s a lot of people that are very dug in against tribal sovereignty in Maine politics, and they’re all, let’s just say, above a certain age,” he said.
After King killed Golden’s bill, lawmakers and tribal leaders alike are aligned in feeling that sovereignty has to start with support at the state level.
That’s why four chiefs, including Nicholas, endorsed Democrat Hannah Pingree for governor last week. Pingree has promised to pass and sign tribal sovereignty legislation in her first 100 days.
Bassett, the sole chief to make an endorsement in the Senate race so far, was also the only chief who did not endorse Pingree.
A working group in the Maine Legislature is currently developing a proposal for state-level changes that would allow the Wabanaki Nations to benefit from all or most federal laws that apply to other Indian tribes.
State and tribal officials are confident that they can make the change at the state level.
A Collins spokesperson in a statement Tuesday reiterated the senator’s support for the applicability of individual federal laws, but declined to take a position on the matter at the federal level. A spokesperson for Jackson said “Troy believes the Wabanaki Nations deserve the same respect, rights and opportunities as other federally recognized tribes,” but did not take a stance on this specific issue.
People like Nicholas and Hill will overlook Collins’ past silence on sovereignty and take the wins — all $6 million of them — that are attainable until the issue is settled at the state level.
“When we get there, I think we’re going to have that discussion, but it’s not right now,” Nicholas said.
Hamel, the Mi’kmaq vice chief, looks at it differently.
“Having a champion for sovereignty at this time in our growth, I think that’s extremely important,” she said. “I think that that’s the fight we need to take on.”
Jackson and Collins both have their shortcomings: Jackson his lack of power and experience, and Collins her unwillingness to lead the charge.
Their supporters are not willing to let these imperfections be the enemy of their good.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 15 to add information about Chief Pos Bassett’s endorsement.
