title: Maine Mariners restocked, eager for more after lengthy playoff run
text:
PORTLAND — Rick Kowalsky sat on a bench at Troubh Ice Arena and flashed a smile as he untied and kicked off his skates following a Maine Mariners practice Monday afternoon.
“My feet are frozen,” he said.
There were more reasons besides the relief of warm shoes for the Mariners’ second-year coach to smile. The start of the new ECHL season is fast approaching, and with training camp in the books, the Mariners are starting the season on much better footing than they did last season, which ended up being among the franchise’s most memorable.
“We feel pretty good about what we’ve got and where we’re at,” Kowalsky said. “We started (last year) with probably 15 skaters, and not even half of those guys ended up sticking with us. … We started camp (last week) with 25, 26.
“It has a completely different feel than last year did.”
The NHL extended its regular season and shortened its preseason this year, speeding up when players landed with affiliated minor league teams. So the Mariners, rather than being largely TBD in early October, arrived for training more fully assembled.
“This is the first time, probably ever, other than when I was in the NHL, where we implemented systems for an exhibition game,” said Kowalsky, a former assistant with the New Jersey Devils. “You feel like you can hit the ground running.”
The season may have a different feel, but Kowalsky and the Mariners hope to build on last year’s success. Maine went deeper in the playoffs than ever before, reaching Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals before falling to Wheeling.
For the 14 players who made that run and are on this year’s roster, there are higher expectations.
“We know our goal, and our standard is to fight for a Kelly Cup,” said forward Wyllum Deveaux, who has served as the team’s captain since January 2025. “From the start of camp, it’s been known. We’ve picked up where we left off.”
A familiar face will be able to help with that. Maine brought back defenseman Connor Doherty, who captained the Mariners from 2021-24 and then played two seasons with the Florida Everblades, where he won the Kelly Cup last year.
As an ECHL veteran, Doherty had the choice of where to continue his career. The Mariners were interested in the reunion, and so was the 33-year-old Doherty, who played all 20 of Florida’s playoff games last season and led the team in plus-minus.
“I loved my time playing here,” Doherty said. “My wife and I wanted to try something for a couple of years, move down south and check that out. Obviously, we had some success in hockey, but now we’re just excited to be back here. I want to keep dragging this organization further and further, and hopefully accomplish something sweet up here.”
He didn’t have to make much of an adjustment.
“I feel like the first couple of days walking into the rink, it’s kind of like ‘Did I ever leave?'” he said.
Both Kowalsky and Deveaux said Doherty’s presence as a veteran leader and championship player will be important for a group of teammates looking to take a step closer to a title of their own.
“Bringing that championship pedigree is huge,” Deveaux said. “He plays the right way, he stands up for teammates and he plays on the edge. And he brings it every night.”
He’ll help anchor a defense that should be strong. Owen Gallatin, Michael Underwood, Nick Anderson and Jaxon Bellamy are back from last year’s playoff roster.
Brad Arvanitis is gone after a strong season in net, but Luke Cavallin (2.02 goals-against average in 10 playoff games) is back after leading the Mariners through the postseason, and Max Lundgren, last year’s Hockey East Tournament MVP at Merrimack College, will battle him for playing time.
“We definitely feel very good about goaltending again,” Kowalsky said. “(And) we’re way ahead of the game with our defense. Last year, we didn’t even have a right-shot defenseman, and I think three of the seven defensemen we started with didn’t even make it until Christmas.”
The big question marks come on offense, where three of the top six scorers from a season ago are gone. Max Andreev, Robert Cronin and Linus Hemstrom bring back some scoring punch, Ryan Francis and Mason Primeau should factor in, and the team also gets Deveaux back for a full season after an injury in last year’s opener limited him to seven regular-season games.
“That’s first and foremost (my focus), is being healthy, playing every single game this year,” he said. “As a leader as well, that’s my biggest thing. Taking care of myself, making sure I’m ready to go and showing the other guys that that’s the standard here.”
Or at least, one of them. The Mariners hope they set a new one last year.
“We feel pretty good about the group,” Kowalsky said. “We want winners, we want leaders, we want character people, that was a big part of my recruiting process, and I think we’ve done a good job of that.”

title: Maine Wildness is the name of the state’s new women’s soccer team
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — The name was announced and was immediately greeted by an extended and hearty ovation.
The Maine Wildness, the newly named amateur women’s soccer club that will be a sister team to the Portland Hearts of Pine, is already a hit. And so is the club’s logo, a blend of new imagery with a clear connection to the Hearts.
“It’s perfect. All of it,” said Nicole Vinal, a native Mainer who lives in Brunswick. Vinal said the name and the story behind it represents her. “I’m scrappy. I’m a hard worker. I love the outdoors, the wilderness.”
Vinal, a season ticket-holder for both the Maine Wildness and the Hearts of Pine, was among a crowd of 500 supporters at Madrid’s in Portland for Thursday’s name and brand reveal.
The Maine Wildness will begin play in the spring and early summer of 2027, competing in the USL W League, which in 2026 had 96 teams across 16 regionalized divisions.
The name and logo were the result of months of planning and community outreach by the organization, which has achieved worldwide recognition for its Hearts of Pine branding and merchandise. Club representatives held town hall-style meetings and an online forum with U.S. Women’s National Team legends, including Michelle Akers, who has become a founding adviser for the Maine Wildness.
Hannah Sirois, the club’s vice president for fan experience and the point person for the women’s team, said the Wildness name was first isolated when staff members were huddled around a campfire, riffing on themes of wilderness and natural beauty.
“It’s about being your unapologetic self,” Sirois said.
Catherine Culley, one of the club’s founding co-owners, had tears in her eyes when the name was revealed and the crowd voiced their wholehearted endorsement.
“I think women need this right now as a positive environment that welcomes women for everything they are,” Culley said. “It’s something I feel the community needed right now. And I think it is important for young girls to see a path forward and it’s equal to the men. Not the same as the men.”
Prior to the name reveal, the audience heard from club personnel about how they had spent hours and hours going over 300-plus names and then shaping the asymmetrical crest logo that pays homage to Maine’s wilderness with stylized imagery of Katahdin, flowing waters and wildflowers.
In the presentation, the qualities of “Wildness” as it relates to Maine women were detailed as five main themes: resilience, communers, work ethic, leadership, and being grounded. Wildness, according to a club press release, connects the physical characteristics of Maine and “the trailblazing spirit” of Maine women.
“The name, it encapsulates everything a Maine women is,” said Justine Satterthwaite of Scarborough. Like Vinal, Satterthwaite is now a season-ticket holder for both the Maine Wildness and the Hearts of Pine.
By incorporating the Hearts of Pine’s distinctive Dirigo Heart image and blue-and-green colors into the Maine Wildness logo, designed by Portland-based artist Pame Chévez, the club was purposeful in connecting its two teams while providing the women’s team with its own identity. The crest emphasizes the natural beauty of wild spaces with images of Katahdin, flowing waters, and resilient flora like wild lupines, thistle, sea rose and fern.
“We asked people across Maine what they wanted for this team and we kept hearing the same response: a love for what we’ve created with Hearts and a deep desire for something distinct to the women of Maine,” said Gabe Hoffman-Johnson, the club’s founder and chief community officer, in a press release. “‘Wildness came from listening to that feedback, finding a name that captures the spirit intrinsic to both this place and the people who make it so special.”
Shortly after the name and brand were revealed, the crowded main room noticeably thinned out. That’s because half of the attendees went to the music venue’s lobby to line up and buy Maine Wildness T-shirts, sweatshirts and other swag. The women’s team items are now available on the club’s online store and its Club Shop at 127 Marginal Way in Portland.
The women’s team will consist of mostly college-age players. Because it is a pre-professional league (think wooden bat baseball leagues for a simple comparison), the players retain their college eligibility. Games are played mostly in May and June. The Maine Wildness will compete in the USLW’s Northeast Division.
The Wildness will immediately be one of top drawing clubs in the USLW. In June, the club sold 5,000 season-ticket deposits in an hour and have converted 4,400 of those deposits into season-ticket sales.
The men’s team, which has averaged 6,239 fans at city-owned Fitzpatrick Stadium this season, has 4,000 season-ticket holders.
The USLW does not report average attendance, but most teams draw less than 1,000 fans. Minnesota Aurora FC is a rare exception, reportedly bringing in over 5,000 fans per match. The Vermont Green, which will be a rival for the Wildness in the Northeast Division, consistently sold out 2,500-seat Virtue Field in Burlington in their first season in 2026.
“This team is intended to set the standard for what a pre-professional women’s team can accomplish,” Sirois said in the press release. “We want to grow the women’s game in this country. Consistently selling out a 6,000-person stadium has never been done at this level, and raising that standard is what we’re rallying this state around.”
The Hearts of Pine ownership announced in August its plans to build its own 9,000-11,000 seat stadium on Cassidy Point in Portland. The hope is to break ground sometime in 2027, with 2029 as the target year for both the men’s and women’s teams to move to their new home.

title: Characters of the County: Katherine Dunn Lives in a Storybook
text:
From a life spent working with animals, Katherine Dunn said she has learned the art of living in the moment.
The director of Apifera Farm in Bremen has dedicated the past 20 years to housing and caring for elderly or abandoned animals, calling it her “soul work.” When she is not tending to her sanctuary, Dunn is in her studio working on her art. Keeping her company while she works on new pottery pieces is Sky Potato, an injured pigeon who now resides in the studio.
Most of Dunn’s artwork is intertwined with her love for animals, anything from a sculpture of a donkey or a book about a cat.
“Well, I’m not going to say animals are better than people, but the older I get, the more I prefer them,” Dunn said. “The more I feel like I’m meant to be with them and not people, or most people. Let’s put it that way.”
Apifera Farm is a sanctuary that takes in animals that are elderly, special needs, or in need of a new home. Currently, she has just over 80 animals on her property, everything from goats, sheep, llamas, donkeys, pigs, geese, horses, and more. She also has an elderly cat sanctuary, which now houses eight cats. The room is housed separately from the other animals and is attached to one of the barns, featuring air conditioning and cat towers.
Originally from Minneapolis, Minn., Dunn went to Hamline University in St. Paul, Minn., where she got an art degree. After graduation, she had dreams of moving to New York City, so she found a marketing job at Ogilvy, an advertising, marketing, and public relations agency.
Before ending up at Ogilvy’s New York City office, Dunn said the people around her told her she wouldn’t find a job in the city as a young person.
“Everybody was shocked, and I loved working there,” Dunn said. “But I was always, you know, it was just a pit stop to get me where I needed to go.”
After New York, Dunn went back to Minnesota, where she worked in the marketing department for different architecture and design firms. In 1996, she decided to become a freelance illustrator.
Art had always been an interest for Dunn; her father was an architect and always having art books during her childhood. She recalled a trip she went on with her friends as a teenager where she met a woman in her 70s who was an artist. After seeing her lifestyle in a cabin, Dunn was inspired.
“It was just like, walking in there, I went, ‘This is what I want to do,” Dunn said. “I want to work alone and I want to paint. And so I did.”
Shortly after 9/11, Dunn moved to Portland, Ore. She said she had needed a change and her brother was living there, so she took the leap to the Pacific Northwest.
The day she moved in, she met the man living next door, who had the same last name as her. That man would become her husband a year later, Martyn.
A few years later, the two started their own farm, which is when Dunn started bringing in elderly animals. The name Apifera comes from the 4,000 lavender plants they had in Oregon, which made the cross-country trek with the couple to Maine.
Farming sent Dunn’s illustrating days “in the toilet,” she said. Despite this, she said she was lucky because of how “stylized” her art is, so she shifted into gallery work and writing.
She has written seven books, mostly memoirs or short stories circling around a specific animal. In her column “Tails and Tales” in The Lincoln County News, Dunn writes from the animal’s perspective.
“The art and the animals is all really merged,” she said.
Dunn has always loved old things, but her love for elderly animals started with one goat. The animal had been abandoned by its owners, Dunn taking him in at 15, which she said is old for goats. He lived to be 22.
She said adopting the goat created a catalyst of her efforts of taking in animals after noticing the amount of people who maybe gets a pony for their kid who then grows up and the family doesn’t want to take care of said pony anymore.
“I was like ‘Wow, people do this,”” she said.
Now, Dunn said if someone came to her with any animal, she is taking them in.
After 15 years in Oregon, Dunn said she had a calling to get out of the state. She asked her husband if he would be interested in moving to the East Coast and the two settled on Maine. After hauling 30 of their animals from coast to coast in 2016, they landed in Bremen.
“We couldn’t really leave the farm,” Dunn said. “We had all these animals. So, long story short, we found this place and totally lucked out.”
When she arrived in Bremen, Dunn said she had enough of raising animals and made the decision to shift into sanctuary work. The same year as their arrival, Apifera Farm became a nonprofit organization. What was originally just a 1760 barn and house has turned into acres of farmland, fencing, and more barns.
Another component of the move for Dunn was the ability to take her animals on the road to different senior living homes. She said the regulations in Oregon were much stricter and she found that in Maine, she was able to start taking them places such as Cove’s Edge in Damariscotta.
Dunn said bringing the animals into the senior homes were to connect elderly residents with something might have loved.
Other than the neglect and surrender cases, Dunn said a lot of her elderly animals come from elderly people as owners realize they are not physically able to care for their animals. There are also many cases where families have gone bankrupt and cannot afford to care for their animals, which then end up at Apifera.
A lot of the times, Dunn said she finds people are doing their best until their animal needs to be given up.
With this work, Dunn said her farm is not a rescue. None of the animals she takes in can be rehomed or sold. Apifera Farm is their new forever home.
After getting heart surgery, Dunn stepped back from taking her animals to senior homes. As she recovered, Dunn and her husband built her clay studio, a passion she had since college.
“I got back into it, so that was great,” Dunn said. “And I still get paid, but I’m really into the whole clay thing right now. I just kind of do what I want to do.”
In a career dedicated to animals and art, both combining into one another, Dunn said she has learned a lot about life and death. The theme is present in a lot of her writing and she said animals have taught her how to let go. Most of her ideas and writing come to her while she is in bed, where she said she brainstorms how to turn her art into stories.
Working with animals has helped Dunn get to where she is spiritually, she said.
“I think that’s probably the main thing, is that they truly live in the moment,” Dunn said.
At 68, Dunn said her new goal is to slow down a little bit.
She does not make appointment before 11:30 a.m. Previously, Dunn said she would work on her paintings until midnight and after dealing with her heart, she didn’t want to rush anymore and needed to set up stronger boundaries.
Dunn’s husband is responsible for some of the heavy lifting but spends most of his time working for Natural Concepts, a landscaping business based in Bristol.
Dunn said she never plans on retiring and that being “stingy” with her time is the closest she will get.
“Artists don’t retire,” Dunn said. “We die.”
Even though Apifera Farm is not usually open to the public, some visitors are invited to the healing barn.
Dunn said the barn was created when she got out of the hospital after her heart surgery. The idea was to bring people to her, one of those groups being the Skidompha Strummers, a ukulele group based from the Damariscotta library.
When the strummers begin playing in the bar, the animals come from all sides to listen. One animal who really loves the music is Dunn’s turkey, Sophie. Every time the music would stop, she said the turkey would start gobbling.
Other than music, Dunn said the purpose of the healing barn is not for school field trips but for more individual connections. She recalled a time where a woman brought in her 100-year-old father who grew up loving horses to see the ones at her farm.
“It was so fun because the horses loved him,” she said.
Bringing people over for experiences also allow Dunn to connect more with her community, she said. In the future, she wants to work more with others, whether that is special needs or elderly, to stop by the farm.
Whether she is tending to her animals or throwing a mug into the kiln, Dunn said her life is like a storybook. She often finds herself asking if she is in the painting or if painting is just what she does. Her life of artwork and animal care has merged together so much she said it is in her soul.
“It’s like my soul is doing what it’s supposed to do and sometimes I even think, well, I really feel that many of the animals, we’re drawn together,” Dunn said.
(Do you have a suggestion for a “Characters of the County” subject? Email [email protected] with the subject line “Characters of the County” with the name and contact information of your nominee.)

title: Fire marshals investigate blaze at Paris mobile home
text:
State investigators are searching for the cause of a fire that destroyed a home on Abby Road in Paris on Wednesday afternoon.
Several pets died in the 3:30 p.m. blaze at 22 Abby Road but no other injuries were reported, officials said.
“Due to the extensive damage, the cause of the fire has been classified as undetermined,” according to a Maine Public Safety news release. “Investigators have not ruled out several possible electrical causes. The fire is not considered suspicious at this time.”
The American Red Cross is assisting the property owners.
Crews from Paris, Norway and Hebron fire departments responded to the scene, along with PACE Ambulance and the Paris Police Department.
When firefighters arrived, the single-family home was fully ablaze and crews worried about the flames spreading into nearby woods, the release said.
Abby Road is a short road that runs off Bumptown Road.

title: New Bangor childcare center with space for hundreds of children sees high demand
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Childcare can be hard to come by in Bangor, and the waitlist is already filling up for a new childcare center with 16 classrooms and space for more than 200 kids.
The Bright Beginnings Child Development Center at 16 Hillside Ave., near the Broadway Hannaford, celebrated its grand opening last month after years of work. The large facility merges three that were run by the social services agency Penquis in leased spaces around the city, now all under one roof with greater capacity.
High demand for spots in the center’s classrooms highlights the need for more childcare options in Bangor, especially for lower income families. Head Start programs, which are federally funded and free for families that qualify based on income, are housed within the Penquis facility in addition to full-day childcare offered at Maine’s market rate.
The center has been opened in phases over the past year, with four classrooms yet to be opened. As of last week, 105 children were enrolled, with more set to start this month, according to Mary Kay Hallett, the Head Start director at Penquis.
The facility includes pre-school classrooms for children ages three to five, as well as smaller classes for infants and toddlers six weeks and older. Families can choose to send their children to Head Start programs lasting from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., or opt for full-day childcare from 7 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.
There is a waitlist for both age groups, and “those applications are being followed up on daily,” Hallett said.
So far, the center has seen especially high demand for the infant and toddler classrooms, which are capped at eight children, Bright Beginnings program director Vivian Perreault said on a recent tour of the building.
The facility is licensed for a maximum capacity of 208.
All 16 classrooms have their own exits to a dedicated outdoor space and their own bathrooms. There are also two large recreation rooms at either end of the building that can be used during winter weather, and a full kitchen where staff prepare fresh food daily. Bright Beginnings has upwards of 40 employees, Perreault estimated.
The building combines services that were previously offered on Davis Road and Venture Way, and at a facility on the Eastern Maine Community College campus. Those centers were phased into the new building gradually, with the Davis Road program moving in most recently in August, according to Hallett.
The new childcare center was intentionally placed near a bus route, Perreault said. The consolidation also adds flexibility for staff and reduces costs as Penquis has faced significant rent hikes at its leased spaces.
Bangor was one of three Head Start centers in the country to be awarded federal funding for a new facility, according to Penquis. The organization raised nearly $1 million in matching funds to finish the new building. The Bangor Daily News was among those who donated to the project.
“This building demonstrates what can happen when a community comes together around children and families,” Kara Hay, president and CEO of Penquis, said. “The generosity and belief shown by so many individuals, businesses, foundations, and partners made this project possible. Bright Beginnings will have an impact not only on the children who learn here today, but on generations of families to come.”
Funds for the project included a $1.5 million grant allocated from the city’s pandemic relief money in 2023, with city memos at the time emphasizing that it represented an investment in healthy childhood environments and affordable childcare.

title: New Orleans jail worker gets 2.5 years in prison for enabling brazen 10-inmate escape
text:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — A New Orleans jail worker received a 2.5-year prison sentence Thursday for enabling 10 inmates to escape through a hole behind a toilet after he turned off its water.
Custodian Sterling Williams, 34, pleaded guilty to one count of malfeasance in office for clearing the way for one of the largest jailbreaks in recent U.S. history. In May 2025, after Williams shut off the water in a cell, 10 inmates removed a toilet, crawled through a gap in the wall and scaled a fence out of the jail. They left behind a scrawled graffiti note reading “To Easy LoL.”
Williams’ attorney, Michael Kennedy, said that Williams did not intentionally help the escapees but acknowledged making mistakes. Williams should have had a work order generated before shutting off the water for the clogged toilet, his attorney said.
“He does admit that he failed to follow protocol in a job as a public employee, and that it is possible that those actions aided in a plan hatched by 10 inmates to escape,” Kennedy said. “But again, without Mr. Williams’ knowledge.”
An additional 2.5 years of Williams’ sentence is suspended, and he will also receive three years of probation. The state dropped 10 charges against him of being a principal to aggravated escape, which carries a sentence of up to 10 years in Louisiana.
All 10 of the inmates were eventually captured, though one convicted murderer remained on the run for five months before being discovered hiding beneath a house in Atlanta. They are all facing charges of aggravated escape and are scheduled for jury trial in April.
Along with Williams, at least 14 other people, many of them friends and family of the escapees, were arrested and accused of aiding in the escape, including by providing food, cash, transport and shelter.
Earlier this year, a grand jury handed down a 30-count indictment against then-Orleans Parish Sheriff Susan Hutson, for malfeasance, obstruction of justice and falsifying public records. While Hutson is not accused of helping the inmates pull off the escape, Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill said a state probe found that Hutson’s poor management led to the jailbreak.
Bianka Brown, the chief financial officer of the sheriff’s office, was also indicted on 20 similar charges.
Hutson and Brown have pleaded not guilty.
___

title: Meet the 81-year-old artist behind thousands of painted rocks
text:
TUALATIN, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - Every morning, rain or shine, painted rocks appear around Tualatin’s Jurgens Park like Easter eggs waiting to be found.
The artist behind the rocks has been a mystery until now.
Phillip Roberts, 81, has spent the last eight years hiding thousands of rocks during his daily walks with his wife.
“I take at least four dozen over a week, so it adds up,” Roberts said.
Roberts is a professional artist whose career has taken him around the world.
“For the past 20 years the pieces that I’ve been working on,” Roberts said, gesturing to his home studio. “I had galleries in Kansas City, I’ve had galleries in San Francisco, I’ve shown in England.”
His inspiration has constantly changed throughout his career.
“I started going to Mexico to find the subject matter of impressionist painters,” Roberts said. “We’d drive around France and Spain, painting.”
All of it has led him back to his home studio in Tualatin, where he spends hours each day.
“I’m usually in here at 1 o’clock, until after 10 in the evening,” Roberts said.
The size of his canvas has changed, and so has the complexity of his subject matter.
“Rather than throwing away the paint on my palette, I started painting rocks,” Roberts said.
Roberts said the rocks are simpler than his oil paintings, and they’re free. His oil paintings are not free.
He gathers his supplies from his backyard, washing and drying the rocks before deciding what to paint.
“I get the rocks from my backyard, I wash them, dry them and look at them,” Roberts said. “Some of them do dictate what they might be.”
Roberts said he is creating animal rocks now, using a hot glue gun and rope.
While the expressive river rocks bring joy to Roberts as he creates them, his real motivation comes from the joy they bring others.
“This lady came up and asked me if we were the ones that put out the rocks and said yes and she said her daughter had a very serious illness, and she said one of the things that got her daughter by was coming over and looking for the rocks,” Roberts said.
Roberts said he plans to continue hiding rocks as long as he can walk.
At 81 years old, Roberts credits his daily three-mile walks for his good health and wellbeing.

title: Authorities investigate letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to congressional, election offices
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities are investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide.
Authorities are urging recipients to treat the letters as “potentially hazardous.”
The Senate was informed of the investigation by a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms that was obtained by The Associated Press.
The mailings come just three weeks before Election Day and are reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when several election offices received envelopes containing the powerful opioid fentanyl.

title: Dementia cases to double worldwide by 2050, study says
text:
(CNN) — A new study suggests the number of people worldwide who develop dementia each year is expected to more than double by 2050.
Researchers studied data from 22 studies involving more than 38,000 people from 18 countries.
After following the participants over a period of time, the researchers estimate there will be nearly 25 million new annual cases of dementia by 2050.
For comparison, more than 11 million people developed dementia in 2023.
The researchers said they found women and those living in low- and middle-income countries were at higher risk of developing dementia.
The study’s authors said the research did not show why those disparities existed, but they highlighted the challenge for countries with lesser health care resources to deal with the condition.
The study was published Monday in JAMA Neurology.

title: Lockheed Martin showered Susan Collins with cash as F-35 program hit turbulence
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In May 2023, the Pentagon’s shiny new fighter jet was not looking so shiny or new.
Already a decade late and nearly $200 billion over its original cost estimate, the F-35 program faced a new crisis. An internal government watchdog report detailed a cascade of new problems with the program, which was in a period of flux amid plans to upgrade the jet’s engine and cooling system.
The report from the Government Accountability Office criticized the Pentagon for lumping those upgrades in with the overall purchase of the planes. Conflating the two, the authors said, would limit congressional insight into cost increases. And they criticized the contractors behind the aircraft for failing to deliver the F-35 in a timely manner.
For Lockheed Martin, the main defense giant overseeing the development of the F-35, the timing was far from ideal. In a few weeks, Congress was set to debate the Pentagon’s mammoth budget — and with it, new funding for the military’s purchase of F-35 jets.
So Lockheed and its lobbyists went on a charm offensive in Washington. The weapons maker shelled out hundreds of thousands over a two-month period, in what the money-in-politics watchdog Open Secrets described as “one of the largest coordinated lobbying efforts” around that year’s military budget.
No member of Congress benefited more than Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who at the time served as the ranking member on the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee.
From May 1 to June 30, 2023, employees and top executives from Lockheed Martin donated $59,500 to Collins’s campaign committee. The donations were outliers during that period: Collins was among the largest recipients of Lockheed cash; the company was her largest single donor over those two months; and it was the largest spending blitz on Collins by Lockheed compared to the same period in other years.
The effort appeared to pay off for Lockheed. In July 2023, less than two months after the release of the Government Accountability Office report, Collins voted in favor of appropriating funds to purchase 83 new F-35 jets. Later that year, when the final version of the military budget was signed into law, Collins celebrated the economic boon she said it would bring to the state of Maine.
In response to questions from The Intercept, Phoebe Keller, a spokesperson for the Republican-controlled Senate Appropriations Committee, said Collins’s support for the jet had nothing to do with donations from Lockheed or any other firm.
“Sen. Collins did not support the F-35 because of donations that she received,” Keller said.
“The F-35 jet program is a longstanding bipartisan defense priority,” Keller said. “Sen. Collins has always publicly supported the F-35 jet program, as dozens of both Republican and Democratic Senators.”
Collins’s position on the Defense Subcommittee of the Senate Appropriations Committee likely played a role in the outsized donations, according to analyst Dan Grazier. And Collins, for her part, would have good reason to approve the spending: The F-35 program, Lockheed claims, has had a nine-figure economic impact in Maine.
FIGHT OF HER POLITICAL LIFE
In the final weeks of the biggest fight of her political career against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, fresh scrutiny on Collins’s donations from defense contractors has become a sore spot for her campaign.
In some cases, the senator’s interactions with defense firms are the routine for Washington: glad-handing, lobbying, contributions, and directing pork-barrel spending back home. Not all of it, though, is standard.
Last month, a bombshell report in ProPublica detailed an FBI investigation into an alleged pay-to-play scheme. A former defense contractor claimed to federal agents that he worked with figures tied to Collins to disguise campaign donations — and got federal contracts totaling $32 million in return. (The FBI probe fizzled after Trump returned to office and purged the bureau; Collins denied wrongdoing, pushing back on elements of the report.)
On Wednesday, more than 250 Mainers signed a letter to the state’s attorney general asking the official to investigate the allegations of corruption, according to Maine Morning Star, a local news outlet.
And earlier this month, The Intercept reported on donations from another defense contractor, AM General, and its parent company, whose employees gave $58,000 to fundraising committees associated with Collins after a damning assessment from the Army put its federal contracts in jeopardy.
As with the AM General donations, the contributions by employees and lobbyists of Lockheed Martin do not indicate wrongdoing by Collins or her donors.
“This is an example of what’s wrong with our approach to buying weapons,” said William Hartung, an analyst who has written critically of defense spending and influence peddling in Washington. “If we buy things because they’re in the state of a powerful member, we’re not going to have a coherent arsenal.”
LOCKHEED GIVING
Collins was not the only member of Congress to push for funding the F-35, which enjoyed broad bipartisan support — especially from lawmakers with eligible firms and facilities in their states. And she was not the only one to benefit from the largesse of Lockheed Martin.
From May 1 to June 30, 2023, Lockheed’s corporate PAC doled out $421,000 in a bipartisan blitz to various campaign political action committees, campaign funds, state parties, and charitable foundations. (Aside from 2024, the year of the presidential election, contributions in that two-month period in 2023 eclipsed subsequent years. In the same period this year, Lockheed’s corporate PAC made 128 donations totaling $236,000; last year, it gave $286,000 across 158 donations during the same period.)
Collins was by far the biggest single beneficiary of the influx of cash — which came at a time when she was not actively campaigning. And, unlike the donations spread out to other campaign committees, the cash going from Lockheed into Collins’s coffers during those months came exclusively in the form of individual donations by employees and executives, including the firm’s CEO and chief operating officer, data from the Federal Election Commission shows.
Lobbyists working for Lockheed contributed another $5,000 to Collins during that period, and corporate PACs for Lockheed’s lobbying firms shelled out another $5,500 total, according to FEC disclosures.
Among individual contributions by Lockheed employees, donations to Collins made up more than 10 percent of all donations during the two-month period surrounding the watchdog report.
Only the firm’s in-house employee PAC, which received 75 percent of all employee donations, took in more from figures tied to Lockheed. Collins got more than twice as much as the next highest recipient, ActBlue, the Democratic Party-aligned fundraising vehicle, which received 4 percent of all Lockheed employee contributions in that period, according to FEC data.
The vast majority donations from Lockheed employees and officials were under $1,000. Of the 60 donations of $1,000 or more during May and June 2023, 56 went to Collins.
Virtually all employee contributions from Lockheed workers and executives to Collins during her current term came during that two-month window, according to the FEC.
Lockheed donations made up a quarter of all contributions during May and June 2023 to Collins’s main fundraising arm, Collins for Senator. The next runner-up was telecom giant Charter Communications, whose employee contributions made up just 8 percent of gifts to the Collins campaign in the second quarter of the 2023 fiscal year.
A spokesperson for Lockheed did not answer specific questions regarding the reason for the sudden influx of individual contributions to Collins in 2023.
“Our employee PAC program continues to observe long-standing principles of bi-partisan political engagement in support of our business interests,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
ANOTHER VEHICLE ARMY DIDN’T WANT
Two years later, a similar pattern played out in miniature when a lesser-known defense firm with a troubled product enjoyed Collins’s support on Capitol Hill.
Collins went out of her way last year to slam the Pentagon for canceling its plans to purchase robotic combat vehicles from Textron and its subsidiary Howe & Howe, the Maine-based developer of the Ripsaw.
Collins has repeatedly hyped the unmanned robotic combat vehicle in Senate hearings and official statements. On June 18, 2025, she took issue with the fact that the vehicle had appeared in a recent military parade, but did not make the cut for further spending.
“It’s the height of irony that you would feature this combat vehicle in your parade as the future of the Army at the same time that you’ve canceled the contract — the cancellation of a contract that was won over a lot of other competitors,” Collins said, describing the decision as “terribly unfair and a real mistake.”
A month later, after the military budget cleared the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins singled out Howe & Howe, and its plant in Waterboro, Maine, as a potential beneficiary of a portion of $44 million allotted to outfit the U.S. Marine Corps with amphibious and autonomous vehicles.
She gave another shoutout to Howe & Howe in January, after the 2026 military budget was signed into law. This May, during the congressional testimony by then-Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, Collins again took the military to task for cutting its planned purchase of the Ripsaw.
Textron’s corporate PAC made contributions totaling $4,000 to various PACs associated with Collins just ahead of her vote on the 2026 military budget. $3,000 of the gifts came days after Collins criticized the military for cutting its plans for the Ripsaw program that would have brought millions of dollars to Howe & Howe.
Later in the year, the Textron corporate PAC donated another $7,000 to Collins for Senator and the Collins-linked Dirigo PAC, according to FEC filings. (A spokesperson for Textron and Howe & Howe did not respond to a request for comment.)
Keller, the Senate Appropriations Committee spokesperson, said that Collins was not a member of the Armed Services Committee that voted on funding the Ripsaw.
“She doesn’t have the agency to fund or not fund the vehicle because it wasn’t through the Appropriations Committee,” Keller said, adding that Collins’s longtime support for the Ripsaw was not motivated by the Textron and Howe & Howe donations.
Employees of Textron and its subsidiary, meanwhile, made contributions to various Collins-linked PACS totaling nearly $15,000 between September 2025 and October 15, 2026, FEC data shows.
The donations, relatively small in the post-Citizens United era of campaign finance, still illustrate a troubling pattern of how influence plays out in Washington, according to Hartung, the analyst critical of military spending.
“A lot of members lobby to get more units of something built in their state, or craft legislation for a system that only their local firm can produce,” Hartung said. “It’s kind of business as usual, but sometimes business as usual causes great harm.”
This story was updated to include further statements from Phoebe Keller, a spokesperson for the Senate Appropriations Committee, that were made after publication.
Originally published on Oct.15, 2026. Republished with permission from The Intercept, an award-winning nonprofit news organization dedicated to holding the powerful accountable through fearless, adversarial journalism. Sign up for The Intercept’s Newsletter.

title: Watch: Fryeburg soccer is the Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Fryeburg Academy soccer
Coach Bob Hodgman-Burns saw signs during a preseason game against Laconia, New Hampshire, that this could be a successful season for the Fryeburg Academy boys soccer team.
“My local players are a year more experienced, and I don’t want to say they suffered through last year, but they had a tough year last year,” Hodgman-Burns said. “I think they learned a lot. So after that first week, it was all coming together.”
With an 8-2-1 record, Fryeburg ranked second in the Class B South Heal point standings heading into Wednesday’s game against Traip Academy. In 2025, the Raiders finished 3-8-3.
Fourth-year player and team captain Abram Grace said the Raiders took a little time to find their footing before settling into the grind of the Western Maine Conference schedule. They had a loss and a tie in their first five games but then won five of their next six.
“Our season started, obviously, not how we’re doing now,” Grace said. “We were struggling with communication, and our passes were a little bit sloppy at times, but throughout the season, we’ve been working hard and getting quite a few wins that we didn’t really expect.”
That includes a 1-0 win over defending Class B champion Yarmouth on Sept. 17 and a 2-1 victory over perennial power Cape Elizabeth on Sept. 22. It’s the first time since 2011 that Fryeburg, ranked 10th in the Varsity Maine poll, has beaten both of those schools in the same season.
Last week, the Raiders offense exploded in a 7-0 win over Lake Region and a 9-1 victory over Sacopee Valley.
The Raiders have scored 39 goals, and nine players have contributed to that total.
“I think that in the games that we come out strong and really try to push from the start and don’t give (opponents) any time, don’t let the team kind of play with the ball, we’re doing better,” Grace said. “So I think for the rest of the season, we’re being aggressive and going at every team we play, because we’re not going to overlook any team.”

title: Scientists knew Doomsday Glacier was melting. They didn’t realize how ‘aggressively’
text:
Scientists knew the Doomsday Glacier was melting. They didn’t realize how ‘aggressively’
The planet’s widest glacier is melting "more aggressively" than previously projected, meaning its impacts on global sea level rise could be double current estimates, according to new research by a team of glaciologists.
Related video above: Explaining why glaciers in the US are melting
Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica — nicknamed the Doomsday Glacier because of the catastrophe its collapse would trigger — is a huge wild card when it comes to forecasting global sea level rise.
The Florida-sized glacier, which lies in one of the least accessible places on Earth, has been retreating for decades, and its melting ice currently contributes around 4% to global sea level rise.
But the mechanisms behind its retreat are exceptionally complex, making it tricky to precisely map out its future.
It’s a vital task, however, as Thwaites holds enough water to raise sea levels by more than 2 feet if it were to collapse. Because it also acts as a cork holding back the vast Antarctic ice sheet, it could ultimately lead to around 10 feet of sea level rise, devastating coastal communities from Miami to Manila.
Glaciologists from the University of California, Irvine and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory have developed a new ice sheet model they say better reflects what is happening underneath this ice giant.
Thwaites’ rapid retreat is driven by processes at its "grounding line" — the point at which the ice rises up from the seabed and starts to float on the ocean as an ice shelf.
But while typical ice sheet models have tended to view the grounding line as something fixed and mostly stable, "we have come to acknowledge a different arrangement beneath Earth’s major ocean-terminating glaciers," said the report’s lead author, Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA who was an Earth system science researcher at UC Irvine at the time of the study.
Satellite data reveals the grounding line is actually a "grounding zone," sometimes miles wide, where seawater constantly flushes in and out with the tides, lifting and lowering the thick ice in a process known as "tidal pumping." This allows relatively warm ocean water to penetrate "deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting," Poinelli said.
When the scientists adjusted models to include the concept of a grounding zone, they found Thwaites could contribute up to 1.2 inches of sea level rise by 2100 — twice previous estimates — even without further global warming, according to the findings published Monday in the journal Nature Communications.
The land on which Thwaites sits slopes downward, meaning that, as the glacier melts, more ice is exposed to warm ocean water. The topography is complicated, however, by two key underwater ridges, which "pin" the ice, holding it back from flowing into the ocean more rapidly.
The melting processes at Thwaites’ grounding zone are accelerating the "unpinning" of ice from a large ridge called the Mouginot Ridge, the study found. There is a 60% chance that it will be unpinned by the end of the century, the study found, after which the glacier is likely to retreat quickly down the sloping bedrock toward the next major ridge.
The findings suggest the impacts of losing Thwaites might have been underestimated. A sea level rise of 1.2 inches may not sound like much, but it’s enough to greatly magnify dangers to coastal populations.
The results "predict greater risk of and exposure for coastal flooding than anticipated in the coming decades," said Eric Rignot, a report author and professor of Earth system science at UC Irvine.
Ted Scambos, a senior research scientist for the Earth Science and Observation Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, who was not involved in the research, said the findings could be "a real game changer for sea level forecasting from Thwaites."
But he and other experts caution that more research is needed to understand the impacts of different grounding zone melting processes, not least by getting direct data from underneath the glacier.
"The reality is that there is a lot we still need to find out about grounding zone processes to be able to make confident predictions about how fast ice will be lost," said Robert Larter, a marine geophysicist at British Antarctic Survey, who was also not involved in the study. The environment beneath Thwaites, which is very difficult to access, is even more complex than the paper describes, he added.
Getting observational data from Thwaites’ grounding line is the next step, Rignot said. The scientists are planning to travel there in 2028 to deploy instruments able to document the flushing in and out of seawater.
"We have been aware of the impacts of climate change on our planet’s sensitive ice sheets for decades," Rignot said. "But a mounting realization gained in recent years of what is really happening on the undersides of glaciers like Thwaites is leading to an even greater sense of alarm."
He said the world must cut planet-heating pollution now to limit the impacts but warned, "even if we do, we can expect higher sea levels in the future resulting from the damage that has already been done."

title: Troy Jackson got $15k from big oil, pharma lobbyists. He’s giving it to charity.
text:
Troy Jackson is donating about $15,000 in political contributions from oil and pharmaceutical lobbyists, his campaign said on Thursday.
Jackson, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, said in a news release that he will donate $5,000 each to Keep ME Warm/Project Heat and the Good Shepherd Food Bank, and $2,500 each to Maine Needs and the Augusta Food Bank.
The lobbyists’ donations are a small fraction of the $20.4 million his campaign says it raised since Jackson secured the nomination on July 25. In giving the donations to charity, Jackson said he’s keeping the”Dirigo Pledge” he made during the abbreviated Democratic primary to replace Graham Platner in July.
“I said I wouldn’t take money from Big Oil or Big Pharma lobbyists, and I meant it,” Jackson said in a written statement. “That money is better spent helping Mainers heat their homes, put food on the table, afford the things they need, and get through a tough winter.”
Jackson also pledged, among other things, to refuse donations from corporate PACs and the pro-Israel AIPAC; to fully disclose his campaign finances; to advocate for a Constitutional amendment to get big money out of politics; and to advocate for a ban on congressional stock trading.
The announcement came hours before his fourth and final debate with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, 73, who has called out the 58-year-old former logger for accepting corporate contributions as state Senate president.
And it comes as polls show that inflation and high gas prices are among the top issues on voters’ minds.
The deadline for campaign finance reports to be filed is midnight Thursday. Jackson has yet to release his full campaign finance report, despite saying in a televised debate that he would release it on Wednesday morning.
Collins, meanwhile, released hers Thursday afternoon, reporting a total of $3.9 million from July 1 through Sept. 30. Her total for the campaign is now nearly $17.7 million. She reported $5.4 million in cash for the final stretch of the campaign.
Despite Jackson’s fundraising, Republicans have a clear money advantage in the Maine’s closely watched race.
So far, Republican-aligned groups have spent or reserved $151.5 million on ads, compared to $110.7 million by Democrat-aligned groups, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

Of all the macho, bald, bearded dudes who sometimes wear logoless baseball caps Jason Statham has played in the last few years, the title character from The Beekeeper is certainly the ones that stands out the most. What a strange concept; a former assassin who once worked for a covert spy group called “The Beekeepers” out for revenge against some scuzzy scam artists after his friend is tricked by a phishing scam and then dies.
Obviously the Beekeeper got his revenge, but that couldn’t be (or bee) the end of the story, could it? Of course not! Now Statham is back in The Beekeeper 2 and this time he’s ... making puns about honey and hives, I hope? In addition to Statham, the film stars Jeremy Irons and Pom Klementieff from the Guardians of the Galaxy movies.

title: UMaine Presque Isle loses blanket approval for new YourPace programs after reports of ‘speed runners’
text:
The accreditor for the University of Maine at Presque Isle has revoked the school’s blanket approval to offer new competency-based degree programs following an investigation into concerns about the rapid speed at which students were getting degrees through its online program, YourPace.
If the University of Maine System wants to introduce new competency programs going forward, it will need to submit them directly to the accreditor for approval.
“Given its concern about the dramatic growth of the YourPace program attributed in part to the speed at which students have been able to complete the credits required to earn a degree, both undergraduate and graduate, the Commission suspends University of Maine System’s general approval to offer competency-based education programs at University of Maine at Presque Isle,” the New England Commission of Higher Education wrote.
In addition, the commission will monitor the university’s progress through reports and requests, including site visits to UMPI and the other system schools that offer the degree programs in spring of 2027.
YourPace is a fully asynchronous competency-based program designed for adults, meaning students can earn credit whenever they demonstrate that they’ve mastered the course content, without set lecture or exam times.
The program — which has seen explosive 700% growth over the last four years and is now behind most of the enrollment growth across whole University of Maine System — came under scrutiny following reporting from The Washington Post that many YourPace students were completing bachelor’s degrees in as little as eight weeks.
The New England Commission of Higher Education, which accredits not just UMPI but the whole University of Maine System collectively, released its decision last Wednesday.
System spokesperson Samantha Warren said forthcoming YourPace programs already approved by the board of trustees, including a Master of Healthcare Administration approved at its latest meeting in September, will not be affected.
In a press release about the decision, UMPI President Ray Rice said YourPace has worked exactly as intended, by recognizing the knowledge and experience working adults already have and “providing an affordable, flexible pathway to a degree that will improve their career opportunities and economic mobility.”
System Chancellor Dannel Malloy, also quoted in the statement, said he was proud of the impact YourPace has had on thousands of adult learners who were able to get a degree while balancing work and their families.
“We welcome NECHE’s continued review and are committed to demonstrating that the innovation and accessibility that make YourPace so impactful are matched by the academic quality and rigor our students, employers and accreditor expect,” Malloy said.
The Post story profiled college “speed runners” who race to get their degrees in as little time as possible by transferring in the maximum number of non-collegiate online tutorial credits, then completing as many YourPace courses as they can in a session.
UMPI offers a flat rate of $1,800 per undergraduate session, so students pay the same cost regardless of how many courses they complete, and students are allowed to transfer in up to two-thirds of the credits needed for a bachelor’s degree.
About 90% of YourPace students get their degree in under a year, and 48% finish in one 16-week semester, according to data from the latest school year. Students transferred in an average of 91 credits, and that number is higher for undergrads.
As is standard practice, the accreditor, known as NECHE, requested a response from the university about the concerns raised in the article. UMPI submitted that update in August, in which it said the Post’s focus on rapid completers, “describes only the end of an academic journey, not the history of that journey itself” and that they make up a minority of students.
The university reported that about a fifth of YourPace students students finished 10 or more courses, or 30 credits, in a semester, and 11% completed 12 courses or more.
About half of the average YourPace student’s credits don’t come from an accredited college source. Nearly half of those noncollege credits are from Sophia Learning, a low-cost online tutorial site.
The school acknowledged a need for more monitoring of students who accelerate through their degrees rapidly, and a hard look at its transfer credit policy. But school and system leaders said they were confident the accreditation review process would not find any issues, since NECHE has accredited the YourPace program at every step of the way.
The commission discussed the university’s response at its latest regular meeting in late September.
NECHE will begin conducting visits to UMPI, the University of Maine at Farmington and University of Maine at Fort Kent — where the system has rolled out a much smaller number of YourPace programs — in order to assess the system’s “oversight and implementation” of its competency-based programs.
The system must also submit a report with detailed data, including faculty-to-student ratios, an analysis of transferred credits, the length of time it took graduates to complete degrees and details about procedures to verify that the students who register for courses are the ones actually completing the work.
System and UMPI representatives must appear before the commission in April 2027 for a review of the evaluation’s results.

title: Gorham volleyball bests Thornton Academy again in late-season test
text:
SACO — The playoffs are approaching fast, and once again, the Gorham volleyball team seems to be finding the right time to hit its stride.
The Rams erased a late deficit in the first set and escaped a double-digit hole in the second set en route to a 3-1 victory Thursday night against Thornton Academy. It was their second win this season over the No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll.
Gorham, the three-time defending Class A champion, won the first two sets by 25-23 scores, dropped the third 25-22, then wrapped up the match with another 25-23 margin in the fourth.
The victory seemed to send a statement: Overlook the champs at your own risk.
“We’ve definitely heard a lot of stuff going on about (how) everyone wants to beat us,” said senior setter Liana Edwards, who had 30 assists — including the 800th of her career — to go with 14 kills. “I feel like we just use that as fuel to win against these big teams.”
KEY MOMENTS
• Gorham (10-3) trailed 20-17 in the first set, but after coach Emma Tirrell called a timeout, the Rams came out recharged. They pulled even at 20, worked to a 23-23 tie, then clinched the set on an Abigail Stevens kill and a Kasey Plaud ace.
• Thornton (11-2), led by three Lotus Porter kills, took a 16-6 lead in the second set, but Tirrell again called timeout, and the Rams again stormed back. Gorham won 12 of the next 13 points, getting three kills from Stevens, and prevailed through a back-and-forth finish when a long Trojans serve and violation broke a 23-23 tie.
• After Thornton stayed alive by securing the final four points of the third set, Gorham won a fourth set that was tied 16 times. The Rams got four kills apiece from Stevens, Edwards and Sophie MacIsaac.
SHOWING POISE
In all four sets, Gorham was the last team to reach 15 points. The Rams won three of them.
Call it big-game experience paying off.
“We’ve all fought (back from) gaps like that,” Edwards said. “It’s just so important that all of us have that grit.”
Stevens said the team has learned not to be phased by being down on the scoreboard.
“It’s just us having confidence in our skills and our practice,” Stevens said. “It’s just trusting each other. We just have to take it point by point, and I think that is a really big game-changer for us.”
SHAKING THE SKID
Earlier this season, Gorham lost three of four matches — to York, Cheverus and Washington Academy — causing it to fall out of the top spot in the Class A Heal point standings. The Rams knew, however, that the short slump did little to affect their championship chances.
“I haven’t had an undefeated (regular) season since 2018, and we lost states that year,” Tirrell said. “We don’t take losses lightly … but we also know that it’s not a big deal, and what really matters is the games in late October.”
UNSUNG HERO
Gorham’s Brooklyn Shaw, a sophomore, came off the bench to make a difference late in the fourth set. She had three kills that put the Rams ahead 16-15, 18-17 and 23-22.
INDIVIDUAL STATISTICS
• Gorham: Liana Edwards (30 assists, 14 kills, two aces), Abigail Stevens (18 kills), Sophie MacIsaac (nine kills)
• Thornton Academy: Sarah Berg (12 kills, six aces), Lotus Porter (nine kills), Ryleigh Light (seven kills, three aces), Sophie von Meyer (six kills)
NOTABLE QUOTES
• “I think this game taught us a lot about ourselves and our team and our starting lineup, and kind of things that we need to work on. We consider this a playoff game, even though it’s the end of the regular season. But from here on out, we’re kind of in playoff mode.” — Thornton coach Kayla Arthurs
• “I don’t think it’s anything we worry about. It’s great matches. That’s definitely something we look forward to.” — Arthurs, on whether losses to Gorham cause frustration.
• “She needs to swing hard, and it always goes our way when she does. … I’m so proud of how aggressive she’s become, because there were games last year when she’d barely swing at all because she was scared. Now she swings all the time.” — Tirrell, on Abigail Stevens

title: Alna Receives Final Permit for Reconstruction of Egypt Road Bridge
text:
The Alna Planning Board approved the town’s application for a shoreland zoning permit for a bridge spanning Ben Brook on Egypt Road at its Oct. 6 meeting.
The Egypt Road bridge has been an ongoing project since April 2021 when the Maine Department of Transportation sent the town a letter warning it of the bridge’s hazardous conditions, according to July 2021 coverage by The Lincoln County News.
The bridge was constructed in 1955 and rehabilitated in 2014. According to the application, the bridge shows signs of structural failure and blocks fish and wildlife from passing upstream.

title: Medicare open enrollment begins: What to expect for 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Open enrollment for Medicare plans begins Thursday and enrollees will face a slew of changes that go into effect in 2027.
During the enrollment period, which ends Dec. 7, people will have the opportunity to choose between traditional Medicare and privately run Medicare Advantage plans in their area, as well as prescription drug plans. Those changes go into effect on Jan. 1.
Open enrollment also comes as inflation adds pressure on seniors whose healthcare costs have risen and as midterm elections are weeks away. Voters have consistently said that the cost of living is a major concern heading into the elections.
The Medicare enrollment period also comes as the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, which translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
New changes to Medicare coming in 2027 include higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies, and new drug price negotiations.
Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, said the open enrollment period offers enrollees “an opportunity to evaluate the coverage they have and see if there might be better options for them in terms of accessing the care that they need at possibly a lower cost.”
Here are a few of the biggest changes:
Medicare Part D
The cap on annual out-of-pocket expenses for Medicare Part D drugs will increase to $2,400, up from $2,100 in 2026, and the standard deductible will increase from $615 to $700.
The temporary Part D premium subsidy will also end early.
The Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums.
It was initially implemented by former President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024 to lower patients’ Medicare Part D prescription drug costs in response to the effects of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected only modest price increases for most people. CMS did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
David Lipschutz, co-director of the Center for Medicare Advocacy, points out that there could be greater disruptions in coverage for some Medicare enrollees since some Medicare Advantage plans are pulling out of specific geographic areas and scaling back benefits, such as dental coverage, while potentially increasing cost-sharing.
Plans, insurance companies make business decisions about what they’re going to offer the following year, if they’re going to offer anything at all. And by that very nature, it causes disruption to the system. And it looks like this time there’s more disruption than usual.
Drug price negotiations
New Medicare-negotiated prices, part of a Biden-era law that allows the haggling for Medicare, will go into effect for 15 drugs, including weight-loss and diabetes medications Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.
Additionally, Trelegy Ellipta, Xtandi, Pomalyst, Ibrance, Ofev, Linzess, Calquence, Austedo/Austedo XR, Breo Ellipta, Tradjenta, Xifaxan, Vraylar, Janumet/Janumet XR, and Otezla will be covered by Medicare as of Jan. 1.
CMS expects the change to lower prescription drug coverage for people enrolled in Medicare by $685 million in 2027.
AARP’s Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Nancy LeaMond said in a statement that “higher healthcare costs are making it harder for older Americans to afford the care they need.”
“It’s more important than ever to shop around, compare your options, and choose the coverage that’s best for you,” she said.
Other Trump administration promises
Along with the changes, President Donald Trump in recent weeks made a series of promises to Medicare enrollees and retirees.
Last week, Trump said his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person in October to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees — or less than one third of enrollees — pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion.
Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients.
According to the CMS website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October.
Trump also announced recently that roughly 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums.

title: Crash during ICE detainment in Sanford prompts local police response
text:
Sanford police responded to the scene of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention Thursday morning after federal agents reported a car crash and unattended children.
ICE detained a man during a traffic stop near Brook and High streets around 9 a.m., Sanford police say. As agents attempted to stop the man, he reversed into one of their vehicles, according to a police account and a video shared with the Portland Press Herald.
Footage captured by a nearby resident’s bird feeder camera shows the two SUVs block the driver in, at which point he reverses into the vehicle behind him. The short clip doesn’t show the rest of the detention.
Sanford police Chief Eric Small said federal agents called dispatch after the crash, prompting a response by Sanford police. Police officers also assisted with a 1-year-old who was found in the man’s car.
Officials say no one was injured, though the 1-year-old was taken to a hospital as a precaution.
Immigration officials did not immediately respond to questions about the man’s detention.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree criticized the incident as “yet another instance of ICE’s aggressive operations putting public safety at risk,” pointing to the fatal July shooting of a Biddeford man during an attempted traffic stop.
‘PRETTY SCARY’
Federal agents told police they used two of their vehicles to block the front and back of the car that the man was driving, according to the Sanford Police Department. A neighbor who witnessed the detention, Wendy Deflaminis, said the man had just pulled out of his driveway when the two ICE vehicles drove up from either side and cornered his vehicle.
The man then reversed, crashing into one of the federal vehicles. Deflaminis said it looked as though the man was trying to navigate around the vehicles until he backed into the one behind him. Small said there was no major damage and that the driver was moving at a “very low speed.”
After the crash, the agents told the driver to stop and put his hands up, and he appeared to comply, Deflaminis said. Federal agents then escorted him into a car.
Once the man had been detained, agents appeared to notice that a 1-year-old was sitting in a car seat in the rear of the vehicle, Deflaminis said. She recalled asking whether someone should call an ambulance to ensure the baby was safe, to which the agents responded that they had already called for one.
“It was pretty scary,” Deflaminis said.
Sanford police say the baby was not properly restrained in a car seat and was taken to MaineHealth Maine Medical Center Sanford out of “an abundance of caution.” Small and Assistant Fire Chief Brian Watkins both said no one was injured.
Small said the police department did not assist with the federal detention and that he did not know the man’s name. Deflaminis did not know the man’s name either but said he lived nearby.
Emergency personnel also evaluated the driver, who is the baby’s father, while he was handcuffed in the back of a federal vehicle, Small said. The man “was under a lot of stress,” Small said, and reportedly told federal agents that he had two more children unattended at his nearby home.
Child Protective Services and the Maine Department of Health and Human Services were contacted to ensure the welfare of the other two children, who are 9 and 2 years old, according to a news release from the Sanford Police Department. Small said those children are now with a family friend who was able to take them in via an arrangement with CPS.
“(The ICE agents) were very forthcoming,” Small said. “They wanted what was best for the children as well.”
Small said the man’s vehicle was towed from the scene.
PINGREE CALLS FOR VIDEO RELEASE
Officials with ICE, U.S. Border Patrol and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond Thursday to requests for more information about the incident.
In a written statement, Pingree, D-1st District, called on the federal agencies to promptly release any footage of the incident, including from body-worn and dashboard cameras.
Referencing the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the congresswoman said that “it is entirely understandable that a father confronted by ICE — with his one-year-old in the car and two more children at home — would be terrified when federal agents box in his car.”
Durán Guerrero, 25, was shot and killed by an ICE agent on the morning of July 13 while driving in a Biddeford neighborhood; officials have said he was not the intended target of ICE’s operation.
A spokesperson for U.S. Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said the senator has been “very clear” about his opposition to how ICE is operating under the Trump administration.
Spokespeople for Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd District, did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this report.

title: 6-year-old fossil hunter makes rare discovery in Nebraska
text:
6-year-old finds rare fossil at a Nebraska state recreation area
A 6-year-old boy in Nebraska made history this summer by discovering a rare fossil at Schramm Park State Recreation Area, the first of its kind found in the state in more than 55 years.
"I found a fossil!" Leo Youngdahl said. "When I was a baby, we would go out in nature, and I would be picking up rocks and putting them in the bucket."
Now older, Leo has learned to identify his findings, saying, "Agates and gemstones and fossils."
Over the years, Leo has discovered several fossils, including brachiopods and shell fossils. But this summer, he found something entirely new.
"This is kind of where I found around right about here," Leo said, pointing to the spot.  
He initially thought the fossil resembled "an upside-down snake shed."
Kelly Ekue, an educator at Schramm Park, was surprised by the discovery.
"Normally, we see six different kinds of fossils here," Ekue said. "I looked at it, and I was like, okay, that's really weird. It looks like a fish. And so we don't have any vertebrates here in our fossil outcrops."
The park is around 28 miles from Omaha.
Local geologists identified the fossil as a conulariid, a type of jellyfish that lived in Nebraska between 200 million and 500 million years ago, when part of the state was underwater. Their soft bodies made them difficult to preserve.
"Certainly for Nebraska history, it's important that we've found one. And the last ones that we found on record were from the 1970s," Ekue said.
Leo’s discovery is now in the care of Schramm Park, where it is being used to educate other children. Meanwhile, Leo remains eager to uncover more fossils.
"Fossils are cool. And I would like to find out all about the things that lived before, because I kind of don't know what all of them are called," he said.
For those looking to find fossils, Leo shared his advice: "I look out for rocks that have kind of lots of nooks and crannies because I think they have more fossils."
