title: Watchdog group seeks to block Jared Kushner from serving in his volunteer envoy role
text:
Watchdog group seeks to block Jared Kushner from serving in his volunteer envoy role
A prominent Washington watchdog group is suing Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, trying to block him from serving as one of the administration’s top envoys without disclosing his personal finances and potential conflicts of interest.
The group, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, argues that Kushner’s role as a chief negotiator in the U.S.’s most prominent ongoing foreign policy concerns means he should be considered an official government employee and comply with all relevant requirements.
Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the U.S. special envoy, are considered to be the president’s closest and most influential diplomats. Neither is Senate-confirmed, and Witkoff is a formal employee, although the wealthy investor does not draw a taxpayer-funded salary.
The White House has repeatedly said Kushner remains a private citizen and is doing his diplomatic duties on a volunteer basis.
But in the lawsuit, CREW said Kushner is representing the United States while simultaneously running an investment firm that manages billions of dollars of foreign-owned assets.
“While his personal business interests abroad raise serious conflict-of-interest concerns, he has not been properly vetted for his government role,” read the legal complaint, filed Wednesday. ”(A)nd he has evaded transparency obligations that aim to ensure that he exercises government authority for the good of the American people and not himself.”
The Constitution’s appointments clause and a post-Watergate ethics law are meant to ensure that federal officials are properly vetted and that their assets are adequately disclosed.
Kushner’s unofficial role has made him central to the biggest foreign policy challenges of the second Trump administration, including the wars between Israel and Hamas, Ukraine and Russia and the U.S. and Iran. He was a primary negotiator of the peace plan that was inked between Israel and Hamas last year, and he regularly travels abroad to meet with world leaders as a representative of his father-in-law.
Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump, were formal government employees during the first Trump administration and filed the appropriate financial disclosures, although neither took a salary. Though Kushner had some domestic policies in his portfolio during Trump’s first term in office, he has been mainly focused on foreign policy the second time around.
Chad Mizelle, an attorney for Kushner, said in a statement on X that the lawsuit is “without merit” and that CREW lacks standing to challenge him.
CREW insists that it is directly harmed because Kushner is depriving it of records that would otherwise be available from government officials.
“Both outside ethics counsel and government ethics attorneys have reviewed Jared Kushner’s volunteer government service and confirmed that his arrangements comply with applicable ethics requirements,” said Mizelle, who served as chief of staff at the Justice Department from the start of the second Trump administration before leaving government service last year.
Meanwhile, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly attacked CREW as an “unserious, Trump-deranged organization that has been attacking President Trump, his family, and his administration since the first term.”
Calling Kushner a “proven dealmaker,” Kelly said his “personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements, which he conducts on a volunteer basis at the President’s request and while paying his own expenses.”
Kushner himself has brushed off conflict-of-interest questions in the past, saying in a CBS News interview last year that his business and financial connections were actually an asset.
“What people call conflicts of interests, Steve and I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world,” Kushner said in the interview, referring to Witkoff. “If Steve and I didn’t have these deep relationships, the deal we were able to get done, that freed these hostages, would not have occurred.”
Kushner was referring to the Israeli hostages who were freed by Hamas as part of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Also named in the lawsuit are Witkoff, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in their official capacities.

title: Trump leans on rallies to boost GOP midterm turnout
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump has held campaign rallies for supporters in Alaska, Arizona and Montana in the past 48 hours, as he works to keep the House and Senate under Republican control in the midterm elections.
Trump used campaign rallies during three presidential campaigns to energize his supporters. He is using the same strategy for the midterms.
Speaking in the Rose Garden on Thursday, Trump said the rallies are energizing his campaign.
“The crowds are unbelievable, actually. And I think we’re having a big impact. The Democrats are saying there’s something bad happening and the the fake news doesn’t want to talk about it, but these are rallies that nobody’s ever seen it,” Trump said.
Some of the president’s supporters have questioned the strategy of visiting states like Montana, which Trump won by almost 20 points in 2024.
White House correspondent Jon Decker asked the president about the Montana trip on the tarmac before Trump boarded Air Force One en route to the state.
“Mr. President, why Montana? It’s a very red state. There are those who are saying you’re playing defense as opposed to trying to go to Michigan,” Decker asked.
“Well, I probably because I’m doing Michigan, too, as you know, I’m doing Michigan in a few days. Montana, because we want to make sure we won. I won, you know, it was one of my best states. I won by 45 points. And really two reasons. Normally I wouldn’t be going, but I like to also pay my respect to places that I don’t have to go there,” Trump said.
“And so I do it to thank them. I also do it because we have some great people there that are running, and I want to make sure they win, because when I don’t run, which, you know, in theory I’m not running, but I feel that I’m running. When I don’t run, we get 49% less turnout. When I do run, we win easily,” Trump said.
More campaign rallies are planned in the days ahead in Ohio, Texas, Georgia and Kentucky. Trump is hoping his MAGA base can match the energy that Democrats say they have this election cycle.

title: Watch: Spruce Mountain soccer is the Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Spruce Mountain soccer
Winning hasn’t come easy for the Spruce Mountain girls soccer team over the past handful of years.
The Phoenix won only eight games from 2023-25. It looked like the 2026 season would be more of the same when they started with three straight losses, but then the victories started to pile up.
Since Sept. 11, Spruce Mountain is 6-0-2, including 6-0 and 3-2 wins last week against Wiscasset/Boothbay and Wells, respectively. The Phoenix were ranked sixth in Class C South Heal points going into Wednesday’s games.
“So I think our team is clicking more … in a sense of just distributing the ball and finding that open player and looking for crosses,” Spruce Mountain coach Jacob Turner said. “I think that’s really helped, and I saw that the most in Wells.”
Both Turner and senior captain Ashley Nelson said three freshmen — midfielder Lexus Hebert, forward Evangeline “Gigi” DiPasquale and defender Harlee Foss — have played a big part in the turnaround.
“I think we have the most talent that we have had in a very long time,” Nelson said. “We’ve had three amazing freshmen (who) have stepped up and (taken) on some very important roles on our team.”
Turner said the Phoenix are well balanced throughout the lineup.
“We have a great back system,” Turner said. “Our midfield is strong, and we’re aggressive in the midfield. We have Lexus Hebert and Natasha (McDonald) that can score on some of these really good teams.”
Nelson said she’s been waiting for a postseason push since entering high school.
“We’ve gone hard at practices; everyone wants to be here,” Nelson said. “We’ve wanted this since I was a freshman. We’ve really wanted to pull through and make playoffs.”

title: Toyota recalls thousands of RAV4s because vehicles could shut down. Here’s why
text:
(CNN) - More than 30,000 Toyota vehicles have been recalled due to a software issue that could cause the car to shut down.
The recall affects the 2026 Toyota RAV4 plug-in hybrid.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said the software issue could cause the hybrid system to reduce power or even shut down when the vehicle is driven at higher speeds.
As a result, the issue could increase the risk of a crash.
Toyota dealers will update the software for free.
Owners will be notified by early December.

title: College student killed in crash after being hit by car going 94 mph in 35 mph zone
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A Clark Atlanta University student died after a crash Tuesday night, and the driver of the other vehicle was arrested, police said.
Officers responded to the crash at Hank Aaron Drive and Glen Street around 11:30 p.m. Tuesday, where 21-year-old Morgan Gamble was found in critical condition, police said. Gamble was taken to the hospital, where she later died.
Driver charged with vehicular homicide
Police believe a vehicle driven by Nikolai Dunford was going 94 mph on Hank Aaron Drive, a 35 mph zone, when it struck Gamble’s car.
Dunford is charged with reckless driving, speeding and first-degree vehicular homicide, police said.
University issues statement
Clark Atlanta University issued a statement Wednesday acknowledging Gamble’s death.
“The loss of a member of our University community is deeply felt, and we extend our heartfelt condolences to Morgan’s family, friends, classmates and all who knew and loved Morgan,” the statement read. “During this time of sorrow, scholars are encouraged to support one another.”
Gamble’s family said she was an extra in Netflix’s reboot of “A Different World.”
The investigation is ongoing.

title: An Maine 11-year-old just shot his first moose
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Logan Grard, 11, shot his first moose Monday evening on the opening day of Maine’s October bull moose season.
Logan was hunting near Greenville with his father, Justin, his grandfather, Kim, and his friend Landon. They had spent the weekend scouting but came up empty-handed Monday morning.
That evening, as they drove down a road, Justin spotted the bull within 50 yards.
He slowed the vehicle as Logan grabbed his grandfather’s .270 rifle. The moose was heading toward a gravel pit behind some short saplings, but when it spotted the hunters, it began trotting away.
The group climbed out and followed the bull into the pit. When it disappeared behind a pine tree, they hurried after it. Justin called to the moose, and it stopped to look over its shoulder.
Logan fired, and the bull fell. When it tried to get back up, Justin fired a second shot, dropping it about 30 yards away.
The bull weighed 620 pounds and had a 33 1/2-inch antler spread.
Logan has been an avid hunter since he was old enough to hold a gun, his mother, Rachel Grard, said.
“He fell in love with the sport,” she said.
He shot a six-point buck in 2023 and a 10-point buck in 2024. This year, he has already taken a bear in September and a turkey a few weeks ago, leaving him one deer away from completing a hunting grand slam.
Logan’s family has entered him in Maine’s moose permit lottery for years, initially applying for bonus points when he was about 6 or 7.
The moose hunt came together in an unexpected way. Justin drew a moose permit last year but had to defer his hunt after tearing a tendon. When Logan drew a permit this year, he wanted his father to join him as his subpermittee.
The family arranged to transfer Justin’s permit to Kim, allowing Logan to hunt with his dad while his grandfather had a chance to take a bull of his own.
Kim, a Navy veteran, traveled from New York to join his son and grandson for the hunt. He was especially thrilled to watch Logan take his first moose with the same rifle Justin used to shoot his first buck.
With Logan’s bull tagged, the family is hoping Kim will get a chance to take a moose of his own before they head home.

title: Obituary: John Patterson Holt
text:
PORTLAND – John Patterson Holt, 88, of Portland, Maine, formerly of Huntington, Mass. passed away peacefully on Oct. 6, 2026, with his family by his side.
John was a devoted husband, father, grandfather, and friend. He is survived by his beloved wife of 66 years, Barbara Holt; his daughter and son-in-law, Bethany and Neil Buitenhuys; and his granddaughters, Emma Ryan, Merritt Ryan and Arielle Buitenhuys.
He was predeceased by his son, John “Jay” Holt.
John proudly served his country in the United States Air Force. Following his military service, he worked for Exxon Mobil for 40 years before retiring. While still working full time, John also raised beef cattle on the family farm in Huntington, Mass. where Barbara grew up. The farm held a special place in their lives and reflected John’s strong work ethic, determination, and dedication.
Above all, John cherished his family and the time they shared together. He also enjoyed traveling to Florida each winter to escape the cold Maine weather. There he loved the warm sun and long walks on the beach everyday.
John will be deeply missed by his family and all who knew him. In accordance with his wishes, a private ceremony will be held at a later date with family and close loved ones to celebrate and honor his life.
John’s family would like to express their sincere gratitude to the Maine Veterans’ Home of Scarborough for the exceptional care he received over the past three years.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in John’s memory to Compassus Hospice in appreciation of the compassionate care and support provided to John and his family.

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Waterville
text:
WATERVILLE — On Nov. 3, Waterville voters can cast their ballots for their next mayor and decide whether to form a charter commission.
In wards 2, 4 and 6 they’ll also select new city councilors, and elect candidates to more local boards.
In person voting is scheduled to take place from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m at the Thomas College Field House, 180 W River Road, and requests for absentee ballots are due by 5 p.m. Oct. 29. Absentee ballots can be delivered to City Hall via a secure drop box outside the main building entrance, or by mail.
Here’s what to expect on the ballot in Waterville.
THE MAYORAL RACE
Incumbent Mayor Michael Morris, a Democrat,will run against Republican Matthew Boulerice in the city’s mayoral election. The pair last faced off in the 2023 mayoral election, when Morris defeated Boulerice by around 600 votes.
Morris said his priorities are fiscal responsibility in the budget, housing stability and increasing sustainable revenues for the city, while Boulerice plans to focus on public safety, including homelessness and recovery, economic growth and “more focused, effective city leadership.” He said he wants to turn good ideas into action as mayor, while Morris said he’d like to see through plans made by existing groups and committees.
To learn more about Waterville’s mayoral candidates, a live candidate forum, open to the public, is set for 6-7 p.m. Oct. 21 in Ayotte Auditorium at Thomas College.
CITY COUNCIL
Candidates are seeking City Council seats in wards 2, 4 and 6, but only Ward 4’s election is contested.
In Ward 4, independent Brian McArthur and Democrat Christopher Rancourt are vying for Councilor Rebecca Green’s seat.
McArthur is a mental health councilor and father of three who said his priorities are economic growth, recreational expansion and public safety. McArthur works with the South End Teen Center to get children outside, and said he believes in having a strong school system to generate community pride.
Running for city council is something he said he sees as a sacrifice, and he doesn’t have loftier political aspirations. But he said he wants to have a say in the city he raises his children in. McArthur and his wife, a Mainer, chose to move to Waterville after spending years doing nonprofit work in South America.
“We came here on purpose,” McArthur said. “We really believe in Waterville. We think it’s a great town, I would love to try to inspire a little bit more community pride.”
A lifelong independent, McArthur said he doesn’t believe party politics should have an impact at the local level.
“Its a lot of what’s wrong in this country and a lot of what got us here today,” McArthur said.
Rancourt is a freight conductor with CSX Railway and he’s lived in Waterville for almost two decades. He wants residents to be able to age in place without being pushed out by high taxes, and said he wants to grow the city’s businesses and community projects.
Rancourt said he’d like to see the council put more forethought into budgeting, and wants to really dig into the city’s spending, which he said is too high without enough long-term planning.
Rancourt comes from a family of central Mainers, and wants to see more stable jobs in the area.
“I grew up in the area, I know what central Maine once was,” Rancourt said. “We ran off factories, paper mills, the wood industry — that’s all gone — we need to start from scratch, but it’s like building a house. We need a good foundation and then we need to get this budget spending under control.”
Rancourt has big ideas about how the city could spend more efficiently on things like roads and development, and he’s ready to get started if he’s elected.
“There’s a lot of stuff I’ve got to learn,” Rancourt said. “But I’m willing to jump in there and start looking at numbers. I’m kind of a numbers guy.”
In Ward 2, Erik S. Thomas is running unopposed for Councilor Flavia DeBrito’s seat. Thomas, the assistant executive director of the Waterville Opera House, previously held the Ward 4 and Ward 7 seats on the council and served as council chair before he lost his bid for reelection in 2021.
Thomas did not respond to the Maine Trust for Local News voter guide survey.
In Ward 6, Councilor Scott Beale is running for reelection after he took over the vacant Ward 6 seat in 2025. In his time on the council, Beale introduced an ordinance to limit how city employees can cooperate with federal immigration agents. Beale said his priorities are supporting growth in the city, protecting Waterville’s immigrant community and expanding the tax base.
MORE LOCAL RACES
Residents will also elect members to the city’s proposed charter commission, with one candidate running from each ward, and choose two of three candidates to be Kennebec Water District trustees.
The board of trustees has four Waterville representatives, and incumbents Sarah Whateley and Alexander Lelchuk will be on the ballot alongside Heather Pelletier, who is also running to be the Ward 2 charter commission representative.
Wards 2, 4 and 6 will also elect candidates to the Board of Education, all of whom are running unopposed.
REFERENDUMS
Waterville residents will decide whether to establish a commission to revise the city charter or establish a new one. The charter is designed to provide a “clear and definitive” overview of the city’s operations and the powers of its officials, and its last revision was approved in 2020.
The candidates for the charter commission will be on the ballot, with one representative from each ward.
COUNTY RACES
Residents will choose between Democrat Joanne Mason and Republican Monte Sylvester for county treasurer. They will also elect a register of deeds, with incumbent Republican Matthew Boucher and Democrat Kevin Lamoreau running.
Maeghan Maloney is running unopposed to retain her role as district attorney.
STATE RACES
Voters in House District 64 will choose between incumbent and current city councilor Flavia DeBrito, who is a Democrat, and Republican challenger Shawn Packard. House District 65 voters will choose between incumbent Democrat Cassie Julia and Republican Jeremy McArthur. McArthur did not respond to the Maine Trust’s voter guide survey.
In the Senate District 16 race, residents will choose between incumbent Republican Scott Cyrway and Democrat Patric Moore. Cyrway did not respond to the Maine Trust’s voter guide survey.
To find your house district and build your ballot, type your address into the voter guide’s search tool.

title: After censure, Sabattus selectwoman must limit contact with town employees
text:
SABATTUS — A selectwoman has been censured by the town board and prohibited from speaking to other town employees outside of official business.
How that is going to work remains to be seen.
At a special meeting Tuesday, the Select Board agreed that Noel Hinkley should be censured after a number of town employees complained about her behavior.
An official complaint from the Sabattus police union prompted an independent investigation that recently concluded.
The investigator, Toby Tiner, an independent human resource consultant, found that some of Hinkley’s comments to other town employees “appear to have crossed some personal and professional boundaries.”
The report also concluded that some former town employees left their positions specifically due to Hinkley’s treatment of them.
Hinkley was accused of referring to one town employee as “a glorified clerk” and publicly blaming that employee for problems at the Sabattus Police Department.
She was also accused of making insensitive remarks, including those about at least one town official’s personal life, and of sending social media messages to one town employee that were perceived as “confrontational and falsely accusatory.”
“The exchange became increasingly personal and escalated unnecessarily,” Tiner wrote in his report.
When that report was released to the public on Wednesday, the four-page document had been heavily redacted, with individual names and specific language blacked out.
Hinkley herself has acknowledged most of the interactions described in Tiner’s investigative report. She described herself as transparent and said most of the issues raised are the result of her speaking frankly.
“If you don’t want an opinion you might not like, don’t ask me,” Hinkley said at the Tuesday night meeting. “If you want to sugarcoat it, you’ll probably want to go to someone else.”
The report concluded that there were a number of town employees who felt “targeted, intimidated and disrespected” by Hinkley.
But not all town leaders agreed that she should be censured.
Select Board Chair Laura Clifford expressed strong opposition to the notion of censuring Hinkley, saying it sends a “troubling message” to voters.
“I’m not suggesting that legitimate complaints should be ignored,” Clifford said at the meeting, “but I am saying that we need to be extremely careful that investigations and legal expenses do not become the answer every time someone’s unhappy with an elected official.
“Sometimes,” Clifford said, “we need to acknowledge our differences and act like adults and move forward.”
It cost the town nearly $4,000 to pay for Tiner’s investigation. And Clifford pointed out that there will also be attorney fees as the town struggles to figure out how a Select Board member can realistically be prohibited from talking to other town employees.
Hinkley, who called the idea “a little absurd,” pointed out that she runs three businesses in Sabattus, including a daycare.
She has friends who are town officials, she said. Occasionally she has to talk with fire officials about a safety program for the children at her daycare.
When Hinkley raised questions about how the censure would work in those contexts, there was uncomfortable muttering and promises to seek clarity in coming days.
“The guidelines for this are being worked out,” Town Manager Raquel Welch-Day said Wednesday.
Those guidelines are expected to be discussed at the town’s next meeting.
In his report, Tiner concluded that complaints about Hinkley were proven valid. He also pointed out that Hinkley expressed “limited concern” about how she is perceived by her peers, at one pointed telling him “I’m not going anywhere.”
It was Tiner’s opinion that intervention by town leaders was the only possible solution.
“In my experience,” Tiner wrote, “entrenched conflicts of this nature are unlikely to be resolved without deliberate intervention. Absent such intervention, it is my opinion that the town is likely to face continued complaints and concerns regarding the work environment, employee morale and retention, and confidence in town leadership.”

title: Fairfield budget articles get OK from voters on 3rd try
text:
FAIRFIELD — Town voters Wednesday passed two budget articles they had rejected twice earlier this year, this time approving as part of a plan officials put forward to draw significantly more from surplus funds than originally proposed.
In all, the articles voters approved at the special town meeting will result in a net of about $2 million less compared with last year’s needed taxpayer funding for the municipal budget. That means the portion of the municipal budget funded by taxes would decrease by roughly 71%, marking a significant change from the 24% increase that would have resulted had voters approved the entire budget as originally proposed in June.
While the property tax rate is set to go down with Wednesday’s approvals, officials said Fairfield property owners could still see increases in their tax bills due to adjustments in property valuations.
The more than 110 voters who turned out to the Fairfield Community Center gymnasium took about an hour to pass the three budget articles.
They approved appropriating $1,209,480 for general government — which includes administrative staff, insurance, general assistance, elections and legal services — and $280,000 for capital improvements, equipment and other reserve accounts, all to come from available undesignated fund balance.
They also approved taking an additional $1,210,520 from the undesignated fund balance to offset taxation.
Voters already had approved using $1.15 million from undesignated fund balance at June’s town meeting. With the $2.7 million appropriated Wednesday, that makes for a total of $3.85 million coming from undesignated fund balance in the 2026-27 budget.
The undesignated fund balance totals municipal funds not assigned to designated accounts. Officials said the recently completed financial audit for the fiscal year ending June 2025 gave them a more accurate idea of how much money is available — about $8.82 million, budget documents show. The audit was not complete when officials first prepared their budget proposal this spring.
In June, voters approved most of an approximately $9 million 2026-27 municipal spending plan. But voters rejected a proposed $1,201,007 for general government and $260,000 for capital accounts.
In the proposal put to voters in September, town officials proposed slight reductions in both articles, and they failed to pass again.
Under the town charter, any budget article not adopted at the annual town meeting reverts to the funding approved in the prior fiscal year until a new budget article passes.
The increase in the approved general government article compared to the original June proposal was due to an increase in the cost of an information technology services contract, town officials said. The increase in the capital accounts article was proposed because of the change to funding the article through undesignated fund balance rather than taxation.
The property tax rate is estimated to decrease from $19.40 per $1,000 of property valuation to about $14.30, Town Council Chairman Timothy Martin said. At the same time, to meet certain state thresholds, property assessments are going up, on average about 30%, he said.
That means, even with the reduction in mill rate, property taxes are not necessarily going down. On average, Town Manager Michelle Flewelling said, a residential property owner should expect to see their tax bill increase about $100.
The municipal budget is only one portion of what factors into residents’ tax bills, typically representing less than half of the total. Somerset County and Maine School Administrative District 49 assessments make up the rest.

title: Why Hannah Pingree is the leader Maine needs
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Charlie Dingman is the chair of the Maine Democratic Party and an attorney based in Augusta. He lives in Leeds.
It will surprise no one that, as chair of the Maine Democratic Party, I enthusiastically support our Democratic nominee for governor, Hannah Pingree.
But my support for Hannah goes well beyond my role as party chair. It comes from watching her work for years and seeing firsthand the kind of leader she is.
I have spent much of my career as a lawyer advocating before all three branches of Maine government. That has given me a front-row seat to state government, both when it works well and when it doesn’t. It has given me the opportunity to see Hannah’s effective leadership during her time in the Legislature and her work leading the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future.
Hannah listens, asks insightful questions, and thinks strategically. She works with focus, determination, and courage to build workable solutions. And I believe she will stand up to anyone who, like our current president, would stand in the way just to accumulate wealth and power.
Good leadership is not just about having the loudest voice in the room. It is about understanding the problems we face, listening to people affected by them, and figuring out how to make things better. That has been a consistent focus of Hannah’s career.
My career has long focused on health care law and policy, so I find Hannah’s approach to that key public concern especially encouraging. Our health care system is enormously complex, often chaotic, and insufficiently focused on health outcomes and affordability. Maine people feel the chaos, cost, and inadequacy as they struggle to afford insurance, find a primary or specialty care provider, or maintain prescription drug therapy when it’s prohibitively expensive.
Ideal solutions will require concerted, nationwide action and investment. Hannah knows we can’t wait for Washington to get there, which may take years even after we reawaken Congress by sending Democratic majorities to the House and Senate. That’s why she’s pledging to create a public health insurance option in Maine. It will not eliminate private or employer-sponsored coverage but will provide another choice — a state-backed plan designed to provide affordable, reliable coverage and use the state’s leverage to help bring down costs.
Her health care plan recognizes something that is especially important in Maine: having coverage does not mean much if you cannot find someone to care for you. She has proposed investing in primary care, strengthening maternity and reproductive health care, and recruiting and retaining more health care workers, particularly in rural communities.
I believe Hannah is the leader we need to seek real improvements in this challenging arena: a governor willing to dig into the details and stay focused on getting results.
We can’t ignore the extraordinary headwinds that any state leader will face from what I view as our currently corrupt and self-absorbed federal government. President Donald Trump’s Republicans have concentrated wealth and power by funding their tax cuts for the ultra-rich with massive cuts to health care and other basic services, while brutally attacking rights and institutions we have long taken for granted.
I think Maine needs a governor who will resist these abuses of power, acting creatively to counteract them to the full extent that a state can do so, while we await a reckoning and a change in direction in Washington. I believe Hannah has the tenacity, the energy, the intelligence, and the compassion we need to lead Maine in this incredibly challenging chapter of our history.
The next four years will bring challenges we can predict and, undoubtedly, some we cannot. Maine needs a governor who cares deeply about the people they serve and knows how to turn good ideas into action. I’ve seen Hannah Pingree deliver exactly that for years in her other leadership roles. I’m excited to be working to elect her as Maine’s next governor.

title: Dunlap, LePage to face off in final televised debate Thursday night
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WAGM) - The two candidates looking to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District in Washington faced off Thursday night in their final televised debate of the campaign.

President Donald Trump visited Arizona and Montana on Wednesday, focusing on gun rights and supporting Republican candidates in tight races before the midterm elections.
President Donald Trump traveled to Arizona and Montana on Wednesday to promote Republican candidates and emphasize key issues ahead of the midterm elections.
In Montana, Trump highlighted the importance of the Second Amendment, warning it would be "under siege" if Democrats win in November. He also announced the Pentagon's plan to create a new military testing site in the state to test advanced weapons and technology.
Earlier in the day, Trump spoke with voters in Arizona to support Republican gubernatorial candidate Rep. Andy Biggs, who is running against incumbent Democrat Katie Hobbs.
Arizona has historically been a GOP stronghold, with registered Republicans outnumbering Democrats and independents by a comfortable margin. However, voters in the state have recently rejected Trump allies and handed top offices to Democrats.
"We had a big day in Arizona and Montana. I think we got a lot of people elected today. The crowds were massive," Trump said. "I'm here whether we win this or not in terms of the Republicans in the Senate and in Congress, but I will tell you I think there's a great thing happening and the people will see what we've accomplished."
The president's visits to Arizona and Montana reflect the administration's focus on closely contested races. According to multiple reports, Trump is expected to attend a rally in Northern Kentucky on Saturday and then will speak with voters in North Carolina and Kansas early next week.

title: Father, child found dead following Amber Alert for the 4-year-old boy
text:
GAINESVILLE, Texas (KXII/Gray News) — A father and 4-year-old child were found dead in Texas on Wednesday amid a search connected to an Amber Alert issued out of Oklahoma.
The Gainesville Police Department said that early Wednesday morning, they got in contact with a relative of Caleb Furley, 25, and missing 4-year-old Andres Furley, who were the subjects of an Amber Alert out of Norman, Oklahoma.
The relative told officers that the two went missing after last being seen at an area business early Monday evening.
A police investigator went to the business when it opened and found surveillance video from Monday that appeared to show the two walking away from the area.
Authorities said they searched the surrounding area for the father and son, which led to the discovery of their bodies.
Gainesville Police Chief Kevin Phillips said their investigation began on Monday after someone reported a suspicious interaction involving a father and son.
“The contact just appeared to be suspicious. So they notified the police department and we responded,” Phillips said.
Officers searched at the time but did not find anyone.
“The officers searched the area extensively, and we also used a drone to search the area, but we weren’t able to locate anyone,” Phillips said.
Police said they also looked for a vehicle possibly associated with the two but were unable to locate it during that initial search.
Norman police confirmed the bodies found were those of 4-year-old Andres and Furley.
Police in Oklahoma said they are working with Texas authorities regarding the case.
“We do extend our deepest condolences to the persons who are impacted,” Phillips added.

title: Hyundai recalls more than 94,000 vehicles over power seat fire risk
text:
Hyundai recalls more than 94,000 vehicles over power seat fire risk
Thousands of vehicles have been recalled over a potential fire risk.
Hyundai Motor America is recalling 94,622 Hyundai Genesis and Genesis G80 vehicles because a power seat motor could overheat and cause a fire, federal safety regulators said.
The recall covers certain 2015 and 2016 Hyundai Genesis vehicles and 2017 through 2020 Genesis G80s.
Related video above | How to stay ahead of recalls
A stuck power seat control switch can cause the front seat motor to overheat, potentially starting a fire while the vehicle is parked or being driven, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
Owners are advised to park affected vehicles outdoors and away from other vehicles or structures until repairs are completed.
Hyundai said a remedy is still under development. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed Dec. 7.
Vehicle identification numbers became searchable on NHTSA’s website on Oct. 13. Hyundai owners can call 1-855-371-9460; Genesis owners can call 844-340-1200. The recall numbers are 308 for Hyundai and 035G for Genesis.

title: Who protects the farmers?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Regarding an Oct. 7 news report (“Maine’s top court rejects eviction appeal by Midcoast farmers”), the farmers’ appeal was reportedly lost because it was found they had “failed to pay rent and grow crops as they had once agreed.”
Crops, for most non-farmers, usually means fruits and vegetables. Not all soils in Maine are suitable for growing fruits and vegetables. Some soils are best used for pasture and hay (a valuable crop) or for growing livestock, which might also be called a valuable crop.
The Maine Farmland Trust ought to carefully review its policies regarding farmers on leased land; the situation that happened in Harpswell will happen again. It is one thing to protect farmland. Who protects the farmers? No farmers, no food.
Jeanne Johnson
Juniper Edge Farm
Brunswick

title: 'Suspicious substances' sent to congressional, election offices nationwide
text:
Authorities investigate letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to congressional, election offices
Federal authorities are investigating letters with “suspicious substances” that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide.
Authorities are urging recipients to treat the letters as “potentially hazardous.”
The Senate was informed of the investigation by a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms that was obtained Thursday by The Associated Press.
The mailings come just three weeks before Election Day and are reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when several election offices received envelopes containing the powerful opioid fentanyl.
Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states.
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement condemning what they said were threats against election staff.
“Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” they said in their statement.

ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) — A firefighter who spent more than 30 years with the St. Louis Fire Department is no longer employed there after he defecated in a cardboard box while working fire protection at Lambert International Airport.
The firefighter was put on administrative leave after the June 10 incident, which was caught on a security camera in an area operated by the airport’s food and beverage concessionaire. His employment with the City of St. Louis ended on Aug. 14, the Department of Personnel confirmed to KMOV.
A photo from security footage showed the man with his pants down, holding a box behind him.
The St. Louis Fire Department is responsible for fire protection at Lambert International Airport. An airport spokesperson previously said fire personnel operate independently at the airport but are on site 24/7.
The St. Louis Fire Department told KMOV that the man started working fire protection at Lambert in 2019.

title: Holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy trial says he was struck by how 'methodical' she was
text:
The lone juror who blocked Lindsay Clancy from being acquitted was influenced by how “methodical” he thought she was while killing her three children, he said during an interview aired Thursday, his first since the trial ended with a deadlocked jury.
Michael Desronvil said he didn’t have any doubt that Clancy was guilty, telling Fox News Channel’s “Fox & Friends” that he was struck by her “thought process” during the killings.
Desronvil was the only juror who opposed clearing Clancy of criminal responsibility, siding with prosecutors who argued that she knew what she was doing. Clancy’s defense argued she was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids.
“The focus has to be on the children,” Desronvil said. “They are the ones who don’t have anyone fighting for them.”
___
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
___
Clancy’s trial ended with a mistrial in early September and generated intense public interest, drawing attention to maternal mental health after childbirth. She had mental health problems that included months of treatment and a stay in a psychiatric hospital before she killed the children and then tried to kill herself at her family’s Massachusetts home in 2023.
Prosecutors have yet to decide whether they will put the case in front of a jury for a second time. They could retry her on first-degree murder charges, seek lesser charges or drop the case entirely.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.
Her former husband Patrick Clancy, who discovered the children’s bodies, has said in interviews that he forgives her.

title: Dunlap and LePage debated, hotly, for the final time. Here are 3 takeaways
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage faced off Thursday— sometimes arguing — for the final time on the debate stage before Election Day.
The Democratic state auditor and Republican former governor are locked in one of the nation’s most competitive races for the U.S. House. The only major poll of the race, conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center in September, found Dunlap with a six-point edge.
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, the second-most rural in the country, has voted for President Donald Trump three times while also electing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden to a House seat since 2018. With Golden not running for reelection, the seat is wide open.
The race is of national importance. Democrats’ path to recapture the House — currently held by Republicans with a four-seat majority — would be significantly bolstered if Dunlap can hold off LePage, one of Maine’s most prominent Republicans.
Those were the stakes for the candidates coming into Thursday’s debate. It was hosted by WABI and WAGM.
Here are three takeaways.
1. There were quite a few spiky moments.
During discussion about declining healthcare access in Maine, Dunlap criticized PL 90, a law championed by LePage during his time as governor that set up a pool of high-risk patients and subsidized their insurance with a fee on all individual health insurance plans in Maine.
“It’s an all-you-can-eat buffet for the insurance companies,” Dunlap said, repeating criticisms about PL 90 from 2012.
“What are you reading?” LePage shot back. “PL 90 lowered the premiums by 76%.”
“That’s not true,” Dunlap said, leaving LePage seemingly exasperated.
“Matt, you’ve been lying a lot this campaign,” LePage said.
Dunlap later accused LePage of calling Social Security a “welfare program,” and quoted from a 2014 press release in which the LePage administration criticized transfer programs, where the federal government sends money to the state, which then disburses funds. The release lumped Social Security in with those programs.
“Quote: ‘It doesn’t matter what liberals call these payments, it is welfare, pure and simple,’ said Gov. LePage,” Dunlap said, pulling from the release. “Including those Social Security payments we just discussed.”
LePage and Dunlap sparred on this for a full minute and a half while moderators Jon Small and Kelly O’Mara attempted to go to a commercial break.
“I’ll just say this,” LePage said, getting the last word in before the halfway point. “If Jared doesn’t retire, you’re not here tonight.”
At the end of the debate, Dunlap challenged LePage about his time living in Florida. LePage has been back and forth between the two states since he left the Blaine House in 2019. He began renting an apartment in Augusta the same month he announced his candidacy for Congress last spring.
LePage said he was a “snowbird,” living in Florida during the winter and Maine during the summer. He said he never spent a full year in Florida and paid his taxes here.
That point emerged again in the candidates’ final remarks.
“He just got a Maine driver’s license right after he declared he was going to run for Congress here,” Dunlap said.
“I never said I didn’t have a Florida driver’s license,” LePage interrupted.
2. Global conflict was, again, a major focus.
The debate began with a question on increasing heating oil assistance. Heating oil, used by about half of Maine households, is hovering near its all-time record price — it rose to over $6 per gallon last month.
Dunlap said heating assistance through the Home Energy Assistance Program should be fully funded, and that the war in Iran was the primary driver of costs. The reduction of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began in February has caused oil prices to spike worldwide.
LePage agreed on the first point — that HEAP should have more backing from the federal government — but challenged the second. Instead of pulling out of Iran, he said, the U.S. Navy and Air Force should force regime change there, though he said the U.S. should not put “boots on the ground.”
“Too many Americans are getting killed in other countries by proxies and the regime in Iran,” LePage said. “So I do believe it’s time to take ’em out.”
“Paul LePage is talking about regime change, and yet not putting any boots on the ground,” Dunlap responded. “I’m not sure how that happens without having American troops committed in a combat situation.”
The moderators also asked about the U.S. trade war with Canada, which has put strain on Maine businesses.
LePage said he has urged the Trump administration to return to the negotiating table, not least because tariffs can be a useful negotiating tool.
Dunlap said he would hope to act instead as a check on Trump, challenging his power to unilaterally impose tariffs.
3. Healthcare kept coming back up.
The most spirited and substantive discussion during the first half of the debate took place in response to a question about healthcare access.
LePage said he wanted to return to the insurance subsidy program he championed as governor, and Dunlap said he hoped to move toward universal healthcare.
LePage had pivoted from a question on immigration to his intent to work across the aisle with Democrats in Congress, and said Dunlap would simply block efforts to take action. Dunlap further pivoted to universal healthcare, saying adopting such a system would, on average, save money. LePage said the cost would be “astronomical.”

title: High schools Thursday: Winslow girls soccer settles for draw with Leavitt
text:
Kennedy Dube scored in the second overtime to give Cony a 2-1 win over Belfast in a Class B North field hockey game Thursday night in Augusta.
Gabby Vachon assisted on the winner as the Rams (9-3-1) knocked off the reigning state champions and jumped ahead of them into third place in the Heal point standings.
Maya Lebrun was the other Cony goal scorer. Kamynn Wadsworth scored for Belfast (9-2).
GIRLS SOCCER
LEAVITT 1, WINSLOW 1: Reese Bilodeau scored off a corner kick with one second left in regulation, and Leavitt (5-6-2) escaped with a tie against Winslow (8-4-1) in Turner.
Winslow took the lead midway through the second half on a goal by Mirra Meak.
MEDOMAK VALLEY 1, ERSKINE ACADEMY 0: Jules Blake scored in the second half as the Panthers (2-10-1) beat the Eagles (6-5-2) in Waldoboro.
Blake finished a ball that deflected to her following a save by Erskine keeper Eryn Young against Liberty Leavitt near the 14-minute mark.
HALL-DALE 8, WINTHROP 0: Clare Sturtevant’s two goals paced the Bulldogs (9-2-2) to their fifth consecutive victory, a shutout win over the Ramblers (4-9) in Farmingdale.
Maya Hammonds contributed a goal and two assists for Hall-Dale, and Robin Asch had one goal and one assist. Lexi Tinkham, Audra Schaab, Megan Inch and Sandra Corpion also scored, while Ella Lawrence, Isabel Tinkham, Vera Krajewski and Fiona Breslin each recorded an assist.
Goalie Genevieve Ciccarelli made three saves for the Bulldogs, who are vying four the second seed in Class C South.
Winthrop’s Kylee Savage stopped 21 shots. The Ramblers are trying to maintain their hold on C South’s eighth and final postseason berth.
BOYS SOCCER
LEAVITT 6, WINSLOW 0: Angelo Toscano scored three times in the first half as the Hornets (8-3-2) jumped out to a 5-0 lead and beat the Raiders (8-6) in Winslow.
Tyler Mates added two goals in the first half and Ryder Sawyer Brown scored on a penalty kick in the second half. Avery Schlobohm, Jacob Gibbs and Sawyer Brown each had an assist.
Leavitt keepers Luke Horn and Andrew Sutton combined for nine saves, while Maddox Lambert made 10 saves for Winslow.
LINCOLN ACADEMY 3, WATERVILLE 0: The Eagles (8-4) got goals from James Hanley, Mat Walther and Jesus Faura Ruiz and shut out the Panthers (0-10-3) in Waterville.
Hanley knocked in a rebound 10 minutes into the first half. Walther volleyed a cross from George Siegel with 18 minutes left in the game, and Ruiz put in a direct kick from 25 yards for the final goal.
Joey Crooker made two saves for the Eagles, while Waterville’s Khaled Alnabelsi stopped 12 shots.
FOOTBALL
LEAVITT 36, NOKOMIS 12: Landon Marquis rushed for two touchdowns and passed for two more, and the Hornets (7-0) defeated the Warriors (2-5) in a Class C game in Turner.
Leavitt capitalized on a Nokomis fumble to open the scoring in the first quarter, as Landon Reny tip-toed his way down the sideline for a 57-yard touchdown run.
Marquis scored on a 2-yard run in the second quarter, and Darren Flagg turned a screen pass into a 68-yard touchdown that made it 22-0 at halftime.
Nokomis threw a scare into the Hornets with two quick touchdowns in the third quarter. First, Maxx Demchak ripped the ball away from a Leavitt defender to catch a 16-yard touchdown pass from Colt Robinson. The Warriors then recovered an onside kick, and Stephone Ross cut the deficit to 22-12 with a 40-yard run.
Leavitt quickly regained control, however, as Marquis capped a drive with a 16-yard run early in the fourth. Cooper Morin caught a 4-yard pass for the final touchdown.
WINTHROP 29, MOUNTAIN VALLEY 7: The Ramblers (6-1) finally pulled away in the second half to earn a Class D South victory over the Falcons (1-6) at Chet Bulger Field in Rumford.
Through the first two-and-a-half quarters, Mountain Valley’s defense rarely allowed the Ramblers extra yards after contact. Winthrop started to break away midway through the third quarter, however, scoring on a 13-yard pass from Porter Lavigne to Clyde Moody for a 15-7 lead.
In the final minute of the third, Tristyan Ortiz added a 28-yard touchdown run. Winthrop’s last touchdown as a 2-yard run by Carter Rand in the fourth, set up a by a 26-yard Moody reception.
Mountain Valley opened the game with an 89-yard kickoff return for a score by Cole Curtis, who made many of the game’s biggest plays. He intercepted two passes, and had a couple of long runs and nice returns.
The Falcons forced a turnover on downs and two punts on Winthrop’s first three drives. On the fourth possession, Rand scored on a 21-yard run, but a missed kick kept Mountain Valley in the lead, 7-6.
Interceptions by Curtis ended the next two Winthrop drives, but in between those, a safety put the Ramblers ahead 8-7. Falcons quarterback Jimmy Arsenault was called for intentional grounding in the end zone.
Winthrop’s defense was stout throughout. Mason Fish had an interception and Canyon Peaslee recovered fumble. For Mountain Valley, Josh Pollis deflected a punt.

title: US reportedly considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ as part of new strike plans against Iran
text:
WASHINGTON — The United States is considering using a so-called “mother of all bombs” as part of new strike plans in the war in Iran.
Military sources told CNN that the plans are in place in case President Trump decides to resume combat operations, either before or after the midterm elections.
What is the MOAB
The GBU-43-B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, is the most powerful non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal.
Using it for the first time in the war with Iran would be a notable escalation.
It has the capability of destroying an area equal to nine city blocks.
Concerns over effectiveness and casualties
However, there are concerns it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough to destroy suspected nuclear facilities.
The big blast radius also raises concerns about civilian casualties.
White House response
When asked about possible military plans in Iran, a White House official told CNN that the president is keeping all options on the table.
Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war, as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the midterm elections.
There is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of U.S. bombing.

title: ‘It feels like punishment’: School district cancels ‘Little Shop of Horrors’ after female cast as male lead
text:
GRAND PRAIRIE, Texas (WFAA) - Grand Prairie ISD has scrapped its production of “Little Shop of Horrors” after district officials learned of the show’s casting and themes, according to the district.
Ana Mota, a senior at South Grand Prairie High School, was cast as the male lead, Seymour, before school leaders told her on Oct. 6 that she would no longer play the role.
Casting changed before cancellation
Ana said callbacks are for specific roles and students do not choose which roles they audition for. She said she initially got the role of Seymour.
“Initially, I got it,” Ana said. “And now we’re here.”
Ana said school leaders offered her the chance to split the female lead with another student instead.
“I was frustrated because I had earned a role and I worked hard for it and I wasn’t allowed to play it,” Ana said.
District cites state law
Grand Prairie ISD canceled the entire production after learning about the casting and the musical’s themes, which include the male lead character developing a romantic relationship with the female lead and an abusive relationship. The district said it plans to find something it called more appropriate.
“It’s not a compromise at all. It feels more like a punishment to everyone in the cast,” Ana said.
In a statement, the district said the decision was made as part of its effort to ensure programs comply with Texas Senate Bill 12 and other applicable laws. The law restricts certain sexually oriented performances on public property in the presence of minors.
Student has played male roles before
Ana said playing male characters is not new for her.
“I played Jack in ‘Into the Woods’ and Pinocchio,” she said.
Ana and her family plans to push back on the district’s decision.
“If we keep our heads down then nothing’s going to get better,” she said.

title: Hunters help save seriously injured woman ‘left out there to die,’ sheriff says
text:
FARGO, N.D. (KVLY/Gray News) - Two friends checking hunting cameras likely saved the life of an injured and bloody 28-year-old woman in North Dakota.
According to Cass County Sheriff Jesse Jahner, the woman was spotted Tuesday on cameras that resident Jay Schueler had set up near County Road 81. The woman was walking alone along the Wild Rice River, appearing to be missing clothing, badly injured and bleeding.
Jahner said Schueler called his friend Jeff Jones, whose property the cameras were located on, and the two went to the area to check on the woman and call 911.
They reached the woman before first responders. Jahner said she had multiple cuts on her neck, describing the injuries as severe and life-threatening, and noted she was wet when they found her.
The woman, who was not immediately identified by police, was treated at the scene, then taken to Sanford in Fargo.
Jahner said the woman had been “left out there to die,” and credited Schueler and his friend with likely saving her life.
Despite her injuries, authorities said she was able to give investigators a suspect’s name and information about a vehicle.
The woman told medical personnel she had been attacked with a knife, Jahner said.
A witness also came forward, helping investigators pinpoint where they believed the assault happened.
Jahner said investigators identified the suspect as 60-year-old Tracy Vaughn Peters.
Cass County authorities and the U.S. Marshals Task Force located and arrested Peters on Wednesday.
Peters was booked into the Cass County Jail on a charge of attempted murder.
Jahner said the reported victim and Peters knew each other but did not elaborate on their connection.
Investigators noted the case remains an open investigation, with deputies continuing to search for the knife that was said to have been used and gathering additional evidence.

Maine's Halloween Season Grows Beyond October 31st Making Parents and Grandparents Jealous
text:
I'm so envious of kids who get to enjoy Halloween all month, instead of the one-day celebration it was when I was growing up.
Halloween in Maine Used to Consist of One Evening, Not a Whole Month
I can't be the only one feeling this way.
When I was growing up, Halloween was only one night.
Parents didn't want to spend a lot of money on your costume for two reasons:
- You would only wear it for an hour or two
- It's so cold in late October that you'd probably wear a coat over it anyway.
So we would dig out the box of past costumes and try to piece something together for the new year.
Maine Trunk or Treat Events Have Changed the Landscape of Halloween
Now, children get to wear their Halloween costumes all month long, so their parents don't mind spending a little more.
They'll wear them over and over all month as they attend trunk-or-treat events.
Maybe they'll even go to Pumpkins in the Park at the Anah Shrine, where they don't have to wear coats.
Then there's the Halloween Glow Party at the Ferris Community Center Complex in Brewer.
My coworkers and I will across the street from the Brewer Community School.
Maine's Month-Long Halloween Celebrations Make Parents Envious
Don't get me wrong, I'm not criticizing the new month-long Halloween celebrations.
In fact, I love it.
I am pretty jealous that we didn't think of it when I was a kid, so I could've worn that costume more than once.
I'll have to drown my sorrows in a bag of Halloween candy, wearing my costume, and watching Charlie Brown get another rock.
