title: Maine's final Senate debate with Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The fourth and final debate in the Maine U.S. Senate race was a spirited affair that plowed some new ground, with Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican Susan Collins weighing in on gun control and the possible reform of the U.S. Supreme Court.
Thursday’s debate at the Gracie Theater at Husson University in Bangor was the only one to have a live audience, invited by the campaigns. It allowed for crowd reactions — and at one point an interruption by a protester — leading to a memorable exchange.
Jackson, a 58-year-old former logger, continued to tie Collins to President Donald Trump, whose actions and policies Jackson argued are driving up the prices of consumer goods, energy and fuel.
Collins, meanwhile, continued to focus on her seniority, which she says has brought $1.5 billion in federal earmarks to Maine in recent years. The 73-year-old has also sought to distance herself from Trump and shift blame onto Jackson for high energy prices, citing his votes in support of solar energy as Maine Senate president.
Here are the major takeaways from the final debate before the Nov. 3 election. It was conducted in partnership with Maine Public, the Portland Press Herald and NEWSCENTER Maine.
1. Protester interrupts, Jackson snaps
About 15 minutes into the debate, someone in the crowd stood up and began shouting about data centers. The moderator took a brief pause as security removed the young man, who appeared to be wearing a press badge.
“That’s obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” Collins quipped.
Jackson shot back.
“Oh shut up,” Jackson said. “I don’t even know that kid.”
Event organizers said the individual was not on the pre-registered media list, but presented a Bowdoin Orient press badge and was allowed in.
In an email Thursday night, the editor-in-chief of the Orient said the student paper did not send a reporter to the debate, and that the credential must have been fabricated.
2. Jackson stumbles on campaign finance
Collins and Jackson each had the opportunity to ask each other a question. And Collins appeared to get the best of both exchanges.
Collins called out Jackson for vowing not to take money from billionaires and corporate PACs. But Collins noted that Jackson’s campaign has been running joint ads with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which she said received money from 28 billionaires and 190 corporate PACs.
Jackson appeared to have been caught off guard, at first confusing the joint ads, which contain his endorsement, with independent super PACs, which he cannot legally coordinate with.
Jackson, who earlier in the day announced he’d give away $15,000 in donations from oil and pharmaceutical lobbyists, also acknowledged that billionaires are supporting his campaign — a statement that drew a reaction from the audience.
“As far as billionaires that I might have on my campaign, that is accurate, but I haven’t made any deals like Sen. Collins has with those billionaires,” he said. “I don’t owe (them) my votes. I’m going to tax those billionaires when I get the U.S. Senate.”
During his turn, Jackson brought up his working class roots and asked Collins if she looks down at him or all working people. Collins talked about how she started working in potato fields in Aroostook County at the age of 10.
“I do not look down on you or on anyone,” Collins said. “I have enormous respect for all the people of Maine.”
3. Supreme Court reform
The two candidates sparred over whether the U.S. Supreme Court needs reforming.
The Democrat said he supports term limits and enforceable ethics standards and would be open to adding members to the court, which he said is currently working for Trump and “the billionaire class.”
“It’s just gross the way that this has ended up,” Jackson said. “And we have to do something meaningful to actually give people’s confidence back.”
Collins disagreed. She said increasing the number of justices would go “completely against the vision of those who wrote the Constitution.” She stuck to her position when a moderator noted that the current number of nine justices was not in the Constitution.
“It’s inconsistent with the whole idea of the Supreme Court being insulated from politics,” Collins said. “That would make it a totally political body.”
Jackson, however, would get the last word.
“We have the best court that money can buy right now,” he said.
4. Through the looking glass on guns
A question about assault weapons produced some surprising answers.
Collins noted that she was a supporter of the original ban on assault weapons passed by Congress in the 90s. She accused Democrats of allowing that ban to expire because they wanted to expand it. And she said she voted to ban bump stocks, which increase the rate of fire in a weapon.
She said she supports “reasonable limits” on magazine capacity and would be open to increasing the age to legally obtain an assault weapon.
Jackson seemed more pro-gun by comparison.
“I’m not in favor of increasing the age,” he said. “It actually comes down to the person. I mean, we do have a culture here in Maine of people being able to buy guns.”
Jackson said he would not oppose an assault weapons ban, but he would oppose taking weapons away from people who already have them.
“I don’t see a good reason for assault weapons,” he said. “You can’t use them for hunting or anything like that. And so I would not be opposed to banning them.”

title: 8 vacant buildings are central to Auburn’s plan for revitalizing Minot Avenue. Here’s where they stand.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The city of Auburn is currently working on a plan to help revitalize Minot Avenue from Washington Street to Court Street, with hopes of finalizing the plan by the end of the year.
Potential changes include upgrading the corridor’s appearance, targeting vacant properties, addressing vehicle and pedestrian safety, and possibly adding more mixed-use development, retail, restaurants and parks to the area.
City officials have been working on the plan for months, gathering feedback from residents and property owners about what they’d like to see.
The plan comes after the city implemented a vacant property ordinance last year in response to a proportionally large number of empty buildings along that portion of the street. One focus of the plan is expected to be the eight vacant buildings in that half-mile stretch of Minot Avenue. All of the buildings are privately owned.
Eric Cousens, Auburn’s director of Public Services, said the city has few enforcement options to motivate owners to use, clean up or upgrade their properties. Available is the new vacant property ordinance, which requires owners of vacant or abandoned properties to register them with the city and pay a fee starting at $100 based on the type of building, ownership and size.
At the time of registration, property owners must also agree to a city inspection of the property to determine the building’s condition. Any that don’t meet the necessary safety codes would need to be fixed by the individual. Once complete, a vacant building permit would be issued.
Among incentives is the use of Tax Increment Financing, or a TIF, which can be used to redirect property taxes toward redevelopment projects. Each would be taken on a case-by-case basis, Cousens said.
In addition, the city could apply for transportation funding from state and federal agencies to address vehicle and pedestrian safety concerns.
Here’s more on the eight vacant properties:
MINOT AVENUE/WASHINGTON STREET ROUNDABOUT
15 Pierce St.
Auburn city records identify 15 Pierce St. as a storage and warehouse, and the former home of Michalak Battery & Core. Constructed around 1928 on .92 acres, it features a steel exterior and asbestos roof cover. It still remains in possession of Michalak Battery & Core and is valued at $178,200.
61 Washington St. North
This property was once home to K.L. Jack, a Portland-based industrial fastener supplier. An employee with the company confirmed that they moved to 279 Washington St. South last year.
There was a banner on the outside of the building on Tuesday stating Maine RC Raceways will be moving to the location. According to its Facebook page, Maine RC Raceways is currently located at 1578 Auburn Road in Turner.
City records show the building was built around 1949 and features a brick exterior and rolled roof cover. Classified as an industrial building with a distribution warehouse, it also has a drive-in door, a showroom and two private offices on .13 acres of land.
The building is owned by Jack Lawrence and is valued at $172,000.
29 Washington St. North
The building is the former home to Seltzer and Rydholm Inc., a local, family-owned bottling business that started in the 1920s, built the building in 1968, and sold the building to Pepsi in 2004.
Pepsico closed the location in 2010, moving the plant to 191 Merrow Road. The facility on Merrow Road no longer bottles, but is being used as a warehouse and distribution facility.
City records indicate 29 Washington St. North was built with a concrete exterior and tar-gravel roof. Classified as an industrial building with a warehouse, it sits on .44 acres and is valued at $290,000. It is currently owned by Keith Morgan.
254 Minot Ave.
The city considers this property vacant, though there is activity at the location. According to Cousens, it’s being used as a furniture warehouse, and the city is working on permitting a new use for the building.
The property has had several owners, including Maine Baking Company, Benson & Sullivan and Stratham Tire. City records indicate the building was built around 1915, featuring a brick exterior and tar-gravel roof. It also has a large basement space, four garage bays and two loading docks.
The building sits on 1.34 acres of land and is owned by Libby Dinan, LLC. Labonte Business Realty, LLC sold the property to Libby Dinan on Jan. 20 for $525,000.
WASHINGTON STREET NORTH TO COURT STREET
1 Minot Ave.
This building is the former home of the Auburn Police Department before the department was relocated to Auburn City Hall in 2011. City records indicate the building was built around the 1990s, with a brick exterior and rubber roof. The property sits on 1.2 acres and is valued at more than $400,000.
67 Minot Ave.
This building was a high-profile mill built in 1908, with additions made until 1914. The four-story brick shoe factory was the home of Lunn & Sweet Shoe Co., one of Auburn’s biggest employers at the time. The Barn was in the space from 1994 to 2015.
The building lies on 2.36 acres and is valued at about $714,000.
81 Minot Ave.
Constructed in 1936, the building was once a car dealership. Classified as a commercial building with a garage, it sits on 1.02 acres and was valued at $153,000. Earlier this month, the Auburn City Council deemed this a dangerous building, informing the owners they have 30 days to either repair or demolish the building.
All three buildings above — 1, 67 and 81 Minot Ave. — were part of a $40 million medical tourism project in 2015 by a Chinese developer to convert the site into a medical facility for Chinese patients wanting medical treatments in the United States. The project never took shape.
60 Minot Ave.
City records indicate this building was built around 1900 and is classified as an auto building with a warehouse valued at more than $500,000. The three-story building is equipped with loading docks, a six-bay garage and an elevator on .79 acres.
Cousens said the property is considered partially vacant, with the top two floors not being used. Scott Hossler, owner of Cameron Tires & Services, recently confirmed that. He said his business uses the lower half for storage and that intends eventually to use the top two floors.

title: Sam Pfeifle for House District 104
text:
Throughout his 12 years on the MSAD 15 School Board, Sam Pfeifle has helped lead the school system to become one of the best in the state, serving both Gray and New Gloucester. He’s learned to work with people who have many views on school policies and funding, and has demonstrated an ability to listen, to compromise, to work hard and to continue learning.
Sam will work for the kinds of things I care about, including making housing and healthcare more affordable. I’m quite confident he won’t give tax breaks for the wealthy that are paid for by reducing assistance to schools and to people in need.
Sam is an experienced elected official who understands how government works. Best of all, he’s an independent thinker who will challenge the status quo. I hope everyone will join me in voting for Sam Pfeifle for House District 104.
Anne Gass
Gray

title: Troy Jackson campaign says it raised $20.4 million in third quarter of Maine U.S. Senate race
text:
Troy Jackson campaign says it raised $20.4 million in third quarter of Maine U.S. Senate race
Jackson's campaign says nearly 200,000 individual donors contributed during the quarter
Troy Jackson campaign says it raised $20.4 million in third quarter of Maine U.S. Senate race
Jackson's campaign says nearly 200,000 individual donors contributed during the quarter
Maine U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson's campaign announced on Thursday that it raised $20.4 million during the third quarter of 2026, fueled by nearly 200,000 individual donors.
According to a news release, the campaign received around 350,000 contributions during the quarter with 95% of those totaling less than $100.
The campaign also said that it received donations from all 16 counties in Maine.
"Working people are tired of a Washington where the people writing the biggest checks get everything they want, while the rest of us struggle to get by," Jackson said in a statement.
Jackson is seeking the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate seat currently held by Sen. Susan Collins.
The fundraising figures were provided by Jackson's campaign and have not been verified independently.

title: What’s on the ballot in Scarborough?
text:
Scarborough residents have a lot of choices to make ahead of the November election, with an array of candidates running for seats on the Town Council, school board and sanitary district, a number town officials say is unprecedented. On top of local elections, residents will be asked to vote in county, state and federal races.
To see the complete ballot and dive more into candidate responses, explore the 2026 Maine Voter Guide.
Here’s what residents can expect to see on their ballots Nov. 3:
REFERENDUM
Scarborough and Old Orchard Beach residents will vote on a $7.4 million upgrade to the radio communications system used by both towns’ public safety, public service and school departments.
Firefighters and police officers in both towns have said they’ve experienced communications problems during emergency situations using the current system, which uses 1950s technology and 1990s infrastructure.
The total cost is estimated at nearly $12.4 million, with Scarborough contributing $9.2 million and Old Orchard Beach contributing $3.2 million. However, other funding sources could reduce that number.
The Scarborough referendum will ask residents to approve borrowing up to $6 million, in anticipation of receiving federal grants. If the towns don’t receive the grants, Scarborough will have to seek out other funding options or return to the voters to bridge the gap.
LOCAL RACES
There are seven candidates for three open seats on the Scarborough Town Council. The terms will expire in 2029. Here’s a brief rundown of what they had to say in our Voter Guide.
Isha Agarwal, a Democrat, is running for office for the first time. She is an emergency room doctor and a mom to three young kids. Her top priorities are strong schools, safe roads and more thoughtful and slower growth. Agarwal is running to support strong schools and safe roads.
Lawrence Cain, who is non-partisan, is the only incumbent running for a seat. He served a partial term starting in June 2025, during which he authored or assisted initiatives including a 20% increase to senior property tax relief, a 3.09% budget tax increase and a short-term rental ordinance. His top three priorities are managing growth, affordability for all residents and quality of life issues. He owned a small business for 35 years and is now retired.
Samuel Cofone is the owner and operator of the Downeaster Motel and a former Cumberland County sheriff’s deputy. Cofone, a Republican, is running for office for the first time. His top priorities are slowing growth so infrastructure can catch up, cutting unnecessary spending of tax dollars, and making town government more transparent and holding town officials accountable. His disciplinary records from his 28 years with the sheriff’s office span 65 pages and show numerous suspensions, reprimands and warnings from 1995 to 2021.
Sean Flaherty served as a member of the Maine House of Representatives from 2008 to 2010. Flaherty, a Democrat, is a lawyer, and his top priorities are accountability and transparency, sustainability and infrastructure, and safe streets and neighborhoods. In 2010, during his previous term as a legislator, Flaherty was arrested for operating under the influence, which was the focus of widespread coverage.
“I hope the voters aren’t really interested in someone who is perfect or claims to be perfect, because I am not. If my mistake from 2010 can help anybody learn to deal with problems or avoid problems, I am happy to be the teaching tool,” Flaherty said this week. “In the 16 years since, I never stopped trying to serve folks in Scarborough and I have the receipts to prove it.”
Denise Hamilton, an assistant controller and small business owner, has closely followed local government and participated in municipal meetings. She is non-partisan and running for office for the first time. Her top three priorities are thoughtful growth, infrastructure and independent research.
Jessica Sargent is a small business owner and conservation policy consultant running for office for the first time. She is a Democrat, a conservation economist and a community volunteer. Her top priorities are resilient infrastructure, balanced growth in appropriate areas and fiscally responsible budgeting.
R. Wayne Werts, a Democrat, is a retired fire chief and paramedic. He was a member of the Maine House of Representatives in 2012 representing House District 70, and he was defeated in 2014 when he ran for reelection. His top priorities are travel and infrastructure, growth and taxes, and curtailing ICE.
There are two candidates running to fill one vacant seat on the Scarborough Board of Education, with a term expiring in June 2028.
Andrew Guillerault is a stay-at-home dad, coach, former district employee and the husband of a teacher. His top three priorities are kids, parents and teachers, and he wants to make transparent policies that support a strong school culture.
Stephen Zamierowski is an outdoor educator with experience as a substitute teacher, wilderness skills specialist and outdoor education guide. His top priorities are supporting school, staff and parents in navigating evolving technology usage, operating within the budget, and preparing for construction and transition to a new school building environment.
There are three seats with three-year terms expiring in 2029 for the Scarborough Sanitary District. Matthew Garrett, Jason Greenleaf, Denis Lafreniere Jr. and Benjamin McDougal are running.
STATE RACES
Scarborough is divided into two Senate districts — 29 and 30 — and three House districts — 124, 125 and 126.
In state Senate District 29, Democratic incumbent Anne Carney is facing Republican Vincent Maietta. In District 30, M. Thad Moody is the Republican candidate going up against Democrat Sophie Bailey Warren, who is currently representing Scarborough in the Maine House of Representatives.
For the Maine House of Representatives District 124 seat, the candidates are Democrat Eric James Nathanson; Independent Mary Shannon Lindstrom, chair of the Scarborough Board of Education; and Republican Scott W. Doherty, a Scarborough town councilor. Democratic incumbent Kelly Maureen Noonan Murphy is the only candidate on the ballot for District 125. For the District 126 seat, Republican Ethan E. Mongue is facing the incumbent, Democrat Andrew Gattine.
Voters will also choose between Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree, Republican nominee Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett for governor.
OTHER RACES
Scarborough residents will vote in the U.S. Senate race between Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
In Maine’s 1st Congressional District, Democratic Rep. Chellie Pingree will face Republican Ronald Russell.
Cumberland County Sheriff Kevin Joyce is the only candidate in the sheriff’s race. Paul Aranson is the only candidate for judge of probate.
Stephanie Anderson, who is independent, and Jacqueline Sartoris, a Democrat, are running for Cumberland County district attorney. The Cumberland County district attorney serves four years and prosecutes all criminal cases, except homicides, which are handled by the attorney general.
HOW TO VOTE
People who want to register to vote must now do so in person at the Town Clerk’s Office. The office will be open late from 5 to 7 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28, for voter registration.
Early voting is taking place from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday-Thursdays at Town Hall, until Thursday, Oct. 29.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Since September 2025, members of the newsroom have traded the responsibility of writing “Voluntary View,” a spotlight on volunteering with nonprofit organizations serving Lincoln County.
Started by former reporter Ali Juell, the column provides a way for the news staff to develop a deeper appreciation for organizations doing good works in our community while also giving back to the region.
So far, the column has featured two food pantries, a historical society, a secondhand book shop, and a land trust. However, for two years running, we have missed the chance to feature possibly the biggest volunteer opportunity of them all: Damariscotta Pumpkinfest and Regatta. This incredibly dedicated group of folks work year-round, coordinating hundreds of details before the 10-day window in October when thousands of visitors will descend on the Twin Villages to see giant pumpkins be weighed, paraded, paddled, and dropped. By comparison, it took four general assignment reporters and the associate editor to be at every marquee event if just to photograph, and that doesn’t include our sports reporter covering the second annual Tour de Gourd!
The fact that the annual festival manages to go off every year without a hitch – or, at least without one visible to the general public – is a true testament to the determination
and diligence of everyone involved.
Perhaps next year, in celebration of the festival’s 20th anniversary, we’ll approach our coverage a little differently, embedding a reporter to volunteer at each of the major events.
To echo Glenn Chadbourne’s statement in this week’s cartoon, we tip our hats to everyone who made the 19th annual Pumpkinfest a smashing success. There’s a lot to be proud of this year, and we can’t wait to see what you come up for next year’s festival.

title: Proudly voting for Susan Collins
text:
Before I was elected to the Maine Legislature, I interned for Sen. Susan Collins for several months. I saw Sen. Collins show up for Maine people every day. She is a leader with impeccable integrity, a hard worker who knows the facts and an independent voice for all Mainers.
When I was elected to the Legislature, I secured part of the funding needed for a state-of-the-art town hall for my constituents in Hollis. The project would not have been completed if not for the federal investment Sen. Collins secured. Sen. Collins came through for Hollis, as she does for all of Maine.
The Maine people couldn’t have a clearer choice. I also served with Sen. Collins’ opponent in the Legislature. The contrast between Collins and Troy Jackson — in terms of ethics, commitment and accomplishments in office — couldn’t be more palpable.
I will proudly vote for Sen. Collins. I hope all Maine voters will do the same.
Nathan Carlow
State Representative, Maine State Legislature
Buxton

title: South Portland youth soccer club under investigation for missing funds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The South Portland Police Department is investigating the misappropriation of funds within the South Portland Strikers, a nonprofit youth soccer organization that plays home games at Wainwright sports complex.
Chief Daniel Ahern said that the department doesn’t know how much money was taken and would not share how many people the department is investigating.
The Strikers board became aware of a former board member potentially using club funds for unauthorized purposes in 2025 and 2026, according to president Gabriel Harp. He said that the club is cooperating with law enforcement in the ongoing investigation.
“We are not characterizing this as embezzlement or making conclusions about criminal conduct,” Harp said.
The soccer club deferred expenses and reduced or eliminated discretionary items from the 2026 budget, according to an email that went out to families. The club spent about $50,000 in 2025, per board meeting minutes, and it was projected to have about $6,500 in reserves for the 2026 year, per the beginning of the budget process.
Last year, the club had more than 270 athletes between the ages of 7 and 13, fielding 20 teams that play their home games at Wainwright sports complex and travel for games across the state.
The club offers scholarships to more than 50 players, or about 19% of the club, so that uniform costs and registration fees aren’t a barrier for children to play soccer. The Strikers are supported through individual donors, grants and local business sponsorships.

title: Trump scraps livestream of Fort Hood shooter’s execution
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled plans to livestream the execution of the gunman responsible for the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting, following bipartisan criticism from lawmakers, religious leaders and some survivors of the attack.
The decision comes just one week after the Pentagon announced that Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others, would be executed by firing squad in a broadcast available to the public.
In a lengthy post on Truth Social, Trump defended the original proposal as a potential deterrent to terrorism but acknowledged concerns about broadcasting the execution.
“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan,” Trump wrote. “But, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
Trump had previously expressed support for the livestream, telling reporters Oct. 9 that he approved of the plan. But the proposed broadcast quickly drew opposition from across the political spectrum.
Vice President JD Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson stopped short of condemning the proposal but said they would not watch the execution. Other lawmakers, including some Republicans, publicly opposed the livestream.
Some survivors of the Fort Hood shooting also raised concerns about broadcasting Hasan’s death, while the Vatican’s Secretary of State criticized the proposed spectacle.
Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. During his military trial, Hasan acknowledged carrying out the shooting and presented his actions as religiously motivated.
Despite canceling the livestream, Trump said the firing squad execution would proceed as planned. However, he clarified that only the victims’ immediate family members would be allowed to watch the event if they chose to.
The controversy has prompted a legislative response. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) introduced legislation Thursday that would prohibit the public broadcasting of military executions, seeking to prevent similar proposals in the future.

title: Ex-fiancé charged nearly 15 years after mother who was on ‘People’s Court’ vanished
text:
ORLANDO, Fla. (Gray News) - Nearly 15 years ago, a Florida mother vanished after she and her former fiancé appeared on “The People’s Court.” Now, he’s accused of her murder.
Orlando Police say 55-year-old Dale Smith Jr. was arrested Wednesday on a charge of second-degree murder in relation to the presumed death of his former fiancée, Michelle Parker.
Parker, 33, disappeared on Nov. 17, 2011, after dropping her then-3-year-old twins off at Smith Jr.’s Orlando home. Hours earlier, Parker and Smith Jr. appeared on an episode of “The People’s Court” in a dispute over a lost engagement ring, WESH reports.
Police say Smith Jr., who has been the prime suspect in the case for years, was the last known person to see or hear from Parker. While Parker’s remains have never been found, all the evidence points to her former fiancé as being responsible for her murder, according to police.
Orlando Police Chief Eric Smith credited the suspect’s arrest to a renewed, focused look at the case over the past year as well as advances in digital forensics.
“This case never stopped being a priority. Our detectives kept working. They kept asking questions. They kept examining the evidence,” said Smith at a press conference.
Nearly 15 years after her daughter’s disappearance, Parker’s mother, Yvonne Stewart, said Smith Jr.’s arrest brings some measure of closure.
“This is the happiest day,” Stewart told The Orlando Sentinel. “I was hopeful this day would come but never really knowing if it will and the fact that he could get away with it and not ever be arrested – that’s just a hard pill to swallow.”
Stewart also said she hopes Smith Jr. will reveal where her daughter’s remains are.
“There’s not one day that’s gone by that I don’t think of her or look at her pictures or talk to her,” she said. “I’m just going to take it minute by minute.”
Smith Jr. has denied having anything to do with Parker’s disappearance.

title: Trump to hold Georgia rally for Collins amid midterm push
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will hold a rally at the Dalton Municipal Airport in Dalton, Ga. Friday in support of Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), as the two Republicans look to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.).
The rally is scheduled to take place at 3 p.m. Eastern Time.
The stop is part of a midterm campaign blitz from the president.
Trump said his previous rallies have set candidates up for success.
“We had a big day in Arizona and Montana. I think we got a lot of people elected today. The crowds were massive. You just saw a crowd that set a record for that arena,” Trump said.
Republicans are increasingly focusing on holding as many Senate seats as possible. Most polls paint a picture that holding the House of Representatives looks out of reach.
The president is campaigning in some states that traditionally have been easy wins for Republicans, such as Texas, Ohio and Kentucky.
Trump said he’s giving his all to the effort, and putting his administration’s record on display.
“I think we’re having an amazing run. And it’s not easy work, you know doing these rallies. They’re big rallies, and you can’t do 15 minutes. You have these people waiting for three days. And the people who see what we’ve accomplished, where there’s never been. It’s a golden age of America, and the Iran War will end very soon,” Trump said.
Trump’s visit to Georgia comes with Collins struggling in the polls. Several different polls show Ossoff ahead by an 8-10 percentage point margin.

title: Doctors say Pope Leo’s lung has recovered well from surgery and say his post-operative tests normal
text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV met with a top aide on Thursday and resumed working from the hospital, as doctors reported his lung had recovered well from surgery to remove a cancerous nodule.
Leo’s post-operative tests remained within normal levels and his physiotherapy session Thursday involved full mobility exercises, with the pope going about his daily activities independently, said the update from Leo’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
“The chest X-ray revealed good recovery of the operated lung,” they reported. “Overall, his postoperative recovery is proceeding as expected.”
Separately, the Vatican said Leo had received the Vatican chief of staff, or “substitute,” Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, and had resumed working from the hospital. Rudelli handles much of the day-to-day administrative work of the Holy See.
For a second day Leo celebrated Mass with other priests in a special chapel set up near his room on the 10th floor of the hospital, spokesman Matteo Bruni said.
The 71-year-old Leo had the lower right lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Asked if any changes to Leo’s planned trip to South America from Nov. 6-17 were expected, Bruni pointed to Leo’s words on Sunday when he announced the discovery of the nodule and impending surgery.
“Thank you for your prayers for the pastoral visit I will make to Peru,” Leo said Sunday in Spanish, in a greeting delivered to a Peruvian group. The trip is also scheduled to include stops in Uruguay and Argentina.
Leo is expected to remain hospitalized until at least Oct. 20.
___
Barry reported from Milan.

title: Outdoor Learning Grows at Miller School
text:
Lindsey Jones’ math lesson was briefly interrupted by a snake.
“I thought it was a worm because of the color!” One third grader exclaimed as the group calmed down and returned their attention to class in a shady corner of the Miller School’s lawn on Friday, Oct. 2.
“Miss Jones,” as she is known to her students, sent her class of 12 across the schoolyard to find different shapes in their environment, leaving their math textbooks and pencils in a neat circle on the grass. It was a warm morning for October, partly cloudy with a light breeze – perfect for taking the classroom outside.
Jones sees that her third graders get at least one lesson outside a day, so, including lunch, they get “two good chunks of fresh air,” she said.
With a new teacher-led committee, state support, and community donations, Waldoboro’s Miller School is making the outdoors a feature of students’ schedules.
“It’s not a change of material – it’s just a change of location,” teacher Abby Lash said.
Lash’s kindergarteners were outside at the same time as Jones’ class, collecting fallen leaves on the blacktop on clipboards to learn about colors and make art. Now in her second year of teaching, Lash was inspired last spring to incorporate the outdoors more into her indoor classroom and became a main initiator of this schoolwide change.
“How can we take learning outside of the four walls?” she wondered.
A committee with staff representing each grade level was formed, and it began working with the Maine Department of Education’s new Trail Guides program to best shape how outdoor learning can work at the school.
Page Nichols, the department’s chief innovation officer, said that Miller School is one of the first to join the free program, which was launched this past spring. The school currently has three “coaches” assigned to support its programming, both virtually and in-person, she said.
So far, the endeavor has been at no extra operational cost to the school.
“Our goal is to try to just make outdoor learning something that’s not super overwhelming for teachers,” Lash said.
Though the outdoor learning block on her first day of school this year was “chaos,” for Lash, her students quickly learned that classroom expectations could also apply outside. Then on week five, she noticed that her students ask less about the next recess or lunch period.
“We get to run, race, and find bugs,” kindergartener Jaxson Oliver, 5, told Lash when asked about why he liked outdoor learning.
In a “lemons-turned-lemonade moment”, as Principal Shawn Strack described it, budget cuts that took away the school’s Spanish program left an open spot in students’ schedules for outdoor lessons at least once a week.
“We’re not forcing any teacher to do this, but the response from the teachers has been incredible,” Strack said. “They’ve really taken it and run.”
New this year to Miller School, Strack said he is a “big proponent of kids being outside” and wants to take full advantage of the existing schoolyard lawn, courtyard space, and small greenhouse. He and the staff committee also oversaw the setup of an outdoor classroom: a circle of 20 cut tree stumps donated by third grade parent Arthur Charles just one week before on Oct. 2.
Charles, a veterinarian at the nearby Medomak Veterinary Services, said he recently had to cut down a large oak tree when he saw the school’s call for tree stumps. He said he does not think his donation was “a very big deal,” and credited the school with making the outdoor classroom happen.
“I’m a big supporter of getting kids outside,” Charles said.
On the other side of the playground from Jones and Lash, the combined first and second grade classes of teachers Leah Brooks and Nancy Farrin sat on the circle of stumps around a willow tree.
The “scientists,” as Brooks referred to them, watched as their teacher lowered a large pumpkin into a tub of water, asking them if they believed it would float.
“I knew it!” yelled one student, who guessed correctly that it would.
After testing the flotation of pumpkins of various sizes, students were tasked with scooping out the inside. To wipe off the pumpkin innards, they had to do was rub their hands in the grass.
“Get dirty!” Brooks encouraged. “This is nature’s slime.”
Many teachers are planning to continue their outdoor lessons through the year, no matter rain or snow. Lash’s students, for example, have an outdoor “classmate:” a tree they will observe throughout the four seasons.
“It’s OK if you’re cold,” she said she hopes to teach her students. “It’s OK if you’re uncomfortable. That’s part of life. That’s part of growing.”
Though, “it’ll be interesting getting kindergarteners in their snow pants twice a day rather than once,” Lash said.
In addition to Charles’ contribution, Dow Furniture donated two Adirondack chairs to the school for teachers, a donation worth almost $400.
“Our community is very important to us and since Miller School is in our backyard, we wanted to contribute to this space,” the store’s general manager, Wilmot Dow, said in an email.
The school is looking to further involve its local community, which Strack said has been “wildly supportive,” into the new program.
“Maine is a great place to be doing outdoor learning,” Strack said.

title: Innocent bystander, 81, killed in gunfire outside Walmart, police say

title: Early voter turnout is strong as major races drive interest in Maine
text:
Early voter turnout is strong as major races drive interest in Maine
Voters in Maine have been able to cast ballots for more than a week, and early numbers show a very high interest in this year's election.
In-person absentee voting for the Nov. 3, 2026, election began on Monday, Oct. 5.
As of Tuesday, Oct. 13, the Maine Secretary of State's Office reported nearly 144,000 absentee ballots had been requested, nearly 141,000 had been issued, and nearly 60,000 had already been returned. In the June primary, 88,176 absentee ballots were cast.
In 2022, the last gubernatorial election, a total of 252,135 absentee ballots were issued.
In Scarborough, election officials said on Thursday they were expecting a higher than average voter turnout this year. In fact, 3,423 ballots were issued in Scarborough's first week of absentee voting, which exceeds the total number of absentee ballots cast in the June primary (2,828).
In Portland, the City Clerk's Office told Maine's Total Coverage on Thursday that they had already issued around 10,000 absentee ballots in just over a week with nearly 4,000 already returned.
"This election certainly is busier than other general elections we've seen in the past," the Portland City Clerk's Office. "We are expecting the polls to be very busy on election day!"
The South Portland City Clerk said on Thursday they had also already exceeded the number of absentee requests from June.
"This is consistent with a November election during a governor or presidential race for South Portland," said South Portland City Clerk Jessica Hughes.
Hughes urged voters in her city to take advantage of extended hours for elections from 8 a.m. until noon on Oct. 17 and 24 at City Hall.
In Sabattus, town officials said there are nearly 3,300 registered voters. As of 8 p.m. on Thursday, 518 ballots had been issued, which is a 15.7% voter participation rate with still more than two weeks to go.
Voters do not need to provide a reason to vote absentee, and those voting in person at the clerk's office do not have to fill out an application in advance.
Voters also can request an absentee ballot online or by mail.
The deadline to request a no-excuse absentee ballot is Thursday, Oct. 29.
Voters must submit completed absentee ballots to their municipality by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Maine residents who are not yet registered to vote still can participate. The state allows same-day voter registration, meaning eligible voters can register and cast a ballot during the early voting period or on Election Day.
In September, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said that absentee voting by mail would continue as normal, after the U.S. Supreme Court rejected a Trump administration effort to dramatically overhaul the system in the name of election integrity.
"We know that many Mainers – particularly seniors and people with disabilities – appreciate the convenience of voting from home, and we are thrilled that our joint legal efforts with states across the country to protect the right to vote by mail have succeeded," Bellows wrote in a news release on Sept. 15. "This is good news for voters and for democracy."
Despite criticizing absentee voting and falsely blaming fraud associated with mail-voting for his 2020 election loss, President Donald Trump is now imploring Republicans to use "every appropriate tool," including mail-in ballots, to vote in the midterms.
The Secretary of State’s Office says Maine is coming off record turnout during the June primary election and is a national leader in voter turnout.
During the June primary, Maine Democrats outnumbered Republicans 3:1 in the turnout of unenrolled early and absentee voters.

title: Widespread rain arrives in Maine Friday
text:
Widespread rain arrives in Maine Friday
Thursday remains dry with showers increasing Friday morning.
Widespread rain arrives in Maine Friday
Thursday remains dry with showers increasing Friday morning.
High pressure will bring Maine one last dry, mild day today before colder, wetter weather arrives for the weekend. Rain will move from west to east Friday morning as a storm passes near the Canadian border.
Most of the state will receive about half an inch to an inch of rain Friday afternoon and evening, with some heavy downpours possible. A few snowflakes could mix in across the western mountains early Friday before changing to rain. Friday night, rain will taper off to snow showers in the mountains and northern valleys as colder air moves in.
Saturday will feel more like late fall, with strong northwest winds and much colder temperatures. Highs will reach the 40s to near 50 along the coast, while mountain temperatures stay in the 30s. Wind gusts could reach 30 mph statewide and 40 mph in the foothills, making it feel like the 20s and 30s. Snow showers are possible in the mountains, and hiking above treeline could be hazardous.
Saturday night will be very cold, with lows in the 20s and lower 30s. Sunday will bring improving conditions as high pressure returns, leading to drier weather and a gradual warm-up. Temperatures are expected to climb back into the 50s and 60s by early to midweek next week.

title: A blueprint for disaster for Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Luisa S. Deprez, Ph.D., of Cape Elizabeth is professor emerita of sociology and social policy at the University of Southern Maine.
Once again, the notorious, dangerous and ultra-conservative Maine heritage foundation, the Maine Policy Institute, has gone out of its way to attempt to undermine the safety and security and well-being of Maine families.
Its newest approach to doing so is described in the recently released 2026 Maine Policy Blueprint, a dictum that leaves no stone unturned when it comes to proposals that will threaten the lives of children and families while undermining communities and, ultimately, the state.
Perhaps the children and families of the institute’s staff and collaborators will not suffer but be assured that hundreds of thousands throughout the state will.
Its impact would be similar to its national predecessor, Project 2025, which Donald Trump and his Republican loyalists used to decimate the federal government and unleash a flurry of executive orders, rule changes and (il)legal maneuvers designed to inflict harm on millions of Americans.
They include cuts to Medicaid and food programs; reduction and elimination of education programs for special needs children and low-achieving communities; decreased regulations of toxic chemicals both in the air and in your food and water; purging of research programs studying cancer, heart disease, diabetes and other chronic diseases; erasure of vaccination protocols; disregard for national park protections; and on the horizon, plans to upend Head Start by “stripping away standards on health and literacy … and brushing teeth.” Who knows what’s in store Social Security and Medicare?
The Blueprint purports to promote a Maine where “people are freer, more prosperous, or better able to afford happy lives.” To do so it suggests overall reforms in every sector.
Among them:
Environmental: End “state-level hostility toward fossil fuel and nuclear power” while removing regulatory and permitting barriers; end vehicle inspection mandates (ever been behind a vehicle with no brake lights on a dark road at night?); repeal all emissions reductions goals as well as nuclear referendum requirements; reduce funding for water quality by 15%; ban subsidies on EV sales.
Education: Allow public schools to transition to a charter school if they wish, reducing state expenditures for public schools and turning over educational standards and curriculum to a private enterprise; eliminate funding for adult education and turn over adult and community education, adult basic education, adult high school diploma programs, high school equivalency diploma testing, family literacy, job skills training, and college transition programs to the private sector; eliminate funding for the Department of Education’s office of student supports; reduce the state reimbursement rate for school administration encouraging central office staffing, and management functions; give authority for public school curriculum and learning wholly to parents.
Housing: Eliminate rent control; eliminate the Housing Opportunity Program targeting low- and moderate-income households and community workforce housing needs; abolish minimum lot sizes and parking mandates.
Health: Repeal the paid family medical leave program; repeal Medicaid expansion (30% of Mainers had MaineCare coverage in 2025, most children and elders); increase state employees’ share of health insurance premiums; contract-out prison medical services.
Food: Eliminate funding for Maine’s universal school meals program; eliminate statewide hunger relief program — breakfast, lunch, after-school, weekends, summer; expand work requirements for those receiving SNAP (about 40,000 of 170,000 current recipients); move food programs to DHHS.
Economy: Repeal the 2% income tax hike on incomes above $1 million for single filers; freeze the minimum wage and deregulate occupational licensing; targeted 10% reduction in central administrative units (567 jobs); lease or concession-manage Maine’s most visited, highest cost parks to eliminate payroll, seasonal staffing, overtime pay and day-to-day maintenance; eliminate funding for international commerce that promotes exports, international student recruitment and overseas trade opportunities for Maine businesses.
Veterans services: A 10% cut focused on outreach, technology and central-office staffing.
Law enforcement: Require all state and local police to cooperate with ICE.
This is not Maine as it should be nor as it is. The intent of the Blueprint is not to ensure that Maine “people are freer, more prosperous or better able to afford happy lives” but to slash expenditures that actually enable Mainers to be freer, more prosperous, safer, and able to live lives of value. Like Project 2025, it guarantees that only the private sector flourishes.
This Blueprint will be the agenda for every Republican up for election in any race in the state. We have seen this played out before. Project 2025 devastated the federal government and the state and continues to do so.
As you go to the polls, ask yourself this question: Do you want this Blueprint to be our future? If you say “No,” know who you are voting for. Be sure they share your sentiments.

title: Trump says Pentagon will not livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter
text:
Trump says Pentagon will not livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter
President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it.
Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But, he continued, “any very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
The Pentagon has said Hasan’s execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, “if they so choose.”
The announcement earlier this month from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan’s execution would be public — and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be livestreamed — prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalization.
When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.
But he continued: “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”

title: ’Some sus s--- going on’: What Nolan Wells’ friends said in texts after he mysteriously disappeared
text:
(Gray News) - Phone records reveal how Nolan Wells’ friends privately talked about his death and what they planned to tell police.
Wells went to Horn Island in Mississippi with friends to celebrate the July 4 holiday but never came home. His body was found two days later on the shore of the island.
The Wells family’s outside analysis of his phone, compiled by Garrett Discovery, has since been publicly released, People reported.
The 292-page report includes private messages from 29 group chats in which Wells’ phone was included.
The messages show Wells’ friends reacting in real time to news that he was found dead as well as to accusations that they were involved in his death.
In a message sent on July 5, a user indicated that Wells seemed fine in the early evening on July 4: “he came and was hanging out with us and around us, he never disappeared with [redacted] when it was time to leave around like 6 he got off our boat with this other guy and thy started walking back to their boat.”
In the early morning hours of July 5, several messages were sent to Wells asking where he was and whether he was OK, CBS News reported.
At 11:59 a.m. on July 5, a user wrote in one of the chats: “There is def some sus s--- going on.”
Soon after, a user said that thousands of people had been “on that damn island and nobody knows who he was with.”
Another user said at 11:12 a.m., “They did sum wit bra.”
And at 12:24 p.m. that day, members of one of the group chats appeared to question the account that Wells had chosen to remain on Horn Island: “if he was gone ride with somebody else why would he leave his phone on the boat,” one user wrote.
In one of the group chats, a user told everyone on July 5 sent at 12:56 p.m., to check their camera rolls for photos or videos in which Wells might appear in the background.
“See if he was talking to anyone we don’t know,” read a message.
One person wrote that Wells appeared in a video recorded at 12:39 p.m., and at 4:28 p.m. on July 5, someone wrote that their friend group was getting blasted on “fb” and warned “dont read that bs or or be running yalls mouth bc ppl will make an inch turn into a mile.”
“No one say anything to anyone out of our friendgroup,” read another message.
On July 5 at 6:52 p.m., a user wrote that police had just contacted them. “They’ve called everyone,” another message reads.
On July 6 at 9:22 a.m., a user issued what they described as “a little advice,” writing that “if we get called in for questioning” then “the smart move is to ask for an attorney and that doesn’t mean we’re guilty it just smart so we don’t get played by some potential bias cop.”
Less than 30 minutes later, a user reported that Wells’ body had been found, writing, “They got him.”
“There’s no [expletive] way,” one user responded, adding that Wells was “the best [expletive] person.”
“I love Nolan he would want us to stay together through this and be there to live on his lecacy [sic],” another message read.
“It’s nationwide,” a message sent at 11:35 a.m. on July 6 read.
On July 6 at 12:44 p.m. one user said “Don’t speculate about s--- yall.”
Another message warned, “Bc they can try to get your ass.” And another advised: “just stick to what you know happened.”
On July 6 at 12:45 p.m., a user wrote, in part, “We have nothing to hide.”
By July 7, the conversation had turned to accusations of a cover-up.
On July 7 at 1:40 p.m., a user wrote, “They posted this update and every single comment is just abt how we’re covering it up.”
On July 13 at 4:08 p.m., a user, identified as Tracestin Shepherd, who was quoted in a July 12 Rolling Stone article, wrote that they were sorry if an interview they had done caused any backlash: “that wasn’t my intention at all was just tryna clear our group of what I know was the truth.”
On July 14 at 9:43 a.m., someone wrote, “We need to go to Nolan’s funeral and get with all our other black friends to prove a statement for the media. It would shut everything down.”
Less than an hour later, someone said, “It’s almost like their brainwashing Nolan’s parents and taking advantage of them while their overwhelmed and grief.”
On July 20, the day of Wells’ funeral, a user reacted to the news that a reward was being offered in Wells’ death investigation.
“They are doing such a disservice at a funeral and so ignorant,” the message read, in part.
The same day, there was a discussion about putting up a cross for Wells. “Bring his flip flops,” a user wrote on the night of July 20. “We can bury those as well.”
Last month, Jackson County’s district attorney announced a Mississippi grand jury found no criminal wrongdoing in Wells’ death.
The grand jury said the position, condition and location of his body, along with the time it was discovered, were “consistent with drowning.”
Liza Park, an attorney on Wells’ family attorney Ben Crump’s team, said the state autopsy found two 2-inch contusions — or bruises — on the back of Nolan’s head. This is consistent with what Dr. Roger Mitchell found when he conducted the independent autopsy.
Park emphasized that Dr. Mitchell found no white blood cells, meaning the injury to Nolan’s head happened within a short period of time before he died.
Park noted that the state autopsy report says the larynx and hyoid bone are without hemorrhages and fractures, and the interior spine was “unremarkable.”
The toxicology results included in the report say chest decomposition fluid contained 270 mg/dL of ethanol. Cannabinoids, nicotine, cotinine and caffeine were all “presumptive positive,” but it said confirmatory testing did not reveal cannabinoids in the decomposition fluid.
Experts said there was no fluid or debris in his airways, his GI tract was “unremarkable” and his stomach was empty.
His lungs and throat did not contain any water.

title: 🎃👻 MAINE, READY TO BINGE?! 3 Stephen King Movies to Watch This Halloween!

3 Best Stephen King Movies to Binge on Halloween in Maine
Planning a night of scary movies this Halloween season? Bangor’s most famous resident is responsible for plenty of them!

3. The Shining
An isolated hotel, an increasingly unhinged caretaker, and an atmosphere of pure dread make The Shining an all-time horror classic. If you're looking for a movie that will leave you feeling uneasy long after the credits roll, this one belongs on your Halloween watchlist. Oh, and the genius of Jack!
So, grab your favorite Halloween snacks, turn down the lights, and get ready for a movie marathon featuring three unforgettable stories from the mind of Bangor's own Stephen King. Just don't blame us if you have trouble sleeping afterward!

title: Lawsuit by 2 women accuses ex-Florida Rep. Matt Gaetz of sex trafficking
text:
Lawsuit by 2 women accuses ex-Florida Rep. Matt Gaetz of sex trafficking
Two women filed a lawsuit Thursday against former U.S. Rep. Matt Gaetz, saying they were sexually exploited by him and other men in violation of a federal anti-trafficking law.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Orlando, comes nearly two years after the House Ethics Committee said the Florida Republican had regularly paid for sex, including once with a 17-year-old girl, purchased and used illicit drugs, and violated state laws while a member of Congress.
Gaetz had left office when the report was released and denied wrongdoing. But the report helped to tank his nomination to become attorney general in President Donald Trump's second administration.
Two women said they were in their early 20s in 2017 when they met Gaetz through Joel Greenberg, who was a tax official in Seminole County and is now in prison for a raft of crimes, including a sex crime.
Gaetz provided drugs and paid the women for sex, out-of-state travel, lodging and other expenses, according to the lawsuit.
"Much of the conduct alleged against me is false," Gaetz said in response.
"The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee report that didn't allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance," he said in a statement.
Gaetz also appeared to mock the women on the social platform X, sharing a 2018 social media photo of the backs of three women in bathing suits looking at the ocean in the Bahamas.
"I'm shocked nobody responded to their repeated cries for help, posted to instagram," he said Thursday.
The lawsuit also names Greenberg, another man and businesses tied to Greenberg's family.
"Every part of this venture ran on an exploitative power imbalance," the women's attorney, Spencer Kuvin, said in the lawsuit. "On one side stood a sitting congressman, an elected tax collector, and a former state legislator, men with public office, private homes, and money to spend. On the other stood young financially vulnerable women in their early twenties."
Gaetz hosts a political talk show on One America News Network. He was recently appointed to the board of Triumph Gulf Coast, which oversees how Florida spends money recovered for damage from the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill.

title: Maine Mariners restocked, eager for more after lengthy playoff run
text:
PORTLAND — Rick Kowalsky sat on a bench at Troubh Ice Arena and flashed a smile as he untied and kicked off his skates following a Maine Mariners practice Monday afternoon.
“My feet are frozen,” he said.
There were more reasons besides the relief of warm shoes for the Mariners’ second-year coach to smile. The start of the new ECHL season is fast approaching, and with training camp in the books, the Mariners are starting the season on much better footing than they did last season, which ended up being among the franchise’s most memorable.
“We feel pretty good about what we’ve got and where we’re at,” Kowalsky said. “We started (last year) with probably 15 skaters, and not even half of those guys ended up sticking with us. … We started camp (last week) with 25, 26.
“It has a completely different feel than last year did.”
The NHL extended its regular season and shortened its preseason this year, speeding up when players landed with affiliated minor league teams. So the Mariners, rather than being largely TBD in early October, arrived for training more fully assembled.
“This is the first time, probably ever, other than when I was in the NHL, where we implemented systems for an exhibition game,” said Kowalsky, a former assistant with the New Jersey Devils. “You feel like you can hit the ground running.”
The season may have a different feel, but Kowalsky and the Mariners hope to build on last year’s success. Maine went deeper in the playoffs than ever before, reaching Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals before falling to Wheeling.
For the 14 players who made that run and are on this year’s roster, there are higher expectations.
“We know our goal, and our standard is to fight for a Kelly Cup,” said forward Wyllum Deveaux, who has served as the team’s captain since January 2025. “From the start of camp, it’s been known. We’ve picked up where we left off.”
A familiar face will be able to help with that. Maine brought back defenseman Connor Doherty, who captained the Mariners from 2021-24 and then played two seasons with the Florida Everblades, where he won the Kelly Cup last year.
As an ECHL veteran, Doherty had the choice of where to continue his career. The Mariners were interested in the reunion, and so was the 33-year-old Doherty, who played all 20 of Florida’s playoff games last season and led the team in plus-minus.
“I loved my time playing here,” Doherty said. “My wife and I wanted to try something for a couple of years, move down south and check that out. Obviously, we had some success in hockey, but now we’re just excited to be back here. I want to keep dragging this organization further and further, and hopefully accomplish something sweet up here.”
He didn’t have to make much of an adjustment.
“I feel like the first couple of days walking into the rink, it’s kind of like ‘Did I ever leave?'” he said.
Both Kowalsky and Deveaux said Doherty’s presence as a veteran leader and championship player will be important for a group of teammates looking to take a step closer to a title of their own.
“Bringing that championship pedigree is huge,” Deveaux said. “He plays the right way, he stands up for teammates and he plays on the edge. And he brings it every night.”
He’ll help anchor a defense that should be strong. Owen Gallatin, Michael Underwood, Nick Anderson and Jaxon Bellamy are back from last year’s playoff roster.
Brad Arvanitis is gone after a strong season in net, but Luke Cavallin (2.02 goals-against average in 10 playoff games) is back after leading the Mariners through the postseason, and Max Lundgren, last year’s Hockey East Tournament MVP at Merrimack College, will battle him for playing time.
“We definitely feel very good about goaltending again,” Kowalsky said. “(And) we’re way ahead of the game with our defense. Last year, we didn’t even have a right-shot defenseman, and I think three of the seven defensemen we started with didn’t even make it until Christmas.”
The big question marks come on offense, where three of the top six scorers from a season ago are gone. Max Andreev, Robert Cronin and Linus Hemstrom bring back some scoring punch, Ryan Francis and Mason Primeau should factor in, and the team also gets Deveaux back for a full season after an injury in last year’s opener limited him to seven regular-season games.
“That’s first and foremost (my focus), is being healthy, playing every single game this year,” he said. “As a leader as well, that’s my biggest thing. Taking care of myself, making sure I’m ready to go and showing the other guys that that’s the standard here.”
Or at least, one of them. The Mariners hope they set a new one last year.
“We feel pretty good about the group,” Kowalsky said. “We want winners, we want leaders, we want character people, that was a big part of my recruiting process, and I think we’ve done a good job of that.”

title: What kind of world are we building for our children?
text:
Ella D. Tabasky is a nonprofit worker, union steward and community organizer. She lives in Midcoast Maine.
Thanks to Ed Sheeran and Macklemore, the struggle for Palestinian liberation was recently thrust back into the mainstream.
The stars’ public dispute revived the familiar question of whether performing artists should “stay out of politics,” as if speaking about the suffering of millions is somehow more political than staying silent.
For me, there is no staying silent. I am Jewish, I am an activist, and I am the daughter of a Holocaust educator. And the fact that this conversation unfolded during the Days of Awe — the 10 days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur devoted to introspection and repentance — felt especially significant.
Judaism, at its core, is not neutral in the face of suffering. We are a people whose story is one of liberation from oppression. We are taught that pikuach nefesh, saving a life, is the most important obligation of every human being.
During the Days of Awe, we are asked to look honestly at ourselves. Teshuvah calls us to acknowledge our mistakes and resolve to do better. Tefillah asks us to engage in deep reflection. Tzedakah calls us to give to those in need.
So what does this require once the holiday is over? For me, it means continuing to look honestly at what is happening to Palestinians and to all oppressed people.
The genocide remains devastating. In June, the United Nations released a paper outlining the deliberate targeting and killing of Palestinian children across occupied Palestine. The Elimination Project, a recent report from B’Tselem, an Israeli human rights organization, documents more than 2,000 testimonies showing Israel dismantling the conditions necessary for Palestinian collective existence in the West Bank.
“Naza,” the new documentary from Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examines Israel’s bombing campaign in Gaza and the systems used to select targets. Its central question is difficult to ignore: What happens when technology and bureaucracy make it easier to reduce human beings to targets?
All people, but especially children, deserve safety and joy.
That conviction is inseparable, for me, from being Jewish. I grew up understanding the Holocaust as a warning about dehumanization and what happens when people decide someone else’s pain is none of their business.
My Judaism does not tell me that someone’s humanity matters more than anyone else’s. Quite the opposite. Jewish safety and Palestinian freedom are not opposing values. Our safety and liberation are intertwined.
And this is where Palestine connects, for me, to what is happening here in Maine. The histories and circumstances of these two places are profoundly different. But questions of power, safety and dignity follow us home.
In January, the federal government launched “Operation Catch of the Day.” The ACLU of Maine reports that roughly 200 people were detained. Maine subsequently enacted three “ICE Out” laws limiting cooperation between federal immigration enforcement and state and local institutions.
Then, in July, 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was murdered by an ICE agent with a well-documented history of violence. Left in the wake of this tragedy were Guerrero’s wife and 3-year-old child.
Again, the situations in Palestine and Maine are not the same. But I keep coming back to the same question: What kind of world are we building for future generations?
I am a member of Jewish Voice for Peace Maine, and we are organizing an event for children and families called From Maine to Palestine: Children Will Be Free on Oct. 18 in Portland. The fundraising event will include music, storytelling and community art-making, and 100% of the proceeds will support the Maine Solidarity Fund and Rawa, a Palestinian grassroots community fund.
The Days of Awe are over. But the work of asking what we owe one another continues. For me, that means continuing to build a world where all children and their families, regardless of their backgrounds, can be safe and experience joy. I invite you to commit to that work. Joining me on Oct. 18 is one way to start.

title: Police: Investigation underway after robot inappropriately touched teen girl
text:
Police: Investigation underway after robot controlled by two men inappropriately touched teen girl
German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men inappropriately touched a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said.
Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday, in which the robot's suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault.
They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online.
Related video: Humanoid robot breaks Usain Bolt’s 100m dash record at 9.39 seconds
Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot's movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time.
Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said.
“We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was "new territory for us.”
Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men's phones were confiscated.
North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground.
The robot, said to be 120 cm (about 3 feet and 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache.
Videos found online appeared to show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street.
One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area.
On the police's Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticized inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim.
___
Associated Press writer Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed to this report.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Snow Mixes With Rain Friday, Colder and Breezy Saturday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Wednesday. We’re finally getting a brief break from the unsettled weather heading into Thursday, with sunshine returning across northern Maine. It will still be breezy and cool, but Thursday will easily be the nicest day of the next few. Our next storm system arrives Friday, bringing widespread precipitation back into the region. Snow will likely mix in at times across northern Maine, especially early in the day and again Friday night, but widespread significant accumulation is not expected. Colder and breezier conditions then settle in for Saturday, with a few lingering snow showers possible.
Tonight remains chilly across the region, with temperatures generally falling into the mid 30s. Presque Isle, Caribou and Houlton all look to bottom out around 36 degrees, while colder locations farther north and west may fall closer to freezing. Northwest winds remain somewhat breezy this evening, with gusts up to around 20 to 25 mph, before gradually easing overnight. Skies remain mostly cloudy for much of the night, with only an isolated shower possible early.
Thursday brings a much quieter day, with mostly sunny skies expected across northern Maine. High temperatures climb into the upper 40s to lower 50s, including around 50 degrees in Presque Isle and 48 degrees in Caribou. Houlton looks to reach the lower 50s. Northwest winds will still be noticeable, generally around 10 to 15 mph with gusts approaching 30 mph at times. Despite the sunshine, the breeze will keep a cooler feel in place.
Thursday night turns significantly colder as winds ease and skies remain mostly clear for part of the night. Temperatures look to fall into the mid and upper 20s across much of Aroostook County, including around 26 degrees in Presque Isle and Caribou and near 25 degrees in Houlton. Cloud cover begins to increase late Thursday night as our next system approaches from the west.
Friday will be a wet and chilly day across northern Maine. Temperatures only climb into the upper 30s and lower 40s across the north, with Presque Isle and Caribou both near 41 degrees and Houlton around 43 degrees. Snow may mix with rain during the morning, especially across northern and higher-elevation locations. As temperatures climb during the day, rain should become the more dominant precipitation type for most locations. Little or no snow accumulation is expected across much of northeastern and southeastern Aroostook County during the daytime hours, though some light accumulation remains possible across northwestern Aroostook County.
Temperatures fall back toward freezing Friday night, which allows rain to mix back with snow in some areas. Presque Isle and Caribou look to fall to around 34 degrees, with colder locations farther north and west dropping into the upper 20s and lower 30s. This is when the better chance for light snow accumulation develops. Most areas that see snow will likely remain below an inch, although locations near the Canadian border and higher terrain could potentially reach one to two inches. Some slick roads cannot be ruled out Friday night as temperatures approach freezing.
Saturday remains unsettled as colder air wraps in behind the departing system. Snow showers will be possible during the morning, with a few rain or snow showers lingering into the afternoon. High temperatures only reach the mid to upper 30s across northern Aroostook County and lower 40s farther south.
Winds also increase behind the system, with gusts generally remaining below the stronger levels we were watching in earlier forecasts. It will still be breezy enough to make temperatures feel colder, with wind chills dipping into the 20s at times.
Conditions improve Saturday night into Sunday, with skies clearing and temperatures falling into the lower to mid 20s. Sunday looks dry and cold, with sunshine returning and highs only reaching the lower 40s.
For more details on Thursday’s brief break, Friday’s rain and snow mix and the colder weather arriving for the weekend, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Maine's Halloween Season Grows Beyond October 31st Making Parents and Grandparents Jealous
text:
I'm so envious of kids who get to enjoy Halloween all month, instead of the one-day celebration it was when I was growing up.
Halloween in Maine Used to Consist of One Evening, Not a Whole Month
I can't be the only one feeling this way.
When I was growing up, Halloween was only one night.
Parents didn't want to spend a lot of money on your costume for two reasons:
- You would only wear it for an hour or two
- It's so cold in late October that you'd probably wear a coat over it anyway.
So we would dig out the box of past costumes and try to piece something together for the new year.
Maine Trunk or Treat Events Have Changed the Landscape of Halloween
Now, children get to wear their Halloween costumes all month long, so their parents don't mind spending a little more.
They'll wear them over and over all month as they attend trunk-or-treat events.
Maybe they'll even go to Pumpkins in the Park at the Anah Shrine, where they don't have to wear coats.
Then there's the Halloween Glow Party at the Ferris Community Center Complex in Brewer.
My coworkers and I will across the street from the Brewer Community School.
Maine's Month-Long Halloween Celebrations Make Parents Envious
Don't get me wrong, I'm not criticizing the new month-long Halloween celebrations.
In fact, I love it.
I am pretty jealous that we didn't think of it when I was a kid, so I could've worn that costume more than once.
I'll have to drown my sorrows in a bag of Halloween candy, wearing my costume, and watching Charlie Brown get another rock.

title: InvestigateTV+: Flock camera concerns
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ digs into the mass surveillance network known as Flock, recording every car that passes, how that data is stored and who gets to see it.
Then, we’ll explain the questions to ask when determining a loved one final wishes after death.
Also, an artist shows us what he’s inspired to do with his leftover paint and how it’s sparking unexpected joy around a local park.
Watching the Watchers
Flock Safety cameras have become a fixture in thousands of communities across the United States. The company’s license plate readers photograph every vehicle that passes and store that information in a searchable database available to law enforcement.
The same system that helps police also captures ordinary people’s movements, and when the technology is misused or gets it wrong, critics say oversight is too weak to allow for proper accountability.
The cremation process
When you choose cremation, you’re trusting a stranger with something irreplaceable. So how do you know it’s really your loved one coming home? Horror stories of mishandled cremations have sparked doubt in some minds.
Our investigation went inside South Carolina funeral homes to find out what you need to know. We came away with three questions you should ask any funeral home.
Disc golf growing in popularity
Disc golf has grown from a niche activity into a sport with a growing following, fueled by low cost and an expanding number of courses across the country.
Painted rocks around the park
Every morning, rain or shine, painted rocks appear around Tualatin’s Jurgens Park like Easter eggs waiting to be found.
The artist behind the rocks has been a mystery until now.
