title: Trudy strengthens to a hurricane as system nears Mexico’s coast with major storm expected
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Trudy intensified into a Category 1 hurricane as it approached the Pacific coast of Mexico, authorities said Thursday.
Trudy was located about 300 miles (480 kilometers) southwest of Acapulco, Mexico, with maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (120 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami.
The hurricane was moving northwest at 9 mph (15 kph) and was expected to approach the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico this weekend, the center said.
Trudy was on track to become a major hurricane on Friday, bringing rainfall of 4 to 8 inches (101 to 203 millimeters) through the weekend across Colima and Jalisco states, the center said.

title: Lincoln Girls Soccer Loses To Falcons
text:
The Lincoln Academy girls soccer team lost 6-2 to Freeport in a battle among two of the top teams in Class B South on Thursday, Oct. 8 in Newcastle.
The score was tied 2-2 at halftime before the Falcons exploded for four goals in the second half to claim the win.
Lincoln Academy dropped to 8-3 with the loss, while Freeport improved to 7-3 and jumped ahead of the Eagles in the Heal Point Standings. The Falcons are now in fourth place in class B South, while Lincoln is right behind them in fifth.
The Falcons jumped out to an 1-0 lead midway through the first half. Several minutes later, the Eagles countered with a goal by Rowan Coffin to tie the score 1-1. Dory Westhaver created havoc in the Freeport defensive end and booted a loose ball off a defender before the advancing Falcons goalie could gather it, and Coffin was there to boot it into the vacant goal.
Freeport reclaimed their lead less than a minute later to make it 2-1.
Ella Soucy tied the match in the closing minutes of the first half, gathering the ball in front of the Freeport net after it had been jarred loose once again by the feisty, attacking Westhaver.
“The girls played a great first half against a really good team,” said head coach Lauren Ober. “We just did not have two strong halves in us today.”
Freeport reestablished the lead, 3-2, early in the second half and then their defense shut out the Eagles the rest of the way. The game was closer than the final score indicates, as the Falcons picked up three goals late in the contest.
Ella Tracy scored two goals and had one assist to lead the Falcons offense. Isla Pattershall and Emily Kelsh each had one goal and one assist, and Ada Shirley and Lexi Richardson each scored once goal.
Natalie Hanna made 12 saves in net for the Eagles, and Freeport goalie Karleigh Costello stopped four Lincoln shots during the game.

title: Holdout juror breaks silence on Lindsay Clancy mistrial in new TV interview
text:
Holdout juror says Lindsay Clancy was 'methodical' in the killing of her 3 children in new interview
Michael Desronvil, the lone holdout juror who wanted to convict Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy of murder in the deaths of her three children, sat down for his first television interview since the jury deadlocked.
Video above: Lindsay Clancy’s attorney requests investigation into holdout juror
In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany, Desronvil said he had no reasonable doubt, despite claims from other members of the jury.
"I had a lot of evidence to back up my claim, but out of respect for the other jurors and the court system, I will put that to sleep for now until they go through the process of the court system," Desronvil said.
The jury was split 11-1 in favor of finding Clancy not guilty of the most severe offense.
Desronvil was accused by Clancy's defense team at the time of being an obstructionist during deliberations, committing misconduct, and breaking the law.
The holdout juror told Fox News he believed Clancy was "methodical" in killing her children Cora, Dawson and Callan.
He said after watching video evidence and listening to courtroom testimony, he came to the decision that Clancy couldn't be found not guilty by reason of insanity.
Clancy's defense team declined to comment on Desronvil's interview.
The full interview aired on Fox News on Thursday morning.
Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz has yet to decide whether to charge Clancy with first-degree murder again and retry her.
Background of the Clancy case:
- Lindsay Clancy, 36, faces three murder charges in the 2023 deaths of her children, Cora, Dawson and Callan.
- She also jumped from a second-floor window, leaving her partially paralyzed.
- In a civil case, Lindsay Clancy alleges a "catastrophic failure" of multiple medical providers in diagnosing and treating her psychiatric condition.
- Her trial began July 20. Although her legal team offered to stipulate to the deaths of the children, she has pleaded not guilty.
- She is being held at Tewksbury State Hospital.
This case involves issues of mental health. If you or someone you know needs help, you can talk with the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or sending a text message to 988, or you can chat online here.

title: New York man shot by ICE officers appears in immigration court
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A man who was shot by federal immigration officers in New York had his first hearing before an immigration judge Thursday, appearing remotely via video livestream from the federal jail where his lawyers say he is being held in solitary confinement.
Oscar Belgal, 28, barely spoke during the brief court session. His injury from the shooting wasn’t apparent on the video feed, but his lawyers say he needs surgery to remove a bullet lodged in the back of his neck.
Belgal, a native of the Dominican Republic, tried to say something to the judge about his living conditions at the jail, but his lawyer advised him against it and cut him off.
Karene Brown, of the Legal Aid Society, said Belgal has been on 24-hour lockdown at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn with no access to a phone to speak with his family.
She told Judge Dara Reid that she has asked Immigration and Customs Enforcement to move him from solitary confinement but it has so far not honored the request. Reid said she has no say in where he’s placed within the facility — the same jail holding former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
ICE officers confronted Belgal on Oct. 8 while he was trying to find a parking spot after picking his son up from school. The boy, age 5, was in the car when an ICE officer ran up and smashed one of the car windows.
In a court filing Wednesday, Belgal’s lawyers said the ICE officer then fired several shots into the vehicle as Belgal attempted to drive away. The officers never identified themselves and wore masks and civilian clothes, the lawyers said.
Department of Homeland Security officials maintain the officers believed their lives were in danger and opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and accelerated toward them.
New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively show how the shooting happened.
Belgal’s next immigration court hearing is Oct. 29. His lawyers have also filed a petition in federal court seeking his release.
___
Associated Press reporter Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this story.

title: Hilary Swank, 52, is pregnant with third child
text:
(Gray News) - Hilary Swank is pregnant with her third child at the age of 52.
The “Million Dollar Baby” star and her family shared the news on social media with a video showing them dancing with glowsticks taped to their bodies, which then revealed the mom’s baby bump.
The caption reads, “A lot of people have been asking what project I’m doing next, this one releases in December.”
In 2023, the Oscar winner gave birth at the age of 49 to twins, daughter Aya and son Ohm.
Swank told People in May that she felt fortunate to be able to prioritize time with her children.
Swank said her career had been a priority earlier in life, describing it as “such a baby of mine.” She won the best actress Oscar in 2000 for “Boys Don’t Cry” and in 2005 for “Million Dollar Baby.”
“I knew I wanted kids someday, but I wasn’t planning what that would look like,” Swank said. “I know it’s so different for everyone, but for me, if I had had a kid in my 20s or my 30s, I think I’d be a much different parent than I am now.”

title: Driver who had 1-year-old inside car allegedly rammed ICE vehicle in Sanford
text:
A driver who had a 1-year-old inside a car allegedly rammed a vehicle driven by a federal immigration agent in Sanford on Thursday morning.
That comes just months after a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed a 25-year-old Colombian man in Biddeford during a traffic stop, renewing scrutiny of the agency’s tactics in carrying out President Donald Trump’s deportation agenda.
Two ICE vehicles tried to box in the vehicle about 9:19 a.m. on Brook Street, near High Street, according to the Sanford Police Department.
The driver then allegedly reversed and rammed one of those ICE vehicles.
A 1-year-old child, who allegedly wasn’t properly secured in a safety seat, was found inside the vehicle, Sanford police said.
The child was taken to Southern Maine Health Care out of an abundance of caution, police said.
Officers later learned that the driver’s two other children, ages 2 and 9, had been left without adult supervision at a nearby home. They were taken into the custody of the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
On July 13, Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero was shot and killed by an ICE agent at the intersection of Pool and Hill streets in Biddeford. Homeland Security claimed initially that he had “weaponized” his vehicle before backing off that statement. Guerrero also wasn’t subject to a deportation order.
Coming on the heels of another fatal ICE traffic stop in Texas, the agency temporarily halted traffic stops, only for Trump to contradict that order after less than a day.
CNN reported earlier this month that ICE laid out new instructions for vehicle stops, requiring agents to complete training courses and to ensure that vehicles are equipped with lights and sirens.

title: Kelly Clarkson and a Brooklyn store are clashing on social media over mechanical bird. Here’s why
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — It was something most people have likely done at one time or another: complain to others about feeling judged or dismissed during an interaction, maybe even take to social media to post about it.
But just because we might all have the same impulse, we all don’t have the same reach and impact. Exhibit A: a dispute between singer Kelly Clarkson and a small store in Brooklyn that’s brought out angry fans and heated commentary.
The conflict from over the weekend, involving a high-priced mechanical bird, is raising more issues than just the quality of customer service. It’s also a case study in power dynamics, and the differential that exists between someone with a high profile and those without.
It started Saturday when Clarkson went to Art of Play, a store in Brooklyn that offers items like books, games and playing cards and also hosts magic shows. But the interaction turned negative, she said in a social media post, when she “was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it” and went on to say the store had “just lost a huge sale.” She named the store and gave it a thumbs down.
A back-and-forth ensued, with the store making its own posts saying initially that the item wasn’t for sale and then adding that they had tried to find her an alternative. Clarkson said that wasn’t true.
Since Clarkson’s initial post, there’s been a barrage of commentary online — and, the store owners say, in the real world. There have been hateful messages and reviews, and even someone showing up at the store, said Adam Rubin, one of the partners.
“I don’t understand why these people are willing to debase themselves on behalf of a celebrity they never met,” he said. Representatives for Clarkson did not respond to repeated attempts to get comment.
The power of celebrity is potent
Celebrities have power in different ways. They can influence what people feel as well as impact what they think or believe, said Alfred Archer, assistant professor at Tilburg University in the Netherlands, who has done research around the ethics and politics of fame.
In a situation like Clarkson’s, the influence is heavily weighted in the celebrity’s favor as a result, he said. That doesn’t mean celebrities should be censored or barred from speaking, but they should be cognizant of that reality in determining what they say and how they say it.
“You can’t hold the celebrity responsible for everything that their followers do, of course,” Archer said, but those who have influence should remember that their words can resonate widely and “be careful about what they put on social media and what they communicate in public for that reason.”
That power can also have positive ripples — like when Ms. Rachel, the children’s educator and YouTube star, asked people on social media for Black-owned businesses to support. She gave recognition to small businesses like a coffee shop in New Jersey, leading to a huge jump in sales and popularity.
“I think really the responsibility here is to use this power in a responsible way,” Archer said. “And of course, what that looks like in any individual case is going to be a decision for a particular celebrity to make. But they do have to think about it a bit more carefully than an ordinary member of the public does.”
Social media changed the equation
While everyday people have always been fascinated by the famous, the explosion of social media and the glut of information — and the way we follow our family and friends right along with our favorite stars — means there’s more of a likelihood that people can develop parasocial, or one-sided, unreciprocated relationships with celebrities. That can lead to the kind of harsh messages and bad reviews that the Brooklyn store says it has experienced.
That aspect of modern life is baffling to Franchesca Ramsey, a writer, podcaster, and content creator.
“I think social media itself has heightened people’s ability to feel a connection to a celebrity or a public person that they don’t know,” she said.
“Back in my day, you liked a musician, you put up a poster on the wall. You read the magazine articles about them. You maybe went to their concert. You watched their music videos. But beyond that, it didn’t feel like a two-way relationship. It felt like I’m the fan and this is the person that I really enjoy,” she said.
“Social media has ... kind of created this false sense of reality where, I really think even the act of watching someone’s content on your phone and it looks like they’re talking directly to you,” she said.
Asked what advice he would give another small-business owner facing this kind of situation, Rubin didn’t have any. “This is not something that a small business owner has the capability to deal with,” he said. “This is something that happens on a level of fame and celebrity that I don’t have access to, (that) most normal people don’t have access to.”
Watching the crowd of reporters from his plumbing supply store next door to Art of Play, Daniel Graffeo couldn’t believe the uproar was still going on several days after the initial encounter, but wasn’t totally surprised. “Nowadays everybody’s looking for something, you know, publicity,” he said.
He hoped it would never find him. “I would not want to be in that situation.”

title: CTE educators gather in Lewiston for statewide fall conference
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON, ME – Hundreds of career and technical education (CTE) instructors and education leaders from across Maine gathered at Lewiston Regional Technical Center on Friday, October 9, for the 2026 Maine CTE Fall Conference, a day dedicated to professional development, collaboration and celebrating the educators preparing Maine students for careers in the skilled trades and beyond.
Hosted by the Maine Administrators of Career and Technical Education (MACTE) in partnership with ACTE Maine, the annual conference brought together educators representing a wide range of technical programs, including construction, automotive technology, healthcare, culinary arts, welding, forestry and many others.
The day began with opening remarks from MACTE President Bill Tracy, followed by an introduction from MACTE Executive Director Consultant Amy Marston and remarks from Maine businessman Shawn Moody. The opening program also included recognition of outstanding CTE educators and leaders whose work is making a difference for students and communities across the state.
“I was impressed by today’s conference and what it brought together,” said Amy Marston, Executive Director Consultant for MACTE. “To have so many CTE educators from all over Maine under one roof, sharing ideas, talking about their programs and learning from each other is pretty incredible. There was so much energy in the building, and you could just see how much these instructors care about what they do and the students they teach. It’s a great reminder of just how much is happening in career and technical education in our state.”
Celebrating Excellence in Career and Technical Education
The conference recognized six individuals for their outstanding contributions to career and technical education:
New Teacher of the Year: Rich Jamison, Automotive Technology Instructor, Hancock County Technical Center, recognized for creating student opportunities through industry partnerships, apprenticeships and automotive program development.
Teacher Educator of the Year: Julie Keblinsky, Director of Teaching and Learning for AOS 91 Mount Desert Island Regional School System and Adjunct Professor in Eastern Maine Community College’s CTE Teacher Certification Program, recognized for her leadership in preparing and mentoring new CTE instructors and strengthening instructional practices across the state.
Counseling and Career Development Professional Award: Hope High, Student Services Coordinator, Hancock County Technical Center, recognized for helping students navigate CTE, college and career pathways.
Carl Perkins Community Service Award: Michelle Cote, Health Occupations Instructor, Hancock County Technical Center, recognized for integrating community service and real-world healthcare experiences into student learning.
Teacher of the Year: Lauren Remington, former Early Childhood Education Instructor at St. Croix Regional Technical Center and current Content Manager for ACTE, recognized for her innovative program development, leadership and commitment to expanding educational opportunities.
Administrator of the Year: Bill Tracy, Director of Hancock County Technical Center and MACTE President, recognized for his leadership in expanding CTE programming, strengthening partnerships and increasing opportunities for students.
Following the opening program, instructors gathered in program-specific technical update sessions, giving educators from similar disciplines an opportunity to discuss curriculum, share best practices, address common challenges and learn from programs across Maine.
Lunch featured food prepared and served by students and culinary programs, including food trucks from Capital Area Technical Center and The Green Ladle at Lewiston Regional Technical Center, providing another opportunity to showcase the hands-on learning taking place in Maine’s CTE schools.
The afternoon featured a variety of professional development sessions focused on helping instructors strengthen their programs and bring new ideas into their classrooms. Topics included transitioning from working in the trades to teaching, engaging students in social media content creation, developing career pathways through apprenticeships, exploring careers in forestry and more.
The annual Fall Conference is one of several opportunities throughout the year for Maine’s CTE educators and administrators to come together, learn from one another and strengthen programs across the state. With Maine employers continuing to face workforce challenges, the work happening in CTE classrooms remains an important part of preparing the next generation of skilled workers.

title: Susan Collins gets the 1st tribal endorsement of her career
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Daily News was the first to report this story. What you’re reading here would likely not be made public without the efforts of professional journalists asking questions, interviewing sources and obtaining documents.
The Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik has endorsed U.S. Sen. Susan Collins in her reelection bid against Democrat Troy Jackson, a first for the five-term Republican.
In a letter to Collins, Chief Pos Bassett of the tribe’s Pleasant Point reservation said the senator had worked “tirelessly to improve the economy of both the Passamaquoddy Tribe and community of Washington County” for 30 years.
The support marks a first for Collins, who has pushed for federal funding and several projects for the tribes. But she is not among the state and federal political figures, including Jackson, who have supported tribal sovereignty. Gov. Janet Mills has opposed it, but it is becoming a consensus issue among Democrats.
With the candidates still meeting with tribal leaders and more endorsements likely to come before Election Day, the new support from one of the two Passamaquoddy reservations is tied to the senator’s major pitch to voters that she brings federal dollars home.
Bassett said Collins met with Pleasant Point leaders last year to discuss imminent threats to the reservation’s wastewater treatment plant, due to increasing height of storm surges, shore erosion and rising tide levels. Failure would impact the tribal elder apartment complex, homes, businesses and the marine environment, he said.
“Susan stepped up and secured $5 million in federal funds to support our efforts to construct a new wastewater treatment plant and collection system — a vital and critical piece of community infrastructure,” the chief wrote. “Her ability to deliver has really made a difference in our community and we are so grateful.”
The senator in a statement said she was honored to receive the endorsement, adding that it was “a community that is so important to the culture of our state.”
“I look forward to our continued work together to ensure Maine’s tribes have the resources they need to strengthen their communities, protect their residents and build a stronger future,” she said.
The endorsement came a few days after Jackson — who was backed by the Mi’kmaq Nation Tribal Council during his third-place gubernatorial run — met with Wabanaki nation members on Indigenous People’s Day and held a virtual roundtable with tribal leaders. Other federally recognized tribes did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Senate race.
The Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980 gave the tribes more than $80 million but allows the state to regulate them like towns and cities without the rights of federally recognized tribes in other parts of the country. Independent Sen. Angus King vocally opposed a proposal from U.S. Reps. Jared Golden and Chellie Pingree that would have let the tribes benefit from future laws on federally recognized tribes. Collins did not take a position on the initiative and has said such decisions are up to the Legislature and governor.
A Collins spokesperson said she supports tribes having governmental authority to manage their own affairs. She also has been willing to back extension of federal programs to the tribes even when involving jurisdictional powers, such as applying the Violence Against Women Act to the tribes.
If proposed changes at the state level require amendments to federal law, the senator will examine them closely to understand their impacts on Maine’s tribes, the spokesperson said.
Jackson in a video posted on X Monday said the federal government had let down Maine tribes throughout the state’s history. He pledged to be “the loudest” senator to get tribes “what every other federal tribe across this country has: the right to self-determination.”
“Just like in the [state] Senate, where Troy championed tribal issues by working to recognize the inherent sovereignty of the Wabanaki, improve water quality and family protections, and foster economic development, in the U.S. Senate Troy will fight for the Wabanaki Nations,” his campaign said in a statement.
The chiefs of Mi’kmaq Nation, Passamaquoddy Tribe at Indian Township, Penobscot Nation and Houlton Band of Maliseets announced endorsements for Democratic gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree last week.

title: Edward Little volleyball downs rival Lewiston/Lisbon
text:
AUBURN — Sarah Ebersole put on a big performance to celebrate Senior Night.
Ebersole had nine aces in the first set and finished with 13 to lead the Red Eddies to a 3-1 win over Lewiston/Lisbon in a Class A match on Thursday.
“Serving is really our strong suit,” said Ebersole. “We’re a really great serving team, and we really use that to our advantage in every game. When we’re having a rough time, our serving pulls us out of it every time. We really focus on that, too. It’s really great to be a consistent serving team.”
The teams split their regular-season matches. Lewiston/Lisbon won 3-1 on Sept. 25.
“It’s our home turf, and I think that they just really wanted to prove we still got it, basically, since we lost to (Lisbon/Lewiston) last time,” Edward Little coach Kristi Gordon said. “They’re like, ‘We have to get them this time.’”
HOW IT HAPPENED
Edward Little (9-5) entered the match 12th in the Class A Heal point standings, but played like a higher seed against Lewiston/Lisbon and moved up to ninth with the win. The top 12 teams qualify for the state tournament.
Fifth-ranked Lewiston/Lisbon (11-2) recorded the first point, but Edward Little scored the next 15 on the way to a 25-11 margin in the first set. The Blue Devils regrouped to win the second set, 25-22.
That momentum carried over into the third set, as Lewiston/Lisbon jumped out to a 10-4 advantage. Edward Little battled back, though, and eventually took the set, 25-21.
The fourth set was back-and-forth, with both teams going on little runs. Edward Little closed it out, prevailing 25-18.
UNSUNG HERO
Edward Little’s Elizabeth Galway did a little bit of everything. Not only did she set up teammates, dive on the floor to save points and tally an ace of her own, she also had the spike that clinched the victory. Her powerful hit ricocheted off a Blue Devils player into the stands.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “We came into this one thinking, ‘We’re going to focus, and we’re going to focus on having a good time, because if it is our last game, we just really want to enjoy ourselves.’ And I think that helped us play a lot better, having a good, positive attitude.” — Mallory Johnson
• “(My players are) looking forward to possibly being in the playoffs. We’re hoping, we’re crossing our fingers, so we’ll see what happens after all these games that are happening this week.” — Edward Little coach Kristi Gordon
• “I’ve had (these players) since they were freshmen. They bought into the program, our ideas, our beliefs, and they want it just as bad as we do.” — Lewiston/Lisbon coach Jennifer Curlee
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Edward Little: Sarah Ebersole (13 aces), Sierra Reynolds (three aces), Mallory Johnson (three aces)
• Lewiston/Lisbon: Myriah Bowden (three aces)

title: Obituary: Jeannine B. Lemelin
text:
LEWISTON – Jeannine B. Lemelin, 87, of Lewiston, passed away on Oct. 7, 2026, at her home. She was born on Sept. 25, 1939, to parents Gerard D. Chouinard and Imelda A. Michaud Chouinard. Jeannine previously worked in shoe shops prior to her disability. She enjoyed spending time with her family and smelling the crisp ocean air. She also loved trains and
airplanes.
Jeannine was predeceased by her parents, her two brothers Albert and Paul, daughter-in-law Susan Cox-Rawstron (son John’s wife), and her husband Richard.
She leaves behind her five children Donna Rioux and husband Arthur Rioux, Robert Rawstron and husband Rod Lisse, John Rawstron, Cheryl and Sharon Rawstron, her sister Laurie Chouinard, four granddaughters, Erica, Cara, Chelsea, Shelly; five great-grandsons and two great- granddaughters.
There will be a service on Friday, October 16, at 10 a.m., at St. Peter’s Cemetery in the mausoleum.
In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation to the blind vision rehabilitation centers or school
for the deaf.

title: Several pets killed in Paris fire that destroyed home, officials say
text:
Several pets killed in Paris, Maine, fire that destroyed home, officials say
The Maine State Fire Marshal's Office said it is investigating a fire that destroyed a home in the town of Paris and killed multiple pets.
The fire at 22 Abby Road was reported shortly before 3:30 p.m. Wednesday. Crews from the Paris, Norway and Hebron fire departments responded to the scene, as well as members of PACE Ambulance and the Paris Police Department.
Officials said several pets died in the house fire, but no people were injured.
The single-family home was deemed a total loss. The American Red Cross is providing assistance to the property owners.
The State Fire Marshal's Office said that due to the extensive damage, the cause of the fire has been classified as undetermined.
Investigators have not ruled out several possible electrical causes, and the fire is not considered to be suspicious at this time.

title: Crumbl Cookies locations closing across the country, reports say
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - Dozens of Crumbl Cookies locations are reportedly closing their doors.
According to a report by Restaurant Business, at least 57 locations have closed this year, with more at risk. The outlet also reported at least 55 franchises were listed for sale.
The closures come even after Crumbl, known for its rotating line of cookies, launched dirty sodas to bring in sales. Rather than improving sales, unit volumes declined by about 16%.
Sales overall didn’t look any better. USA Today reported that sales in August were 70% lower than two months before.
Co-founders Sawyer Hemsley and Jason McGowan stepped down from the company earlier in the year.
Still, the company has more than 1,000 locations and 29,000 employees, according to its website.
Crumbl was formed in 2017 in Utah and was generating $1 billion in revenue each year within its first seven years, Restaurant Business reported. The company went viral during and after the pandemic and became widely known for its pink boxes across social media.

title: Healthy Acadia invites you to discover a path to peace with a guided meditation
text:
Healthy Acadia will host “Discover the Path of Peace: A Guided Meditation for Inner Alignment,” with Julie Daigle on Thursday, Nov. 5 from 5 to 6 p.m. The free online event is the latest installment in Healthy Acadia’s Monthly Mindfulness series.
Daigle will offer a guided meditation session to foster peace, clarity and to encourage us to identify and rest within our most authentic, heartfelt desire. Participants should be prepared to rest fully, lying down if possible, on a comfortable surface. You can use a yoga mat if you have one, but it isn’t necessary if you don’t; a comfortable spot to relax fully into stillness is the essential requirement. We will also have a few minutes at the end to journal the experience, so please bring paper and a pen or pencil or other drawing/writing tools if you prefer.
Pre-registration is required for this free event. Upon registering, you’ll receive a confirmation that includes the information needed to join the Zoom session. Register online at https://bit.ly/mindful-110526.
Julie brings over 40 years of mind-body-spirit practice, which informs her current classes in yoga nidra and tai chi in coastal Maine. She began a traditional Chinese medicine-based martial arts practice in the early 80s, received her third-degree black belt in the 90s, acquired her 200-hour RYT with the Yoga Alliance in the early 2000s and nine years ago, became both a certified instructor for the Tai Chi for Health Institute and a certified Yoga Nidra instructor. She credits this foundation in mindfulness and moving meditation-based practices for building a resilience accessible to all through consistent, gentle practice.
For more information about this event, future mindfulness offerings, or other programs that support mindful living, subscribe to Healthy Acadia’s e-newsletter or visit healthyacadia.org/hpm-mindfulness-for-health.
Celebrating 25 years, Healthy Acadia is a 501(c)(3) community health organization dedicated to building vibrant communities and making it easier for everyone to lead healthy lives. Serving Washington and Hancock counties, the organization provides community health support and leadership across Maine. For more information, visit healthyacadia.org.

title: States sue AI giant OpenAI, saying ChatGPT is hurting children and deceiving adults
text:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit.
The company’s chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to commit suicide or hurt or kill others, the lawsuits said.
At the same time, the lawsuits contend that chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and on teenagers, the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence.
“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.
The states also accused OpenAI of giving life to rogue AI models — or “cyberhacking agents” as one lawsuit called them — that hacked into other companies, lied to human users and wrote themselves new mission instructions.
In a statement, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model. It also said it is reviewing what it calls “misaligned models” and that it had found nothing close to the rogue incident discovered in July when an AI agent hacked into another AI company.
States join together in lawsuits
The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.
Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”
In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends.
The states say that the risks and harms — to teenagers and to the broader public from rogue agents — were foreseeable, but that OpenAI has misled people into thinking that ChatGPT undergoes adequate safety testing while the company undermines safety in the pursuit of profit.
“Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm — including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse — due to (OpenAI’s) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content,” Idaho wrote in its lawsuit.
ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits.
The AI landscape is evolving
It’s possible all of the allegations in the states’ lengthy lawsuits date to incidents and findings before August, when OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT designed for teenagers, with stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats.
Still, the states said it is far from clear that the current version is any less dangerous.
A watchdog group, Common Sense Media, said last week that some of OpenAI’s protections in its ChatGPT for Teens product don’t work as intended and it urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until it can offer a safe product for teens.
Coordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit.
In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an $18 billion landmark legal settlement that ended a trial over teen social media addiction and settled claims filed by nearly every state.
Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures.
OpenAI is making a similar appeal.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company is committed to working with states on “advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.”
OpenAI also said it works with external experts who review its policies and ChatGPT’s behavior.
ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens is designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said.
Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said.
But Laura Zimmerman, Common Sense Media’s director of youth AI research, questioned the value of OpenAI’s statistics.
For one thing, ChatGPT can do a student’s homework in seconds, so even 15 minutes can have a big impact on a teenager’s development, Zimmerman said. She also questioned whether OpenAI knows which users are teenagers or children, given that her organization’s testing found that ChatGPT couldn’t or didn’t detect which user is a child.

title: Bath Iron Works to highlight shipbuilding careers at job fair
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works is inviting recent high school and college graduates and others considering a career change to learn about opportunities in shipbuilding at an occupational trade show.
Representatives from engineering and design firms will share information on working with BIW, while attendees can learn about its apprenticeship program, which combines paid work experience with training toward an apprenticeship certificate and a college degree.
BIW’s human resources team will be available to answer questions about the hiring process and to provide information on pay and benefits.
The event is open to the public and runs Saturday, Oct. 17, from 9 a.m. to noon at BIW’s Training Academy at 8 Leavitt Drive in Brunswick.
A business unit of Reston, Virginia-based defense contractor General Dynamics (NYSE: GD), Bath Iron Works employs 6,800 shipbuilders in Bath. It ranked as Maine’s fourth-largest employer in the 2026 Mainebiz Book of Lists.
Seven Arleigh Burke-class destroyers are currently under construction at the shipyard.

title: Southwest Standers and Bar Harbor Resisters want everyone to get out and vote
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — The Southwest Standers and the Bar Harbor Resisters will host national No Kings rallies on Oct. 17 in their respective towns. Both groups are encouraging everyone to get out and vote early this year.
The Standers event will take place at 315 Main St. in Southwest Harbor, from 11 a.m. to 12 p.m. The Resisters event will be held on the Bar Harbor Village Green from 10 to 11 a.m. Both events are part of the nationwide No Kings demonstrations.
Last year, according to Mark Sullivan, a member of the Standers, the rally drew 650 people.
“In October of last year, we had 650 people come just for an hour to Southwest Harbor downtown and totally peaceful protest, people using their voice to express their feelings about current political conditions and current leadership,” said Sullivan.
This will be the fourth national No Kings participation by the Standers.
Organizers plan to set up a voter-information table for island residents covering the different options available. “Nationally, there’s going to be a lot of voter education, and we’re going to do that as well. We’re going to have a table hosted by us, you know, folks from the island talking about, you know, the existing early voting options, absentee ballots, mail-in ballots, what to expect on Election Day,” explained Sullivan.
The Bar Harbor Resisters will also have voter information available, including resources for locating and getting to the nearest polling location, according to Resister Grace Nagiecka.
Sullivan and Nagiecka both said their respective groups wanted to see people coming together and voting to make change.
“It’s about people expressing opposition to the increasing power and influence of the billionaire class,” Sullivan said. He referenced the rising costs of fuel, housing, food, and other things people need to survive slowly getting out of reach for the average American. “It’s killing everybody’s cost of living except for the billionaires themselves.”
“I think more and more people, regardless of party, have realized this is out of control. My voice is being taken away, and I’m subject to whatever it is that billionaires want to put in front of me and make available to me and price. So I think this is going to be a really fantastic day nationally for people to stand up and to say ‘People have the power.’”
Sullivan hopes the rally will bring people together and offer an opportunity for different sides of the political spectrum to find common ground. “This one that has such a positive message for every single voter, regardless of party,” he said.
He noted that anyone who wants to participate can find information on the No Kings website at mobilize.us/nokings and register there or find information on a rally near you. The group encourages anyone participating to register so organizers can plan accordingly.
“We’re preparing for around the same number as last year, and if anything, this is a more inclusive and, you know, a more nonpartisan event. But people — everybody is fed up, and the only way any one of us is going to start getting the changes and improvements we want is by voting.”
Sullivan described the event as a chance to counter isolation and doom-scrolling by coming together in person. He expects a positive, energetic gathering centered on voting and civic participation in Southwest Harbor and even across the nation.
He also confirmed that trained peacekeepers and “Yellowcoats” will be present at the rally. The Standers have developed a playbook, site plan, and designated locations for pairs of peacekeepers trained in de-escalation in case of any heated discussions happen at the rally; they make sure people are not parked at local businesses and are accessible to the general public.
At past larger rallies, the Southwest Harbor Police Department has been on site. Sullivan praised the department and Chief John Hall for their professionalism and willingness to uphold the constitutional rights of those participating.
“We have a great relationship with them, and the chief is really articulate about, hey, it’s our job to make sure that anybody expresses themselves within their legal and constitutional rights,” said Sullivan.
Kate Henry, who is the head organizer for the SWH Standers, is also encouraging people to “bar hop” and go to the rally in Bar Harbor first, and then head over to Southwest.

title: 1 dead in Bangor apartment building fire
text:
One person died and two others were treated for smoke inhalation following an apartment building fire in Bangor on Wednesday morning.
The Bangor Fire Department responded to 72 Cedar St. for a structure fire at about 6:35 a.m., Maine Department of Public Safety spokesperson Shannon Moss said in a news release Thursday.
One occupant was unable to escape the building, Moss said.
Two other residents were transported to Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center to be treated for smoke inhalation, Moss said, and have since been released.
The identity of the deceased is being withheld pending an examination by the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, Moss said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation.

title: Why stop there, Sec. Hegseth?
text:
“High-testosterone” Department of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan by firing squad — the first military execution in the U.S. since 1961 — would be available to “livestream.”
To ensure the proper barbarity for the spectacle, and simultaneously to help fight our growing deficits, Hegseth should sell the rights to a “pay-per-view” showing, even to Fox News, perhaps at halftime of a football game.
Americans could have been charged, say, $40 to witness the killing. Hegseth could make a guest appearance and demonstrate his warrior nature by doing push-ups and then shooting one of the guns. With just three million subscriptions, the revenue would have been $120 million, more than enough to cover the $84 million that his department spends on erectile dysfunction medicine annually.
Although President Trump may flip-flop on the livestream, he has never missed an opportunity to use the media to make money.
Paul Josephson
Vinalhaven

title: Berwick appoints police chief as interim town manager
text:
The Berwick Select Board has appointed police Chief Timothy Towne as interim town manager while it searches for someone to take on the role permanently.
The board voted unanimously at an Oct. 6 meeting to appoint Towne, with a start date this week. Five days into his new post, Towne said he’s inherited a lot of responsibility.
“I’m walking into things, you know, that have been taking place for quite some time, so getting caught up to speed on things is a little challenging,” he said Thursday. “I’m doing a lot of reading, a lot of research, so I can get informed enough to make sure things continue as they should.”
Towne has spent more than 30 years serving Berwick, starting at the police department in 1993 as a reserve officer. He then served as a detective and a sergeant before rising to the chief position in 2001.
He took the interim job “simply because there’s a need for it.” He knew the Select Board was in a bind when former Town Manager Arthur Capello announced he was stepping down and taking on a city administrator role in Missouri.
“It’s not easy to find a town manager that’s willing to just walk through the door,” Towne said.
So when the Select Board approached him, he didn’t have to think too hard about it before he took the job.
He’ll be serving both roles — police chief and interim town manager — concurrently with the help of others at the police department but admits he’s an exceptionally busy man.
Towne’s also preparing for Nov. 3, when his neighbors will decide whether he should be elected House District 149 representative. The Republican’s in a two-way race with South Berwick Town Council Vice Chair Mallory Cook, a Democrat.
(House District 149 encompasses portions of North Berwick and South Berwick and is currently represented by Democrat Tiffany Roberts, who’s termed out of office.)
Towne said he’s happy to help for now, but that he has a soft agreement with the town come November. If he’s elected as a state representative — a goal he committed to before taking on the interim role — then he’ll step away from his town hall position.
“I just want to keep it stable for the people that work here,” Towne said. “The town is progressing very well. There’s a lot of things going on in town, and you don’t like to see things have to take a back seat.”
The Select Board is actively searching for Berwick’s next manager and said at the Oct. 6 meeting that it’s seeking a recruiting firm to help find that person.

title: Three Maine football storylines to follow against Bryant
text:
It’s been two weeks since the University of Maine football team dropped its fifth straight game with a 24-16 loss to Sacred Heart on Oct. 3 in Orono. Maine had a bye last week, during which it fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters.
The Black Bears (1-5, 1-2 Coastal Athletic Association) return to action when they host Bryant (4-2, 2-0 CAA) at 1 p.m. Saturday (FloSports; ABC in Bangor market). Here are three storylines to watch as Maine looks to end the skid.
Green-er pastures?
With Waters gone, running backs coach Sean Green takes over as interim offensive coordinator. Green is well-known in Maine, having won state titles as head coach of Cape Elizabeth High School in 2021 (Class C) and Portland in 2024 (Class A).
Green takes over a Maine offense ranked 121st of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in points per game (14.5). In Monday’s CAA press conference, coach Jordan Stevens said the goal is to “continue to find ways to be more balanced” offensively and praised his team’s response to the change.
“I thought the guys have handled that type of change really well in how they’ve approached practice, and Coach Green has done an excellent job,” Stevens said. “This is not something that’s foreign to him in calling plays; it’s something he’s done in the past, so I have full confidence in his ability.”
The quarterback question
Through the first four games, Eddie Buehler was Maine’s unquestioned starter at quarterback. Yet in the second half at Elon on Sept. 26, Caden Drezek took over under center. Buehler again got the start against Sacred Heart before Stevens turned to Drezek in the second quarter.
So, with a new offensive coordinator, what will the plan be this weekend? Will Buehler make his seventh straight start? Will the Black Bears turn to Drezek instead? Or will we see some combination of the two, as has been the case the past two games?
“In a perfect world, you’d always probably have one guy,” Stevens said. “I don’t have any answer for you on that right now, but we are working through the quarterback position and how we’re going to manage that this week.”
Up-and-down Bulldogs
On one hand, Bryant boasts an impressive 21-14 win over Princeton, which is 3-1. Yet the Bulldogs also needed a miracle — 10 points in the final 40 seconds — to pull out a win over North Carolina A&T, which might be the worst team in the CAA. Bryant also lost 28-13 at Brown.
This is an opportunity, then, for the Black Bears, who have had two weeks to prepare. The numbers don’t suggest a lopsided game — in fact, ESPN’s SP+ has the Bulldogs as just 1.3-point favorites. A win will be difficult, but it’s not impossible — and if Maine can pull it off, the trajectory of the season could change.

title: Hannaford app, website still offline over 2 days after company identified security issue
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford’s website and mobile app remained offline Friday, more than three days after the supermarket’s parent company says it disabled some systems as a precautionary measure while addressing a network cybersecurity issue.
Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch food giant that owns Maine’s largest grocer, announced in a brief news release late Monday that it was experiencing an internal network issue and had taken some systems offline to protect them, including the Hannaford website and app.
Online ordering has been disabled since then, though stores have remained open as usual.
On Thursday morning, the notification of the outage on Hannaford’s website was updated to include a note that customers can still shop online via third-party delivery services such as DoorDash, Instacart and Uber Eats.
Caitlin Cortelyou, a spokesperson for the Scarborough-based grocery store chain, said in an email Thursday that Hannaford is continuing to work with Ahold Delhaize to resolve the issue. While the investigation into the outage is ongoing, Cortelyou said, the companies “have no evidence at this moment that customer or associate data was taken in this cybersecurity incident.”
Ahold Delhaize says it has contacted external cybersecurity experts to help with its response and is “engaging with the appropriate authorities” as necessary.
“We know how important it is for our customers to be able to shop with us when and how they choose, and we apologize for the disruption,” Cortelyou said. “We appreciate our customers’ continued patience and understanding as we work to resolve the issue.”
If the cybersecurity issue is deemed to have been a data breach, then Maine law requires it be reported to the Office of the Maine Attorney General. The AG’s office said neither Hannaford nor Ahold Delhaize had reported the issue as of Wednesday.
A 2024 breach of Ahold Delhaize’s systems affected more than 95,000 Mainers and over 2 million people worldwide. Hannaford said most of the Mainers whose information was exposed were current or former employees.
Ahold Delhaize, one of the world’s largest food retailers, operates more than 2,000 U.S. stores under several brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant Food. Hannaford is the state’s largest grocer, with almost 70 stores across Maine.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 16 to indicate that the outage has continued into Friday.

title: Maine artists are exhibiting on a bigger stage: The world
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In July 2022, as we emerged from the COVID pandemic, the art newspaper Artnews published a story with the headline: “Forget the Hamptons. Artists, Dealers, and Advisors Are Congregating in a New Bucolic Contemporary Art Hub: Maine.” Whether this still holds true, especially during the dead of Maine winter, is hard to verify. Statistics are not easy to come by. But certainly Maine art — which has a long and storied legacy as a mecca for artists — is looking particularly vital on the world stage at the moment.
Currently online through Oct. 29 is “A Look at ME: Paintings from Maine,” hosted by international art gallery Taymour Grahne Projects, which was first established in New York and now has gallery space in Dubai and an office in London. The virtual exhibition features 29 painters, all but four of them alive and actively working in the state. In Arkansas, “Down East,” an exhibition of eight Maine contemporary women artists, just closed at Pond Gallery, an artist-run space in Fayetteville. On display from Oct. 29 through Dec. 17 at Concord Art in Concord, Massachusetts will be “Magnetic North,” which will showcase 17 Maine-based artists.
Creatives working in Maine have always individually sought representation in the larger urban art centers, particularly New York and Boston because of their proximity. But what is happening now feels different: national, international and online exhibitions that highlight groups of Maine artists as a collective rather than individuals, conveying the idea of Maine as particularly fecund ground for contemporary art.
It would be preposterous to suggest Maine art is any one thing, of course. As I write in my forthcoming book, Contemporary Maine Art (Monacelli, Spring 2027):
“I do not believe there is something remotely like a brand called ‘Maine art.’ This in itself prescribes confining boundaries for a phenomenon that is uncontainable and perpetually evolving and changing. That is why, when I talk about Maine art, I talk about ‘art in Maine’ rather than the ‘art of Maine.’ The difference in prepositions is an important one, for taken as a whole, art made here represents a staggering pluralism of styles, ideas, genres and media.”
What’s more, in all these exhibitions, the common narrative of the state as primarily a generator of painting of landscapes, seascapes, lighthouses and fishing scenes is almost nowhere in evidence. Instead, the artists featured are tackling current issues — politics, climate change, racism, sexuality and gender — as well as more universal themes such as time and memory, domesticity, loss and spirituality.
To what can this trend be attributed? Many artworld watchers point to a renewed interest in regional art. The website AmericanRegionalism.com, a “reference archive for study, preservation and celebration of American Regional art,” detected a shift that began in the 2020s with what it describes as “a renewed interest in authenticity, community and the emotional truth of local experience. As digital culture accelerates and global aesthetics become increasingly homogenized,” the site reads, “many artists and audiences are seeking work that feels grounded, human, and connected to real places.”
Lebanese-Finnish dealer Taymour Grahne has witnessed this on a global scale. “People are looking outside the centers — New York, Los Angeles, London — to networks and collectors in other cities,” he observes. “There are a lot of great artists in New York, but it’s interesting to see what is happening outside of that world.”
Marc Mitchell, the curator of the Fayetteville show, who is director of exhibitions at the School of Art, University of Arkansas, also points to social media. “There is a way that we can get information that has been very beneficial,” he says. “With social media and the internet, there really is no place we can call isolated any more.”
Another recent contributor to the enhanced consciousness about Maine artists, believes Falmouth and Portland art dealer Elizabeth Moss, is the Lynne Mapp Drexler syndrome. Though Drexler exhibited widely during her days in New York in the middle of the 20th century, she was largely eclipsed by her husband, the painter John Hultberg. After eschewing the New York art world and moving to Monhegan Island where she lived until her death, she could be found selling her work to tourists for $50.
“We’ve exhausted all the male abstract expressionists,” believes Moss. “People are looking at the art of women who were overshadowed in that time.” As part of this reappraisal, Drexler’s work has gained astonishing notoriety, collected by celebrities like John Legend and breaking auction records with prices in excess of $2 million.
MAINE, DUBAI AND THE WORLD
When Grahne opened his new Dubai gallery this past September, the inaugural exhibition was “Arranging Flowers,” a solo show of paintings by Maine artist Gail Spaien, who the gallery has represented for years. When asked what led to this decision rather than concentrating on one of the many Middle East artists he has championed over the last 15 years, Grahne says, “Dubai is an international hub, one of the most cosmopolitan cities in the world. Opening with Gail was a signal that Dubai is a space where this art can be shown. She already had a following here. The show sold out.”
It might seem strange to hear that Spaien’s cozy paintings of Maine interiors overlooking the water — with their wood-burning stoves, curled up cats, braided rugs and floral arrangements — has such a powerful draw halfway across the globe. But Grahne knows why. “Domestic space is sacred and such a big part of our world in Arab culture,” he says. “While Gail’s art is Maine-specific, it also has a universal appeal.”
Spaien adds that “nature motifs and patterns are part of [Arab] reverence for the natural world.” The online exhibition, she says, “was Taymour’s idea. He asked me to organize a show of Maine artists.” The 29 painters Spaien selected were a mixture. Some are what she calls “old guard” artists such as Katherine Bradford, Mark Whetli and the late Carlo Pittore and Robert Hamilton (as well as Drexler). Another group is current “megastars” such as Tessa Greene O’Brien, Jarid del Deo and Anne Buckwalter. There are emerging artists such as Cody Castle-Stack, Grace Hager and Meg Hahn too. And others — the late Beverly Hallam (“totally unrecognized”) and Natasha Mayers — are little known outside Maine’s borders.
“We’ve had nine or ten sales so far,” Grahne said. They include works by Castle-Stack, Spaien and Jay Stern, and they sold to collectors in Dubai, Jordan, Texas and Maine. There has also been considerable interest in paintings by Bradford and Drexler. Grahne doesn’t believe this trend is anywhere near ebbing. This past summer, he sent a team to Maine to scout artists for potential exhibition and representation. “I like that Maine is not market-centric, but artist-centric” Grahne says. “It’s created something very special.”
DOWNEAST, ARKANSAS
The “Down East” exhibition in Fayetteville came about through a vast network of personal connections. “I know a lot of artists in Maine because I went to graduate school at Boston University,” says Mitchell. While attending in the early 2000s, two of his classmates were Meghan Brady and Kayla Mohammadi. He also studied with John Walker, Mohammadi’s husband. “John used to make all his students go up to Maine and paint,” Mitchell recalls. “Ever since then, I try to get there,” which he did for a time through work with the Tides Institute in Eastport.
Before the pandemic, not long out of graduate school, Mitchell recalls, he was a fellow artist in residence with Eleanor Conover at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville. And when he got to Fayetteville, he met Samantha Sigmon, who ran an alternative artist-run space there called Backspace and has since become assistant curator at Bates Museum of Art in Lewiston. Significantly, Sigmon’s first curating foray at Bates after her arrival was a show she titled “Across Common Grounds: Contemporary Art Outside the Center” in 2024, which picked up on the regionalism trend.
“The more I thought about it, there was a common ethos between Arkansas and Maine,” Mitchell says, ticking off a list that includes, “resilience, an appreciation for nature and culture, a history of storytelling.”
Mitchell’s desire to do a woman-centric exhibition dovetailed with these synergies between Arkansas and Maine, so he contacted Brady and Conover to begin a conversation about who should be in the show. The nine women selected include Mohammadi, Conover and Brady, but also ceramist Ariela Nomi Kuh, sculptor Elizabeth Atterbury and fresco artist Barbara Sullivan.
Since the university’s Edward Durrell Stone-designed fine arts building was closed for renovations, Mitchell partnered with Pond Gallery for “Down East.” The show received several inquiries about buying the work, which were redirected to the artists’ galleries. And, says Mitchell, “The outpouring of compliments and support on social media was really nice.”
CONCORD BOUND
Painter Elizabeth Awalt has been coming to Swan’s Island from her Concord, Massachusetts home every summer for years. “I was seeing this kind of growth and strength of artists going on in Maine,” she says. “You can’t say that about New Hampshire or Cape Cod, at least not any longer. And they’re doing things that you wouldn’t expect. I wanted to share that in the Boston area because they’re doing wonderful work and you don’t see a lot of them down here.”
So Awalt leveraged her position on the exhibitions committee of Concord Art — an artist association incorporated in 1922 by painter Elizabeth Wentworth Roberts and located in the 18th-century John Ball House — to propose an exhibition of Maine artists. The institution agreed, so Awalt called environmental and installation artist Pamela “Posey” Moulton, who she had met some years before on Swan’s Island, to connect Awalt to Maine artists who were doing interesting work.
The two have curated “Magnetic North,” a show that intentionally challenges the established identity of Maine art. Jocelyn Lee’s photographic, often nude, portraits of aging people. Dylan Hausthor’s subtly uncomfortable images of rituals conducted by hermetic religious communities. David Wilson’s beautiful yet spooky woodland scenes based on fables and myths. All of them, says Awalt, “have this weird, almost surreal quality to them.”
To Awalt, that felt in perfect congruence with Concord’s history as a nexus for Transcendentalist thinkers like Ralph Waldo Emerson, Sophia Ripley and Henry David Thoreau (who published his travel narrative “The Maine Woods” in 1864). The Transcendentalists, of course, were a fringe movement. But that, too, feels perfectly aligned with Maine’s history of attracting free thinkers and iconoclasts.
Interest in art produced in Maine will certainly get another national profile boost from former Portland gallery owner Peggy Greenhut Golden’s upcoming documentary, “Away from It All: Maine’s Place in American Art.” The film is scheduled to air this spring — locations to be determined — and chronicles the development of American art through a Maine lens. The film is narrated by actor Tony Shalhoub, an alumnus of University of Southern Maine.
For Maine artists themselves, believes Spaien, it is all about a pride of place and a desire to spread the enthusiasm far and wide. “The folks working in Maine right now want to share Maine,” she believes. “They want to be connected to those in the outer world but also want to remain Mainers and bring others into the picture.” The time for this, apparently, is now.
Jorge S. Arango has written about art, design and architecture for over 35 years. He lives in Portland and can be reached at [email protected]. This story is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.

title: Maine’s new women’s soccer team set to unveil branding Thursday
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - The Portland Hearts of Pine is preparing to unveil the branding behind Maine’s new women’s soccer team Thursday, ahead of its inaugural season next spring.
The team will compete in the USL W League, beginning play in May 2027.
Gov. Janet Mills has proclaimed Thursday as the second-ever “Maine Day of Soccer” in celebration of the new women’s franchise.
“The Hearts of Pine have brought a tremendous amount of pride and energy to Maine during their first two seasons, and I can’t wait to welcome their new women’s team to Portland,” Mills said in a statement Wednesday.
The first “Maine Day of Soccer” came in April 2024 when the men’s Hearts of Pine team launched its name, crest and brand identity.
According to Gabe Hoffman-Johnson, founder and chief community officer for the Hearts of Pine, the addition of the women’s team has been a vision since the beginning.
“This is a moment we’ve imagined for a long time, and to see it become real with so much support from people across the state is incredibly meaningful,” said Hoffman-Johnson.

title: Who protects the farmers?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Regarding an Oct. 7 news report (“Maine’s top court rejects eviction appeal by Midcoast farmers”), the farmers’ appeal was reportedly lost because it was found they had “failed to pay rent and grow crops as they had once agreed.”
Crops, for most non-farmers, usually means fruits and vegetables. Not all soils in Maine are suitable for growing fruits and vegetables. Some soils are best used for pasture and hay (a valuable crop) or for growing livestock, which might also be called a valuable crop.
The Maine Farmland Trust ought to carefully review its policies regarding farmers on leased land; the situation that happened in Harpswell will happen again. It is one thing to protect farmland. Who protects the farmers? No farmers, no food.
Jeanne Johnson
Juniper Edge Farm
Brunswick

title: A 14-year-old was shot in the face, losing his eye. His friend is now facing charges
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - A 14-year-old South Carolina boy is traumatized after he was shot in the face and lost an eye. His 17-year-old friend is now facing charges, police say.
Derrick Simmons, 14, is facing a long road to recovery after he was shot in the face Friday, losing his left eye. His mother, Davida Simmons, says the incident has changed her son’s life.
“He was like, ‘Mom, I can’t play football no more.’ And I tell him, ‘You can still do anything that’s possible. Don’t let this hinder you,’” Simmons said.
Charleston Police say officers responded to a downtown apartment complex around 1 p.m. Friday and found Derrick with a gunshot wound to the face. Police say the 14-year-old and a 17-year-old friend were handling a gun when the older teen pointed the gun at Derrick and fired.
A call from the hospital changed everything for Derrick’s mother.
“I got the first call around 1:35. I had, like, 20-something missed calls... So, I was panicking,” Simmons said. " So, I came down to the hospital and talked to one of the nurses. She was telling me that my son was shot twice. He was shot once in the eye. Then, he was shot once in the shoulder. So, I asked the doctor, ‘Can you save his eye?’ His eye is not savable at all. His eye is completely gone."
Simmons says her son is recovering from surgery, but the trauma is still with him.
“He was telling me that he was scared, and I told him, ‘The best birthday gift was you still here,’” Simmons said.
She says her son has had nightmares since the shooting.
“He was trying to figure out why he can’t open his eyes. He was trying to open his eyes. So, he finally grasped the idea last night when I told him, ‘You can’t open your eyes because your eye is not there anymore.’ So, he started crying because he was trying to figure out why. Why did this happen to me?” Simmons said.
As her son begins a long recovery that will include getting a prosthetic eye, Simmons is urging gun owners to make sure children can’t access their firearms.
“If you own a firearm, the best thing for you to do, if you have kids that’s active or any situation, it’s best to keep it locked up because things like this can happen. I don’t want another mother to go through what I’m going through,” she said.
Police say the 17-year-old suspect admitted to shooting Derrick. He was arrested and charged with assault and battery of a high and aggravated nature, possession of a firearm during the commission of a violent crime and possession of a firearm under 18.
He was booked into the South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice.
Keeping guns out of teens’ hands
Jerome Smalls, developer of youth outreach for the Charleston Police Department, said preventing gun violence takes a community effort.
“There’s a culture around firearms, right? Around it being exciting or cool or part of a facade or an identity. We need to do a better job, both in schools and our communities and as a whole, in changing that culture and that narrative of what it means to be cool and to be associated with firearms,” Smalls said.
Smalls said many young people access firearms through unlocked vehicles.
“The kids call it poking, where they go pull loose door handles, and if it’s unlocked, that’s the number one way firearms are getting in the hands of not just young people but other folks in our community,” he said.
Smalls said the department is working with local organizations, including Representation Matters, on youth programs focused on keeping guns out of young people’s hands.
“If we can get a better hold in marketing and understanding that hey, you have a very dangerous piece of machinery that you own, and you need to be accountable and responsible with that machinery, I think that right there – it doesn’t end it all – but it can curve a lot of young people getting their hands on firearms,” he said.
Carlos DeVeaux, co-executive director of the Representation Matters Foundation, said he works directly with the teen suspect and his family.
“It’s a very unfortunate situation, and it’s kind of personal because I work hand-in-hand with the children in the community. The teenager that it happened to, I work hand-in-hand with him and his parents,” DeVeaux said. “I just think that parents need to pay more attention to the children and don’t give them too much options... But most of all, men, more Black men need to step up and get into these children’s lives, pay attention to their movement, pay attention to what bothers them because too much guns are getting into these children’s hands.”
DeVeaux said his organization works to show young people role models who look like them.
“If you show a child that somebody that looks like them have done it before, they feel that they can do it,” he said.

title: Firefighter who defecated in box while working at airport no longer with department
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) — A firefighter who spent more than 30 years with the St. Louis Fire Department is no longer employed there after he defecated in a cardboard box while working fire protection at Lambert International Airport.
The firefighter was put on administrative leave after the June 10 incident, which was caught on a security camera in an area operated by the airport’s food and beverage concessionaire. His employment with the City of St. Louis ended on Aug. 14, the Department of Personnel confirmed to KMOV.
A photo from security footage showed the man with his pants down, holding a box behind him.
The St. Louis Fire Department is responsible for fire protection at Lambert International Airport. An airport spokesperson previously said fire personnel operate independently at the airport but are on site 24/7.
The St. Louis Fire Department told KMOV that the man started working fire protection at Lambert in 2019.
The firefighter was not identified by name.
