title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, as Zelenskyy says he feels betrayed by Trump
text:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine attacked a Russian oil refinery Thursday, abandoning a brief truce involving energy-related targets that it said Moscow did not heed, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow in Russia’s Ryazan region, according to the Russian Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov. Russia’s Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv’s relations with Trump, which have soured again in recent days amid deepening tensions with Washington.
Zelenskyy said he was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks.
Despite going along with Trump’s demand for a truce, Zelenskyy complained, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes, and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. Both are vital for the Ukrainian military.
He said his patience had run out, telling the Financial Times in an interview published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume.
“We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying.
A senior Ukrainian official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to speak publicly, confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
Zelenskyy slams US deal to buy Russian diesel
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Ukraine never stopped its strikes on refineries that have hurt Russia. It wasn’t possible to independently verify each side’s claims.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov labeled Ukraine’s strikes on oil facilities as a “direct and crude challenge to President Trump.”
Another point of tension with Ukraine is a deal Trump made with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
In an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist’s YouTube show, Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink limits that restricted the use of Ukrainian drones.
“Really, yes, between us,” Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. “Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump.”
He said the behavior of the U.S., including restricting the Starlink system, “was really strange.”
Zelenskyy says U.S. position isn’t ‘on the right side of history’
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “losing a strong partner” in the United States.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he’s in the middle,” he said.
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is “not the right side of history.”
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
A Ukrainian official said the country has not received an explanation from either SpaceX, the company that maintains the Starlink satellites, or the Pentagon, on the slowdown. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive situation.
The Pentagon has not answered questions about the slowdown from The Associated Press either.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn’t stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Ukraine looks to Europe for more help
Amid fears that the Trump administration may be withdrawing support for Ukraine, Zelenskyy went to Brussels on Thursday for talks with European Union leaders attending a two-day summit.
Zelenskyy said he would meet with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, French President Emmanuel Macron, and the prime ministers of Poland, Denmark and Belgium.
The previous day, he visited London, where he won pledges of more help from U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Asked whether the EU still trusts Trump, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, replied: “We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender.”
“Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that is why Europe is standing beside Ukraine,” Kallas told reporters.
Russian strike in Ukraine kills 3 civilians
In other developments, three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine’s Emergency Services said Thursday.
Between midnight and Thursday morning, Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, Zelenskyy said on X, adding that the barrage came “precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted.”
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security.”
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian air force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
A Ukrainian missile destroyed six warplanes at an airfield in southwestern Russia, Zelenskyy said. The aircraft were used to launch powerful glide bombs, he said.
“Russia is dragging out the war, so our long-range operations will continue,” he said on social media.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight and that Russian forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.
___
Associated Press writers Samya Kullab in Kyiv, Ukraine; Lorne Cook in Brussels; and Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed.

title: A zoo's flamingo produces chicks at record-setting 60 years old
text:
A zoo's flamingo produces chicks at record-setting 60 years old
Six flamingo chicks have joined the flock at a Kentucky zoo, including two hatched by a mother who is making history.
Queen, a 60-year-old Chilean flamingo, is believed to be the oldest female flamingo to produce chicks at a zoo accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums, according to James McKinney, the Taxonomic Curator of Birds at the Louisville Zoo.
"The oldest female to produce a chick is 50 years old, so her being 10 years older by that much — and she’s produced two chicks this year — is pretty wild," McKinney said.
Flamingos can go years without nesting, making Queen’s successful breeding season even more remarkable.
“To have a female that’s 60 years old produce fertile eggs and hatch them out — and the chicks do great — that’s pretty awesome,” McKinney said.
Queen’s two chicks are only a few weeks old. They are among six new chicks visitors can see at the zoo.
Depending on the time of day, guests may also spot the young birds walking with their handlers. The supervised outings help the chicks get the exercise they need while developing.
"We have to make sure they’re getting plenty of exercise as they’re growing because they do grow really fast," McKinney said. "They’ll be full size by 70 to 80 days old."
Although the chicks will quickly reach their adult size, it can take up to two years for them to develop flamingos’ signature pink coloring. Until then, the young birds will retain their gray plumage as they grow alongside the flock.

title: California orders lenders to report on their handling of insurance payouts to LA fire survivors
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California officials on Thursday will order mortgage lenders, including banks and credit unions, to report on how they have handled insurance payouts to survivors of the 2025 Los Angeles-area fires.
The California Business and Consumer Services Agency and the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation seek to speed up the release of insurance proceeds that lenders hold before distributing them to homeowners. DFPI has received more than 160 complaints about payment delays or other issues since January 2025. The state is giving lenders two weeks to submit their reports.
“It’s unacceptable that after running through a gauntlet of paperwork to file insurance claims, some wildfire survivors still have not gotten access to the funds they need to rebuild,” said Rohit Chopra, secretary of the Business and Consumer Services Agency.
The Palisades and Eaton fires destroyed more than 16,000 homes and other structures as they tore through residential neighborhoods in and around Los Angeles. Very few homes have been rebuilt since.
In July, Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote a letter to bankers’ associations and credit unions, saying fire victims rebuilding their homes reported that lenders sometimes hold on to those payouts for weeks before releasing them. He ordered the state to collect data on lenders that take longer than 10 days to distribute insurance proceeds and don’t develop a plan to speed up those payouts.
He signed a law last year requiring banks and credit unions to pay homeowners interest on insurance payments they hold.
Newsom said the state is taking crucial action Thursday to support families and business owners as they rebuild.
“The last thing survivors need is unnecessary red tape, delays, and barriers standing between them and the relief they deserve,” he said in a statement.
More broadly, questions about who should bear the financial costs of California’s wildfires have persisted throughout Newsom’s nearly eight years as governor. He took office in 2019, months after the deadliest and most destructive fire in state history, and immediately had to grapple with who should cover the costs of fires caused by utility equipment. In his final legislative session as governor, Newsom pushed a plan that would have required home insurers to bear more of the cost. But the deal fell apart when lawmakers couldn’t agree on a solution.
DFPI Commissioner KC Mohseni said the department will take action, including potentially through fines, against banks and credit unions that unnecessarily delay insurance payouts.
“It is critical that as homeowners and families continue to rebuild and recover, lenders do not stand in their way,” he said in a statement.

title: Bear wanders into hospital, stops to eat Halloween candy
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - A bear walked into a hospital early Monday and treated itself to Halloween candy.
A black bear roamed the hallway at a hospital on Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson around 2 a.m., stopping only when it found a bucket of donated Halloween candy.
“This is like being in a tunnel with a bear,” said Sherri Warnke, who had been at the hospital helping her mother settle in after being transferred.
Warnke, who does not work at the hospital, said she was walking toward the exit through the emergency department when the bear stepped out of a side hallway ahead of her. She said the bear was about 30 feet away.
“And if I was like 15 seconds faster, we would have ran into each other,” she said.
The doors along the hallway she was in open only with a badge.
“I don’t have a badge,” Warnke said. “I can’t get through any doors. They’re all locked.”
The closest way for her to get out was a door about 60 yards behind her. So she began backing away, slowly and quietly, betting the bear had not spotted her in the dim hallway.
The bear suddenly stopped and started digging in something.
“I got a whiff of what I thought initially was trash,” Warnke said.
It was not trash. Doctors later told her the bear had found a Halloween candy donation bucket.
Soon after, an announcement over the intercom warned that a bear was in the building. Shortly after the announcement, several doctors working in the building came down the hallway to take a picture of the bear.
“They wanted pictures,” Warnke said. “But approaching a bear that’s having this dessert is not my first option.”
Warnke started taking video and pictures. In one of her videos, she said, she can be heard calling out, “Exit plan, guys, because the bear thinks you’re going to steal his food.”
Warnke said she was worried that there would be a lag between one of the doctors swiping their badge and a door unlocking.
“And that delay can be a death sentence to you if a bear is really mad at you,” she said.
The candy, however, bought everyone time.
“I was like, candy, donation, he’s going to be there for a while, he’s not going to give up that candy, that’s for sure,” Warnke said.
Staff let her out through a back way, and she did not see how the bear left the building.
When Warnke returned the next day, she said a door leading into the main part of the hospital was closed, and the staffer at the emergency department front desk told her it had been shut because of the bear. Staff said the bear left the same way it came in.
The staffer also showed her a photo of the bear standing at the same front counter where she stood. Staff joked that the bear had been checking in.
“I said, ‘Well, actually, I think he’s checking out now,’” Warnke said.
Warnke said she is not easily rattled by wildlife.
“I was born and raised in Alaska,” she said. “So I’m in the mountains all the time, and I’m a mountain runner.”
Warnke said it was not her first encounter with a bear, but she was surprised to see one in the hospital.
“And this is not a small bear,” she said. “He was a pretty big black bear.”
With hibernation approaching, the bear looked well fed already.
“And he was fat and ready for hibernation,” Warnke said. “I was like, ‘Well, did you eat something before you came for dessert?’”
Warnke told a friend the bear had simply been out trick-or-treating, “and good thing he chose the treat and not for me to do a trick.”

title: A new Medicare season begins, but some shifts will arrive in 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Open enrollment for Medicare plans begins Thursday and enrollees will face a slew of changes that go into effect in 2027.
During the enrollment period, which ends Dec. 7, people will have the opportunity to choose between traditional Medicare and privately run Medicare Advantage plans in their area, as well as prescription drug plans. Those changes go into effect on Jan. 1.
Open enrollment also comes as inflation adds pressure on seniors whose healthcare costs have risen and as midterm elections are weeks away. Voters have consistently said cost-of-living is a major concern headed into the elections.
The Medicare enrollment period also comes as the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, which translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
New changes to Medicare coming in 2027 include higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies, and new drug price negotiations.
Here are a few of the biggest changes:
Medicare Part D
The cap on annual out-of-pocket expenses for Medicare Part D drugs will increase to $2,400, up from $2,100 in 2026, and the standard deductible will increase from $615 to $700.
The temporary Part D premium subsidy will also end early.
The Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums.
It was initially implemented by former President Joe Biden’s administration in 2024 to lower patients’ Medicare Part D prescription drug costs in response to effects of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected only modest price increases for most people. CMS did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
Drug price negotiations
New Medicare-negotiated prices, part of a Biden-era law that allows the haggling for Medicare, will go into effect for 15 drugs, including weight-loss and diabetes medications Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.
Additionally, Trelegy Ellipta, Xtandi, Pomalyst, Ibrance, Ofev, Linzess, Calquence, Austedo/Austedo XR, Breo Ellipta, Tradjenta, Xifaxan, Vraylar, Janumet/Janumet XR, and Otezla will be covered by Medicare as of Jan. 1.
CMS expects the change to lower prescription drug coverage for people enrolled in Medicare by $685 million in 2027.
AARP’s Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Nancy LeaMond said in a statement that “higher healthcare costs are making it harder for older Americans to afford the care they need.”
“It’s more important than ever to shop around, compare your options, and choose the coverage that’s best for you,” she said.
Other Trump administration promises
Along with the changes, President Donald Trump in recent weeks made a series of promises to Medicare enrollees and retirees.
Last week, Trump said his administration will make one-time payments of $90 per person in October to help more than 20 million Medicare enrollees — or less than one third of enrollees — pay for their Part B premiums. It will cost about $2 billion.
Not eligible are roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, millions of other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients.
According to the CMS website, eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate this month, with most getting a direct deposit. Others will receive a paper check from the Treasury Department later in October.
Trump also announced recently that roughly 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums.

title: Crash during ICE detainment in Sanford prompts local police response
text:
Sanford police responded to the scene of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention Thursday morning after federal agents reported a car crash and unattended children.
ICE detained a man during a traffic stop near Brook and High streets around 9 a.m., Sanford police say. As agents attempted to stop the man, he reversed into one of their vehicles, according to a police account and a video shared with the Portland Press Herald.
Footage captured by a nearby resident’s bird feeder camera shows the two SUVs block the driver in, at which point he reverses into the vehicle behind him. The short clip doesn’t show the rest of the detention.
Sanford police Chief Eric Small said federal agents called dispatch after the crash, prompting a response by Sanford police. Police officers also assisted with a 1-year-old who was found in the man’s car.
Officials say no one was injured, though the 1-year-old was taken to a hospital as a precaution.
Immigration officials did not immediately respond to questions about the man’s detention.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree criticized the incident as “yet another instance of ICE’s aggressive operations putting public safety at risk,” pointing to the fatal July shooting of a Biddeford man during an attempted traffic stop.
‘PRETTY SCARY’
Federal agents told police they used two of their vehicles to block the front and back of the car that the man was driving, according to the Sanford Police Department. A neighbor who witnessed the detention, Wendy Deflaminis, said the man had just pulled out of his driveway when the two ICE vehicles drove up from either side and cornered his vehicle.
The man then reversed, crashing into one of the federal vehicles. Deflaminis said it looked as though the man was trying to navigate around the vehicles until he backed into the one behind him. Small said there was no major damage and that the driver was moving at a “very low speed.”
After the crash, the agents told the driver to stop and put his hands up, and he appeared to comply, Deflaminis said. Federal agents then escorted him into a car.
Once the man had been detained, agents appeared to notice that a 1-year-old was sitting in a car seat in the rear of the vehicle, Deflaminis said. She recalled asking whether someone should call an ambulance to ensure the baby was safe, to which the agents responded that they had already called for one.
“It was pretty scary,” Deflaminis said.
Sanford police say the baby was not properly restrained in a car seat and was taken to MaineHealth Maine Medical Center Sanford out of “an abundance of caution.” Small and Assistant Fire Chief Brian Watkins both said no one was injured.
Small said the police department did not assist with the federal detention and that he did not know the man’s name. Deflaminis did not know the man’s name either but said he lived nearby.
Emergency personnel also evaluated the driver, who is the baby’s father, while he was handcuffed in the back of a federal vehicle, Small said. The man “was under a lot of stress,” Small said, and reportedly told federal agents that he had two more children unattended at his nearby home.
Child Protective Services and the Maine Department of Health and Human Services were contacted to ensure the welfare of the other two children, who are 9 and 2 years old, according to a news release from the Sanford Police Department. Small said those children are now with a family friend who was able to take them in via an arrangement with CPS.
“(The ICE agents) were very forthcoming,” Small said. “They wanted what was best for the children as well.”
Small said the man’s vehicle was towed from the scene.
PINGREE CALLS FOR VIDEO RELEASE
Officials with ICE, U.S. Border Patrol and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond Thursday to requests for more information about the incident.
In a written statement, Pingree, D-1st District, called on the federal agencies to promptly release any footage of the incident, including from body-worn and dashboard cameras.
Referencing the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the congresswoman said that “it is entirely understandable that a father confronted by ICE — with his one-year-old in the car and two more children at home — would be terrified when federal agents box in his car.”
Durán Guerrero, 25, was shot and killed by an ICE agent on the morning of July 13 while driving in a Biddeford neighborhood; officials have said he was not the intended target of ICE’s operation.
A spokesperson for U.S. Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said the senator has been “very clear” about his opposition to how ICE is operating under the Trump administration.
Spokespeople for Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Rep. Jared Golden, D-2nd District, did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this report.

title: Maine Black Bears react to Quinnipiac’s Alex Kostov’s high hit on Chris Romaine on Saturday
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The Maine men’s hockey team earned a split over the weekend with No. 6 Quinnipiac at Alfond Arena.
An early Bobcats major charging penalty and game misconduct caused a scary situation on Saturday.
Alex Kostov left his feet to deliver a high hit on Chris Romaine along the boards behind the Black Bears’ net in the first period.
Romaine was motionless on the ice before slowly being helped by his teammates to the Maine locker room.
Quinnipiac is a member of the ECAC, and the conference keeps disciplinary actions, like suspensions, confidential.
“Any time that happens to anyone, on your team or even on the other team, it’s definitely a scary incident. Those hits definitely should not be in a game,” said Owen Fowler, graduate forward.
“It’s always scary when you see someone just not move there for a little bit. But, he was moving there shortly after, so when you’re on the bench, at least you know he’s moving around. He’s gotten a little bit better every day, it seems like,” said Ben Barr, head coach.
Romaine is day-to-day to return.

title: Investigation underway after fake hostage situation at jewelry store
text:
Investigation underway after hackers fake hostage situation at jewelry store
Police shut down a major roadway in Massachusetts Sunday evening after responding to a reported hostage situation, which was later determined to be a hoax at King Jewelers in Cohasset, Massachusetts.
Cellphone video shared with Hearst sister station WCVB showed officers shutting down the busy roadway and focusing on the jewelry store.
“There’s 10 cruisers in front; they’re waiting for somebody,” a person said in the video.
Cohasset police confirmed that a man called the regional dispatch center, claiming he was barricaded inside King Jewelers and holding two hostages at gunpoint with a pistol and rifle.
“The caller stated he was armed with both a pistol and a rifle and demanded money in exchange for the hostages’ safe release,” police said.
Tactical officers from five agencies surrounded the building and eventually made their way inside, finding no hostages. Police determined the call was an elaborate hoax.
Video below: Wild video shows moment man climbs through Taco Bell drive-thru window
Authorities said the caller hacked into the business’s video surveillance system, which allowed him to accurately describe the inside and outside of the store to dispatchers.
Police are now investigating who made the fake call and how they accessed King Jewelers’ surveillance system.
Cohasset police Chief William Quigley commended the dispatchers for their response to the situation.
“Dispatchers kept the caller on the phone for an extended period, remained calm and professional, and gathered a tremendous amount of information that will be valuable to our detectives as they work to identify the person responsible,” Quigley said.
Quigley reminded everyone that fake calls like this are far from harmless, saying they put officers at risk and take them away from real emergencies.

title: Wrong to remove George Mitchell’s name without evidence or proof
text:
Douglas Rooks is the author of “Statesman: George Mitchell and the Art of the Possible” (Down East Books, 2016.) He welcomes comment at [email protected].
The University of Maine System Board of Trustees voted 9-5 on Sept. 28 to remove former Sen. George Mitchell’s name from university programs and scholarships — the latest in a series of such moves following release of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
The removal of Mitchell’s name from scholarships and institutes began back in February in Ireland, which had recognized Mitchell’s central role in the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, a deal that has brought lasting peace to Northern Ireland.
They never knew Mitchell as well as we do here in Maine.
One of the dissenting UMS trustees, Donna Loring, explained her position in a Bangor Daily News op-ed, writing, “My vote was not a declaration that every allegation concerning Mitchell is false. I do not know that. But neither has there been a finding that he committed wrongdoing. The university’s own task force acknowledged that fact.”
Loring’s point is inarguable. Before we remove names, portraits and statues from the public square, there must be an effort to establish the facts, and discern the truth as far as it can be known. Judging from its report, the task force did not attempt this, instead citing “serious allegations” and potential “reputational harm” to the university as deciding factors.
“I worry about a standard in which reputational harm can outweigh the absence of a finding of wrongdoing,” Loring wrote. We should all be worried.
Although the chaotic release of the Epstein files in 2025 by order of Congress was widely assumed to be in the public interest, there are serious doubts. Unedited investigative files and reports — such as those just inadvertently released by the Maine Attorney General’s Office — can be profoundly and unfairly damaging to lives and reputations. If such releases became routine, there would be few reputations left worth having.
Suspicions and allegations that would not normally be public are spread worldwide, with instantaneous reactions and conclusions that then drive policymakers to treat accusations, however serious, as facts, and suspicions as warranted.
News accounts focused on 300 “mentions” of Mitchell’s name among 2.5 million pages of documents; Donald Trump’s name appears more than 30,000 times. By itself, these numbers mean nothing. To this day, no one has been charged with any criminal offenses (except Epstein and his enabler, Ghislaine Maxwell).
If we use suspicion and allegation as the standard, we’re on a slippery slope. It’s a short distance from here to the 1950s McCarthyite “Red Scare,” where guilt by association among “fellow travelers” ruined lives, careers and reputations.
At least the UMS trustees made some attempt to balance the accusations against Mitchell’s lifetime of service. In his hometown, Waterville’s school board swiftly voted 5-2 to remove his name from an elementary school after a handful of complaints. The Legislature’s presiding officers, with no process at all, removed Mitchell’s portrait from the State House, where it had been installed to bipartisan acclaim in 2014.
There are public places in Maine and recognitions in Washington to which Mitchell’s name is still attached. This is far from unanimous.
We should also balance the accusations with an accounting of Mitchell’s achievements. Along with his unique contributions to world peace — among dozens of wars and rebellions in our times, there is hardly another example like it — Mitchell represented Maine with distinction in the U.S. Senate for 15 years. As majority leader, he shepherded dozens of important bills to passage — landmarks in protecting the environment, creating affordable housing and providing better lives for persons with disabilities. Surely this should count.
I am of course not privy to the UMS trustees’ deliberations. As Mitchell’s biographer, however, I can offer testimony from years of research, interviews and discussions involving his family, his staff, political supporters and opponents, those who knew him best in his personal and public life.
In all that time, I never heard of any lapses in personal integrity lending credence to the anonymous, unsourced Epstein allegations. Rather the reverse — in campaigning, in fundraising, in the sometime regrettable business of politics, Mitchell was a stickler for following the rules.
It may be impossible ever to lay to rest the suspicions created by the Epstein files. As so often in the digital age, we are drowning in data of variable quality, with understanding nowhere to be seen.
In the absence of proof, I suggest no further “de-namings” of Mitchell, with its implied public censure, until some reliable standards can be established. Ultimately, history will assess his virtues and flaws, like those of any other human being. The trustees’ majority judgment should not be the last word.

title: Can Maine use natural methods to stop shoreline erosion?
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND — On a mild afternoon, sailboats glided across Casco Bay while Southern Maine Community College students sat at picnic tables studying, knitting and talking politics. Just steps away, however, this beloved stretch of coastline is crumbling.
Back-to-back winter storms battered the Willard Beach area three years ago, eating away at fragile bluffs beneath a campus science building and city pump house and closing a popular shoreline walking path.
Now city, regional and state officials are coming together to try to protect the shoreline and infrastructure, using natural methods when they can and hoping to forestall rising seas and worsening storms for as long as they can.
The proposal to protect this small stretch of shoreline, which would involve the combination of riprap, vegetation and a relocated walking path, is one of three that the Greater Portland Council of Governments is using federal grants to help draft.
The plans for South Portland, Mitchell Field in Harpswell and the Yarmouth wastewater treatment plant are far from complete. Variations abound. Nothing is permitted. Nobody knows who might foot the bill.
“It’s clear that something has to be done,” said Sara Mills-Knapp, the sustainability director at Greater Portland Council of Governments and the leader of a nature-based shoreline erosion workshop at Willard Beach on Wednesday.
The Willard Beach workshop serves as a crucial test case for how vulnerable communities can adapt, if not turn back, rising waters without smothering their shorelines under a rigid granite seawall. Instead of concrete, think plants, coir logs and buried trees to rebuild the dune system.
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection now favors such methods during permitting, said Nathan Robbins, the department’s climate change specialist. The state is publishing a new reference guide to help promote nature-based erosion control this week, Robbins said.
Maine sea levels have been rising at a rate of about a half-foot a century. The pace has sped up as the world burns more fossil fuels, producing heat-trapping emissions that warm both air and sea.
Maine sea levels are projected to rise between 1.1 and 3.2 feet by 2050 and 3 and 9.3 feet by 2100, depending on how successful and quick we are at curbing global emissions rates, according to the scientists who advise the Maine Climate Council.
The $800,000 to $1 million Willard Beach proposal would give engineers room to replace the steep, failing bank with a gentler sloped bluff. Unlike hard seawalls that reflect wave energy downward and scoop out beach sand, the sloped bluff dissipates waves.
Heavy vegetative riprap — stone embedded with deep-rooted native plants — would bind the slope, paired with a newly engineered sand dune at the base. As much as they wanted to avoid stone, the consultants agreed Willard Beach requires a mixed approach.
“Plants alone just won’t cut it,” said Lisa Vickers, senior coastal specialist at GEI Consultants.
The proposal, which is about 30% complete, would require moving the walking path a couple hundred feet inland, behind the science building. But that extra space means it will not encroach upon the sandy beach below, a favorite among sunbathers and dog walkers.
Nature-based methods have sparked some tension. Hard seawalls offer immediate structural defense, while living shorelines require two to three growing seasons for native roots to bind sands. Marine contractors are used to dumping heavy granite boulders, not installing soil lifts.
And they could fail with the next winter storm, warned Pete Slovinsky, a marine geologist with the Maine Geological Survey. But so could traditional seawalls and even jettys, even with a high price tag and the harder-to-win permits required to build them, he said.
At the workshop Wednesday, Slovinsky told a crowd of about 30 people that ranged from local residents to engineers working on other erosion control projects that the proposed bluff project would help protect the city pump house for now, but the city should plan to eventually move it.
“The one thing I can guarantee you is that the sea will keep rising,” Slovinsky said. He pointed at the pump house behind him, which sits a couple dozen feet back from the 22-foot bluff. “That’s going to fail. Maybe not today, or next year, but sooner than you think.”
For state leaders, however, these pilot designs mark an essential turning point.
“Rocks don’t have roots,” Robbins said. “Plants have roots, deep roots that can help stabilize from the top of the bluff to the dunes to the beach. And rocks are expensive and require maintenance. Over time, plants will take over and do a lot of our work for us.”

title: Man wanted in South Portland thefts arrested after reports of person walking in traffic
text:
Man wanted in South Portland thefts arrested after reports of person walking in traffic
Authorities say Joshua Maloney, 30, was identified as a person of interest in two theft incidents
Man wanted in South Portland thefts arrested after reports of person walking in traffic
Authorities say Joshua Maloney, 30, was identified as a person of interest in two theft incidents
A man suspected in two felony thefts at a South Portland sporting goods store was arrested after police received reports of someone walking in traffic Wednesday evening.
South Portland police say officers received multiple calls around 6 p.m. about a man walking in and out of traffic near 555 Maine Mall Road. Callers reported the man was wearing all black and appeared intoxicated.
Officers who responded to the scene identified the man as 30-year-old Joshua Maloney.
Police say officers recognized Maloney as a suspect in two felony theft-related incidents at Dick's Sporting Goods.
According to police, Maloney was out on bail for unrelated charges involving possession of cocaine, possession of fentanyl and violation of conditions of release.
Officers say Maloney was found with a liquid substance that tested positive for a fentanyl compound or methamphetamine.
Maloney was taken to Cumberland County Jail, where he faces two felony theft counts, possession of scheduled drugs and violation of conditions of release.

title: Mt. Blue field hockey bests Messalonskee in double overtime
text:
OAKLAND — The Mt. Blue field hockey team is finding its stride with the playoff quickly approaching.
The Cougars earned the fifth straight win Thursday, beating Messalonskee 2-1 in double overtime. With the win, Mt. Blue (8-5) overtakes the Eagles for fourth place in the Class A North Heal point standings.
Reese Nye scored the first goal for the Cougars, and the game-winner was an own-goal after a scramble in front of the cage with 6:34 left in the second overtime.
“We knew we had to play strong,” said Nye, a senior. “The way we practice really translates to how we play on the field. The way we push ourselves and prepare (is key). And our pregame mentality has been really good.”
Senior Addie Hafford scored for Messalonskee (6-7), which is now fifth in A North.
How did they get there?
Pure grit. The Cougars put constant pressure on the Eagles, but goalie Baylee Dillon, who finished with 12 saves, and Messalonskee were able to knock away every attack.
Nye gave Mt. Blue a 1-0 lead with 6:05 left in the first quarter. Hafford tied it just two minutes later.
“We just pushed each other and kept each other going,” Nye said. “We just keep telling each other to keep our heads in the game.”
From there, it was a midfield battle for the remaining three quarters, and then some, before the Cougars prevailed.
What does it mean?
Mt. Blue continued its winning streak and continues to climb up the A North standings. The Cougars trail No. 1 Skowhegan (12-1), No. 2 Mt. Ararat (12-0), and No. 3 Camden Hills (10-2).
“It’s not where you start, it’s where you finish,” said Mt. Blue coach Julie Lajoie of her team’s current streak.
The Cougars wrap up the regular season at Oxford Hills (3-9-1) on Monday.
Messalonskee is 1-2 in its last three games and remains in the middle of the A North playoff mix. The Eagles finish at Skowhegan on Friday.
Unsung hero
Mt. Blue senior goalie Gwen Lesperance had four saves, including a key stop on a breakaway opportunity in the first overtime.
“That’s a very hard thing to do, to get a save in overtime, point blank (on a breakaway),” Lajoie said.
Statistical leaders
• Mt. Blue: Reese Nye (1 goal), Gwen Lesperance (4 saves)
• Messalonskee: Addie Hafford (1 goal), Baylee Dillon (12 saves)

title: Car registered to man accused of planning mass shooting was at Hindu temple he targeted, police say
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Illinois authorities believe a 19-year-old man charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago entered the building’s parking lot on Sunday, hours before police arrested him near his home after receiving a tip about the alleged attack plan.
Authorities announced Wednesday that they had arrested Alexandros Paporakis and provided the additional detail about his suspected movement during a news conference Thursday. The leaders of Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in a statement said a security threat had “targeted our Temple” and announced an increased security presence.
Palatine Police Chief William Nord said a red Acura RDX registered to Paporakis entered a temple parking lot on Sunday around 12:25 p.m. and left less than 15 minutes later. He was seen alone inside the car around 2 p.m. near his home in another suburb.
Paporakis faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle. Prosecutors have said his co-workers at a Taco Bell location called 911 after Paporakis told them he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” and said Sunday would be the “special day.”
Temple adds security after threat
Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, around 40 miles west of downtown Chicago, said leaders were in contact with police.
“Please know that the safety of our devotees, employees and volunteers is our highest priority, and we have implemented additional security measures effective immediately, including increased armed security presence at the Temple,” a statement said.
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois’ 8th congressional district, said he was at the Hindu temple on Sunday.
“I visited not knowing that there was an attacker lying in wait with a sinister motive to commit a mass shooting, and only because his AR-15 weapon jammed was he not able to commit a massacre that day,” Krishnamoorthi told The Associated Press on Thursday.
Krishnamoorthi said he had increased his security in response to the alleged planned attack. He called on the FBI to “investigate and prosecute this particular matter as a hate crime,” and the Trump administration to release federal nonprofit security grants to bolster security at religious institutions.
“People are really shaken up,” he added.
Court records detail the accused attacker’s words
Paporakis told a coworker on Sunday afternoon that his gun jammed and he left quickly, but promised to “retry,” according to prosecutors. He sent the coworker a video showing an AR-style rifle and a photo of himself wearing a tactical vest, they added.
Paporakis also sent the coworker an eight-page document in which he used racial slurs to describe non-white people and outlined a plot to kill as many of them as possible, according to prosecutors. He also described himself as a white supremacist and a neo Nazi who fantasized about mass murder.
Police arrested Paporakis later that day near his home in Palatine, which is located about 40 miles (64.37 kilometers) northeast of the temple. Detectives who searched his home found an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines and “hundreds of rounds” of ammunition, a gas canister labeled with a slur referring to South Asians, a tactical vest and a patch depicting Nazi symbolism, authorities say.
Paporakis’ mother was questioned, but she is not cooperating with the investigation, police said on Thursday.
At a Wednesday court appearance, a judge ordered Paporakis to remain in detention. His next court hearing is scheduled for Oct. 30.
“This case is in the earliest stage of what will likely be a lengthy process,” the office of the Cook County Public Defender, which is representing Paporakis, said in a statement emailed to the AP. “We would remind the public that statements made by police and prosecutors are only allegations and that cases can change significantly as they continue to be investigated.”
The targeting of the Hindu temple is another example of heightened threats in the last few years against South Asians in the U.S., according to Stop AAPI Hate, the national reporting center for anti-Asian hate incidents. Online slurs and threats have risen significantly, co-founder Manjusha Kulkarni said in a statement.
“We are grateful this violent plot was thwarted and that no one was hurt -– but it doesn’t erase the fear Hindu, Indian, and South Asian people feel after years of escalating hate,” Kulkarni said. “Violence against South Asian people is not inevitable. It is fueled when leaders stoke fear of immigrants and people of color for political gain.”
She attributed some of the anti-South Asian sentiment to the Trump administration’s rhetoric around Indian immigrants who hold work visas. She also pointed to a Texas Republican last month posting a social media video of South Asian students cheering at a University of Texas football game and referring to them as “foreigners.”
The temple, like other Hindu temples and households around the country, has been celebrating Navratri, a Hindu festival that lasts nine days. It “should be a time for celebration and unity, not terror and hate,” Kulkarni said.
___
Associated Press writer Terry Tang in Phoenix contributed to this report.
___
Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Nurse’s office latest, and ‘counter(ing) negative’ with positive
text:
Wiscasset Middle High School was closer Oct. 13 to getting its next nurse, after Sommer Maybee's arrest on an OUI charge last month and her subsequent resignation.
Two candidates were set to be interviewed for the job, WMHS Principal Chris Hennessey told the school committee.
In the meeting and in his written leadership update, Hennessey described the challenge from what the update called "our nurse situation."
Hennessey said Wiscasset Elementary School Nurse Nicole Appleton has been spending significant time at WMHS and several WMHS staff received training in first aid basics and in giving medication. He thanked Appleton, Brandon Rogers, Stephanie French, Beth Bluteau, Sandy Aloisio, Mindy Turner, Ashley Major, Xantha Morse, Alyson Graham, Molly Carlson, Tyler Hilchey and Patti Sims for the nurse's office being covered.
On a question from Vice Chair John Merry, Hennessey said, "We've been covering (the office). I'm not going to tell you though that it's been ideal. It's been a challenge ... I'm usually anchored (near) the nurse's office anyway (and) Sandy Aloisio has just been incredibly invaluable, and probably the biggest MVP in stepping up to fill that void." He added, Appleton's presence has been "very professional (and) calming. She's been wonderful."
Said Hennessey, "Yeah, we're getting it done. Not easy, though."
Former WES nurse Alaechia Ellis has been covering at WES as a substitute two days a week so that Appleton can go to WMHS, Superintendent of Schools Dr. Kim Andersson said.
And in public comment, former school committee member Brycson Grover said "recent events ... with one of the employees ... has yet again brought negative attention, a black cloud over (the) Wiscasset district, which is very unfortunate." When he then recalled concerns raised last year about students spending time in the nurse's office, Chair Tracey Whitney said, "I need you to not discuss a specific staff member."
"I'm saying nurse's office," Grover said. When Whitney let him resume, he instead said "a certain office, that I believe the board all knows what I'm talking about. Concerns were raised about students being in there when they should not have been," and the superintendent failed to handle it, Grover said. And the committee in June did not order an independent investigation of last school year's incident "that involved that certain employee ... Any information is good information. And now fast forward, here we are again, with the same individual."
Post-meeting, Andersson had no comment on Grover's comments. In June, Grover and fellow member at the time Jonathan Barnes had supported the outside probe and Whitney, Doug Merrill and Christopher Hart abstained. In that June meeting, the committee nodded 5-0 Andersson's proposal for a "two schools beneath one roof" committee to examine issues with shared spaces and times when middle and high schoolers are together.
Last May, then-senior D'Antae Dawkins was charged with aggravated assault on a middle schooler during a gym class officials have said Maybee was covering. Sept. 22, a half hour after she left school, Maybee was arrested under the last name of Harding in the Wiscasset Marketplace plaza parking lot on a Class D OUI charge; she made bail, was placed on paid administrative leave and an internal investigation began.
In the Oct. 13 meeting, the committee voted to "receive" Maybee's resignation. The committee typically votes to "accept" a resignation, usually accepting it "with regret." Asked Oct. 14 about the committee's wording the night before, Andersson said: "Receive and accept have the same meaning in this case."
Also Oct. 13, Andersson spoke of the department's continuing effort to work to "get the good word out on all of the amazing things that are happening in our schools every single day." Executive Assistant/Data Specialist Cynthia Young has been “crushing it” on Facebook, Andersson said. Young has been putting out press releases on activities such an alumnus visiting Wiscasset Elementary School to share with students his work as a marine biologist; and a “Crazy Hair Day” students earned by being safe, responsible and respectful.
Andersson said it is believed to take "10 positive articles to counter one negative (one) ... The students and staff are phenomenal, we’re off to a great start this year, and we just want to keep that positive momentum going.”
And she urged committee members to be spreading the word that the town vote on the third, 2026-27 budget offer is Nov. 3. “We can’t tell people how to vote, but we can tell them to vote, and we can tell them that frequently,” she said.
She recapped that costs are down 1% from 2025-26 and the local ask is down 2.5%.
“You guys have worked really hard. We’ve had a lot of meetings. And it’s time to start the fiscal year ’28 budget (work), so if you could tell all your friends frequently to make sure they vote Nov. 3, if they haven’t voted already, absentee.”
Whitney reminded residents the committee's recorded budget sessions are all on the school department's YouTube channel. "Please feel free to go back and see this path that we have taken because it has been a long and winding road ... We have been doing some work here and I ask you all to see where we've come (from) and where we are now."
In other business, no teachers have applied yet for projects through "gifted and talented" funding, Andersson said. Hennessey said he and others have been bugging students to eat breakfast and lunch. "It is incredible how few kids want to eat. We're all really trying to push to make sure that they do that." And he said the new, separate student handbooks for the middle and high schools are almost ready.
The committee nodded hiring James Andretta, high school girls soccer coach; Phil Di Vice, middle school boys soccer coach; Alicia West, volleyball coach; Billy Pinkham, JV basketball coach; Dana Lawrence, girls varsity basketball; Jamey Roy, boys varsity basketball; Nori Lund, high school swim; Jay Bailey, high school baseball; Kelly Johnson, WES educational technician; and, pending documentation, Hann Paulsen and Nathaniel Gapski as educational technicians.
Whitney said she is delighted to have been hearing "wonderful things about the start of the new school year ... It's nice to know that things are being handled beautifully and I really appreciate that. So thank you," she said in closing oral remarks in her first "Notes from the Chair," a feature the committee has added to its regular meetings.

title: North Korea holds first underwater-launched missile tests in nearly 3 years
text:
North Korea holds first underwater-launched missile tests in nearly 3 years
North Korea performed its first underwater-launched missile tests in nearly three years on Wednesday, likely from an as-yet-deployed submarine that it says is designed to launch nuclear weapons.
Related video: Trump reduces military training with South Korea, citing "great respect" from North Korea's Kim Jong Un, August 2026
The high-profile tests come as North Korea is dialing up weapons demonstrations in an apparent bid to pressure the United States to offer greater concessions if it wants a resumption of diplomacy.
The official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday the military tested two types of strategic cruise missiles in the country’s eastern waters. It said the tests were aimed at assessing the readiness of North Korea’s underwater combat systems and demonstrating the reliability of its nuclear deterrent.
KCNA didn't say what launch platform was used. But the agency's photos of the launch suggested the country mobilized the “Hero Kim Kun Ok” submarine that was unveiled in 2023 with great fanfare but drew outside skepticism about its claimed capabilities.
If confirmed, Wednesday's missile launches were the first public weapons tests from that submarine, which implies North Korea began testing weapons systems for the vessel before its deployment in what would be a major threat to South Korea and the U.S., experts say.
Weapons testing likely signals impending submarine deployment
North Korea for years has been developing various missiles designed to be fired from underwater, which was a worrying development for its rivals because such launches would be difficult to detect in advance.
Before Wednesday's tests, all North Korean underwater launches were made from a 2,000-ton-class submarine with a single launch tube. Many experts call it a test platform rather than an operational submarine in active service.
In September 2023, North Korea launched the “Hero Kim Kun Ok,” saying the submarine was capable of launching tactical nuclear weapons from underwater. State media photos showed the submarine has at least 10 missile launch tubes in addition to its torpedo tubes.
At the time, many foreign experts were skeptical the submarine would work as North Korea described, saying it was likely a modification of an existing, aging diesel-fueled submarine.
A lack of known weapons tests from the submarine in the past three years signaled it had some technical issues including an ability to right itself. But Wednesday's tests indicated North Korea had resolved those issues and started testing the weapons to be carried by the submarine, according to analyst Shin Jong-woo at South Korea’s Defense and Security Forum.
North Korea will likely also test ballistic missiles from the submarine before it is deployed by the navy, Shin said.
The submarine's deployment “would pose a significant threat” to South Korea and the U.S. because underwater-launched missiles are “formidable weapons that we don't know when and where they would be fired,” said Moon Keun-sik, a submarine expert who teaches at Seoul’s Hanyang University.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches and concluded the missiles were launched from a submarine, with one fired from a vertical launch tube and the other from a torpedo tube. The South’s military didn’t immediately specify the North Korean submarine that it believed was involved.
North Korean leader wants to pressure Trump
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un recently turned his focus to strengthening the navy after a decade of expanding the country’s ballistic missile program. In March 2025, North Korea unveiled its first nuclear-powered submarine under construction, but it’s unclear when the construction would be completed.
Wednesday's launches were the first underwater testing activities since January 2024. They extended a recent run in weapons demonstrations, including tests of various hypersonic missile systems on Sept. 20 and Oct. 3 that the North said were aimed at advancing its arsenal of weapons designed to overwhelm missile defenses in South Korea and Japan.
The tests came after North Korea in August rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump’s apparent effort to revive diplomacy with Kim by scaling back a military drill with South Korea. North Korea said shortening the duration of the drill won't change its hostile nature.
North Korea has previously said it could return to diplomacy if the U.S. abandons its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drops demands for the North’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.
North Korea's latest submarine-launched tests were part its efforts to gain leverage in potential negotiations with the U.S., Moon said.
“North Korea would want to say it would never give up its nukes,” Moon said. “It's sending a message to the U.S. saying that ‘We’ve perfected land-abased nuclear weapons and are deploying nuclear weapons to the maritime domain so that you shouldn't demand our denuclearization any longer.'”

title: Kitten guided out of drain pipe by custom equipment
text:
Custom remote-controlled crawler used to get stuck kitten out of drain pipe
A kitten found in a drain pipe in Utah was safely rescued, thanks to a custom piece of equipment.
West Valley City Government shared a video on Facebook showing a remote-controlled crawler helping guide a small kitten out of a drain pipe on Oct. 12.
Watch the rescue in the video player above
"Our Storm Water Crew in the Public Works Department got a little surprise call on Monday—a kitten in a drain pipe! They used a pole camera to locate the cat and tried to coax it out, but it wouldn’t budge," the post said.
Officials then used R2D2, a custom remote-controlled crawler with a live camera and lights, to help.
"R2D2 is usually used to inspect pipes, but now it can add 'kitten rescuer' to its list of functions," West Valley City Government continued. "R2D2 gently nudged the kitten out of the pipe and into the arms of one of the crew."
The kitten did not appear to be injured.

title: Amber B. Bowie (1992-2026)
Closing up camp for the season
text:
The kids have all gone back to school, the nights are getting colder and it’s time to close up camp in Maine. Before packing the car for that last trip home, a little work now can help prevent frozen pipes, unwanted guests and unpleasant surprises come spring. Here are five things to check before turning the key for the season.
ANTIFREEZE FRAME OF MIND
Keeping pipes and fixtures from freezing is the number one winter task at hand for any homeowner. Be sure to completely drain the water and plumbing system before shutting off the water. This includes drainpipes, toilet tanks and faucets. Be sure to leave faucets open and remove any plugs from tubs and sinks after draining. Unplug the refrigerator and empty the ice maker. The jury is out on adding antifreeze to your pipes: it’s a known toxic material that’s harmful to surface water and the ground. If everything is drained properly, you should be okay, but if you’re undecided, low-toxicity antifreeze is the better choice.
EXPERT TIP: Pack up liquid cleaning supplies to avoid an explosive mess in the spring.
PLAYING CAT AND MOUSE
It only takes a hole the size of a dime for your summer escape to become a winter squat for mice, bats, rodents, birds and a whole menagerie of animals looking to escape the elements. Inspect for loose clapboard, space around pipes, open chimney flues and tunneling near the foundation. Then, do an extra wipe and sweep of all cabinets, cupboards and underneath appliances for crumbs or even a kibble of pet food. Protect mattresses, cushions, linens and bedding with plastic, and include good, old-fashioned mothballs or cedar planks for woolens.
EXPERT TIP: Sometimes, you simply need a professional, and pests are often one of those times. A reputable pest control service, or professional property management company can make opening day in the spring even more pleasurable.
SAFETY AND SECURITY
It isn’t just the woodland or seaside critters to be wary of. No matter how modest or remote your summer dwelling may be, chances are that if you love it, an uninvited human might too. Double-check window latches and all locks on doors, sheds and recreational items. Don’t leave anything over the season that you couldn’t bear to lose.
EXPERT TIP: Research remote monitoring security systems that can withstand the elements. Check with the local police or fire departments for localized recommendations, but a trail camera or security doorbell is a common solution.
KEEP A ROOF OVER YOUR HEAD
If you’re comfortable climbing a ladder and have a spotter, clear the roof of all leaves and debris. Check for possible water entry points around piping, shingles and wires. What about cracks in caulking, chimney flashing and gaskets? If need be, clear out gutters to ensure there’s no clogging. If you’re afraid of heights or don’t have experience on the roof, hire a professional. Swallowing your pride is much less painful than a broken leg.
EXPERT TIP: Just like your year-round home, trimming back tree branches will reduce roof pileups, water damage and critter access.
DON’T FORGET TO TURN OFF THE STOVE
It seems like common sense, but sometimes we forget the most basic things. After you unplug all appliances, be sure to call the gas and electric companies to shut off the flow and/or turn off any propane lines.
EXPERT TIP: Now is the time to schedule a radon test. Levels rise in the colder weather so you can make plans to mitigate in the spring.

title: Las Vegas officials release the ID of a man whose body was found in a barrel in Lake Mead
text:
Las Vegas officials release the ID of a man whose body was found in a barrel in Lake Mead
Las Vegas officials identified a homicide victim Thursday whose remains were found in a rusted barrel on a shore of Lake Mead after the lake’s level was depleted amid drought.
Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse identified the victim as Edward Lelburian Jackson, who was from Arkansas and in his mid-to-late 50s when he died.
The discovery by boaters in 2022 sparked memories of the city’s mob era, which ended in the mid-1980s. Organized crime helped build up the city, and a body stuffed in a barrel was known to signify a mob killing.
But while Jackson had a brief criminal history in the early 1980s in Salt Lake City, Utah, which included one charge of aggravated arson and conspiracy of fraud, investigators said Thursday they do not have information to support theories that the man's death was mob-related.
Jackson's family told investigators that he liked to travel, but it is unclear why he was in Las Vegas.
Authorities had already said the man was shot, and they estimate he was killed between the mid-1970s and early 1980s, based on the type of shoes found with him.
The man had been wearing a button-down short-sleeve shirt, light blue jeans, a silver wristwatch, and blue-and-white tennis shoes.
The Mob Museum in Las Vegas had suggested the victim could be connected to the mob. Speculating it could be George “Jay” Vandermark, a gambling machine cheater trusted by the mob to oversee slot machine operations at the Stardust casino; William Crespo, a drug-runner who became a federal informant; or Johnny Pappas, who owned a boat at Lake Mead and worked in the casino industry.
All three disappeared, and their bodies were never found.
Lake Mead is at a historic low due to years of overuse, longstanding drought and increasing temperatures. The water level of the 90-year-old reservoir has dropped, exposing areas that were previously underwater. Historians predict more bodies could be found.
Several other sets of remains were found at Lake Mead in 2022. That May, another set of skeletal remains was discovered, and they were identified as a drowning victim from 2002. Skeletal remains found in August were identified as a 52-year-old Las Vegas resident who disappeared in 1998. A set of remains found in October 2022 were determined to be an accidental drowning from 1974, according to Clark County.
In August 2026, more human remains were discovered.
Lake Mead and the upstream Lake Powell are the largest human-made reservoirs in the U.S., part of a system that provides Colorado River water to more than 40 million people, tribes, agriculture and industry in Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and across the southern border in Mexico.
In 2022, the dropping lake level exposed Las Vegas’ uppermost drinking water intake, forcing the regional water authority to switch to a deep-lake intake it completed in 2020 to keep serving the city’s 2.4 million residents and visitors, casinos and suburbs. Las Vegas attracts around 40 million tourists per year.

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate for a final time
text:
The fourth and final debate between Troy Jackson and Susan Collins is here.
After a whirlwind two weeks in which the candidates repeatedly faced questions from Maine journalists, they will meet for a final time onstage Thursday in Bangor.
Tonight’s debate is hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and NEWSCENTER Maine.
As always, we’ll be following along live. The event starts at 7 p.m., and you can watch a livestream below.
And that’s a wrap!
Thanks so much for following along with us, not just for this debate, but for all the debates!
We’ll see you next time.
A Maine Mount Rushmore?
The candidates ended by answering a question about who should be on a Maine-themed Mount Rushmore, if such a thing were to exist.
Collins took a beat before answering Joshua Chamberlain, who fought for the Union in the Civil War. Jackson said Frances Perkins, the former Labor Secretary, and the first woman to hold a Cabinet position.
Collins said she is a strong supporter of Ukraine and that she “adamantly opposed” the Russian invasion of the country. She noted that she signed a letter criticizing Trump’s recent move to buy some oil from Russia.
Jackson said he’s not in favor of increasing the age limit to buy the weapons, but said he’s not opposed to banning them. He noted he would not advocate for taking away the weapons from people who already have them.
“We are resilient and strong. I’ve seen the executive branch over the years, regardless of whether it was Democratic president or a Republican president, try to get more and more power,” Collins said.
Jackson seems to be settling in
If he was stilted in previous debates, Jackson seems to be finding more a comedic stride tonight. He’s slipped in a number of these one-liner jabs such as his jab about the Supreme Court, and they’re playing well in the room.
“What we want is a Supreme Court that is insulated from politics,” Collins said.
Jackson shot back with a joke.
“We have the best court that money can buy,” Jackson said.
Jackson criticized Collins for not doing enough for everyday Mainers.
Jackson countered that as senator, Collins has presided in a huge spike in gas prices.
Jackson was asked why he prefers Customs and Border Protection to take over ICE’s responsibilities given that CBP officers fatally shot a Minnesota man earlier this year.
Jackson said she wouldn’t give immigration officers a “blank check” like Collins did.
This is an emerging theme of the night: Jackson expresses a number of things he wouldn’t do, but doesn’t express clearly what he would do.
A note on the audience
The audience is getting rowdy. People were laughing and “oohing” and “ahhing” at several of the pithier lines in Jackson’s answer to Collins’ question about his campaign finance filing
She also reiterated Iran should not be allowed to make a nuclear weapon.
When pressed on the beginning of the war, Collins said Congress should have been consulted on the war.
“Under the War Powers Act, the president, as commander-in-chief, for the first 60 days, has very broad authority to do whatever he wants, essentially, when it comes to a military conflict,” Collins said. “After 60 days, that’s when I voted every single time with the Democrats to bring the conflict to a halt.”
She pivoted to talking about how heating assistance has been funded at record levels, and noted that she supports social safety net programs.
Jackson said he may have gotten some support by billionaires, drawing a reaction from the room. But he said he still plans to tax them.
“They know that I don’t owe them a thing like Sen. Collins,” Jackson said.
However, he noted he would vote to impeach Hegseth, Trump’s Defense Secretary.
Does Collins regret RFK vote?
Collins noted the areas where she disagrees with the controversial U.S. Health and Human Services department secretary. For example, she doesn’t believe vaccines cause autism — a link Kennedy has made in the past.
But she said she agrees with him on his focus on chronic diseases. Overall, she’t said she didn’t regret the vote.
A look at the instigator from the room
A young man just stood up from the fourth row and interrupted Collins before she could answer a question. He was quickly escorted out of the room to applause.
Jackson’s response was muffled, but it sounded like he said, “oh, shut up,” noting he didn’t know the person.
“I don’t know what world Sen. Collins is in where she started out, we had $4 trillion in debt, now we have $40 trillion in debt under her watch, and somehow it’s my fault,” Jackson responded. “In Maine, we have a balanced budget. Has it grown? Yes. But it’s still balanced.”
He noted that tax cuts for wealthy Americans contribute to the debt.
Collins noted Maine is running a potential budget deficit of about $1 billion — you can read about that here — and Jackson noted that he hasn’t been in the Legislature since 2024.
Pressed on that point, Collins pivoted to attacking Jackson, arguing she’d vote the Democratic party line if elected.
Jackson contended that Collins would be a rubber stamp for Trump in her sixth term, and the two squabbled over how often Collins supports Trump.
When asked the same question about her party, Collins said her party has worked to secure the border.
But Collins also said she would vote independently during her sixth term.
“We need more people in the center. We don’t need more people who are going to vote a straight party line,” Collins said.
Jackson’s opening statement hits on chaos in our politics
Following a familiar line of attack, Jackson hit Collins for voting to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Collins did not ultimately support the measure, but Jackson has repeatedly attacked her for a vote to advance the bill. (She’s argued it would have made the floor anyway, and that because of her vote, she was able to get a $50 billion fund for rural hospitals amended onto it.)
“I ask for your support so I can continue my work for you,” Collins said.
Jackson’s campaign finance report is in
He promised to deliver the numbers Wednesday morning. They came about 36 hours later — though still before the statutory deadline.
Take a look at our rundown of the third quarter fundraising by Collins and Jackson. The Democrat had a heck of a quarter — but he’s still being badly outraised by Collins and her allies.
The candidates take the stage
The candidates have arrived! The room is full mostly of Collins and Jackson supporters, who broke out into applause as the candidates took the stage. The two met in a cordial handshake and are now at their podiums taking last minute notes.
Pictures tell the story
Here’s a look a the scenes outside the debate. Might be a bit more raucous inside than the past three.
Coming into tonight, Jackson’s campaign said the former logger will try to focus on healthcare — something that he’s done in each debate so far. He will undoubtedly continue to tie Collins to President Donald Trump, who’s deeply unpopular here.
Expect Collins to continue to highlight her seniority in the Senate as a strength and try to shift blame for the high cost of — whether its property taxes or electricity rates — onto Jackson, who served as state Senate president for six years.
Let’s hope the candidates break some new ground. But after three televised debates in two weeks, that may be difficult to do.
Update from on the ground from Bangor
Just under an hour before the candidates are set to take the stage, supporters of each have gathered in the parking lot outside the venue. Jackson’s supporters are blasting music and holding a large banner that reads “Let them eat road salt” — a zinger from the first debate.
Across the lot, Collins supporters are doing a call-and-response with the senator’s first and last name in front of a large tour bus.
One hour to go!
We are about an hour from go time.
Get caught up on our past debate coverage before we get started. You can read our takeaways from the first debate here, from the second debate here and from the third debate here.

title: Maine Wildness is the name of the state’s new women’s soccer team
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — The name was announced and was immediately greeted by an extended and hearty ovation.
The Maine Wildness, the newly named amateur women’s soccer club that will be a sister team to the Portland Hearts of Pine, is already a hit. And so is the club’s logo, a blend of new imagery with a clear connection to the Hearts.
“It’s perfect. All of it,” said Nicole Vinal, a native Mainer who lives in Brunswick. Vinal said the name and the story behind it represents her. “I’m scrappy. I’m a hard worker. I love the outdoors, the wilderness.”
Vinal, a season ticket-holder for both the Maine Wildness and the Hearts of Pine, was among a crowd of 500 supporters at Madrid’s in Portland for Thursday’s name and brand reveal.
The Maine Wildness will begin play in the spring and early summer of 2027, competing in the USL W League, which in 2026 had 96 teams across 16 regionalized divisions.
The name and logo were the result of months of planning and community outreach by the organization, which has achieved worldwide recognition for its Hearts of Pine branding and merchandise. Club representatives held town hall-style meetings and an online forum with U.S. Women’s National Team legends, including Michelle Akers, who has become a founding adviser for the Maine Wildness.
Hannah Sirois, the club’s vice president for fan experience and the point person for the women’s team, said the Wildness name was first isolated when staff members were huddled around a campfire, riffing on themes of wilderness and natural beauty.
“It’s about being your unapologetic self,” Sirois said.
Catherine Culley, one of the club’s founding co-owners, had tears in her eyes when the name was revealed and the crowd voiced their wholehearted endorsement.
“I think women need this right now as a positive environment that welcomes women for everything they are,” Culley said. “It’s something I feel the community needed right now. And I think it is important for young girls to see a path forward and it’s equal to the men. Not the same as the men.”
Prior to the name reveal, the audience heard from club personnel about how they had spent hours and hours going over 300-plus names and then shaping the asymmetrical crest logo that pays homage to Maine’s wilderness with stylized imagery of Katahdin, flowing waters and wildflowers.
In the presentation, the qualities of “Wildness” as it relates to Maine women were detailed as five main themes: resilience, communers, work ethic, leadership, and being grounded. Wildness, according to a club press release, connects the physical characteristics of Maine and “the trailblazing spirit” of Maine women.
“The name, it encapsulates everything a Maine women is,” said Justine Satterthwaite of Scarborough. Like Vinal, Satterthwaite is now a season-ticket holder for both the Maine Wildness and the Hearts of Pine.
By incorporating the Hearts of Pine’s distinctive Dirigo Heart image and blue-and-green colors into the Maine Wildness logo, designed by Portland-based artist Pame Chévez, the club was purposeful in connecting its two teams while providing the women’s team with its own identity. The crest emphasizes the natural beauty of wild spaces with images of Katahdin, flowing waters, and resilient flora like wild lupines, thistle, sea rose and fern.
“We asked people across Maine what they wanted for this team and we kept hearing the same response: a love for what we’ve created with Hearts and a deep desire for something distinct to the women of Maine,” said Gabe Hoffman-Johnson, the club’s founder and chief community officer, in a press release. “‘Wildness came from listening to that feedback, finding a name that captures the spirit intrinsic to both this place and the people who make it so special.”
Shortly after the name and brand were revealed, the crowded main room noticeably thinned out. That’s because half of the attendees went to the music venue’s lobby to line up and buy Maine Wildness T-shirts, sweatshirts and other swag. The women’s team items are now available on the club’s online store and its Club Shop at 127 Marginal Way in Portland.
The women’s team will consist of mostly college-age players. Because it is a pre-professional league (think wooden bat baseball leagues for a simple comparison), the players retain their college eligibility. Games are played mostly in May and June. The Maine Wildness will compete in the USLW’s Northeast Division.
The Wildness will immediately be one of top drawing clubs in the USLW. In June, the club sold 5,000 season-ticket deposits in an hour and have converted 4,400 of those deposits into season-ticket sales.
The men’s team, which has averaged 6,239 fans at city-owned Fitzpatrick Stadium this season, has 4,000 season-ticket holders.
The USLW does not report average attendance, but most teams draw less than 1,000 fans. Minnesota Aurora FC is a rare exception, reportedly bringing in over 5,000 fans per match. The Vermont Green, which will be a rival for the Wildness in the Northeast Division, consistently sold out 2,500-seat Virtue Field in Burlington in their first season in 2026.
“This team is intended to set the standard for what a pre-professional women’s team can accomplish,” Sirois said in the press release. “We want to grow the women’s game in this country. Consistently selling out a 6,000-person stadium has never been done at this level, and raising that standard is what we’re rallying this state around.”
The Hearts of Pine ownership announced in August its plans to build its own 9,000-11,000 seat stadium on Cassidy Point in Portland. The hope is to break ground sometime in 2027, with 2029 as the target year for both the men’s and women’s teams to move to their new home.
