title: Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland dedicates 100th home in Standish
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland dedicates 100th home in Standish
The home is the 10th Habitat for Humanity has built in the Standish neighborhood and the eighth designated for a single mother and her family
Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland dedicates 100th home in Standish
The home is the 10th Habitat for Humanity has built in the Standish neighborhood and the eighth designated for a single mother and her family
Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland celebrated a major milestone Thursday, dedicating its 100th home and welcoming a new homeowner and her family to a neighborhood where the organization has helped other single mothers achieve homeownership.
Michelle Demers and her family are preparing to move into their new home next week. The home is the 10th Habitat for Humanity has built in the Standish neighborhood and the eighth designated for a single mother and her family.
For Demers, the opportunity marks the end of a six-month experience and the beginning of a new chapter.
“It's exciting. Little nerve wracking. It's been a great six months, great experience. So, to finally kind of come to the end, the grand prize, so to speak. It's great,” Demers said.
She learned about the opportunity after her oldest daughter saw it advertised online and encouraged her to apply.
Habitat for Humanity of Greater Portland Executive Director Chad Mullin said the organization hopes the home will provide stability and peace for the family.
“We believe that homes, create an environment of safety and shelter, of comforts, of ease, of peace. Right. And so for her family, I think it's going to mean just that,” Mullin said.
The milestone also comes as the organization faces the challenge of rising construction costs. Mullin said each home costs about $400,000 to build, including all expenses, putting homeownership out of reach for many families.
To help manage costs, Habitat partners with a modular home dealer to set the homes. Volunteers then help complete work such as flooring, trim and siding before families move in.
The organization is continuing construction in the neighborhood, with plans to finish two additional homes in December.
For Demers and her daughter Jurnee, the wait is nearly over. Jurnee said she is looking forward to having friends over and decorating the house for the holidays.
The dedication also coincides with the 50th anniversary of Habitat for Humanity International, giving the local organization another reason to celebrate its work helping families find affordable places to call home.

title: Fact checking Maine gubernatorial debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Fact checking WMTW Maine gubernatorial debate
Rick Bennett, Bobby Charles and Hannah Pingree met in our studio for the final gubernatorial debate of this cycle on Wednesday.
Fact checking WMTW Maine gubernatorial debate
Rick Bennett, Bobby Charles and Hannah Pingree met in our studio for the final gubernatorial debate of this cycle on Wednesday.
Immigration officers at Maine polling locations and accusations into candidates pasts were among the claims made by gubernatorial candidates when they met in our studio on Wednesday night.
"Bobby Charles was recorded on tape inviting ICE to come to our polls," Democrat Hannah Pingree said about her Republican opponent.
"No, I never invited them into the polls. That's false," Charles responded.
Late this summer, Charles was recorded during a campaign stop saying he would call Pres. Donald Trump's border czar and ask him to send ICE agents to Maine.
"I'm gonna actually 3 or 4 weeks before the election, maybe three. I'm going to make an appeal for ICE and Marshals ," Charles said in an audio recording obtained by Maine's Total Coverage.
Maine state law says that federal immigration officers cannot be within 250 feet of a polling location.
The Charles campaign does not dispute the audio recording but told Maine's Total Coverage on Thursday that Charles has not called Tom Homan on this matter.
Another claim we're looking into, Charles alleging it is a conflict of interest that a housing grant was awarded to a non-profit that Pingree was helping lead while she was also working on housing issues at the state level.
"You've sent your money not to Lewiston or Bangor, but to [North] Haven," Charles said. "North Haven doesn't need extra funding, and your family didn't need that money."
Charles continuing to double down on social media after the debate, posting videos from our conference room and parking lot.
"These are the documents that prove in December 2022 when she was running the office that the money went to the organization that she was running," he said in a Facebook video.
"Maine Housing awarded a grant I was not on," Pingree said.
"You were in charge of affordable housing, and $1 million went to your family. How do you how do you defend that?" Charles interrupted.
Charles is referring to an $840,000 grant that was awarded to the non-profit North Haven Sustainable Housing by MaineHousing.
The purpose of the grant, as stipulated by MaineHousing, was the build affordable housing in island communities.
15 island communities, including North Haven, are eligible.
Pingree was the president of North Haven Sustainable Housing and also the director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future at the time the grant was awarded.
MaineHousing is not part of that office and Pingree has never worked for MaineHousing.
State law allows a member of the governor's cabinet to also serve as president of a nonprofit, assuming they follow the state's conflict of interest laws and they do not financially benefit from it.
Federal tax documents for North Haven Sustainable Housing show the only paid employee of the non-profit was the executive director in 2022.
That same document discloses the executive director, Sam Hallowell, is the domestic partner of Pingree's sister.
Pingree's father, Charlie Pingree, is also on the board.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal probe, AP source says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Washington D.C. U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also probing issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the Democrat for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

title: 5 killed, including 3 children, in shooting at Oregon elementary school, officials say
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - Five people are dead after a shooting occurred at an elementary school in Oregon.
Police confirmed that three children -- ages 5, 8 and 11 years old -- a teacher, and the shooter were killed.
EN ESPAÑOL | Cuatro muertos en tiroteo en una escuela primaria de Oregon
The Bend Police Department said officers responded just before 1 p.m. to the Silver Rail Elementary School after a first call reported a person fired a gun into a car.
Within minutes, more callers reported a person walked into the school and started shooting.
A person at the school shot and killed the shooter, the chief said. Police did not release the shooter’s name or age Thursday.
Later in the evening, CNN reported the shooter was a 16-year-old boy.

Sen. Ron Wyden also issued a statement Thursday saying his heart goes out to the victims and their loved ones.

title: Trump administration advances plan for peptide drugs favored by RFK Jr.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. health officials are moving ahead with a plan to allow specialty pharmacies to produce certain peptides, a class of largely unregulated injections that have become popular among followers of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other wellness influencers.
Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services submitted a peptides “interim access policy” to the White House for review, according to a posting Thursday on a government website. The plan was sent to the Office of Management and Budget, which reviews federal rules and regulations with the potential for significant economic impact.
HHS officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon.
Peptides are the building blocks of more complex proteins, triggering hormones inside the body needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss.
But the ones at issue here haven’t gone through that rigorous vetting process. Nevertheless, they have gained a foothold among Americans interested in bulking up, looking younger or boosting energy. Those uses are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration and most of the data on peptides comes from animal studies.
Before joining the administration, Kennedy publicly declared that “FDA’s war” on peptides and other wellness products would soon end.
After becoming health secretary, Kennedy said U.S. compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans were increasingly turning to “gray market” peptides made in China and other countries. Those products remain widely available for purchase via online platforms like TikTok.
The White House filing doesn’t give specifics of the new policy, but two people familiar with the plan say it is intended to allow pharmacies to temporarily compound some of the most popular peptides, including BPC-157, a chemical promoted to build muscle and heal injuries. The people spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations.
The update is the latest indication that Kennedy and other Trump administration officials are looking to ease access to unproven products that are popular within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Some of the biggest MAHA figures sell peptide injections and supplements.
The FDA previously placed BPC-157 and more than a dozen other injectable peptides on its list of substances that are too risky to be compounded by pharmacies. Possible risks include contamination, allergic reactions and tumor growth, according to the FDA.
But earlier this year, Kennedy directed the agency to reconsider a short list of chemicals that have been widely promoted by wellness influencers and fitness celebrities.
In July, a panel of external FDA advisers recommended the agency drop its restrictions on six of the seven peptides put before them. That recommendation went against the scientific conclusion of FDA’s staff scientists, who reiterated that none of the peptides had been studied enough to establish their safety and effectiveness.
The new policy sent to the White House would essentially assure compounding pharmacies — specialty businesses that mix customized medications that aren’t available from traditional drugmakers — that they won’t be targeted for producing certain peptides, according to the people familiar with the plan. That approach, known as enforcement discretion, allows the FDA to selectively choose to not enforce some of its own regulations.
Formally adding the peptides to FDA’s list of drugs that are safe for compounding would require federal rulemaking, a process that could take years and involves multiple rounds of public comment. It was not immediately clear if the administration still plans to pursue that process.
The proposal was quickly praised online by some Kennedy allies who sell peptides.
“This is huge,” Brigham Buhler, a wellness clinic operator who sells peptides through an online service, posted on X. “This isn’t about whether you’re for or against peptides. It’s about whether you’re for or against MEDICAL FREEDOM.”
The panel of outside experts that met in July was selected by Kennedy’s health department and included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field.
The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers and Noom. Both companies recently announced plans to offer peptides to their customers if the federal government eases access. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth $2 billion to $3 billion.

title: ‘He’s not violent’: 911 call made before man allegedly kills aunt, grandmother with chainsaw
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — Transcripts reveal a call for help was made before police in Alabama said a 47-year-old man killed two of his family members.
Crime scene tape surrounded a home on Carolina Court in Mobile on Oct. 12 as investigators canvassed the area.
911 call details
According to transcripts, a woman called 911 after 11 a.m. on Monday.
In the call, she said her nephew, later identified as Thomas Steele, was “off his medication for Lithium” and she wasn’t “sure who to call or contact.”
“He gave away his phone and giving his car away. He’s doing some bizarre things, and I don’t know if that’s good. He says he’s just going to live for God and not going to have any kind of electronics,” the woman said to 911 dispatchers.
The operator asked if she needed medical help.
The woman said Steele is bipolar and “it’s in his mind. He’s following God.”
As the call continued, the caller said her nephew was acting out.
The operator asked what she meant and if he was being harmful.
“I just needed to figure out what to do. I called 988 and tried to talk to him. He’s calm! He’s not violent or anything. So, I guess I’ll just let it play itself out,” the caller responded.
The operator gave the woman the number for the police department and the call ended.
Police respond to home
According to a source, about two and a half hours later, police were called to the home and were told Steele was waiting outside.
Officers said they found Steele’s grandmother and aunt inside the home decapitated with a chainsaw.
Mobile police identified the victims in the double homicide on Carolina Court as Christy Deloach, 65, and Dora Boone, 85.
The source also told FOX10 News that a woman with special needs was inside the home at the time of the killings. She was unharmed.
Steele remains behind bars without bond.
It is unclear how long after the 911 call the aunt and grandmother were killed. It is also unclear if the caller was able to reach Mobile police after the operator gave her that number.

title: US considering using 'mother of all bombs' against Iran, CNN sources say
text:
US considering using 'mother of all bombs' against Iran, CNN sources say
The U.S. military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should President Donald Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter.
Using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal, for the first time in the conflict with Iran would mark a notable escalation, even though there are doubts over how effective it would be in accomplishing any of Trump’s stated strategic objectives or tipping the balance of the war, multiple sources familiar with internal military planning discussions about potentially deploying the weapon said.
Trump is facing pressure to bring an end to the deeply unpopular war — as Republicans brace for potential political backlash from voters in the upcoming midterm elections and there is little indication the two countries are close to a negotiated resolution after more than six months of U.S. bombing.
While the U.S. military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against outstanding Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that incorporates those plans in a way that could actually end the war — something only the president has the power to do.
For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could act as a “definitive” end to the war, at least from a messaging point of view, aware of how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans.
Video below: President Trump rejects Iran's latest proposal as war enters its eighth month
While some administration figures have characterized the war as essentially won, Trump has been more guarded in recent remarks, stopping short of declaring victory and saying the U.S. still has unfinished business in the country.
Behind the scenes, Trump has also cast doubt on some outside allies who have encouraged him to simply bring U.S. troops home and move on. Doing so, Trump has argued, would look like defeat.
Over the course of the last several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterms, several advisers said privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before Election Day.
Trump has ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets that include “a lot of energy infrastructure” and the potential use of a MOAB, one of the sources told CNN. The same source said the phrasing used was that this attack would come “prior to U.S. retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” indicating the administration could launch the additional strikes, attempt to declare victory and quickly pull everyone out.
A second source told CNN that military plans for striking Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, also explicitly call for using the MOAB. In recent months, Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe, where the U.S. and Israel believe Tehran has stored components of its nuclear program, even after pausing full combat operations earlier this year, and Trump continues to emphasize that his goal is to ensure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon.
Doubts MOAB would be effective
Another U.S. official noted that when the military plans, it develops a menu of options for policymakers that range from the high-end to low-end. Higher-end targets, including those that are located deep underground, require bigger bombs, and the MOAB is the biggest, the official added.
But there are questions around whether the MOAB would be an effective munition to use against Iran’s nuclear facilities and other sites that are located deep underground. While the GPS-guided bomb is capable of destroying an area equivalent to nine city blocks, it likely lacks the capability to penetrate deep enough under the surface to destroy the suspected nuclear facilities at Pickaxe, which is believed to be fortified by layers of granite, and other remaining Iranian nuclear sites, sources said.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a third source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”
If used, the MOAB would have devastating effects on the area that it impacts but likely only at the surface level, the sources noted. And the bomb’s massive blast radius would almost certainly raise concerns about the prospect of civilian casualties — particularly if it is used to target Iranian infrastructure targets located near populated areas and in close proximity to non-military sites.
Still, Trump could opt to use the MOAB as a psychological weapon at a time when the Iranian regime appears dug in and unwilling to bend to his diplomatic demands. While U.S. officials warn that deploying it is unlikely to force Iran’s capitulation or achieve a strategic military victory — it could provide Trump with an additional option, short of restarting full combat operations, to alter the conflict’s current status quo.
“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level … you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the third source familiar with recent planning discussions added.
Many within the administration as well as outside analysts agree that the only way to decisively defeat Iran would be through a major operation involving ground troops, a commitment that could potentially cost thousands of American lives. The Pentagon considers all scenarios, so those plans exist, but as of now no one in the administration is arguing for such drastic action.
Trump has indicated he has little interest in putting U.S. boots on the ground in Iran but his desire to end the conflict as soon as possible presents a political dilemma for a president who is keenly aware of how unpopular the war has become yet has been unable to secure a diplomatic agreement that would bring it to a close.
Top Trump administration officials and military planners have been focused, for weeks, on finding an off-ramp that gives Trump a “symbolic” win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, CNN has reported.
A fourth source familiar with the Pentagon’s recent planning discussions on Iran told CNN that military officials had developed some options that would amount to a “fireworks show,” with the goal of providing Trump an off-ramp from the conflict even if those strikes fail to accomplish his stated goals for starting the war in the first place.
And despite Trump’s recent pledge to hold off on launching additional strikes before the midterms, the U.S. military already appears to be preparing for potential Iranian retaliation should the president give the go-order.
The next turnover of U.S. troops deployed to CENTCOM is also expected to take place within the next few weeks, according to a fifth source, a U.S. official who acknowledged it is possible some of the personnel who rotate out of the region, may not be replaced by fresh service members.
Asked about the plans, a White House official told CNN that they do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon.”
In response to CNN’s request for comment, a Pentagon official said: “The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.”
MOAB developed for ‘psychological operations’
Developed during the Iraq War, the MOAB is an air blast-type warhead that explodes before hitting the ground to project a massive explosion from all sides.
During the final stages of testing in 2003, military officials told CNN the MOAB was mainly conceived as a weapon employed for “psychological operations.”
Military officials said then they hoped such a huge blast would rattle Iraqi troops and pressure them into surrendering or not even fighting.
As originally conceived, the MOAB was to be used against large formations of troops and equipment or hardened above-ground bunkers. The target set has been expanded to include targets buried under softer surfaces, such as caves or tunnels.
Trump was the first U.S. president to deploy the MOAB, during his first term when he authorized the military to use its most powerful non-nuclear bomb on ISIS positions in Afghanistan in 2017.
That strike targeted a network of fortified underground tunnels that ISIS had been using to stage attacks on government forces — killing 36 ISIS fighters, Afghan officials said. The blast destroyed three underground tunnels as well as weapons and ammunition, but no civilians were hurt, Afghan and U.S. officials added at the time.
At the time, the bombing marked a dramatic change in attitude for Trump, who advocated an isolationist, “America first” foreign policy during his first election campaign.
Following the 2017 strike, U.S. military officials were pressed on whether the 21,600-pound bomb was necessary for that particular target and would likely face similar questions if the munition is deployed against Iran.

title: Al Pacino to get lifetime achievement award from the Screen Actors Guild
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Al Pacino has been named the next recipient of the SAG-AFTRA Life Achievement Award.
The 86-year-old star of “Dog Day Afternoon,” “Scent of a Woman” and a trilogy of “Godfather” films is the 62nd actor to receive the highest honor handed out by the Screen Actors Guild -American Federation of Television and Radio Artists.
“I wondered and wandered most of my life but have always felt at home with a script and my fellow actors. It’s the work and the actors along the way that have been among the greatest joys of my life,” Pacino said in a statement Thursday. “It’s an honor to be recognized by SAG-AFTRA in celebrating the journey.”
He’ll pick up the prize on Feb. 28 at the 33rd annual Actor Awards at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles. The show will stream live on Netflix.
The award also honors humanitarian work, and the guild cited Pacino’s charitable efforts for disaster relief, fighting hunger and poverty and his support for local theater companies, including the Shakespeare Center of Los Angeles.
The native New Yorker was a young actor best known for his stage work when director Francis Ford Coppola tapped him to play Michael Corleone in 1972’s “The Godfather” against the wishes of a studio that wanted an established star in the coveted part.
He would be nominated for an Oscar for the role and become regarded as one of the finest actors of his generation. He got annual Academy Award nominations for the next three years, for “Serpico,” “The Godfather Part II” and “Dog Day Afternoon.” He would not win until he took best actor for “Scent of a Woman” in 1993, a year when he was also nominated for supporting actor for “Glengarry Glen Ross.” He’s been nominated nine times overall, most recently in 2020 for “The Irishman.”
Pacino has also won two competitive Actor Awards from SAG-AFTRA, two Emmys, four Golden Globes and the Globes’ lifetime achievement honor, the Cecil B. DeMille Award.
“I have spent my life in awe and appreciation of the force of nature that is Al Pacino,” SAG-AFTRA President Sean Astin said in a statement. “When you watch him perform, you are witnessing a student and a master. Al Pacino is an artist of extraordinary courage, intensity and heart whose work has always set an exceptional standard of skill and talent. All of that and he’s just plain fun to watch.”
The SAG-AFTRA Life Achievement Award dates to 1962. Previous winners include Barbara Stanwyck, James Stewart, Pearl Bailey, Frank Sinatra, James Cagney, Katharine Hepburn, Audrey Hepburn, Paul Newman, James Earl Jones, Jane Fonda and Harrison Ford.

title: Androscoggin County EMA begins move into former Maine Public building in Lewiston
text:
LEWISTON — The Androscoggin County Emergency Management Agency last week began the long process of moving into new space at the former Maine Public building at 1450 Lisbon St.
The agency is leaving its longtime home on Oak Street and will eventually be joined by the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office, ending a yearslong effort to find a new location for a county public safety building.
The move gets the agency out of the basement of the Lewiston Fire Department’s central station, providing more space and making communication between county offices more efficient, officials said.
For EMA Director Chad Arris, one aspect of the new office stands out.
“Having windows,” said Arris, laughing. “We don’t have to rely on security cameras to tell us whether it’s raining out or sunny out. Just looking out and watching the traffic every now and then is a nice touch.”
The agency, which works with communities to prepare, respond and recover from emergencies, hopes to be up and running in the new building by July 2027. Arris said they are waiting on a direct fiber-optic line to connect the Lisbon Street office to the Androscoggin County Building in Auburn, which will gain them access to all the necessary servers and to operate as an emergency center.
That is expected to be complete within the next couple of months, Arris said. Once that’s done, he said they’ll start moving more of the central parts of the emergency operations center. For now, the agency will continue operating out of the Oak Street station.
Sheriff’s office personnel will begin moving into the location sometime next year, according to Androscoggin County Administrator Jeff Chute.
Androscoggin County purchased 1450 Lisbon St. in August for $1.4 million with the goal of getting county operations under one roof.
The county had previously bought the former Evergreen Subaru dealership at 774 Center St. in Auburn in 2022 for the same purpose, using $4.5 million from a federal grant. However, following years of discussion, concerns over the cost of renovation and permitting issues led county commissioners to vote early this year to sell the property and seek another location for a public safety building.
The new building will have county law enforcement, the criminal investigation division, civil, records and administration on the first floor, and EMA and dispatch services on the second.
With the new space being much bigger and more open, Arris and Holly Williams, planner for Androscoggin County Emergency Management Agency, say they envision being a “command center” for other statewide EMA’s, inviting them in for large group trainings and tabletop exercises to practice skills and see where they need to improve and help each other.
They also plan to offer more programs for the public to access, with ideas including CPR and first-aid classes.
Unlike the EMA’s Oak Street office, Williams and Arris said, the new office is ADA compliant, with an elevator and an electric chairlift to help people with mobility issues. The agency has seen an increase in the number of volunteers for its Community Emergency Response Team increasing, and a lot of them are older.
“We worried about that a lot at the other place,” said Arris. “We don’t want to exclude anybody, but now we can do all these preparedness classes just to make people prepared for emergencies.”
More room also allows the agency to communicate with the departments they work with more efficiently. The agency works with all the communities in Androscoggin County and in the case of an emergency, there’s plenty of room for everyone needed.
“We can all be in the same room at the same time making the same decisions with the same information,” said Arris.

title: Water cooler stops falling tree just inches away from crushing man and his dog
text:
PRESCOTT, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) - A water cooler miraculously saved a man and his dog from a falling tree in Arizona, authorities say.
Deputies with the Yavapai County Sheriff’s Office responded Sunday afternoon to reports that a massive tree fell onto a van parked in a camping spot just outside of Prescott.
“When deputies arrived, they braced for the worst. Instead, they found a man and his dog, miraculously unharmed, though the van itself was a total loss,” officials said in a statement.
Deputies looked inside the van to see what could’ve stopped the tree from crushing the man and dog and found an ordinary Igloo water cooler.
“As the tree smashed into the vehicle, the sturdy cooler took the brunt of the impact, stopping the trunk just inches from crushing the man in the driver’s seat,” officials said.
High winds and saturated soil can make falling trees an unpredictable and deadly hazard, officials said. Avoid parking under large, dead or leaning trees, especially during high winds.

title: Black Panther Party stalwarts to celebrate 1966 founding in Oakland, programs that aided the poor
text:
The legacy of the Black Panther Party lives on six decades after its founding, in the work of a Seattle medical center started to address systemic health disparities in the African American community, particularly among Black children.
Originally known as the Sidney Miller Free Medical Clinic in 1969, it put into practice the national Black Panther Party’s Ten-Point Program to uplift African Americans as the Black Power movement gained momentum. Now, as the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center, it, along with the affiliated Country Doctor Community Clinic, sees tens of thousands of patients in a year.
As the celebration begins Thursday for the Black Panther Party’s Oct. 15, 1966, founding in Oakland, California, former members are looking beyond the iconic black leather jackets, berets and clenched fists to highlight programs aimed at healing disenfranchised and forgotten communities.
From free medical clinics and pushing nationally for sickle cell anemia testing to providing free breakfasts for children and community schools promoting education and literacy, the Black Panthers understood what was needed during the racially turbulent 1960s, said Fredrika Newton, widow of co-founder Huey P. Newton.
“We sought to meet the basic needs of the Black community, not only the Black, but all oppressed communities,” she told The Associated Press Tuesday. “Children were going to school hungry. People couldn’t get medical care. People were sleeping in the streets, just like today.”
A planned four-day conference this weekend in downtown Oakland includes a gala. Surviving original members and other Black Panther Party veterans are expected to attend.
Pushing for Black empowerment and against racist policing
Co-founders Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale were students at Merritt College in Oakland, where they formed the Panthers during the Civil Rights Movement. Both became active in Bay Area politics during the mid-1960s and believed the Civil Rights movement may have addressed the plight of Blacks in Southern states, but it failed to bring about any real change in the U.S. West and North.
With Newton as minister of defense and Seale as the group’s chair, the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense advocated for political and economic empowerment and initiatives to improve life for the city’s Black residents in addition to standing up to what they saw as racist and heavy-handed policing in the Black community.
“We knew that Black people were getting brutalized by the police,” said Fredrika Newton, who joined the Black Panther Party in 1971 after meeting Huey P. Newton. “We wanted to make sure that they were getting educated and taught how to protect themselves.”
Confrontations with law enforcement — broadcast to households across the country — galvanized Black support for the organization but also worried many white people. Seale, declaring that the Second Amendment right to bear arms also applied to Blacks, led a small group of armed Panthers in 1967 into the California state legislature.
The Black Panther Party was targeted by the FBI, which put its leaders and members under surveillance and operated a yearslong disruption and discrediting campaign.
John “Bunchy” Crear was caught up in the maelstrom of race and politics sweeping across California in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Crear, along with some friends, began attending Black Panther political education classes in 1970. He joined at age 19.
“I was at home in my bedroom listening to my music when my mother comes in and says two white gentlemen from the FBI were in the living room wanting to talk to me,” recalled Crear, 74, who lives in Houston. “I walked in and there were the men in black. They asked if I was a member of the Black Panther Party, then pulled a book out with photos asking if I knew this person, if I knew that person.”
“’Well, John, if you stay in school and get you a good job, you’ll never hear from us again,’” Crear said the men told him before leaving.
Healthcare part of community survival programs
The Black Panther Party purchased buildings and homes that served as safe houses and centers for their community survival programs, which mostly addressed food insecurity, lack of healthcare, unequal education and other issues in Black communities.
Chapters were started in about 70 other cities. The chapter in Seattle started one of the 13 original Black Panther Party-founded healthcare clinics across the country and is the only one still in operation.
“Thinking especially about Black folks in the 1960s and 70s, it was impossible to try to address one need and not all because they were vulnerable and under threat in so many areas,” said Brandy Taylor, chief executive of the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center and Country Doctor Community Clinic.
“It wasn’t just about medical care. It was about free speech, social services, food security and knowing your rights. There were so many doors closed that you couldn’t survive without addressing them all,” she said.
From the end to emulation
The Black Panther Party folded in 1982 after years of police surveillance, as well as dwindling national membership, infighting, allegations of embezzlement and scandals in which Huey P. Newton was implicated and criminally charged.
Newton’s addictions to alcohol and drugs overtook him. He was murdered in Oakland, California, in 1989 by a drug dealer.
In 2021, a bronze bust of Huey P. Newton was unveiled in Oakland.
However, some see similarities in why the Black Panthers were started with the emergence of the Black Lives Matter movement following the 2013 acquittal of the man who killed Trayvon Martin, a Black teenager in Sanford, Florida.
“We want to let young people know exactly what we did and what could be done,” said Fredrika Newton, who also is president and co-founder of the Huey P. Newton Foundation.
“This is not a blueprint for what they can do now, but they can certainly see what we did, take what we did, apply them to the conditions today and organize,” she said. “Organize around the needs that exist today.”
_____________
Williams is a Detroit-based member of AP’s Race & Ethnicity team.

title: Watch: Spruce Mountain soccer is the Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Spruce Mountain soccer
Winning hasn’t come easy for the Spruce Mountain girls soccer team over the past handful of years.
The Phoenix won only eight games from 2023-25. It looked like the 2026 season would be more of the same when they started with three straight losses, but then the victories started to pile up.
Since Sept. 11, Spruce Mountain is 6-0-2, including 6-0 and 3-2 wins last week against Wiscasset/Boothbay and Wells, respectively. The Phoenix were ranked sixth in Class C South Heal points going into Wednesday’s games.
“So I think our team is clicking more … in a sense of just distributing the ball and finding that open player and looking for crosses,” Spruce Mountain coach Jacob Turner said. “I think that’s really helped, and I saw that the most in Wells.”
Both Turner and senior captain Ashley Nelson said three freshmen — midfielder Lexus Hebert, forward Evangeline “Gigi” DiPasquale and defender Harlee Foss — have played a big part in the turnaround.
“I think we have the most talent that we have had in a very long time,” Nelson said. “We’ve had three amazing freshmen (who) have stepped up and (taken) on some very important roles on our team.”
Turner said the Phoenix are well balanced throughout the lineup.
“We have a great back system,” Turner said. “Our midfield is strong, and we’re aggressive in the midfield. We have Lexus Hebert and Natasha (McDonald) that can score on some of these really good teams.”
Nelson said she’s been waiting for a postseason push since entering high school.
“We’ve gone hard at practices; everyone wants to be here,” Nelson said. “We’ve wanted this since I was a freshman. We’ve really wanted to pull through and make playoffs.”

title: Baby sleepers sold on Amazon recalled due to suffocation risk
text:
Baby sleepers sold on Amazon recalled due to suffocation risk
Parents are being urged to stop using a recalled baby sleeper because it could put infants at risk.
Papablic is recalling about 248 convertible bedside sleepers because they can pose suffocation, entrapment and fall hazards, officials with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission said Thursday.
Related video above | How to stay ahead of recalls
The recalled sleepers can be used as bassinets or play yards.
Their mattresses may shift, leaving a gap where a baby could become trapped and suffocate. The products’ locking mechanisms also may fail, causing them to collapse, federal officials said.
The recall covers model PAPA03001AI, which has a gray exterior and a stars-and-moon print inside.
The model number is on a label beneath the mattress pad. The sleepers were sold on Amazon and Papablic’s website from April 2025 through July 2026 for about $190.
No injuries have been reported. Consumers should stop using the sleeper immediately and contact Papablic for a full refund. For more information, click here.

title: College student killed in crash after being hit by car going 94 mph in 35 mph zone
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — A Clark Atlanta University student died after a crash Tuesday night, and the driver of the other vehicle was arrested, police said.
Officers responded to the crash at Hank Aaron Drive and Glen Street around 11:30 p.m. Tuesday, where 21-year-old Morgan Gamble was found in critical condition, police said. Gamble was taken to the hospital, where she later died.
Driver charged with vehicular homicide
Police believe a vehicle driven by Nikolai Dunford was going 94 mph on Hank Aaron Drive, a 35 mph zone, when it struck Gamble’s car.
Dunford is charged with reckless driving, speeding and first-degree vehicular homicide, police said.
University issues statement
Clark Atlanta University issued a statement Wednesday acknowledging Gamble’s death.
“The loss of a member of our University community is deeply felt, and we extend our heartfelt condolences to Morgan’s family, friends, classmates and all who knew and loved Morgan,” the statement read. “During this time of sorrow, scholars are encouraged to support one another.”
Gamble’s family said she was an extra in Netflix’s reboot of “A Different World.”
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Hannaford app, website still offline over 2 days after company identified security issue
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannaford’s website and mobile app remained offline Friday, more than three days after the supermarket’s parent company says it disabled some systems as a precautionary measure while addressing a network cybersecurity issue.
Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch food giant that owns Maine’s largest grocer, announced in a brief news release late Monday that it was experiencing an internal network issue and had taken some systems offline to protect them, including the Hannaford website and app.
Online ordering has been disabled since then, though stores have remained open as usual.
On Thursday morning, the notification of the outage on Hannaford’s website was updated to include a note that customers can still shop online via third-party delivery services such as DoorDash, Instacart and Uber Eats.
Caitlin Cortelyou, a spokesperson for the Scarborough-based grocery store chain, said in an email Thursday that Hannaford is continuing to work with Ahold Delhaize to resolve the issue. While the investigation into the outage is ongoing, Cortelyou said, the companies “have no evidence at this moment that customer or associate data was taken in this cybersecurity incident.”
Ahold Delhaize says it has contacted external cybersecurity experts to help with its response and is “engaging with the appropriate authorities” as necessary.
“We know how important it is for our customers to be able to shop with us when and how they choose, and we apologize for the disruption,” Cortelyou said. “We appreciate our customers’ continued patience and understanding as we work to resolve the issue.”
If the cybersecurity issue is deemed to have been a data breach, then Maine law requires it be reported to the Office of the Maine Attorney General. The AG’s office said neither Hannaford nor Ahold Delhaize had reported the issue as of Wednesday.
A 2024 breach of Ahold Delhaize’s systems affected more than 95,000 Mainers and over 2 million people worldwide. Hannaford said most of the Mainers whose information was exposed were current or former employees.
Ahold Delhaize, one of the world’s largest food retailers, operates more than 2,000 U.S. stores under several brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Giant Food. Hannaford is the state’s largest grocer, with almost 70 stores across Maine.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 16 to indicate that the outage has continued into Friday.

title: Trump leans on rallies to boost GOP midterm turnout
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump has held campaign rallies for supporters in Alaska, Arizona and Montana in the past 48 hours, as he works to keep the House and Senate under Republican control in the midterm elections.
Trump used campaign rallies during three presidential campaigns to energize his supporters. He is using the same strategy for the midterms.
Speaking in the Rose Garden on Thursday, Trump said the rallies are energizing his campaign.
“The crowds are unbelievable, actually. And I think we’re having a big impact. The Democrats are saying there’s something bad happening and the the fake news doesn’t want to talk about it, but these are rallies that nobody’s ever seen it,” Trump said.
Some of the president’s supporters have questioned the strategy of visiting states like Montana, which Trump won by almost 20 points in 2024.
White House correspondent Jon Decker asked the president about the Montana trip on the tarmac before Trump boarded Air Force One en route to the state.
“Mr. President, why Montana? It’s a very red state. There are those who are saying you’re playing defense as opposed to trying to go to Michigan,” Decker asked.
“Well, I probably because I’m doing Michigan, too, as you know, I’m doing Michigan in a few days. Montana, because we want to make sure we won. I won, you know, it was one of my best states. I won by 45 points. And really two reasons. Normally I wouldn’t be going, but I like to also pay my respect to places that I don’t have to go there,” Trump said.
“And so I do it to thank them. I also do it because we have some great people there that are running, and I want to make sure they win, because when I don’t run, which, you know, in theory I’m not running, but I feel that I’m running. When I don’t run, we get 49% less turnout. When I do run, we win easily,” Trump said.
More campaign rallies are planned in the days ahead in Ohio, Texas, Georgia and Kentucky. Trump is hoping his MAGA base can match the energy that Democrats say they have this election cycle.

title: How do I know my loved ones’ ashes are real? Behind the scenes of the cremation process
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Death can be an uncomfortable conversation, but leaving your loved ones without a plan puts you at risk of ending up in the wrong hands.
Cremation has surpassed traditional burial in popularity in the country. The North American Cremation Association said in 2025 the cremation rate was 62.8%.
Dr. Joe Paciarelli, a grief counselor in Greenville, has seen the importance of ashes to loved ones through his work.
“There’s one case of somebody who, they had such a powerful emotional connection and attachment with their spouse that they actually kept the urn on their body, in a bag,” Paciarelli said. “When they were sleeping, when they were at work, when they went on vacation.”
Paciarelli said the concern comes up a lot.
“People mention maybe offhandedly, I don’t really know if it’s actually them or not,“ Paciarelli said. ”There’s no way for me to tell."
Does it include a private viewing?
For Jay McAfee, the CEO of Thomas McAfee Funeral Homes, the death care industry isn’t just business; it’s a century-old promise to his community. McAfee’s great-great-grandfather started the company in 1913, making him and his cousin the fifth generation of McAfees to run the business.
“We’re going to operate with absolute transparency,” McAfee said. “If anybody wants to come in and you know, get a behind the scenes look to our facilities, we are absolutely willing to be open about that.”
McAfee said one of the ways they ensure the integrity of the cremation process is through a private family viewing.
“It’s going to serve two purposes,” McAfee said. “They’re going to confirm the identity of their loved one who’s in the cremation container at the time... The second purpose it serves is as a meaningful way to say goodbye.”
McAfee said the viewing takes place in a serene setting and they work hard to make sure it’s not a clinical or transactional experience that many people fear.
Thomas McAfee offers public tours as part of their “Unmasking the Mysteries of Cremation” program. The next session will be held on May 28 at the Northwest location on White Horse Road.
How do they track the process?
Funeral Director Trevor Buchanan at Robinson Funeral Home said if a funeral home isn’t transparent, it’s a sign to walk away.
“You deserve transparency,” Buchanan said. “If a funeral home cannot answer your questions without hesitation, that is a major red flag.”
Buchanan took FOX Carolina Investigates through each step of their cremation process and how Robinson Funeral Home logs it all.
After a private family viewing, the family signs an identification form stating they saw their loved one. Then a barcode is placed on the loved one’s ankle, which is tracked through a software system.
Barcodes are also on the retort equipment and scanned at the start of cremation, for any changes during the cremation and at the end of cremation. Nothing can be scanned out of order.
“We take multiple steps that are above what the law requires,” Buchanan said. “Including having the cameras that record everything that occurs in our cremation center.”
A numbered medallion corresponding with the number of the cremation certificate also stays with the body the entire time and is attached to the bag of cremains.
“That medallion is the physical link to a family’s loved one’s identity after the cremation process,” Buchanan said.
Do they operate a crematory on-site?
Both Thomas McAfee and Robinson Funeral Homes operate their own crematories, and have rooms with a viewing window into the area where the retort is located.
“Any family that wishes to be present at the start of their loved ones’ cremation, this is the room that they come to,” Buchanan said.
Families can even push the button to start the loading process, which is important in some religious practices.
Both Buchanan and McAfee said they want the community to know that just because you choose cremation doesn’t mean you can’t have a service or a meaningful experience.
“We can do a memorial service, a celebration of life, a full service where your loved one is present in a casket for an open casket visitation and service,” Buchanan said.
“I wish families understood that cremation doesn’t have to be transactional,” McAfee said. “There’s so many options that they have when they choose cremation. We just see so often families coming to us with anxiety, you know, because they don’t know what to expect. And so, our job is to educate them and help them understand what the experience is going to be like for them and hopefully ease that anxiety.”
Pre-plan end of life
Experts say that pre-planning is crucial to protecting the people you leave behind from confusion and last-minute decision making.
They say guesswork can become a burden fast, especially when families are left to decide what their love one wanted. That includes how to pay for it and who has the authority to say yes.
“If you’re not legally divorced, that spouse has to sign,” Buchanan told us. “If you have five kids across the United States, all five of those kids would need to sign for cremation to occur.”
Pre-planning can give you your own voice in the legal process. In certain states, you can sign your own cremation authorization and pre-planning can lock in prices.
But the plan doesn’t have to start with a funeral contract. Experts suggest you write down your wish and put them somewhere your family can find them.
The more open of a conversation you have with loved ones about end of life care will mean less guesswork later on.

title: Maine veterans file FEC complaint against Sen. Susan Collins over donor funds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A group of Maine veterans announced Thursday they have filed a formal complaint with the Federal Election Commission against Sen. Susan Collins, her authorized campaign committee, 1820 PAC and convicted defense contractor Martin Kao.
The group detailed the filing at a 10 a.m. press conference Thursday.
What the complaint alleges
Complainant Jason Tkacs and the veterans allege Kao made campaign contributions to Collins and an allied super PAC in connection with earmark-style naval research funding.
The filing further alleges Kao privately admitted to law enforcement that the naval project funded by the appropriations was neither sought nor deployed by the U.S. Navy.
The complaint also alleges the Collins campaign failed to surrender the funds to the U.S. Treasury, as required under federal campaign finance rules and precedents. Instead, the campaign has said it donated the money to help rebuild a school in Frenchville, Maine, after a fire.
Organizers said the funding issue was raised in three recent Senate debates.
Veterans speak out
Melinda Swayne, of Bryant Pond, a U.S. Navy veteran, spoke at the press conference:
“Maine Veterans like us put everything on the line to defend our country. Our national defense budget, which Sen. Collins plays a key role in setting should protect the people who serve, not be used as an ATM for her political donors. I feel deeply betrayed by our current Commander in Chief who derailed the FBI’s investigation into whether or not our senator sold us out and now I want answers from Sen. Collins. Maine Veterans deserve a senator who will fight for them.”
Organizers said veterans from southern, central, Downeast and northern Maine participated.
Collins campaign responds
In a statement, the Collins campaign rejected the allegations:
“These Troy Jackson supporters are reaching a new low. They are now criticizing a legal and proper donation to a school that burnt down in Frenchville, Maine. They have displayed absolutely no understanding of the law, they don’t know the facts, and are today filing a complaint with the FEC which fully cleared Senator Collins and her staff almost five years ago.”
The campaign also pointed to a statement from former FEC Commissioner Sean Cooksey, who served when the FEC investigated Navatek in 2021:
“At no time did the FEC have any evidence that 1820 PAC or Senator Collins’ campaign knew or did anything wrong. We dismissed or took no action on every potential violation against the PAC, and pursued significant civil penalties against the company. Those are the facts. Any suggestion otherwise is hackery.”

title: Troy Jackson raises $20.4M in a furious Maine Senate campaign ramp-up
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Democrat Troy Jackson raised $20.4 million in his first three months in the U.S. Senate race, four times what Republican Sen. Susan Collins brought in, but he spent it in a furious ramp-up and entered October with less cash than the incumbent.
Jackson’s report, filed with the Federal Election Commission minutes before the candidates met for their final debate Thursday in Bangor, is the first look at his finances since Maine Democrats nominated him at a special convention in July. He replaced Graham Platner, who left the race over sexual assault allegations.
The reports underline the national stakes of a race that could decide control of the Senate. Both candidates got about 85% of their disclosed contributions from outside Maine. Meanwhile, outside groups have spent or reserved $139.1 million on ads since late July, nearly four times what the campaigns and their party partners have, according to AdImpact data.
Jackson’s campaign touted the haul in a release Thursday, saying he had nearly 200,000 donors and that nearly 95% of contributions were under $100. It left out what the campaign spent and has left.
Jackson spent $16.5 million and had $4 million on hand at the end of September, along with roughly $1 million in debt to a vendor. Collins raised $5.2 million and spent $10.9 million over the same quarter, ending it with $5.4 million and no debt.
The Democrat’s money runs largely through ActBlue, the online fundraising platform, which processed $17.1 million, about 90% of what he raised from individuals. His average gift there in July and August was about $50. September’s haul won’t be disclosed until next week.
The report was a flashpoint at debates on Tuesday and Thursday. At the first one, Collins noted that Jackson had not disclosed his fundraising yet. He responded with a pledge to release the report on Wednesday morning, a day before it was due. His campaign did not submit it until minutes before the Thursday debate.
“It was my first one,” Jackson said then. “I had to make sure it was right.”
Jackson has said he will not take corporate PAC money, a pledge that does not cover labor unions. Nearly 80 PACs gave him $352,000, many of them unions. They include the machinists and painters unions, which gave $5,000 each and paid Jackson as a consultant just before and during his run for governor that ended with a third-place June primary finish.
The report lists 960 donors who gave at least $3,500, the per-election maximum, including 130 from Maine. Many gave $7,000, which is allowed because the special convention that nominated Jackson counts as a separate election under federal rules. The campaign designated about $1.1 million to that contest.
Collins is leaning more on outside help. Groups backing her have put $85.3 million into ads since late July, nearly seven times what she and her party partners have spent. Outside groups have spent $53.9 million backing Jackson since he took over the nomination.

title: Speaker Johnson dismisses skeptics as he campaigns for House GOP in Maine battleground
text:
BANGOR — Speaker Mike Johnson made a campaign swing Wednesday through Maine’s picturesque second congressional district, convinced Republicans will defy history and maintain their House majority, as he worked to boost GOP candidate Paul LePage in what is one of the party’s best hopes to flip a Democratic-held seat.
The speaker told a small crowd at the Sea Dog Brewing Co. that he disagrees with the polling and the growing sense that Republicans are heading toward defeat on Nov. 3. Instead, he said he believes that the party in power will maintain its narrow grip on the House — thanks in part to candidates like LePage, the two-term former governor.
“I’m telling you, we’re going to surprise them,” Johnson told the few dozen gathered for lunches of burgers, fish and chips and pot pies at the Bangor eatery.
Johnson has been crisscrossing the country in a campaign blitz that will total more than 20 states and 40 districts in October, in a final sprint ahead of the elections that will determine control of Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term in the White House.
Republicans have increasingly been forced to play defense in the final weeks, trying to shore up their candidates in GOP strongholds nationwide as voters reel from high gas prices, Trump’s tariff policies and the war against Iran. Democrats are reaching deep into districts where Trump has had support, trying and preparing a first 100-day agenda if they win back control.
Johnson said what he’s seeing on the campaign trail tells a different story — of crowds turning out to support the party’s candidates, including earlier this week in southern Texas, a key battleground region.
“Now we have to defy history to do this,” Johnson said, noting that rarely does the president’s party win in midterm elections.
But he said, echoing Le Page’s own message to the room, “voter turnout is critical.”
With a narrow split, every House district matters
While much of the attention in Maine has been on the state’s volatile Senate race between incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, the House race for the open seat held by retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden is another key battleground.
LePage and Democratic state auditor Matt Dunlap are vying for the sprawling district that encompasses much of the rural northern part of the state. The two are set to debate this week.
LePage acknowledged that getting out the vote is what will make the difference.
The district is one Trump carried in the past, but that Golden has held as a leader of the conservative Blue Dog Coalition, a caucus of more centrist Democrats. The retiring congressman has at times bucked House Democratic leadership in voting with Republicans.
It’s also one of the few remaining Trump-won districts represented by a Democrat, which makes it a prime opportunity for Republicans as they work to backfill losses elsewhere and keep their majority.
This week, the main House Republican super PAC aligned with Johnson, the Congressional Leadership Fund, canceled spending in four House races, including Iowa and New Jersey, and increased its investment in others from Texas to Pennsylvania.
Democrats, however, are confident they will seize control, as they begin planning an ambitious agenda focused on affordability issues and anti-corruption investigations of Trump and his administration.

title: Trump, after bipartisan backlash, says Pentagon won't livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday that the Pentagon will no longer livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it.
Trump said on social media that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan.”
But, he continued, “any very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
The Pentagon has said Hasan’s execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, “if they so choose.”
The announcement earlier this month from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan’s execution would be public — and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be livestreamed — prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalization.
When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.
But he continued: “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.

title: Deputies: 9 kids endured day-long wall squats in house of ‘horror’
text:
ETNA TOWNSHIP, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) - Nine children have been removed from what investigators describe as “appalling and unsafe living conditions” in Ohio.
“The living conditions were horrific, disgusting,” said Captain Jay Cook with the Licking County Sheriff’s Office.
Detectives arrested Jonathan Parr and Jacqueline Coleman on child endangerment charges Tuesday after carrying out a search warrant at a home in Etna Township, according to the Licking County Sheriff.
Twelve people lived at the home, including nine children, detectives said.
“Part of the disclosure from the children was the abuse. Sometimes it was punishment. Sometimes it was for no good reason at all, where they would have to stand with their back against the wall. As like a wall squat type situation. It was reported that they would have to sometimes stand there all day,” Cook said. “There was a disclosure of nails in the floor, and it was mentioned that it was there for like a marker to put their feet.”
All nine children are now in the custody of child protective services.
The sheriff’s office said additional charges against the suspects are possible.
