title: Winslow to request review of tax assessment after complaints of high bills
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WINSLOW — The Town Council voted Tuesday to seek a review of its tax assessment after residents complained of high bills and councilors said they were blindsided.
After the municipal budget saw a 16% increase for the 2027 fiscal year and a statistical revaluation shook up property values, Winslow residents told councilors they were surprised to see steep increases in their tax bills.
Councilors said they were surprised, too, after a mill rate of $14.50 per $1,000 of assessed valuation signified a drop from Winslow’s previous mill rate of $14.85.
At the meeting, council Chair Fran Hudson said the council was not looking to throw the tax assessor under the bus, but wanted “to make sure that it was done correctly, fairly and was equitable to every taxpayer.”
“It’s our responsibility,” Hudson said.
The council voted to instruct Town Manager Marc Amaral to contact Maine Revenue Services, part of the Department of Administrative and Financial Services, to conduct a review or evaluation of the tax process after Hudson consulted with the Maine Municipal Association.
Hudson said MMA informed her that seeking an assessment from the revenue services department was legal and acceptable.
The council asked the town manager to ensure all councilors receive updates from the assessment in writing. If the revenue services department cannot go in depth enough on the tax assessment process, Hudson said, the town would consider hiring a private auditing company.
“We have heard you loud and clear, we agree with you,” Councilor Doris Labranche said in a message to the taxpayers. “We want to make sure everything was done fair and equitably among all property types.”

title: A long search for a new priest in Aroostook County
text:
St. John’s Episcopal Church in Presque Isle had more pews than people as a dozen parishioners spread out in the dimly lit church at a recent Saturday service. The Rev. Robert Smith shook each attendee’s hand during the sign of peace — a quick task in a small congregation.
Halfway through the service, the congregants joined Smith in a prayer about the church’s ongoing search for a new leader.
“May the Holy Spirit guide our search committee to speak and listen faithfully in this time of transition,” they said. “Bless the priest you are preparing to join this cluster and prepare us to welcome new leadership with love.”
St. John’s and two other associated Episcopal churches in Aroostook County — St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Fort Fairfield and Church of the Good Shepherd in Houlton — have been without a spiritual director since the priest they shared retired late last year. Smith, who held the role before retiring more than a decade ago, has been filling in to lead services once a month as the congregations search for someone new to take over full-time.
For small, rural churches in shrinking denominations such as the Episcopal Church, finding new clergy can take months or years. Between 2015 and 2024, the Episcopal Church, a mainline Protestant denomination that separated from the Church of England after the American Revolution, lost almost a third of its regular attendees in Maine.
“There are more full-time jobs available across the whole church, across the whole country, than there are priests looking for jobs,” said the Rev. Suzanne Roberts, transition and deployment officer for the Episcopal Diocese of Maine. The church is currently hiring for five clergy positions in Maine, but only the Aroostook one is full-time, with the three congregations pooling their resources to pay a rector.
Rural churches often serve important functions beyond their congregations, Roberts said, hosting addiction recovery programs, managing or supporting food pantries, and serving as community gathering places.
“If a church closes,” Roberts said, “that resource and that safe space for the community is lost.”
Aroostook County has lost at least three Episcopal churches — in Caribou, Mars Hill and Limestone — since the 1990s. Members of the remaining churches, which each have their own space and ministries but pool resources for operating costs and staff as part of what the church calls the Aroostook Cluster, say their congregations are small but vibrant. Though the search for a priest has been long, their faith isn’t wavering.
“We’re not under any illusions that this is going to be fast, but we’re doing OK,” said Dory Smith, who was baptized, confirmed and married at St. John’s and serves on the search committee for the cluster’s new priest.
A careful search
When the Aroostook Cluster’s most recent rector, the Rev. Kevin Kinsey, retired, it kicked off a well-defined process.
Before churches can post a clergy job listing, Roberts said, parishioners have to go through what they call a “discernment process.” That involves forming a search committee and spending time describing the congregation’s identity and hopes for a new clergy member. The Aroostook Cluster’s search committee, made up of three members from each congregation, spent six months on this process before the diocese posted the job in May.
Since Kinsey’s retirement, the three small congregations with a combined weekly attendance of roughly 70 people have welcomed a mix of retired local priests and visiting clergy to lead services and have held morning prayers led by lay members.
In more densely populated states, Roberts said, congregations sometimes consolidate and sell off buildings to save money. But in a rural state, the distance between communities means this is less of an option. Two thirds of Maine’s Episcopal churches don’t employ a full-time priest, and the Aroostook churches were the first to pool their resources to support joint positions.
Episcopal priests in Maine often have jobs outside of ministry, live in double-income households or have already retired and taken on a part-time posting, Roberts said.
The Rev. Ginny Urbanek became an Episcopal priest in her 60s while living in Houlton. She reached the mandatory retirement age of 72 in 2018, but she still leads at least one service almost every weekend, covering for the Aroostook Cluster and other churches, including an Episcopal congregation in Winn and a Lutheran congregation in New Sweden.
Before her retirement, Urbanek served as a part-time priest at Good Shepherd. The church joined the Aroostook Cluster in 2021, three years after she left, extending the cluster’s range south by 40 miles.
“I’m retired now; I just turned 80,” Urbanek said. “However, I am busy because there is a lack of clergy in the northern part of the state, and people ask, and I say yes.”
Smith remembers when St. John’s was full enough to support a priest on its own. As a child, she said, the Sunday school had up to 90 children, but now the church averages just over a dozen attendees, most of whom are retired.
Even though the Presque Isle church is smaller now, Smith said, it’s still a family. Janet Scott, who has been a member since 2000 and also serves on the search committee, agreed.
“It’s the community that I hold dear,” Scott said, “and, unfortunately, that community has faded, mainly because we’ve had parishioners who’ve passed away.”
‘We’re doing just fine’
On a recent Sunday, two stuffed bears slowly wound their way through the pews, getting hugs and prayers from each of the roughly three dozen attendees at St. Paul’s in Fort Fairfield.
The bears — one tan, one black — were bound for relatives and friends in Bangor and Eastport going through difficult times.
Dan Foster, who was baptized at St. Paul’s in 1956 and played piano at the service, said the church’s ministry goes beyond structured initiatives such as the prayer bears and financial support for the Presque Isle emergency homeless shelter. Much of the church’s influence, he said, comes from parishioners supporting each other and their community in little ways, “constantly projecting a very loving, caring persona in a world that can be very cynical and hard.”
After the service concluded, parishioners filed into the church’s entry hall, passing by a fake tree with colorful paper leaves, each one with a good deed someone had done to support the environment. Most of the attendees stayed for a potluck meal of sandwiches, zucchini bread and cookies — a weekly occurrence after every service.
Ann Spinney, who moved to Aroostook County and joined St. Paul’s in 2021, said the congregation has been an important part of her social life since her move. She joined the Caribou Choral Society and a community band after meeting parishioners who took part in those groups.
During the search for a new priest, the church has welcomed a couple of new members.
“It would be great to find an exceptional spiritual leader for what we’ve really grown, and I don’t think we need to settle for anything less. And if that is going to take a while to get, I think that’s perfectly fine,” Dan Foster said.
John Foster, Dan Foster’s brother, is leading the search committee for a new priest, which is now in what could be a long waiting period for applicants. The church was more full when he was a kid, he said, but he thinks it’s more welcoming and loving today despite its small size.
“Having a priest that’s another cog in that family is really a great thing,” he said. “Every congregation is not for everybody, and we feel that we have a truly unique situation, but it has to be a unique situation that lines up with somebody else.”
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Why autoimmune disease is harder to catch in older adults — and what helps
text:
(Aging Untold) — Autoimmune conditions like type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus can be especially tricky to spot for older adults because the immune system naturally changes with age.
The good news is that early diagnosis can make a real difference in managing symptoms long-term.
What does “autoimmune” actually mean?
Autoimmune disease is a condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy body tissues, according to the National Institutes of Health.
“Think about it like your body has an army that’s there to protect you, and that’s your immune system,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “And it no longer knows who the enemy is. So it fights itself. And that’s what an autoimmune disease is.”
Rheumatoid arthritis affects the joints and bones, and lupus is systemic, Cradduck said. “It, unfortunately, can go after everything.”
Cradduck also shared her own experience being diagnosed.
“I was going to the doctor for well over a year and seeing a very good rheumatologist, and my lab work and my symptoms weren’t meeting the criteria all at the same time,” she said.
She said she would have symptoms, but her lab work would look OK.
Then she would have “terrible lab work,” but symptomatically she was OK.
“And sadly, oftentimes the treatment is worse than the disease in some ways, because the treatment only targets lowering your immune system and leaving you more susceptible,” Cradduck said.
Finding the source of inflammation
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, compared it to a “big ball of confusion.”
“It’s really the system is confused, so it doesn’t know what’s going on,” Rogers said. “So wherever that weakest link is, that’s where it’s going to attack. I think probably at the time when you were diagnosed several years ago, we didn’t have the recognition that we have now.”
Rogers said inflammation is usually the driver.
“Key is, you have to find out what drove it in the first place. Where is the inflammation coming from that’s allowed these other organs to get hit? It’s much more complex than people realize,” Rogers said.
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, offered a way to picture it.
“I had another doctor friend explain that these symptoms are like smoke, and you want to get to the fire, which is the inflammation,” Ambrose said.
Rogers pointed to the gut as a common source.
“And usually a lot of times it’s coming from the gut,” Rogers said. “So I tell people, if you figure out that you have some GI issues, and the breakdown there, go back to the foundation — go back to nutrition, go back to the sleep. You have to say, hey, my body is on fire. Am I going to use water or gas to put it out?”
Leaning on friends and community
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, talked about what she’s learned from a friend living with Crohn’s disease.
“She has a really great diet. I let her pick all the restaurants out because she knows what she can eat on any given day. And so I really encourage people that have friends that have autoimmune too, when they’re having a day that’s not a particularly great day and they’re tired and they’re worn out, be with them,” O’Rourke said.
And celebrate the good days.
“And then when they have a better day, celebrate that victory. Like, be there through thick and thin. Because it can be an inconsistent condition and some of the symptoms might preempt a plan that you might have had — and just be OK with that,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck added that the invisible nature of these conditions can be one of the hardest parts.
“What I found was so hard was everybody was saying, ‘But you look so good,’” Cradduck said. “When I felt so terrible... I couldn’t prepare a meal without having to take a break when I was first sick.”
It’s rarely just one cause
Rogers emphasized that autoimmune disease develops from a mix of factors, not a single trigger.
“It’s multifactorial. You also have to look at a combination of lifestyle factors and genetics. Genetics plays a huge role,” Rogers said. “And it’s an autoimmune disease — I tell people it’s not like catching a cold. You didn’t just catch it. It’s a combination of things that have led up to this point.”
So, you need to figure out what’s driving it.
“Keep looking for answers,” Ambrose said. “Because today many people are living longer, fuller lives, and there could be answers out there that make a difference.”
Key takeaways
When managing an autoimmune disease, keep these points in mind:
- It’s internal friendly fire. The immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissue, damaging joints, skin, nerves or organs.
- It’s often an invisible battle. These conditions rarely have visible signs, yet heavily impact daily life, careers and family.
- There are clues before crisis. Pay attention to early warning signs, make proactive choices and practice strong self-advocacy to help your body function at its best.

title: Gorham group asks court to overturn town’s approval of Amazon facility
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A group of Gorham residents is asking Cumberland County Superior Court to overturn the planning board’s approval of Amazon’s proposed 146,280-square-foot distribution center.
The appeal, filed by citizens group Gorham United, alleges that the planning board failed to apply some of Gorham’s land use ordinances in its Sept. 14 approval of Amazon’s project. The group argued the megaretailer’s application did not present full evidence the project would comply with town standards governing traffic, public safety, wetlands and stormwater.
The appeal contends that the board approved Amazon’s project without a sufficient plan to mitigate significant traffic and wetland impacts, and that the project will “affect Gorham United members’ property, neighborhood conditions, traffic safety, environmental resources, public infrastructure, and interests.”
The warehouse is projected to see over 3,000 daily truck, van and car trips and impact 34,918 square feet of freshwater wetlands on 94 acres.
“Amazon should not be held to a different standard,” said Josh Trombley, a leader of Gorham United. “Our town should hold every applicant to the standards established to protect Gorham residents and the community.”
The group is asking the court to overturn the planning board’s approval, calling it “arbitrary, capricious, unreasonable, and ultra vires (‘beyond the powers’ in Latin),” and mandate further review. The same residents are circulating a petition for a moratorium that would temporarily block Amazon’s plans at the local level by banning industrial developments that generate over 1,500 daily vehicle trips.
Community Development Director Tom Poirier said that the town stands behind the planning board’s decision on Amazon’s application, and that it thoroughly addressed the topics outlined in the appeal, took public input into account and required revisions to Amazon’s proposal.
“(The planning board’s) review included technical submissions, town staff and consultant comments, and extensive public input, including concerns raised by neighbors and Gorham United,” Poirier said. “The revised plans and information required careful consideration of detailed technical information alongside the concerns of the community.”
The town review process of Amazon’s plans lasted six months, spanning a sketch plan meeting, two public hearings, a workshop and a final review. Residents’ testimony has largely opposed the project, citing concerns about impacts on traffic, the environment, local businesses and overall quality of life in town.
According to the town attorney, the board must review site plans for general consistency with the town’s comprehensive plan and ordinances and approve the plans if they appear to meet standards.
The proposed warehouse is still awaiting approvals from the Department of Environmental Protection, the Department of Transportation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which are expected to make decisions and issue Amazon permits in coming months.
The DEP is assessing the project’s wetland impacts, and the DOT is reviewing Amazon’s traffic impact study and said it will work with town officials in Gorham and Westbrook to identify road improvements needed to address “unreasonable congestion” or “unsafe conditions” it could create.
Gorham United’s appeal claims that the planning board should not have relied on future permits and studies and post-approval reviews to prove compliance with town ordinances.
Amazon revised its initial plans based on planning board and resident feedback throughout the review. Developers proposed shorter lighting poles and higher fencing, and reduced the number of van parking spaces to make room for an earthen berm on the western side of the development, pulling it back from homes on Shamrock Drive.
The company also proposed widening Main Street in front of the site to add a two-way turning lane and introducing signaling improvements to the intersection of Mosher Road (Route 237) and Main Street.
Members of Gorham United, some of whom live on Shamrock Drive, say those changes aren’t enough.
“An industrial-sized trucking facility does not belong in the middle of a town village,” Trombley said.

title: Why stop there, Sec. Hegseth?
text:
“High-testosterone” Department of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan by firing squad — the first military execution in the U.S. since 1961 — would be available to “livestream.”
To ensure the proper barbarity for the spectacle, and simultaneously to help fight our growing deficits, Hegseth should sell the rights to a “pay-per-view” showing, even to Fox News, perhaps at halftime of a football game.
Americans could have been charged, say, $40 to witness the killing. Hegseth could make a guest appearance and demonstrate his warrior nature by doing push-ups and then shooting one of the guns. With just three million subscriptions, the revenue would have been $120 million, more than enough to cover the $84 million that his department spends on erectile dysfunction medicine annually.
Although President Trump may flip-flop on the livestream, he has never missed an opportunity to use the media to make money.
Paul Josephson
Vinalhaven

title: AMHC Receives Funding to Improve Technology
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - If you visit AMHC, you may see some changes. The organization recently received federal funding to improve their technology and infrastructure. After Maine senators renegotiated $190 million for Maine’s rural health transformation program AMHC was awarded $651,000.
AMHC CEO Christy Daggett says improving patient access and their patients’ experience is their goal. “AMHC uses technology a ton to afford telehealth services to people. So, being up to date and cutting age in technology is really, really important to AMHC. Healthcare now isn’t about just counting appointments. It’s about being sure that we’re measuring outcomes and we’re helping people get well, and cybersecurity and privacy is very important in behavioral healthcare. So, this grant will help us on both those counts too.”
“We’re improving our electronic health record. We are improving equipment for people in the field who do mobile crisis work and most critically for patients we’re using AI assisted clinical documentation. Basically, using it as a tool to make clinicians’ lives easier. So, they can spend more time face-to-face with clients. Never diagnosing or communicating independently with clients,” Daggett continued.
Daggett says keeping up with current technology and infrastructure is important in rural communities like Aroostook County. Anyone with questions can contact AMHC at 554-2352.
